en: One who is about to sacrifice with the New Moon or Full Moon oblation prepares the curdling agent for the oblation beforehand—either one day or two days prior, according to the season. Now, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "He curdles it with sour milk for the sake of association with Indra; he curdles it over the remnants of the Agnihotra for the continuity of the sacrifice."
Having ascertained that the moon is waning, or having recognized it as full, he adds fuel to the fires:
he places three logs on the Gārhapatya fire, three on the Anvāhāryapacana, and three on the Āhavanīya;

they sweep around them, thereby creating the form of the Upavasatha day. Then, while he is observing his vow, he cuts a branch of the Palāśa tree, either facing east or north, remaining silent until he thinks he has reached the desired spot.
He cuts off a branch that is facing east or north, which has many leaves and many twigs, but whose tips are withered, with the formula:

"For food thee! For strength thee! With it he drives away the calves, saying: "Ye are winds; ye are approachers. Then he sends forth their mothers, saying: "May the god Savitṛ impel you for the most excellent rite. Swell, O inviolable ones, as the portion of the gods—full of vigor, full of milk, rich in offspring, free from disease, and free from sickness. Let no thief master you, nor the evil-doer; may the bolt of Rudra avoid you."

"May you be many and firm under this cowherd," with these words he looks at the sacrificer. Then, having carried this branch around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, having brought it in through the eastern door, and having placed it behind the Gārhapatya fire on the northern half of the wagon-stand within the fire-hall, [he says]: "Protect the cattle of the sacrificer. This is the case if he performs the *saṃnayana* offering;
but if he does not perform the *saṃnayana*, there is simply the laying down of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

Then, standing behind the Gārhapatya fire, he takes up either a knife or a horse-rib, saying: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee. Having taken it, he consecrates it, saying: "Thou art the cry of the sacrifice."

He heats [the sacrificial grass] at the *gārhapatya* fire, saying: "The *rakṣas* is burnt up; the enemies are burnt up. Then, three times, he proceeds toward the *āhavanīya* fire, saying: "This prayer has gone forth toward the sacrificial grass, fashioned by Manu and adorned with the *svadhā*-offering. The seers bring it from the front for the gods as something pleasing. With the words, "Sit here upon the sacrificial grass," he looks back at the altar. Then he goes in that direction where he thinks he will find the sacrificial grass.

He takes hold of a bunch of *darbha* grass as much as he deems sufficient for the *prastara* bundle, saying, "Thou art the portion of the gods, gathered around. Then he strokes it upwards, saying, "Thou art grown by rain. He grasps it with a knife, saying, "O divine *barhis*, do not let me cut thee lengthwise nor crosswise; may I succeed in [reaching] thy joint. He cuts it, saying, "May I, the cutter, not be harmed. He touches the places where he has cut, saying, "O divine *barhis*, grow with a hundred shoots! and, "With a thousand shoots may we grow! He touches himself. He cuts this entire bunch.
Having made it into a bundle, he places it down with the formula, "Protect from contact with the earth.

Thereafter, he silently cuts off an odd number of handfuls—three, five, seven, nine, eleven, or as many as he deems sufficient. Then, having made the cord threefold by winding it around, he winds it to the left with the formula, "Thou art the girdle of Aditi."
Having placed that [bundle] with its tip pointing northward,
he gathers the prastara-bunch upon it, saying, "I gather thee well-gathered," and binds it together, saying,
"The binding for Indrāṇī."

"Pūṣan makes a knot for you; may Pūṣan tie the knot"—saying this, he hides it from behind toward the east with the words, "May it not slip away from you. Then he lifts it up with, "I lift you up with the two arms of Indra," and places it upon his head with, "I carry you on the head of Bṛhaspati. Having gone forward with, "Go through the wide atmosphere," he sets it down to the north of the Gārhapatya fire, not on the ground, with, "You are one that goes to the gods."
He places it as if upon that [spot] where he considers it to be hidden. He silently cuts the food for consumption;

he cuts it in a single stroke for the ancestors. Then, having likewise made a cord with three windings, he binds together the fuel of eleven pieces of wood with the formula: "Since you, having assumed the form of a black antelope, entered the trees, therefore I gather you together in eleven parts, well-gathered."

He makes the altar (vedi) with knees [shaped] like a calf for one desiring cattle; it is made of *mūta* grass for one desiring food; it is triple-layered (*trivṛt*) for one desiring splendor; and it has its tip pointing upward for one desiring heaven. He prepares the altar prior to the northern boundary-stroke (*parigrāha*), and then in the afternoon he performs the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.

Then, having cut off the leaves from this branch, he scatters them in front of the Gārhapatya fire. Then, having stripped the bark from below, he places the thick part behind the Gārhapatya for the purpose of the *upaveṣa*. Then, having measured a span from it and wound it with blades of *darbha* grass, he makes a threefold branch-strainer (*śākhāpavitra*) with the verse: "Threefold on the *palāśa* tree, made of *darbha*, measuring a span—may that most purifying strainer in the sacrifice make my milk and oblation pure."

Then, when the evening agnihotra has been offered, having spread grass to the north of the gārhapatya fire, he places four items upon them: the milking vessel, the strainer, the two *sāmnāyya*-heating pots, and the cooking pot; then he sprinkles them with water, saying three times, "Be purified for the divine rite, for the sacrifice to the gods. Then, sitting behind the gārhapatya fire, he draws out embers toward the north with the *upaveṣa* stick, saying, "Thou art the heat of Mātariśvan."
Upon them he places the vessel for the *sāṃnāyya* milk over the fire, saying: "Thou art heaven; thou art earth; thou art the all-sustainer; by the highest support, stand firm, do not waver!
Into it he places a branch-strainer with its tip pointing eastward, saying: "Thou art the strainer of the Vasus, hundred-streamed; thou art the strainer of the Vasus, thousand-streamed."

Having taken hold of that [calf], he remains silent; then he waits for the cows as they approach, [reciting]: "These come hither, yielding honey, rich in offspring, glorious, and of every form; becoming many as they are born again and again—may Indra cause you, O cows, to delight here," or "May Mahendra" if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra. Then he says, "Tell me when she has been let loose to the calf. When she has been let loose, they announce it; while she is being milked, he consecrates her with the mantra: "The drop is offered, the speck is offered; to Agni, the great vault of heaven, Svāhā!"
[He says] "To Heaven and Earth. Then, as [the cowherd] brings [the second cow] from the east toward the west, he asks, "Which one did you milk? The other replies, "That one.
He consecrates that [cow] with the mantra, "She is the life of all.
As he brings the second [cow], he asks, "Which one did you milk? The other replies, "That very one."
He addresses her with the mantra, "She who is all-pervading...
When she is bringing the third [milking], he asks, "What have you milked? The other replies, "That one."
He addresses her with the three verses beginning "She, Viśvakarman...

When the three [cows] have been milked, he releases his speech with the formula: "May she yield much milk for Indra; may the oblation swell again for the gods; may it be fit for milking again for the calves and for men. Or, if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra, he says "for Mahendra.
Having released his speech, and without touching [the cows], he causes the remaining ones to be milked silently.

Having brought water for washing after the milking, he pours it in [with the formula]: "Be united, O you who possess immortality, you who have waves, most honey-sweet, pleasant, for the winning of wealth. Then, having heated this [milk], having removed it from the fire toward the north, and having cooled it, he mixes it with curds across a strainer [with the formula]: "I mix thee with Soma; for Indra I mix thee," or "for Mahendra I mix thee," if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra.

As soon as he thinks he will cause [the milk] to curdle, he brings the remains of the *agnihotra* offering and pours it over [the mixture], saying: "Thou art the continuity of the sacrifice; I continue thee, the continuity of the sacrifice. Then he covers it with a water-holding vessel or a cup, saying: "Thou art a receptacle; for Viṣṇu, for the sacrifice, I cover thee. With waters from a non-empty vessel, those which flow pure around. He places it as if on top where he considers it to be hidden, saying: "O Viṣṇu, protect the oblation. At this time, he silently drives away the calves for the morning milking by means of *darbha* grass.
Then, in the morning, after the Agnihotra has been offered, he rubs his hands together with the formula: "May I be able for you two for the sake of the work for the gods.
These fires remain strewn around as they were at night;

however, if they have not been strewn around, he first strews around the Āhavanīya fire from the front, then from the south, then from the west, and then from the north; in this same manner, he strews around the Anvāhāryapacana fire.
In this manner [he prepares] for the Gārhapatya fire;
then, having strewn grass in front of the Gārhapatya, he places the sacrificial implements upon them in pairs, with their openings facing downwards.

The wooden sword (sphya), the potsherds, the Agnihotra-ladle, the winnowing basket, the black antelope skin, the yoke-pin, the mortar, the pestle, the lower grinding stone, the upper grinding stone, the Juhū-ladle, the Upabhṛt-ladle, the Sruva-spoon, the Dhruvā-ladle, the vessel for the Prāśitra-portion, the Iḍā-vessel, the stirring-stick, the flour-sifter, the vessel for leading forward the water, the butter-pot, the Veda-broom, the wooden trough, the thong, the scrapings of the Veda, the fire-stirring stick, the wood-cutter, and the Anvāhārya-pot.

Having prepared the *madantī* water and whatever other vessels there may be in pairs, and having seated the Brahman priest to the south, he spreads the *pṛṣṭhyā* line continuously from the Gārhapatya fire to the Āhavanīya fire with the formula: "Thou art the continuity of the sacrifice; I spread thee for the continuity of the sacrifice; I spread thee for the continuity of the sacrifice. Then he prepares two strainers (*pavitra*) from the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), each a span long, equal in size, with untrimmed tips, and not cut by the fingernails, [with the thought]: "These two are the out-breath and in-breath, the limbs of the sacrifice in their entirety."

"May they move about, swelling, the two purifiers that cleanse the oblation. Then he wipes them with water, saying: "You are the two purifiers; you belong to Viṣṇu; you are worthy of sacrifice; you are purified by Vāyu; you are purified by the mind of Viṣṇu; you are the purifiers of the sacrifice. Then, having sat down to the north of the Gārhapatya fire, he asks for either a *kamaṇḍalu* or a cup for the carrying forward of the *praṇītā* waters. Pouring water across the strainers into it, he says: "O Brahman, I shall carry forward the waters; O sacrificer, restrain your speech."

Having been born together with the vital breaths, holding [the vessel] and pouring [the water] out, he carries it around the north of the Āhavanīya fire, places it upon *darbha* grass, covers it with *darbha* blades, takes up the strainer, turns to the right, and running back toward the west, he takes up the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle with his right hand and the winnowing basket with his left, saying, "For the sake of service (*veṣāya*).
He heats them over the Gārhapatya fire, saying, "The Rakṣas is burnt away; the enemies are burnt away," three times. Then, behind the Gārhapatya, the cart stands facing the fire.

He touches its northern yoke-pole with the mantra: "Thou art the yoke-pole; injure the injurer; injure him who injures us; injure him whom we injure. He consecrates the cart with the formula: "Thou art the most liberal of the gods, the most fulfilling, the most beloved, the best bearer, the best invoker of the gods; thou art the unswerving vessel of the oblation; be firm, do not waver. Then, having stepped upon the southern felly of the wheel with the words "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu," and having ascended, he places the winnowing basket on the front-board (prauga), the offering-ladle in the basket, and the two strainers in the ladle.

Then he looks at the materials for the sacrificial cakes with the formula: "I look upon you with the eye of Mitra; do not be afraid, do not tremble, may I not harm you. With the words "Wide open the wind," he throws away a blade of grass or a stalk of *kiṃśāru*. Then, having touched water and explained the *daśahotṛ* formula, he addresses the sacrificer, saying, "I shall pour out the oblation," and pours it out using the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle provided with a strainer.

If, however, there is no space, he places the wooden sword (sphya) behind the Gārhapatya fire; upon the wooden sword he places the vessel (pātrī), and into the vessel he pours the grains for the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa). Then he touches the front part of the vessel, saying: "Thou art the yoke-pole (dhur); injure him who injures us; injure him whom we injure. Thou art the most bountiful, the most fulfilling, the most beloved, the best bearer, the best invoker of the gods among the gods. Thou art the unerring vessel of the oblation; be firm, do not waver. Then...

He gazes at the materials for the sacrificial cakes, saying, "I gaze upon you with the eye of Mitra; do not fear, do not tremble, may I not harm you. With the words, "Wide open for the wind," he throws away a blade of grass or a *kiṃśāru* awn. Then, having touched water and explained the *daśahotṛ* formula, he addresses the sacrificer, saying, "I shall pour out the oblation. He pours it out using the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle provided with a strainer, while the sacrificer gives permission, saying, "Om, pour out! Then he pours it out three times with this sacrificial formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour you out, acceptable to Agni. He performs this three times with this same formula.

Having once silently performed this very introductory rite (*pratipad*), he says, "To Agni and Soma" at the full moon sacrifice; "To Indra and Vaimṛdha" and "To Indra and Agni" at the new moon sacrifice; "To Indra" for one who does not offer the *saṃnaya* (curd-mixture), or "To Mahendra" for one who is a sacrificer to Mahendra. Then, having poured out the portions, he touches them with the formula, "This is for the gods," and "This is ours together" for those that remain over.

"For prosperity, not for misfortune," he says; then he gazes at the Āhavanīya fire, saying, "May I behold the light of Vaiśvānara, the sun. Then he looks toward the houses, saying, "May the dwellings be firm within heaven and earth. Then, taking them up, he rises, saying, "Go through the wide atmosphere. Having gone, he places them down to the north of the Gārhapatya fire, saying, "I place you in the lap of Aditi," and he addresses the Gārhapatya, saying, "O Agni, guard the oblation."

Then, having poured water across the strainer into this very *sruva* ladle, he purifies it three times with two strainers whose tips point northward, reciting verse by quarter: "May the god Savitṛ purify you with a flawless strainer, with the rays of the Vasu Sūrya. Then, exalting them, he stands up over the waters, saying: "O divine waters, flowing forward, flowing ahead, lead this sacrifice forward; place the lord of the sacrifice in front. Indra chose you for the slaying of Vṛtra; you chose Indra for the slaying of Vṛtra. With these very waters, he sprinkles the waters.

"Ye are sprinkled, ye are sprinkled," saying this three times, he then sprinkles the materials for the sacrificial cakes with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I sprinkle you, acceptable to Agni; [acceptable] to Agni-Soma, to such-and-such [deity], to such-and-such"—repeating thus three times according to the respective deity.

Having turned the vessels face upwards, he sprinkles them with the formula: "Be purified for the divine rite, for the sacrifice to the gods," saying this three times. Then, having set aside the remaining sprinkling water, he places it down.

He shakes the black antelope skin with its neck pointing upward, having turned toward the north, saying: "Shaken off is the Rakṣas; shaken off are the enemies. Then he spreads it out in front [of the fire] with the neck facing westward and the hair side up, saying: "Thou art the skin of Aditi; may the Earth recognize thee! Upon it he places the mortar, saying: "Thou art the wooden pressing-slab;
may the skin of Aditi recognize thee! Into that he pours the grains for the sacrificial cake, saying: "Thou art the body of Agni, the release of speech; I take thee for the enjoyment of the gods."

He places the pestle [with the formula]: "Thou art a wooden one, born of a tree; may it prepare this oblation for the gods with good effort. Then he calls the preparer of the oblation three times: "O preparer of the oblation, come! O preparer of the oblation, come! And [he says] "Strike together! Then, striking the upper and lower grinding stones loudly with the sound of a bull's roar, he says: "Proclaim food, proclaim strength, proclaim splendor; may we conquer the assembly. Having pounded [the grain] and removed the husks, he places the winnowing basket to the north [of the mortar] with the formula: "Thou art increased by rain."

Into that [mortar] he pours the grains for the sacrificial cake, saying, "May that which has grown by rain recognize thee. Then, turning toward the north, he winnows them, saying, "The *rakṣas* is winnowed away; the enemies are winnowed away.

Having seized the husks with his left hand, he throws them out in this direction, saying, "Thou art the portion of the *rakṣas*. Then, having touched water, he separates [the grain from the husks], saying, "May Vāyu separate you.

He causes the rice grains to fall into the pan, saying, "May the divine Savitṛ, the golden-handed, receive you. Handing them over to the one who threshes, he says, "Thresh them three times; report to me when they have been thrice-threshed."

They say that when the rice grains are being husked, whatever husk remains is the portion of the Rakṣases; "May the waters carry it away from here," with these words he pours the washing of the rice within the altar or in the region of the rubbish-heap (utkara). At this time, he milks the cows for the morning milk-offering using a strainer with its fringes pointing northward;
he does not curdle it here.

Then, when the three grains have been husked, he likewise shakes the black antelope skin with its neck pointing upward, turning toward the north, saying: "Shaken away is the Rakṣas; shaken away are the enemies. Then he spreads it out in front [of the mortar], with the neck toward the west and the hair facing upward, saying: "Thou art the skin of Aditi; may the earth recognize thee! Upon it, he places a yoke-pin with its knob pointing northward, saying: "Thou art the support of heaven; may the skin of Aditi recognize thee! On that pin, he sets down the lower grinding stone facing eastward, saying: "Thou art the bowl belonging to the mountain; may the support of heaven recognize thee!"
He places the lower grinding stone upon the upper with the formula: "Thou art the supporter, daughter of the mountain; may the mountain-daughter recognize thee.

Upon it he pours out the grains for the sacrificial cake with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour thee out, acceptable to Agni; [acceptable] to Agni-Soma, to such-and-such, to such-and-such," according to the respective deity.
He pronounces the formula over them as they are poured: "Thou art grain; satisfy the gods, satisfy the sacrifice, satisfy the lord of the sacrifice, satisfy me, the performer of the sacrifice."
He looks at his two arms while grinding [the flour], saying: "For out-breath thee, for in-breath thee, for diffused breath thee!

He causes the ground grains to fall upon the black antelope skin, saying: "May the god Savitṛ, the golden-handed, receive you for long-extended life, for the sake of longevity! "Devo vaḥ savitā hiraṇyapāṇiḥ pratigṛhṇātu. (May the god Savitṛ, the golden-handed, receive you.)

Handing over the oblation to the one who grinds it, he says, "Grind it without scattering; make it fine. They grind the materials for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and set aside those for the cooked grain offering (*caru*).
If he is going to prepare a *caru* offering, they should divide the grains for the *caru* and the *puroḍāśa* before the pouring of the grains.

Then, having washed these potsherds (*kapāla*), he places them behind the *Gārhapatya* fire—eight to the south and eleven to the north. Then, sitting down behind the *Gārhapatya*, he takes up the fire-stirring stick (*dhṛṣṭi*) with the formula, "Thou art the *dhṛṣṭi*; bestow spiritual power (*brahman*)," and addresses the *Gārhapatya* fire with the formula, "O Agni, drive away the Agni who eats raw food."
With the words, "Drive away the flesh-eater," he throws out the southern ember and then turns another one toward him with the words, "Bring the one who sacrifices to the gods."

He places that [brick] in the middle of the southern potsherds with the formula: "Thou art the firm one; make the earth firm, make life firm, make offspring firm; encompass the kinsmen for this sacrificer. He then rolls a coal over it with the formula: "The Rakṣas is burnt up, the enemies are burnt up. Then he places the one on the eastern side with the formula: "Thou art the support; make the atmosphere firm, make the out-breath firm, make the in-breath firm; encompass the kinsmen for this sacrificer. Then he places the one on the western side with the formula: "Thou art the foundation."

"Make firm the sky; make firm the eye; make firm the ear; make firm the kinsmen for this sacrificer—thus he says as he piles them around. Then he places one on the southern half: 'Thou art the support; make firm the quarters; make firm the womb; make firm the offspring; make firm the kinsmen for this sacrificer—thus he says as he piles them around. Then he places the first enclosing-stone: 'Ye are piled; pile up offspring for him, wealth for him, and kinsmen for this sacrificer—thus he says. And so likewise the subsequent one."
He places two [potsherds] in the north, touching each other, with the formula: "Ye are piled; pile offspring for this man, wealth for him, kinsmen for this sacrificer.

Then he covers them with embers, saying: "Be heated by the heat of the Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases. Then he yokes them with the yoking-formula: "The potsherds which the wise arrange upon the cauldron—may Pūṣan and Indra-Vāyu yoke them in the observance of the rite. In this very same way he places the subsequent potsherds. They kindle the potsherds, they set fire to them, they place the cooking-pot [upon them], and they put on the baking-vessels.
The waters for mixing the flour are heated.

Then, having sat down to the north of the Gārhapatya fire, remaining silent, he pours the flour from the black antelope skin into the vessel across the strainers, according to the respective deities: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour thee out, acceptable to Agni; [acceptable] to Agni-Soma, to so-and-so, to so-and-so. Then he says to the assistant: "Bring water, bring it! The one who gives the command brings it, having drawn from the *praṇītā* waters with the *sruva* spoon, supporting it with the *veda* grass-bundle, or placing his hand between them; likewise from the *madantī* waters.

As both kinds [of flour] are being brought, he addresses them with the mantra: "May the waters unite with the waters; may the plants unite with their sap; O wealthy ones, be united with the moving [waters], and full of sweetness with those full of sweetness. Then he pours water over them, saying: "You are born from the waters; be united with the waters. He mixes them, saying: "I mix you for the sake of generation.

Having mixed and stirred them, he touches them, saying: "For Agni thee! For Agni-Soma thee! For so-and-so, for so-and-so! He forms the cake according to the respective deity, saying: "Thou art the head of Makha."
Having pushed back the coals toward the southern potsherds, he places [the cake] upon them with the formula, "Thou art the Gharma, the life of all.
He spreads it out with the formula, "Spread wide; may the lord of the sacrifice spread wide for thee.
As he is spreading it, he fashions it into the shape of a tortoise.

"All the potsherds he spreads over," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Then, across the strainers, he pours the clarified butter into the butter-pot with the formula: "The milk of the great ones, the sap of the plants; of thee, the imperishable, I pour out for the sacrifice to the gods. Then, having drawn out embers mixed with ashes from the north, he places [the pot] upon them. In the same manner, he places the second cake upon [the embers]. Then [he takes] the boiled rice, then the curd. Having poured water into a vessel, he causes the skin of the southern cake to form, saying three times: "Take on the skin! Take on the skin! Then [he does so] for the northern one.

He carries fire around [the cakes] three times, saying, "The Rakṣas is enclosed; the enemies are enclosed. Then he bakes the southern sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), addressing the Gārhapatya fire with the formula: "May the god Savitṛ bake thee on the highest vault of heaven; may Agni not burn thy body; O Agni, guard the oblation. In the same manner, he bakes the northern sacrificial cake. Then, having covered the southern sacrificial cake with ashes, he covers it with the Veda-grass-bundle, saying three times: "Be united with the Brahman; be united with the Brahman. Then [he does the same] for the northern one.

Saying, "Cook without burning," he releases his speech. Then, having heated this washing-water from the *pātrī* vessel over a coal from the *gārhapatya* fire and brought it forward, he pours it out westward within the altar onto three lines, saying: "To Ekata, Svāhā! To Dvita, Svāhā! To Trita, Svāhā! Then he takes up the *veda* grass-broom, saying: "This *veda* has found the earth, which was hidden in secret, in the depths and in caverns; may it find a world for the sacrificer; may the one of many deeds make the sacrifice flawless."

With the *veda* he sweeps the altar thrice: "With the *veda* they found the earth; that earth spread out over the earthly realms. She bears the germ within the worlds; from thence the sacrifice is born, bestowing all."

Then, standing behind the altar, he takes up the wooden sword (*sphyam*) with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee. Having taken it, he consecrates it: "Thou art the right arm of Indra, thousand-edged, hundred-pointed. Then he whets it upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the formula: "Thou art Vāyu, sharp-edged; thou art hundred-edged, made of wood, the slayer of enemies. Then he places the sacrificial grass with its tips pointing northward within the altar with the formula: "Thou art the armor of the earth; be an armor for the sacrificer."

He strikes it with the wooden sword (*sphya*) [saying]: "O Earth, place of sacrifice for the gods! May I not harm your root, O herb! [Saying]: "Araru has been struck away from the earth," he takes it up;
[saying]: "Go to the enclosure, go to the cow-pen," he carries it; he looks toward the altar [saying]: "May the sky rain for you."

Having taken [the clod], he scatters it on the rubbish-heap (utkara) with the formula: "Bind, O God Savitṛ, in the furthest distance with a hundred fetters him who hates us and whom we hate; do not release him from there. He strikes a second time with the formula: "O Earth, place of divine sacrifice, may I not harm the root of your plant. With the formula, "Araru is driven away from the Earth, the place of divine sacrifice," he takes [the clod].
With the formula, "Go to the fold, the stall of cattle," he carries it away.
He inspects the altar with the verse, "May the sky rain for thee.

Having carried [the earth], he scatters it upon the rubbish-heap (utkara) with the formula, "Bind him, O God Savitṛ, in the furthest distance with a hundred fetters—he who hates us and whom we hate—do not release him from there.

He strikes a third time with the formula, "O Earth, place of sacrifice to the gods, may I not harm the root of thy plant. With the words, "Araru, the non-sacrificer to the gods, is driven away from the earth," he takes up [the clod].
"Go to Vraja, go to Gosthāna," he says as he carries [the earth]; "he observes the altar"; "May the sky rain for you," he says as he has carried it;

he pours it out on the rubbish-heap (utkara) with the formula: "Bind him, O God Savitṛ, in the furthest distance with a hundred nooses—he who hates us and whom we hate—do not let him loose from there. With the formula, "May your arrow not leap up to heaven," he turns [the hoe] back here.

He silently draws the fourth layer together with the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Then he performs the first tracing of the altar: on the south side with the formula, "May the Vasus enclose thee with the Gāyatrī metre"; on the west side, "May the Rudras enclose thee with the Triṣṭubh metre"; on the north side, "May the Ādityas enclose thee with the Jagatī metre. Then he mutters the *karaṇa* formula: "O men, come and prepare this altar, rich in Vasus, rich in Rudras, rich in Ādityas, upon the expanse of heaven, at the navel of the earth, so that this [sacrificer]..."

"Lest the sacrificer come to harm," [he thinks]. Then, with the wooden sword (*sphya*), he digs up the eastern part of the altar (*vedi*) with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, the wise perform the rite. He then says to the Āgnīdhra, "O Āgnīdhra, bring [the earth] from there three times!
When the Āgnīdhra has brought it three times, he issues the call: "O Brahman, I shall perform the second enclosure."

Having produced [the earth], he takes hold of the subsequent enclosure: "Thou art Truth" on the south; "Thou art the seat of Truth" on the west; "Thou art the glory of Truth" on the north. Then he levels the altar towards the west with the wooden sword (sphya), saying: "Thou art support, thou art self-support; thou art wide and thou art wealthy. O thou of great power, who didst take up the earth before the creeping of the cruel one, the giver of life, whom the wise brought forth with offerings in the moon—beholding her, the wise perform sacrifice. Then, having fixed the wooden sword crosswise within the altar.

He utters the direction: "Place the *prokṣaṇī* waters; set down the fuel and the sacrificial grass; wipe the *sruva* and the *sruk* ladles; gird the wife; bring the clarified butter. Having filled these *prokṣaṇī* waters, the Adhvaryu, carrying them with his right hand, pours them out upon the wooden sword (*sphya*) and sets them down in the track of the *sphya*. Then he strikes the *sphya* into the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), saying: "O Gods, whoever hates me with the heart, with the mind, or with speech; whoever hates me with sacred knowledge or with ritual action; whoever hates me with learning or with a longing heart—Indra, with his thunderbolt, shall cut off his head!"

Having washed his hands, he washes the wooden sword (*sphya*) and sets it down; they set down this fuel and sacrificial grass (*idhmā-barhis*), with the fuel to the south and the sacrificial grass to the north. Then he takes up these spoons: with his right hand the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) and the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* spoons, and with his left the *dhruvā* spoon, the vessel for the *prāśitra* portion, and the fringes of the *vedī* cloth. He heats them over the *gārhapatya* fire, saying: "Burned away is the demon; burned away are the enemies; I heat you with the most brilliant splendor of Agni. Then he cleanses the dipping-spoon, saying: "May I not wipe out the cow-pen; I cleanse you, the vigorous one, the subduer of rivals."

Having wiped the handle with the roots [of the grass] three times on the inner side, three times on the outer side, and likewise three times [on the other side], and having touched it with water and heated it, he hands it back. Then he wipes the *juhū* [ladle] with the formula: "May I not wipe away speech or breath; I wipe you, the vigorous one, the overcomer of rivals. Having wiped it in that same manner, and having touched it with water and heated it, he hands it back. Then he wipes the *upabhṛt* [ladle] with the formula: "May I not wipe away sight or hearing; I wipe you, the vigorous one, the overcomer of rivals."

In the same manner, having wiped it, touched it with water, and reheated it, he hands it back; then he wipes the *dhruvā* [spoon] with the formula: "May I not wipe away the offspring and the womb; I wipe thee, the vigorous one, the subduer of rivals. In the same manner, having wiped it, touched it with water, and reheated it, he hands it back; then he wipes the *prāśitraharaṇa* [ladle] with the formula: "May I not wipe away the form and color from the cattle; I wipe thee, the vigorous one, the subduer of rivals."

In the same manner, having wiped [the ladle], touched it with water, and heated it, he hands it back. Then, having touched these wiping-straws with water, he throws them into the Gārhapatya fire with the formula: "The craft of heaven is spread out, resting upon the peaks of the earth; by means of that which has a thousand branches, we destroy our rival, svāhā! Then, having strewn grass in front of the rubbish-heap (utkara) and placed the ladles upon them, he causes the wife to step between the altar and the utkara, behind and to the south [of the latter].

Having seated her to the north of the *gārhapatya* fire, he girds her with the *yoktra* (girdle) with the mantra: "Desiring goodwill, offspring, and prosperity for our bodies, having become devoted to the service of Agni, I gird myself for the sake of good deeds.
Then he makes her recite: "May it be joined; may the blessing be joined to my desire."

Then, across the filter, he causes her to sip water with the mantra: "The plants are full of milk; the milk of the creepers is full of milk. Whatever milk is in the milk of the waters—with that, O Indra, unite me. Then he causes her to place fuel-sticks on the Gārhapatya fire with the mantras: "O Agni, lord of vows, I shall perform the vow; may I be able to do it, may it be successful for me, Svāhā! O Vāyu, lord of vows! O Āditya, lord of vows! O lord of vows among vows, I shall perform the vow; may I be able to do it, may it be successful for me, Svāhā! Then...

She sits down behind the *gārhapatya* fire with the mantra: "O Agni, we, possessing good offspring and good husbands, have approached you, who crush the rivals, the undeceivable, and the one who cannot be deceived. May I not become a widow, but like Aditi, may I be blessed with good sons. O *gārhapatya*, for the sake of non-widowhood and for the sake of good offspring, I sit down near you. Then she recites: "My sons are slayers of enemies, and my daughter is a sovereign (*virāj*). And I am a conqueror; my fame as a husband is supreme. Then he makes her recite: "May what is deficient be made full," and "May what is redundant be placed [in its proper order]."

Then he makes her look at the Gārhapatya fire with the formula: "O Agni, lord of the house, invite me; O wives of the gods, invite me. O wife, this is your place; homage be to you; do not harm me. Then he makes her look at the clarified butter with the formula: "Thou art the milk of the great ones, the sap of the plants; I look upon thee with unimpaired vision for the sake of good offspring. Then he places it over the Gārhapatya fire with the formula: "Thou art splendor."

Having taken up a fuel-stick, he carries it forward, saying, "Follow after the luster. Then he places it over the Āhavanīya fire, saying, "May Agni not take away your luster. At this point, he places that fuel-stick in the middle of the Āhavanīya with the formula, "Svāhā!

Then, having carried it around the *prokṣaṇī* waters along the front, and having placed it on the southern half of the altar, he causes the sacrificer to look at the clarified butter. "He should look while closing his eyes," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Then, having carried it back around as it was brought, and having placed it on the northern half of the altar, the Adhvaryu looks at it, saying: "Thou art the tongue of Agni, the well-being of the gods; for every station, for the gods, for every sacrificial formula, be thou present! Then he purifies it three times by bringing it back again toward the north with two strainers whose tips point northward, saying: "Thou art the bright, thou art the light, thou art the splendor. Then he purifies the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling waters, verse by verse, saying: "May the god Savitṛ purify you with a flawless strainer, with the rays of the Vasu Sūrya."

Having placed two strainers into the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling-vessels, he takes up the *sruva* ladle with his right hand and the *juhū* offering-spoon with his left, resting them upon the *vedī*. Having established them there, he draws [the clarified butter] into the *juhū*, taking four portions with the formula: "I take thee, the bright one, for the bright one, for every station, for the gods, for every sacrificial formula. Having taken it thus and touched it, he hands it over. Then he draws into the *upabhṛt* spoon; taking eight portions with the formula: "I take thee, the light, for the light, for every station, for the gods, for every sacrificial formula," he takes fewer portions of clarified butter while taking more [substances] into the ladle.

Having touched it in the same manner, he hands it over; then he takes [the butter] from the *dhruvā* with this *yajus*: "I take thee for the flame, in the flame, for every abode, for the gods, for every *yajus*. Having taken four portions and filled [the ladle], he touches it in the same manner and hands it over.

Then, having placed this vessel of clarified butter together with the *sruva*-ladle behind the altar, he stands up while pouring out the sprinkling waters, saying: "O divine Waters, you who flow first, you who move first, lead this sacrifice forward; place the lord of the sacrifice at the forefront. Indra chose you for the slaying of Vṛtra; you chose Indra for the slaying of Vṛtra. With these very waters he sprinkles the waters, saying three times: "You are sprinkled; you are sprinkled. Then, having loosened the fuel, he sprinkles it, saying: "Thou art black, dwelling in the clefts; for Agni, thee, Svāhā! He sprinkles the altar, saying: "Thou art the altar; for the sacrificial grass, thee, Svāhā!"

He sprinkles the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the formula, "Thou art the sacrificial grass; for the ladles, svāhā! They bring this sacrificial grass between the *praṇītā* water and the *āhavanīya* fire. Having placed it within the altar with its knot facing eastward, he sprinkles it: "For heaven, thee! over the tips; "For the intermediate space, thee! over the middle parts; and "For earth, thee! over the roots.

Having sprinkled the knot from the front toward the west together with the *sruva*-ladle, he pours out the remaining *prokṣaṇī* water from the southern hip to the northern hip [of the altar], saying: "Svadhā to the Fathers who sit upon the sacrificial grass; become strength; go to the earth with strength! Having removed the vessel for the *prokṣaṇī* water and loosened the sacrificial grass, he takes up the *prastara* bundle from the front, saying, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s tuft," or silently; he inserts the two strainers (*pavitra*) into it, saying, "I place the out-breath and in-breath in the sacrificer," or silently.

He hands it over either to the sacrificer or to the Brahman priest; then he stretches out these grass-binding cords from the southern hip of the altar toward the north. Then, at the southern edge of the altar, he spreads a handful of sacrificial grass with the formula: "O divine grass, soft as wool, I spread thee, a good seat for the gods."

He spreads that abundant grass in front, facing westward, in three layers, not so thick as to be visible through. Then, holding the *prastara* bundle in his hand, he moves forward toward the east and lays down the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), beginning with the middle one: "Thou art Gandharva Viśvāvasu; from all [evil] protect the sacrificer; thou art the praised enclosure of the sacrificer, O *iḍā*. Then the southern one: "Thou art the right arm of Indra; thou art the praised enclosure of the sacrificer, O *iḍā*. Then the northern one: "May Mitra and Varuṇa enclose thee from the north with firm law; thou art the praised enclosure of the sacrificer, O *iḍā*."

Then he girdles [the fire] from the front with the verse, "May Sūrya protect you from the front against any imprecation. He places two upright fuel-sticks: the southern one with the verse, "O Sage, we enkindle thee, the inviter to the sacrifice, the brilliant, the great Agni at the rite," and the northern one silently. Having placed them, he lays down two separating-blades (vidhṛtī) across the altar with their tips pointing northward, saying, "Ye are the restrainers of the people. Upon the two separating-blades, he places the sacrificial grass-bunch (prastara), saying, "May he sit in the seat of the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas."

On the *prastara* [grass-bundle], he places the *juhū* with the formula: "Thou art the *juhū*, ghee-dripping by name; sit on thy dear seat with thy dear name. He places the upper *upabhṛt* with the formula: "Thou art the *upabhṛt*, ghee-dripping by name; sit on thy dear seat with thy dear name. He places the upper *dhruvā* with the formula: "Thou art the *dhruvā*, ghee-dripping by name; sit on thy dear seat with thy dear name. Then, he touches the ladles that have been set down with the formula: "These have sat down in the world of good deeds; protect them, O Viṣṇu! Protect the sacrifice! Protect the lord of the sacrifice! Protect me, the sacrificer!"

Then he consecrates the clarified butter with the formula: "Ye are Viṣṇu's portions; ye are Viṣṇu's abodes; ye belong to Prajāpati. Then, taking the butter-pot together with the dipping-spoon in his right hand and the vessel and the Veda-grass-bundle in his left, he turns to the right, hastens back toward the west, and sits down behind the Gārhapatya fire. He spreads a double layer of butter in the vessel with the verse: "I prepare for you a pleasant seat; I fashion it well-favored with a stream of ghee."

"Sit in that nectar; be established in it, O essence of rice, being well-disposed. Then, taking the *dhṛṣṭi* (the stirring-ladle), he pushes away the embers from the southern sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) with the formula: "Here I push away the face of the attacking army. Then he shows it [to the sun] with: "O Sun, shine as light for great power. Having cleared it of dust with the *veda* (grass-broom), he pours clarified butter over it with: "May Agni, whose source is ghee, swell; may he approve the oblations. Anoint the opening, anoint the skin; I pour ghee upon you, who are well-formed and a finder of wealth, for Agni, as one dear to him, with the splendor of cattle."

Or whichever deity it belongs to, he then removes it [from the fire] with the verse, "Cooked, he rises up; the progenitor of thoughts. He thoroughly satiates it with clarified butter. With the verse, "Moist, spreading, the guardian of the world," he first anoints it on the bottom and then smears it on top. [He says,] "Anoint that self of yours which has entered into the animals. In this same manner, he removes the subsequent sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). Then [he prepares] the cooked [rice], then the curd, then he adorns the *sāṃnāyya* offering with the verse, "That self of yours which has entered into the animals, which has spread out according to the stations of the gods."
"O Soma, having become possessed of self and possessed of clarity, go to the gods and find the light for me, the sacrificer," with these words he responds;
then, counting them, he removes the potsherds with the formula, "May the prosperity of the earth and its essence not depart," for the sake of the sacrificer's protection, so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Then, having filled the *sruva* ladle with clarified butter, he places it between the two *puroḍāśa* cakes; then, grasping them together, he sets them down within the altar (*antarvedi*) with these *vyāhṛti*s: "Bhūḥ! Bhuvaḥ! Suvaḥ! He sets down the two *puroḍāśa* cakes in the middle, the boiled milk (*śṛta*) to the south, and the curd (*dadhi*) to the north. Then, having carried that *sruva* around the front of the offering-ladles, he places it on the *prastara* grass to the south of the *juhū* with the formula: "Be pleasant for me, sit well-seated upon the earth; extend me with offspring and cattle in the heavenly world."

"Sit in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space; may I become superior, and let my rivals be inferior! Having thus carried him back the way he was brought, he places him upon the *dhruvā* [ladle] with the formula: "Thou art the bull, belonging to the Śakvarī meters, the son of the *ghṛtācīs*; sit in the dear seat with thy dear name.

Then, taking a fuel-stick from the faggot, he says: "Recite for the fire being kindled! And when he recognizes the Hotṛ reciting "Forward your strengths, O ye that go to heaven," he then places the first stick upon the fire.

At each utterance of the *praṇava*, he places [a fuel-stick] upon the fire; then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ's recitation, "O Agni, kindled, with the oblation," he finally places one upon it at the end.

He leaves over a piece of the fuel-stick. Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ’s call, "Sacrifice! Pay honor!", he fans the Āhavanīya fire three times with this Veda-broom. When the *sāmidhenī* verses have been recited, having taken a portion from the *dhruvā* ghee with the dipping-spoon and supported it with the Veda-broom, he pours the *prājāpatya* oblation crosswise, saying mentally, "To Prajāpati, svāhā! Then he issues the command: "O Āgnīdh, sweep the fires three times each! Thereupon, the Āgnīdhra, taking hold of the cord used for binding the fuel and the wooden sword (*sphya*), [proceeds].

He cleanses the enclosing sticks: three times the middle one, three times the southern one, and three times the northern one; he fans the Āhavanīya fire three times with the formula: "O Agni, winner of booty, I cleanse thee—the Agni who is about to go forth for booty, who is about to win booty, the vigorous winner of booty—for the sake of winning booty; [I cleanse] Agni, the eater of food, for the sake of eating food. Then, standing in front of the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* spoons, he makes an añjali gesture toward the east with the formula: "Thou art the world; spread thyself out, O Agni, sacrificer; this is homage. Then he takes up the *juhū* with his right hand, saying: "Come, O *juhū*; Agni calls thee for the sacrifice to the gods."
With his left hand, he takes up the *upabhṛt* [ladle] and mutters while stepping across it with his left foot: "O *upabhṛt*, come hither! God Savitṛ calls you for the sacrifice to the gods.
He says: "O Agni and Viṣṇu, may I not step upon you; move apart, do not scorch me; create a world for me, O you two world-makers!"

While the sacrificer maintains contact with him, he prepares a place for Viṣṇu with the formula, "Thou art the place. Having touched the middle enclosing-stick, he pours the straight Āghāra-libation continuously toward the east, without interruption, [with the mantra]: "From here Indra performed heroic deeds; may the sacrifice of the Lord of Sacrifice rise up, reaching to heaven, unassailed, O Indra, let the two winds blow it, svāhā!

He lifts the ladle upward with the words, "Great light! Then, without letting the two ladles touch each other, stepping northward, he mutters: "O Agni, protect me from evil conduct; grant me a share in good conduct."

He anoints the *dhruvā* with the *juhu*, [saying]: "Thou art the head of Makha; may light be anointed with light," three times. Then, having placed the two ladles in their respective places, he chooses the *pravara*. Having taken the faggot-binders in his hand on the *utkara* mound, the *āgnīdhra* priest follows close behind him along the back.

Then he causes [the Hotṛ] to announce: "O announce! Let there be hearing! Agni, the divine Hotṛ, shall sacrifice to the gods—he who is wise and perceptive—like Manu, like Bharata, like so-and-so, like so-and-so, like the Brahman; may he sacrifice here. The Brāhmaṇas are the protectors of this sacrifice; such-and-such is the human [Hotṛ]. Thus he takes the name of the Hotṛ. Having stood up, the Hotṛ releases [his breath];
once released, the Adhvaryu sits down and remains seated, awaiting the impulse (prasava).

Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ’s utterance, "O Adhvaryu, take up the butter-spoon," he takes the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, steps across, calls for the *śrauṣaṭ*, and says, "Recite the offering-verse for the *samidhs*.
At the *vaṣaṭ*-call, he makes the offering. Saying "Recite!
Recite! for each, when about to sacrifice the fourth time, he pours half of the butter from the *upabhṛt* into the *juhū*.

Having performed the five *prayāja* offerings, he steps northward and, with the residue of the oblation, sprinkles the sacrificial portions (*havīṃṣi*) in successive order: first the *dhruvā* ladle, then the southern cake, then the *dhruvā* ladle again, then the northern cake, then the boiled milk, then the curds, and finally the *upabhṛt* ladle; then, taking four portions of clarified butter, he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni," and having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to Agni."

When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers [the oblation] facing the fire with extended arms in the eastern part of the northern half. Then, having stepped across to the north and taking four portions of clarified butter, he says, "Recite for Soma. Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to Soma. When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers it facing the fire with extended arms in the eastern part of the southern half. Then, having spread an underlayer of butter, while cutting from the eastern half of the southern sacrificial cake, he says, "Recite for Agni. Then he worships it [with the formula]: "Do not fear; do not tremble; may I not harm you; may your brilliance not depart."

Then he touches it with: "Support Bharata, pour out for Manu; I shall offer the portions to you in return; homage be to you, do not harm me. Having cut a portion from the eastern half, he cuts from the western half, pours clarified butter over it, and anoints the place of cutting. With the formula: "Whatever I have done contrary to the natural order of my self while cutting the portions for you, I anoint that back together with clarified butter; may it swell again for you," he steps across, calls for the *śrauṣaṭ*, and says, "Sacrifice to Agni."

When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he makes the offering. Then, taking four portions of clarified butter, he says, "For Prajāpati," in a low voice; "Recite the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*)," loudly. Having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Prajāpati," in a low voice; "Recite the offering verse (*yajyā*"), loudly. When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he makes the offering. Then, having spread an underlayer [of butter], while cutting from the rear half of the northern cake, he says: at the full moon sacrifice, "For Agni and Soma"; or "For Indra Vaimṛdha"; and at the new moon sacrifice, "For Indra and Agni. For one who does not offer the *saṃnāya*, [he says] "For Indra"; for one who offers the *saṃnāya*, "For Mahendra" if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra. The spreading of the underlayer is the same.
Having made the equalizing touch, he cuts from the rear half and then cuts from the front half;
he pours clarified butter over it, makes the equalizing touch again, steps across, calls for the *śrauṣaṭ*, and says, "Recite the offering prayer for Agni and Soma.

At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers the oblation. Then, having spread a base of butter, while cutting twice from the sacrificial cake, he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for Indra," or "for Mahendra" if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra.
He cuts twice from the sacrificial cake, twice from the boiled milk, and twice he pours clarified butter over the curds.
Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for Indra," or "for Mahendra" if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra.

At the *vaṣaṭ* call, he makes the oblation. Then, having spread a base of clarified butter, while cutting from the northern half of the southern sacrificial cake, he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt."

He cuts once from the northern half of the southern cake, once from the *dhruvā* ghee, once from the northern cake, once from the boiled milk, and once from the curds; he pours ghee over it twice, but does not re-anoint what has been cut off. When the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering has been performed, he offers the two *pārvaṇa* oblations with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), [reciting]: "We worship the full moon, the bull, the vigorous one; may it yield for us excellent offspring and thousandfold abundance of wealth. To breath, the bounteous, to the full moon, svāhā!"—thus at the full-moon sacrifice.

The new moon is fortunate and very gracious; like a cow, she swells again and again. May she milk for us excellent heroic strength and thousandfold increase of wealth. "To the new moon, the bountiful one, for the sake of out-breathing, svāhā!"—thus [he offers] on the night of the new moon.
Having stepped across [the altar], and having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "Sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt."

At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering in the eastern part of the northern half, passing over the previous offerings; here he throws this stirring-stick (*mekṣaṇa*) into the Āhavanīya fire, and then he pours the residue of the oblation over it. Then, having stepped out toward the north and having poured water into the *juhū* ladle, he pours the rinsing water inside the enclosing sticks with the formula: "In Vaiśvānara I offer this oblation; may this thousandfold, hundred-streamed spring go to our father, grandfather, and great-grandfather in the heavenly world, swelling with the *svadhā*—homage!"

Having washed the *sruk* spoon, heated it, and filled it with water, he pours it out outside the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the mantra: "This ocean, a hundred-streamed fountain, spreading itself in the midst of the world; yielding ghee for mankind, O Agni, do not harm Aditi in the highest heaven. At this point, he pours all of that clarified butter from the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū*. Then, having placed the two spoons in their respective places, he cuts off the *prāśitra* portion from the northern half of the southern sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), the size of a barleycorn, or even less than a barleycorn, with the formula: "Let this be prepared by the archer's aim."

"May we not cause harm to the sacrifice; this oblation is pure and well-offered"—having thus sprinkled it with the spoon-handle and placed it behind the *praṇītā* waters, he touches the spoon-handle with water and sets it down.
Then he asks for either a *kaṃsa* vessel or a cup (*camasa*) as an assistant's portion (*vedopahavana*).

Having placed it within the altar (*antarvedi*), he makes an under-layer of butter in it and, breaking off a piece from the southern half of the southern sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), he places it [into the vessel] with the formula: "I cut off [the portion] from the southern half, unbroken, single-faced, seen by Manu, having ghee as its foot, and impelled by Mitra and Varuṇa."

Having divided the second portions, he places them down. Then, from the eastern half of the southern *puroḍāśa*, having well-saturated a piece three or four finger-breadths wide with clarified butter, he places the sacrificer’s portion in front of the *dhruvā* vessel. He takes two portions from the *dhruvā* butter, twice from the northern *puroḍāśa*, twice from the boiled milk, and twice from the curds; he then anoints the Hotṛ’s fingers twice and, after smelling it, consumes it.
He cuts off the four *avāntareḍā* portions; he spreads [the butter] underneath, cuts twice, and pours [butter] over.

The Adhvaryu, the Sacrificer, the Brahman, and the Āgnīdhra touch it together. Then, when he recognizes from the Hotṛ's recitation, "The divine Adhvaryus are invited; the human ones are invited," he divides the southern cake into four parts and places them upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Then, when he recognizes from the Hotṛ's recitation, "This sacrificer is invited," the Sacrificer, looking at the Hotṛ, should meditate on Vāyu with his mind. When the *iḍā* has been invited, he places the six-fold portion for the Āgnīdhra.

He spreads [the underlayer of ghee], places the oblation, and pours [ghee] over it; he spreads [another underlayer], places the oblation, and pours [ghee] over it. They consume [the portion] and purify themselves. Then he says, "Bring the *prāśitra* portion for the Brahman."
They carry away the *pari-prāśitra*, following it with water and the *brahmabhāga* by means of the *veda*;
then he asks for the *anvāhārya* rice, and they set aside this sacrificial remnant.
Then he issues the call: "O Brahman, we shall proceed; O Āgnīdh, having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, cleanse the fires once each."
Having been born, he places this fuel-stick in the middle of the Āhavanīya fire.

Then this Āgnīdhra priest cleanses the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) with the faggot-bands themselves: once the middle one, once the southern one, and once the northern one; he fans the Āhavanīya fire once with the formula: "O Agni, winner of booty, I cleanse thee who hast run for booty, who hast won booty, the vigorous winner of booty, for the sake of winning booty; I cleanse Agni, the eater of food, for the sake of eating food. Then, having touched these faggot-bands with water, he throws them after [the fire] into the Āhavanīya with the formula: "Rudra, who is the overlord of beings..."

"The bull that moves within the sacrificial ground—do not harm our cattle; let this be your oblation, Svāhā! Then, taking up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, stepping forward, and calling for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to the gods!
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering. He sacrifices three subsequent offerings (*anūyāja*), saying, "Sacrifice! Sacrifice! while moving westward.

Having sipped water, he then separates them; having stepped out toward the north and set down the two offering-spoons (srucau) in their respective places, he spreads them apart with two Vājavatī verses. With the verse, "By the impulse of strength, with the uplifting, he has lifted me up," he lifts up the Juhū spoon with his right hand. Then, with the verse, "By the pressing-down, Indra has made my rivals lower," he presses down the Upabhṛt spoon with his left hand. With the verse, "The gods have increased the Brahman through the uplifting and the pressing-down," he moves the Juhū eastward. Then, with the verse, "May Indra and Agni scatter my rivals in all directions," he moves the Upabhṛt westward.
He anoints the enclosing sticks from the east: with "For the Vasus thee" the middle one, with "For the Rudras thee" the southern one, and with "For the Ādityas thee" the northern one.

Then, having touched the *upabhṛt* ladle with water and placed the two ladles in their respective places, he anoints the *prastara* bundle in the ladles: the tips in the *juhū* with "Licking what has been anointed"; the middle parts in the *upabhṛt* with "May the birds depart"; and the roots in the *dhruvā* with "May I not wipe away offspring and the womb. Then, having plucked a blade of grass from the *prastara*, he places it in the *juhū*.

Then he causes [the Āgnīdhra] to announce: "Ośrāvaya! Let it be heard! *Astu śrauṣaṭ*! The divine Hotṛs have been impelled for the auspicious proclamation; the human [Hotṛ] has been sent forth for the Sūktavāka. Recite the hymns!

He throws [the wooden sword] forward as if above, neither throwing it too far ahead, nor tossing it back from the front, nor letting it rest against anything, nor scattering it in all directions; he raises it upward with the formula: "May the waters and plants swell! You are the speckled ones of the Maruts. Go to heaven; from there, send rain down upon us! Then he looks toward the Āgnīdhra, saying, "O Āgnīdh!"

The Āgnīdhra says to him, "Converse [with the Śrauṣaṭ]. The Adhvaryu says, "The Āgnīdhra has come. The Āgnīdhra says, "He has come. The Adhvaryu says, "Make it heard. The Āgnīdhra says, "Śrauṣaṭ. The Adhvaryu says, "Say this. The Āgnīdhra says, "Throw after [the firebrand]. He throws it after.

"Welcome to the divine *hotṛ*s; well-being to the human ones; pronounce the *śaṃyuvāka*. Then, having risen, he worships the *āhavanīya* fire with the formula: "O Agni, you are the protector of life; protect my life. O Agni, you are the protector of sight; protect my sight. Then he touches this earth with the formula: "You are firm. He throws the middle enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) into the fire with the verse: "O divine Agni, that enclosing-stick which you placed around yourself while being seized by the Paṇis—that very one I bring back to you according to your pleasure, so that it may not be alienated from you. Then he throws the other two together with the formula: "Come together to the path of the sacrifice. Then he makes an offering over them with the residue of the oblation.

He pours the contents of the *upabhṛt* ladle into the *juhū* with the formula: "O great ones who abide on the *prastara*, you who dwell on the *barhis* and possess shares in the remnants—O all you gods, accepting this speech, sit upon this *barhis* and rejoice, Svāhā! Then, having turned to the right and hastened back toward the west, he releases the two ladles at the pole with the formula: "I place you in the seat of Agni, whose house is free from serpents; for the sake of bliss, O blissful ones, bestow bliss upon me; O you two who bear the burden, protect the burden-bearers.
If, however, there is no pole, he releases them on the rubbish-heap (*utkara*) with the *sphya* using that same mantra.

Then, taking the vessel of clarified butter together with the *sruva* spoon in his right hand and the *juhū* ladle in his left, having handed the *veda* grass-bundle to the *hotṛ*, and having turned to the right, they both run back toward the west. The *adhvaryu* passes to the south of the *gārhapatya* fire, and the *hotṛ* to the north; behind the *gārhapatya*, they sit down facing east, the *adhvaryu* on the south and the *hotṛ* on the north. Then the *adhvaryu*, making the *veda* the *upabhṛt* and taking four portions of clarified butter, says loudly, "O *āgnīdhra*, announce for Soma! Having called for the announcement, he says softly, "For Soma," and loudly, "Recite the offering-verse (*yajya*) for Soma! At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering.

Taking four portions of clarified butter, he says [the offering formula] "to Tvaṣṭṛ" in a low voice; having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* loudly, he says "to Tvaṣṭṛ" in a low voice; he says "recite the *yajyā*" in a low voice; and when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he makes the offering loudly.

Taking four portions of clarified butter, he says [the invitatory verse] "To the wives of the gods" in a low voice; having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* loudly, he says "The wives of the gods" in a low voice; "Sacrifice! loudly; and when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers to the wives of the gods within the enclosed space (*pariśrita*). Then, taking four portions of clarified butter, he says [the invitatory verse] "To Agni Gṛhapati" in a low voice; having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* loudly, he says "Agni Gṛhapati" in a low voice; "Sacrifice! loudly; and when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers in the eastern part of the northern half, passing beyond the previous offerings. Then, having passed by the front of the Hotṛ, he anoints two finger-breadths of the Hotṛ's [finger].
Having smelled it and consumed it, he completes the *iḍā* with four portions;

the Adhvaryu and the wife both touch the clarified butter together. When the *iḍā* has been invoked, he places the six-fold portion for the Agnīdhra; they both eat it and perform the ritual purification.

Then, having taken four portions of clarified butter into the *sruc* ladle and turning away toward the left, he offers an expiation-oblation (*prāyaścitta*) in the *anvāhāryapacana* fire with the mantra: "Whatever has adhered to the mortar, the pestle, and the winnowing basket; whatever on the grinding stone, the black antelope skin, and the potsherds—those droplets and scattered drops I unite in sacrifice. May all the gods enjoy this oblation. Whatever many droplets exist in the sacrifice, I offer them all, well-sacrificed and united, into the fire: *svāhā*!"

Having taken another fourfold portion and having placed the wood-chips upon the Anvāhāryapacana fire itself, and having poured in the husks, he offers the husk-oblation with the mantra: "O Agni, of unassailable life-force, of cool body, protect me today from heaven; protect me from bondage; protect me from ill-sacrificed offerings; protect me from bad food; protect me from evil conduct; make our food free from poison; make our dwelling-place easy to sit in; Svāhā! Then, having returned by the same way he came, he makes the sacrificer recite over the Veda-bundle from the beginning of the section until the end: "The Veda art thou, the acquisition art thou... and so on.

Having handed over the Veda to the Hotṛ, he unties the wife [with the formula]: "I unloose this bond of Varuṇa which Savitṛ, the kindly-minded, has bound; in the womb of Dhātṛ, in the world of good deeds, I make it pleasant for me together with my husband. Then, having placed the cord in her joined palms, he pours water from the vessel [saying]: "Together with life, together with offspring, together again with splendor, O Agni!"

"May I go united with my husband; may my self be united with my body," she says. Then she wipes her mouth with the verse: "O Sarasvatī, whatever honey is in your waters, in your cows, and in your horses—with that, O winner of prizes, cleanse my mouth, O Sarasvatī. She pours out water; for it is said in the Brāhmaṇa, "Having assumed the form of the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), she rises. Then, in the same manner, she makes her sip water across the strainer with the verse: "The plants are full of milk; the milk of the creepers is full of milk. With that milk which is the milk of the waters, unite me, O Indra."

Then he causes her to place fuel-sticks on the *gārhapatya* fire with the formulas: "O Agni, lord of vows, I have performed the vow; I was able to do it; may it be successful for me, svāhā! O Vāyu, lord of vows! O Āditya, lord of vows! O lord of vows among vows, I have performed the vow; I was able to do it; may it be successful for me, svāhā! Then, having led her out by the way she entered, he goes eastward and causes the *dhruvā* ladle to swell: "May the *dhruvā* swell with clarified butter for every sacrifice for those seeking the gods."

"The udder of Sūryā, the lap of Aditi, the wide-streaming Earth—at this sacrifice. Then, dipping the *sruva* spoon into the *ājya*-pot, he offers the expiations (*prāyaścitta*), [reciting]: "Whatever in the sacrifice was under-intoned, over-intoned, accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ*-call, or over-recited; whatever is redundant in the rite or deficient—may the sacrifice, knitting together its joints, go forward, making it right."

"May the offering consecrated with *svāhā* go to the gods, *svāhā*! Then he offers for the prosperity of the sacrifice: "To those who are sacrificed for, *svāhā*; to those not sacrificed for, *vaṣaṭ*, *svāhā*; a remedy for the ill-sacrificed, *svāhā*; for restoration, *svāhā*; for misfortune, *svāhā*; for the divine bodies, *svāhā*; for success, *svāhā*; for prosperity, *svāhā*; for total prosperity, *svāhā*; *bhūḥ* *svāhā*; *bhuvaḥ* *svāhā*; *suvaḥ* *svāhā*; *bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ* *svāhā*! To this my [prayer], O Varuṇa; I implore you, O Tattva; you, O Agni, for us; you, O Agni, for us."

O Agni, you are *ayāsya*, established with a mind that is *ayās* (unwearied/unwavering); being *ayās*, you carry the oblation; being *ayās*, bestow healing upon us—*svāhā*. O Agni, you are *ayās*, free from reproach; truly you are *ayās*; held by an *ayas* (unwavering) mind, you carry the invocation as *ayās*; being *ayās*, bestow healing upon us—*svāhā*. Whatever we have done amiss in this rite, whether in respect of the mantra or the ritual action...

By this oblation, I pacify all that; may the gods be satisfied and shower down ghee, *svāhā*. Whatever in this ritual I have done in excess, or whatever I have done here deficiently—may Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the wise one, make all that well-sacrificed and well-offered for me. To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the consumer of well-offered oblations, the fulfiller of desires of offerings, *svāhā*. O Prajāpati, none other than you has encompassed all these created beings.
With whatever desire we sacrifice to you, may that be ours; may we be masters of riches, *svāhā*.

Then, having torn off portions from the blades of the sacrificial grass, he anoints them upon the *dhruvā* ladle with the formula: "May the sacrificial grass be anointed with the oblation, with clarified butter; may it be united with the Ādityas, with the Vasus, and with the Maruts."

"May it be anointed with Indra, with all the gods," he says; then he throws it after [the oblation] into the Āhavanīya fire with the words, "May it go to the celestial firmament, svāhā! Then, having stood up and stepped onto the altar with his right foot, he offers the *samiṣṭayajus* with the *dhruvā* spoon: "O gods who know the way, having found the way, go upon the way; O Lord of the Mind, O God, place this sacrifice of ours among the gods, svāhā! To Speech, svāhā! To the Wind, place it, svāhā! He lifts up the *sruk* ladle, pours out the *praṇītā* waters, and the sacrificer, having stood up, strides the *viṣṇukrama* steps with his right foot.
The oblation for either the new moon (*āmāvāsya*) or the full moon (*paurṇamāsya*) is completed;

then the formal announcement (*upavyāharaṇa*) is prescribed: "At the beginning of a rite, one should desire the success of that rite; at the beginning of a constituent part of the sacrifice, one should desire the success of that constituent part.

Having spread out *darbha* grass with the tips pointing eastward, the sacrificer sits upon it facing the east and mutters: "Those [streams] which flow from the front, those from above, and those from all sides—with these rays as my strainers, I commence faith and the sacrifice. O gods who know the way, find the way for the sacrifice."

"May the sacrifice be set in motion by the god Manasaspati, by Vāta. "O Śraddhā, come! I call you with truth. Thus he performs the invocation with the *ākūti* (intention). "I place you before me for intention, for desire, for prosperity—for immortality and for life. "For his protection, I place the divine *ākūti* before him; may she, the mother of the sacrifice, be easy for me to invoke, so that I may obtain this which I desire in my mind, having entered it into my heart with my will"—thus he forms the mental resolve three times, and three times aloud.
"One desiring all objects shall establish the sacred fires"—thus at the establishment of the fires;

"one desiring heaven shall sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices"—thus at the New and Full Moon sacrifices; and "one desiring heaven shall sacrifice with the Four-Monthly sacrifices"—thus at the Four-Monthly sacrifices.
"One desiring heaven shall sacrifice with an animal"—thus in the Animal Sacrifice (*paśubandha*);

"one desiring heaven shall sacrifice with Soma"—thus in the Soma Sacrifice; "one desiring heaven shall pile the fire-altar"—thus in the Piling of the Fire-altar (*agnicaya*). In an *ahīna* or a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), one sacrifices according to one's desire or for whatever specific purpose one desires.

"May that be successful for me; may that be fully successful for me; may that desire be fulfilled for me"—this is the response of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). "May that be successful for you; may that be fully successful for you; may that desire be fulfilled for you"—this is the response, "Om, so be it. Then he asks the officiating priests for the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), [addressing] the Adhvaryu: "O Adhvaryu, give me the sacrificial ground."

"May the divine Āditya, the divine Adhvaryu, grant you a place for sacrifice"—to this he replies, "Om, so be it. "O Brahman, grant me a place for sacrifice"—to this he replies, "May the divine Candra, the divine Brahman, grant you a place for sacrifice"—to this he replies, "Om, so be it. "O Hotṛ, grant me a place for sacrifice"—to this he replies, "May the divine Agni, the divine Hotṛ, grant you a place for sacrifice"—to this he replies, "Om, so be it."

"O Udgātṛ, give me a place for sacrifice to the gods," he says to the Udgātṛ. "May the divine Parjanya, the divine Udgātṛ, grant you a place for sacrifice to the gods. "Om, so be it," is the reply. "O Sadasya, give me a place for sacrifice to the gods," he says to the Sadasya.
"May the divine Ākāśa, the divine Sadasya, grant you a place for sacrifice to the gods. "Om, so be it," is the reply. "O Hotrakas, give me a place for sacrifice to the gods," he says to the Hotrakas.

"May the divine waters, the divine Hotṛ-priests, the Sinsis, grant you the place for sacrifice. "Om, so be it," is the reply. "O Camasādhvaryus, grant me the place for sacrifice. "O rays, the gods, the divine Camasādhvaryus, may they grant you the place for sacrifice. "Om, so be it," is the reply.
Or rather, he does not ask for the place for sacrifice; from the very beginning, having bathed at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), he emerges, puts on a new, unwashed garment, and [proceeds].
Pure, clean, purified, fit for sacrifice, free from evil, and practicing celibacy, the student—regarded as an assistant—should perform the Vedic rites while observing the ritual up to the fourth act.

Facing east, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), and moving clockwise (*pradakṣiṇa*), he performs the rites for the gods; facing south, moving counter-clockwise (*prasavya*), and wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he performs the rites for the ancestors. These rites end either toward the east or toward the north.

Standing, sitting, or bowing down as is appropriate, according to the *Chandoga-brāhmaṇa*: "Just as the right hand is [superior], so is the sacrificial ground for the gods (*devayajana*); just as the left, so is the sacrificial ground for the ancestors (*pitṛyajana*). As is the sacrificial ground for the ancestors, so is the making of a cemetery (*śmaśānakaraṇa*); as is the making of a cemetery, so it is in the case of the *iṣṭi*, animal, and *soma* sacrifices performed for malevolent purposes. From the very beginning, the sacrificial ground for the gods should be to the east of water; from which one would not find another sacrificial ground for the gods nearby to the east, one leaves a space the size of a sacrificial ground beyond to the north."

Now, the selection of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is prescribed: the priests shall be Brāhmaṇas endowed with noble birth, lineage, sacred learning, and good conduct; they must have no physical defects, no moles, and must not have crossed over a ditch [in their ancestry], nor be outcasts, nor born of low-caste women, nor those who have not studied the Vedas. One should exclude those whose fathers were plowmen or shepherds, the sons of appointed daughters (*putrikā*), those born of another’s field (*para-kṣetra*), those born of a pregnant bride (*sahoḍha*), those born of an unmarried woman (*kānīna*), those born after a younger brother (*anujāvara*), and those with two ancestral lineages (*dvipravara*). The Adhvaryu should be of the Aṅgiras clan, the Brahman of the Vasiṣṭha clan, the Hotṛ of the Viśvāmitra clan, the Udgātṛ of the Ayāsya clan, and the Sadasya of the Kauṣītaka clan. The remaining priests may be of the Bhṛgu or Aṅgiras clans. According to some, birth, conduct, and learning are the criteria for qualification.

If he should choose them, let him choose only those whose limbs are unimpaired: an *adhvaryu* who does not have deformed nails, a *brahmā* who is not afflicted with leprosy, a *hotṛ* who is not mutilated, an *udgātṛ* who is not hideous, and a *sadasya* who is not afflicted with skin disease (*śipiviṣṭa*).

Now, the *pratiprasthātṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, and *unnetṛ* are the attendants of the *adhvaryu*; the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*, *āgnīdhra*, and *potṛ* are the attendants of the *brahmā*; the *maitrāvaruṇa*, *acchāvāka*, and *grāvastut* are the attendants of the *hotṛ*;
the *prastotṛ*, *pratihartṛ*, and *subrahmaṇya* are the attendants of the *udgātṛ*; and the *abhigara*, *dhruvagopa*, and *saṃśrāvaka* are the attendants of the *sadasya*.
Some say they are either self-dependent or not self-dependent;
it is known that there are ten or eleven *camasādhvaryu* priests who are hired with other sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Therefore, for the *agnihotra* sacrifice-rite, there is only one officiating priest (*ṛtvij*).
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there are four officiating priests (ṛtvij): the Adhvaryu, the Brahman, the Hotṛ, and the Āgnīdhra;
in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the Pratiprasthātṛ is the fifth;
and in the Paśubandha sacrifice, the Maitrāvaruṇa is the sixth.

At every gentle sacrifice, he should choose each one of them for their respective offices; having approached each, he should direct them, saying: "I, so-and-so, approach you for the office of the Adhvaryu;
may your honor officiate as my priest," and likewise for the office of the Brahman, the Hotṛ, the Udgātṛ, and the Sadas.
Some say that there is no *sadasya* (member of the assembly); some say that the *hotraka*s are [distinguished] by their respective duties, while others say they are not.
The *hotṛ*-priests, the *camasādhvaryu*s, and the *adhvaryu*—for the *adhvaryu* is the first among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) to be appointed; by him the *stoma* is to be harnessed.
"The Sun is the divine *adhvaryu*; he is my *adhvaryu*. O *adhvaryu*, I choose you as *adhvaryu*," [with these words] he chooses the *adhvaryu*.
