"Āditya is the divine Adhvaryu; he is your Adhvaryu. With his permission, I shall perform the ritual act. "Om, so be it," is the reply. "Candra is the divine Brahman; he is my Brahman. O Brahman, I choose you as Brahman. [The Brahman replies: "Candra is the divine Brahman; he is your Brahman. With his permission, I shall perform the ritual act. "Om, so be it," is the reply. "Agni is the divine Hotṛ; he is my Hotṛ. O Hotṛ, I choose you as Hotṛ. [The Hotṛ replies: "Agni is the divine Hotṛ; he is your Hotṛ. With his permission, I shall perform the ritual act. "Om, so be it," is the reply. Thus for the Hotṛ.

"Agni, the divine, is the divine *hotṛ*; he is your *hotṛ*. With his permission, I shall perform the ritual act. "Om, so be it," is the reply. "Parjanya, the divine, is the divine *udgātṛ*; he is my *udgātṛ*. O *udgātṛ*, I choose you as *udgātṛ*. [Thus one chooses] the *udgātṛ*. "Parjanya, the divine, is the divine *udgātṛ*; he is your *udgātṛ*. With his permission, I shall perform the ritual act. "Om, so be it," is the reply. "Ākāśa, the divine, is the divine *sadasya*; he is my *sadasya*. O *sadasya*, I choose you as *sadasya*. [Thus one chooses] the *sadasya*.
"Ākāśa is the divine Sadasya; he is your Sadasya. With his approval, I shall perform the rite. "Om, so be it," is the response.
"The Waters are divine; the divine Hotrās are present. Those Hotrās are present for me. O Hotrakas, I choose you as Hotrakas"—thus [he chooses] the Hotrakas.

"O divine Waters, you are the divine Hotrāśamsins; permitted by you as the Hotrāśamsins, we shall perform the rite. "Om, so be it," is the response. "The rays are the divine Camasādhvaryus; O Camasādhvaryus, I choose you as my Camasādhvaryus"—thus [he chooses] the Camasādhvaryus.

The rays are the gods; they are the divine *camasādhvaryu*s. Being permitted by them with the words, "We shall perform the ritual act," the response is "Oṃ, so be it. Each one who has been chosen mutters: "Greatness you have spoken for me; glory you have spoken for me; fortune you have spoken for me; splendor you have spoken for me; austerity you have spoken for me; praise you have spoken for me; arrangement you have spoken for me; enjoyment you have spoken for me; the All you have spoken for me; the Whole you have spoken for me; everything auspicious you have spoken for me—let that protect me, let that enter me, let that quicken me; by that..."

"May I enjoy; may the god go to the god; may Soma go to Soma"—thus [is the mantra]. "Om, so be it," is the reply. "May my anger be in the tiger; may my internal disease be in the panther; may my hunger be in the wolf; may my devouring [instinct] be in the horse;
may my thirst be in the desert; may my voracity be in the royal palace; may my weariness be in the stone; may my hemorrhoids be in the donkey."
In the thorn-bush is my shame; in the *aśvattha* tree is my trembling;
in the tortoise is my bodily ailment; in the bladder is my discharge; in the *apriya* is my death; in the rival is my evil;
in the adversary is my destruction; in ill-repute is my failure.
May my lack of prosperity be in the *parasvat* deer;

may my affliction be in the rhinoceros; may my blindness be in the gayal; may my deafness be in the cow; may my grief be in the bear; may my exhaustion be in the iguana; and may my cold be in old age.
Fear in the black bird, a foul odor in the whip, fear of owls in me, cowardice in dogs, and envy in the crow.

May my prosperity be in the monkey; may my joy be in the falcon; may my delight be in the young camel; may my weariness be in the female deer; may my woolly garment be in the sheep; may my fragrance be in the perfume box;
and may my ornament be in the maiden.
The sow has brought moisture to my heart; the viper has brought sleep to me; the python has brought bad dreams to me; the lightning has brought arrogance to me; and greed has brought dampness to me.
May my sin and misfortune be in the locust;
may my falsehood be in women; may my harshness be in goats; may my affliction be in the Vratya.

In the Śūdra is my theft; in the Vaiśya is my failure to perform duty; in the kinsman of a Rājanya is my ignorance; in the Niṣāda is my Brahman-murder; in the Kuliṅga is my sneezing; in the Ulūla is my wantonness; in the Udriṇī is my vomiting;
in the Kiṃpuruṣa is my weeping; in the Dvīpin is my [evil] desire; in the Hastin is my leprosy.

In Śunī I have difficulty in hearing; in the Snāvanya country I have the Mleccha; in Videha I have the Śīpatha; in Mahāvarṣa I have the Glau; in the Mūjavat mountains I have the Tapnā; in Dundubhi I have the Kāsika; in the Ikṣvākus I have bile; in Kaliṅga I have impurity;
in the mule I have childlessness.
In the dog is my evil conduct;
in the mouse is my tooth-disease; in the fly is my scab; in the parrot is my jaundice.
May my chatter be in the peacock;
may my old age be in the bull;
may my slander be in the blue jay; may my fatigue be in water; and may my sin be in one who abandons the Veda.

"Go away, O Evil One! You have been driven away from us again, O Evil One! Enter the world of those who do good deeds, O Evil One; enter there undisturbed. O Evil One, whoever does not leave us—him we abandon you. May he who hates us be destroyed; destroy him whom we hate.
Then, with joined palms, he strikes the water, saying: "May the waters and the plants be friendly to us."

He pours out these waters toward that direction in which he has an enemy, saying: "May they be ill-disposed toward him who hates us and whom we hate. Then, having touched water, they enter as they came.

Now, regarding this establishment of the fires (agnyādheya), what is the commencement of that rite? The seasons and constellations have been stated, and the preparatory observances for oneself have been stated; how, then, is the sequence here established?

Having performed the bathing, purifying, sprinkling with mantras, and the recitation of the *puṇyāha* (auspicious day), having summoned faith and made the mental resolve (*ākūti*), having uttered the preparatory formulas (*upavyāhṛti*), having chosen the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and honored them, having requested the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) and secured it, and having taken up the wooden sword (*sphya*), he enters by way of the designated space between the altar (*vedi*) and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*). Standing behind the *gārhapatya* fire, he digs up the site of the *gārhapatya* towards the east with the wooden sword, [reciting]: "May what is being dug up remove from this earth the impure and the evil of the sacrificer!"

"May the four quarters be auspicious to us; may Mother Earth be propitious to our offspring. Then he sprinkles it with water: "May the divine waters be for our aid, for our drink; may they flow toward us with health and well-being. In this very manner he digs out the site for the Anvāhāryapacana fire, and likewise for the Āhavanīya, and so for the other two, if he intends to perform them. Then, having gone out northward by way of the space between the altar and the rubbish-heap (utkara), they go in that direction where his ritual materials have been prepared.

Alternatively, all the ritual materials (saṃbhāra) are prepared to the north of the hall; or else, within the altar (antarvedi), he collects each material one by one in their proper sequence with a single Yajus formula.

Having gathered sand with the formula, "The form of Vaiśvānara on earth, the flowing moisture—may they enter us as something pleasant," he deposits it. In this very same way, having gathered each subsequent material with each subsequent Yajus formula, he deposits them one after another: saline soil, sand, the mole-heap, an ant-hill, mud, the earth dug up by a boar, a lotus leaf, and gravel—these are the eight earthly materials. Then, with a subsequent Yajus formula, he brings six pieces of gold; then, with the formulas for the trees, the wooden materials.

He brings branches that are moist, with shoots and leaves, along with their sprouts, a span in length, and with undried tips; or rather, he brings them according to availability. From a variegated *aśvattha* tree, he brings three fire-logs—moist, with shoots and leaves, along with their sprouts, a span in length, and with undried tips—from a variegated *aśvattha* tree: "You are gathered from the variegated *aśvattha*, fashioned as great bodies."

"Measured by Prajāpati, the mouth of the sacrifice, are these three pairs consisting of triplets for the sake of procreation. Then he brings a nest of *muñja* grass, [saying]: "O Agni, that vigorous body of yours which has entered into the plants..."

"I gather that [fire-drill] for you here," he says, and then he brings him two fire-drills (*araṇī*): one made of *aśvattha* wood from the heart of a *śamī* tree, or even one not from the heart of a *śamī* tree; four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in height, twelve finger-breadths in width, and sixteen finger-breadths in length—or alternatively, a span (*prādeśa*) long, equal on all sides, and four finger-breadths in height. While it lies face upwards, they fashion its lower part as the birth-place (*prajanana*), with the grain of the wood following the direction and sloping towards the west;
the upper fire-drill (*uttarāraṇi*) is of the same dimensions.

Then he brings these [materials]: "From the *aśvattha* tree, the bearer of oblations, I gather the sacrificial body born of Agni, whose womb is peaceful, the heartwood of the *śamī*, for the sake of generating Agni. "The *aśvattha* tree which has grown from the heartwood of the *śamī*, dwelling together with you—that I bring for you by means of sacred prayer (*brahman*), along with the sacrificial signs. Then he gathers again those well-prepared materials: "O Jātavedas, you whom I have gathered together, as a body hidden among beings—being thus gathered, sit down, auspicious to our offspring; you who know, lead us to a wide world."
Now, indeed, it comes about that Indra, having slain Vṛtra and defeated the Asuras, returned on the new moon day;
the ancestors arrived on the preceding day,
and the sacrifice went to the ancestors.
The gods begged for him back;
they did not give him back to them. They said, "Let us choose a boon: we shall give him back to you, provided that he is prepared for us on the very day before. They gave him back to them.
"Therefore, it is performed on the day before for the ancestors;
in that he performs it for the ancestors on the day before, the sacrificer, having ransomed the sacrifice from the ancestors, spreads it out"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Now, if he does not obtain a cow, he obtains a ram or a goat; or else, having cooked rice for gambling, he pours over it abundant clarified butter or milk, and performs all that which is to be done with a cow. And it is known: "Clarified butter or milk is indeed the seed of the milch-cow, and rice-grains are the seed of the bull."

A cow indeed, because of the commonality of its body parts, enters even when well-concealed; or it enters either a frying pan or a heating vessel; or it enters even the *aupāsana* fire itself. They perform half of the *aupāsana* rite, or they perform the entire *aupāsana* rite using the *brāhmaudana* fire.
For it is indeed offered right here;

thus the ritual procedure is the same up to the pouring of the *saṃbhāra* materials. Then, having divided the *saṃbhāra* materials into three parts, one places them in the *sabhya* and *āvasathya* fires, or in the *āhavanīya* fire, or in both the *sabhya* and *āvasathya* fires.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the placing of the fuel sticks (*samid-ādhāna*).
He offers five fuel-sticks each from various trees after anointing them;
what is the sequence here? The *aśvattha*, the *udumbara*, the *parṇa*, the *śamī*, and the *vikaṅkata*—this is the sequence here.
And how indeed does one proceed at the end of the offerings to Indra-Agni and Aditi? At the end of the offerings to Indra-Agni and Aditi, he should let loose a horse that has stepped in water.

The statement, "Then one should draw out another for the purpose of the *daśahotr*," is appropriate only in the *Tantrasamāsa*, and not elsewhere; because the fire that has been carried forward (*praṇīta*) becomes mundane (*laukika*), and the rule is that "the fire in which an oblation has been offered by the *hotṛ* is to be maintained until the end of the ritual"— thus, when the ritual is concluded, it becomes mundane.
The oblations for the Tanū offerings are well-known;
he gives the well-known dakṣiṇās for the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya).
If he should not obtain these, he should give as many parched grains (mantha) or boiled rice (odana) as there are [of those dakṣiṇās].
"By that very means, he attains this desire;

therefore, one should give even a single cow as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)," so says the Paiṅgalāyani Brāhmaṇa. However, one must certainly not be without the consecrated fires (*anāhitāgni*). For it is known: "He who has established the sacred fires is indeed one of the gods. Now, when he takes out the fire, by that he secures a thousand wish-fulfilling cows; and when he offers the Agnihotra, by that [he secures] a thousand. Thus, what is stated here is truly immeasurable.

Now, on the day of preparation for the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), he procures: a cow, a ram, an unhemmed garment, four water-jars, three stakes of *udumbara* wood, a ladle of *udumbara* wood, one omentum-spit of *udumbara* wood that is branchless, all other materials required for the ancestral sacrifice (*paitṛyajñika*) except for the cooked rice-offering (*sthālīpāka*), two mats of *eraka* grass, collyrium and ointment, clarified butter, a handful of grass, the wooden sword (*sphya*), and a cord;
all this is placed to the south within an enclosed space.

Within this enclosed space, while he is facing eastward, he performs the tonsure of his hair. Having silently applied three bunches of *darbha* grass, he shaves him with the formula: "I shave; I shave well, impelled by the god Savitṛ and sharpened by the sacred word (*brahman*). May those hairs of mine which are above this [place] be for my well-being. Then, when his hair and beard have been shaved and his nails clipped, he makes him recite as he pours water from a water-pot over him: "May these waters be auspicious to me; may they carry away my evil deeds. Being purified, may we perform our sacred rites."

Having bathed, having stepped out toward the east, having put on a new garment, and having adorned himself, he anoints his eyes. Then, having purified him silently with twenty-one bunches of *darbha* grass divided into three groups of seven each, and having taken a vessel of water, he leads him to this direction; at a crossroads, while he gazes into that very vessel of water, he makes him recite the formulas for the deposits of evil: "O Simha, my wrath! O tiger, my internal disease! Having uttered this entire section up to its end, and having poured out the water, they cast away the vessel and return without looking back.

Having washed his hands and feet, he returns by the same way he came and causes the sacrificer to recite the section beginning with *pavamānaḥ suvarjanah*. He purifies himself with water. Having kindled the *idhma* from the *āmātya* fire, having placed it at the time of the *anvāhāryapacana* rite, having cleansed it, and having strewn it around with sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he melts the clarified butter (*ājya*), purifies it, and places these items to the north: four water-jars, three pits made of *udumbara* wood, three spits made of *udumbara* wood, one *udumbara* ladle, and one unbranched *udumbara* omentum-spit; and to the south, [he places] the same.

He prepares everything else for the ancestral sacrifice (*paitṛyajñika*) other than the *sthālīpāka*: the materials for the fire, a mattress and pillow, collyrium and ointment, clarified butter, a handful of grass, the wooden sword (*sphya*), and a cord;

these he places to the south, making a gaming-ground (*adhidevana*). Therein he pours out forty-nine dice. Then, taking up the wooden sword, he digs once toward the south, saying: "Struck down are the Asuras, the Rakṣasas, and the Piśācas who dwell upon the earth! Let them go elsewhere, wherever their mind has gone!"

Then he sprinkles it with water, [reciting]: "May the fathers who are below, those who are above, and those who are in the middle—those Soma-loving ones who have gone to the life-breath, who are free from malice and knowers of the *ṛta*—may they protect us, O fathers, at our invocations.

Then he takes up a firebrand, [reciting]: "The Asuras who, assuming new ancestral forms by means of the *svadhā*, wander about; those who carry away the outer forts and the inner forts—may Agni drive them away from this sacrifice. With that [firebrand], he heats the dug-out spot, [reciting]: "May the purifying Agni, making auspicious days, drive the Asuras far away from here, those who, having assumed the color of the fathers, desire a share here."

He completes [the rite] right here; he lets a drop of clarified butter drip onto that firebrand. He spreads sacrificial grass (barhis) with its tips pointing southward: "I bring you, O sacrificial grass, soft as wool and pleasant, for the sake of the fathers. May my fathers, worthy of Soma, sit upon this, along with their grandfathers and great-grandfathers and their followers. Then he invokes the fathers: "May our Soma-worthy fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers rise up and be present here with their followers—those who reach the breath of life, who are joined with truth, and who are free from malice; may the fathers come today to our invocation."

"Come here, O Fathers, to eat the oblation; having sat down upon the sacrificial grass at this sacrifice, do not deprive us of our hero. Then he offers them a seat and a bed made of *eraka* grass, saying: "These [seats] are for the two of them; they have arrived, worthy of Soma. Having become dear to our people, be auspicious and bringers of well-being. Then he brings them drinks: a drink of honey, a drink of milk, a drink of barley meal, or whatever else is available.

He gives one thing to the Brahmins and pours out another, saying, "O fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, this is your drink. At this point, he sprinkles them with a single water-pot silently. Then four people—the father and his sons—sit around the dice:
the father in the east, the eldest son in the south, the next-born in the west, and the youngest in the north. The father cuts twelve dice;
that is the victory.
The elder brother conquers twelve,
while the younger brother conquers twelve.

That [wood] prevails; then those that remain, the younger [relative] collects them together. Now, if there are two, the father is twice as long; if there is one, the wife is the third part. And if there are none at all, both husband and wife are twice as long.
This same rule applies to three, this same rule applies to two; having performed what was to be done, they depart.

Having said, "The cow has been won," they rise up; then, taking sacrificial grass (barhis) for them, he dedicates the cow with the formula: "I dedicate you, who are dear to the fathers, to the grandfathers, and to the great-grandfathers.
According to some, [he does this] silently. Then he sprinkles it with water with the formula: "I sprinkle you, who are dear to the fathers, to the grandfathers, and to the great-grandfathers.
According to some, [he does this] silently.
They immolate it right here with its head toward the west and its feet toward the south.

Once it has been immolated, he revives its vital breaths by sprinkling it with water. Having silently extracted the omentum each time, he removes the heart and the recognized portions of the meat, as well as the two kidneys. Having placed these upon those very spits, they cook them on this very fire.
When the omentum is cooked, he offers five oblations with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*).

Āḥ! Those waters that arise from the east and those from the north—with those waters, the sustainers of the entire world, I place an interposition between myself and my father; svadhā, obeisance, svāhā!

I have hidden myself within the mountains, within the great earth, within the sky, and within the infinite directions; I have placed a barrier between [myself] and the Grandfather—svadhā, obeisance, svāhā!

I have placed myself between [the worlds] by means of all the seasons, days and nights with their proper junctions, and half-months and months; I have established this interval from my great-grandfather. Svadhā! Namaḥ! Svāhā!
Whatever my mother, acting without restraint, caused me to be excited while she was unfaithful, may my father take that seed of mine; let another man come to her. Svadhā! Homage! Svāhā!

Whatever limb of yours the flesh-eating Jātavedas has burned while leading you away or guiding you to other worlds—that I now cause to enter back into you. O Fathers, be whole with all your limbs! Svadhā! Namaḥ! Svāhā!

Having divided the omentum into three parts, he offers it with a ladle made of *udumbara* wood: "To Soma, accompanied by the fathers, the impetuous one, we offer this oblation. O vigorous one, enjoy this of ours; as one born of ourselves, [offer] the oblation to the gods and the fathers. *Svadhā! Adoration! Svāhā!* I invoke Yama, who is accompanied by the Aṅgirases for our protection, and who is attended by the fathers. O son of Vivasvat, eat this of ours; as one born of ourselves, [offer] the oblation to the gods and the fathers. *Svadhā! Adoration! Svāhā!* O Agni, carrier of the *kavya*, when you sacrifice to the fathers who increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*),..."

"Carry the oblation to the gods and to the ancestors; O self-born one, carry the oblation to the gods and the ancestors! Svadhā! Homage! Svāhā! Having silently placed the ladle upon the fire, he offers these portions according to the procedure for the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*): first the heart, then the left kidney, then the right. "This for thee, father N.N., and for those who follow thee, and for those whom thou followest here. This, father, is thy imperishable *svadhā*; as great as the earth is, so great is thy measure; this measure, having become such, I give to thee. Thou art measured by the earth; do not perish for my sake, father."

He gives the second [portion]: "This is for you, grandfather N.N., and for those who follow you and those whom you follow here; this, grandfather, is your portion of *svadhā*. As great as the intermediate space is, so great is your measure; I give you this measure as it has come to be. You are measured by the intermediate space; do not fail the grandfather."

He gives the third [portion], saying: "This is for you, O great-grandfather [Name], and for those who follow you, and those whom you follow here; this, O great-grandfather, is your imperishable *svadhā*. As vast as the sky is, so great is your measure; I give you this measure as it truly is. You are measured by heaven; do not perish for the sake of the great-grandfather. Having said, "O ancestors, rejoice here according to your respective portions," he silently sprinkles [the offerings] there with one water-pot.

Then, having approached the cow from behind, he causes blood to flow forth: "May those Rakṣases who have a share in blood, and those Pitṛs who carry away and scatter [the offerings], be satisfied with this blood! Those miscarried fetuses of ours who wait upon us as sharers in blood—to them be self-born *svadhā* and obeisance; may they be satisfied and rejoice! Those who are raw, those who are cooked, and those wicked ones who fall upon us—to them be self-born *svadhā* and obeisance; may they be satisfied and devour!"
To those boys, to those women, and to those unknown ones who fall upon us—to them be self-born *svadhā* and homage; may they be satisfied and may they rejoice.

Having arrived, he gives collyrium, then he gives ointment, then he gives garments; then he worships with six salutations in reverse order; then he asks for a hero; then, having raised them up and carried them out, he invokes the mind with three verses: "We invoke the mind hither," "May our mind return to us," and "O Fathers, may our mind come back to us. At this point, having given a new garment to a Brāhmaṇa who knows thus, and having put on another garment to be worn, he goes toward the south and purifies himself with water.

In which both fragrances and flavors, as well as colors and strength, are deposited—may those waters be auspicious for me; may they carry away my evil deeds. Those waters sent by the gods that sprinkle vigor upon the earth—may those waters be auspicious for me; may they carry away my evil deeds. From whose emergence this entire world is born—may those waters be auspicious for me; may they carry away my evil deeds. Those waters by whose splendor and glory these three worlds are encompassed—may those waters be auspicious for me; may they carry away my evil deeds.

May those waters be auspicious for me; may they carry away my evil deeds. Those waters which flow—whether eastward, southward, westward, northward, or upward—which are wealthy, honey-sweet, and bright.

"May those waters be auspicious for me; may they carry away my evil deed"—saying this, he removes that garment which was to be worn [during the rite], puts on another, and rises from the fire with the verse addressed to Prajāpati: "O Prajāpati, none other than you... Then he throws the firebrand back [into the fire] with the verse: "Jātavedas has become the eater of the oblation; having made the offerings fragrant, he has carried them to the fathers, and they have eaten them with the *svadhā* call. Knowing [the way], O Agni, come back again to the gods."

There he gives these portions to the Brahmins: first the heart, then the left foreleg, then the right; he prepares food according to his faith and, having made this hare into a cow, he bestows it as a choice gift upon the Brahmins.

Whoever obtains a share of this cow, they all indeed become partakers of cattle through it. Having offered the *jayas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*, he offers the *āmātya* oblations. This is indeed the *upavasatha* (fast-day), for the gods dwell upon it, thinking, "In the morning we shall win desirable wealth. That which belongs to Agni on eight potsherds is indeed the desirable wealth of the gods; desirable wealth comes to him for whom one, knowing this, prepares this cow.
He overcomes every evil, he overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin.
"Furthermore, one conquers death," said Prajāpati.

"These are indeed called the *kūṣmāṇḍas*, or the *kājavas*, or the *vāmātya-homas*, or the *atīmokṣas*. Whatever evil deed one performs in this world, from all that he is released; free from debt, he goes to the heavenly world," so said Prajāpati.

One who is about to establish the sacred fires procures eight earth-related materials: saline soil, sand, a mole-heap, an ant-hill, mud from a pool, ground dug up by a boar, a lotus leaf, and gravel; and then the wood-related materials: an *aśvattha* tree, an *udumbara* tree, a *parṇa* tree, a *śamī* tree, a *vikaṅkata* tree, a tree struck by lightning, a *śamī*-enclosed branch, a nest of *muñja* grass, and three moist fuel-sticks from a conspicuous *aśvattha* tree, complete with shoots and leaves.

Six pieces of gold, each a span long and with unshriveled ends; three of gold and three of silver; a horse that has previously drawn a chariot; a chariot wheel; *brāhmaudana* rice-grains; all kinds of herbs; the hide of a red bull; new sacrificial vessels—these he brings for him. Then he brings the two fire-drills (*araṇī*) with the verse: "The Aśvattha tree which grew from the womb of the Śamī, that I bring to thee by means of the sacred word (*brahman*) along with the sacrificial signs. Now follows the consideration of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*):
one should establish the sacred fires under the Kṛttikās; one should establish the sacred fires under Rohiṇī.
One should establish the sacred fires under the two Punarvasus, or under the first Phalgunīs, or under the second Phalgunīs, or under Citrā; now, therefore, follows the consideration of the seasons:
a Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in spring.
A Rājanya should consecrate himself in summer,
a Vaiśya in autumn,
and a Rathakāra in the rainy season; moreover, he should indeed establish the sacred fires at whatever time faith may come upon him.
That indeed is his prosperity.
Thus, for one who is afflicted, or for one who is excessively endowed with faith, there is this Brāhmaṇa passage:
"He who establishes the sacred fire under Rohiṇī surely prospers; he ascends all heights."

The new moon that occurs after the full moon of Vaiśākha coincides with the constellation Rohiṇī once a year; on that day he should establish the fires. Now, for him, a hall or a shed has already been prepared beforehand on a chosen sacrificial ground (devayajana);
they make two doors for it, one to the east and one to the south, and they prepare the site for the Gārhapatya fire in the middle.
Twelve steps to the east of the Āhavanīya fire, or at a point marked by the range of vision;

or to the south of the Viṣuvant, or at a point marked by the range of vision of the Anvāhāryapacana fire—having thus dug up the ground in three parts so that two parts lie toward the east and one part toward the west, and having sprinkled it with water, he shaves his hair and beard and clips his nails; the wife does likewise, except for the hair.
Both are adorned with human ornaments and wear unwashed garments. He causes her to cook the food to be offered for the vow; they both eat of it, mixed with clarified butter and mixed with milk.

Then, when the sun is over the trees, he calls for the collection of all medicinal herbs, a vessel of clarified butter together with a dipping-spoon, a ladle, sacrificial grass, a garment, fire-sticks, and chips of wood; having taken these, they proceed while remaining covered, toward either a frying pan or a heating-plate.

Having scattered pieces of *dīpyā* wood into that fire, having strewn it around with sacrificial grass (*barhis*), having melted the clarified butter (*ājya*) and purified it, he offers all the medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadha*) with his joined palms, having first spread a base of butter and then poured more over it, saying: "To Agni, who possesses all herbs, for nourishment and procreation, Svāhā! Then, having offered the *jayas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*, he offers the *amātya-homas*. Then, having taken four portions of butter into the ladle (*sruca*), he offers the oblation to Prajāpati with the verse: "O Prajāpati, these [beings] are thine alone; no other than thou... Having again taken four portions, he offers the *anukhyā* oblation with the verse: "Agni Jātavedas, the first, has looked toward the forefront of the dawns; he has looked toward the days."

"Following the many rays of the sun, he has extended across heaven and earth—Svāhā! Then the sacrificer takes those embers in either a pan or a shallow bowl, saying: "I take you for long life; I take you for brilliance; I take you for heat; I take you for vigor; I take you for spiritual luster. Then, taking them up, he stands up, saying: "May long life enter me; may prosperity enter me; may spiritual luster enter me."

Having handed those over to the Adhvaryu, they go out while the sacrificer maintains contact with him. Returning by the same way they came, having gone around the north of the hall and entered by the eastern door, he pours them out in the place of the Gārhapatya fire and adds fuel.
They strew sacrificial grass around it;
the Brahman and the sacrificer sit down to the south. Then he spreads out a red bull’s hide behind the fire, with the neck facing east and the hair side up.

At the time of carrying it away, he pours out four measures of rice-grains for the Brahman, either with the formula, "I pour out what is pleasing to the Brahman," or silently. Then, having touched the poured-out grains with the formula, "For intention thee, for desire thee, for prosperity thee," he places those rice-grains in a winnowing basket, sprinkles them with water, and spreads them out upon a hide. Then, having placed the mortar and pestle upon that very hide, he threshes them.
Then, with that same vessel, he pours in four vessels of water, provided that the cooking-pot is sturdy.
If it is uncrushed, or five, or more, it becomes equal to water;

having cooked it with a full supply of fuel by anyone who is skilled, he pours ghee over it and sets it aside toward the north. Then they announce it to the officiating priests (ṛtvij) as it approaches. These priests approach it, and having washed that vessel and spread a base of ghee within it, he draws it out into it as if without striking it.

Having made a channel for pouring ghee and having brought a large quantity of clarified butter, he then offers an oblation from this very boiled rice, or stands near it, saying: "To the wise, the seer, the holy one, the bull, the vigorous one—may that word which is worthy of praise be offered. From whatever there is fear, may we have freedom from fear; I sacrifice to the gods who are to be appeased, svāhā! Then, having seated these four *ārṣeya* priests to the north, each in his respective direction, and having caused them to sip water in order, he pushes this [boiled rice] toward them while touching the ground and as if not cutting it off, after they have eaten three mouthfuls, saying: "Peace! It is accomplished; your *brahmaudana* is ready."
To them he gives a castrated young bull; then this Brāhmaṇa, sitting to the north, eats the scrapings from the pot.

To him he gives whatever is prepared for him; then, with what remains of the clarified butter (*ājya*), he anoints the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and offers them, [reciting]: "Serve the fire with fuel-sticks; awaken the guest with clarified butter. Offer the oblations into him—*svāhā*! O Agni, let the ladles full of clarified butter, rich in oblations, approach you, O beloved one. Accept my fuel-sticks—*svāhā*! We magnify you, O Aṅgiras, with fuel-sticks and clarified butter. Blaze forth brightly, O youngest one—*svāhā*! For a Brāhmaṇa, these verses are in the *gāyatrī* meter.
With *triṣṭubh* verses he sprinkles Agni for a Kṣatriya: "I sprinkle thee with [the milk of] a ruddy cow; do thou sprinkle me with long life, O Agni, enjoying the oblation.

With *jagatī* verses he sprinkles it for a Vaiśya: "The guardian of the people has been born, the watchful one; O Agni, the human clans praise thee," and "Seven are thy kindling-sticks, O Agni, seven thy tongues.
At the kindling-sticks, he gives a heifer.
Then, handing him the two kindling woods, he says: "You shall remain restrained in speech; give instructions regarding that which you are to instruct.
He replies: "Have the Brahmins fed; guard the horse; set down the ritual materials. For him, the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) becomes one characterized by abundance.
This is the prosperity of the *agnyādheya*.

Regarding this, they say: "One should not offer a cow at the *agnyādheya*, for it is of a terrible form. One may indeed do so, or one may not; or one may even offer many. According to Kātya, there should follow for him a meritorious and peaceful benediction. Then he hands him the two kindling sticks (*araṇī*).

The Earth, the mistress of the people, accepts him at the seat of the Cosmic Order; she, the supporter of riches, turns toward him. You two, pregnant with the kinsman Jātavedas, generate for the sacrifices one who goes before them. Ascend my ten fingers, O Agni, together with immortality, long life, and splendor.

"Living long, may we see each subsequent year; may I perform the sacrifice at the New Moon and the Full Moon as it ought to be performed. Then he hands them over with the formula: "You two are possessed of the proper season, having Agni as your seed; receive the embryo. I take that from you two. That is the truth: that you two bear a hero and will give birth to a hero. You two shall procreate through me in the morning; you two, being procreated, shall cause me to procreate through offspring, cattle, spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and the heavenly world."

Then he leads him from untruth to truth, from the human to the divine, saying: "Here I pass from untruth to truth; I pass from the human to the divine; I restrain my speech. They remain for the night keeping him awake while he maintains silence.

With wood-shavings they kindle the fire that night. [The sacrificer recites: "Kindling the fire with wood-shavings, may I win both worlds; prospering in both worlds, may I cross over death. With this verse, he binds a spotted goat to the north of the Gārhapatya hearth. With it, he makes the fire about to be established look upon him [the goat], [reciting: "O Agni, cause the progeny and the quarters to dwell together with the cattle; bestow upon him the kingdoms that belonged to Savitṛ’s impulsion."

Then, at the latter part of the night, the Adhvaryu, having hastened there, heats the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) with the verse: "O Jātavedas, pour here the seed of the world, that which shall be born from fervor (*tapas*). Producing Agni, the bearer of oblations, from the *aśvattha* tree and from the womb of the *śamī*—he who is the source of bliss. "Here is thy seasonal womb, from which being born thou didst shine; knowing it, O Agni, ascend it, and then increase our wealth. Then, having placed this fire in a vessel, they sit to the south keeping it aflame.

Then he smears these fire-places with a lump of cow-dung. Then, taking a third portion of the ritual materials, he pours it out upon the site of the Gārhapatya fire with the formula: "That immortal essence of the earth which arose together with thee—that Agni gave to Agni; in that may this [fire] be established."

Wherever he goes to fetch fuel-sticks, he mutters: "Whatever black there was here in the moon, that too is here. Then he places them [on the fire] with: "With the vigor of heaven, with the greatness of earth, with the nourishment of the intermediate space—I place you, possessing all cattle. Then he mixes them together with: "I unite your hearts; may your minds be united; may your breath be united. Those bodies of yours which are dear, and your dear hearts—[may they be united]."

"May you be dear to me, and may my bodies be dear to you"—with these words he then arranges them: "May Heaven and Earth be in harmony; may the waters and plants be in harmony; may the fires, being of one vow, be in harmony separately for my preeminence—those fires which are of one mind between heaven and earth."

"May the two spring seasons, as they prepare themselves, enter [the fire] together, just as the gods enter Indra. Then, taking half of the remaining materials and carrying them out by the southern door, he pours them into the site of the *anvāhāryapacana* fire with the formula: "That immortal essence of the atmosphere which came into being together with thee—Vāyu gave that to Agni; may this [essence] be placed therein.
When he reaches the saline soil (*ūṣa*), he mutters: "Whatever black there is in the moon, let that also come here"; thus he places it.

He mixes it in such a manner and prepares it in such a manner; then, returning by the same way he came, taking the remaining materials and carrying them out by the eastern door, he pours them into the site of the Āhavanīya fire with the formula: "That immortal essence which arose from heaven in union with thee—that the Āditya gave to Agni; may this [essence] be placed therein.
Wherever he finds the saline soil (ūṣa), there he mutters: "Whatever blackness was here in the moon, that has come hither too."
He places [the butter] in that manner, he mixes it in that manner,
he prepares it in that manner; then he gives instructions to the guardian.

He says, "The fires have been distributed; let no one pass between them. Then the Adhvaryu, having turned to the right and hastened westward, places a nest of Muñja grass upon the materials at the site of the Gārhapatya fire. Having placed the lower churning stick (*araṇi*) upon it with its cutting edge facing westward, he places the upper churning stick (*uttarāraṇi*) with the *Daśahotṛ* formula.
He then says, "Churn!"
The sacrificer churns first; the sacrificer churns last;
he generates [the fire].

When [the child] is born, he utters the words, "I grant a boon," and then he worships him with the verse: "Mortals have brought forth the immortal, the tireless, the swift, the firm-jawed; may the ten unwedded sisters, moving together, grasp the newborn male. Then he breathes upon him: "With the breath of Prajāpati, I breathe upon you for the nourishment of Pūṣan, for my long life of a hundred autumns, for a hundred years of life, for vitality, for splendor, for living, and for merit."

"In breath I place you as immortality, as an eater of food for the sake of eating food, as a protector for protection"—having said this, he says to the Udgātṛ, "Recite the Rathantara," and then he places him.

"Bhūr bhuvaḥ! The Gharma is the head; may this Agni become dear to the cattle. Grant protection to our children and progeny. With the formula, "O Lord of Vows, I establish you with the vow of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases," he should establish [the fire] for those of the Bhṛgu and Aṅgira lineages. With the formula, "O Lord of Vows, I establish you with the vow of the Ādityas, the gods," [he establishes it] for other Brāhmaṇa subjects. With the formula, "O Lord of Vows, I establish you with the vow of King Varuṇa," [he establishes it] for a king. With the formula, "O Lord of Vows, I establish you with the power of Indra," [he establishes it] for a Rājanya.
"O Manu, O Grāmaṇī, O Vratapati, I establish you with the vow," [he says] for a Vaiśya;

"Of the Ṛbhus, of the gods, O Vratapati, I establish you with the vow," [he says] for a Rathakāra. According to the *ṛṣi* and according to the *gotra*, he throws a piece of gold to the north with the words, "With your own body, become united. Then he hands over this silver [piece] to a *vṛṣala* or an unknown person; "He hands over misfortune itself," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Then he worships him [the fire] with: "I am you; you are me. This is mine; this is yours. You are my womb; I am your womb. Being mine alone, O Agni, carry the oblations, O son, making the world for your father, O Jātavedas! With a good household-fire, burning away the enemies, bringing each dawn more auspicious than the last, O Agni, driving away our rivals, bestow upon us abundance of wealth, food, and vigor.
Then they take up this fire which has been gathered together in that vessel.

Having led it out by the southern door, he establishes the Anvāhāryapacana fire with the formula: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ! O Vāta, breath, may this Agni become dear to the cattle; cook the food, well-savored for our children and descendants. With the words, "O Lord of Vows, I establish thee by the vow of these gods," according to the Ṛṣi and according to the Gotra, and with the verse, "By the Gāyatrī metre," he throws a chip of gold to the north, saying, "Be united with thine own body. Then he hands over this silver [chip] to a Śūdra or an unknown person; "He hands over misfortune itself," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Alternatively, one establishes the Anvāhāryapacana fire from the Gārhapatya fire.

According to this Brāhmaṇa passage: "Prajāpati created Agni; he was afraid, thinking, 'He will burn me up. He divided his greatness into three parts for the sake of peace and to prevent burning. Then he stands before it [the Anvāhāryapacana] with the mantra: "May these riches come to me; may I dwell here together with these offspring."

"May Iḍā, the multiformed, stand here; shine in the midst of wealth, O Jātavedas! Having said this, he returns by the same way he came and places the fuel for the leading forward. He places it in such a way that he thinks: "The Āhavanīya fire will be established when the sun has half-risen."

When he has thus prepared himself, while they are arranging the supporting stones, this horse—already washed—is standing in front, facing eastward. Then he says to the Udgātṛ, "Recite the Vāmadevya! Then he lifts it up with the formula: "I lift thee for vigor, for strength; for manly power, for long life, for splendor! Thou art the overcomer of rivals, the overcomer of Vṛtra. That greatness of thine which is heavenly among the gods, that soul of thine which has entered into the cattle, and that prosperity of thine which has spread among men—with that, O Agni, come hither, being well-pleased."

"From heaven, from earth, from the intermediate space, from the wind, from the cattle, and from the plants—from wherever, O Jātavedas, you have come into being, from there, O Agni, come to us with favor. "He carries [the fire] a little further forward; then a little more, then a little more; he carries the head lower and lower," so says the Brāhmaṇa. "While taking it up, he should accomplish these measures"—this is another [instruction]. They lead the horse in front.

He addresses it with the mantra: "Go forward along the eastern quarter, O wise one; O Agni, be an Agni before us here. Shining forth, illuminate all the quarters; bestow strength upon our bipeds and quadrupeds. At the midpoint they stop, [saying]: "Stride out, for you are great; as the knower of the altar, be watchful for men in the three worlds. Then they approach, [reciting]: "Agni, the first Jātavedas, has looked toward the forefront of the dawns; he has looked toward the days."

"Following the many rays of the sun, he has extended across heaven and earth"—saying this, he makes the horse step forward from the north side onto the ritual materials, so that the embers of the fire already laid down may fall upon them; then, having turned it clockwise and sprinkled it with water, he releases it toward the north.

This [offering] belongs to the Adhvaryu; he gives another to the Brahman. Then, having turned to the right, he establishes the fuel (idhma) with the verse: "That which is of heaven, that which is of earth—may the two worlds, being in agreement, come together. Upon their back may Jātavedas sit, bringing welfare to offspring and being pleasant to the body. With the words, "I place you, the breath, in immortality; the eater of food for the sake of eating, the protector for the sake of protection," he then says to the Udgātṛ: "Sing the Bṛhat, the Vāravantīya, and the Śyaita! He issues all these directions.

While the *Bṛhatī* is being sung, he establishes the Āhavanīya fire with the formula: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! Arka is the eye; that is yonder sun, and that is this fire. May it become well-beloved by the cattle! O pure one, with that which is your pure luster, your pure body, your pure and imperishable light—with that shine for me; with that I establish you. O Agni, with Agni and with the sacred word (*brahman*), O Lord of Vows, I establish you by the vow of these gods."

According to the ṛṣi and according to the lineage, he throws a piece of gold to the north with the words, "With the Gāyatrī metre; be united with your own body. Then he hands over this silver [plate] to a Śūdra or an unknown person; "He hands over misfortune itself," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Then he worships it with the words, "I have attained; I have pervaded; I have pervaded a full lifespan. At this point, he establishes these two fires, the Sabhya and the Āvasathīya, and he rolls the chariot-wheel continuously from the Gārhapatya fire to the Āhavanīya fire.

At the New and Full Moon sacrifices, having appeased the fires with all kinds of herbs and the *vyāhṛtis*, he anoints five fuel-sticks each from various trees and places them on the fire with these five verses beginning, "Being kindled, he is the first law," omitting the verse, "O Agni, giver of life, enjoying the oblation. Then, having turned to the right and hastened westward, standing behind the *gārhapatya* fire, he worships with the "limbs" [verses]: "O Agni, those two auspicious forms of yours, the Virāj and the Svarāj—may they enter me; may they quicken me."

"O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Sovereign (*samrāj*) and the Overpowering (*abhibhū*), may they enter me; may they quicken me. O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Pervading (*vibhū*) and the Encompassing (*paribhū*), may they enter me; may they quicken me. O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Mighty (*prabhvī*) and the Abundant (*prabhūti*), may they enter me; may they quicken me. O Agni, with those auspicious bodies of yours, I establish you"—with all [these formulas] he establishes the *gārhapatya* fire, with all the *anvāhāryapacana*, and with all the *āhavanīya*.

Then he assigns the terrible forms: "O Agni, with those forms of yours which are terrible, go to so-and-so. At this point, he meditates in his mind upon him whom the sacrificer hates. Then, having touched water, he worships with the Virāj-krama formulas at the Gārhapatya fire:
"O manly one, protect my offspring for the sake of immortality and life—those born and those yet to be born—established in immortality and truth."

"O Atharvan, protect my food; protect the essence, the nourishment here for the sake of long life—O you of unerring life-force, O you of cool body, making the food free from poison," [with these words] he addresses the Anvāhāryapacana fire. "Be auspicious; protect my cattle—those that are two-footed and those that are four-footed, O Agni, those here with eight hooves and those that are one-hoofed and swift-moving," [with these words] he addresses the Āhavanīya fire. "O wide-extending one, protect my assembly hall; and those who are members of the assembly, those sitting in the assembly—make them full of sensory power; may they sit through a full span of life," [with these words] he addresses the Sabhya fire.

"O lowest one, protect my mantra, which the seers who know the three Vedas know—the *ṛc*s, the *sāmans*, and the *yajus*s; for that is the immortal glory of the virtuous. Thus [concluding] the *āvasathīya* rite.

Then, at the *gārhapatya* fire, having melted the clarified butter and purified it, and having taken four portions into the offering-spoon (*sruc*), he offers a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the *āhavanīya* fire while it contains a fuel-stick, with the verse: "Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues..."

At the *pūrṇāhuti*, he grants a boon; then he sets down these cleansed *agnihotra* vessels to the north of the *gārhapatya* fire—either on a grass-mat or on a wooden chopping-block—namely, the pot together with the dipping-spoon (*srava*), the offering-ladle (*sruk*), the fire-brand for lighting, and the fuel-stick. Then, having stationed the *agnihotrī* cow to the south facing north, a Brāhmaṇa milks her.

"One should milk the two front [cows], one should milk the two rear; one should not touch them together; one should milk two for one desiring cattle"—having thus placed [the milk] on the fire, he brings in the latter [portion]; then, having carried this *agnihotra* around the front of the *āhavanīya*, having brought it in through the eastern door, and having set it down behind the *gārhapatya*, he performs the ritual procedure for the *agnihotra* therein, and having offered a kindling-stick, he carries it forward toward the east.

He places it near the Āhavanīya fire on a grass-bunch; he then silently places this fuel-stick in the middle of the Āhavanīya. When it has caught fire, he makes two offerings facing it, wiping upwards and wiping downwards, for the Brāhmaṇa says, "He obtains both. Having twice tasted [the ghee] with his finger and having turned toward the north, he consumes [the remainder] from the ladle whose handle points eastward.
Having washed the ladle, heated it, and filled it with water, he pours it out toward the north.

"He gratifies the Seven Seers indeed," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Having offered the oblation, he adds fuel for the sake of kindling spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). He pours out water; "He has made it the form of the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*)," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Then he sends a servant to fetch sacrificial grass, or he prepares it with a Yajus formula. Then, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and led forward the waters, when about to offer the cake on eight potsherds for Agni, he should recite the Daśahotṛ formula.
When about to recite the *sāmidhenī* verses, he should recite the Daśahotṛ formula.
Having cooked [the oblation], he sets it down;

for this [offering] there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, five *prayāja*s, and two *vārtraghna* *ājyabhāga*s; furthermore, the two *saṃyājyā*s for the principal oblation are the two *triṣṭubh* verses beginning with "Agni is the head" (*agnirmūrdhā*) and "He has become" (*bhuvaḥ*).

Having placed the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) for the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*); he gives them up to twelve, or he may give more at his will. This sacrifice is concluded with the pouring out of the full vessel and the *viṣṇukrama* steps.
He releases his vow;

then, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and led forward the waters, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra-Agni and a pap for Aditi. This pap for Aditi is prepared in ghee; when the milk has nearly boiled, he pours in the clarified butter.
Having cooked [the oblation], he sets it down.

For this sacrifice, there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, five *prayāja* offerings, and two *ājyabhāga* offerings dedicated to Vṛtra-slayers. Then, for the two principal oblations: "Indrāgnī rocanā divaḥ" and "śnathadvṛtram" are for the offering to Indra and Agni; "aditir na uruṣyatu" and "mahīm ū ṣu mātaram" are the two *triṣṭubh* *saṃyājyā* verses for the offering to Aditi.
Having set down the *anvāhārya* rice and having drawn out this *caru*, four *ārṣeya* priests consume it;
"He offers in the very light of the quarters," so says the Brāhmaṇa. This sacrifice concludes with the *pūrṇapātra* and the *viṣṇukrama* steps;
he releases his vow.
Thereupon he observes this vow for twelve days;
his vow is this: he speaks no untruth, nor does he eat meat.
He does not approach a woman; they do not wash his clothes by means of washing; he drinks from vessels other than those made of clay; he does not become defiled by the food-leavings of a Śūdra;
and he washes his own feet himself.
He does not eat salt nor *kauśī* grain, except for sesame;
before the morning excretion, he himself brings fuel and lies down at the edge of the fires; these fires remain unextinguished for him for twelve days.

No Brahmin who has not fasted dwells in his house; or rather, the sacrificer becomes one whose vow consists of the remnants of the *agnihotra*. His wife brings him food. Then, when twelve [nights] have dawned, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhya* line and having carried forward the waters, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pavamāna;
having cooked it, he places it down.

For this [offering], there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, five *prayāja*s, and the two *ājyabhāga*s are the *vārtraghna* hymns; for the oblation, the two *saṃyājyā*s are the two *triṣṭubh* verses, "O Agni, you purify our lives" (*agna āyūṃṣi pava-se*) and "O Agni, purify yourself" (*agne pavasva*).
Having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives gold weighing thirty *māna*s.
This sacrifice concludes with the *pūrṇapātra* and the *viṣṇukrama* steps;
he releases his vow.
Then, at that very moment, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the waters, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pāvaka and to Agni Śuci.
Having cooked [the oblation], he sets it down.

For this [offering], there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, five *prayāja* offerings, and two *ājyabhāga* portions dedicated to Vṛtrahan. Then, for the two principal oblations (*havis*), the invitatory and offering verses (*saṃyājye*) are the two *triṣṭubh*s: "O Agni, the Purifier" (*agne pāvaka*) and "May that Agni, the Purifier" (*sa naḥ pāvaka*), and "O Agni, most pure in thy vows" (*udagne śucayas tava*).
Having placed the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives away gold weighing thirty *mānas* and forty *mānas*. This sacrifice concludes with the pouring out of the full vessel and the *Viṣṇu-strides*;
he releases his vow.

Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the *anvārambha* (the taking hold from behind). He performs the *anvārambha* of the full-moon sacrifice so that the fast-day (*upavasatha*) is common to both. Then, in the morning, after the *agnihotra* has been offered and before the carrying forward of the waters, he melts clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire, purifies it, takes four portions into the *sruva*-ladle, and, having mentally recited the *caturhotṛ* formula, offers it into the *āhavanīya* while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, saying "Svāhā!
Having taken another four portions, he offers the two *sārasvata* oblations.

Having run through the verse, "Full in the west," he offers with the formula, "O Agni and Soma. Having taken another fourfold portion of clarified butter and having run through the verse, "The establisher, the gatherer of riches," he offers with the formula, "That portion which the gods assigned to you. Then, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, having carried forward the waters, he pours out an oblation on eleven potsherds for Agni-Viṣṇu, a pap for Sarasvatī, and an oblation on twelve potsherds for Sarasvant;
having cooked them, he places them down.

For this [offering], there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, five *prayāja*s, and two *ājyabhāga*s dedicated to Vṛtra-slayers; then for the oblations, the two *saṃyājyā* verses are in the *triṣṭubh* meter: "O Agni-Viṣṇu," "O Agni-Viṣṇu," "Forward for us," "O Goddess," "From heaven," "The swelling one," "Of Sarasvat," and "Those waves of yours, O Sarasvat. Having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives a pair of cattle as a gift.
This sacrifice concludes with the *pūrṇapātra* and the *viṣṇukrama* steps;
he releases his vow and then performs the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha sacrifices.
The establishment of the fires (agnyādheya) is concluded; the establishment of the fires is concluded.

One who is about to re-establish the fires (punarādheya) becomes one who has already performed the sacrificial formulas (kṛtayajus) and gathered the materials (saṃbhṛtasaṃbhāra). Regarding this, they say: "The materials need not be gathered, nor should the sacrificial formulas be performed. However, on the other hand, the materials must indeed be gathered and the sacrificial formulas for the re-establishment must be performed, for the sake of its successful completion.

He prepares a repaired chariot, a mended garment, a bull that has been let loose again, a nest of *darbha* grass, three *darbha*-made rings for the fingers, and the well-known ritual materials required for the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*).
That new-moon day which occurs before the full moon of the month of Āṣāḍha coincides with the *punarvasu* constellation once a year; on that day he should establish the fires.

On the day of preparation for that [sacrifice], having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇī*), having gone down, having churned out the fires, and having spread them out, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and one on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara, intending to extinguish the fire. That well-known sacrifice is completed. Then, at that very moment, having sprinkled the fires with water and cooked the *brahmaudana* (the Brahmin’s rice-porridge), he observes the fast. Then, in the morning, the ritual of the establishment of the fires (*āgnyādheya*) is commenced; it is exactly the same, except that what was there a nest of *muñja* grass is here a nest of *darbha* grass, and what was there the fuel for the leading forward of the fire is here rings made of *darbha* grass.

He establishes the Gārhapatya fire with *darbha* grass, the Anvāhāryapacana fire with *darbha* grass, and the Āhavanīya fire with *darbha* grass. At the establishment of the fires, he recites the *Sarparājñī* verses beginning with "The earth by its abundance, the sky by its expanse" over the Gārhapatya; four of these are recited over the Gārhapatya and three over the Āhavanīya. The ritual procedure up to the chariot wheel is the same; only this much differs.
That which was the silent *agnihotra* there, here one offers with the verse, "Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues.
That which was the eight-potsherd offering to Agni there, here it is a five-potsherd offering to Agni;

into its *prayāja* offerings he places four case-endings: "O Agni, come for the feast," "O Agni, let the fuel-sticks partake of the clarified butter," "We choose Agni as the messenger," "Let Tanūnapāt, O Agni, partake of the clarified butter," "By Agni is Agni kindled," "O Agni, let the *iḍā*-invocations partake of the clarified butter," "May Agni slay the Vṛtras," and "O Agni, let the sacrificial grass partake of the clarified butter."
The first fore-offering (*prayāja*) is naturally accomplished as the best. Now, therefore, follows the deliberation regarding the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*).
Some say the two butter-portions should be those containing the word "slayer of Vṛtra" (*vārtraghna*);

some say they should be those containing the word "increasing" (*vṛdhanvat*). Some say these two should be: "Awaken Agni with a hymn" (*agnim stomena bodhaya*) and "O Soma, you [are] for us" (*tvaṃ naḥ soma*); some say these two should be: "O Agni, you purify our lives" (*agne āyūṃṣi pava se*) and "O Agni, purify yourself" (*agne pavasva*).

That which is the *pavamāna* is the form of Soma; [he recites] "O Agni, bring that today" and "For you, O Agni," and then, with the verses "Again with vigor" and "Together with wealth," he offers two oblations on both sides of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). He pronounces the *sviṣṭakṛt* formula over the fire, and recites the two *saṃyājyā* verses: "Today for you... and "With these our hymns...";
then, having placed the *anvāhārya* rice, he proceeds.

He gives the sacrificial fee for the re-establishment of the fires: a repaired chariot, a mended garment, and an ox that has been let loose again. At its *anūyāja* offerings, he inserts two *vibhakti* verses: "The mortal who, through his thoughts and prayers, has enjoyed the service of Agni—may he, being foremost, grant us food for our protection. "May the divine *barhis* accept the gift at the winning of wealth; may it partake of the treasury of riches. O Agni, we meditate upon the effective hymn today, reaching unto heaven.
May the divine Narāśamsa, seeking wealth, partake of the treasury of riches at the winning of wealth. The final *anūyāja* is performed spontaneously.
This sacrifice concludes with the *pūrṇapātra* and the *viṣṇukrama* steps;
he releases his vow.
Then, at that very moment, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, he causes water to be brought forward and subsequently offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Varuṇa.
Having cooked it, he places it [on the altar].

For this [offering], there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, five *prayāja* offerings, and two *ājyabhāga* portions dedicated to Vṛtrahan; furthermore, the two *saṃyājyā* verses for the oblation are the two *triṣṭubh* verses beginning with "tvaṃ no agne" and "sa tvaṃ no agne."

Having placed the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives a bull as a gift; this sacrifice concludes with the *pūrṇapātra* and the *viṣṇukrama* steps. He releases the vow, and the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*) is completed.

Thus, indeed, [concerning] the *vṛddhi* and the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*). Now it is said: "He who establishes the fire after the time for the *punarādheya* has passed should offer these oblations."

At the third establishment of the fires, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of the five-potsherd cake for Agni, he offers oblations with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), saying: "Leka, Saleka, Suleka—may those Ādityas, enjoying the clarified butter, partake of it, Svāhā! Keta, Saketa, Suketa—may those Ādityas, enjoying the clarified butter, partake of it, Svāhā! Vivasvant, Aditi, Devajūti—may those Ādityas, enjoying the clarified butter, partake of it, Svāhā! Thus the third establishment of the fires is concluded;
then, for one whose fires have been carried away or whose kindling-wood (*araṇī*) has been lost, he proceeds by means of the *brahmaudana* alone.
The establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*) is successful.

Having kindled the *gārhapatya* fire before sunset and having brought the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, he draws out the flaming *āhavanīya* for the evening oblation. Having kindled the *gārhapatya* fire before sunrise and having brought the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, he draws out the flaming *āhavanīya* for the morning oblation.

With speech as the Hotṛ, with breath as the Udgātṛ, with the eye as the Adhvaryu, with the mind as the Brahman, and with the ear as the Agnīdh—by means of these five divine officiating priests, I lift you up. *Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ*, being lifted up, lift me up from evil! Whatever I have done unknowingly or knowingly, whatever sin has been committed by day, from all that, being lifted up, release me! Thus at evening. "Whatever sin has been committed by night, from all that, being lifted up, release me! Thus at dawn.

He places the fire: "I offer the immortal oblation into the immortal; I offer Agni upon the earth for the winning of immortality. Through that, may we win from here our endless desire, which Prajāpati won first. I offer immortality into Agni Vaiśvānara, Svāhā!"—thus at evening. "I offer immortality into Sūrya, into Agni Vaiśvānara, Svāhā!"—thus in the morning.
In this manner, the wife attends the fire both at evening and in the morning.

"In the evening, in the evening," say some; then he sets down these washed Agnihotra vessels to the north of the Gārhapatya fire—either on a grass-mat or on a wooden board—the pot together with the dipping-spoon (sruva), the offering-ladle (sruk), the fire-lighter, and the fuel-stick. Then, having stationed the Agnihotra cow to the south facing north, a Brāhmaṇa milks her.

One should milk the two front [cows] for the eldest son of the eldest wife, or for one who has attained prosperity; one should milk the two rear [cows] for the youngest son of the youngest wife, or for one who desires to thrive. One should not touch [the two milks together]. For one desiring cattle, one should milk both. Having placed [the vessel] over the fire, he brings the upper [milk] into it. Then, having carried this Agnihotra around the front of the Āhavanīya, having brought it in through the eastern door, and having set it down behind the Gārhapatya, he then sprinkles it, saying at evening:
"I sprinkle thee, the Right, with Truth. Thus he sprinkles at evening.

"Truly, I sprinkle you with truth," he says; having offered in this same manner in the morning, he sprinkles [the coals]. Then, having turned clockwise, having run back toward the west, and having sat down behind the Gārhapatya fire, he draws out the embers toward the north, makes them separate, places the vessel upon them, and illuminates it with a lighted stick, saying, "May your brilliance not burn me.
With the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), he pours water over it, saying, "Thou art immortality.
Having illuminated it once more, he carries fire around it three times, saying, "The Rakṣas is enclosed; the enemies are enclosed."

Having prepared the path and carried [the fire] out toward the north, and having pushed back the embers, he takes up the *sruva* spoon with his right hand and the fuel-stick (*samidh*) with his left, and the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle with his left hand, saying: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee."

He heats [the ladle] over the *gārhapatya* fire, saying: "The *rakṣas* is burnt away; the enemies are burnt away. Then, having placed the *sruk* on the grass-bundle (*kūrca*), he addresses the sacrificer: "Om, I shall draw up [the butter]; Om, draw it up," and the sacrificer gives his permission. Then he draws up four spoonfuls, either full or not full, saying: "Much is the *iḍā*, the *iḍā* of the earth; much is the *iḍā*, the *iḍā* of the mid-air; much is the *iḍā*, the *iḍā* of heaven; much is the *iḍā* of the earth, mid-air, and heaven. Having set the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) back into the vessel, he then touches them both together, saying at evening: "In harmony with the gods who go at evening, may the gods who go at evening lead me safely across with cattle. At morning, he says: "In harmony with the gods who go at morning... (and so on).
"In harmony with the gods who come at dawn, may the gods who come at dawn convey me safely with my cattle.

At this point, having taken hold of this fuel-stick on the handle of the offering-ladle, he places it behind the Gārhapatya fire on a grass-mat, saying: "Homage to Īśāna! May my progeny and cattle increase; may I, the sacrificer, not come to harm."

Having hurried up from the *daśahotr* formula, he carries it eastward, saying: "Bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, suvaḥ! O Urū, follow the intermediate space! This is the wide path leading to the gods, by which the seers desiring heaven went; by that I go to the highest firmament, so that I may not be separated from the presence of those who have performed good deeds.

He places it down behind the *āhavanīya* fire on a grass-bunch, saying: "Homage to the Lord! May my progeny increase; may I, the sacrificer, not come to harm. At this point, he places a fuel-stick in the middle of the *āhavanīya*.

"I place you, the silver-colored, whose light is fire, who possesses the wind, who leads to heaven—the imperishable brick, the night—for the sake of the heavenly world. I place immortality in my breath; may Prajāpati settle you. With this, he performs the *tayādevata* rite: "By that deity, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, sit firm! Then he performs the *sūdadohas* rite: "These dappled cows, yielding milk for him, mix the Soma; they are the clans of the gods at their birth, in the three luminous realms of heaven. Thus [he recites] at evening.

Then in the morning, [with the formula] "Thee, the tawny one, with the light of the sun, accompanied by Vāyu, leading to heaven, for the sake of the heavenly world, I place as a brick that is uninjured; I place immortality in my out-breathing; may Prajāpati settle thee," he places it.
Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he performs the *sūdadohas* verse.
When it has been kindled, he offers oblations facing it, saying at evening: "Agni is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā!"
"Sūryo jyotir jyotir agniḥ svāhā" at dawn—this is the combined formula;
then the uncombined: "Agnir jyotir jyotir agniḥ svāhā" in the evening, and "Sūryo jyotir jyotiḥ sūryaḥ svāhā" at dawn.

Then, having once lifted the *sruk* over the *kūrca* and placed it down, he turns to the right and gazes at the *gārhapatya* fire, saying: "Come hither, come together; let not the portion of those who have a share be lost."

"May the world of the Seven Seers, where their good deeds reside, support this sacrifice and the sacrificer here"—having said this, he offers the second oblation after the first, kindling the fire more intensely with the formula, "To Prajāpati, svāhā! mentally. Then, having moved the spoon three times beyond [the fire], he places it on the grass-bunch (kūrca), wipes it downward, and with his hand turned westward and downward, he wipes off the residue upon the plants with the formula, "For the plants, thee! Refresh the plants! In the same way, having wiped it a second time, he wipes it off upon the plants. To the south, wearing the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he wipes it off toward the west with the formula, "For the fathers, thee! Refresh the fathers!"—this is for the evening.

Then, in the morning, having wiped upwards, he wipes the smear from the herbs with his palm turned upwards, saying, "From the herbs, thee; quicken the herbs. Having wiped downwards in the same manner a second time, he wipes it down upon the herbs themselves, saying, "For the fathers, thee; quicken the fathers," while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) toward the south. Then, having touched water, he eats twice with his finger, saying, "Progeny, light. Then, having turned toward the north, he consumes [the remainder] with the ladle whose handle points eastward.

"May this oblation be productive for me, with ten heroes, with all my kin, for well-being; may it win me self, offspring, cattle, safety, the world, and rain. May Agni make my progeny abundant; may you bestow upon us food, milk, and seed; may he maintain for us the increase of wealth, nourishment, and vigor—Svāhā! Thus at evening. At dawn, [he says]: "May Sūrya make my progeny abundant.
Having wiped the ladle, heated it, and filled it with water, he pours it out toward the north, saying: "Gladden the Seven Seers! Quicken the Seven Seers! Svāhā to the Seven Seers!"

"He thereby gratifies the Seven Seers," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Then, behind the Gārhapatya fire, he pours out water, saying: "Here I offer immortality into Agni Vaiśvānara, Svāhā!"; "In the imperishable, I offer an imperishable oblation, Svāhā! He pours it out within the sacrificial altar. Having offered and kindled [the fire], he says: "He has made it a kindling of spiritual luster. "He pours out water; he has thus made it the form of the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha)," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Then, when the evening *agnihotra* has been offered, having put on the sacrificial cord (*yajñopavīta*) and sipped water, standing in the sacrificer’s place, he worships the *āhavanīya* fire with the six verses beginning with "upaprayanto adhvaram," each according to its meter; and with the next six verses addressed to Agni-Pavamāna, he worships the *āhavanīya* itself: "O Agni, thou purifiest our lives," "O Agni, purify," "O Agni, the Purifier," "May Agni, the most pure in his vows, [purify us]," and "O Agni, thy purifiers [are bright]."

Then he worships the Āhavanīya fire with: "O Agni, you are the giver of life; give me life. O Agni, you are the giver of splendor; give me splendor. O Agni, you are the protector of the body; protect my body. O Agni, whatever is deficient in my body, fill that up for me. Then he worships the night with: "O Citrāvasu, may I reach your end in safety. Then he places a fuel-stick on the Āhavanīya fire with: "Kindling you, may we kindle you for a hundred winters—resplendent, full of vigor, bestowing vigor, glorious, bestowing glory, and possessing excellent heroes, O invincible one."

"O Agni, the subduer of rivals, upon the highest firmament, Svāhā!"—having said this, he worships the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra: "O Agni, you have united with the splendor of the Sun, with the praise of the Ṛṣis, and with your beloved abode. You, O Agni, possess the splendor of the Sun; unite me with long life, splendor, and progeny. Now it is indeed said:

"Just as a man, a horse, or a cow grows old, so does the fire, once established, grow old. After a year has passed, one should worship it with the *Āgnipāvamānī* verses. Thus, after a year has passed, he worships the Gārhapatya fire with the *Āgnipāvamānī* verses.
"He makes him new again and ageless," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Then he pays homage to the houses and the cattle: "I behold the offspring, the human progeny of Iḍā; may they all remain in our house. You are water; may I partake of your water. You are greatness; may I partake of your greatness. You are power; may I partake of your power. You are vigor; may I partake of your vigor. O wealthy ones, rejoice in this world, in this cow-pen, in this dwelling, in this womb. Stay right here; do not depart from us. May you become many for me."

Then he touches the calf of the Agnihotrī cow with the formula: "Thou art united, possessing all forms; come to me with vigor, with abundance of cattle, and with increase of wealth. May I thrive in your thousandfold prosperity; may your riches rest within me. Then he worships the Gārhapatya fire with two-footed and three-footed verses: "O Agni, day by day, we approach thee with prayer, O thou who dwellest in the darkness, bringing homage. Shining in thine own abode, the ruler of sacrifices, the guardian of the Eternal Law, the radiant one, ever increasing."

"O Agni, be easy of access to us like a father to his son; attend to us for our well-being. O Agni, be our closest relative, our protector, and our auspicious shelter. To you, O most radiant and shining one, we now pray for the sake of our friends' welfare. Agni, the Vasu of renowned wealth, come hither as the most glorious one; grant us riches! Having said this, he then pays homage to both the houses and the cattle.

"With vigor I behold you; behold me with vigor. With the increase of wealth I behold you; behold me with the increase of wealth. You are *iḍā*s, honey-makers; enter me, being pleasant and intoxicating. May I thrive through your thousandfold prosperity; may your riches rest upon me. Then he worships the Āhavanīya fire with: "We meditate upon that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he impel our prayers. Thus he worships the Āhavanīya itself: "O Brahmaṇaspati, make Soma the one who brings forth light."

"Kakṣīvantaṃ ya auśijam"—with these words he worships the Night: "Never art thou barren, O Indra; never dost thou fail the donor. More and more, O Maghavan, may thy divine gift be increased. Then he worships the Gārhapatya fire: "O Agni, we set thee around us as a fortress, thee the wise one, O powerful one—thou of bold hue, day by day, the breaker of the treacherous."

Then he worships the Gārhapatya fire with the formula: "O Agni, lord of the house, may I be a good lord of the house through you as my lord of the house; may you be a good lord of the house through me as your lord of the house. For a hundred winters, I invoke this blessing for myself and for N.N.; I invoke that radiant blessing for N.N., for N.N."—he mentions as many sons as have been born to him, ending with the word "progeny" (*tantavaḥ*). Now it is said: "He who worships the fire facing it directly consumes it; he who worships turning away from it is deprived of offspring and cattle. He should worship so as to be somewhat turned aside."

He approaches from the side, neither facing toward nor away from [the fire], as he is about to perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. He prepares: sacrificial grass (barhis) cut in a single stroke, darbha blades for the strewn covering, rice grains, a winnowing basket, a washed mortar and pestle, a cooking pot, a dipping-spoon (sruva) together with a stirring-stick (mekṣaṇa), a mat of eraka grass and a pillow, ointment and unguent, a fringe of cloth, a wooden sword (sphya), a water-pot, and the sacrificial implements; then he strews grass around the Anvāhāryapacana fire.

To the north of that, he places each item one by one: a mattress of *eraka* grass, ointment and oil for anointing, a fringe, the wooden sword (*sphya*), a water-pot, and the sacrificial implements. Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) and sitting behind the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, he pours out rice grains into a pot containing two strainers, either with the formula, "I pour you out, acceptable to the ancestors," or silently. Having placed the lower and upper millstones on this very skin and set down the mortar and pestle, he threshes [the grain] only once.
