Then, facing south, having separated these [grains], he pours water into this very pot across the strainer, places it over the fire, and pours the rice grains into it across the strainer.

Then he pours out the clarified butter and places the clarified butter on the fire; having carried fire around both, he cleanses the stirring-ladle and the dipping-spoon. Then, having cooked this sacrificial porridge and poured the clarified butter over it, he removes it from the fire toward the north. Then, having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder and having kindled the Anvāhāryapacana fire, he offers three oblations, taking portions with the stirring-ladle, saying: "To Soma, drunk by the fathers, svadhā! Adoration! Svāhā! To Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the fathers, svadhā! Adoration! Svāhā! To Agni Kavyavāhana, the maker of good offerings, svadhā! Adoration! Svāhā!"—this in the eastern part of the southern half of the fire.

Having silently placed the stirring-stick (mekṣaṇa) on the fire, having arranged the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta), having dug up the earth to the south of the Anvāhāryapacana fire with the wooden sword (sphya) and sprinkled it with water, and having spread sacrificial grass (barhis) with its tips pointing southward, he purifies [the site] with water, saying: "May the fathers be purified; may the grandfathers be purified; may the great-grandfathers be purified. Then, with the dipping-spoon (sruva), he offers three balls of rice (piṇḍas), each underlaid and overlaid with clarified butter, saying: "This for you, O father, N.N., and for those who follow you; this for you, O grandfather, N.N., and for those who follow you; this for you, O great-grandfather, N.N., and for those who follow you."
Having said, "O fathers, following you, rejoice according to your respective portions," he turns toward the north and waits until the steam has subsided;
for they say, "The steam has subsided. Then, having turned back, he smells this sacrificial porridge (caru), saying:

"Those fathers who are equal and of one mind in the realm of Yama—for them is the world, *svadhā*, and homage; may the sacrifice be prepared among the gods. Those kinsmen of mine who are living among the living, equal and of one mind..."

"May their prosperity be ordained for me in this world for a hundred years"—having said this, he then purifies them with water in the same manner, saying: "May the fathers purify themselves; may the grandfathers purify themselves; may the great-grandfathers purify themselves. Then he gives collyrium, saying: "May the fathers apply collyrium; may the grandfathers apply collyrium; may the great-grandfathers apply collyrium. Then he gives ointment, saying: "May the fathers anoint themselves; may the grandfathers anoint themselves; may the great-grandfathers anoint themselves."

Then he gives them garments, saying: "O fathers, these are your garments; O grandfathers, these are your garments; O great-grandfathers, these are your garments. According to the Brāhmaṇa, [the rule is]: "One should have his hair cut when in the latter part of life."

Then one attends upon the reversal with six salutations: "Homage to you, O fathers, for the sap; homage to you, O fathers, for the vigor; homage to you, O fathers, for the life; homage to you, O fathers, for the *svadhā* offering; homage to you, O fathers, for the wrath; homage to you, O fathers, for the terrible [power]. O fathers, homage to you who abide in this world—may they follow you! O fathers, homage to you who abide in that world—may I follow you! O fathers, homage to you who abide in this world—may you be the most excellent among them! O fathers, homage to you who abide in that world—may I be the most excellent among them!"

"May I become like Vasiṣṭha," he says, and then he entreats the hero: "O Fathers, give me a hero; O Grandfathers, give me a hero; O Great-Grandfathers, give me a hero. May I be possessed of fathers through you; may you be possessed of good offspring through me. Then he causes them to rise: "Arise, O Fathers, go forth, O heroes, along the ancient path of Yama."

"May he bestow upon us wealth and that which is auspicious; may he declare us as sharers among the deities. Then he dismisses them: "May the fathers go to their respective worlds with the speed of thought; depart, O Soma-loving fathers, by the deep, ancient paths!"

Then [he recites], "The well-disposed fathers who rejoice in the company of Yama. Then he invokes the mind with three verses: "We invoke the mind hither; let the mind come back to us again; O fathers, give us back our mind. At this point, he throws these rice-balls together with the sacrificial grass (barhis) into the fire. Then they take up two of each of those implements. Having put on the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavīta), he worships the Gārhapatya fire with the verse addressed to Prajāpati: "O Prajāpati, none other than you... At this point, he mutters this second verse: "That which is in the atmosphere, on earth, and in heaven..."
The Piṇḍapitṛyajña is concluded.

During the rainy season, one who intends to perform the Āgrayaṇa offering of Śyāmāka grains has its well-known Upavasatha day. Then, in the morning, after the Agnihotra has been offered, having strewn the Pṛṣṭhyā line and having carried forward the waters, he offers a pap of Śyāmāka grains dedicated to Soma.

Having released his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviskṛt*), he melts the clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire, purifies it, takes four spoonfuls into the offering-ladle (*sruc*), and offers the *ājyānī* oblations into the *āhavanīya* fire with the verse beginning, "To him of a hundred weapons, of a hundred powers... Having cooked five [portions], he sets them down.

For this [offering], there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, five *prayāja* offerings, and the two *ājyabhāga* portions belong to the Vṛtra-slaying deities; then the oblation [is offered] with the verses, "Swell up" (*āpyāyasva*) and "Be united" (*saṃ ta*).
The two *saṃyājyā* verses are in the *triṣṭubh* metre.

Having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives a garment as a gift; then he eats the sacrificer’s portion with the mantra: "May Agni eat first, for he knows how the oblation is; may he, who beholds all people, make the plants auspicious for us.
This sacrifice concludes with the pouring out of the full vessel and the *viṣṇukrama* steps; [the sacrificer] releases his vow.

Now, when one is about to perform the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice of rice in autumn, its *upavasatha* day is well known. Then, in the morning, after the *Agnihotra* has been offered, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the waters, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni, a pap for the Viśve Devas, and a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth.

Having released his speech with the words "The oblations have been offered," he melts the clarified butter over the *Gārhapatya* fire, purifies it, takes four portions into the ladle, and offers the *ājyānī* oblations into the *Āhavanīya* fire with the five verses beginning, "To him who has a hundred weapons, a hundred powers..."
Having cooked [the oblation], he sets it down.

For this [offering], there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, five *prayāja*s, and two *ājyabhāga*s dedicated to Vṛtra-slayers; then for the oblations: "Indra and Agni, the luminaries of heaven... is for the offering to Indra and Agni; "The All-gods, the All-gods... is for the offering to the Viśve Devās.
"May Heaven and Earth, the first-born parents," [he says]; these two *triṣṭubh* verses are the *saṃyājyās* for the offering to Heaven and Earth.

Having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives away the first-born calf; then he eats his portion of the sacrifice with the mantra: "O gods, you have led us from good to better; through you as our protection, may we attain prosperity. Enter us, O food, as a source of delight; be auspicious to our offspring and pleasant to our bodies."
This sacrifice concludes with the *pūrṇapātra* libation and the *viṣṇukrama* steps; he then releases his vow.
Now, when it is springtime and he intends to perform the *āgrayaṇa* offering of barley, its *upavasatha* day is well known.

The ritual procedure is the same as that for the *vrīhyāgrayaṇa*, with this much difference: he eats the sacrificer’s portion [with the mantra], "They have ploughed this barley, mixed with honey, upon the bank of the Sarasvatī; Indra, the lord of a hundred powers, was the master of the plough, and the Maruts, the givers of good gifts, were the ploughmen.
This sacrifice concludes with the pouring out of the full-vessel and the *viṣṇukrama* steps; he releases his vow.

One who is about to go on a journey [from his fires] puts on the sacrificial cord (*yajñopavītin*), sips water, circumambulates the *āhavanīya* fire from the front, and, standing in the sacrificer’s station, worships the *āhavanīya*: "O Jātavedas, that name which my father and mother first gave me at birth—bear that for me until we meet again; O Agni, I shall bear your name. Then, restraining his speech, he departs; he releases his speech only when out of the vicinity of the fires. He stays away sleeping on the ground, eating meat, and approaching women;
he does not stay away for more than twelve nights.

Without entering the sacrificial hall, he prepares the fuel-sticks on the road while returning; having looked back at the fires, he restrains his speech and worships only the Āhavanīya fire with the verse: "O Jātavedas, our names and yours, as we move about like two people putting on garments, let us exchange them again for the sake of long life and living, each according to its proper place."

Then he worships the Gārhapatya fire: "Homage to Agni the unpierced, homage to the unassailable, homage to the sovereign! Agni is invincible, of great fame, all-conquering, triumphant, the most excellent Gandharva. Then he worships the Anvāhāryapacana fire: "O Agni, from you come the fathers, the gods, the oblations, and the utterances; unite me with long life, unite me with lordship, and establish me in well-being. Then he worships the Āhavanīya fire:
"This Agni is the most excellent, this is the most blessed, this is the best winner of a thousandfold; may there be for me heroic strength through him."

If they report to him a failure in the sacrifice, saying, "He has not offered," then, having melted clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire and purified it, and having taken four ladlefuls into the *sruc*, he offers the *saṃtanī* oblation in the *āhavanīya* with the mantra: "May the mind, as light, enjoy the clarified butter; may it join together this interrupted sacrifice. Those dawns and those sunsets that have been sacrificed—those I unite with the oblation of ghee, *svāhā*. Then he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tantumat, and gives a shallow earthen bowl (*śarāva*) as the sacrificial fee.

That [offering] concludes with the established formula; then he offers expiations for those [verses] that have been omitted. For by this means, indeed, the ancient Vedic scholars who were seekers of truth, desiring splendor, desiring fame, and desiring holy luster, used to perform the worship.

But that practice has fallen into disuse because of the excessive weight of the vow. Now, therefore, follows the worship according to the Vairāja [metre]: "O Manly One, protect my offspring"—with these words he worships the Gārhapatya fire;
"O Atharvan, protect my food"—with these words the Anvāhāryapacana fire; "Be auspicious, protect my cattle"—with these words the Āhavanīya fire.
"O wide-extending one, protect my assembly," [with this he addresses] the member of the assembly;
"O abyss-dwelling one, protect my counsel," [with this he addresses] the member of the household. He travels abroad for an indefinite period.
Upon returning, on the path, he prepares fuel-sticks. Having looked back at the fires, he restrains his speech. Having arrived, he pays reverence with this very same formula.
The expiation is the same.

Then, on the day of the Upavasatha, having put on the sacrificial cord (yajñopavītin), having sipped water, having gone around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, and having sat down in the sacrificer’s place, he sips water across the strainer, [reciting]: "The plants are full of sap; the sap of the plants is full of sap."

"O Indra, unite me with that essence which is the essence of the essence of the waters. Then he places fuel-sticks on the Āhavanīya fire, saying: "O Agni, Lord of Vows, I shall perform the vow; may I be able to do it, may it be successful for me, Svāhā! O Vāyu, Lord of Vows! O Āditya, Lord of Vows! O Lord of Vows among vows, I shall perform the vow; may I be able to do it, may it be successful for me, Svāhā! Then, on the following day, he addresses the sacrificial oblation as it is being poured out: "I invoke here Agni the Hotṛ; we invoke here the gods who are worthy of sacrifice."

"May the gods come with benevolent minds; may the gods depart from my oblation"—having uttered this, he restrains his speech until the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*); having released his speech at the call for the preparer of the oblation, he yokes the sacrifice with the formula: "Who yokes you? May He yoke you. At the proper time, he yokes the potsherds with the verse: "The potsherds which the wise ones pile up upon the *gharma*, those belong to Pūṣan in his vow; O Indra and Vāyu, yoke them!"

Of those [verses] made into *yajus*-formulas, whatever is broken, he throws that onto the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), saying: "Unbroken is the Gharma, the swift-giver; from where it was taken, thither has it gone again."

Then, having melted the clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire, purified it, and taken four portions into the ladle, he offers the *saṃtanī* oblation into the *āhavanīya* fire with the mantra: "The fuel, the altar, and all the enclosing sticks follow the life of the sacrifice. To those thirty-three threads who have stretched them out and who sustain this sacrifice with their own power—to them I offer this nourishment, Svāhā! Then he releases another [ladle] with the words, "May the Gharma reach the gods. Now it is indeed said: "If it should be lost, he should offer a cake on two potsherds to the Aśvins and one on a single potsherd to Heaven and Earth."

That well-known sacrifice is concluded; then, in the same manner, having melted the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire and purified it, and having taken four portions in the ladle, he offers the *saṃtanī* oblation in the Āhavanīya fire with [the verse]: "The fuel, the altar, and all the enclosing sticks follow the life-span of the sacrifice."

"Those thirty-three threads which have been stretched out, who by their own power sustain this sacrifice—for them I restore what has been cut; Svāhā! Then he lets another [thread] go forth with the formula, "May the Gharma go to the gods. Now, if anything of the clarified butter or the Sāṃnāyya spills elsewhere than on the sacrificial grass before the final fore-offering, he collects its essence with the formula:
"I pour thee together with the Yajus for progeny, long life, and wealth; impelled by Bṛhaspati, may the sacrificer not suffer harm here."

He consecrates the spilled [ghee] with: "To the Lord of the Earth, svāhā! To the Lord of the World, svāhā! To the Lord of Beings, svāhā! Then, having proceeded with whatever remains, he causes the sacrificer to look at the clarified butter (ājya) with: "Thou art ghee; thou art truth; thou art the overseer of truth; thou art the oblation; thou art Vaiśvānara, belonging to all the gods, with purified vigor, possessing true power. Thou art force; thou art overcoming; overcome the enemies, overcome those who act as enemies; overcome the hostile armies, overcome those who attack us. Thou art of thousandfold heroism; may that [heroism] be mine."
"Quicken! You are the essence of the clarified butter; you are the truth of truth; you are the life-span of truth; you are the vigor of truth. With truth I sprinkle you. May I partake of you.

Then, as each portion of the clarified butter is taken, he consecrates it with four formulas over the *juhū* ladle: "I take you for the restraint and support of the five winds; I take you for the restraint and support of the five seasons; I take you for the restraint and support of the five directions; I take you for the restraint and support of the five peoples."

"With eight [verses] I take for you from the *upabhṛt* ladle; for the restraint and support of the five-holed [sacrificial post], I take you; for the splendor and restraint of the *brahman*, I take you; for the vigor and restraint of the *kṣatra*, I take you; for the people and their restraint, I take you; for heroic power I take you; for good offspring I take you; for the increase of wealth I take you; for spiritual luster I take you."

With the four [verses], "Firm is the earth for us; our oblation is for the gods, the blessings for the sacrificer," he consecrates the vessel as it is being filled with, "I take thee for the deities of the gods. He consecrates the enclosing-sticks as they are being laid around with, "I take thee for desire.

He consecrates the middle enclosing-stick with, "Thou art firm; may I be firm among my kinsmen, wise, perceiving, and a finder of wealth. He consecrates the southern one with, "Thou art fierce; may I be fierce among my kinsmen, fierce, perceiving, and a finder of wealth."
"Thou art the conqueror; may I be the conqueror among my kinsmen, a conqueror, a perceiver, and a finder of wealth"—with these words he recites the subsequent [verse].
Then he yokes the fire with a formula: "I yoke thee with the divine prayer for this oblation to be carried, O Jātavedas."

While the two fuel-sticks are being placed upon the fire, he mutters: "Kindling thee, may we live long with good offspring and brave sons, bringing tribute to thee. Then, within the altar, he consecrates the oblations that have been set down: "O Agni, whatever of this sacrifice of mine may be injured, or whatever of the clarified butter may spill, O Viṣṇu—with that I slay the ill-fated rival; I place him in the lap of Destruction. Then, with the *vyāhṛtis*—"Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ"—he should set down the *agnihotra* offering. For the *agnihotra* is the mouth of the sacrifice, and these *vyāhṛtis* are the Brahman; thus he places the Brahman at the very mouth of the sacrifice.
"When the year has come around, he should set them down with these very [syllables]; thus he encloses the year on both sides by means of the Brahman," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said:

"One who is about to perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices should set down the oblations with these *vyāhṛtis*; for the New and Full Moon sacrifices are the mouth of the sacrifice, and these *vyāhṛtis* are the Brahman; thus he places the Brahman at the very mouth of the sacrifice."

"When the year has come around, he should set them down with these very [formulas]; verily, by means of the Brahman, he encloses the year on both sides," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is indeed said: "One who is about to perform the Cāturmāsyas should set down the oblations with these *vyāhṛtis*; for the Cāturmāsyas are the mouth of the sacrifice, and these *vyāhṛtis* are the Brahman; thus he places the Brahman at the very mouth of the sacrifice."
"When the year has come around, he should set them down with these very [verses]; thus, by means of the Brahman, he encompasses the year on both sides," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Now, it is further said: "Whatever part of the sacrifice is performed with a Sāman, the blessing of that sacrifice goes to the ruling class (rāṣṭra); whatever part is performed with a Ṛc, the blessing of that sacrifice goes to the common people (viś). Thus, the Brāhmaṇa performs the sacrifice with that which lacks a blessing."
When about to recite the *sāmidhenī* verses, one should place these *vyāhṛti*s at the beginning; thus one makes the *brahman* itself the introductory step (*pratipad*).
"In this way, the Brāhmaṇa sacrifices with a sacrifice that possesses a blessing," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is also said:

"If one should desire, 'May the blessing of this sacrifice go to the sacrificer's rival,' he should place these *vyāhṛtis* in the *puro'nuvākyā*; for the *puro'nuvākyā* has the rival as its deity, and thus the blessing of his sacrifice goes to the rival—so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, there is also this [further teaching]:

"If one should desire, 'May the blessing of the sacrifice reach all these sacrificers equally,' he should place one of these *vyāhṛtis* at the half-verse of the *puro'nuvākyā*, one before the *yājyā*, and one at the half-verse of the *yājyā*;
thus the blessing of the sacrifice reaches them equally," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, furthermore, it is said:

"Just as Parjanya, when well-rainfed, pours down rain, so does the sacrifice pour down blessings for the sacrificer; just as they enclose water on dry land, so does the sacrificer enclose the sacrifice with his prayer"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. He begins with the *vyāhṛtis* for a Brāhmaṇa, with the *hiṅkāra* for a Rājanya, and with a *ṛc* for a Vaiśya; however, one may perform all three of these. He then consecrates the fuel being placed upon the fire with a mantra.

"O Agni, be one who withers for the sacrificer; be one who withers for him who assails us. O Agni, kindled by the gods, kindled by the mind, sweet-tongued!"—with these words he addresses the Pravara as it is being invoked. "I sprinkle upon your head, O immortal Hotṛ, for the increase of wealth, for good progeny, and for heroic vigor"—with these words he addresses the Āghāra-libation as it is being poured with the *sruva*-ladle. "You are the mind belonging to Prajāpati; enter me with the mind and with existence."

He consecrates the *āghāra* libation being poured with the mantra: "Thou art speech, belonging to Indra, the destroyer of rivals; enter me with speech and with power. He consecrates each of the *prayāja* offerings as they are offered with the formulas: "Of the seasons, I gratify the spring; may it, being gratified, gratify me. Of the seasons, I gratify the summer; may it, being gratified, gratify me. Of the seasons, I gratify the rains; may they, being gratified, gratify me. Of the seasons, I gratify the autumn; may it, being gratified, gratify me. Of the seasons, I gratify the winter and the cool season; may they, being gratified, gratify me."

He consecrates the two portions of clarified butter that have been offered with the formula: "Through the sacrifice to the gods Agni and Soma, may I become possessed of sight. He consecrates the offering to Agni that has been made with the formula: "Through the sacrifice to the god Agni, may I become an eater of food. He consecrates the Upāṃśuyāja offering that has been made with the formula: "Thou art a deceiver; may I be undeceived; may I deceive so-and-so," at which point he meditates in his mind upon whomever the sacrificer hates. Then, having touched water, he consecrates the two offerings to Agni and Soma that have been made with the formula: "Through the sacrifice to the gods Agni and Soma, may I be a slayer of Vṛtra. [Then the offering] to Indra...

He consecrates the offering to Agni with: "Through the sacrifice to the god Indra-Agni, may I become possessed of power and an eater of food. He consecrates the offering to Indra with: "Through the sacrifice to the god Indra, may I become possessed of power.
He consecrates the offering to Mahendra with: "Through the sacrifice to the god Mahendra, may I attain victory and greatness.
He consecrates the offering to Sviṣṭakṛt Agni with: "Through the sacrifice to the god Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, may I, long-lived, attain a firm foundation through this sacrifice."

While the *prāśitra* is being cut off, he mutters: "May Agni protect me from ill-performed rites; may Savitṛ protect me from evil intent. Regarding the portion belonging to the sacrificer, he says: "Whoever near or afar acts as an enemy, may I conquer him with this. As the *iḍā* is being brought forward, he addresses it, beginning with "O thou of beautiful form and rain-like color, come! and continuing with "O bountiful one. Then, while the intermediate *iḍā* is being consumed, he addresses it: "Thou art delight; delight us; thou art delightful to us; may I attain thy delight. Then, within the altar, he purifies himself with water, [reciting]: "May the mind, the light, enjoy the clarified butter; may it join together this severed sacrifice."

"Bṛhaspati protect this for us; may all the gods rejoice here"—with these words he consecrates the *puroḍāśa* cake placed upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). "O radiant one, swell; may there be no depletion for me who gives; may there be no exhaustion for me who acts"—with these words he then requests the *anvāhārya* rice, and when it has been set down within the altar (*antarvedi*), he consecrates it until the end of the section: "Thou art the portion of Prajāpati, full of vigor, full of milk."

He consecrates each *anūyāja* offering as it is offered: "Through the sacrifice to the gods, may I be rich in offspring by means of the *barhis*; through the sacrifice to the gods, may I be rich in cattle by means of the *narāśaṃsa*; through the sacrifice to the gods, may I, long-lived, attain a firm foundation by means of the *agni sviṣṭakṛt*. Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ's recitation, "Agni has enjoyed this oblation," he makes the sacrificer recite the formula for victory: "May I follow Agni’s victory with my own. The spreading apart of the two *vājavatī* verses is performed according to the specific desire expressed.

Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ saying, "This sacrificer, so-and-so, desires," he causes the sacrificer to recite the milking of the sacrifice: "These blessings have come, desiring to be milked; accompanied by Indra, may we win them; may we milk offspring and food.

He then addresses the *prastara* being thrown into the fire with the mantra: "May Agni cause you to go to the deity by means of the ruddy horse; may Indra cause you to go to the deity by means of the two bay horses; may Sūrya cause you to go to the deity by means of the dappled horse."

He addresses the enclosing-sticks as they are being released: "I loosen your cords, I loosen the reins, I loosen the thongs and whatever fastenings there are. Bestow upon us wealth and that which is auspicious; declare us as sharers among the deities.
He addresses the *śaṃyuvāka* when it has been recited: "Through the sacrifice and the worship of the gods, may I attain a firm foundation in the peace of Viṣṇu.
He addresses each of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings as it is offered.

"Through the sacrifice to the god Soma, may I, possessing good seed, deposit seed; through the sacrifice to the god Tvaṣṭṛ, may I nourish the form of cattle. Then he combines the other two [portions] with the formula: "The bird of the gods, Agni the lord of the house, is the pair of the sacrifice; through the sacrifice to these two gods, may I prosper by means of that pair.
At the Veda [bundle of grass], he causes the sacrificer to recite from the beginning of the section until its end: "Thou art the Veda; thou art acquisition; may I acquire."

He recites the mantra over the *dhruvā* ladle while it is being replenished: "May the *dhruvā* be replenished with clarified butter for each sacrifice performed by those seeking the gods; she is the udder of Sūryā, the lap of Aditi, the wide-streaming Earth in this sacrifice. Then he consumes the sacrificer’s portion, saying: "Prajāpati’s world is named Vibhān; in that I place you, together with the sacrificer," or "The lord of the sacrifice has attained his blessing. At this point, he asks for the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*).

Having placed that [vessel] within the altar (antarvedi), he makes the sacrificer recite over the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*): "In the assembly, may you be mine; you are everything, may you be everything for me. You are full, may you be full for me. You are imperishable, may you not perish for me. Then he distributes [the water] toward the quarters: "May the gods and the officiating priests purify themselves in the eastern quarter; may the months and the ancestors purify themselves in the southern quarter; may the houses and the cattle purify themselves in the western quarter; may the waters, the plants, and the trees purify themselves in the northern quarter; [may they purify themselves] in the upward quarter."

"In the direction, let the sacrifice, the year, and the lord of the sacrifice purify themselves"—with these words he pours out the water. "I send you forth to the ocean; being inexhaustible, go back to your own source. May I be unimpaired in my offspring; may your milk not be spilled from me.
Then, having risen, he strides the Viṣṇu-strides with his right foot, reciting four verses according to their meters, the fourth following after the third:

"Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of the adversary; with the Gāyatrī meter, I stride across the earth. He whom we hate is excluded. Thus he strides with the four verses, one after another in order of their meters.

He does not step toward the fourth [quarter], nor does he pass beyond the Āhavanīya fire; rather, standing right there, he worships the Āhavanīya with: "We have gone to heaven; we have gone to the light of heaven. Do not cut me off from your sight; do not destroy me for that heat of yours. Then he worships the Sun with: "Thou art well-being, the best of rays; thou art the bestower of life, bestow life upon me; thou art the bestower of luster, bestow luster upon me. Then he banishes his rival from these worlds, saying: "Here I banish this rival from these quarters, from this sky, from this atmosphere, from this earth..."
"From this earth, from food, I exclude him; excluded is he whom we hate," and then, having touched water.

With the words, "May I be united with light," he touches his chest toward himself; then he turns around to the right, saying, "May Indra turn me back"; then he turns toward the north, saying, "May I be united with offspring, and may offspring be united with me; may I be united with the increase of wealth, and may the increase of wealth be united with me. Then he places a fuel-stick on the Āhavanīya fire, saying, "O Agni, being kindled, shine for me; may I, as your kindler, shine, Svāhā! Then he stands in worship before the Āhavanīya, saying, "The sacrifice is wealthy."

"May I become more prosperous," he thinks; then he worships the Gārhapatya fire with two *pāvamānī* verses addressed to Agni: "O Agni, you purify our lives" (*agna āyūm̐ṣi pavase*) and "O Agni, purify yourself" (*agne pavasva*). Then he worships the Gārhapatya again: "O Agni, lord of the house, may I become a good lord of the house through you as my lord of the house; may you become a good lord of the house through me as your lord of the house for a hundred winters. He invokes this blessing: "For me, for so-and-so, I invoke that luminous blessing; for so-and-so, for so-and-so," naming as many of his sons as have been born, ending finally with the word "progeny" (*tantavaḥ*). Now, indeed, there is this [text]:

"He who, having yoked the sacrifice, does not release it, indeed becomes without a firm foundation. With the words, "Who yokes you? May he release you," he releases the potsherds at the proper time. "The potsherds which the wise ones collect for the *gharma*—may Pūṣan and Indra-Vāyu release them according to their vow. Then, having returned by the same way he came and sat down in the sacrificer's place, he sips water across the filter in the same manner: "The plants are full of milk; the milk of the creepers is full of milk."

"Whatever essence is in the essence of the waters, with that, O Indra, unite me"—having said this, he places fuel-sticks on the Āhavanīya fire, saying: "O Agni, Lord of Vows, I have performed the vow; I was able to do it; it has been successful for me, Svāhā! O Vāyu, Lord of Vows! O Āditya, Lord of Vows! O Lord of Vows among vows, I have performed the vow; I was able to do it; it has been successful for me, Svāhā! Then, having stood up, he mutters the formula for the re-attainment of the sacrifice: "The sacrifice came into being; it has come into being; it was born; it has grown."

"He became the lord of the gods; may he make us lords. May we be masters of riches. Then, having stepped forward toward the east, he mutters: "O Agni, may this sacrifice be rich in cattle, rich in sheep, rich in horses, possessed of manly friends, ever unassailable, rich in *iḍā*, O Asura, rich in progeny, long-lasting wealth, broad-based, and possessed of an assembly. Then he issues the command: "Let him satisfy the Brāhmaṇas!"

Intending to perform the duties of the Brahman priest, having put on the sacrificial cord (*yajñopavīta*), sipped water, and walked around the front of the *āhavanīya* fire, he stands to the south facing north and approaches the seat of the Brahman priest with the formula: "Homage to Brahman! Homage to the seat of the Brahman! Then, from the seat, he throws away a blade of grass with the formula: "O son of two wives, go away; sit on the seat of another who is more foolish than we. He sits down with the formula: "May I go up from the low ground and up from the high ground. Then he looks at these two [the earth and the sky] with the formula: "Protect me today, O Heaven and Earth. Having sat down, he mutters the following.

Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Suvaḥ! Who shall be the Brahman here? He shall be the Brahman here. I am joined with Prāṇa, the Lord of Creatures; I am yoked with the Brahman, like a swift steed well-yoked to the pole, like a draft-ox yoked for the journey. I shall carry the oblation to the deities. Bhūr, I take refuge in; Bhuvaḥ, I take refuge in; Suvaḥ, I take refuge in; Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ, I take refuge in. I take refuge in Vāyu; I take refuge in the Brahman; I take refuge in the Kṣatra; I take refuge in the unbreakable stone.
"I take refuge in the Brahman-treasury of Prajāpati; I take refuge in the deity Speech, which is free from affliction; I take refuge in *Oṃ*.

With these words, the sacrificer chooses the Brahman priest, saying: "O Lord of the earth, O Lord of the world, O Lord of the great Being, we choose you as the Brahman; as the domestic priest for the one whose oblations are accepted, by whom the Aṅgirasas, the gods, went to the highest heaven, to the sky."

Chosen, the Brahman priest mutters: "I am the lord of the earth; I am the lord of the world; I am the lord of the great being. Impelled by the god Savitṛ, I shall perform the office of the officiating priest. You have chosen me as the Brahman, as the domestic chaplain at the Vītahavya sacrifice, by whom the Aṅgirases, the gods, went to the highest heaven. O god Savitṛ, they choose you here as Bṛhaspati, the divine Brahman. That I declare to the mind; the mind to the Gāyatrī; the Gāyatrī to the Triṣṭubh; the Triṣṭubh to the Jagatī."

In the world, the *anuṣṭubh* [verse] is for the *anuṣṭubh* [meter]; the *paṅkti* is for the *paṅkti*; Prajāpati is for Prajāpati; the Viśvedevas are for the Viśvedevas; Bṛhaspati is for Bṛhaspati; the Brahman is for the Brahman; "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ"—Bṛhaspati is the Brahman of the gods, and I am the Brahman of men. "O Bṛhaspati, protect the sacrifice. When he says, "O Brahman, I shall lead forward the waters; O sacrificer, restrain your speech," then the Brahman gives the impulse.

"O God Savitṛ, lead forward the sacrifice; prosper these deities. May the sacrificer be on the back of the firmament, in the world of heaven. Where the world of the Seven Seers who have performed good deeds is, there place this sacrifice and the sacrificer—Om, lead forward! He remains restrained in speech while the *praṇītā* waters are being led forward, until the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*).

When the *sāṃnāyya* milk is being milked, he then says: "May she yield much milk for Indra, for the gods, the oblation"—or "for Mahendra," if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra. He restrains his speech at the time of pouring [the grain] until the placing of the potsherds (*kapāla*).
He restrains his speech during the pouring [of the grains] until the covering [of the altar];

while the *stambayajus* is being carried away, he restrains it until the placing of the *prokṣaṇī* waters. When the Adhvaryu says, "O Brahman, I shall perform the second tracing of the altar," then the Brahman gives the impulse: "O Bṛhaspati, enclose the altar; with the sacred word (*brahman*), enclose this sacrifice. Where the world of the seven seers who have performed good deeds is, there place this sacrifice and the sacrificer—*oṃ*, enclose it! He restrains his speech while the clarified butter (*ājya*) is being taken up, until the placing of the *dhruvā* ladle.
While the *sāmidhenī* verses are being recited, from the time of the *pravara* invocation until the *puro’nuvākyā* has been recited, until the *vaṣaṭ*-call,

and while the *prāśitra* portion is being cut off, they carry it for him up to the signal for the oblation; he gazes upon that *prāśitra* as it is being carried along the front of the *āhavanīya* fire.
"I behold you with the eye of the Sun," he says; then he receives it with both hands, saying, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, I receive you with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan.

Then he sets it down, saying, "I set you down on the navel of the Earth. Then he gazes at it, saying, "I gaze upon you with the eye of Suparṇa Garutman. Then, grasping it with his thumb and ring finger, he places it first beyond the teeth and then on the tip of his tongue, saying, "I consume you with the mouth of Agni."

Having consumed [the portion] and sipped water, he swallows it down together with water, saying: "With the belly of Bṛhaspati, the Brahman. Then, having sprinkled himself with water, he touches his vital organs (prāṇas), saying: "Speech in my mouth; breath in my nostrils; sight in my eyes; hearing in my ears; strength in my arms; vigor in my thighs; may all my limbs be unharmed; may my body be with my body; homage be unto you; do not harm me! Or [he says]: "In me are the breaths, in me are the breaths. He places the consumed portion of the *brahmabhāga* in the *prāśitraharaṇa* vessel. Then he asks for the *anvāhārya* rice;
once it has been placed within the altar (*antarvedi*), he addresses it with a mantra.

"O Brahman, you are the Brahman; homage to you, O Brahman! Protect me, the Brahman, from the unoffered today; may everything be offered for me. Then, having cut off a portion as large as [the thumb], he places it in the *prāśitraharaṇa* vessel with the formula: "Thou art glory; come to me; may I become possessed of food and an eater of food. Then, as it is being led northward in front of the ladles, he addresses it with the mantra: "May the sacrifice ascend to heaven; may the sacrifice go to heaven; by that path which leads to the gods, may the sacrifice reach the gods."

When he says, "O Brahman, we shall set forth; having placed the fuel-stick, O Agnīdh, cleanse the fires once each," then the Brahman gives the impulse: "O God Savitṛ, you have announced this to him; impel it and sacrifice it! Bṛhaspati is the Brahman; protect the sacrifice, protect the lord of the sacrifice, protect me! Om, stand firm!"—thus he proceeds in the Pravargya rite.

He remains right there until the offering of the *samiṣṭayajus*. Once the *samiṣṭayajus* has been offered, he rises and stands in worship before the *āhavanīya* fire, reciting: "Jātavedas has carried the sacrifice of the oblation; undeceived, he has sat down first at its end. Granting gain after gain, release us with a good release. Bestow upon us wealth, O Jātavedas, and whatever is auspicious.
By this very [formula], he becomes the Brahman priest for the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Cāturmāsya offerings, the animal sacrifice, and the Sautrāmaṇī.
Having set out the oblations, he addresses the Hotṛ.

Wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder and having sipped water, he rubs his two hands together with the formula: "For the work of you two, for the gods, may I be able; for the power of you two, for the good deed of you two. Then, with two verses, he takes Agni into himself: "I take Agni first into myself; that Agni who is ours... Then he enters between the altar (vedi) and the rubbish-heap (utkara), saying: "I enter Truth; I enter Order; I enter Immortality; I enter the dear, uninjured body of Prajāpati. With this fifteenfold thunderbolt, [I strike] my enemy..."

"I step upon my rival, whoever hates us and whomsoever we hate; Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Suvaḥ, I stand in the station of Viṣṇu"—having spoken thus, he steps with his right forefoot across to the northern edge of the altar and stands there.

When he hears, "Recite for Agni as he is being kindled," then he mutters this *hautra* formula: "I take refuge in Ka; I take refuge in him. That meter which is your shelter, O Prajāpati, in that I take refuge. As much as I know of you, O Viṣṇu, so much shall I perform. Impelled by the god Savitṛ, I shall perform the office of the officiating priest. Homage to Agni, the overseer; homage to Vāyu, the listener; homage to Āditya, the beholder. Today may I utter speech that is pleasing to the gods and worthy of being heard by men."

"Full of *svadhā* for the ancestors, a firm foundation for every being—*bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. O Praśāstṛ, through myself, my offspring, and my cattle, I take refuge in Prajāpati; may there be safety for me. I shall recite the *prājāpatya* [section]; I take refuge in speech; speech shall perform the office of the *ṛtvij*. For glory, for splendor, for power, for prosperity—may the sacrifice and the sacrificer grant great protection!
Having uttered the *abhihiṅkāra* three times here, he joins the next verse without interruption from the *abhihiṅkāra*:
"Forward your strengths, reaching toward heaven"—he recites this first verse three times.

Having recited the final verse three times, he breathes out the entire *sāmidhenī* formula verse by half-verse. After the verses have been recited, he invokes the deities and, having made a span-measure on the ground, sits down, saying: "With the Gāyatrī metre, with the Trivṛt stoma, with the Rathantara Sāman, with the Vaṣaṭ-call as a thunderbolt, I drive away my hateful rival; the hateful one is driven away.
He remains sitting while looking at the Āhavanīya fire, or between the two fires, or he looks at them while saying "lead" or "bring"; thus, he is born from this [fire] without being timid.

When he knows [the response], he mutters: "Agni the god is the Hotṛ. Then he recites: "O God Savitṛ, they choose you here for the Agnihotra, together with your father Vaiśvānara. Then, having stood up, he takes hold of the Adhvaryu on his right shoulder with his right hand, and the Āgnīdhra on his right shoulder with his left hand; or, if he himself responds to the call, he should take hold of him on the right hip, saying: "We take hold of Agni, the domestic priest at the choosing of the Hotṛ, by whom the gods and the Aṅgirases went to the highest heaven, to the sky."

"O gods among gods, exert your prowess! Let the first ones [be victorious] over the second, the second over the third; you eleven, seize them together! Then he announces his name to the Adhvaryu, turns toward the southern shoulder of the altar, saying, "May Indra turn me back," and then, while proceeding toward the Hotṛ’s seat, he mutters:

"May the six wide ones protect me with joy: heaven and earth, day and night, water and plants; may they guard me, may they protect me; homage to them! Then he throws away a blade of grass—either dry or one with its tip broken off—at the junction of the south and the west, saying, "The *parāvasu* is cast out. Then, having touched water and having spread [grass] underneath, he sits down, saying, "I sit here in the seat of Arvāvasu. He sits with his right foot uppermost. Then, turning to the right, he gazes at the *gārhapatya* fire.

"O Viśvakarman, you are the protector of bodies; protect my body," with these words they both look at the Āhavanīya fire. "O Agni and Viṣṇu, may we not step upon you; leave what remains of your vigor; do not burn me; O makers of space, create a place for me—this indeed is your place. With this, he creeps slightly toward the north. Then he mutters three verses: "O All-Gods, instruct me how, having been chosen as the Hotṛ priest here and having sat down, I may think [the ritual]; tell me clearly my share, so that by which path I may carry the oblation to you."

May I today utter that first word by which we gods may overcome the Asuras. O eaters of strength, worthy of sacrifice, you five peoples, enjoy my oblation! Homage to the great, homage to the small, homage to the young, homage to the old! Let us sacrifice to the gods if we are able; may I not fall away from the peace of the elder gods. Thus [he says].

Then, having caused the two offering-spoons to be taken up by means of the *srugādāpana* formula, he sacrifices the oblation according to the respective deity. Then follows the consecration of the *vaṣaṭ*-calls: "O *vaṣaṭ*-call, do not choose me away; I invoke you with the great mind through Mātariśvan. Do not take away my breaths; carry my speech as an oblation to the gods. Might, force, force—might! Speech!
If, however, the *vaṣaṭ*-calls are very close together, he consecrates them with this much alone: "Might, force, force—might! Speech! Then he anoints the Hotṛ's fingers twice.
He wipes what was previously mentioned onto his upper lip with the formula: "I consume thee, offered to Vācaspati, for food and for out-breathing.
He wipes it onto his lower lip with the formula: "I consume thee, offered to Sadasaspati, for strength and for in-breathing.
Then, having touched water, he causes the *iḍā* to be cut four times; with an open hand, not closed, he invokes the *iḍā*, held level with his mouth.

The Rathantara has been invoked together with the earth, together with Agni, together with food, and together with speech; may the Rathantara invoke me together with the earth, together with Agni, together with food, and together with speech. The Vāmadevya has been invoked together with the intermediate space, together with Vāyu, together with breath, and together with cattle; may the Vāmadevya invoke me together with the intermediate space, together with Vāyu, together with breath, and together with cattle. The Bṛhat has been invoked together with heaven, together with Āditya, and together with sight; may the Bṛhat invoke me together with heaven, together with Āditya, and together with sight.
The stationary world has been invited; let the stationary world invite me.
The moving world has been invited; let the moving world invite me.
The seven officiating priests have been invited; let the seven officiating priests invite me.
The cows have been invited together with the food; may the milch-cow with the bull invite me.
The milch-cow with the bull has been invited; may the milch-cow with the bull invite me.
Ida and rain have been invited; may Ida and rain invite me.

"The food has been invited; may the friend, the food, invite me as a friend. Having uttered this invitation, he invites [the *iḍā*] loudly and with articulated speech: "The *iḍā* has been invited; O thou who art invoked, do thou enjoy me, O *iḍā*!

Now, if he intends to eat the whole [of the *iḍā*], he should first eat the portions placed in his hand and then eat from the cup itself. But if he intends either to give it away or to set it aside, he should cut off a piece of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and eat it, saying: "Thou art the *iḍā*; thou art pleasant; thou art the maker of pleasantness. Bestow upon us abundance of wealth and good offspring. For the glory of my face and for the fragrance of my mouth, I eat thee."

Having consumed [the remnants] and sipped water, he pours out a line of water toward the east or the north, silently; for this is indeed the rule regarding the clarified butter. Then he mutters this prayer: "May the mind, as light, enjoy the clarified butter;

may it join together this severed sacrifice. May Bṛhaspati extend this for us; may all the gods rejoice here. Having performed the after-offerings (*anūyāja*) and uttered the *śaṃyuvāka*, he makes a hollowed gesture (*añjali*) upon the sacrificial grass and performs the expiation: "O Sacrifice, welfare be mine and prosperity be mine! O Prajāpati, O Sacrifice, whatever in thee is deficient and whatever in thee is redundant—whatever rite of thine, O Sacrifice, is in Prajāpati, let that be so."
Then, having placed the *veda* grass-bundle on the southern half of the altar, he causes the sacrificer to recite:

"O divine *veda*, by that means through which you became a *veda* for the gods, by that means become a *veda* for us! You are the *veda*; you are acquisition; may I acquire offspring, cattle, and the heavenly world. You are action; you are compassion; may I perform meritorious action. You are gain; you are the winner; may I win this. May the *veda* grant me wealth—abounding in ghee, providing a home, nourishing, thousandfold, and vigorous."

Having performed the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings and having offered the *phalīkaraṇa* oblation, he makes the wife recite over the *veda* grass-bundle: "Thou art the *veda*, thou art acquisition; may I acquire that. Thou art action, thou art compassion; may I perform that action. Thou art gain, thou art the gainer; may I gain that. May the *veda* grant me prosperity of wealth, thousandfold, full of ghee, nest-like, and vigorous.
Having untied the *veda*, he gives half of it to the wife;
she either places it between her thighs or holds it with her right thigh.

Then, turning toward the east and spreading the other [grass-blades], he goes forward with the mantra: "Stretching the thread, follow the light of the mid-region; guard the paths of light prepared by wisdom; weave them out without flaw for the singers; be a Manu and generate the divine folk. Then, having thrown those blades which remain onto the *barhis* grass with the mantra: "Thou art the filler; fill me with offspring and cattle," he goes out by the way he entered, circumambulates the Āhavanīya fire from the front, and stands to the south.

Standing facing north, he worships the Āhavanīya fire with this verse: "Jātavedas has carried the sacrifice of the oblation, undeceived, seated first within it. Granting gain after gain, release us with a good release. Bestow upon us wealth, O Jātavedas, and whatever is auspicious. By this prayer, O Agni, grow strong—whether by our power or by what we have done through knowledge. Lead us toward greater prosperity; unite us with your benevolence that brings strength."

"O Varuṇa, those hundred and those thousand great sacrificial bonds that are spread out—may Agni, Indra, Bṛhaspati, the Viśvedevas, and the Maruts of beautiful praise release us from them. These indeed are the recitations for the New and Full Moon sacrifices, for the Cāturmāsya offerings, for the animal sacrifice, and for the Sautrāmaṇī.
Now, they are placed upon the altar at the animal sacrifice.

When he knows [the signal] "Recite for the fire being churned," then he mutters these two verses: "Whatever vows of yours we may violate, Whatever, being simple-minded and weak-willed, Mortals do not perceive in the sacrifice— May Agni, the Hotṛ who knows the ritual, The most skilled sacrificer, worship the gods in due season. With the words, "The cows chose you for kingship; the Maruts, chanting beautiful hymns, call upon you. Seated at the height, at the peak of dominion, from there, O fierce one, distribute wealth to us," the Adhvaryu makes the sacrificer recite this over the staff of the Maitrāvaruṇa.
Taking it by the front, he hands it to the Maitrāvaruṇa with the formula, "I hand you over by the command of Mitra and Varuṇa, the two directors.

He receives it from the thick end with the formula, "I receive you by the command of Mitra and Varuṇa, the two directors. Holding it with the right hand above, he wipes it upward with the formula, "May I be straight and not crooked.
Taking it, he issues the direction: "Let the Hotṛ worship Agni, well-kindled with a good kindling-stick—thus for the end of the fuel of the animal sacrifice."
One who is about to sacrifice with an animal victim prepares:

enclosing-sticks of *pūtudru* wood, bdellium, fragrant *tejana* wood, a tuft of white wool from between the horns of a ram, two ropes—one double-stranded and one triple-stranded, two omentum-spits—one forked and one unforked—a heart-spike, enclosing-sticks made of *kārṣmarya* wood, a staff for the Maitrāvaruṇa priest made of *udumbara* wood reaching up to his mouth, sacrificial fuel and grass, fuel for the fire to be led forward, a branch of the *plakṣa* tree, a vessel for the *iḍā*-portion, barley-flour from barley-bearing fields for the sake of an offering of flour.

[He prepares] curds for the speckled butter and gold; then, having sacrificed with the New Moon oblation or under a [favorable] lunar mansion, he melts the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire, purifies it, and taking four portions in the ladle, he offers it in the Āhavanīya fire while mentally reciting the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ formula, as the sacrificer maintains contact with him, saying "Svāhā! Having taken another four portions, he offers the oblation for the sacrificial post (*yūpāhuti*) with the verse: "O Viṣṇu, stride out widely; grant us ample space for our dwelling."

"O you whose source is ghee, drink the ghee; further extend the lord of the sacrifice—svāhā! Having taken another fourfold portion of ghee, he then requests the vessel of clarified butter together with the dipping-spoon, the sacrificial grass, gold, and a water-vessel. They call for the carpenter with his axe, saying, "Come, O sacrificer! Having gone out by the eastern door, they proceed in that direction where his sacrificial post (yūpa) is visible, or where he thinks he will find it.

He approaches that tree which grows on level ground from its own womb, having many leaves and many branches, with unshriveled tips, and leaning toward the west: "I have passed beyond others, I have not approached others; I have found you on this side of those beyond, and beyond those on this side. You, the one belonging to Viṣṇu, I choose for the sacrifice to the gods. Then he anoints it with clarified butter, saying, "May the god Savitṛ anoint you with honey. He raises the sacrificial grass (barhis) with its tip pointing upward, saying, "O plant, protect him!
With the axe, he strikes it across, saying, "O axe, do not harm him!"

The first chip that falls away, he sets it down in a known place. Without splitting it, he cuts a branch that has no knots, either facing east or north as it moves forward. He consecrates it with the mantra: "Do not scratch the sky with your tip; do not injure the mid-air with your middle; be united with the earth. Then, having placed gold upon the cutting-block and strewn grass around it, he makes an offering over it with: "O Lord of the Forest, grow forth with a hundred shoots, svāhā!"

With the words, "May we grow with a thousand branches," he touches himself; he causes the branches to sprout from the tip downwards. With the words, "The axe, sharpening itself, has led thee forth for great good fortune," he should cut that [branch] which is five cubits long; this is the shortest among those possessing the Brāhmaṇa-text.
He trims it at the place of the *caṣāla* so that it is at most a full embrace [in girth] and at least a span, with the words, "Uninterrupted is wealth and heroic sons."
Of that which is the uppermost part, he cuts off four finger-breadths for the *caṣāla*;

having made it either four-cornered or eight-cornered, he carries it away or causes it to be carried away; having carried it away, he finishes it and makes the *svaru* from the very shavings. Now, on the previous day, this altar for the animal sacrifice has already been measured out: ten steps across at the back, twelve steps eastward, and eight steps across at the front;
having strewn around that [altar], he performs the *stambayajus* rite.

This very well-known procedure for the sacrificial cake (pauroḍāśika) is followed: he performs the first tracing of the altar three times with the sacrificial formula (yajus) and the fourth time silently;
he mutters the Karaṇa formula; he digs up [the earth]; from the dug-up spot, the Āgnīdhra carries it away three times;
when the Āgnīdhra has carried it away three times, then he asks for the wooden sword (sphya), a water-vessel, sacrificial grass (barhis), and the yoke-pin (śamyā).

Having taken this up, he says, "Come, O sacrificer," and having dug up with the wooden sword (sphya) to the north of the altar at two or three steps' distance, and having sprinkled it, he measures out the pit (cātvāla) with the yoke-pin (śamyā), saying, "Thou art my path to wealth. To the east, he draws a line with the wooden sword from west to east along the inside of the northern handle of the yoke-pin.

With the formula, "Thou art the path of bitterness for me," he scratches inside with the wooden sword (sphya) using the southern end of the cord turned eastward; with "Protect me from distress," he scratches behind with the northern end of the cord turned eastward; with "Protect me from agitation," he scratches on the north with the southern end of the cord turned eastward. Then, having placed sacrificial grass (barhis) in the pit (cātvāla), he strikes it with the wooden sword, saying, "Agni knows thee by the name Nabhas; O Agni Aṅgiras, [know] him who is upon this earth. He takes it up with "Come with life as thy name," and having carried it away, he pours it out on the high altar (uttaravedi) with "I establish thee with that name of thine which is unassailable and worthy of sacrifice."
He strikes the second [brick] with: "May Agni find thee; O Agni Aṅgiras, thou who art on the second earth. He takes it up with: "Come with life as thy name!

Having carried it, he deposits it on the high altar (uttaravedi) with: "With that name of thine which is unassailable and worthy of sacrifice, with that I establish thee. He strikes the third [brick] with: "May Agni find thee; O Agni Aṅgiras, thou who art on the third earth. He takes it up with: "Come with life as thy name!"
Having taken it, he pours it out on the *uttaravedi* with the formula, "With that which is thy invincible, sacrificial name, with that I establish thee";

the fourth time he carries it silently together with the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Then the Adhvaryu digs up the loose earth from the *catvāla* pit with the wooden sword (*sphya*), and then he says to the Āgnīdhra, "O Āgnīdhra, carry [the earth] from here three times. Thereupon, the Āgnīdhra carries it three times.
When the Āgnīdhra has carried [the earth] three times, then the Adhvaryu mixes the soil for the high altar (*uttaravedi*), saying, "Thou art a lioness; thou art a buffalo.
He spreads it out, saying, "Spread wide! May the lord of the sacrifice spread wide for thee!
He strikes it with the wooden sword (*sphya*), saying, "Thou art firm," and then he sprinkles it with water.

With the words, "Be purified for the gods," and "Be beautified for the gods," he strews sand over it. Having made that [mound] one span high and four-cornered, he measures it around with a yoke-pin. Having raised the northern navel and covered it, he takes up the spade with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee. Having taken it, he consecrates it with: "Thou art the spade; thou art no woman."

With that [formula], he traces around the pit for the sacrificial post so that half of it shall be within the altar and half outside the altar: "The *rakṣas* is traced around; the enemies are traced around. Here I cut off the neck of the *rakṣas*; him who hates us and whom we hate—here I cut off his neck. Then he says to the Āgnīdhra: "O Āgnīdhra, come! Dig this pit for the sacrificial post, level with the top; throw the excavated earth toward the east; do not dig deeper than four finger-breadths from the top. He either digs it himself or has it dug.
As long as the Adhvaryu is busy there, so long does this Pratiprasthātṛ add fuel to the fire for the leading forward of the waters;
they prepare the supporting grass-bunches,
and the Adhvaryu takes from the Cātvāla pit the "Indra's roar" sprinkling waters for himself.

He gives fivefold-drawn clarified butter to the attendant; the ritual materials are placed for the Brahman priest, and then he issues the command: "Recite for the fire being led forward! Agnīdh, follow along with the single-ridge wooden sword! When this has been uttered three times, they lift up [the fire].
They go toward the Hotṛ's place; they proceed along the north of the altar and maintain this fire.
Then the Adhvaryu sprinkles the high altar with the *prokṣaṇī* waters accompanied by the *indrighoṣavatī* verses.
"May Indra-ghoṣa protect you from the east with the Vasus"—thus [he protects] from the east;
"may Manojava protect you from the south with the Pitṛs"—thus from the south; "may Pracetas protect you from the west with the Rudras"—thus from the west.

"May Viśvakarman protect thee from the north with the Ādityas"—with these words he sprinkles from the north. Now, whatever remains of the *prokṣaṇī* water, he pours it out to the south of the high altar (*uttaravedi*).
"Whatever there is cruel, that he pacifies by means of this," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then, having placed gold between [the altar and himself], he sprinkles [the altar] crosswise with five-fold taken ghee.

"Sim hīrasi sapatnasāhī svāhā!"—thus on the right shoulder; "Sim hīrasi suprajāvaniḥ svāhā!"—thus on the left hip; "Sim hīrasi rāyaspoṣavaniḥ svāhā!"—thus on the right hip; "Sim hīrasyādityavaniḥ svāhā!"—thus on the left shoulder;

"Sim hīrasyāvaha devān devayate yajamānāya svāhā!"—thus in the middle. Then, with the words "For the beings, thee," he lifts up the ladle; then he lays down the enclosing sticks made of *pūtudru* wood.

“You are the life of all; steady the earth!”—with these words he places the middle [brick]. “You are firmly seated; steady the atmosphere!”—with these words he places the southern one. “You are immovably seated; steady the sky!”—with these words he places the northern one. Then he pours out the remaining materials: bdellium, fragrant ointment, and a tuft of white wool, saying, “You are the ash of Agni; you are the soil of Agni. Then he pours clarified butter over them with the residue of the oblation. Then, having turned clockwise, he establishes the fuel, saying: “O Sacrifice, be established in a good mind, most auspicious; may riches enter into you in many ways.”

"Bestowing long life upon the sacrificer, now anoint the singer with immortality"—having thus loosened it and made it capable of bearing the oblations, he offers over it the *adhvara* oblations: "May Agni, knowing the way, lead the sacrifice; may those who destroy the sacrifice not find it. Proclaim the sacrifice to the gods; further on and further on lead the lord of the sacrifice, *svāhā*!"

May Vāyu, knowing [the way], lead the sacrifice; may those who destroy the sacrifice not find it. Proclaim the sacrifice to the gods today; further on and further on, advance the lord of the sacrifice. Svāhā!
May Sūrya, knowing the way, lead the sacrifice; may those who destroy the sacrifice not find it. Proclaim the sacrifice to the gods; further and further extend the lord of the sacrifice. Svāhā!

"May the sacrifice, knowing [the way], lead the sacrifice; may the destroyers of the sacrifice not find it. Proclaim the sacrifice to the gods today; further on, promote the lord of the sacrifice—Svāhā! Then the sacrificer himself offers these oblations: "Agni is the eater of food, the lord of food; he rules over food; may he give me food—Svāhā! Vāyu is the giver of breath, the lord of breath; may he give me breath—Svāhā!"

"Āditya is the giver of much; he is the lord of the most numerous cattle. May he grant me the most numerous cattle, svāhā! Having performed the second tracing around while it contains fire, having leveled the ground, and having fixed the wooden sword (sphya) across, he issues the call: "Set down the sprinkling waters; place the fuel and the sacrificial grass; cleanse the spoon, the knife, and the ladles; silently prepare the vessel for the speckled butter; gird the wife; and bring the clarified butter and the curds. When the sprinkling waters have been brought, he throws away the wooden sword.

Having swept [the altar], having placed the fuel and the sacrificial grass, having turned to the right, and having stepped back facing west, he cleanses the *sruva* ladle, the *svadhiti* knife, and the offering spoons; he silently cleanses the vessel for the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*). He girds the wife and goes out with the clarified butter and the curds. Having purified the clarified butter and the sprinkling waters in the usual manner, and having taken the portions of clarified butter, he spreads a base layer in the vessel for the speckled butter with the formula: "Thou art the milk of the great ones."

Having placed two blades of *barhis* grass between [the vessel and the fire] with the formula, "The bodies of all the gods," he pours curds [into the vessel] with the formula, "May I prosper today; thou art the draught of the speckled ones. Having removed the two blades of *barhis*, he then sprinkles [the curds] with the formula, "Thou art the heart of Viṣṇu" over the first [portion], and "Viṣṇu has stepped along thee for food" over the second.
Then he rises up with the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling waters and sprinkles the fuel, sprinkles the altar, and sprinkles the *barhis* grass.
Having sprinkled the sacrificial grass (barhis) that has been placed nearby and poured water over it, he takes the prastara-bunch from the front.

Having spread the fivefold sacrificial grass, holding the prastara in his hand, he moves forward to the east and lays down the enclosing sticks (paridhi) made of *kārṣmarya* wood; he places two upright fuel-sticks (samidh) and sets down two separating blades (vidhṛti) crosswise.

Having touched together the two *vidhṛtī*s, the *prastara* on the *vidhṛtī*s, the *juhū* on the *prastara*, and the other sacrificial grasses (*barhis*) with the formula, "These have sat down," he turns to the right, runs back toward the west, and calls for: "Prokṣaṇī water containing barley, a handfull of *barhis*, the butter-pot with the *sruva*-ladle, the *svaru* chip, the rope, the staff of the Maitrāvaruṇa, a splinter from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), gold, and a vessel of water. Having placed these nearby, he washes the sacrificial post with the verse: "O Lord of the Forest, may the waters that cleanse away whatever a skillful carpenter has struck with his hand or with the axe, remove that from you."

This sacrificial post (yūpa), washed and brought forward, lies to the east of the hole (avaṭa) with its top-ring (caṣāla) already fitted. Standing to the north of the Āhavanīya fire, facing away [from it], he sprinkles it with the formula: "For the earth thee! For the atmosphere thee! For the sky thee! He pours water into the hole with the formula: "May the world, the seat of the fathers, be purified.
He scatters barley-grains [into the hole] with the formula: "Thou art barley; ward off our haters; ward off our enemies."

Intertwining the sacrificial grass held in his hand, he spreads it out with the formula, "Thou art the seat of the Pitṛs. He inserts a chip of the sacrificial post with the formula, "Thou art easy of access; thou art the leader of leaders; the Lord of the Forest shall stand upon thee; take note of him! Then he takes up the vessel of clarified butter together with the dipping-spoon, the wooden sword, the rope, the staff for the Maitrāvaruṇa, and a vessel of water. Having taken these, he says, "Come, O sacrificer! The sacrificer follows behind him, and the wife follows behind the sacrificer. Having gone around the front of the sacrificial post, they stand to the south facing north—the Adhvaryu in front, the sacrificer behind him, and the wife behind the sacrificer.

Then, having removed the *caṣāla*, he anoints the top of the sacrificial post with the formula, "May the god Savitṛ anoint thee with honey," both inside and out, making it well-anointed; he then fixes the *caṣāla* with the formula, "For the plants that bear good fruit. Then, while pouring clarified butter over the corner facing the fire with the *sruva*-ladle, he says, "Recite for the post being anointed"; he anoints it right to the end, for by anointing the very end, he anoints the sacrificer himself with splendor; he does not anoint the part beyond [the end].

The wife anoints it from all sides; he strokes it all around so as not to exclude any part, for thus he bestows brilliance upon it—so says the Brāhmaṇa. As he raises it, he says, "Recite for the one being raised. He raises it with the verse: "Support the sky, fill the mid-region, and make firm the earth with your base. Then he fashions it with two verses addressed to Viṣṇu: "Behold these your abodes, O Viṣṇu, the deeds of Viṣṇu," and [the second], "Those wise ones ever behold that highest step of Viṣṇu. At the point where he aligns the corner facing the fire (agniṣṭhā-aśri) with the Āhavanīya fire, there he gazes at the top-ring of the Dhruva post: "That highest step of Viṣṇu, the wise ever behold."

"Like an eye stretched out in the sky"—with these words, he then piles earth around it from left to right, saying: "I pile thee around, winner of the *brahman*, winner of the *kṣatra*, winner of good offspring, winner of the increase of wealth.

He strikes it with the staff of the Maitrāvaruṇa, saying: "May I strike down the *brahman*; may I strike down the *kṣatra*; may I strike down offspring; may I strike down the increase of wealth. Having laid it down neither deficient nor excessive, and having poured out a vessel of water, he then folds this three-stranded rope thrice and, while winding it around at the height of the navel with the middle strand, he says: "Recite for that which is being encircled!"

He winds [the cord] around three times from left to right with the formula: "Thou art the encircler; may the divine subjects encircle thee; may this abundance of wealth encircle the sacrificer among men. He interlaces [the strands] at the ends and twists them toward the end. He winds the thicker part over the thinner part. Then, to the north of the corner facing the fire (agniṣṭhāmaśri), he hides the sacrificial chip (svaru) in the middle loop with the formula: "I hide thee on the ridge of the atmosphere. He releases the sacrificial post provided with the chip.
Then, having brought this washed animal between the *cātvāla* and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), he causes it to stand in front of the post, facing west.

Taking two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the formula, "For darkness thee," he performs the introductory rite (*upākaraṇa*) with: "Thou art the invoker; the divine hosts have come forward, the carriers, the eager ones. O Bṛhaspati, bestow riches! May the offerings be palatable to thee. O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, make them beautiful! O wealthy ones, rejoice! Born of Prajāpati, this animal—O Lord of Animals, it is yours today. I dedicate you, acceptable to Indra and Agni" (or whichever deity it belongs to). Having set aside the two blades of grass that were previously prepared, he places the splinter for churning upon the fire-drill (*araṇi*) with the formula: "Thou art the birthplace of Agni."

"O you two bulls, moving downward, you are bulls," [he says]. Then he takes up the two kindling woods with the formula, "Thou art Urvaśī; thou art Āyu Purūravas. Then he anoints these two together in the vessel of clarified butter with the formula, "Anointed with ghee, do ye two produce a bull. Then he causes him to recite the procreational verses: "Be born after the Gāyatrī metre; be born after the Triṣṭubh metre; be born after the Jagatī metre. Then he says, "Recite for the fire being churned";
when it is born, he says, "Recite for the fire that has been born"; as he throws it [into the fire], he says, "Recite for the fire being thrown."

He strikes [the victim] with the verse, "May you strike us together with one mind," and having struck it, he makes an oblation into the fire with the verse, "Fire moves, having entered into fire. Then he takes up the cord with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee.
With that [cord], he binds the animal crosswise on its right side, at the middle of the head, with the formula, "I seize thee, the divine oblation of Truth, with the noose."
He joins the two ends of the cord that is double-stranded and triple-stranded together with the formula, "Overpowering men.
He then fastens it with the formula, "From the waters, from the plants, for Indra and Agni, I sprinkle thee,
acceptable [to them]," or with whichever deity the animal belongs.

"He makes it drink [the water] with the mantra, 'Thou art the drinker of waters. [With the words,] 'O divine waters, may this oblation, which is indeed well-tasted, be made savory,' he sprinkles it from above and then sprinkles from below;
thus he makes it pure on all sides," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Having moved aside the vessel for the sprinkling water,
and then taking a fuel-stick from the faggot, he says, "Recite for the fire being kindled," and places the faggot [on the fire],
leaving one stick behind; he fans it with the *vedā* grass-bundle, and when the *sāmidhenī* verses have been recited, he pours the *āghāra* libation with the *sruva* spoon.
After wiping the two offering-spoons,
he then, without letting them touch each other, steps northward and anoints the animal with the *juhū* at the forehead,
saying: "May your breath unite with the wind."

With the formula "May the limbs be united with the sacrificial objects," he places [the offering] on the hump; with "May the lord of the sacrifice be united with his blessings," on the southern buttock.
Then, having set down the two ladles in their respective places, he chooses the *pravara*.

Having chosen the Hotṛ in the prescribed manner, he then causes the announcement to be made: "Ośrāvaya! Astu Śrauṣaṭ! Mitrāvaruṇa are the two Praśāstṛs; from the office of the Praśāstṛ—'Asau Mānuṣaḥ' (so-and-so is the human one)," thus he pronounces the name of the Maitrāvaruṇa. Then he causes the announcement to be made; if he does not cause the announcement here, he says: "Ośrāvaya! Astu Śrauṣaṭ! Agni is the leader of the divine clans, and this sacrificer is the leader of the human ones. May their household-fire shine without failure for a hundred winters. May the two of them prosper together, their bodies united yet distinct. Thus the Hotṛ sits down.
He awaits the impulse;
once impelled, having taken up the two offering-spoons and stepped across, he calls for the *āśrāvaṇa* and says, "Prompt for the *samidhs*";
when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering, saying, "Prompt! Prompt!"
Pours together [the butter] at the fourth and eighth [prayājas]; at the eighth, he pours together the entire residue; he leaves over the remainder for the *svāhākṛti* offerings.
Having performed ten *prayāja* offerings, having stepped across toward the north, he asks for the *svaru* and the *śāsa*.
Having anointed the two [spatulas] with the *juhū*, he anoints the victim with them, saying, "Anointed with ghee, may you two protect the victim," and hands [the spatu] over;
he hides the sacrificial knife and inserts the *svaru* [into the ground].

Then, having set down the two offering-ladles (*srucau*) in their respective places, he says, "Recite for the fire being carried around. Then the Āgnīdhra, taking a fire-brand from the Āhavanīya fire, goes three times clockwise around [the victim]—between the *cātvāla* pit and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), to the north of the place of immolation (*śāmitradeśa*), in front of the animal, and behind the ladles—and following this circumambulation, he offers the *apāvya* oblations with the verse: "The ancestors who receive [the offerings], knowing [them], for whom Paśupati is the lord of animals;
those wild beasts of every form that are bound after the one being bound—releasing them, [they are] the seed of the world."

Having placed the firebrand in the Āgnīdhra shed, he returns three times again by the same way he went; then they set out with the firebrand first, the Śamitr following behind with the animal, and the Adhvaryu follows the animal, taking hold of it with the two omentum-roasting spits.

The sacrificer holds the two omentum-spits; then, having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he issues the command: "O Hotṛ, give the impulse for the oblations to the gods. Then, as this animal is being led northward between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, he addresses it with two verses: "May the breath of the sacrificer be separate from the animal; O wealthy ones, enter the lord of the sacrifice in a pleasant manner. At the point where the Āgnīdhra places the firebrand, he throws down sacrificial grass (*barhis*) in front of or to the north of the animal being slaughtered, with the formula: "Protect [it] from contact with the earth."

Then, having said, "Slay this animal with its head toward the west and its feet toward the north; let it be quieted without making a sound," they return by the same way they came and sit for the occasion of the *pṛṣadājya* (spotted butter), saying: "May offspring of every form rejoice here in this sacrifice, all-knowing and dripping with ghee; dwelling together around Agni as their home, may they favor us with milk and ghee.

When it has been quieted, he offers the *saṃjñaptāhuti* (the oblation for the quieted one) with the verse, "If the animal has made a sound... Then he approaches, saying, "O slaughterers, come hither!"

He consecrates with the mantra "Aditi, release this bond" the animal being released from the noose; having fastened it with a branchless twig, he throws it away toward this direction (the south) with the formula, "I make him who acts as an enemy low; upon him whom we hate, I fasten the bond. Then the Pratiprasthātṛ leads the wife forward, having made her rise with a water-pitcher; then he makes her look up at the sun with the formula, "Homage to thee, O outstretched one. Then, having gone out northward between the *cātvāla* and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), leading her eastward, he causes her to recite: "Go forward, unassailable."

"Along with a stream of ghee, together with offspring, together with the increase of wealth"—with these words, as she has arrived, the Adhvaryu makes her recite over the waters: "O divine waters, you who seek purity, pure yourselves, carry the gods; pure, may we, being served, become the servers for you.

He then causes the vital breaths of the animal to swell in succession: "May speech swell for thee," he says to speech; "May breath swell for thee," he says to breath; "May sight swell for thee," he says to sight.

"May your hearing swell," he says; with this, he again touches those very [limbs]. "Whatever pain has gone to your breaths, whatever to your sight, whatever to your hearing, whatever is harsh in you, whatever is settled [within], may that swell for you; may that be purified by this.
