"May your navel swell," he says; "may your anus swell," he says; having grasped the anus, he washes the feet [with the formula]: "Purity for our movements, peace for the waters, peace for the plants, peace for the earth."
With the formula "By peace and by day," he pours out what remains to the south along the back;
they lead the wife away, and they turn the animal over onto its back.

Along the opening of its southern side, he places sacrificial grass (barhis) with its tips pointing eastward, saying, "O plant, protect him! He places the knife across it, saying, "O knife, do not harm him!
He cuts the grass, saying, "Make a skin! Then he takes a small portion from that very same sacrificial grass.

Having smeared both ends of the thickest [portion] with blood, he throws it out toward this direction [the south], saying: "Thou art the portion of the Rakṣases; I lead this Rakṣas into the lowest darkness—he who hates us and whom we hate; here I lead him into the lowest darkness. Then, having touched water and spread out a wider space, he extracts the omentum, saying: "For food thee! (iṣe tvā).

With [the formula], "O Heaven and Earth, be covered with ghee," he covers the two omentum-spits with a branchless [twig] and places them underneath. With [the formula], "Uninterrupted be wealth and good heroes," he then turns her (the victim) to the right, sprinkles her with water, and heats her over the *śāmitra* fire. Then they proceed, led by the fire-brand;
the Adhvaryu follows with the omentum, and the sacrificer again takes hold of the two omentum-spits from behind.

"Come! Enter the atmosphere!"—saying this, he throws the tip of a blade of *barhis* grass onto the outermost embers of the Āhavanīya fire for the omentum (*vapā*) as it is being heated, with the formula: "O Vāyu, partake of the drops! Then, having carried it between the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the Āhavanīya fire, the Pratiprasthātṛ, standing to the south and facing north, roasts it; then he makes an offering over it with a spoonful, saying: "Thee they have established as the bearer of oblations. Then he says: "Recite the invitatory prayer for the drops!"

When the *stokīyā* verses have been recited and the omentum has been cooked, he takes the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, steps forward, causes the announcement to be made, and says, "Prompt for the *svāhākṛtī*s. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering. Then, having stepped back toward the north, he sprinkles the clotted butter (*pṛṣadājya*) with the residue from the ladle and sprinkles the omentum. Then, having spread an underlayer of ghee twice with the *sruva* spoon, while cutting off portions of the omentum, he says: "Recite the invitatory verse for the fat of the goat's omentum being cut off for Indra and Agni."

He sprinkles [the offering] twice, steps across, causes the announcement to be made, and says, "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the fat of the goat's omentum set forth for Indra and Agni. Then he offers a spoonful before the *svāhā*-utterance, saying, "Svāhā to the gods!"

When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers the omentum with [the verse]: "O Jātavedas, go to the gods with the omentum; for you have become the first Hotṛ. Increase their bodies with clarified butter; may the gods eat the oblation consecrated by *svāhā*, *svāhā*! Then, after the utterance of *svāhā*, he offers a spoonful of oblation with the formula "To the gods, *svāhā*! At this point, he throws the two omentum-spits into the fire—the one with a forked end facing eastward and the one without a fork facing westward—with [the formula]: "O *svāhā*, go to the Maruts of the upward sky! Then he joins these two together...
He offers with the residue. Then, having stepped out toward the north and set down the two ladles in their respective places, they step forward and purify themselves at the *cātvāla* pit.

They call for the wife; they call for the *hotṛ*; they call for the *brahman*; they call for the *pratiprasthātṛ*; they call for the *praśāstṛ*; they call for the *āgnīdhra*. "Come, O Sacrificer! [he says]. "O Waters, carry away this day whatever is blameworthy and whatever is impure; whatever falsehood I have committed by assault, and whatever curse I have uttered against the innocent—release me from my oaths, and release me from Varuṇa."

"Having released me from the fetter of Yama, from every sin against the gods and likewise from sin against men"—with these words, he takes water in his joined palms and sprinkles it toward that quarter in which the person whom he hates resides, saying: "May the waters and plants be friendly to us; may they be unfriendly to him who hates us and whom we hate.
Then, having touched water, they sit down in their respective places.
Then he issues the command: "O Āgnīdh, prepare the sacrificial cake for the animal sacrifice; O Pratiprasthātṛ, dissect the animal.
This Āgnīdhra prepares the cake on eleven potsherds for Indra and Agni.

Then the Pratiprasthātṛ gives instructions to the slaughterer: "Prepare the heart, the tongue, and the breast together; prepare the two kidneys together; prepare the left foreleg and one shoulder-bone together; keep the two sides separate; prepare the right hip and the rectum together; prepare the right foreleg, the left hip, and the three parts of the anus together; prepare the large intestine and the tail separately; cut the animal into many portions; move the animal three times; and of the animal moved three times, make the heart the last."
When the animal has been cooked, he asks for the animal-cake;

having placed it on the sacrificial grass and sprinkled it with clarified butter, he removes it from the fire and sets it down within the altar. Then, while spreading a base of ghee in the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for the cake being portioned out for Indra and Agni.
Having taken a portion from the eastern half, he takes a portion from the western half and sprinkles it with clarified butter.

He anoints [the offering-spoon] again; then he cuts once from the northern half for the Sviṣṭakṛt, pours clarified butter over it twice, does not anoint it again, steps across, causes the announcement to be made, and says:
"Prompt the offering of the cake set forth for Indra and Agni."
When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he makes the offering. Then, while pouring together [the butter], he says, "Recite for Agni"; having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Prompt for Agni.

When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering in the eastern part of the northern half, passing over the previous offerings. Then, having stepped out toward the north and placed the two ladles in their proper places, he cuts off the *prāśitra*. Having cut off the *iḍā*, when the *iḍā* has been invoked, he places it for the *agnīdh*. They consume the portion consisting of six cuttings and perform the ritual purification (*mārjana*).

Then he issues the command: "O Āgnīdh, place the northern sacrificial grass; O Pratiprasthātṛ, converse regarding the animal sacrifice. Then this Āgnīdhra hides the *iḍasūna* (the portion for the *iḍā*) within a branch of the *plakṣa* tree;

that becomes the northern sacrificial grass. Then the Pratiprasthātṛ, having divided the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) and poured it into the *juhū* ladle, goes out northward between the *cātvāla* pit and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), and asks: "O Śamitṛ, is the oblation cooked? Now this Śamitṛ stands to the north, holding the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*).
He replies, "It is cooked.
Having stepped forward in the same manner, he asks the second one, and the other replies in the same way.

Having stepped across in that same manner for the third time, he questions him, and the other replies in the same way. Then, taking the heart-spit from the *śamitr*, having pierced the heart with it, and having handed it over to the *śamitr*, he bastes the heart with speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) with the mantra: "May your mind be united with [my] mind; may your breath be united with [my] breath; may this offering, pleasing to the gods and rich in ghee, be consecrated with Svāhā!"

Having performed the *viyūha* and said, "Carry [the organs] away," he returns by the same way he came and spreads [grass] under the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, as well as the two *iḍādhāna* vessels, and that vessel in which he intends to take the *vasāhoma* offering. They bring that animal between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, between the sacrificial post and the *āhavanīya* fire; having brought it forward, he places it to the south for the *pañcahotṛ* formula. By this same path they carry the *yūpa* (the sacrificial post), and by this same path the *iḍāsūna*.
Then, having placed the heart on a branch of the *plakṣa* tree, while cutting its tip with the knife, he says, "Recite for the *manotā* as the oblation is being cut."

First he cuts twice from the heart, then from the tongue, then from the chest, then from the thin membrane, then from the two kidneys, then from the left foreleg, then from the right rib, then from the left rib, then from the right hip, and from the tail. Having divided the rectum into three parts, he sets aside the smallest portion for the *iṣṭakṛt* offering; the largest he sets aside for the *upayaj* offerings, and having divided the middle part into two, he places it in the *juhū* ladle. Then, having placed the fat of the kidneys into the broth, he covers the *juhū* with it.

He sprinkles it with broth and bastes it; then, for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he cuts off portions from all three limbs into the *upabhṛt* ladle once each. Having cut a piece of flesh from the right foreleg, he places it [in the ladle]; then from the left hip, a small portion; and from the rectum. Then, having placed the kidney-fat into the broth, he covers the *upabhṛt* ladle with it and sprinkles it with broth.

He pours clarified butter over it twice; then, having placed the heart, the tongue, the breast, the two kidneys, and the rectum into the vessel, he sprinkles them with broth and pours clarified butter over them. Then, in either a *kaṃsa* or a *camasa* cup, he takes the portion of the fat (*vasāhoma*), sprinkles it with broth, and pours clarified butter over it. Then he touches the portions of the animal victim, saying: "May Indra’s out-breath settle limb by limb; may Indra’s in-breath manifest limb by limb. O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, let your many forms come together, for though you are of diverse shapes, you become uniform."

"May the mother and the fathers rejoice after you as you go among the gods for protection, O friend!"—with these words, he then stirs the fat-oblation with his right side from the pot, [saying]: "Thou art glory; may Agni cook thee; may the waters flow together for thee; for the gliding of Vāta, for the delight of Pūṣan, for the growth of the waters and the plants.
They carry the tail of the slaughtered animal toward the west and carry it around the animal.

Then, taking up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, he says: "Recite the invitatory verse for the oblation of the goat for Indra and Agni. Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "Prompt the Hotṛ to recite the offering verse for the oblation of the goat set forth for Indra and Agni.
The Pratiprasthātṛ stands to the north, holding the *vasā-homa* (fat-oblation).

At the half-verse of the offering verse, he offers the *vasā-homa*, saying: "O drinkers of ghee, drink the ghee; O drinkers of fat, drink the fat! You are the oblation of the intermediate region; *svāhā*! To the intermediate region, *svāhā*!"

When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers the oblation. Following this offering, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers to the quarters with the remnants of the fat-offering (*vasāhoma*), saying: "To the quarters, to the intermediate quarters, to the directed quarters, to the sub-quarters, to the upward quarters—*svāhā*! Homage to the quarters, *svāhā* to the quarters! Then, having turned clockwise and dipping the spoon into the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), he says: "Recite for Vanaspati! Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Prompt for Vanaspati! When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering on the eastern part of the northern half, passing over the previous offerings. Then, while pouring together [the portions], he says: "Recite for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt! Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Prompt for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt!"

At the utterance of "vaṣaṭ," he offers [the oblation] in the eastern part of the northern half, passing over the previous offerings. Then, having stepped out toward the north and placed the two ladles in their respective places, they lift up the *iḍā* for the Hotṛ. When the *iḍā* has been invoked, he places the sixfold portion, including half of the *vaniṣṭhu*, upon the Āgnīdhra; then they consume the half-*vaniṣṭhu* together with the fat. They perform the ritual purification (*mārjana*). Then he says, "Hand over the breast to the Brahman."

Brahman accepts it with the formula: "O Soma, we, bearing our minds within our bodies according to your law, may we obtain offspring. Then he issues the command: "O Āgnīdh, bring the embers for the supplementary offerings (aupayaja); O Upayaṣṭṛ, sit down; O Brahman, we shall set forth; having placed the fuel-stick, O Āgnīdh, cleanse the fires once each. They bring those embers for the supplementary offerings from the Śāmitra fire; the Hotṛ pours them down in front of himself, and the Upayaṣṭṛ sits down with the third part of the entrails (guda). Then the Adhvaryu, having divided the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) and poured it into the Juhū ladle, having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, says:
"Prompt for the gods (*devebhyaḥ preṣya*)."

When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers; saying "Prompt! Prompt! in this very manner, the *upayaṣṭṛ* performs the secondary offerings (*upayaja*) with these eleven [verses], beginning with "Go to the ocean, svāhā! for each cut-off portion of the rectum.

"Go to Agni Vaiśvānara, Svāhā!"—with this, he finally throws everything after [the fire]. Then he wipes his hands on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the formula: "From the waters, from the plants; grant me mind and heart. Then he gazes at its smoke, saying: "May I attain body, skin, son, and grandson. Having performed eleven after-offerings (*anūyāja*), he steps out toward the north, places the *svaru* in the *juhū* ladle, and standing facing west while looking eastward, he offers it with the formula: "May your smoke go to heaven, your flame to the intermediate space; fill the earth with ashes, Svāhā! Then...
Having set down the two offering-spoons in their proper places, he separates them with the two *vājavatī* verses;

having scattered the *prastara* and the enclosing-sticks with the *śaṃyu* formula, having poured out the remnants from the spoons and released them, they perform the *saṃyājana* of the wife with the tail of the victim. He sacrifices to Soma and Tvaṣṭṛ with clarified butter alone. With the tail held upward, he sacrifices to the wives of the gods;
with it held downward, he sacrifices to Agni Gṛhapati.
From the upward-turned tail-tendon, the Hotṛ portions out the *iḍā*;
from the downward-turned [portion], the Āgnīdhra [takes] the sixfold portion; they both eat it and perform the ritual purification (*mārjana*).

Then, having taken four portions of clarified butter into the *sruc* ladle and turning away toward the left, he offers an expiation on the *anvāhāryapacana* fire; he does not, however, perform the offering of the husks (*phalīkaraṇa*). Then, having gone forward to the east and replenished the *dhruvā* vessel, he offers three *samiṣṭayajus* oblations with the *sruva* spoon: "O Sacrifice, go to the sacrifice; go to the lord of the sacrifice; go to your own womb, svāhā! With the *sruva* spoon alone, he offers the second: "This is your sacrifice, O lord of the sacrifice, accompanied by the *sūktavāka*, rich in heroes, svāhā!"

"O gods who know the way, having found the way, go along the way; O Lord of the Mind, O God, place this sacrifice of ours among the gods—Svāhā! In speech, Svāhā! In the wind, place it, Svāhā! With these words, he lifts up the *sruva*-ladle.

Then he calls for the wooden sword (*sphya*), a vessel of water, and the heart-spit (*hṛdayaśūla*). Having taken these, he says, "Come, O Sacrificer! The Sacrificer follows behind him, and the wife follows after the Sacrificer. Having gone out northward between the *cātvāla* pit and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), and having dug up the ground with the wooden sword in front of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and sprinkled it, he disposes of the heart-spit at the junction of the dry and the moist.

"O Agni, burn him, burn against him who hates us and whom we hate. Then they purify themselves with water, saying: "From every bond, O King Varuṇa, release us; from whatever we have sworn by the waters, the inviolable ones, O Varuṇa, from that, O Varuṇa, release us. Then they return without looking back, for the sake of escaping the reach of Varuṇa.

While on the journey, he prepares the fuel sticks, saying, "Thou art fuel; may we prosper through thee," and having arrived, he places them upon the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "Thou art a fuel stick; thou art brilliance; bestow brilliance upon me. Then they worship the Āhavanīya, saying, "I have followed the waters; we have united with their essence. Rich in milk, O Agni, I have come; unite me with that splendor. Then he burns the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) upon the *aupayajika* fire with the verse: "Whatever debt remains unpaid by me, for which I move about as an offering to Yama..."

"Remaining right here, I pay off that debt; O Agni, through this I become free from debt. Then, with his joined palms, he offers the parched groats—which have been spread out and sprinkled with ghee—into the forest fire, saying: "O Viśvalopa, I offer you to Viśvadāva, Svāhā! He then rubs his hands together, saying: "One has eaten, one has not offered; one has acted with a single mind. May they all provide us with healing, a dwelling, strength, and what is desirable. He makes a second offering, saying: "Whatever debts I owe, whatever remains unpaid, for which I move as a tribute to Yama—while remaining right here, we discharge that; being alive, we pay this back to the living, Svāhā!"
"Two hands move apart; one is from the cooked offering, one from the uncooked offering. May they, being of one mind, provide us with healing, a dwelling, strength, and what is excellent.

With this he offers the third oblation: "May we be free from debt in this world, free from debt in the next, and free from debt in the third world. May we, free from debt, traverse all paths—those traveled by the gods and those traveled by the fathers—svāhā!"

Two hands are joined together: one is from the cooked [oblation], one is from the uncooked; they are of one mind. May they provide us with healing, a dwelling, strength, and what is desirable. Then he worships the deities: "This one before us with the mist," [addressing] Agni; "Do thou, O Lord of the Mist, for us," [addressing] Vāyu; "O God, making us swell," [addressing] Āditya. Then he worships the sacrificial post: "Hoping for excellent offspring, abundance of wealth, and good horses; established by Bṛhaspati through wealth, stand firm for me, the sacrificer. Then he consigns the former fire into a wood-shard with the verse: "This is thy seasonal womb."
He pours it into the middle fire with two verses, "Being invoked" and "Awake, O Agni.
Then, having added fuel to the middle fire, he offers the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the middle fire with the verse, "Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues.
At the full-oblation, he gives a choice gift.
"One should give an excellent cow or an excellent bull," so said Baudhāyana. The animal sacrifice (paśubandha) concludes; the animal sacrifice concludes.

One is about to perform the Vaiśvadeva oblations on either the full moon day of Phālguna or Caitra. Some say the performance should be according to the lunar asterisms (nakṣatra); others say one should perform it during the northern course of the sun, on an auspicious day of the waxing fortnight.

He prepares a three-pronged porcupine quill, a razor of red metal, four potsherds for the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), four vessels for the cooked rice (*caru*), as many stirring-spoons (*mekṣaṇa*) as there are vessels, two portions of milk—one for the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) and one for the curdling of the oblation (*havir-ātañcana*), sacrificial grass (*barhis*) tied in three bundles which are then tied together as one, and a *prastara* bundle with its tip pointing forward. Then, on the day of fasting, he offers the introductory sacrifice (*ārambhaṇīyā-iṣṭi*) consisting of two oblations: a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara and a cooked rice offering for Parjanya.
That well-known sacrifice is concluded; then, on this day, the calves are driven away for the Viśve Devas.

Having caused the milk for the Vaiśvadeva to be milked, he observes the fast according to the procedure for the Sāṃnāyya, or silently. Then, in the morning, after the Agnihotra has been offered and before the carrying forward of the waters, he melts the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire, purifies it, and having taken four portions into the ladle, he offers it into the Āhavanīya fire while mentally reciting the Pañcahotṛ formula and with the sacrificer maintaining contact, saying "Svāhā! Then, having strewn the Pṛṣṭhyā line and carried forward the waters, he offers an oblation on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, a cake on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ, and a pap for Sarasvatī.
[He prepares] a *caru* for Pūṣan, a cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts, *āmikṣā* for the Viśve Devas, and a cake on one potsherd for Dyāvāpṛthivī;
at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), he releases his speech.

The ritual procedure is the same up to the pouring [of the grains]; having poured them, he places eight potsherds on the southern half of the *gārhapatya* fire. Then, having brought water across the strainers from the north, he places it over the *caru* for Soma. Then, to the north, he places twelve potsherds for the offering to Savitṛ.

Then, having poured water across the strainers from the north, he places [the milk] over the fire for Sarasvatī and Pūṣan; then, to the north, he arranges seven potsherds for the Maruts; then, having poured milk across the strainers from the north, he places it over the fire for the curdled milk (āmikṣā); then, to the north, he arranges a single potsherd for Heaven and Earth. They kindle the potsherds and they heat the cooking vessels.

Having prepared and ground the flour, he pours it out and mixes it, then covers it; he places an eight-potherd cake for Agni across the strainer, pours the grains for the Soma-oblation into the pot, and then covers it; he places a twelve-potherd cake for Savitṛ across the strainer, pours the grains for Sarasvatī and Pūṣan into the pot, and then covers it; he places a seven-potherd cake for the Maruts across the strainer; he pours curds into heated milk, which becomes the *sāmicī* (clotted curd).

Whosoever is skilled [in this] cooks it by thoroughly kindling the fire, removes the fat, and places it where there is no heat; then he piles [the earth] over it with the formula, "To Heaven and Earth, one cake on one potsherd.
Having caused the skin of the sacrificial cakes to be taken up, having cooked them, and having covered them, he goes eastward, pours out water for the Āpyas, and performs the *stambayajus* rite.
This is well known as the procedure for the sacrificial cakes (*pauroḍāśika*): he recites the formula three times and silently a fourth time; he performs the first tracing of the altar.
The *karana* formula; he mutters it, digs up [the earth], and from what has been dug up, the *āgnīdhra* carries away the earth three times.

When the *āgnīdhra* has carried it away three times, then, having performed the second tracing of the altar, having leveled it, and having fixed the wooden sword (*sphya*) across [the altar], he issues the call: "Place the sprinkling waters; set down the fuel and the sacrificial grass; cleanse the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) and the offering-ladles (*sruc*); silently prepare the vessel for the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*); gird the wife; and bring the clarified butter and the curds! When the sprinkling waters have been brought, he throws away the wooden sword, purifies them, sets down the fuel and the sacrificial grass, turns to the right, hastens back toward the west, and [takes] the dipping-spoon and the offering-ladles.
He cleanses the vessel for the speckled butter silently.

He girds the wife with the cord. Having risen, he purifies the clarified butter and the sprinkling waters with both curds and clarified butter. Having taken the portions of clarified butter along with the speckled butter in the prescribed manner, he stands up with the sprinkling waters and sprinkles the fuel and sprinkles the altar.
He sprinkles the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
Having sprinkled the sacrificial grass that has been placed down and having poured water over it, he takes up the *prastara* bundle from the front, consisting of young shoots.

Having spread the threefold sacrificial grass, holding the *prastara* in his hand, he moves forward to the east and lays down the enclosing sticks made of *kārṣmarya* wood; he places two fuel-sticks upright.
He places the two *vidhṛti*s crosswise;

upon the two *vidhṛti*s he places the *prasūmaya* grass-bundle; on the *prasūmaya* bundle the *juhū* ladle; and the other ladles on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Having touched them all together with the formula, "These have sat down," he turns to the right, hastens back toward the west, and takes down the oblations in their proper order: the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśas*), which have been spread with a base of butter and sprinkled over, and the cooked rice-porridges (*carus*), after having sprinkled them with butter.

It is well known that from the *māruta* [oblation], one draws out the *āmikṣā* into either the *kaṃsa* or the *camasa*, pours the *vājina* over it, and then sprinkles it with [clarified butter]. Then, having removed the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) and brought it forward, he turns its back upward. Then, having taken hold of these [offerings] together, he places them within the altar (*antarvedi*) with these *vyāhṛti*s: "Bhūḥ! Bhuvaḥ! Suvaḥ! As for the *vājina*, he places it either on the rubbish-heap (*utkara*) or in the open space.
Then, according to the procedure for the fire-drilled (*nirmanthya*) oblation, he proceeds with the fire-drilled oblation, having cast it into the fire and offered it.
Then, taking a fuel-stick from the faggot, he says, "Recite for the fire being kindled," and he places the faggot on the fire, leaving one stick aside.

He fans the fire with the *vedā* grass-bundle; when the *sāmidhenī* verses have been recited, he pours the *āghāra* libation with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), and after it has been wiped clean, he pours the second libation with the two offering-spoons (*sruc*).
Then, without touching the two offering-spoons, having stepped across toward the north and having anointed the *dhruvā* with the *juhū*, and having set down the two spoons, he chooses the *pravara*.
He chooses the *hotṛ* in the established manner;
the *hotṛ* sits down.
He awaits the impulse;
once impelled, having taken up the two offering-ladles and stepped across, he calls for the *āśrāvaṇa* and says, "Recite the offering-verse for the *samidhs*.
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the oblation. Saying "Recite, recite," he pours together [the butter] at the fourth and eighth [recitations]; at the eighth, he pours out the entire remainder.

Having performed the nine *prayāja* offerings, he steps out toward the north and, with the residue of the oblation, successively sprinkles the sacrificial portions (*havīṃṣi*). Then he proceeds with the two *ājyabhāga* offerings for Agni and Soma, and thereafter he proceeds with the sacrificial portions in their regular order.

Having announced, "Recite for the Viśvedevas from the Mārutas; sacrifice to the Viśvedevas," he proceeds with the *āmikṣā*. He proceeds silently with the cake on one potsherd. Having announced, "Recite for Heaven and Earth; sacrifice to Heaven and Earth," he then proceeds with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. At this point, he throws these stirring-sticks (*mekṣaṇas*) into the Āhavanīya fire. Then he makes an oblation over them with the remnants of the ghee. Then, having stepped out toward the north and placed the two ladles in their proper places, he cuts off the *prāśitra* portion and then cuts off the *iḍā*. When the *iḍā* has been invoked, he places it for the Agnīdhra. They consume the six-fold portion.
They cleanse themselves; then he says, "Carry the *prāśitra* to the Brahman.
They carry the *prāśitra* around, followed by water and the Brahman’s portion with the *veda*;
then he asks for the *anvāhārya*.

Into that [fire] he gives the first-born calf; they take down this sacrificial remnant and set aside the whey (*vājina*). Then the Adhvaryu issues the call: "O Brahman, we shall proceed; O Āgnīdh, having placed the fuel-stick, cleanse the fires once each. Then the Adhvaryu, having divided the speckled butter and poured it into the *juhū* ladle, steps across, calls for the *śrauṣaṭ*, and says, "Sacrifice to the gods! (*devān yaja*).

When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers the oblation. Having performed nine after-offerings (*anūyāja*) with the calls "Sacrifice! Sacrifice!", he steps out toward the north, sets the two offering-spoons (*sruk*) in their proper places, and separates the two spoons with the two *vājavatī* verses.

Having scattered the *prastara* and the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) together with the *śaṃyu* formula, having poured out the remnants from the spoons, and having released them, he then asks for either a wooden cup (*kaṃsa*) or a bowl (*camasa*) that is not smeared with clarified butter.

Having placed it within the altar (*antarvedi*), while pouring the *vājina* (the whey) into it upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he says, "Recite for the *vājins*. Having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Sacrifice to the *vājins*!"

When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers with "To the Vājins, svāhā! Having offered when the *anuvaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he carries away the portion for consumption. Having sought permission from as many officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) as there are, the sacrificer alone consumes it directly, saying: "Whatever semen of mine is shed, whatever of mine increases, or whatever is born again, or whatever of mine is firmly established—with that, make me vigorous; with that, make me possessed of semen; with that, enter me auspiciously. Of thee, who art drunk by the Vājins, who art drunk by the Vājins—of thee, the honeyed, being invited, I, invited, consume."

Then the Adhvaryu, having turned to the right, having run back toward the west, having performed the offerings for the wives (*patnīsaṃyāja*), and having gone eastward and replenished the *dhruvā* ladle, offers three *samiṣṭayajus* oblations pertaining to the animal sacrifice with the formulas: "O Sacrifice, go to the Sacrifice; this is thy sacrifice, O Lord of Sacrifice; O Gods who know the way. Then, having proceeded with the full-vessel rite and the *viṣṇukrama* steps, he releases his vow.

Then, having performed the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha sacrifices and sitting in the sacrificer’s station, he has his hair cut and shaved all around with a three-striped porcupine quill and a razor of red-hot iron: "The *Ṛta* alone is the Supreme Lord; nothing whatsoever transcends the *Ṛta*. Upon the *Ṛta* the ocean is established; upon the *Ṛta* this earth rests. With sharp flame, Agni has overcome the heat with the *uṣṇihā*; the head is placed within the heat by the splendor of Vaiśvānara. By the *Ṛta* I cut it off; by the Truth I shave it around."

"By means of austerity I follow after him; by means of what is auspicious I turn toward him; by means of what is beneficial I advance toward him. That is the Order (ṛta) of the head, that is the Truth (satya), that is the Vow (vrata); may I be able to perform that, may I be capable through that, may I prosper through that"—thus [he says] first toward the east, then toward the south, then toward the west, then toward the north, and then from above.
The Vaiśvadeva oblations are concluded with the words, "He prays for the well-being of the year-long [sacrifice]," and thus he prays.
Now, therefore, when he is about to sacrifice with the Varuṇapraghāsa oblations four months later, he procures the following:

a three-striped porcupine quill, a razor of red iron, four potsherds for the sacrificial cakes, five cooking-pots for the rice-mash, as many stirring-sticks, two portions of milk—one for the speckled butter and one for curdling the oblation—and *śamī* leaves, *karīra* fruits, and barley-meal; a winnowing-basket made of reeds; and for each person, including one extra, vessels of *karambha* (barley-flour mixed with curd) made from slightly parched barley ground with their husks remaining.
From these same materials, they fashion a ewe and a ram.
The ram has horns and the ewe is hornless;
they are both covered with white wool. There are two Adhvaryu priests and two sets of sacrificial vessels.
There are two sets of fuel-sticks and sacrificial grass, and two altars;
of these, the northern one is like that for the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), and the southern one is like that for the new- and full-moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).

These two altars are level toward the west and uneven toward the east, separated by a distance of a span (*pr̥tha*). On this day, moreover, the calves are driven away from their mothers in two groups: those for the Maruts and those for Varuṇa.

Having caused two cows to be milked for the *sāṃnāyya*—either according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya* or silently—he observes the fast. Then, in the morning, after the *agnihotra* has been offered, having spread the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and led forward the waters, he pours out the oblations: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, and so on, the five "moving" offerings; a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra-Agni, clotted curds (*āmikṣā*) for the Maruts, clotted curds for Varuṇa, and a cake on one potsherd for Ka. At the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), he releases his speech. The ritual procedure is the same up to the carrying of fire around the offerings (*paryagnikaraṇa*). At this point, they carry fire around these: the *karambha* vessels, the ewe and the ram, the *śamī* leaves, the flour of *karīra* fruits, and a winnowing basket made of reeds.

Having caused the sacrificial cakes to take on their crusts, having cooked them, and having covered them, he goes eastward; having poured out water for the *āpyas*, the two of them carry away the *stambayajus*—the Adhvaryu carries it away on the northern altar and the Pratiprasthātṛ on the southern one. Of these two carrying it away, the Adhvaryu goes first; of the two returning, the Pratiprasthātṛ goes first. This well-known procedure of the cake-offering (*pauroḍāśika*) is performed: three times with the formula and the fourth time silently. They perform the two preliminary enclosures (*parigrāha*), and the Adhvaryu alone mutters the *karaṇa* formula. Once the earth has been dug up, the Āgnīdhra carries away the dust from the two dug-up spots three times.

When the Āgnīdhra carries [the earth] three times, the Adhvaryu alone, according to the procedure for the *cātvāla*, traces around the *cātvāla*; according to the procedure for the *uttaravedi*, he pours out the *uttaravedi*; having set aside the *uttaranābhi*, the two [priests] lead forward the two fires according to the procedure for the fire: the Adhvaryu, having placed the fire on the northern altar, makes offerings over it with the *adhvara* oblations;
the Pratiprasthātṛ, having placed the fire on the southern [altar], makes offerings over it silently.

Having performed the two subsequent enclosures with the formula containing the word *agni*, having leveled [the ground] and fixed the wooden sword (*sphya*) crosswise, the Adhvaryu alone issues the call: "Place the sprinkling waters; set down the fuel and the sacrificial grass; cleanse the *sruva* and the *sruk* ladles; silently [cleanse] the vessel for the speckled butter; gird the wife; and come forward with the clarified butter and the curds. When the sprinkling waters have been brought, he throws away the two wooden swords, purifies them, sets down the fuel and the sacrificial grass, turns to the right, moves back toward the west, and cleanses the *sruva* and the *sruk* ladles, as well as the vessel for the speckled butter silently.

The Adhvaryu should cause the wife to gird herself with two portions of clarified butter and curds; having purified the clarified butter and the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling waters, the Adhvaryu takes the clarified butter together with the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) on the northern altar, while the Pratiprasthātṛ takes the materials for the New and Full Moon sacrifices on the southern altar. Then, rising up with the *prokṣaṇī* waters, they sprinkle the two fuel-sticks (*idhma*), sprinkle the two altars, and sprinkle the two bundles of sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Having sprinkled the sacrificial grass that has been placed down and poured water over it, they take the two *prastara* bundles from the front.
The Adhvaryu spreads fivefold sacrificial grass on the northern altar, and the Pratiprasthātṛ spreads it threefold on the southern one.

Then, moving forward with the prastara-bunches in their hands, they lay the enclosing sticks made of *kārṣmarya* wood around the fires; they place the fuel-sticks upright and the separating blades crosswise, and they set down the prastara-bunches upon the separating blades.

Having touched them together with the formula, "The two Juhū-ladles have sat upon the two Prastaras; the others upon the two Barhis-grasses," they turn to the right and run back westward—the Adhvaryu from the south and the Pratiprasthātṛ from the north. They take down the oblations in order: the Adhvaryu takes down those beginning with the one for Agni; the offering for Indra-Agni and that for the Maruts are well-known. Having scooped out the curdled milk (āmikṣā) into either a vessel or a cup, the Pratiprasthātṛ places the ewe therein, and then he pours into it the śamī-leaves, karīra-fruits, groats, and the curdled milk.
Having brought the whey (*vājina*), the Adhvaryu then pours it over [the mixture].

In the same manner, having drawn out the curd (*āmikṣā*) into either a vessel (*kaṃsa*) or a cup (*camasa*), he places a ram into it. Then he scatters for him the *śamī* leaves, the flour of *karīra* fruits, and the curd;
having brought the whey, he then pours it over.

Having removed the cake on one potsherd in that same manner and having brought much [fuel], he makes it with its back exposed. Then, taking hold of these [cakes], they place them within the altar. The Adhvaryu places those beginning with the one for Agni on the northern altar; the Pratiprasthātṛ places the one for Indra-Agni and the one for the Maruts in the established manner; the Adhvaryu places the one for Varuṇa on the southern altar, and the one for Ka on the northern altar. Likewise, regarding the whey—whether in the *utkara* or in the *viśaya*—the Adhvaryu alone performs the rite with the churned butter according to the procedure for churning, having cast it into the fire and offered it.
Then, taking a fuel-stick from the faggot, he says, "Recite for the fire being kindled," and places two fuel-sticks upon it, leaving two remaining.

They fan the fires with the two *vedas*. When the *sāmidhenī* verses have been recited, the two of them pour the two *āghāra* libations using the *sruva* ladles. The Adhvaryu alone issues the command: "O Āgnīdh, wipe the fire three times each!
Once wiped, the northern fire becomes purified, while the southern remains unwiped. Then the Pratiprasthātṛ asks the wife, "Wife, who is your lover? She replies, "Such-and-such."
"Let Varuṇa seize him," he points out;

for if he were not to name the paramour who is there, he would obstruct a dear kinsman. "He should point him out, saying, 'This one is my paramour'; by pointing him out, he causes him to be seized by the noose of Varuṇa"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.

At this point, having performed the *paryagnikaraṇa* rite around these vessels of groats (*karambhapātra*), he places them together in a winnowing basket made of *aiṣīka* grass and hands them to the wife.

The wife places those [pots] upon her head. Then, having caused her to go out by the southern door and having gone around both altars to the south of the Anvāhāryapacana fire, while leading her eastward, he makes her recite: "We invoke the Praghāsya Maruts, the carriers of the sacrifice, who are well-pleased with the *karambha*. Then, standing in front of the southern fire facing west—the Adhvaryu on the north, the Sacrificer on the south, and the wife on the south—he hands these *karambha* vessels from the wife to the Sacrificer.

The sacrificer places those [stalks] upon his head; then he recites the invitatory verse (*puro’nuvākyā*): "O Indra, do not strike us in battles, O God; may we be thy partakers, O Mighty One, for great indeed is the bounty of this Bounteous One. The song of the one possessing oblations lauds the Maruts. Then both the offering verse (*yājyā*) and the wife [recite]: "Whatever sin we have committed in the village, whatever in the forest, whatever in the assembly, whatever in our senses, whatever toward a Śūdra or an Ārya, whatever under the law of another—this is the expiation for that, Svāhā! At this point, he throws the winnowing basket made of *eṣīkā* grass into the fire, or alternatively, having sprinkled it with water, they consume it.

Moving apart, the Adhvaryu consecrates them with the mantra: "O performers of the rite, you have performed the rite well, together with speech that brings bliss; having performed the rite for the gods, go to your home, O bounteous ones. Then the Pratiprasthātṛ cleanses the southern fire; both pour the two libations (āghāra) into the ladles, and the Adhvaryu alone chooses the *pravara*.
He chooses the Hotṛ in the established manner, and the Hotṛ sits down.

Desiring the impulse for procreation, having taken up the two offering-spoons at the time of the birth [of the sacrifice], having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Recite the offering-verse for the *samidhs*.
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, they both offer. Saying "Recite, recite," they offer at the fourth and eighth [verses]. At the eighth, the Adhvaryu pours out the entire remainder.

The Pratiprasthātṛ retains the remnants for the after-offerings (*anūyāja*s). Having performed nine fore-offerings (*prayāja*), he steps out toward the north, and having stepped across, both [the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ] successively pour clarified butter over the oblations (*havīṃṣi*) using the two remnants. The Adhvaryu pours over those beginning with the one for Agni; the Aindrāgnī and Mārutī are well-known;
the Pratiprasthātṛ [pours over] the Vāruṇī, and the Adhvaryu [pours over] the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) for Ka.

Then they proceed with the two butter-portions (ājyabhāga) for Agni and Soma; then the Pratiprasthātṛ desists; then the Adhvaryu proceeds in due order with the oblations starting from that for Indra-Agni; then the Adhvaryu desists; then the Pratiprasthātṛ, while taking portions for the Maruts, says, "Recite the invitatory verse for the Maruts!
With the first portion he takes portions of *śamī* leaves, *karīra* fruits, groats, and curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*);
with the second portion he places *śamī* leaves, *karīra* fruits, groats, the curd-mixture, and a ewe, and pours clarified butter over them.
Having stepped across and caused the announcement to be made, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for the Maruts.

At the *vaṣaṭ* call, he makes the offering. Then the Pratiprasthātṛ stops. Then the Adhvaryu, while taking a portion from the oblation for Varuṇa, says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for Varuṇa," and with the first portion he takes portions of *śamī* leaves, jujube fruit, parched flour, and curdled milk.

With the second cutting, he places the *śamī* leaf, the *karīra* fruit, the groats, the *āmikṣā*, and the ram; he sprinkles them with clarified butter, anoints them back, steps across, causes the announcement to be made, and says, "Sacrifice to Varuṇa. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering. He proceeds with the cake on one potsherd for Upāṃśu, saying, "Recite for Ka," and "Sacrifice to Ka. Then they proceed with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; the Adhvaryu cuts portions from the offerings beginning with that for Agni, while the Pratiprasthātṛ cuts the portion for Indra-Agni and the portion for Māruta in the established manner.

The Adhvaryu pours clarified butter twice over the vessel for Varuṇī and the cake on one potsherd; he does not turn back, but having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt."

When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, they offer two oblations, bypassing the previous offerings, in the eastern halves of the northern parts [of the fires]. At this point, they throw these stirring-sticks (*mekṣaṇa*) after [the offerings] into the Āhavanīya fires. Then they make offerings over them with the two remnants of the ladles. Then, having stepped out toward the north and set down the two ladles in their proper places, he cuts off the *prāśitra* portion and then cuts off the *iḍā*. The Adhvaryu cuts portions for those [deities] beginning with Agni; the Pratiprasthātṛ [cuts] for the one belonging to Indra-Agni, and the Adhvaryu [cuts] for the one belonging to Māruta and Varuṇa in the established manner. He pours clarified butter over the cake baked on a single potsherd (*ekakapāla*). Then the Pratiprasthātṛ approaches the northern altar (*uttaravedi*).

When the *iḍā* has been invoked, he places [the portion] for the *āgnīdhra*; they consume it in six portions and perform the ritual purification (*mārjana*). Then he says, "Carry around the *prāśitra* for the *brahman*";
they carry the *prāśitra* around, followed by water and the *brahman’s* portion with the *veda*-grass bundle.
Then he asks for the *anvāhārya* rice; into it he gives as much as he pleases. They remove that sacrificial remnant and set aside the two portions of whey (*vājina*).

The Adhvaryu alone gives the summons: "O Brahman, we shall proceed; O Āgnīdh, having placed a fuel-stick, cleanse the fires once each. Then the Adhvaryu, having divided the speckled butter and poured it into the *juhū* ladle, steps across, calls for the *śrauṣaṭ*, and says, "Sacrifice to the gods! At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, they both sacrifice. Having performed nine after-offerings (*anūyāja*s) with the calls "Sacrifice! Sacrifice!", he steps across toward the north, sets the two ladles down in their proper places, separates the two ladles with the two *vājavatī* verses, scatters the *prastara* grass-bundle and the enclosing sticks together with the *śaṃyu* formula, pours out the remnants from the ladles, and releases the ladles.
In the same way, they ask for two vessels or cups that have not been smeared with clarified butter. The procedure for the whey (*vājina*) is the same.

The Adhvaryu alone, having turned to the right, hastened westward, performed the *saṃyāja* offerings to the wives, and having gone eastward, replenished the *dhruvā* ladle; he then offers three *samiṣṭayajus* oblations pertaining to the animal sacrifice, while the Pratiprasthātṛ offers one pertaining to the New and Full Moon sacrifices in the southern fire. Then, having performed the rites with the full-vessel water and the *viṣṇukrama* steps, he does not release his vow.

Then he asks for the vessel of clarified butter together with the *sruva*-ladle, the *sruk*-ladle, sacrificial grass, two garments for wearing, the dregs of the offering to Varuṇa, and the husks; having taken all this, he says, "Come, O sacrificer! The sacrificer follows behind him, and the wife follows behind the sacrificer. Having gone out northward between the *cātvāla* pit and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), they go to where there is water.

The *avabhṛtha* rite is performed in the established manner, except that he does not recite the *Sāman* chant nor the formula, "O divine waters, this is your embryo. Then they return without looking back, in order to remain hidden from Varuṇa.

On the road, while preparing the fuel sticks, he says, "Thou art fuel; may we prosper through thee," and having arrived, he places them on the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "Thou art a fuel stick; thou art brilliance; bestow brilliance upon me. Then they stand in worship before the Āhavanīya with the verse: "I have followed the waters; we have united with their essence. O Agni, I have come full of milk; unite me with splendor. At this point, he releases his vow.

Then, having performed the Full Moon sacrifice and the Vaimṛdha offering, he sits upon the sacrificer’s seat and, with a three-striped porcupine quill and a razor of red-hot iron, he has his hair trimmed at the front and shaved all around, [reciting]: "When the Gharma turned around the teeth of the earth and of heaven, Agni, ruling by his might, Varuṇa together with the prayers, Indra with his friends the Maruts—Agni with his sharp flame, the heat, the *uṣṇihā* verse, and the head were placed upon the ascetic heat by the splendor of Vaiśvānara."

"By the *ṛta* I turn him back; by the *satya* I turn him around; by *tapas* I follow after him; by the auspicious (*śiva*) I bring him near; by the beneficial (*śagma*) I turn him toward me. "That is the *ṛta* of his head, that is the *satya*, that is the vow (*vrata*), may I be able to perform that; through that may I be able, through that may I prosper"—thus [they proceed] first to the east, then to the south, then to the west, then to the north, and finally above;
thus the Varuṇapraghāsa oblations are concluded. "May he pray for well-being for the coming year"—thus he prays.

Now, therefore, when he is about to sacrifice with the Sākamedha oblations after four months have passed, he procures a three-striped porcupine quill, a razor of red iron, four sets of potsherds for the sacrificial cakes, four cooking-pots for the rice-messes, as many stirring-sticks, curds for the speckled butter, and then, on the day of preparation for the full moon, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Anīkavant; that well-known sacrifice concludes with the rising of the sun together with the sun. Then, at midday, he offers a rice-mess to the Maruts Sāṃtapanas.

That well-known sacrifice is concluded. Then, on this day, the calves are driven away from their mothers for the Gṛhamedhin Maruts. When the evening Agnihotra has been offered, having cooked the Gṛhamedhīya rice-pap (caru) in the milk of all the cows over the Gārhapatya fire, he pours clarified butter over it and removes it toward the north. Then, having washed that vessel and spread a layer of ghee in it, he draws out the pap into it as if without crushing it.

Having made a hollow for pouring the clarified butter and having poured in abundant ghee, he places it within the altar. Then he proceeds with the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), [saying] "To Agni" and "To Soma."
Then, having spread an underlayer of clarified butter, while taking a portion from the eastern half of the *caru*, he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for the Maruts, the Gṛhamedhins.
Having taken the portion from the eastern half, he takes a portion from the western half, pours clarified butter over it, and replenishes the spot from which the portion was taken.
Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ* cry, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for the Maruts, the Gṛhamedhins."
When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he makes the offering; then he proceeds with the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation. The *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice concludes with the *iḍā*.
He leaves over the residue from the scraping of the cooking vessel for the *pūrṇadarvya* offering.
They cook food for the neighbors, women, and children. Having eaten, they anoint themselves and smear themselves with oil; they let the calves stay with their mothers.

On this very night, they tie up the calf of a cow that has a calf of its own. Then, the Adhvaryu, having hastened there in the latter part of the night, offers the Agnihotra with the milk from a cow that has its own calf. Having cleansed this ladle and spread an underlayer of ghee in it, he places all of this [the scrapings] into it, making it as smooth as possible;

he pours ghee over it twice. Then he recites the invitatory verse: "O ladle, fly away full; fly back again well-filled. Let us barter for it like merchandise—food and strength, O Lord of a Hundred Powers!"

He sacrifices with the formula: "Sacrifice! Give to me; I give to thee. Bestow upon me; I bestow upon thee. Bring to me what is brought to me; I bring to thee what is brought. He should sacrifice at the bellowing of the bull with the words, "O Bull, come!"—for this is the *hiṃkāra* of the Brahman. This is another [offering]: he sacrifices in the *gārhapatya* fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, saying "Svāhā! Then, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the waters, he offers a cake on seven potsherds to the sporting Maruts, simultaneously with the rising of the sun.

That well-known *iṣṭi* is concluded; then, at that very time, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the waters, he offers the five *saṃcara* oblations: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra-Agni, a pap for Indra, and a cake on one potsherd for Viśvakarman. Having caused the cakes to form a crust, having baked them, and having covered them, he goes eastward, pours out water for the *āpyas*, and performs the *stambayajus* rite. This is the well-known procedure of the *pauroḍāśika* section: he recites the formula three times and silently a fourth time; he performs the first tracing of the altar.
He mutters the *karaṇa* formula; he digs up [the earth]; from what has been dug up, the Āgnīdhra carries it away three times.

When the Āgnīdhra has carried it away three times, then, according to the procedure for the *cātvāla*, he traces around the *cātvāla*. According to the procedure for the *uttaravedi*, he pours out the *uttaravedi*. Having leveled the *uttaranābhi*, according to the procedure for the fire, he leads forward the fire. Having performed the second tracing of the altar, having leveled it, and having fixed the wooden sword (*sphya*) across, he issues the call: "Set down the sprinkling waters; place the fuel and the sacrificial grass; cleanse the *sruva* and the *sruk* ladles; silently prepare the vessel for the speckled butter; gird the wife; [prepare] the clarified butter and the curds."

When the *prokṣaṇī* waters have been brought with the call "Codehi" (Come here), he cleanses the wooden sword (*sphya*), places the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmā-barhis*) down, turns to the right, and having stepped back toward the west, he cleanses the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) and the offering-ladles (*sruc*). He silently cleanses the vessel for the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya-grahaṇī*). Having girded the wife, he goes out with the clarified butter and the curds. Having purified the clarified butter and the *prokṣaṇī* waters, the rite concludes in the established manner, just as the *vaiśvadeva* oblations do, except for the whey-offering (*vājina*). Then, having performed the *pūrṇapātra* and the *viṣṇukrama* steps, he does not release his vow.

Intending to perform the Mahāpitṛyajña, he prepares rice and barley, six potsherds, milk from a cow that suckles another's calf, a half-vessel, two new vessels, a stalk of sugarcane, three leaf-cups, sacrificial grass with its roots, a large kindling-stick, the enclosure for the fuel, a mattress and a pillow, collyrium and ointment, a fringe, a wooden sword, two water-pitchers, and the sacrificial implements; then he strews grass around the Gārhapatya fire.

To the north of that, he places each item separately: a cushion and a pillow, collyrium and ointment, a fringe, the wooden sword (sphya), two water-pitchers, and the sacrificial implements; then, having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder, he sits down to the north of the Gārhapatya fire and, using the Agnihotra-ladle provided with strainers, pours out the oblation with the formula:

"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour thee out, acceptable to Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs. He pours out four handfuls of rice with this same introductory formula, saying: "I pour thee out, acceptable to the Pitṛs seated on the Barhis," and likewise four handfuls of barley.

Having performed this very same procedure, [he says] "I offer what is pleasing to the Agniṣvātta ancestors," and takes four barley grains; he causes the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*) to be raised over the rice grains themselves. They lift up the barley grains, and at the call of the preparer of the oblation, he releases his speech. The ritual action is the same up to the pouring [of the grains]; having poured them, he places six potsherds on the southern half of the Gārhapatya fire-altar. Then, having crushed these barley grains in a mortar, and having placed a single potsherd on the Gārhapatya fire, they roast them.
Having made the grains multiform, half of those grains remain as grains while they turn the others into groats;
having poured together the prepared and ground [grains], he mixes them and places the cake on six potsherds.

Then, having drawn out embers mixed with ashes toward the north and placed a new vessel upon them, he pours clarified butter across the strainer and throws the grains across the strainer. Then he asks for a half-vessel of milk from a cow that has recently calved.

Having poured groats upon that [fire] across the strainer, he stirs it with a single cane-splinter; "He stirs from the right, he stirs without grasping," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Then, having drawn out embers mixed with ashes from the north, he places [the vessel] over them.
Having caused the sacrificial cake to take on its skin and having sprinkled it, he pours out the water for the Apya deities right here.
To the south, this level mound has been prepared;
there he draws this square altar (vedi), but he does not dig it.
Having kindled the Anvāhāryapacana fire in the middle of that [altar], he performs the Stambayajus rite;

this is the well-known procedure for the cake-offering (pauroḍāśika), performed three times with the Yajus formula and silently a fourth time. He performs the first tracing of the altar, mutters the Karaṇa formula, digs up the earth, and from what has been dug up, the Āgnīdhra carries away the earth three times.

When the Āgnīdhra has carried [the earth] three times, [the Adhvaryu], having performed the second tracing of the altar, having leveled it, and having fixed the wooden sword (sphya) across [the altar], issues the call: "Set down the sprinkling waters; place the fuel and the sacrificial grass; cleanse the dipping-spoon (sruva) and the offering-ladles (sruc); bring the clarified butter! When the sprinkling waters have been brought, he throws away the wooden sword, purifies it, places the fuel and the sacrificial grass, turns to the right, hastens back toward the west, and cleanses the dipping-spoon and the offering-ladles; then he goes out with the clarified butter, and having purified both the clarified butter and the sprinkling waters—
Having taken the clarified butter that has been prepared— either fivefold or sixfold portions— he rises with the sprinkling waters; he sprinkles the fuel,
he sprinkles the altar,
and he sprinkles the sacrificial grass.

Having sprinkled the sacrificial grass (barhis) that has been placed down and having poured water over it, he takes up the prastara-bunch together with its roots from the front part [of the grass] silently.
Then, having shifted his sacred cord over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta), he goes around three times from left to right while spreading the grass,
first more closely together and then more widely apart.

Then, having again put on the sacrificial thread in the same manner as before, he goes around three times in the opposite direction; then, with the *prastara* bundle in his hand, he lays down two enclosing sticks—the middle one and the southern one—and places two fuel-sticks upright. He sets down the two *vidhṛti* grass-blades crosswise.
He silently places the *prastara* grass-bundle together with its roots upon the two *vidhṛti* separators;

he places the *juhū* ladle on the *prastara*, and the other two ladles (*upabhṛt* and *dhruvā*) on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Having touched them all together with the formula, "These have sat down," he turns to the right, runs back toward the west, and takes down the oblations in their proper order: having sprinkled the cake (*puroḍāśa*) which has been spread with a base of ghee and poured over it, he then sprinkles the parched grains (*dhānāḥ*) and the groat-mash (*karambha*).
They cite these one by one in their proper sequence:

he places the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) to the south, the parched grains (dhānā) to the north, and the groats (karambha) to the north; to the south, he sets down this enclosure, the cushion and pillow, the eye-salve and ointment, the fringe of the garment, and the wooden sword (sphya). To the north, he places two water-jars.
To the south sit the Brahman and the sacrificer; to the north, the Adhvaryu and the Agnīdh.

Then, taking a fuel-stick from the faggot, he says, "Recite for Agni, for the gods, and for the fathers, as he is being kindled. He places the faggot [on the fire] once or thrice, leaving one stick remaining; he fans it with the *vedā* grass-bundle, and when the *sāmidhenī* verses have been recited, he pours the *āghāra* libation with the *sruva* spoon.

Having wiped the two offering-ladles (sruk) together from top to bottom, then moving northward without letting the two ladles touch each other, having anointed the *dhruvā* with the *juhū*, and having set down the two ladles, he chooses the *pravara*. Then he causes the announcement to be made: "O announce! Let it be heard! May Agni, the divine Hotṛ, worship the gods and the Pitṛs; may he sit. This much is the *pravara*;
the Hotṛ sits down.
He awaits the impulse; once impelled,

having taken up the two offering-spoons, stepped across, and caused the announcement to be made, he says, "Recite the offering-verse for the fuel-sticks," and offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.

Having offered four *prayāja* oblations, omitting the one for the *barhis*, with the call "Sacrifice! Sacrifice!", he steps northward and pours clarified butter over the oblation-materials (*haviṣ*) in their proper sequence using the residue of the offering-ladle.

Then he proceeds with the two *ājyabhāga* portions for Agni and Soma. Having stepped northward again and placed the two ladles in their respective places, they put on their sacred threads over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*).
Turning around, these officiating priests exchange positions; he places the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) to the north.

To the south is the vessel for the groats; parched grains are placed to the north. The Brahman and the Sacrificer sit down to the north, while the Adhvaryu and the Āgnīdhra sit to the south. Then they enclose it, making the door on the northern side.
He who is the strongest among them, taking a water-pitcher, goes around three times from left to right, sprinkling a continuous stream;

he does so accordingly, having set down the pitcher, returning three times again by the same way as he came, and then, having spread an underlayer of ghee, while cutting off a portion from the eastern half of the sacrificial cake, he says:
With the formula, "To Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs, svadhā!

he cuts portions from the eastern half of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), from the eastern half of the parched grains (dhānāḥ), and from the eastern half of the groat-mash (karambha); he then pours clarified butter over them.

He anoints [the offering] after having cut off the portion from the south; he steps across toward the north with "Oṃ svadhā!"; having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, the *adhvaryu* responds with "Let there be *svadhā*!"; [the *hotṛ* then says] "Make *svadhā* for Soma accompanied by the fathers!"
Having uttered "svadhā" as the āgūra, or "svadhāmaha," or "svadhā namaḥ," he pronounces the vaṣaṭ;
when the vaṣaṭ has been pronounced, he makes the offering.
Then, having spread an underlayer of ghee, while taking a portion from the middle of the roasted grains, he says, "Recite for the Barhiṣat Pitṛs: Svadhā!
He takes a portion from the middle of the roasted grains and from the middle of the groats.
He pours clarified butter over the middle of the sacrificial cake,
anoints it back,
cuts a portion from the south side, steps across toward the north, causes the announcement to be made with "O Svadha!", and receives the response with "Let there be Svadha!"
"For the Pitṛs seated on the sacrificial grass, Svadhā!"—
having thus made the *āgū* call, saying either "Ye svadhā! or "We [offer] svadhā," he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call as "Svadhā namaḥ."

When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he makes the offering. Then, having spread an underlayer of ghee, while cutting a portion from the rear half of the *karambha*, he says, "For the *agniṣvātta* fathers, *anu svadhā*! He cuts a portion from the rear half of the *karambha*, from the rear half of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and from the rear half of the parched grains (*dhānā*). He pours clarified butter over them and anoints the place from which the portions were taken.
Having cut the portions from the right side, he steps across toward the north; he causes the announcement to be made with "O Svadhā! and the response is given with "Let there be Svadhā!";
he says, "Make the Svadhā-offering for the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs," and they respond with "Yes, Svadhā! or "We [accept] the Svadhā!"
He utters *vaṣaṭ* with the words "Svadhā! Homage!

and when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he makes the offering. Then, having spread an underlayer of ghee, while cutting off a portion from the southern half of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt; svadhā!
and he cuts off a portion from the southern half of the sacrificial cake.
From the southern half of the grains and from the southern half of the karambha,
he pours clarified butter twice; he does not re-anoint them.

Having cut off the portions from the south, he steps across to the north, saying "O Svadhā! He causes the announcement to be made with "Let there be Svadhā! The response is "Let there be Svadhā! [He offers] to Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, saying "Make the Svadhā!
Having uttered the *āgūr* formula "Ye Svadhā! or "Ye Svadhāmaha!
or "Svadhā Namaḥ!", he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call.

When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers [the oblation] in the eastern part of the southern half, passing over the previous offerings; at this point, he throws the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) and the splinter (*śalākā*) into the fire, and then pours the residue (*saṃsrāva*) over them. Then, having stepped across to the south and placed the two ladles (*srucau*) in their proper places, they put on their sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*).
Turning around, these officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) exchange the sacrificial foods; he places the cake (*puroḍāśa*) to the south.
To the north is the porridge (karambha) and the parched grains (dhānā) are indeed placed;
to the south sit the Brahman and the sacrificer, while to the north are the Adhvaryu and the Āgnīdhra; then, having cut off the Prāśitra portion, he cuts off the Iḍā.

When the *iḍā* has been invoked, he places [the portion] for the *āgnīdhra*; having eaten it with the *nidhana*, they deposit it on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Then, having placed their sacred threads over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), he mixes together the sacrificial cake, the parched grains, and the groats in a vessel.
He gives three balls at the three corners of the pits containing the leaf-fragments, saying: "This is for you, O father, N.N., and those who follow you," at the southern buttock of the altar.

"O grandfather, [name], and those who follow you—this for you!"—thus he wipes the smear on the right shoulder. "O great-grandfather, [name], and those who follow you—this for you!"—thus he wipes the smear on the left shoulder and on the northern hip. Having said, "This is yours; this is ours; may we, living and alive, follow after this [offering]," and "O fathers, rejoice here according to your portions," they go out toward the north, put on their sacred threads over the left shoulder (yajñopavīta), and stand before the Āhavanīya fire, saying: "O Maghavan, may we delight in you, who are so fair to behold."

"Now indeed, O you whose chariot-seat is full, being praised, you go according to your will. Harness now, O Indra, your two bay horses"—with these words they stand by [the fire] until the signal is given; then they worship the Gārhapatya fire with the verse: "They have eaten and rejoiced; they have shaken off their dear [impurities]. The inspired singers, self-luminous, have been praised with a most recent hymn. Harness now, O Indra, your two bay horses."

They stand by [the fire] until it goes out; then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta), they approach the Anvāhāryapacana fire, saying: "The fathers have eaten, the fathers have rejoiced, the fathers have been satisfied, the fathers have cleansed themselves. Depart, O Soma-loving fathers! They stand by [the fire] until it goes out. Then he who is strong says to him: "Go around, sprinkling with this water-pitcher in a continuous stream, moving three times from right to left.
He does so.

Having set down the pitcher as before, he goes around it three times again in the opposite direction. He gives a cushion and a pillow, as well as collyrium and ointment, for the sake of pleasure at the bringing [of the offerings]. Then he gives garments. Then he worships with six salutations in reverse order. Then he asks for a hero. Then, having raised them up and carried them out, he invokes the mind with three verses: "We call the mind hither," "May our mind come back to us," and "O fathers, give us back our mind. At this point, he throws these rice-balls together with the leaf-cups into the fire. They dismantle the enclosure.

Then they put on their sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*). Then he issues the direction: "O Brahman, we shall set forth; having placed a fuel-stick (*samidh*) [on the fire], O Āgnīdhra, cleanse the fires once each. Then, taking the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to the two gods!
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering.

Saying "Sacrifice, sacrifice," he performs two after-offerings (*anūyāja*) without the *barhis* grass. Having sacrificed, having stepped across toward the north and placed the two ladles in their respective places, he separates the two ladles with the two *vājavatī* verses.

Having scattered the *prastara* and the enclosing sticks with the *śaṃyu*-formula, having poured out the remnants from the two ladles and released them, he offers the *samiṣṭayajus* right here. Then they recite two verses each for these *śastra*s. Then, having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavīta*), they worship the Gārhapatya fire with the verse addressed to Prajāpati: "O Prajāpati, none other than you... At this point, he mutters this second verse: "That which is the mid-region, the earth, and also the sky... The Mahāpitṛyajña is thus concluded.

While the Adhvaryu is busy with his duties here, the Pratiprasthātṛ bakes the Traiyambaka cakes—one for each person, plus one extra—on a single potsherd over the Gārhapatya fire. Having baked them without pouring clarified butter over them and having removed them from the fire, he places them in a basket, a winnowing basket, or the hollow of an old leather bag, and sits waiting. Then he calls for two threads, blue and red, the last leaf [of the Palāśa tree], a firebrand from the edge of the house, and a vessel of water. Taking these things, they stand by the Gārhapatya fire, saying: "For as many as we are of the household, for them I have performed this rite; you are the refuge of cattle."
"May there be protection for the sacrificer; grant me protection," he says. Then, having gone out toward the north, they proceed in that direction where a well-known, permanent crossroads exists;
or, if such one does not exist, they depart by means of a cart or a chariot.

Having kindled that single firebrand and strewn it all around, he takes a portion from each of all the *traiyambaka* cakes at once onto a leaf placed at the edge and offers them with the formula: "Rudra is indeed one; there is no second who stands with him. O Rudra, this dog is your animal; accept it! This, O Rudra, is your share together with your sister Ambikā; accept it! A remedy for the cow, a remedy for the horse, a remedy for man—and furthermore, a remedy for us, a good remedy, so that it may be well-being for our rams and ewes. O Mother Rudrāṇī, we have appeased you."

"To the god Tryambaka—so that he may make us better, so that he may make us wealthier, so that he may make us possess cattle, so that he may incite our resolve—svāhā! At this point, he throws away the last leaf of the palāśa twig at the path where the cattle pass, directed toward him whom he hates.

If, however, he does not hate anyone, he deposits [the cakes] in a hole dug by a rat; then he hands over one of these *traiyambaka* cakes to each of them, and two to the sacrificer. Then they walk three times around this fire from left to right, striking their right thighs, [reciting]: "We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity. Like a cucumber from its stem, may I be released from death, not from immortality. Having walked around once, they stand to the north; they dig up [the cakes], saying, "For Bhaga, thee!"—desiring to obtain them. In the same way they walk around a second time, and likewise a third time.

Then she, desiring a husband, goes around three times to the left, striking her left thigh, while reciting: "We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the finder of a husband; like a cucumber from its stalk, may I be released from here, but not fall [into the next world]. Having gone around once, she stands facing the north and pulls up [a blade of grass] with the words, "For fortune (bhaga) thee! She thus desires [a husband]. In this very same way she goes around a second time, and likewise a third time.
Then he pours them into the joined palms of the sacrificer with the words,
"I unite thee with offspring, as surā with māṣara";
the sacrificer pours them into the joined palms of his wife with the words, "I unite thee with offspring and cattle, as surā with māṣara."
The wife [says], "I unite you with fortune, as one mixes *surā* with *māsara*, for my daughter who desires fortune.

Then, having poured them into a vessel and tied them together with two threads—one blue and one red—she fastens them either to a dry stump or to a forked branch, saying: "This is your portion, O Rudra; enjoy it! With this favor, pass beyond the Mūjavat mountains, with your bow unstrung and the *pināka* in your hand, clothed in a skin. They stand there until the stars appear. Then, having poured out the water, they depart, casting aside the vessel without looking back.

Having washed his hands and feet, he returns by the same way he came and, having returned, offers a *caru* oblation to Aditya. "Aditi is indeed this [earth]; it is upon her that they find firm support," so says the Brāhmaṇa. That sacrifice concludes in the established manner; at this point, he releases the vow.

Then, having performed the Full Moon sacrifice and the Vaimṛdha sacrifice, he sits in the sacrificer’s station and, with a three-striped porcupine quill and a razor of red iron, he has his hair trimmed on top and shaved all around, [reciting]: “He who set this great earth in motion according to the seasons; he who, upon the skin of this earth, causes the plants to grow back—Agni, ruling by his might, Varuṇa together with his thoughts, Indra with his friends the Maruts. Agni with his sharp flame, with heat, has stepped over the *uṣṇihā*.”

"By the heat of Vaiśvānara, which was placed upon your head through asceticism, I turn it back by means of *ṛta*; I turn it around by means of *satya*; I follow it with asceticism; I turn it toward you with auspiciousness; I turn it toward you with power. That is the *ṛta* of the head, that is the *satya*, that is the vow; may I be able to do that, may I be able through that, may I prosper through that. Thus [the formulas] are performed first in the east, then to the south, then to the west, then to the north, and then above. The *Sākamedha* offerings conclude with the words, "He prays for the well-being of the year-long [cows]. Thus he prays.

Now, therefore, when he is about to sacrifice with the Śunāsīrīya oblations after four months have passed, he procures a three-striped porcupine quill, a razor of red iron, five sets of potsherds for the sacrificial cakes, five cooking-pots for the rice-messes, as many stirring-sticks, and curds for the speckled butter; then, on this night, the calves are driven away from their mothers for Vāyu.

In the morning, he causes the milk for Vāyu to be milked either according to the procedure for the *saṃnāyya* or silently. Then, after the morning *agnihotra* has been offered, having spread the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and carried forward the waters, he pours out the oblations: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, and the five "moving" offerings—a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra-Agni, a pap for the Viśve Devas, a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra Śunāsīra, milk for Vāyu, and a cake on one potsherd for Sūrya.

Having caused the cakes to take on a crust, having baked them, having covered them, having gone toward the east, and having poured out water for the Āpyas, he performs the *stambayajus* rite. This is well-known as the procedure for the cake-offering (*pauroḍāśika*): he recites the formula three times with the *yajus* and the fourth time silently. He performs the first tracing of the altar; he mutters the *karaṇa* formula; he digs up [the earth]; from the dug-up spot, the Āgnīdhra carries it away three times.
If he prepares the *uttaravedi*, it is concluded in the same manner as the *mahāhavīṃṣi*.

If, however, he does not prepare the high altar (uttaravedi), the sacrifice concludes in the same manner as the Vaiśvadeva offerings, except for the whey-offering (vājina); then, having performed the rites with the full-vessel (pūrṇapātra) and the Viṣṇu-strides (viṣṇukrama), he releases his vow.
