Then, having performed the Full Moon sacrifice and the Vaimṛdha offering, he sits down in the sacrificer’s place and, with a three-striped porcupine quill and a razor of red iron, he trims his hair and has it shaved all around, [reciting]: "Parameṣṭhin released one month for the sake of creatures; thereby he brought great prosperity to them, bringing immortality to mortals. You are born again according to your offspring; that indeed is your immortal nature, by which months, half-months, seasons, and years are formed. By which, O Prajāpati, they turned back for you as you were sacrificing."
Therefore, by means of this sacred formula (*brahman*), I turn it back for his life. With a sharp flame, Agni has overcome the heat; with the *uṣṇih* meter, the head has been placed upon the heat.

By the splendor of Vaiśvānara, I turn it back by means of *ṛta*; I turn it around by means of *satya*; I follow it along by means of austerity (*tapas*); I turn it toward him by means of what is auspicious (*śiva*); I turn it back toward him by means of what is efficacious (*śagma*). "That is the *ṛta* of the head, that is the *satya*, that is the vow (*vrata*); may I be able to do that; by that may I be able; by that may I prosper"—thus [he says] first in the east, then in the south, then in the west, then in the north, and then from above.
The Śunāsīrīya offerings are concluded; he pronounces the benediction, "May he obtain well-being for the year," and so he pronounces it. He is about to sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma;

he procures a black antelope skin and a black antelope horn, a garment and a girdle—this girdle is to be made of broad braided hair, threefold and with a single loop on one side—and twenty-two bunches of *darbha* grass, fresh butter and ointment, a reed-shaft with its tuft, a staff of *udumbara* wood, a wooden cup, and a vessel for the giving of the vow, along with its sling, ladle, and stirring-spoon.

These thirteen items the sacrificer places around his wife: a water-pot, a head-net, a garment, a yoke-tie, an unlimited number of bunches of *darbha* grass, fresh butter, collyrium, a reed-stalk with its tuft, a clay vessel, a wooden pin, a cooking-pot with its sling, and a stirring-ladle.
A sacrificial hall has been constructed on a consecrated site for the sacrifice to the gods.
"One should cause him to sacrifice on a site for the divine sacrifice where the oblation is prepared beforehand"—among these options, he chooses whichever he prefers.
They construct a hall with its ridge-pole facing east, with openings toward the quarters, and higher toward the south;
they make four doors for it: facing east, south, west, and north. To the south, they construct a fire-hall for cooking the sacrificial food, and behind that, the wife’s chamber.

Now, if the sacred bathing-place (tīrtha) is at a distance, they construct two straw-mat enclosures to the north of the hall: the eastern one for the sacrificer and the western one for his wife; they provide them with doors facing east and have water-jars placed within them. Then, having either performed the New Moon sacrifice or offered an oblation under an auspicious constellation, he causes the fires to be mounted onto the two chariots and proceeds toward the hall. Having gone around the north of the hall and entered it by the eastern door, he churns the fire on the site of the Gārhapatya, spreads out the fires, and ties the King Soma to the central beam.
They strew grass around [the fires].

The Brahman and the sacrificer sit down to the south. Then, having melted the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire and purified it, and having taken four portions into the offering-spoon, he mentally recites the Saptahotṛ formula and offers it into the Āhavanīya fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, saying "Svāhā!
Having again taken four portions, he offers the oblation for the sacrificial post (yūpāhuti), provided that he performs this offering here.

In the forenoon itself, they tie up the two calves of the two cows that provide the sacrificial milk; then he has the food for the undertaking of the vow cooked, and the two of them eat of it—mixed with ghee and mixed with milk. Then the Adhvaryu asks for the ritual materials from the riverbank, and says, "Come, O Sacrificer! Having gone out by the eastern door, they go to where there is water; then, while the Sacrificer is facing eastward, he moistens his right temple-locks with water.

"May the waters moisten you for life, for long life, and for splendor"—with these words he raises the blade of *barhis* grass with its tip pointing upward; "O herb, protect him!"—with these words he places the axe across [the grass]; "O axe, do not harm him!"—with these words he shaves [the hair], saying, "O god-hearer, shave these."

With the words, "May I attain what is auspicious and superior," he touches the part where the hair was cut off. By this same procedure, he moistens the hair for the second shaving of the beard (*godāna*) with water, either with a Yajus formula or silently.
Handing the razor to the barber, he says: "Let the barber announce me as one whose hair and beard have been shorn and whose nails have been clipped.
He announces him accordingly. Then he sprinkles him with water, saying: "May the waters, our mothers, cleanse us; may those who purify with ghee cleanse us with ghee."

Having rubbed [his hands] together, he sprinkles dust over himself with the mantra, "May they wash away all impurity from us; may they carry off our sin. He emerges from the water saying, "Pure from the waters, purified, I come forth.
Covering himself with the edge of his garment, he sips water, for the Brāhmaṇa says, "He eats the waters.

Then, moving clockwise, he puts on a new, unwashed garment with the mantra, "Thou art the body of Soma; protect my body. Now, fresh butter, having been stirred, lies nearby in a shallow vessel of water.
Having rubbed it thoroughly with his two hands, he first anoints his face with the formula: "Thou art the milk of the earth; thou art the bestower of luster; bestow luster upon me.
Another person anoints him from head to foot in the direction of the hair, and then anoints his back. Now, this collyrium, ground on a stone slab, lies ready along with a tufted reed-shaft.

While he faces east, [the teacher], sitting facing west, anoints his right eye with his left hand, saying: "Thou art the pupil of Vṛtra; thou art the protector of sight; protect my sight. He does this three times for each eye, twice for the upper one; for the Brāhmaṇa says, "He should anoint five times. Thus he anoints the right eye five times and the left eye five times. Then he purifies him with twenty-one tufts of *darbha* grass, saying: "May the Lord of Thought purify thee; may the Lord of Speech purify thee; may the god Savitṛ purify thee with an unbroken filter, with the rays of the bright sun."

He causes the sacrificer to recite: "O Lord of the Purifier, by means of your purifier, may I be able to accomplish that for which I purify myself. Then, having placed him in his left hand, he leads him into the hall with the verse: "O Gods, we approach you whose laws are true at the sacrifice; O Gods worthy of worship, since we have made this invocation to you."

He causes him to enter the hall by the eastern door with the formula, "Indra and Agni, Heaven and Earth, Waters, Plants. Then, having led him around the front of the Āhavanīya fire and seated him to the south facing north, he makes him look at the Āhavanīya with the formula, "Thou art the overlord of consecrations," and [makes him look] at himself with, "Protect me while I am here.

While the Adhvaryu is occupied here, the Pratiprasthātṛ moistens the wife's right armpit with water silently; he silently thrusts up a blade of sacrificial grass with its tip pointing upward, and silently lays down the razor crosswise.
He sows silently;
having sown silently, he touches the end [of the hair] with this same procedure. He moistens the other armpit with water;
silently handing the razor to the barber, he says: "Barber, report that my armpits have been shaved and my nails have been clipped."
Having addressed her thus, he then sprinkles her with water silently;
having washed away the dust silently, he causes it to float away silently;
he rises from the water silently; having covered himself with the edge of his garment silently, he sips water silently.

Silently she puts on a large garment; silently she anoints herself; silently she applies collyrium. Then he purifies her with an unlimited number of bunches of *darbha* grass, each time silently. Then, having led her in by the western door and brought her into the hall, while leading her toward the east, he makes her recite: "May the wife of Brahmaṇaspati go forward; may she sit upon the altar with splendor. And I, desiring [her], shall dwell here in my own world. Then she sits down behind the Gārhapatya fire, saying: "We, possessing good offspring and being well-wedded, have approached you."

"O Agni, the subduer of rivals, you who are undeceived, the undeceivable one"—having recited this, and having performed the *pṛṣṭhya* libations and brought forward the waters, he offers the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice consisting of a cake on eleven potsherds dedicated to Agni-Viṣṇu.

For this [offering], the tenfold set is omitted: he does not lead the sacrificer to the vow; he does not gird the wife; he does not prepare the sacrificer’s portion, nor the Brahman’s portion, nor the cake placed on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); he does not request the *anvāhārya* mess of rice; he does not perform the oblation of the husks; he does not offer the *samiṣṭayajus*; he does not make the sacrificer recite over the full vessel; and he does not take the *viṣṇu-steps*. Then the Adhvaryu, having turned to the right and hastened westward, having performed the offerings for the wives, goes eastward.
Having replenished the *dhruvā* ladle and poured [the remainder] back into the *ājya-sthālī*, he offers the *dīkṣā-hutis* by dipping with the *sruva* from the *ājya-sthālī*:

"To Ākūti, to Prayuj, to Agni, svāhā! To Medhā, to Manas, to Agni, svāhā! To Dīkṣā, to Tapas, to Agni, svāhā! To Sarasvatī, to Pūṣan, to Agni, svāhā! Then, having taken four portions into the *sruk* ladle, he offers the fifth oblation with the *sruk*: "O divine waters, vast, bringing all-blessing, may Bṛhaspati increase us with our oblation—Heaven and Earth, the wide mid-region—svāhā!"

Furthermore, having taken four portions of clarified butter, he offers the *audgrahaṇa* oblation with a full ladle, saying: "Every mortal should choose the friendship of the divine Leader; everyone seeks wealth, let him choose glory that he may prosper—*svāhā*! At this point, he pours out the full vessel within the altar (*antarvedi*). Then, having carried it around in front of the *āhavanīya* fire, he hands it to the sacrificer, along with the black antelope skin, the black antelope horn, the garment, the girdle, the Udumbara staff as the fifth, and the turban as the sixth.

Then the Pratiprasthātṛ hands over to the wife the water-pot (*kumbha*), the head-net (*kurīra*), the garment (*vāsaḥ*), the girdle (*yoktra*), and the peg (*śaṅku*). Then, on the sacrificer’s seat, he spreads out a black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and the hair upward; he touches its white and black parts, placing his thumb on the white part and his finger on the black part, saying: "You two are the artistic forms of the Ṛg and Sāman; I take hold of you both. Protect me until the conclusion of this sacrifice. Then, bending his right knee, he creeps forward, saying: "O God Varuṇa, sharpen this prayer of one who strives, and sharpen his will and skill."

"By which we may cross over all difficulties; let us mount the boat that is easy to cross. Having said this, he makes a lap and winds the girdle around it from left to right with the formula: "Thou art vigor, belonging to Aṅgiras; soft as wool, grant me vigor; protect me, do not harm me. He ties a knot that can be untied. At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ girdles the wife with a yoktra with two verses: "Desiring goodwill, I gird thee... and so on. Then he covers the sacrificer with a garment with the formula: "Thou art the protection of Viṣṇu, the protection of the sacrificer; grant me protection."
He causes [the sacrificer] to recite over the openings of the garment: "Protect me from the appearance of the stars.

Having drawn back the ends of the garment, he wraps his head with the turban in a clockwise direction, saying: "With prosperity I wrap your head; for prosperity, for glory, and for spiritual luster. At this moment, the Pratiprasthātṛ silently places a basket of hair-sieve upon the wife's head.
Then he gives this black antelope horn of his— having three or five ridges, tied with a hempen cord like a cluster of flowers— to the sacrificer, [with the words] "Thou art the womb of Indra.
The sacrificer receives it [with the words] "Do not harm me."
Having tied that end of the garment to the fringe, he digs up a clod of earth within the altar with it, saying: "For the sake of cultivation, for good crops, thee!"

With the words, "For the plants with good fruit," he scratches the hair-parting on the right side of his head; at this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ ties a pin to the wife's garment, saying, "Scratch yourself with this. Then he hands him a staff made of Udumbara wood with its tip pointing upward, reaching up to his mouth. The sacrificer receives it with the formula, "May the divine tree be well-established; standing upright, protect me until the end. Then he makes him recite the formula for taking hold of the sacrifice: "Svāhā! To the sacrifice with the mind, Svāhā!"

"To Heaven and Earth, svāhā! From the wide mid-air, svāhā! I take hold of the sacrifice from the wind, svāhā!"—at this point he closes his fists and restrains his speech. Then he announces: "This Brahmin here has been consecrated; he is of such-and-such a lineage, the son of so-and-so, the grandson of so-and-so, the great-grandson of so-and-so. We announce him to Indra and Agni, to the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Viśve Devas, and to the Soma-drinking Brahmins.
He says this three times in a low voice; thus he announces him to the gods.
"Having gone out three times with a loud voice, he announces him to both gods and men," so says the Brāhmaṇa; then he instructs him.

"You are initiated; speak as one who is initiated. Speak only the truth; do not speak untruth. Do not smile; do not scratch yourself; do not uncover yourself. If you should smile, you must smile with your mouth covered. If you should scratch yourself, you must scratch with a black antelope horn. If you should release speech, recite a verse addressed to Viṣṇu. Let not the sun rise over you while you are elsewhere than in the initiation-hut, nor let it set over you there. As for the names of the deities, call them by their proper names as they are known; but as for those names that are not of the deities, call them as they are known."

"Place the discerning [fire] above; speak speech that is pleasing and full of discernment; do not cut off from the black antelope skin nor from the staff"—in this very way he performs all this. Then, at the time of adding fuel, standing to the north of the Āhavanīya fire, he issues the call: "Make the fires radiant! O initiated one, restrain your speech! O wife, restrain your speech!"

Having given the command, while the two [officiants] observe the vow of silence, they cause the milk to be drawn. Then the Adhvaryu, having gone out by the eastern door and caused the milk to be drawn, returns by the same way he came, performs the Agnihotra procedure at the Gārhapatya fire, heats the milk, removes it from the fire toward the north, cools it, and then—whether having curdled it or not—suspends it on a sling in the northern part of the shed. Then the Pratiprasthātṛ, having gone out by the southern door and caused the milk to be drawn, returns by the same way he came, heats the milk for the vow-oblation, removes it from the fire toward the north, cools it, and then—whether having curdled it or not—suspends it on a sling in the southern part of the shed.

Then, when the stars have risen, the sacrificer, having fastened on the black antelope skin and having gone out by the eastern door, stands before the hall and releases his speech three times, saying: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! Perform the vow! Perform the vow! Then, he utters speech that is welcoming and far-seeing for the sake of approaching the guests.

If he happens to come upon something impure, he mutters: "The mind is unbound, the eye is poor; Sūrya is the best of lights. O consecration, do not abandon me! And if it rains upon him, he mutters there: "O flowing waters, bestow strength, bestow vigor, bestow strength! Do not destroy my consecration, do not destroy my austerity!

These two *yajus* formulas of his remain in use until the completion of the rite. Then, at the proper time, he spreads a black antelope skin for the sacrificer in the sacrificer’s station, with the neck pointing eastward and the hair side upward.

If there is a great deal spread out, he lies down without anything intervening from the black antelope skin; then he mutters the verse for lying down: "O Agni, do thou keep watch well; may we rejoice. Protect us for our welfare; give us back to awakening. He lies on the right side;
this indeed is the place of the sacrificer; he lies in his own place. Having turned toward the fire, he lies down; "Having turned toward the deities, he lies down," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then this wife lies down behind the Gārhapatya fire silently.

Then, having approached at midnight, the Adhvaryu makes him recite the awakening formula: "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows, a god among mortals; you are to be praised in the sacrifices. He then sips water, saying: "We meditate upon the divine thought, the very gracious one, for our aid; may she, bestowing splendor and carrying the sacrifice, be easy for us to cross. Then, having poured [the remainder] into a bronze vessel or a wooden cup, he hands over the *vrata* (vow-food) to him.

Having enclosed the area to the south of that [fire], he partakes of the fast-food with the Yajus formula: "O gods born of mind, yoked by mind, very skillful, sons of Dakṣa—may they protect us, may they aid us; homage to them, svāhā to them! Having partaken of as much as is required for the fast, he silently partakes of more. At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ pours out [the fast-food] into the wife's vessel and hands it to her.

Having enclosed that [milk] with a filter, he observes the vow silently; having washed the vessels, they hand them over. Then, in the same manner as before, prior to the disappearance of the stars, having issued the call, the two who have restrained their speech milk the sacrificial food. Then, when the sun has risen, the sacrificer, having fastened his black antelope skin and having gone out by the eastern door, standing in front of the hall, releases his speech three times, saying: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! Perform the vow! Perform the vow! The release of speech is the same; the formula for lying down is the same; the formula for waking up is the same; the sipping of water is the same; and the observance of the vow is the same.
Then he sends out messengers for the gift-giving.

Whomever he thinks will not refuse him, to him he sends first, saying: "May all the gods favor me with the gift; may Pūṣan with his bounty, Soma with his wealth, and the god Savitṛ as the giver of riches. Upon seeing one bringing [the gift], he murmurs: "Do not bring it away! O Soma, give this much, bring more! May I, while giving, not fail through my generosity; may I not fail in life! He accepts it according to its form.

With the words, "Thou art moon-ointment," he accepts gold; with "Thou art cloth," a garment; with "Thou art dawn," a cow; with "Thou art a steed," a horse; with "Thou art a goat," a goat; and with "Thou art a ram," a ram. Furthermore, whatever has not been specifically prescribed by a Brāhmaṇa, he accepts it with the formula, "Thou art belonging to Prajāpati; be for my enjoyment. Having gathered these together, they guard them.

Of those [cows], the one that perishes or dies, he assigns to Vāyu with the words, "To Vāyu, thee!"; the one that dies in water or by a snare, he assigns to Varuṇa with the words, "To Varuṇa, thee!"; the one that is shattered or falls into a pit, he assigns to Nirṛti with the words, "To Nirṛti, thee!"; and the one that a serpent or a tiger kills, he assigns to Rudra with the words, "To Rudra, thee! Of these, three go away to the distant regions; now, as for this one that has been lost—if they should find it, what would happen? It should remain unassigned; this is one view. Furthermore, she should obtain a recipient who is better than herself.
"One should give them away together with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*): this is one view; 'One should sacrifice with this [cow] dedicated to Vāyu': this is another.
Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the departure.

When the consecrated person finds security of possession (*yogakṣema*) elsewhere than at the place of sacrifice, or when he is consecrated elsewhere than at the place of sacrifice, they mix the two portions of the fast-milk (*vrata*)."
They tie up the two cows that yield the milk for the vow; when there is material to be offered, they place the *gārhapatya* fire in the nest and the *āhavanīya* fire on the front part of the chariot.

Alternatively, having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇī*), he sets out with a verse addressed to Bṛhaspati: "Go forth from good to better; may Bṛhaspati be your leader. Now, if he comes upon the time for the vow while traveling, he places the two kindling woods to the north, encloses the area to the south, and performs the vow.

He remains silent while seeking grass and water; then, if he comes upon water that is not bridged, he mutters: "O divine waters, O son of the waters, may I not step upon that wave of yours which is fit for oblation, full of power, and most intoxicating; may I follow the unbroken thread of the earth.
He either plunges into it or crosses over it; "Having made a bridge, he passes over," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Then, where he intends to dwell, he settles there with the verse, "Now we have settled on the best spot of the earth. Then he worships the rising sun with the verse, "Drive away our enemies, O thou with all heroes. Then, where he is about to perform a sacrifice, he settles there with the verse, "We have come to this place of divine worship on the earth," reciting until the end of the section.
Now follows the fast-day preceding the purchase [of the Soma].

He prepares a moon (candramas), a goat, two tufts of wool—one black and one white—an turban, two garments, two black antelope skins, and the Soma-purchase cow; she is ruddy-brown, tawny, and one year old. There are two oxen for carrying the Soma, a Soma-carrying cart with its planks removed and washed, a red bull's hide, two sets of sacrificial fuel and grass, enclosing sticks made of *kārṣmarya* wood, a *prastara* bundle of *aśvavāla* grass, two separating blades of *ikṣu* grass, and a cooking pot.
The foot-rest consists of a cloth for catching the fibers; there is a golden throne-seat made of Udumbara wood. Its legs are navel-high, and its crossbars are a cubit long.

It is woven with cords of Muñja grass, single-stranded, and slightly thicker than the Samrāḍ-āsandī. If the Soma sacrifice includes the Pravargya rite, then the Adhvaryu, having hastened there during the latter part of the night, gives the command: "Have the three-teat milk for the vow-milk (vrata) brought."

When the sun has risen in the morning and speech has been released, he settles upon the sacrificial ground while standing in front of the hall, provided it has not already been settled. Then he says, "Come, O sacrificer," and having caused him to enter the hall by the eastern door, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, and having carried forward the waters, he offers the *āditya-caru* as the *prāyaṇīyā* sacrifice.

Having released his speech with the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), he melts the clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire, purifies it, and offers a spoonful (*sruva-āhuti*) in the *āhavanīya* fire with the verse: "The sage extends the path of the sacrifice upon the back of the firmament, in the luminous realm of heaven."

"By which you carry the oblation, you go as a messenger from here, being wise there and more bountiful there—*Svāhā*! Then, having gone out, he issues the command: "O Soma-seller, purify the Soma! At the time for the *uparava* holes, let a Brāhmaṇa sit to the south on a red bull-hide near water. Let those cows not go far; among them are the cow for the purchase of Soma and the two bulls for carrying the Soma. Wash the Soma-carrying cart, having removed its side-boards."

They perform according to the directions. Then, returning by the same way they came, having cooked this *caru* oblation, having sprinkled it with clarified butter, and having removed it from the fire towards the north, he places the *Prāyaṇīya* offering down with the *Ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula. The ritual procedure is the same up to the *Prayāja* offerings.

Having offered five *Prayāja* offerings, having stepped across to the north, and having sprinkled the *dhruvā* ladle five times with the residue, he sprinkles the *caru*. Finally, taking four portions of clarified butter, he says:

With the formula "To Pathyā Svasti," he recites the invitatory verse in a low voice; having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for Pathyā Svasti" in a low voice, and "Svāhā! loudly at the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ*. He makes the offering in the eastern half. Then, taking four portions of clarified butter, he says, "To Agni," reciting the invitatory verse in a low voice; having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for Agni" in a low voice, and "Svāhā! loudly at the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ*. He makes the offering in the southern half.

Then, taking four portions of clarified butter, he says loudly, "For Soma," while whispering, "Recite the invitatory verse"; having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says loudly, "For Soma," while whispering, "Sacrifice"; when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers in the rear half. Then, taking four portions of clarified butter, he says loudly, "For Savitṛ," while whispering, "Recite the invitatory verse"; having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says loudly, "For Savitṛ," while whispering, "Sacrifice"; when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers in the northern half. Then, having spread an underlayer of butter, while cutting a portion from the eastern half of the rice-pap, he says loudly, "For Aditi," while whispering, "Recite the invitatory verse."

Having cut a portion from the eastern half, he cuts a portion from the western half, sprinkles clarified butter over it, and anoints the place from which it was taken. Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says "Aditi" in a low voice and "Sacrifice! loudly; when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers the oblation in the middle. Now, it is indeed said: "Having sacrificed to Aditi, he recites a verse addressed to the Maruts: 'O Maruts, since you are from heaven... Then, having spread an underlayer of butter, while cutting a portion from the northern half of the *caru*, he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Now, it is indeed said: "The portion for the Sviṣṭakṛt consists of eight cuttings; the *iḍā* consists of twelve cuttings."

He pours [ghee] over it twice but does not smear [the ladle]. Then, handing this stirring-spoon (mekṣaṇa) down from the two ladles to the Āgnīdhra, he says: "Do not let it fall beyond; do not throw it away. Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "Sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt."

At the utterance of "vaṣaṭ," he makes the offering in the eastern part of the northern half, passing over the previous offerings. At this point, having pushed this stirring-spoon (mekṣaṇa) across the Āhavanīya fire, sprinkled it with water, and set it down to the north, he steps out toward the north, places the two ladles (srucau) in their respective places, cuts off the Prāśitra portion, and cuts off the Iḍā portion. When the Iḍā has been invoked, he places the six-fold portion for the Agnīdhra; they consume it and perform the ritual purification (mārjana).

Then he instructs those who are moving about: "Without making yourselves defiled by food-remnants, having drawn out this sacrificial porridge (caru), you should eat it; then set aside these four things for the concluding offering (udayanīya)—this pot for the porridge, with its scrapings not removed, this stirring-spoon, this altar-grass (veda), and this sacrificial grass (barhis).
The introductory offering (prāyaṇīya) concludes with the Śaṃyu-formula.

At this point, he pours out this full vessel within the altar. Then, having replenished the *dhruvā* butter and taken four spoonfuls into the offering-ladle (*sruk*), he ties a piece of gold with a *niṣṭarkya* knot using a cord, fastens it to a stalk of *darbha* grass, and places it into the ladle with the formula: "This is thy bright body, this is thy luster; unite with it, go to radiance! At this point, holding that *darbha* stalk against the handle of the ladle, he offers it into the *āhavanīya* fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, saying: "Thou art swift, held by the mind, pleasing to Viṣṇu; of thee..."

"At the impulse of Satyasavas, may I attain the restraint of speech; Svāhā! Having taken another fourfold portion [of clarified butter], he then asks for the wooden sword (sphya), a vessel of water, sacrificial grass (barhis), and gold. Taking these together, he says, "Come, O sacrificer! The sacrificer follows behind him, and the wife follows after the sacrificer, taking the pot and the foot-supporting stone. Having gone out by the eastern door and standing in front of the hall, he makes the sacrificer look at the clarified butter with the formula: "Thou art bright; thou art nectar; thou art the oblation for the All-gods. Then, having placed the gold in between, he causes him to gaze at the sun.

"I have mounted the eye of the sun, the pupil of the eye of Agni; when you go with your coursers, O radiant one, wise one. Then they lead this cow for the purchase of Soma northward past the front of the hall. He addresses her with the formula, "Conscious art thou, mindful art thou," until the end of the section. Then he says, "Choose the seventh step on the southern shoulder.
He follows after her six steps.

"Thou art Vasvī; thou art Rudrā; thou art Aditi; thou art Ādityā; thou art Śukrā; thou art Candrā"—with these words he takes hold of the seventh footprint. "May Bṛhaspati make thee rejoice in happiness; may Rudra with the Vasus take heed of thee. Then, having placed gold upon that footprint and having strewn grass around it, he makes an offering over it with the formula: "I sprinkle thee on the head of the Earth, on the place of sacrifice of the gods, on the station of Iḍā, rich in ghee—Svāhā! Having removed the gold, he traces around the footprint with either the wooden sword (sphya) or the black-antelope horn, saying: "The Rakṣas is traced around; the enemies are traced around. Here I cut off the neck of the Rakṣas."
"Whoever hates us and whom we hate—here I cut off his necks," he says.

Then, taking it up with the wooden sword (sphya), he pours it out upon the foot-print of the sacrificial post as much as is moistened, saying, "Wealth for us, wealth for us. Having said this three times, he hands it to the sacrificer with the words, "Wealth for thee."

"O King, [be] whole," says the sacrificer to his wife; then he causes the wife to look at the Soma-purchase cow with the words, "O Goddess, look together with the goddess Urvaśī. Then the wife looks at the sacrificer with the words, "May I, accompanied by Tvaṣṭṛ, consort with you, bearing good seed and depositing seed, obtain a hero in your sight. Then the sacrificer looks at the Soma-purchase cow with the words, "May I not be separated from the abundance of wealth. Then, having washed this gold with water, he ties it on the middle finger. Then he pours water upon the footprint.
They release the Soma-purchase cow, lead away the wife, and they place down the footprint.

Then, standing right there, he asks for the moonstone, a goat, two tufts of wool—one black and one white—an turban, two garments, two black antelope skins, and the Soma-purchase cow; then he asks, "O Soma-seller, is your Soma pure?
and the other replies, "It is pure."

Having well-investigated the king, he approaches him from the front with the portions, saying: "Tell Soma for me: 'This is your Gāyatra portion'; tell Soma for me: 'This is your Triṣṭubh portion'; tell Soma for me: 'This is your Jagatī portion'; tell Soma for me: 'May he attain the sovereignty of the Chandomas. Then, having spread out a red bull-hide with the hair side up, he spreads over the northern half of the hide a double-folded garment with its fringes pointing eastward, and then [an offering] with gold.

He touches the King Soma with his hand, saying: "May your stalk be joined with my stalk; may joint be joined with joint; may your fragrance favor my desire; may your unswerving juice be for exhilaration; you are the companion; the *śukra* is your cup. Then he measures it out with a *aticchandas* verse; he measures it out one by one as they are poured out; with each measure that is not exhausted, he measures him out with that which is not exhausted.

He holds the thumb against all [fingers] while reciting: "I praise that god Savitṛ, the one of wise insight, from the two palms; him whose impulse is true, the bestower of jewels, the beloved thought; he whose lofty splendor has shone forth at his impelling; the golden-handed one of good wisdom has measured it out with his form—Svaḥ.

Measuring ten times—five times with the sacrificial formula and five times silently—he measures up to the middle point for the King (Soma). Then, having gathered the remainder, he pushes the King toward the subjects with the words, "For the sake of the subjects, thee!
Having gathered together the ends of the garment, he ties it around with the turban from left to right, saying, "For the sake of breath, thee."

With the words, "For the diffused breath (vyāna) thee," he ties it on; then, having made a space above with his finger, he makes the sacrificer look at it, saying, "Breathe after the offspring; let the offspring breathe after you. Then he places it upon the skin;
Kautsa takes it from there, sprinkles it with water, and spreads it out upon the skin.
Then, having stood up, he asks, "O Soma-seller, is your Soma for sale?"
"It is for sale," says the other. "From Mūjavat," says the other, for [the Soma] is from Mūjavat. Then he bargains for it with a cow: "I will buy it from you for a cow."

"The Soma has been purchased," says the Soma-seller. "Declare the birds! [The sacrificer replies: "This is your Soma-purchase cow; the ewe is yours; the goat is yours; the garment is yours. Then he bargains for it with gold.

"I purchase Soma for you—full of vigor, full of milk, full of strength, and overcoming adversaries. With the bright I purchase the bright; with the radiant the radiant; with the immortal the immortal. Having said, "The cow is yours," he hands it over to the sacrificer, saying, "May the radiance be with us. Then he bargains for it with its neck facing westward: "Thou art the body of austerity, the color of Prajāpati; of thee, who prosperest with a thousandfold increase, I purchase [the Soma] with the last animal. Thou art our kinship. He looks at the sacrificer, saying, "May thy riches rest in me," and then at himself.
Then, having turned her clockwise and sprinkled her with water, he releases her toward the north;
this [verse] belongs to Kautsa: "As a friend, come to us, O bestower of good friends. Then he takes the Rājana from the Kautsa: "As a friend, come to us, O bestower of good friends."

He places it on the right thigh of the sacrificer with the formula: "Enter the thigh of Indra, the right one; desiring him who desires thee, being pleasant, enter the pleasant one. Then the sacrificer uncovers it after sprinkling it with water. He gives the turban either to a descendant of Kutsa or to an attendant. Then he fastens a tuft of white wool onto the sacrificer with the formula: "Light for us! and then he ties this black [wool] underneath with the formula: "Here I tie around the necks of the biting serpents."

With [the formula], "Thou piercest the Soma-seller; in the Soma-seller, darkness," he strikes the Soma-seller. Then he points out the Soma-purchases: "O Svāna, Bhrāja, Aṅghāri, Bambhāri, Hasta, Suhasta, Kṛśānu—these are your Soma-purchases; guard them, let no one deceive you. Then, taking hold of him, he stands up with [the formula]: "Up with life, with good life, with the sap of the plants, with the vigor of Parjanya, I have risen after the immortals. To the south, this Soma-carrying cart stands ready, with its pole directed eastward and its yoke prepared.

With the formula, "Do thou go toward the wide mid-region," he places the black antelope skin in its nest with the formula, "Thou art the seat of Aditi," and sets the King [Soma] upon the black antelope skin with the formula, "Sit upon the seat of Aditi."

Then he worships him with the verse: "The Bull propped up the sky; he measured out the breadth of the mid-region; the Sovereign sat down upon all beings—all these are the ordinances of Varuṇa. Then he envelops him with a garment with the verse: "In the forests he has spread the mid-region; he placed vigor in the horses, milk in the cows, will in hearts, fire among the people, the sun in heaven, and Soma in the mountains. Then, with the solar verse, "Upwards that Jātavedas," he [covers] the black antelope skin.

He fastens the girths from front to back; then he addresses the two Soma-carrying oxen as they are being led forward: "O oxen, come hither! You are bearers of the yoke, not deaf, not slayers of heroes, and impellers of the sacred word.
Of these two, he yokes the southern one first with the formula, "Thou art the support of Varuṇa," and he drives in the pin with the formula, "Thou art the release of Varuṇa's support."
With the formula, "The noose of Varuṇa is cast off," he yokes the northern ox in the same manner as before. Then, having taken hold of the southern pole, he issues the command:
"Recite for the purchased Soma being carried forward; O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā hymn! But do not you invoke it—the sacrificer shall invoke it."

When the sacrificer calls out three times in a low voice, then this Subrahmaṇya priest, standing between the two sacrificial posts and holding a branch of the *palāśa* tree, invokes the Subrahmaṇyā formula: "Subrahmaṇyoṃ! Subrahmaṇyom! When it has been uttered three times each, they cause [the Soma] to move forward with the words: "Move forward, O Lord of the world, toward all your abodes; let not the waylayers find you, let not those who lie in wait find you, let not the malevolent wolves find you; let not Viśvāvasu the Gandharva harm you; becoming a hawk, fly away to the house of our sacrificer, where it is consecrated by the gods."

They carry the King [Soma] around clockwise; then the Adhvaryu and the Sacrificer approach him directly. For the Sacrificer’s well-being, he recites: "We have entered upon the path that leads to well-being, free from danger, by which one avoids all enemies and finds wealth. Then, standing in front of the hall while the King is being carried, he addresses him with the mantra: "Homage to the eye of Mitra and Varuṇa! Pay homage to that great, far-seeing light born of the gods, the banner of heaven, the son of Dyaus!"
"Recite for Sūrya! Then they bring this wagon that carries the Soma forward of the hall, with its pole facing north, and they steady it with the formula, "Thou art the pillar of Varuṇa.
With the formula, "Thou art the release of Varuṇa's pillar," he drives the pin upward; and with the formula, "Varuṇa’s noose is released," he unfastens the yoke-tie.
Now, it is indeed said:
"One ox is unyoked, while the other remains unyoked; then he receives the guest-offering for the continuity of the sacrifice. "The wife takes hold [of him]," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then he says: "Come, O Sacrificer!"

Having entered the hall by the eastern door and having crossed over the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, he brings forward the water and offers the guest-offering (*ātithya*) while the wife maintains contact with him; then, having performed the introductory formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ... and so forth.

Having performed this same introductory formula—"Thou art the guest-offering for Agni; I offer thee, acceptable to Viṣṇu"—and having performed this same introductory formula—"Thou art the guest-offering for Soma; I offer thee, acceptable to Viṣṇu"—and having performed this same introductory formula—"Thou art the guest-offering for the Guest; I offer thee, acceptable to Viṣṇu"—and having performed this same introductory formula—"Thee for Agni, the giver of increase of wealth; I offer thee, acceptable to Viṣṇu"—and [finally] with the sacrificial formula, "Thee for Śyena, the bearer of Soma; I offer thee, acceptable to Viṣṇu," he offers five times.

Having released his speech at the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviskṛt*), he unyokes the northern ox by this same procedure. Then these four Brahmins take up the throne-seat (*āsandī*). Then the sacrificer takes the King [Soma] from the seat (*nīḍa*) with the verse: "May all those abodes of yours which they worship with oblation encompass this sacrifice. They proceed first toward the throne-seat; the King follows behind, the sacrificer follows behind him, and the Śūdra follows behind with a water-pot.

He causes [the Soma] to enter the hall by the eastern door with the mantra: "O Soma, increasing the dwelling, furthering us, accompanied by brave sons, bringing no harm to our heroes, come into the dwellings. Then, having carried this throne-seat around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, they set it down to the south.

Upon it he spreads a black antelope skin with the mantra: "Thou art the seat of Aditi. With the mantra: "Sit upon the seat of Aditi," he places the King [Soma] upon the black antelope skin. Then he pays homage to him with the mantra: "Thou art Varuṇa, whose vow is firm; thou art of Varuṇa."

Having gathered the edges of the black antelope skin and tied them together with a cord, he fastens it to a bamboo pole with the verse, "May we not be severed from the friendship of the gods, O Ādityas. Then, between the two feet of the western throne-seat, a Brāhmaṇa consecrates him while a Śūdra washes him, [with the thought] "May we not cut ourselves off from the work of the gods. Then he attends to him with a verse addressed to Varuṇa: "That I implore of thee, adoring thee with prayer... Then he gives this instruction: "Let no one pass between the King and the Āhavanīya fire; let no one pass armed, nor with a staff, nor..."
"Let him not come with an umbrella, nor without a turban, nor without sandals," [they say]. Then they announce to him the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) and the cow.

The Adhvaryu gives instructions regarding the cow; they cook this oblation for the guest (*ātithya*), dedicated to Viṣṇu, on nine potsherds. With that, he places the boiling water (*madantīḥ*) on the fire.
This fuel and sacrificial grass for the guest-offering (ātithya) is "artistic" (śilpavat):

it consists of enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) made of *kārṣmarya* wood, a *prastara* bundle of *aśvavāla* grass, and two separating-blades (*vidhṛti*) made of sugarcane. Having thus made it artistic, he causes the cake to be covered with its skin, bakes it, covers it [with ashes], and goes eastward. Having poured out water for the *āpyas*, he performs the *stambayajus* rite. This is well-known as the procedure for the cake-offering: he draws the line three times with the *yajus* formula and a fourth time silently; he performs the first tracing of the altar (*parigrāha*).
He mutters the *karaṇa* formula; he digs up [the earth] and from that dug-up spot the Āgnīdhra carries away [the earth] three times.

When the Āgnīdhra has carried it away three times, then, having performed the second tracing of the altar and having leveled it, he fixes the wooden sword (*sphyam*) crosswise and issues the call: "Set down the sprinkling waters; place the fuel and the sacrificial grass; cleanse the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) and the offering-ladles (*sruc*); bring the clarified butter. When the sprinkling waters have been brought, he throws away the wooden sword, cleanses it, places the fuel and the sacrificial grass, and turning to the right, running back toward the west, he cleanses the dipping-spoon and the offering-ladles. He brings the clarified butter, purifies both the clarified butter and the sprinkling waters, and [proceeds] in the established manner.
Having taken four or five portions of clarified butter, he rises with the sprinkling waters; he sprinkles the fuel,
he sprinkles the altar,
and he sprinkles the sacrificial grass.
Having sprinkled the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) that has been placed nearby and poured water over it, he takes the *āśvavāla* grass as the *prastara* from the front;

having spread the fivefold-layered sacrificial grass, with the *prastara* in his hand, he moves forward to the east and lays down the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) made of *kārṣmarya* wood. He places two upright fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and sets down two transverse *vidhṛti* sticks made of sugarcane. Upon the *vidhṛtis*, he places the *āśvavāla* *prastara*; upon the *prastara*, the *juhū* ladle; and the other two ladles upon the sacrificial grass.

Having touched them with the formula, "These have sat down," and having turned to the right and run back facing westward, he then takes out that sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), which has been spread with a base of ghee and sprinkled with ghee, and places it down for the guest-offering (ātithya) while reciting the Caturhotṛ formula. At this point, he recites the formulas for the ritual materials (saṃbhārāḥ). Then, he proceeds with the fire-drilling according to the procedure for the churning-fire;

having cast the fire into the hearth and offered the oblation, he takes a fuel-stick from the faggot and says, "Recite for the fire being kindled. He places the faggot on the fire, but does not add a separate kindling-stick (samit).
Having fanned the fire with the Veda-grass-bundle, he pours the Āghāra-libation with the dipping-spoon (sruva) once the Sāmidhenī verses have been recited.

Having wiped the two offering-ladles (*sruk*) with the cloth from left to right, then stepping northward without letting the two ladles touch each other, he anoints the *dhruvā* with the *juhū*, sets down the two ladles, and chooses the *pravara*;
he chooses the *hotṛ* in the established manner.
The Hotṛ sits down and awaits the impulse;
once impelled, he takes up the two offering-spoons, steps forward, calls for the *śrauṣaṭ*, and says, "Sacrifice to the kindling-sticks (*samidh*)."

When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers; at the fourth [offering], when about to sacrifice with the call "Sacrifice, sacrifice," he pours all of this *ājya* from the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū*. Having performed five *prayāja* offerings, having stepped across to the north and sprinkled the *dhruvā* with the residue, he sprinkles the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), but not the *aupabhṛta* ladle.

Then he proceeds with the two portions of clarified butter for Agni and Soma; he proceeds with the oblation in a low voice. He says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Viṣṇu," and "Sacrifice to Viṣṇu. Then he proceeds with the Sviṣṭakṛt offering. The guest-offering (Ātithya) concludes with the Iḍā-portion. At this point, he pours out that full vessel within the altar. Having replenished the Dhruvā ladle with clarified butter, he asks for either a bronze cup or a wooden goblet. Having placed it within the altar, he takes up the Tānūnaptra water in it, saying: "I take thee for the protector; I take thee for the one who protects from all sides; I take thee for Tanūnapāt; I take thee for Śākvara; I take thee for the most powerful in strength."

As many officiating priests as there are, they touch it together while he causes the sacrificer to recite: "Unassailable is this, unassailable is the vigor of the gods; a protector against curses, beyond the reach of curses.
He then causes him to recite: "May the Lord of Consecration approve my consecration; may the Master of Austerity approve my austerity; may I straightway attain truth; place me in prosperity.

Having sought permission from all those officiating priests, the sacrificer himself smells it three times, saying: "I offer thee in Prajāpati, in the mind. Then, having poured water over it, he sprinkles it to the north and says: "O Agnīdh, the waters are rejoicing!"
"Rejoicing, the immortal goddesses, increasers of cosmic order (*ṛta*)"—with these [verses], he says, "Come hither.

Then, having touched the *madantī* waters, having risen, having loosened [his hair], and having placed gold [on his head], they cause the King [Soma] to swell with the formulas: "O divine Soma, may every stalk of yours swell for Indra, the winner of the single prize; may it swell for you, O Indra; may you swell for Indra. He causes the sacrificer to recite: "Make your friends swell with gain and wisdom; O divine Soma, may I safely reach the pressing. Then, having touched water, they sit down in their respective places. Then the Adhvaryu separates the two ladles with the two *vājavatī* verses.

Having torn off the *prastara* from the two *vidhṛtis*, he anoints it three times without making it crackle; he does not call for the *āśrāvaṇa* for the *prastara*, nor does he throw the *barhis* after it.

Having placed it on the southern half of the altar, they perform the *nihnuvana* (silent recitation) over it from south to north, saying: "Desired riches for the impulse, for fortune; to those who speak the truth, to Ṛta—homage to heaven, homage to earth!"

He places the wood-shavings upon the enclosing-sticks; he ties the sacrificial grass to the *prastara* with as much of the cord as is necessary, and having shifted it over the *āhavanīya* fire and sprinkled it with water, he sets it down to the north. Then he initiates the sacrificer into the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*) with the formula: "O Agni, Lord of Vows, you are the lord of vows among vows. That body of mine which is here, let it be in you; that body of yours which is here, let it be in me. O Lord of Vows, may the vows of us two who observe the vow be united. Then he instructs him: "Draw the girdle tighter around me; draw it tighter..."

"Form fists! Be one whose vow is heated! Purify yourself with the *madantī* waters! Release the vow first! That body of yours, O Agni, which is Rudra-like—with that protect us! To that body of yours, *svāhā*! With this [formula], he says, "From here on, observe the vow.

He performs all this in this very manner. Then he proceeds with the *pravargya* according to the procedure for the *pravargya*. Now, taking up the wooden sword (*sphya*), he says: "O Āgnīdh, place the *madantī* waters on the fire; place the oblation on the fire; come and sit down! Into these very *madantī* waters, he pours more water and places the clarified butter (*ājya*) on the fire.
Then, having gathered the sacrificial butter from this very *barhis* that has been spread out as far as its edge, he carries away the *stambayajus*.
This is the well-known procedure of the *pauroḍāśika*: three times with the *yajus* formula and a fourth time silently.
He performs the first tracing of the altar, mutters the *karaṇa* formula, digs up the earth, and from what has been dug up, the *āgnīdhra* carries it away three times.

When the Āgnīdhra has carried [the coals] three times, [the Adhvaryu], having performed the second tracing of the altar, having leveled it, and having fixed the wooden sword (sphyá) crosswise, issues the call: "Set down the boiling water; set down the fuel and the sacrificial grass (idhmā-barhis); cleanse the dipping-spoon (sruvá) and the offering-ladles (srúc); bring the oblation! When the boiling water has been brought, he throws away the wooden sword, cleanses it, sets down the fuel and the sacrificial grass, turns to the right, hastens westward, and cleanses the dipping-spoon and the two offering-ladles. He says, "Bring the oblation," and having purified both the oblation and the boiling water, he takes eight portions into the juhú ladle.
Having poured out the third portion from the *upabhṛt* ladle into the *ājyasthālī*, he rises with the *madantī* waters; he sprinkles the fuel,
he sprinkles the altar,
and he sprinkles the sacrificial grass.

Having sprinkled the sacrificial grass (barhis) that has been placed nearby and poured water over it, he takes the prastara-bunch made of *aśvavāla* grass from the front; having spread the sacrificial grass in a single layer, with the prastara in his hand, he moves forward toward the east and lays down the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) made of *kārṣmarya* wood. He places two upright fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and sets down two crosswise separating-blades (*vidhṛti*) made of sugarcane. Upon the separating-blades he places the *aśvavāla* prastara, upon the prastara the *juhū* ladle, and the other two ladles upon the sacrificial grass.

Having touched them together with the formula, "May these sit down," and having turned to the right, having run back toward the west and sat down behind the Gārhapatya fire, he recites the names of the wives of the gods. Then, returning by the same way he came, taking a kindling-stick from the faggot, he says, "Recite for the fire being kindled! He places the faggot on the fire once or thrice, but he does not leave any kindling-stick remaining.
He fans the fire with the Veda-grass-bundle, and when the Sāmidhenī verses have been recited, he pours the Āghāra-libation with the dipping-spoon (sruva).
When [the altar] has been swept, he does not [use] the two offering-spoons for the subsequent [rite];
then he chooses the *pravara* (ancestral invocation), then he causes [the *āgnīdhra*] to announce: "Ośrāvaya! Astu śrauṣaṭ! Sīda hotar!"—this much is the *pravara*;
the *hotṛ* sits down.
He desires the impulsion; once impelled, taking up the two offering-spoons, he says "To Agni" in a whisper, "Recite the invitatory verse" loudly;

having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says "To Agni" in a whisper, "Sacrifice" loudly; when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers in the eastern half at the halfway mark. Then, standing right there, he says "To Soma" in a whisper, "Recite the invitatory verse" loudly; having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says "To Soma" in a whisper, "Sacrifice" loudly; when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers in the middle. Then, while pouring back [the butter], he says "To Viṣṇu" in a whisper, "Recite the invitatory verse" loudly; having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says "To Viṣṇu" in a whisper, "Sacrifice" loudly; when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers the whole [remainder] in the west.
He offers the oblation. Then, having stepped out toward the north and placed the two ladles in their respective places, he says, "O Agnīdh, the waters are rejoicing!

[The Agnīdh responds: "The divine waters rejoice, immortal, increasers of cosmic order (*ṛta*). [The Adhvaryu says: "Come hither with them. Then, having touched the *madantī* waters, having stood up, having loosened his garment, and having placed gold [in the cup], they cause King Soma to swell, [reciting]: "O divine Soma, may each stalk of thine swell for Indra, the winner of the single prize; may Indra swell for thee; mayest thou swell for Indra."

He causes the sacrificer to recite the *ativākya*: "Swell thy friends with gain and wisdom; O divine Soma, may I attain well-being at the pressing. Then, having touched water, they sit down in their respective places. Then the Adhvaryu separates the two spoons with the two *vājavatī* verses;
having plucked the *prastara* from between the two *vidhṛtis*, he anoints it three times without crushing it, but he does not cause the announcement for the *prastara*.
He does not throw the *barhis* after [the fire].

Having placed it in the southern half of the altar, they conceal it there from left to right with the formula: "Desired riches for the impulse, for fortune; to the speakers of truth, to Ṛta, obeisance to Heaven, obeisance to Earth.

Having turned back toward the *prastara* in his left hand and having dipped the *sruva* into the butter-pot, he offers the first *upasad* oblation with the verse: "O Agni, that body of thine which is insatiable, most excellent, dwelling in the depths—with that fierce word I have struck away [evil], with that brilliant word I have struck away [evil]; Svāhā!"

He places the wood-shavings upon the enclosing-sticks and the sacrificial grass upon the *prastara*, tying them with a cord. Having pushed them across toward the *āhavanīya* fire, sprinkled them with water, and set them down to the north, he steps out and issues the call: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā; give the three-breasted vow-food. The Subrahmaṇya invokes the Subrahmaṇyā and gives the three-breasted vow-food. Then, in the afternoon, he proceeds with the afternoon *pravargya* and *upasad* rites;
the procedure for these two is identical, differing only in this respect.

They conceal [the vessel] with the left hand over the right; then, having gone out, he issues the call: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā; have the three-teat milk for the vow! The Subrahmaṇya invokes the Subrahmaṇyā, and they have the three-teat milk for the vow.
At midnight, he hands it over.
Then the Adhvaryu, having hastened there in the latter part of the night, gives the instruction: "Have the two-teat milk for the vow!"

When the sun has risen in the morning and speech has been released, he proceeds with the two middle Pravargya and Upasad rites; here he offers the *rajāśayā* oblation. Then, having gone out, he issues the call: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā hymn; give the two-breast vow-milk. The Subrahmaṇya invokes the Subrahmaṇyā and gives the two-breast vow-milk.
He first strides six steps forward from the Āhavanīya fire.
He drives that stake;
it is the stake at the front of the hall (śālāmukhīya).
From the stake at the front of the hall, he strides thirty-six steps eastward.
He drives that stake;
that is the stake for the sacrificial post-hole.
From the stake at the front of the hall, he strides fifteen steps to the south and fifteen to the north.
He drives those pegs into her two hips. From the peg at the sacrificial post-hole, he strides twelve steps to the south and twelve to the north.
He drives in stakes at those [intervals],
measures them out crosswise according to the measurement, and encloses them all around with a cord;
he stretches the *pṛṣṭhyā* line.
From the peg at the sacrificial post-hole, he strides twelve small steps westward;
that is the middle peg for the Uttaravedi. From the middle peg of the Uttaravedi, he strides five small steps southward and five northward, and there he drives in those pegs.
From the peg at the sacrificial post-hole (yūpāvaṭīya), he strides four small steps to the south and four towards the north;
there he drives in two pegs.
Having measured that [altar] by means of a diagonal measurement from shoulder to shoulder, he encloses it on all sides with a cord;

he stretches the *pṛṣṭhyā* line from the middle *śaṅku* of the Uttaravedi, and following the cord, he strides six steps westward and the seventh to the south; there he places the wooden sword (*sphya*).

That is the time for the *uparavas*. Then, from the *śaṅku* at the northern shoulder of the great altar (*mahāvedi*), he strides twelve steps westward along the edge of the altar and a thirteenth step northward; that is the place where the *Āgnīdhra* sits down.

That is the time for the *utkara*. Then, from the place of the *uparavas*, he carries away the *stambayajus*—this being the well-known procedure of the *Pauroḍāśika* section—with the sacrificial formula three times and silently a fourth time. He performs the first tracing of the altar boundary.

"O men, perform the rite; come and prepare this altar, which is rich in Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, and Viśvedevas, on the height of heaven, at the navel of the earth, so that this sacrificer may not suffer harm. Thus they dig it up. From the dug-up soil, the Āgnīdhra carries away three portions.

When the Āgnīdhra has carried away the three portions, then, standing in front of the hall, he issues the command: "O makers of the altar, fashion the altar! Break up the high places! Fill in the hollows! Cast out the thorny brambles! Complete the altar, sloping toward the east and the north!"

They perform according to the directions; then, from the northern shoulder-mark of the great altar (mahāvedi), he strides three steps westward along the edge of the altar and a fourth step toward the north.

Having covered it with the procedure for the *catvāla*, he traces around the *catvāla*; having covered it with the procedure for the *uttaravedi*, he pours out the *uttaravedi* earth; having raised the *uttaranābhi* and then covered it over, he performs the afternoon *pravargya* and *upasad* rites. Then, having gone out, he issues the call: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā; have the two-teat *vrata*-milk milked! The Subrahmaṇya invokes the Subrahmaṇyā and has the two-teat *vrata*-milk milked. He delivers that at midnight.
Then the Adhvaryu, having hastened there in the latter part of the night, gives the instruction: "Have the one-teat *vrata*-milk milked!"
When the sun has risen in the morning and speech has been released, he proceeds with the two final Pravargya and Upasad rites;

here he offers the oblation in the *harāśayā* vessel. Then, having gone outside, he issues the command: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā; give the half-udder vow-milk. The Subrahmaṇya then invokes the Subrahmaṇyā.

He then offers the vow of the half-breast; immediately thereafter, having combined the afternoon *pravargya* and *upasads*, they go out and issue the call: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā! O Pratiprasthātṛ, set down the *pravargya* according to the procedure for the *pravargya* for the purpose of removal.
They divide this station into three parts.

He places a third portion on the *gārhapatya* fire, a third in the supporting ladles (*upayamanī*), and deposits a third [in the pit]. Then, according to the procedure for the *pravargya*, he sets down the *pravargya* vessel; according to the procedure for the fire, he leads forward the fire. Having performed the second tracing of the altar (*parigrāha*) while it possesses fire, having leveled the ground, and having held the wooden sword (*sphyam*) crosswise, he issues the call: "Set down the sprinkling waters! Place the fuel and the sacrificial grass! This much is the call here. He spreads this sacrificial grass along the edge of the altar; this very same fuel and sacrificial grass is for the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma.
"One should lie down around it," some say. Now, these two carts of his—washed, brought forward, and prepared—are standing on both sides of the hall;

of these two, the southern one is larger and the northern one is smaller. The southern one has its planks removed, while the northern one has its planks not removed. That which is bound to the axle of those two, he unfastens. Then they turn them into the interior of the sacrificial ground (antarvedi). Then, having placed them in front of the hall at a distance of one cubit (aratni) on both sides of the cord, he sprinkles them with the formula: "O you two belonging to Viṣṇu, be purified for Viṣṇu! Then he says: "Come, O sacrificer!"

Having entered the hall by the eastern door, having melted the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire and purified it, and having taken four portions in the offering-spoon, he offers the oblation to Savitṛ on the Śālāmukhīya fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, [reciting]: "The inspired ones harness the mind and they harness the thoughts of the great, wise, and inspired one."

"He alone, knowing the ways, has established the priestly offices; great indeed is the praise of the god Savitṛ. Having taken another fourfold portion with the cry of *svāhā*, he then requests the vessel of clarified butter, the *sruva* ladle, the wooden sword (*sphya*), a water-pot, sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and gold. Taking these together, he says, "Come, O sacrificer! The sacrificer follows behind him, and the wife follows behind the sacrificer. Taking a third of the footprint-measure, they go out by the eastern door, approach the axle behind the southern *havirdhāna* cart, dig up the earth with the wooden sword on the southern track, sprinkle it with water, and [place] the gold.

Having placed [the vessel] and strewn [the grass] all around, he makes an oblation with the mantra: "Viṣṇu strode through this; in three places he planted his step; gathered together is it in his dust—svāhā! Then he pours half of the dust from those footprints into the joined palms of his wife, and then he sprinkles them with the residue of the oblation.

With her right hand turned palm upwards, she anoints the southern axle-hole with the formula: "May a hero be born to us, skillful in action, upon whom we all may depend, who shall be the lord of many. Having taken another four spoonfuls of ghee, having approached the rear of the northern *havirdhāna* cart, having dug up the earth on the northern track with the wooden sword (*sphya*), having sprinkled it with water, and having placed gold upon it and strewn it around, he makes an offering over it with the formula: "O you two, be full of nourishment, rich in cows, abounding in good pasture for Manu, and glorious! Viṣṇu has propped apart these two worlds; he has supported the earth on all sides with his rays. Svāhā!"
Then he pours all these foot-dust particles into the joined palms of his wife; he then sprinkles them with the residue of the ghee.
With her hand turned upward, she anoints the northern axle-end; the anointing is the same for both. Then he hands those implements over to the Pratiprasthātṛ.
They lead the wife and summon the Hotṛ; then, having taken hold of these two together, he issues the call:
"Recite for the two Havirdhāna carts as they are being set in motion!"

When [the verse] has been recited three times, they set it in motion with the words: "Go forward, O sacrifice; prepare the rite; lead the sacrifice upward; do not falter! Now, if the axle creaks, he mutters there: "O divine axle, speak fair words! Then these two, the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ, proceed directly, having gone around the north of the two *havirdhāna* carts and passed between the two front poles; from the middle *śaṅku* of the northern altar, they step out three steps westward along the cord.

"Therefore, delighting in these two which are established at the chin, may you two delight here on the surface of the earth"—with this verse containing a benediction, "O Viṣṇu, whether from heaven or from the earth," the Adhvaryu drives in the wedge to the south of the southern *havirdhāna* cart; then he fastens it securely with a cord. In the same manner, the Pratiprasthātṛ drives in the wedge to the north of the northern *havirdhāna* cart with the verse, "I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu."

Then he secures it with a cord, fastening it well with this same mantra. Then the Adhvaryu, having measured an aratni eastward from the front corner (cubuka) of the southern *havirdhāna* cart and having set the mark at that spot, causes a pit to be dug. Then, having measured a fore-arm's length eastward from the southern end of the yoke and having set the mark at that spot, he causes a pit to be dug. To the north of those two, he causes another pit to be dug. In the same manner, the Pratiprasthātṛ causes three pits to be dug on the northern side, and likewise on the western side. Upon these, they erect pillars with their tops turned toward the east.

They erect two bamboo poles pointing toward the north and fix them in front; he places the Visnu-forehead with the formula, "Thou art the forehead of Viṣṇu," and he lays down the middle roof-panel with the formula, "Thou art the back of Viṣṇu";
then those two which are on both sides—with the formula, "Ye are the corners of Viṣṇu"—they enclose [the shed] from the south and from the north.

They make two doors, one facing east and one facing west. Then, having placed a handful of *kuśa* grass against the southern door-post, he weaves a needle of *darbha* grass through it; on the needle, he fastens a cord with the formula, "Thou art the needle of Viṣṇu," and makes a knot with the formula, "Thou art the firmness of Viṣṇu. Having immediately loosened that [knot], he says, "Without making knots, finish [the work] with manual skill. In this very same manner, [he treats] the northern door-post.

In this manner, he fashions the other two door-posts; then he touches it with the formula, "Thou art Vaiṣṇava; for Viṣṇu, thee! Then the Adhvaryu, having turned to the right and hastened westward, strides six steps eastward from the Śālāmukhīya peg along the cord, and places the wooden sword (sphya) at the seventh step toward the south;
that is the place for the Audumbarī post, and from that spot of the Audumbarī post, he takes up the wooden sword.

"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee"—having taken [the spade] thus, he consecrates it, saying, "Thou art a spade; thou art no woman. With that [spade], he traces around the pit for the Udumbara post, saying: "The Rakṣas is traced around; the enemies are traced around. Here I cut off the neck of the Rakṣas. He who hates us and whom we hate—here I cut off his neck. Then he says to the Udgātṛ: "O Udgātṛ, come here! Dig this pit for my Udumbara post; throw out the earth toward the east.
He either digs it himself or causes it to be dug.

Therefore, he measures out the hall so that there are three roof-coverings across, three towards the east, and three towards the north; or alternatively, so that there are two parts to the north cord and one to the south.
He then has pits dug for the three-fold ladder-steps.
Therefore, having run forward from there, he measures out the *uparava* holes in front of the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart; they are a span wide and a span deep.

Then he says to the *unnetṛ*: "O *unnetṛ*, dig these *uparava* holes—a span wide and a span deep, an arm’s length long, not breaking through [the bottom], and connected above and below. He either digs them himself or has them dug. Then he pours their earth in front of the support of the southern *havirdhāna* cart.

He makes that mound square and then covers it with sand so that it is not visible. Then, from the location of the *uparava* pits, he takes up the wooden spade (*abhri*) with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee. Having taken it, he consecrates it: "Thou art the spade; thou art no woman."

With that [formula], he traces around the pit for the sacrificial post so that half of it shall be within the altar and half outside the altar: "The *rakṣas* is traced out; the enemies are traced out. Here I cut off the neck of the *rakṣas*; him who hates us and whom we hate—here I cut off his neck. Then he says to the Āgnīdhra: "O Āgnīdhra, come! Dig this pit for the sacrificial post, level with the top [of the ground]; throw the excavated earth toward the east; do not dig deeper than four finger-breadths from the top. He either digs it himself or has it dug.

While the Adhvaryu is busy here, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having measured the Udumbara post together with the sacrificer, places a layer of grass beneath it with the formula, "Uninterrupted be wealth and good heroes. Then the Adhvaryu, having turned to the right and hastened westward, calls for: "Prokṣaṇī water containing barley, a handful of sacrificial grass (barhis), a vessel of clarified butter with its spoon, the staff of the Maitrāvaruṇa, gold, and a water-vessel. Having taken these, he says, "Come, O sacrificer! This Udumbara post has been washed and brought forward;
it lies to the east of the pit. He sprinkles it from the far side toward himself.

With the words, "For the heaven thee! For the atmosphere thee! For the earth thee! he pours water into the pit. With the words, "May the world, the seat of the fathers, be purified," he scatters barley grains. With the words, "Thou art barley; keep away our hatred, keep away our enemies," he interlaces his hands holding sacrificial grass (barhis) and spreads it down with the words, "Thou art the seat of the fathers."

Then, having placed this gold beneath it, he makes an offering with the dipping-spoon, saying, "Svāhā to the Fathers! Then he raises it up, saying, "Supporting the sky, fill the atmosphere, steady the earth! Then he fixes it so that its ear-holes face eastward, saying, "May Dyutāna Māruta fix thee by the firm law of Mitra and Varuṇa! Then he heaps soil around it from left to right, saying, "I heap thee around as the winner of the Brahman, the winner of the Kṣatra, the winner of good progeny, and the winner of increase of wealth."

With the staff of Mitra and Varuṇa he strikes it, saying: "Strengthen the Brahman, strengthen the Kṣatra, strengthen the progeny, strengthen the increase of iron! Having set it down without deficiency or excess, and having poured out a vessel of water, he then places gold upon its two prongs and makes an offering with a spoonful, saying: "O Heaven and Earth, be filled with ghee, svāhā! He lets the remainder flow down to the very end; "He thus anoints the sacrificer himself with splendor to the very end," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Then they announce it to the Udgātṛs; they perform whatever rites they know regarding it. Following its erection, they erect stakes with their tips pointing eastward.

They project the northern rafters and lay them down; they place the middle roof-covering with the formula, "Thou art the seat of Indra," and those on both sides with, "For the shelter of all people. For one desiring splendor, he should erect nine roof-coverings;
thus, there are exactly three each for all of them.

He makes the southern ones northern; he thus makes those which were southern northern. He makes them intermediate; [he does so] for the sake of distinction. Thus, at the joints, he throws down rolls of grass.
They are now inside; then they enclose it with the verse: "O lover of songs, may these songs encompass you on every side; may they, increasing after the Increaser, be pleasing and well-received.

They enclose it both from the south and the north, making two doors facing east and west. Then, having placed a handful of *kuśa* grass against the southern door-post, he weaves a needle through it with the formula: "Thou art Indra’s needle"; and he makes a knot with the formula: "Thou art Indra’s firm [knot]."
Having immediately loosened that [cord] and not making it into a loop, they finish the knots with manual skill;

in this very manner they finish the other two door-posts and the two door-arms. Then he touches it, saying, "Thou art Aindra's; for Indra thee! Then, from the northern shoulder-mark of the great altar to the edge of the altar, he strides eighteen steps westward;
there he measures out the Āgnīdhra shed so that half of it shall be within the altar and half outside the altar.
Then, having leveled it, they enclose it;
they make its door on the south side. The Mārjālīya is explained as being equal to the side-measure of the Āgnīdhra shed, which is five aratnis;
they make its door on the north side.

Then, standing right there, he asks for a spade, sprinkling-water containing barley, sacrificial grass in his hand, a vessel for clarified butter with its dipping-spoon, a skin for pressing, two pressing-boards, six pegs, the pressing-stone, gold, and a water-vessel; having taken all this, he says, "Come, O sacrificer," and having caused him to enter the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door, he spreads this skin in the interior of the southern *havirdhāna*.

They set down the other [implements] in front of him. Then, from the place of the *uparava* holes, he takes up the spade with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee. Having taken it, he consecrates it with: "Thou art a spade, thou art a woman. With that [spade], he traces around the *uparava* holes, beginning with the southern one of the two in front: "The *rakṣas* is traced around; the enemies are traced around. Here I cut off the neck of the *rakṣas*. Whoever hates us and whom we hate—here I cut off his neck. He does this for all of them in successive order.

He digs with the formula, "I dig the Rakṣas-slayers, the spell-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu. Thus he digs all of them in succession. Then he throws up the earth from them with the formula, "Here I throw up that spell which our kinsman or our stranger has buried; here I cast him down lower, he who, whether kinsman or stranger, acts as an enemy. With the Gāyatrī metre, the spell is crushed out"—with these words, he throws up the earth from beneath the feet of the sacrificer, starting from the southern one of the two eastern pits.

With the formula, "By the Triṣṭubh metre," he throws [the dust] from the southern of the two rear [stones]; with "By the Jagatī metre," from the northern of the two rear; and with "By the Anuṣṭubh metre," from the northern of the two front stones. At this point, he scatters these foot-dusts on a place where no path is frequented, and there he meditates in his mind upon whomsoever the sacrificer hates. Then, having touched water, both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer touch them; the Adhvaryu touches the southern one of the two front stones, and the sacrificer touches the northern. Then the sacrificer asks, "Adhvaryu, what is here? and [he replies], "Auspicious."
"May that be for us both," [the sacrificer says]. Then the Adhvaryu asks, "O Sacrificer, what is here?
"Auspicious," [he replies].
"May that be for us both."
Whichever [of the two] the Adhvaryu leaves behind, that one the Sacrificer touches.

Of the two southern [stones], the Adhvaryu touches the rear one, and the Sacrificer the front one. Here the Adhvaryu asks, and then the Sacrificer [asks]. Of the two western [stones], the Adhvaryu touches the northern one, and the Sacrificer the southern one. Here the Sacrificer asks, and then the Adhvaryu [asks]. Of the two northern [stones], the Adhvaryu touches the front one, and the Sacrificer the rear one. Here the Adhvaryu asks, and then the Sacrificer [asks]. The Sacrificer asks first, and the Sacrificer asks last; then he touches them [all] with the formula: "Thou art Virāj, the slayer of rivals."

"You are the sovereign, the slayer of rivals; you are the self-ruling, the slayer of the arrogant; you are the all-ruling, the slayer of all destructive spirits"—with these words he sprinkles them all in succession.
