Having taken it, he consecrates it with: "Thou art the spade; thou art a woman, the performer of the sacrifice for the gods. Then, taking it, he stands up with: "Arise, O Brahmaṇaspati! We, seeking the gods, call upon thee. May the Maruts, the bounteous givers, come forward. O Indra, be swift as our ally."

"May Brahmaṇaspati go forward; may the goddess Sūnṛtā go forward; may the gods lead our sacrifice toward the hero, the manly one who bestows fivefold wealth. Then he stands near the prepared clay, saying, "O divine Heaven and Earth, consent to me. He strikes with a clod of earth from a cloud, saying, "May I succeed today at the head of Makha.
He carries it away, saying, "For Makha.
He pours it out to the north upon a black antelope skin, saying, "For the head of Makha," and having carried it away, he performs the standing prayer.

In this same manner he carries away the second; likewise the third; the fourth silently. Having gone around her, he approaches the place trampled by a boar and strikes with the spade, saying, "So great wast thou in the beginning. He carries it away with the formula, "May I succeed today at the head of Makha," and "For Makha thee. With the formula, "For the head of Makha thee," he pours it out upon the black antelope skin to the north, after having carried it away and performed the standing-rite.
In this same way he carries away the second;

likewise the third; silently the fourth; having gone around it, he leaves a remnant. Then he stands by the ant-hill with the verse, "O divine ants, first-born of this being, observers of the cosmic order (ṛta). With the formula for the spade, "May I succeed today at the head of Makha," he strikes.
With "For Makha, thee," he carries it away.
With the formula, "Thee for the head of Makha," he pours [the earth] onto the black antelope skin from the north. Having moved away, he performs the worship (upasthāna) in this very same manner;

he carries the second [load] in the same way, and the third in the same way; the fourth he carries silently. He leaves a remnant of this [earth]. Then he worships a clump of *uṭīka* grass or a clump of *vādara* grass with the formula, "Thou art the vigor of Indra. With the wooden sword (*abhri*), he strikes it down with the formula, "May I succeed today at the head of Makha.
With the formula, "For Makha thee," he carries [the earth] away.

With the words, "Thee for the head of Makha," he scatters [the earth] upon the black antelope skin to the north; having pushed aside the place of worship, he carries away the second [portion] in this very same way, and likewise the third. The fourth he carries silently. He leaves a remnant of that which has been carried around. Then he worships with goat's milk, saying, "Thou art born of Agni, the seed of Prajāpati. He places the spade down with the words, "May I prosper today at the head of Makha.
With the words, "For Makha thee," he carries it away.

With the formula, "The head of Makha art thou," he lets [the milk] drip onto the clay on the black antelope skin from the north; having moved away for the prayer, he lets it drip a second time in the same manner, and a third time likewise; the fourth time silently. Together with the fourth [drip], he pours all of this goat's milk from the vessel onto the clay. At this point, they either throw these remnants into the water, or scatter them right there, or let them remain as an expiation.
Then they take up the *pravargya* vessel, bending down their faces and not breathing over it; they do not allow the *pravargya* and the sun to be separated from one another.

It is known from tradition that many carry it. Then they bring it forward with the mantra: "May Brahmanaspati come; may the goddess Sūnṛtā come. May the gods lead us toward the sacrifice, which provides heroes, is manly, and bestows fivefold wealth."

Then the ass brings him down [from the cart] with the formula: "Bestow life; bestow out-breathing; bestow in-breathing; bestow diffused breathing; bestow sight; bestow hearing; bestow mind; bestow speech; bestow the self; bestow a firm foundation; bestow me; bestow [all this] in me. Then, having mixed him with potsherds from a slaughterhouse, with pebbles ground with collyrium, with goat hair, and with hair from a black antelope skin, he moistens the mixture with boiling water, saying, "May honey make thee honey-sweet," and fashions a lump, saying, "Thou art the head of Makha."
With the words, "You two are at the station of the sacrifice," he presses down with his two thumbs. Then, having cut off a third portion from the clay, he makes three lumps;

he gives one of them to the maker (the potter) with the words, "Thou art Gāyatra," and with that he makes its base. With the words, "I make thee with the Gāyatrī metre," he gives half of the remaining clay, saying, "Thou art Traiṣṭubha."
With that [formula], "I fashion you with the Triṣṭubh metre," he fashions its middle;
finally, he hands over all the clay with the formula, "You are Jāgata. With that, he fashions its cavity with the formula, "I fashion you with the Jāgata metre."

He makes that [piece of wood] one span long, broad at the base, and fixed in the middle; then he pierces two parts of it with a bamboo shaft, and that becomes its milking-pail (*pinvana*). Then, at a distance of three or four finger-breadths from it, he winds a girdle (*rāsnā*) around it, saying, "Thou art the girdle of Makha. Then he takes hold of its opening, saying, "May Aditi take hold of thy opening with the *pāṅkta* metre. Then he heats it over the sun, saying, "Be heated by the heat of Sūrya. Then he places it upon the mound (*khara*).

He consecrates the one that has been set down with the formula, "Thou art Makha. In this very same manner he prepares the second Mahāvīra, and likewise the third; [he prepares] the two *pinvana* vessels silently, as well as the two *rauhiṇaka* potsherds and the butter-pot. Then, with the clay that remains over, he causes it to dry in a windless spot by exposing it to the wind. When they have dried, he prepares twenty-one balls of dung from a stallion, the *abhri* hoe, the fire, and the baking-vessel. Then, having kindled a horse-dung fire-brand, he fumigates the principal Mahāvīra with the formula: "Thou art the dung of the stallion; may Varuṇa, whose vow is firm, fumigate thee with the steadfast law of Mitra and Varuṇa."

Having thoroughly fumigated it both inside and out, he places it down; in this very same manner, he fumigates the second *mahāvīra*, and likewise the third. He fumigates the two *pinvana* vessels, the two *rauhiṇa* potsherds, and the *ājya* vessel. Then, to the north of the hall, he has a wide pit dug as if for a cauldron. Having spread out the *pacana* grass within it, he causes the *mahāvīras* to be brought and laid down therein, facing either east or north, with the two *pinvanas* in front.
Then, on the western mound, he places the vessel for the clarified butter (ājyasthālī) in the northern half; having covered these with the cooking pot from above, he smears them with clay.
He leaves an excess of four finger-breadths on each side for the purpose of kindling, and then he sets fire to them:
with "For the flame, thee! to the east; with "For the radiance, thee! to the south; and with "For the light, thee! to the west.
"To austerity, thee!"— thus [he places it] to the north;
for by day or by night they are ripened,
if he fasts in the morning and approaches [the fire] in the evening.

If, in the evening or in the morning, when those [milk products] have been prepared, he procures cow’s milk, goat’s milk, a stirring-stick, a stone for grinding, a vessel, a lid, a winnowing-basket, a sling, and a black antelope skin—having taken all this together, he approaches [the fire] while reciting: "By his greatness Mitra has become co-extensive with heaven; and by his glory, with the earth. The glory of the god Mitra, the supporter of the people, is winning; his splendor is most wonderful in renown. Then he takes up the stirring-stick with the words: "For success, thee!"

With that [ladle], he scoops out the coals from the principal *mahāvīra* vessel, saying: "May the god Savitṛ, with good hands, good fingers, and good arms, scoop thee out by his power. Then he raises it up, saying: "Arise, become great; stand upright, thou art firm. Then he establishes it in its place, saying: "Not falling upon the earth, mayest thou fill the regions and the quarters."

Then he gazes at it with the formula: "I gaze at thee with the eye of Sūrya; for the upright, for the good, for a firm dwelling, for prosperity. Then he surrounds it with loose earth from left to right, according to the respective [social] class, with the formula: "Here I surround so-and-so, the son of such-and-such, with subjects, cattle, and the splendor of sacred knowledge."

Then, having grasped it with a pair of tongs and placed it in a vessel, he curdles it with goat’s milk, saying: "I curdle thee with the Gāyatrī metre; I curdle thee with the Triṣṭubh metre; I curdle thee with the Jagatī metre. May Vāc curdle thee; may Ūrj curdle thee; may the oblation curdle thee. Make the speech curdle, make the strength curdle, make the oblation curdle. O God, go before [the sacrifice]; may I succeed. Having thus made it well-curded both inside and out, he proceeds.

He causes it to overflow with cow's milk; in this very manner he sprinkles the second *mahāvīra*, and likewise the third. He silently pours [milk] into the two *pinvana* vessels, the two *rauhiṇaka* potsherds, and the butter-pot. Now, if a crack or a fissure occurs, one should scatter powdered stone into goat’s milk, sprinkle that over [the vessel], and heat it with a firebrand while reciting the two verses: "The fissure that has opened... and "Even though apart from union... It will indeed heal completely.

If, however, it breaks completely, he grinds these very potsherds with unguents, mixes them with that clay which lies set aside for expiation, kneads it, bakes it, and having let it cool, sets it down. When their hissing has ceased, he places them in a pit, covers them from above with a black antelope skin, and hangs them on a sling in the northern part of the hall in such a way that the wife does not see them.
They remain lying there until that time, and then they perform the subsequent *śānti* rite with the mantra: "May Vāta, Mātariśvan, blow auspiciously for us.

On the following day, when the purchase of the King (Soma) is to take place, he prepares the following: a throne-seat (*samrāḍ-āsandi*) made of Udumbara wood, a pillar made of Udumbara wood, a milking-vessel (*godohanī*) made of Udumbara wood, a peg for the she-goat made of Udumbara wood, a support for the hoof [of the goat] made of Udumbara wood, a *sruva*-ladle made of Udumbara wood, two *sruc*-spoons made of Udumbara wood, two unpolished *rauhiṇa-havaṇī* offering-spoons made of Udumbara wood, two fire-stirring sticks (*dhṛṣṭī*) made of Udumbara wood, three fans (*dhavitrāṇi*) made of black antelope skin with handles of Udumbara wood—or, according to some, with handles of bamboo.

Six chips of *udumbara* wood, a fuel-stick of *vaikaṅkata*, thirteen enclosing sticks of *vaikaṅkata*, a *vaikaṅkata* offering-spoon (*pracaraṇī*), enclosing sticks made of *kārṣmarya* wood, two plates of gold and silver, two cows that yield the *gharma* milk—one a cow and the other a she-goat—two altars made of *kuśa* grass, one altar made of *muñja* grass that has not been weathered, a rope made of *muñja* grass, cuttings of *muñja* grass, flour of *rohiṇa* beans, and sand for the mounds; then he proceeds with the introductory sacrifice (*prāyaṇīya*), and having performed the introductory sacrifice, he proceeds with the footprint rite (*pada*).

Having performed the *pada* rite and having purchased the King Soma, he prepares the guest-offering (*ātithya*). Having performed the guest-offering, they proceed to the first *śānti* with the formula, "Homage to speech! Then, having strewn grass in front of the *gārhapatya* fire, they set down this sacrificial grass-bundle (*rsava*) for the *parigharma* ceremony; here they place the throne of the sovereign (*samrāḍ-āsandī*), here the pillar, here the *godohanī* (milk-pail), and here the peg for the goat. Then, to the north of the *gārhapatya*, having dug up the ground with the wooden sword (*sphya*) and sprinkled it with water, he pours down sand.

He makes that [place] one span wide, circular, and a mound for burning, and then he makes it radiant with sand. Then, to the north of the Āhavanīya fire, having dug up the ground with the wooden sword and sprinkled it, he pours down sand;

he makes that a mound for spreading out, one span wide and circular, and then he makes it radiant with sand. Then, on the northern edge of the pit, having dug up the ground with the wooden sword and sprinkled it, he pours down sand.

He makes that [mound] square, with a runoff channel, and a rim for the leavings; he makes it firm with sand and provides a border of pebbles. Then the Adhvaryu, having grasped the Mahāvīra vessel used for the Pravargya rite with two hooves, places it on the mound prepared for heating. He then covers it with a screen made of Muñja grass. Then, having carried this throne-seat around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, he sets it down to the south.

Upon that [black antelope skin], he spreads another black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and the hair facing upward. Then, having taken up these two *mahāvīra* vessels used for lying near [the fire] by means of the two Veda-bundles, and having carried them around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, he places them on the black antelope skin on the southern side of the royal throne (*samrāḍāsandī*), with their openings facing eastward. Then, having carried this clay mold around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, he places it on the black antelope skin on the southern side of the royal throne. Then, having carried this remaining clay around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, [he places it] on the black antelope skin on the southern side of the royal throne.

He places [the vessel] down. Then, having taken this pillar for the milking-cow, the peg for the goat, and so forth, and having walked around the south of the Gārhapatya fire along its rear, he carries them out through the southern door. Having fixed the pillar in the sight of the Hotṛ, they bind the calf of the Gharma-milch cow with a cord of muñja grass. Having fixed a peg to the north of that, they tie up the goat;
they turn the kid over on its back.
Then, having returned by the same way they came, they cause [the sacrificer] to go out;
they summon the Śūdras, they summon the Hotṛ, they summon the Brahman, they summon the Pratiprasthātṛ, they summon the Prastotṛ, and they summon the Āgnīdhra.
They enclose the doors in the wife’s hall and enclose the wife.
They strew [the grass] around; the Brahman and the sacrificer sit down to the south. Here they perform the first *praśānti* (appeasement) for those for whom it has not yet been performed.

Then the Adhvaryu, taking up the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling waters together with the strainers, says: "O Brahman, we shall proceed with the *pravargya*; O Hotṛ, recite the hymn for the *gharma*; O Agnīdh, place the two cakes on the fire; O Pratiprasthātṛ, spread out the *pravargya* vessels; O Prastotṛ, chant the *sāmans*."

Then Brahmā gives his impulse: "Thee, joined with the *yajus*, anointed with the *sāmans*, approved by all the gods and the Maruts, extended by the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇās*), capable of carrying us across—may the chanters carry thee while thou art well-disposed. Bestow radiance upon us, being free from anger! *Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ*! Om! Accompanied by Indra, proceed! Then the Adhvaryu sprinkles the Mahāvīra vessel intended for use, saying: "For Yama thee! For Makha thee! For the heat of Sūrya thee! As he reaches each subsequent set of ritual materials, he sprinkles them one after another.
The Pratiprasthātṛ disposes that very Pravargya vessel; then he lays the enclosing-sticks made of Kārṣmarya wood around the Āhavanīya fire.

He places near [the fire] six chips of Udumbara wood, a fuel-stick of Vikaṅkata, thirteen enclosing-sticks of Vikaṅkata on the Gārhapatya fire, two plates—one of gold and one of silver—cuttings of Muñja grass, and the flour for the Rauhiṇa cakes. Then the Āgnīdhra, sitting behind the Gārhapatya, draws out embers toward himself with two stirring-sticks and places upon them the two Rauhiṇa potsherds. Then, having mixed the flour with water, he places the two Rauhiṇa sacrificial cakes on the fire, and then the clarified butter.

He offers the oblation, then places the clarified butter on the fire; having carried fire around both, he bakes the two *rauhiṇa* cakes. At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ wipes with a mat of *muñja* grass the vessels intended for the oblation: the *mahāvīra*, the *sruva* ladle, the two *pinvana* milking-pots, the two *rauhiṇa-havanī* offering-spoons, and the supporting tray (*upayamana*). Then the Pratiprasthātṛ, having purified the clarified butter, having taken out the two *rauhiṇa* cakes after spreading a base of butter and pouring butter over them, and having grasped them with the two *rauhiṇa-havanī* spoons, places one within the altar along the southern joint of the enclosing sticks.

He joins the northern joint of the enclosing-sticks; those [two] in the forenoon are directed eastward, and those in the afternoon are directed westward. Then the Adhvaryu, having grasped the Mahāvīra vessel used for the performance with its two handles and having turned it into his left hand, offers seven continuous *prāṇa*-oblations over the Gārhapatya fire without pausing, using clarified butter taken once from the *ājyasthālī* [ladle], with the formulas: "To Prāṇa, svāhā! To Vyāna, svāhā! To Apāna, svāhā! To the Eye, svāhā! To the Ear, svāhā! To the Mind, svāhā! To Speech, Sarasvatī, svāhā!"

He offers four subsequent oblations according to their occurrence: "To skill, svāhā! To resolve, svāhā! To vigor, svāhā! To strength, svāhā! Then he anoints it with clarified butter, saying, "May the god Savitṛ anoint you with honey. At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ hides a silver plate within the mound for heating on the *khara*. He says, "Protect the earth from heat. Then, having intertwined blades of *muñja* grass, he kindles them, saying, "Thou art flame; thou art glow; thou art light; thou art heat. Having scattered them over the mound for heating, he places the Mahāvīra vessel to be heated upon them.

"Sit down; you are great. Shine forth, O best invoker of the gods! O Agni, worthy of sacrifice, emit your ruddy smoke, O praised one, beautiful to behold! Then he fills it with clarified butter: "Him whom the inspired poets anoint as if spreading him out, heating him with fire like a fatty oblation—the most beloved *gharma* has sat upon the lap of Agni, as a son upon his father's lap. Then, with a span's measure, he establishes its directions: "Invincible in the east, under the overlordship of Agni, grant me long life"—thus in the east. "Possessing sons in the south, under the overlordship of Indra, grant me offspring"—thus in the south.

"To the west, under the overlordship of the god Savitṛ, [I say] 'Grant me breath'; thus [is the response] from the west. To the north, under the overlordship of Mitra and Varuṇa, [I say] 'Grant me hearing'; thus [is the response] from the north."

"Support! Above, under the sovereignty of Bṛhaspati, grant me the Brahman; grant me the Kṣatra; bestow splendor upon me; bestow luster upon me; bestow glory upon me; bestow austerity upon me; bestow righteousness upon me"—thus [he says] above. Then he touches this [earth]: "Thou art the mare of Manu, mother of many sons; protect me from all destructive powers; may I be easy to sit upon for thee; do not harm me. Then, with the two poking-sticks, he draws out the embers toward the north: "Burn, O Agni, the enemies within; burn the foe who harms us; burn the one who seeks to injure another. Burn, O Vasu, thou who art observant, the unobservant; let those who are ageless and tireless stand apart from thee."

With [the formula], "You are the piled; you are the surrounding; svāhā! Be surrounded by the Maruts," he surrounds it on the right. Then the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ surround it with thirteen enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) made of *vaikaṅkata* wood:

the Adhvaryu places two facing east with [the formulas] "Thou art the measure" and "Thou art the fore-measure," and the Pratiprasthātṛ places two facing north with [the formulas] "Thou art the measure" and "Thou art the fore-measure."

He addresses those two [fire-sticks] in this very manner: "You are interwoven; you are measured together; you are measured apart; you are raised up. Then he fixes the thirteenth enclosing-stick on the south side with its tip pointing upward, saying, "You are the interior of the atmosphere. Then he covers it with a golden plate, saying, "Protect the sky from heat. Then he stands over it, reciting: "With these songs, O radiant one, another [form] of yours is worthy; you bear arrows and a bow. When it has flared up, he removes the golden plate.
Then he takes up the fans: "Thou art Gāyatra! with one; "Thou art Traiṣṭubha! with another; "Thou art Jāgata! with the other.

With these, he fans him from behind while facing eastward, holding his knees upright, saying "Honey, honey" repeatedly. He hands two fans to the Pratiprasthātṛ standing to the north, and he hands one of those two to the Āgnīdhra. Then they walk around him three times clockwise, fanning at each *praṇava*.

Having gone around three times, they stand to the north; then he takes up the fans. To the Pratiprasthātṛ, who has gone around by the rear and stands to the north, he gives two fans; of those two, he hands one over to the Āgnīdhra. Then they sit down around him; the Adhvaryu sits behind him, facing east.
The Pratiprasthātṛ sits in front facing west, and the Āgnīdhra on the north facing south;
they remain there in this very manner, fanning [the fire] at every *praṇava* and causing the embers to swell for the sake of the Mahāvīra.

Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ’s recitation, "With those [rays] by which you released the swallowed quail," the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer rise toward it and cause it to shine with this Anuvāka beginning, "Ten rays in the east, ten thou shinest in the south."

Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ’s recitation, "O Aśvins, may our speech be effective," they lift up the fans. Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ’s recitation, "The dappled one has shone at the head of the dawns," having said, "The Gharma has shone," they walk back around three times as they came, set down the fans, and stand worshipping while looking through the openings with the verse beginning, "I have seen the herdsman," and continuing with "May we obtain thee; do not harm me. Then he stands worshipping the Gārhapatya fire with the verse, "Thou, O Agni..."

"You are the head of all human clans; O youngest one, protect us with a hundred fortresses! May you, the joyous one, protect your kindler for a hundred winters, O tireless one, you who possess a radiant heart! May the gifts be right here!"—when [the fire] has been covered, the Pratiprasthātṛ makes the wife recite this over the Veda. "May I consort with thee, accompanied by Tvaṣṭṛ"—he recites this until the end of the section. At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the southern Rauhiṇa cake with the mantra: "May Day, with its light, enjoy [the offering] through its banner; may the beautiful light, through the lights, [enjoy it]—Svāhā!"

Then he takes up the cord with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee. Having taken it, he consecrates it with: "Thou art the girdle of Aditi.

The Pratiprasthātṛ, having gone around by the west, [takes] the two milking vessels with the formula: "O Ka, thou art the swelling [vessels]. Then he calls this cow that yields the Gharma-milk three times in a low voice by the names of the gods: "O Iḍā, come! O Aditi, come! O Sarasvatī, come! Three times he calls aloud, having gone out through the southern door: "O so-and-so, come! O so-and-so, come!"—using whatever name she may have—and then he fastens her with the cord with the formula: "Thou art the turban of Aditi."

With the formula, "Vāyu is its calf," he touches the calf of the Gharma-cow; then he lets it loose with the formula, "May Pūṣan let you loose; may the Aśvins cause you to give. He addresses the cow while she is suckling with the verse: "That breast of yours which is inexhaustible, which is refreshing, by which you nourish all desirable things—that breast which is a bestower of jewels, a finder of wealth, and a giver of good gifts—O Sarasvatī, make that available here for her to suck.
When she has been milked, he draws [the milk] up with the formulas: "O Dawn, leave some of the Gharma! O Dawn, protect the Gharma! Leave some for the Gharma!"

Having enjoined and consecrated it, he approaches it with the formula, "May Bṛhaspati approach you. He strokes the udders with the formula, "Ye are givers, ye are protectors; O all-encompassing ones, [I touch you] with blood. Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ's recitation, "With the ten [fingers] of Vivasvat," at that moment he causes the milk to flow into the two milking vessels (*pinvana*) with the formulas: "Flow for the Aśvins! Flow for Sarasvatī! Flow for Pūṣan! Flow for Bṛhaspati! Flow for Indra! Flow for Indra! He causes the remainder to be milked into a pot. At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ silently causes a she-goat to yield milk into the two milking vessels.

Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ reciting, "Arise, O Lord of Prayer," he hands over the two milks to the Pratiprasthātṛ; having returned by the same way he came, he takes up the two hoof-holders, saying "Thou art Gāyatra" over one, "Thou art Traiṣṭubha" over the other, and "Thou art Jāgata" over the supporting vessel.

Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ’s utterance, "O milk-milkman, come with the milk to the cow-pen," as the two milks are being brought, he consecrates them with: "Come together with a portion of vigor; O Indra and Aśvins, drink the Gharma of the honeyed bees; O Vasus, you who are worthy of sacrifice, vaṭ! Then, having sat down facing west in front [of the fire], the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ pour the two milks into the Mahāvīra vessel; the Adhvaryu pours first, [with the formula]: "Svāhā! I offer thee for the rain-winning ray of the sun."

With "Svāhā! he then gazes at its steam, saying, "Thou art honey, the oblation; heat the heat of Sūrya. At this moment, the Pratiprasthātṛ pours goat's milk silently. Having combined both, the Adhvaryu pours a third portion. Whatever remains of the milk there, he pours into the *upayamana* vessel. Then, having pushed back the embers, the Adhvaryu grasps the *pracaraṇīya* Mahāvīra with two hooves.

With the formula, "I enclose you with heaven and earth," he wipes beneath [the fire] with the *veda* and supports it with the supporting-wood (*upayamana*), saying, "I support you with the intermediate space. Then, taking it up, he stands up, saying, "May I be able to bear you, permitted by the gods and the ancestors."

"Thou art brilliance; carry forward the brilliance! Follow after the brilliance! May Agni protect me from the earth, Vāyu from the intermediate space, and Sūrya from the sky! Do not harm me, O toucher of the sky! Do not harm me, O toucher of the intermediate space! Do not harm me, O toucher of the earth! Thou art the light; grant me the light! Grant me the sky! Protect me from the sky! Then he recites the names of the winds: "To the ocean, hail! To thee for the wind, hail!"—thus five times without taking breath; in the same manner, two further [sets].

"Six additional [oblations] according to the procedure: 'To Agni with the Vasus, svāhā! To Soma with the Rudras, svāhā! To Varuṇa with the Ādityas, svāhā! To Bṛhaspati with the Viśve Devas, svāhā! To Savitṛ with the Arbhus, Vibhus, Prabhus, and Vājins, svāhā! To Yama with the Aṅgirases and the Pitṛs, svāhā!'—with these he gazes at the Brahman seated to the south, saying, 'All the quarters are established in the south.'"

"Viśvān devān ayāḍ iha" (He has sacrificed here to all the gods)—saying this, while stepping over the Hotṛ seated behind with his left foot, he mutters: "O Aśvins, drink of the honeyed Gharma consecrated by Svāhā; Svāhā to Agni worthy of sacrifice; may it be auspicious through the Yajus-formulas.

He causes the sacrificer to recite: "O Aśvins, drink the Gharma that gladdens the heart; day after day, with your protections, may Heaven and Earth grant you approval. Having loudly called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Recite the offering-verse for the Gharma," and when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers the oblation with "Svāhā to Indra!"

Having offered at the second *vaṣaṭ*-call with the formula, "Svāhā! O Indra, drink! he causes [the sacrificer] to recite: "The Aśvins have drunk the Gharma, the heart-gladdening one, day by day with their aids; Heaven and Earth have approved of you both. May that which is to be protected go as it was found. Homage to Heaven, homage to Earth! Thus, place this sacrifice in heaven; place this sacrifice in heaven. Go to heaven, go to the intermediate space, go to the earth, go to the five directions, go to the gods who drink the Gharma, go to the ancestors who drink the Gharma—at this time."

The Pratiprasthātṛ, having dipped the *pinvana* ladle into the supporting vessel (*upayamana*), fills the *pracaraṇīya* Mahāvīra with milk. Then the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ together cause it to swell within the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), reciting in a low voice: "Swell for food; swell for strength; swell for the Brahman; swell for the Kṣatra; swell for the waters; swell for the plants; swell for the trees; swell for Heaven and Earth; swell for well-being; swell for spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); swell for the sacrificer; swell for me. Having thus spoken in a low voice, he then says aloud: "Swell for preeminence! (*jyaiṣṭhyāya pīpihi*).

Then he causes himself to swell toward each of the quarters, saying: "For brilliance thee! For splendor thee! For power thee! For prosperity thee! At this point, he pours the milk that was in the *mahāvīra* into the supporting vessel (*upayamana*). Then, having stepped out toward the north, he places this supporting vessel within the altar with its opening facing east. At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ hides the silver disk (*rukma*) in the mound (*khara*) belonging to the *udvāsanīya*;
upon it, he places the *mahāvīra* used for the ritual performance.

"You are the Dharma, the well-established Dharma; maintain the *brahmans* for us, maintain the *kṣatriyas*, maintain the *vaiśyas*. Let not the wind cause you to fall away. Now, if he should practice sorcery, [he says]: "I place you in the breath of so-and-so; go to ruin along with him—him who hates us and whom we hate. Then, having touched water, he asks for six chips of *udumbara* wood.

Having taken up one of them from the supporting ladle, he lets it drip into the eastern half of the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "To Pūṣan, the sharp-edged, svāhā! Then he places it so that it touches the middle enclosing-stick at its inner end. In the same way, having taken up the second from the supporting ladle, he lets it drip into the very same eastern half of the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "To the pressing-stones, svāhā! He places it likewise so that it touches the middle enclosing-stick at its inner end.
In the same way, having taken up the third from the supporting ladle, he lets it drip into the middle of the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "To the Pratirebas, svāhā!"

He places that inner ointment so as to touch the middle enclosing stick; in the same way, having taken [the butter] from the supporting ladle with the fourth [verse], he lets it drip on the rear half of the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "To Heaven and Earth, svāhā! Then he hides this upper ointment within the ashes. In the same way, having taken [the butter] from the supporting ladle with the fifth [verse], he lets it drip on the southern half of the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "To the Fathers who drink the Gharma, svāhā! Then he places this outer ointment upon the southern enclosing stick.

Having touched [the vessel], he causes it to settle. Then, having taken that sixth wood-splinter, having smeared it with all the residues and having finally dipped it into the supporting grass-bundle (*upayamana*), he lets it drip onto the northern part of the Āhavanīya fire, saying: "To Rudra, who belongs to the Hotṛ, Svāhā! Then, without looking back, he throws it out through the opening on the north side of the hall, saying: "Go away to ruin along with so-and-so, whoever hates us and whom we hate. Then, having touched water, he [dips] the remaining wood-splinters into the water.

At this time, while the Āhavanīya fire is being touched, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the northern *sauviṣṭakṛta* oblation with the formula: "May Day, the light, be pleased with its banner; may the good light [be pleased] with the lights, svāhā! At this point, he silently places that fuel-stick in the middle of the Āhavanīya. When it has caught fire, he makes two offerings facing it with the formula: "bhūḥ svāhā. Then, having placed that supporting tray (*upayamana*) within the altar with its opening directed eastward, he performs the Agnihotra procedure over it.

Having sought permission from as many officiating priests (ṛtvij) of the Pravargya rite as there are, the sacrificer alone consumes [the remnant] directly, saying: "The oblation is offered; the honeyed oblation, O Indra-like Agni, is for thee. Thou art our father; do not harm me. O divine Gharma, may we enjoy thee who art honeyed, full of vigor, full of nourishment, belonging to the Aṅgirases, and possessed of the Svadhā-call; do not harm me."

Then, having cleansed this supporting tray (upayamana) either on the mound of remnants (ucchiṣṭakhara) or by the Āgnīdhra, and having placed it within the altar with its opening facing east, they cast two gold and silver plates into it, pour in the boiling waters (madantī), and purify themselves with the four verses beginning, "Golden-hued, pure, and purifying. Having poured those boiling waters right there, he offers the expiations for the Gharma, dipping the spoon into the vessel of clarified butter, with these two sections of mantras beginning, "To Prāṇa, svāhā! To Pūṣan, svāhā!"

Then, having placed this supporting tray (upayamana) within the altar with its opening facing east, and having grasped it, while calming the heat (gharma), he says, "Recite for the Gharma as it is being set down. Then, having carried this supporting tray around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, he places it on the black antelope skin upon the royal throne (samrāḍāsandi) to the south, with its opening facing east, saying, "Svāhā! To thee, for the rays of the sun! Then they perform the northern pacification (śānti), saying, "May the wind, Mātariśvan, blow auspiciously for us. Then, in the afternoon, he proceeds with the afternoon Pravargya;
whatever is prescribed for that [morning rite] is indeed prescribed for this one as well.

The ritual procedure is the same up to the offering of the southern *rauhiṇa* cake; then he offers the southern *rauhiṇa*: "May Night, the light, enjoy [the offering] with its banner; may the fair-lighted one [enjoy it] with the lights, Svāhā! In the same way, he offers the northern *rauhiṇa*. The ritual procedure is the same up to the placing of the fuel-stick (*samidh*). At this point, he places this fuel-stick in the middle of the Āhavanīya fire: "Thou hast carried me across from day; protect me from night! This is thy fuel, O Agni; by it mayest thou be kindled; grant me life; anoint me with luster! Thus in the evening. In the morning: "Thou hast carried me across from night; protect me from day!"
From that point forward, he adds fuel in the forenoon with the morning mantra and in the afternoon with the evening mantra.
When that fire has been kindled, he offers oblations twice facing it: in the evening with "Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā! and in the morning with "Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā!"
The ritual procedure is the same up to the formal summons (*saṃpraiṣa*).

Then, having carried this supporting tray (*upayamana*) around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, he places it on the black antelope skin upon the royal throne (*samrāḍāsandi*) to the south, with its opening facing west, saying: "Svāhā! To thee for the constellations! Then they perform the subsequent pacification rite (*śānti*), saying: "May Vāta Mātariśvan blow auspiciously for us.
He proceeds with the Pravargya ceremony in this very manner for three days, six days, twelve days, a year, or four months, while the fire is being heated.

"Having consumed the Pravargya, for one year he should not eat meat, nor approach a woman, nor drink from an earthen vessel, nor should anyone drink his leavings; for thus he composes his own brilliance," so says the Brāhmaṇa. When he is about to remove the Pravargya, he prepares three fire-sticks, fuel, three seats, two water-pitchers, curds mixed with honey, a handful of *grumuṣṭi* grass, a bundle of *avakā* plants, twenty fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood, cuttings of *muñja* grass, flour of *rauhiṇa* grains, and sand for the mounds (*khara*).

Here they perform the preliminary pacification with the mantra, "Homage to speech! Then, having strewn grass in front of the Āhavanīya fire, they set down together all these items belonging to the Gharma rite: here the throne for the Sovereign (Samrāj), here the pillar, here the milking-vessel, and here the peg for the she-goat. Then, having poured out the two pits separately into their respective vessels, they set them down together right here. Then, either the attendant or the Āgnīdhra, having poured the contents of the *ucchiṣṭa* pit into its vessel, carries it out through the southern door to the Mārjālīya area.
Having offered the oblation, they return by the same way they came and cause the Śūdras to go out;

they summon the wife, they summon the Hotṛ, they summon the Brahman, they summon the Pratiprasthātṛ, and they summon the Prastotṛ. They enclose the Āgnīdhra shed and the doors; then they screen the seated wife with a garment whose fringes point northward.

They strew the sacrificial grass. The Brahman and the sacrificer sit down to the south; they perform the first *śānti* (appeasement) for those whose [ritual] has not yet been entered upon. Then, at the *gārhapatya* fire, having melted the clarified butter, he purifies it. At this time, the *pratiprasthātṛ*, having kindled the *śālāka* fuel on the *āhavanīya* fire and holding it at the height of his mouth, stands in front facing west.

The *adhvaryu*, standing behind him facing east, offers an oblation with the *sruva* ladle, saying: "O Gharma, that heat of yours which is in heaven, which is in the *gāyatrī* metre, which is in the Brāhmaṇa, and which is in the *havirdhāna*—that I appease for you with this; svāhā!"
Having thrown that very [fuel] right there and having kindled another, he stands in front facing west while holding it at the height of his navel;

standing behind him facing east, the Adhvaryu makes an offering with a spoon, saying: "O Gharma, whatever heat of yours is in the intermediate space, in the Triṣṭubh metre, in the Rājanya, or in the Āgnīdhra—by means of this, I appease that of yours, svāhā!
Having thrown that very [fuel] right there and having kindled another, he stands in front facing west while holding it at the height of his knees.

Standing behind it facing east, the Adhvaryu makes an offering over it with the dipping-spoon (sruva), saying: "O Gharma, that heat of yours which is on the earth, which is in the Jāgata metre, which is in the Vaiśya, which is in the assembly—by this [offering], I appease that of yours; svāhā!

Having thrown it right there and having opened the doors, they then take up the Pravargya vessel and go out by the eastern door, reciting the two verses: "May Anumati favor us today... and "...O Anumati, do thou favor us...".
Then, having stepped onto the Mahāvedi, he says to the Prastotṛ: "Prastotṛ, chant the Sāman!"
"The Prastotṛ follows with the Sāman; he reaches the Nidhana thrice;
'every single person reaches the Nidhana,' so says the Brāhmaṇa."
Then they step forward with the mantra:
"For the protection of heaven, protect us; protect the bodies of the intermediate space; by the law of the earth, we step forward for new prosperity."

At the equinox (viṣuvat), they perform the second *nidhana* and then step forward, saying: "For the protection of the Brahman, guard the bodies of the Kṣatra; by the law (*dharman*) of the Viś, we step after you for new prosperity. At the time of the *uparava* holes, they perform the third *nidhana* and then step forward, saying: "For the protection of the breath, guard the bodies of sight; by the law of hearing, we step after you for new prosperity. Then they stop to the north of the *uttaravedi*.
He who is strong, he says to him: "Go around three times to the right, sprinkling [the water] with this water-pitcher in a continuous stream.
He does so.
While it is being sprinkled, he causes the sacrificer to recite: "Thou art auspicious, O bringer of peace; a child of the nourisher of men; bring us peace and bring us prosperity all around."

Having set down the water-pot as before, he goes around it three times again in the opposite direction; then he touches the northern navel with the formula: "The navel of the Cosmic Order has four corners, the seat of all life, wide protection; may we drive away hatred and crookedness; let us follow another path of the Law. Then he scatters those two mounds to the north of the northern navel;
with two fire-stirring sticks, he makes that mound long from east to west.

Having placed gold and bullion upon that [spot], he spreads out a black antelope skin with its neck to the east and its hair upwards; then, having scattered the *rauhiṇa* flour over it and smoothed it with cuttings of *muñja* grass, he scatters sand over it. Then the Adhvaryu, grasping the *pracaraṇīya* Mahāvīra vessel with two hooves, fills it with curds mixed with honey, saying: "O Gharma, this is your food, this is your soil; through it, grow and swell; and may we also grow and swell."

"May we drink," [he says]. Then he fills it with: "Thou art the milk of the great ones; thou art ordained among the gods as light; thou art the radiance of the trees and the sap of the plants. We, who are strong, pour thee down, who art strong. Then he places it on the eastern half of the mound with: "The mind is directed upward toward heaven."

Then, having taken these two *upāśaya* Mahāvīras with both hands and filled them with curds mixed with honey, he places them so that they touch the front of the *pracaraṇīya* Mahāvīra. Then, having filled this *pracaraṇī* ladle with curds mixed with honey, he places it upon the Mahāvīras with its opening facing westward. Then, having smeared these two gold plates (*rukma*) with curds mixed with honey, he places them so that they touch the *pracaraṇīya* Mahāvīra on both sides. Then these two *pinvana* vessels [are filled] with curds mixed with honey.
Having filled the *pracaraṇī* ladle all around, he places it so that it touches the great *mahāvīra* pot at its western opening.

Then, having untied this girdle made of muñja grass, he anoints it with curds mixed with honey and spreads it out, touching the large cauldrons (*mahāvīra*) with its tip pointing westward. Then, having anointed these two hoof-shaped pieces (*śapha*) with curds mixed with honey, he places them behind the large cauldron used for the ritual performance (*pracaraṇīya*), with their tips crossing each other transversely and touching. Then, having anointed these two Rauhiṇa-offering spoons with curds mixed with honey, he places them with their tips pointing westward, touching the tips of the two hoof-pieces. Then, these ten [spoons] made of udumbara wood...

Having anointed the fuel-sticks with curds mixed with honey, he spreads them out behind the Rauhiṇa-offering ladle so that their tips point westward and they touch one another; then, having untied this Veda made of Kuśa grass and anointed it with curds mixed with honey, he spreads it out behind the Mahāvīra vessel used for the performance, touching it with its tips pointing westward; then these two posts, having anointed them with curds mixed with honey, he places them down behind the two hoof-prints so that their tips point westward and they touch one another; then this supporting tray with curds...

Having filled it with honey-mixed [milk], he places it upon the two pillars with its opening facing westward. Then, having untied this cord for the fire-drill, he anoints it with honey-mixed curds and sets it down right there upon the support. Then, having untied these enclosing sticks made of *kārṣmarya* wood and the handles of the fans, he anoints them with honey-mixed curds and spreads them out above the support, with their tips laid crosswise, interlaced, and touching one another. Then, having anointed this hoe with honey-mixed curds—

He places [the two posts] behind the two pillars so that they touch them with their tips turned crosswise; then he anoints these two fire-stirring sticks (*dhṛṣṭi*) with curds mixed with honey and places them behind the two spoons so that they touch them with their tips turned westward.

Then, having anointed these two fans with curds mixed with honey, he places them down so that they touch each other behind the *dhṛṣṭi* ladle. Then, having anointed these ten fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood with curds mixed with honey, he spreads them out behind the two fans so that their tips point westward and they touch one another. Then, having filled this vessel of clarified butter with curds mixed with honey, he places it down behind the wooden shovel (*abhri*) so that it touches it. Then, he anoints this fan with curds mixed with honey.

Therefore, he covers the vessel of clarified butter; then, having anointed these two Rauhiṇa potsherds with curds mixed with honey, he places them behind the vessel of clarified butter so that they touch it. Then, having filled this dipping-spoon (sruva) with curds mixed with honey, he places it behind the vessel of clarified butter, between the two Rauhiṇa potsherds, so that its bowl faces westward and it touches them. Then, having untied this Veda-bundle made of Kuśa grass and anointed it with curds mixed with honey, he places it behind the vessel of clarified butter with its tips facing westward so that it touches it.

Then, having loosened this seat (āsandī) and spread it out, he anoints it with curds mixed with honey and places it right here to the north, touching [the clay]. Then, having anointed the remaining clay with curds mixed with honey, he pours it down between the two thighs.

"O Gharma, this is your food, this is your soil; grow with it and swell with it, and may we also grow and swell. Then, having scattered sand over it and covered it with cuttings of *muñja* grass, and having scattered the flour of the *rauhiṇa* cakes over it, he covers it with a black antelope skin, with the neck pointing eastward and the hair side up. Alternatively, he encloses the *mahāvīra* vessel used for the ritual on all sides like the circle of the sun; then he worships it [with the verse]: "He who is in human form, may he be in our mouth..."

"You stand; neither above nor across am I fashioned according to your fashion, but you are fashioned according to my fashion. Who you are, that am I; who I am, that are you. Ascend to the firmament together with the sacrificer."

Then, taking a handful of grass, he sprinkles it with curds mixed with honey, saying: "The sky has leaped over the earth; the young bull has leaped over the cows. May this entire world leap; may the sacrifice leap and procreate. From what has leaped, it was born; it has been procreated. From what has leaped, the bull is born; from what has leaped, may we procreate. Then he says to the Prastotṛ: "O Prastotṛ, sing the Vārṣāhara Sāman and the Iṣṭāhotrīya. He who is strong, him he addresses: "Go around three times to the right, sprinkling continuously with this water-pitcher."

While the water is being sprinkled, he causes the sacrificer to recite the Gandharva-formulas, beginning with: "Thou art Ranti by name, the divine Gandharva; Indra recognized the skill of the unimpaired. Having set down the pitcher there, he returns three times again in the same manner as he went. Then he stands over it [the Gharma] and worships it, saying: "O divine Gharma, thou as a god hast gone to the gods; here I, a man, go to men. Come after me to the Soma-drinking, together with offspring and together with abundance of wealth. Then he scoops up water with his joined palms, saying: "May the waters and the plants be friendly to us."

He sprinkles water toward that direction in which he has an enemy, saying: "May they be ill-disposed toward him who hates us and whom we hate. Then, having touched water, he worships the sun with the *jyotiṣmatī* verse, "Upward from the darkness... He then covers it with a load of *avakā* plants and instructs a guardian: "Guard the Mahāvīra vessel from birds;

O Prastotṛ, follow after it with the Śyaita chant. He says this to the Prastotṛ. Then, returning by the same way he came, he offers two spoonfuls of oblation on the Gārhapatya fire with the verses, "Upward that [sun]... and "The bright..."

Then they stand by the Āhavanīya fire, reciting: "Proclaim this for us, O Agni, among the gods—this newest Gāyatra song, this gain. Then, having run to the place of the Āgnīdhra, they perform the subsequent *śānti* rite at the place of the Āgnīdhra, [reciting]: "May the wind blow auspiciously for us, O Mātariśvan..."

Now, therefore, we shall explain the expiations for the *gharma* ceremony. If the sun should set while the *pravargya* has not yet been performed, one should offer three spoonfuls of oblations into the *gārhapatya* fire with the words "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ," and having performed the *upasad* rite, one should proceed with the *pravargya* on the following day. If the sun should set while the *pravargya* has already been commenced, one should offer three spoonfuls of oblations into the *gārhapatya* fire with the words "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ"; then, having tied a piece of gold with a thread at the western door—

If it should then become active and fall into the *gārhapatya* fire, one should offer three spoonfuls with the formula, "bhūḥ bhuvaḥ suvaḥ. Then he raises it up with two verses: "ūrdhva ū ṣu ṇa ūtaye" and "ūrdhvo naḥ pāhy aṃhasaḥ.

Then he fills it with clarified butter with the verse, "añjanti yaṃ prathayanto na viprāḥ. Now, if a fissure or a crack should appear, one should mix powdered stone with goat's milk, sprinkle that over it, and heat it all around with a firebrand with two verses: "vidhuṃ dadrāṇaṃ" and "yadṛte cid abhiśriṣaḥ. It will surely heal completely.

If, however, it should break entirely, he should grind these very potsherds with unguents, mix them with that clay which lies set aside for expiation, fashion [another vessel], bake it, let it cool, and set it down; then he prepares another *mahāvīra* for use. Now, if they should pass by [the fire] while distracted, he should offer three spoonfuls on the *gārhapatya* fire, saying: "Bhūḥ! Bhuvaḥ! Suvaḥ!"

Then, with the words, "Return again with strength and wealth," they walk around it again. Now, if it should fly up while being raised, he should offer three spoonfuls of oblations into the *gārhapatya* fire with the words, "Bhūḥ! Bhuvaḥ! Suvaḥ! Then he touches it with two verses: "O Gharma, do not cause us distress; do not trouble us; do not [afflict] us with our censured intentions. Thus with these two.

Now, if a bird should cause the Gharma-milch cow or the Mahāvīra vessel to flow [with blood], one should wash them with warm water while reciting, "O Mitra and Varuṇa, come here to our aid. Then, one should offer nine spoonfuls of oblations in the Gārhapatya fire with the verses: "Hear this my call, O Varuṇa," "To that I go for refuge," "Do thou, O Agni," "So do thou, O Agni," "O Agni, thou art Ayāsya," "We two from out of the darkness," "Upwards that light," and "The fair-winged birds. Now, if one cannot find the Gharma-milch cow, one should have another milked; and if one cannot find another, then a goat.

If he should not find a goat, he should proceed with the milk of an *arka* plant; if he should not find the milk of an *arka*, he should mix together barley flour, rice flour, or millet flour with water and proceed with that—even with water alone he may proceed—but he must certainly not fail to proceed. "Thou art the milk of the great ones," with these words the pouring into the *mahāvīra* is prescribed. "The sky has descended upon the earth," with this he consecrates what has been spilled. Now, if lightning should strike, he should offer a spoonful in the *gārhapatya* fire with the verses beginning, "That lightning which fell in the east," according to the specific form [of the direction].

"Oblation to Prāṇa, svāhā! Oblation to Pūṣan, svāhā!"—these are the expiations for the Gharma; and whenever any part of the Gharma ritual is performed out of order, one should offer these oblations: "Homage to thee, O Gharma, Lord of the Earth, svāhā! Homage to thee, O Gharma, Lord of the World, svāhā! Homage to thee, O Gharma, Lord of Beings, svāhā! To Gharma, svāhā! To the Aśvins, svāhā! To Indra, svāhā! To Bṛhaspati, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! To Brahman, svāhā!"

Then, having placed the *aṣāḍhā* brick marked with three lines and the *uttara-lakṣman*, he places here the *gharmeṣṭakā* and the *kulāyinī*. He places the *gharmeṣṭakā* with the verse, "Out of his vigor [arose] the sun," and the *kulāyinī* with the verse, "Those which are thy wet wombs, O Agni. Having worshipped the piled fire with Sāmans and praised it with an Uktha, standing at the northern corner of the hip, he touches the fire while reciting this Anuvāka: "Thou art Agni; thou art Vaiśvānara. At this point, he gives a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Adhvaryu: either a hundred, a thousand, or as many as the bricks.

At the Soma sacrifice accompanied by the *pravargya* ceremony, they consume the *dadhigharma* with the anuvāka beginning, "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! May that great power of Indra [be mine]! Then he assigns the terrible forms (*tanūḥ*):

"O Agni, those terrible forms of yours—*tanūḥ*, *snīhī*, *snīhiti*, *snīhiti*—these are the terrible forms; *dhuni* and *dhvānta*," thus the group belonging to the *rājasūya*; "and *ugra* and *dhuni*," thus the group belonging to the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicityā*). Now, if a thief should steal either the Gharma-milch cow or the Mahāvīra vessel, one should offer a spoonful in the Gārhapatya fire with the verse, "May Day and Night drive him away."

"Khaḍiti" means cruel words. Now, if [the victim] cries out like a single-eyed hawk, he addresses him with the mantra: "O Indra, as you wander, let loose the cows. Then he should throw a firebrand burning at both ends toward him, saying: "O Agni, converse with Agni; O Death, converse with Death. Then he stands over him, saying: "One time, O Agni, obeisance to thee; twice, obeisance to thee; thrice, obeisance to thee."

Now, if a vulture should cry out, he addresses it with the mantra: "The blood-mouthed one, indistinct with gore. Then, if distressed speech should arise, he addresses it with the mantra: "When this [speech], having become a wolf... Then, if a jackal or a *kākapiñjaka* should cry out, he addresses it with the mantra: "Whether impelled or whether acting of its own will... Then, if a female hyena should cry out, he addresses it with the mantra: "O long-faced one, O evil-jawed one... Then, if an owl or a female owl should cry out, he addresses it with the mantra: "Thus indeed, O owl..."

It has flown down. Now, if mad speech should arise, he addresses it with the mantra: "When you have entered into these beings... Now, if a bird should alight upon the *gharmadughā* cow or the *mahāvīra* vessel, he addresses it with the mantra: "Spreading out your thighs, you fly... Now, if worms should infest the *gharmadughā* cow or the *mahāvīra* vessel, he should wash them away with water, saying: "With the *Atriṇ* spell, I kill you, worm! Now, if an enemy should approach the *pravargya* rite while it is in progress, [he should address him] at the *gārhapatya* fire...
He should offer a libation with the *sruva* ladle, saying, "O bringer, cut off!

Then, when he is about to pronounce a curse against someone, he should pronounce it against him, saying, "I curse you by means of the Brahman. Then, he should shake the right arm of the door-post of the person whom he hates, saying, "Sting, O thou that art born of *śimi*! If anyone else should bark at these [three], he should throw a firebrand burning on both ends at him, saying, "Sting, O thou that art born of *śimi*! Then, if the wind should blow as if shaking everything, he addresses it with the mantra: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ, bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ, bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ; the world has been established, the world has been established, the world has been established."

Now, if he should enter the hall uninvited, he should enter with these verses, namely with the verse, "Whatever of ours is deficient here"; but if he is indeed invited, he should enter with this very same verse.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*). During the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious constellation, having had his hair and beard shaved and having performed the introductory rite as before, he goes out from the village toward the east or the north. Having established the fire on a barren spot where no roof-cover is visible, having strewn grass around it, and having placed the boiling water (*madantī*) over the fire, he performs the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the first Anuvāka. Then, with *darbha* grass, he prepares seats for the deities of the Pravargya ceremony, saying: "I prepare a seat for the Pravargya; I prepare a seat for the Gharma; I prepare a seat for the Mahāvīra; I prepare a seat for the Sovereign (*samrāj*)."

"To the south of the fire, I prepare [the seat] for Brahmā; 'for Prajāpati, I prepare,' [he says] to the north of the fire; 'for the Ṛṣis, the makers of mantras, the lords of mantras, I prepare; for the gods who drink the Gharma, I prepare. Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), to the south, he says: 'For the fathers who drink the Gharma, I prepare; for Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the fathers, I prepare. Then, having touched water, to the north, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), he says: 'O Rudras, for Rudra the Hotṛ, I prepare. Then, having touched water, he says: 'For all the deities of the Pravargya, I prepare.'"

Having sprinkled water around the fire from left to right and having placed fuel sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood with the *vyāhṛtis*, he gratifies the deities of the *pravargya* rite with the *madantī* waters, saying: "I gratify the *pravargya* in front of the fire; I gratify the *gharma*; I gratify the *mahāvīra*; I gratify the sovereign (*samrāj*)."

To the south of the fire, [he says] "I satiate Brahmā; I satiate Prajāpati"; to the north of the fire, [he says] "I satiate the seers, the makers of mantras, the lords of mantras; I satiate the gods who drink the Gharma. Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), to the south, he says, "I satiate the ancestors who drink the Gharma; I satiate Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the Pitṛs. Then, having touched water, to the north, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), he says, "I satiate Rudra, the Hotṛ Rudra. Then, having touched water again, he says, "I satiate all the deities of the Pravargya."

While he causes him to place four fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood—whose tips are not dried out and which have been anointed with clarified butter—he causes him to recite these mantras one by one: "The earth is the fuel-stick," and so forth.

Then he worships the deities: "O Agni, lord of vows, I shall perform the Śukriya vow; may I be able to do so, may it be successful for me. O Vāyu, lord of vows; O Āditya, lord of vows; O Lord of Vows among vows, I shall perform the Śukriya vow; may I be able to do so, may it be successful for me. Then he causes him to recite the introductory verses of these Anuvākas, or those of the first and the last. Or else, he instructs him: "Close your eyes and restrain your speech. Then, with an unwashed garment, he wraps his head three times from left to right, facing forward.
He encloses [the altar] with the formula, "Ye are the piled [bricks], the surrounding ones; svāhā! Be enclosed by the Maruts.

Having sprinkled water around the fire from left to right, having placed fuel sticks of *vikaṅkata* wood with the *vyāhṛtis*, and having gratified the deities of the *pravargya* with the *madantī* waters, he performs the rite of peace (*śānti*) with the final *anuvāka*. Then, after the sun has set, they go to the village.

Restraining his speech, he should remain standing during this night, or sit, or lie down; then, in the morning when the sun has risen, having gone out from the village toward the east or the north, and having established the fire in a barren spot where no roof is visible, having strewn grass around it, having placed the boiling water on the fire, and having performed the pacification with the first Anuvāka, he prepares seats for the Pravargya deities with Darbha grass. Then, having removed his garment with the verse "The birds, the fair-winged," he shows him these six things: fire, water, the sun, a cow, a Brāhmaṇa, and gold.

Having first shown three [verses], and having shown the others as they occur, he should sprinkle water around the fire from left to right, place fuel-sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood with the *vyāhṛtis*, satisfy the deities of the *pravargya* rite with the *madantī* waters, perform the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the final *anuvāka*, and then instruct him in the observances of his vow: "He shall not mount a vehicle; he shall not climb a tree; he shall not descend into a well; he shall not hold an umbrella;
he shall not wear sandals; he shall not sleep on a couch."
He should not converse with a woman nor with a Śūdra; if he must converse, he should converse with a Brāhmaṇa;
he should not eat in the evening.

If he eats, let him eat unkindled food; he shall not bathe; on the eighth day and on the festival days (parvan) he shall fast, but on that [eighth] day he may bathe; he shall remain silent and stand during the day, and sit or lie down during that night. Upon seeing something impure, blood, a corpse, or an outcast vessel, he shall look at the heavenly lights. Having seen something impure, he mutters: "The mind is unbound, the eye is poor; Sūrya is the best of lights; O Consecration (Dīkṣā), do not abandon me! Now, if it rains upon him, he mutters: "O flowing waters, bestow strength, bestow vigor, bestow strength; do not destroy my consecration, do not destroy my austerity."
One should observe this vow for a year, for one does not transcend the vow for a year; however, one may study this very [text] during that year.
Or, if one does not study it during that year, one should observe this vow for as long as the study lasts; then, when the year has elapsed, one may teach or cause others to hear it.

Having performed the introductory rites as before, having gone out from the village toward the east or the north, having established the fire in a desolate place where no roof is visible, having strewn grass around it, having placed the boiling water on the fire, and having performed the *śānti* rite with the first *anuvāka*, he prepares seats for the deities of the *pravargya* ceremony using *darbha* grass. Then he offers oblations for the expiation of transgressions of the vow (*avratyaprāyaścitta*) with the two verses, "Whatever flaw has occurred in my self" and "Agni has given back my sight. Having sprinkled water around the fire clockwise and added fuel-sticks of *vikaṅkata* wood with the *vyāhṛtis*, he satiates the deities of the *pravargya* ceremony with the boiling water.

Having caused four Udumbara fuel-sticks—whose tips are not dried out and which have been anointed with clarified butter—to be placed upon the fire, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite the formulas, one by one, beginning with "The sky is the fuel-stick. Then he worships the deities, saying: "O Āditya, lord of vows, I have performed the Śukriya vow; I was able to do it; may it be successful for me. O Vāyu, lord of vows... O Agni, lord of vows... O Lord of vows, lord of all vows, I have performed the Śukriya vow; I was able to do it; may it be successful for me. Having gratified the deities of the Pravargya rite with the boiling waters (madantī), he performs the propitiatory rite (śānti) with the final Anuvāka.
One should prescribe for him the days when study is forbidden, and he himself should not study when the sun has set, nor when it has not yet risen, nor when there are water droplets falling.
Not when it is turned away, nor in the shade of a cloud, nor near domestic animals, nor near wild animals.
Not at the edge of water, nor while looking at green barley, nor at mansions,
nor at corpses.
Not having seen blood spurt forth,
nor having eaten me, nor having consumed the funeral offering (śrāddha).
He does not shave his hair and beard,
nor does he let his hair hang loose, nor does he brush his teeth.
He does not anoint himself, he does not rub oil on his body, nor is he wet.

One should not study while wearing wet clothes, nor when one is oneself wet. Then, having sat down on *darbha* grass to the west of the fire, holding *darbha* grass in his hand, he should recite the *svādhyāya* facing away from the fire. Wherever he perceives anything that has not been consecrated with peace (*śānti*), he should perform the *śānti* rite again and then recite. Having finished the recitation, he should go out for the *pravargya* ritual with the final verse; until he has entered the village, he should not study anything else—he should not study anything else.

Intending to collect the fire-pans (ukhās), he prepares a horse and a donkey; for these two, two reins made of muñja grass or of kuśa grass; a hoe with a wooden handle; earth obtained from a Brāhmaṇa’s field that has been prepared and is fit for use; a mound from an anthill; a black antelope skin and a lotus leaf; a yoke-halter; a water-jar; gold; potsherds from an old, broken vessel; gravel; powdered ointment-unguents; wool from a ram; hair from a black antelope skin; a Vaiśya who possesses seventeen [qualities]; a knife for cutting; a skilled artisan who has fashioned the pans; and then, either by means of the New Moon sacrifice (amāvāsya) or—
Having performed the oblation with clarified butter under an auspicious constellation, he causes a pit to be dug in front of the hall at the point where the pegs are set;
he then coats it with the prepared earth and makes it level with the mouth of the pit.

He places near [the fire] a black antelope skin, a lotus leaf, a yoke-tie, a water-pot, and gold. Then, at the midpoint, having dug up with the wooden sword (sphya) and sprinkled [water], he places a mound of earth from an anthill;
a Vaiśya sits to the south guarding it. Then, having dug up with the wooden sword in front of the northern part of the hall and sprinkled [water], he pours down sand;
he makes that into a circular mound (khara) and then covers it with sand so that it is shining.

Having covered it with young *kuśa* shoots and knots of *dūrvā* grass, they then enclose it; they make a door for it facing north. He places near it shards of pottery, pebbles, ground collyrium, black goat hair, black antelope skin with its hair, a slaughter-stool, a fire-pot, and a skilled butcher. Then these two, a horse and a donkey, stand at the front of the hall, having been washed; he places the wooden sword (*abhri*) within the altar, and the two ropes at the northern edge of the altar.
They strew grass around [the fires].

The Brahman and the sacrificer sit down to the south. Then, having melted the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire and purified it, and having taken four portions into the ladle, he offers the Sāvitra oblations in the Āhavanīya fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, reciting the six verses beginning with "yuñjānaḥ prathamaṃ manaḥ," followed immediately by the verse "deva savitaḥ" and the formula "eṣa no deva savitaḥ. This is the ritual procedure.

He completes [the rite] with either a *ṛc* or a *yajus*. Having offered the ninth oblation, he worships with the verse, "With a *ṛc*, may he fulfill the *stoma*. Then he takes up the wooden shovel (*abhri*) with the four sections beginning, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ.

Having carried it around in front of the *āhavanīya* fire, he hands it to the Brahman priest seated to the south. Then he takes up the rope with the verse, "They took hold of this rope of Order," and with it he fastens the horse, saying, "O steed, run forward! In the same manner, he takes up a second rope.
With her, he yokes the donkey with two verses: "Yoke ye the donkey, you two, at every yoking, the most powerful one," and "The more vigorous one.

They lead the horse first; he consecrates it with the formula: "Come forward, overleaping the curses. Following behind, he addresses the donkey: "Together with Pūṣan as thy companion, from the seat of the earth, come hither for Agni Purīṣya in the manner of Aṅgiras."

The Vaiśya indeed circumambulates the Vaiśya; the men ask, "What do you seek? and they reply, "We seek Agni Purīṣya in the manner of Aṅgiras. Then he stands by the ant-hill, saying, "We shall carry Agni Purīṣya in the manner of Aṅgiras. Then they go forward with the horse, [reciting] the two verses: "Agni Jātavedas, the first, has looked along the forefront of the dawns, along the days; he has extended himself along the many rays of the sun and along heaven and earth," and, "Having come, O steed, from the path, having stepped upon the earth, O steed. With these two [verses], he causes the horse to step upon the clay while facing eastward.

Then his back is rubbed with the verse: "The sky is your back, the earth your seat, the atmosphere your self, and the ocean your womb. Having looked out with your eye, trample upon those who attack. At this point, he meditates on whoever the sacrificer hates as being beneath the horse's feet. Then he makes it step forward facing east with two verses: "It has stepped out; it has stepped forth. Then he sprinkles that footprint with water.

"Release the divine waters, honey-sweet, for the health of offspring; from their place let the plants rise up with goodly fruit. Then, having taken four portions of clarified butter in the ladle, having placed gold in the southern intermediate hoof-print, and having strewn grass around it, he offers an oblation with the verse: "I sprinkle Agni with mind and with ghee."

Furthermore, having taken four portions of ghee and having placed gold in the northern intermediate hoof-print, and having strewn grass around it, he makes an offering upon it with the verse, "I besprinkle thee with speech and with ghee. Having removed the gold and taken up the spade, he traces around the footprint with the three verses, "The wise lord of booty," "Around thee, O Agni, like a fortress," and "Thou, O Agni, with thy days.
He digs with the two verses, "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ" and "Thee, O Agni, full of light, of fair countenance."

Then, having spread out grass-blades with their tips pointing eastward on the northern side for the ritual materials, he spreads over them a black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and the hair facing upward. Then, bringing a lotus leaf with the formula, "Thou art the back of the waters," he places it upon the black antelope skin and touches both of them together with the two verses, "Ye two are a refuge; may ye be united. Having removed the lotus leaf, he takes eight portions of clay.

"Purīṣya asi viśvabharā"—of these verses, four are *gāyatrīs* and four are *triṣṭubhs*. He carries the clods one by one with these verses; or rather, he carries a single clod with all eight verses. Then, having filled this pit with earth from all sides, he moistens it with water, [saying]: "May Vāyu Mātariśvan join together what was disjointed in the heart of thee who art stretched out."

"To him who moves by the breath of the gods—to him and to you, O Goddess, let there be *vaṣaṭ*! Having thus placed a lotus leaf upon the clay from above and gathered together the edges of the black antelope skin, he binds them with the yoke-cord, saying: "Well-born together with light, thou hast sat down as a refuge and a protection; O Agni, radiant one, clothe thyself in this all-formed garment. Then, taking it up, he stands up with two verses: "Arise, O performer of the fair sacrifice! Stand upright for our protection!"

Then he brings him [the fire] with the verse: "O Agni, you are the newborn child of the two worlds, beautiful and distributed among the plants; the bright infant, anointed, has overcome the darkness, crying out from his mothers. Then the donkey seats him [the fire] with the formula: "Be firm, O you of strong limbs; be swift, O racer, O steed; be broad and easy to sit upon, you who carry the soil of Agni. Then he stands over him with the formula: "Be auspicious toward the human offspring, O Aṅgiras;
do not burn against heaven and earth, nor the atmosphere, nor the trees. They lead the horse first.

He addresses them with the mantra: "Let the vigorous steed go forward, neighing loudly; let the ass go following behind, braying loudly, flying along with the sound of the chariot. Carrying Agni Purīṣya, may he not fall before his full span of life. The ass, neighing loudly, well-yoked to your chariot, O you two stallions—he shall carry from here the swift messenger, Agni Purīṣya, for you both. Carrying the stallion Agni, the embryo of the waters, the essence of the ocean—O Agni, come for the feast! Then they look at these two [the horse and the ass], saying, "Order! Truth! Order! Truth! and they cause the Vaiśya to circumambulate them clockwise.

The Vaiśya asks, "O men, what are you carrying? They reply, "We are carrying Agni Purīṣya, like Aṅgiras. Then they bring him down onto the mound (khara) with two verses: "May the plants receive this Agni; O plants, rejoice in him! Having sprinkled him with water, they release the horse and the donkey; they throw the two ropes into the water, or alternatively, having sprinkled them with water, they consume them.

Then he loosens him [the fire] with the verse, "Shining forth with broad radiance... On that day, he pours water over him with the three verses, "O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss," according to their respective meters.

Then he mixes it with potsherds from a broken vessel, gravel ground with *añjana*, goat-hairs, and the hairs of a black antelope skin, with the two verses: "Mitra, having mixed the earth, I mix thee for freedom from disease.
Then he gathers it together with [the verse], "The Rudras, having gathered the earth," and fashions it into a lump with [the formula], "Thou art the head of Makha."
With the words, "You two are at the station of the sacrifice," he presses down with his two thumbs. Then, having cut off a third portion from the clay, he fashions three lumps;

he gives one of them to the person who has prepared the mouth [of the image], and consecrates it with the formula, "United with the Vasus and Rudras. He gives half of the remaining clay to the person with the words, "May the Vasus fashion you with the Gāyatrī metre," and consecrates it with, "O Sinīvālī of the beautiful braids! He gives the other half with the words, "May the Rudras fashion you with the Triṣṭubh metre."

He gives all the remaining clay, saying, "Make the fire-pan as much as you are able," and he consecrates it with the formulas: "May the Ādityas fashion you with the Jagatī metre; may the Viśve Devas, belonging to Vaiśvānara, fashion you with the Anuṣṭubh metre. Now it is said:
"He restrains it with some [formulas] and consecrates it with others for the sake of pairing;
he makes it three-layered."
In that he carries [the earth] three times and anoints it three times, thereby it becomes three-peaked;

he makes it one span high, immeasurable across. Then, at its [corner], either three finger-breadths or four finger-breadths from the edge, he winds a girdle around it with the formula, "Thou art Aditi’s girdle. Then, along each of its directions, he raises eight corners;
and at the junctions of the girdle and the junctions of the corners, he forms eight teats.
"One should make it nine-cornered for one practicing black magic," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

He makes the ninth [corner] at the breast; then he takes its opening with the formula, "May Aditi take thy opening with the *pāṅkta* metre. Then he places it on the mound (*khara*) while reciting the rest of the section beginning with, "Having made this great fire-pan (*ukhā*). In the same way he makes a second, and likewise a third. [He makes] five *ṛṣabha*-bricks and three *maṇḍala*-bricks silently.
Then, with the clay that remains, he causes it to dry by exposing it to a windless spot.

When those breezes have subsided, prepare twenty-one balls of dung from a stallion, as well as a hoe, a fire, and a cooking vessel. Then, having kindled a horse-dung fire-brand, he fumigates the principal *ukhā* pot, beginning with: "May the Vasus fumigate thee with the Gāyatrī metre," and continuing with "May Varuṇa fumigate thee," both internally and externally.

Having fumigated it well, he deposits it; in the same way he fumigates the second, and likewise the third. [He places] five *carṣabha* bricks silently, and three *maṇḍaleṣṭakā* bricks. Then, to the north of the hall, he has a pit dug that is as wide as a large jar, with the formula: "May the goddess Aditi, accompanied by the Viśvedevas, dig thee, O pit, in the dwelling-place of the earth, in the manner of Aṅgiras."

Having spread that [clay] with the fire-pan (*pacana*), he places the primary and secondary [bricks] upon it with the formula: "May the divine wives of the gods, accompanied by the Viśvedevas, place thee, O *ukhā*, in the lap of the earth, like Aṅgiras. In this very same way he places the second, and likewise the third. He silently lays down five *ṛṣabha* bricks and three *maṇḍala-iṣṭakā* bricks; he extends them either eastward or northward. Then, having covered them from above with the fire-pan, he smears them with clay.
He leaves a space of four finger-breadths in each direction for the purpose of kindling, and then he sets them on fire.

With "May the Dhiṣaṇās protect you," he places [the fire] in the east; with "May the Agnāyah protect you," in the south; with "May the Varūtrīs protect you," in the west; and with "May the Janayas protect you," in the north. Then he entrusts them, saying: "O Mitra, bake this fire-pan; may it not break. I entrust it to you so that it may not break. These are baked either by day or by night.

If he fasts in the morning, he approaches [the sacrifice] in the evening; if in the evening, then in the morning.
