When those [milk products] have been cooked, he prepares cow’s milk, goat’s milk, a fire-stirring stick, a stone for grinding, a pair of tongs, a winnowing basket, a sling, and a black antelope skin. Having taken all this together, he approaches [the altar], reciting: "By his greatness, Mitra has become co-extensive with this heaven; and by his glory, with the earth. Of Mitra, the god who sustains the people, the glory is victorious."

With the verse, "Glory, most wonderful in fame," he then takes the *dhṛṣṭi* (stirring-ladle) and draws out the embers from the principal fire-pan (*ukhā*) with the formula: "May the god Savitṛ draw thee out, he who is fair-handed, fair-fingered, and fair-armed by his power. Then he raises it up with the formula: "Arise, become great; stand upright, thou steadfast one. Then he establishes it in its place with the formula: "Not falling away, mayest thou fill the regions and the quarters of the earth. Then, having grasped it with a pair of tongs and placed it in the vessel (*sata*), he heats it thoroughly with goat's milk.

"May the Vasus anoint you with the Gāyatrī metre," he begins; "may the Viśve Devas, belonging to all men, anoint you with the Anuṣṭubh metre. Having thus anointed it on both the inner and outer sides, he causes it to overflow with cow's milk. In this same manner he anoints the second, and likewise the third. [He prepares] five bull-bricks and three Maṇḍala-bricks silently. Now, if a crack or a fissure occurs, he throws powdered stone into goat's milk, sprinkles [the brick] with that, and heats it with a firebrand;
it then rises up whole once again.

If, however, it should break entirely, he grinds these very potsherds into powder, mixes them with that clay which remains for the purpose of expiation, kneads it, bakes it, and after it has cooled, sets it aside. When their hissing has ceased, he places them in a pit, covers them from above with a black antelope skin, hangs them on a sling in the northern part of the hall, and they remain there until the appointed time.
Now, in this very same context of the preliminary position, he performs a sacrifice with an animal dedicated to Vāyu;
for him, that which is prepared for one intending to sacrifice with an animal is ready: the heads of a horse and a Vaiśya killed in battle, while they play at dice, they cook a bull.
They bring a bull and a goat; this is the "serpent-head" [offering]. Now, on the previous day, this altar for the animal sacrifice (paśubandha) is prepared;

having strewn it around, he performs the *stambayajus* rite. This is well-known as the procedure for the cake-offering (*pauroḍāśika*): three times with the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) and a fourth time silently.
He performs the first tracing of the altar, mutters the *karaṇa* formula, digs up the earth, and from the dug-up spot, the Āgnīdhra carries away the earth three times.

When the Āgnīdhra carries [the earth] three times, then he traces around the *cātvāla* pit according to the procedure for the *cātvāla*; he pours out the *uttaravedi* altar according to the procedure for the *uttaravedi*; having leveled the *uttaranābhi*, he leads forward the fire according to the procedure for the fire; having performed the second tracing of the altar, having leveled it, and having fixed the wooden sword (*sphya*) across [the altar], he issues the call: "Set down the sprinkling waters; set down the fuel and the sacrificial grass; cleanse the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), the knife (*svadhiti*), and the offering-ladles (*sruc*); silently [cleanse] the vessel for the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*); gird the wife; [prepare] with the clarified butter and the curds."

"O Pratiprasthātṛ, pierce the heads of the sacrificial animals," says the Adhvaryu; he then performs the well-known rites pertaining to the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*). Then the Pratiprasthātṛ makes a request for twenty-one beans, a *parṇa*-branch, a lump of clay, a vessel of water, a hoe, an anthill-clod split sevenfold, and a pair of tongs. Having taken these, he approaches the heads of the animals. To the south lies the head of the human victim, and the others lie in front of it. Then, having placed the sacred thread over his right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), he scatters seven beans around the human head and sweeps around it three times from right to left with the *parṇa*-branch.

"Day after day leading away cattle, horses, men, and all living beings, Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is never satiated; with these seven [verses] concerning the five types of men, he drags them along while they are surrounded. In the realm of Vaivasvata, King Yama, those people are separated: those who here desire truth and those who are speakers of untruth—with these seven [verses], he drags them along while they are surrounded. O King, they are separated here, and then they come into your presence."

And those who bow to the gods and honor the Brahmins—then he takes up the ant-hill earth with his right hand and the human head with the pincers held in his left; having joined the vital breaths (prāṇas) together, he places the ant-hill earth in its receptacle. Then, having sprinkled this human head, scraped it, and washed it, he coats it with clay, taking care not to coat the vital breaths. As for the other [heads], they finish them with the same threefold process: having scraped them, washed them, and coated them with clay, they likewise take care not to coat the vital breaths.
Then he places them down after sprinkling them with water; they remain lying there until the [proper] time.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the *sāmidhenī* verses of the animal sacrifice.
"Forward your strengths, O ye who seek the heavens"—this is one [verse];
"May the years, O Agni, and the seasons increase thee"—these are ten.

Having extracted from among them the verse containing the word *jyotis* (light), he places nine in the position for the *dhāyyā*s; then he places two *dhāyyā*s containing the word *pṛthupāja-*; then he places this verse: "Yoke, indeed, those who best invoke the gods."

These verses, being recited in their forward order, amount to twenty-four; however, he recites the *jyotiṣmatī* verse last. Then he pours the *āghāra* libation with the verse, "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning. Now follows the deliberation regarding the *āprī* verses: "His fuel-sticks are upright," and so on—there are twelve of them.
From these, he removes the *tānūnapātī* verse for the Vasiṣṭhas and inserts the *nārāśaṃsī* verse; for other lineages (*gotras*), he removes the *nārāśaṃsī* verse and inserts the *tānūnapātī* verse.

Now, if [the sacrifice] is mixed, [the verses are assigned as follows]: "O thou with thick food, for wealth... for the omentum; "He who gives breath, he who gives the self... for the animal cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*); and "Hither to Vāyu with our teams... for the oblation (*havis*).

But if it belongs entirely to Vāyu, then two of these verses—"O thou with thick food, for wealth..."—are for the omentum, two for the animal cake, and two for the oblation. And if it belongs entirely to Prajāpati, then two of these verses—"He who gives breath, he who gives the self..."—are for the omentum, two for the animal cake, and two for the oblation.

They perform all the formal rites for the animal victim; then, having carried fire around these heads of the victims, he suspends them in slings on the northern part of the shed. Then, having tied this head of the serpent with a cord, he fastens it to the loop of the sling.
These remain there until the appointed time, and then the dark fortnight begins.
He prepares the bricks and the sacrificial fees for the fire-altar, if he intends to perform the sacrifice after maintaining the fire for a night;
however, if he maintains it for a year, he need not concern himself with this, thinking, "The path is long."

He prepares a principal seat made of Udumbara wood; its legs are a span high, its head-boards and side-boards are a cubit long, it is woven with cords of Muñja grass, and its planks are spread out, smeared with clay. He also prepares a sling of Muñja grass with six or twelve strands, a nest-like basket of Muñja, a piece of Krumuka wood mixed with clarified butter, two fuel-sticks—one of Vikaṅkata wood and one of Śamī wood—seven fuel-sticks of Udumbara wood, three fuel-sticks of various trees, and a gold disk with twenty-one knobs.

The materials for the Agniṣṭoma have been prepared; a hall has been constructed on a consecrated sacrificial ground. Then, having brought him from the bathing-place (tīrtha) and purified him, he performs the three-offering initiation sacrifice (dīkṣaṇīyā-iṣṭi), consisting of a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Viṣṇu, a pap in ghee for Aditi, and a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara.

For her, as many [oblations] perish as there were for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice. Then, having turned to the right, the Adhvaryu hastens westward, performs the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, goes eastward, replenishes the *dhruvā* ladle, pours it back into the *ājyasthālī*, and, dipping with the *sruva* spoon from the *ājyasthālī*, offers the *agni-dīkṣā* oblations.

"To Ākūti, to Agni Prayuj, Svāhā! To Manas, to Medhā, to Agni Prayuj, Svāhā! To Citta, to Vijñāta, to Agni Prayuj, Svāhā! To Vāco Vidhṛti, to Agni Prayuj, Svāhā! To Prajāpati Manu, Svāhā! To Agni Vaiśvānara, Svāhā! Then, having taken four portions of clarified butter into the *sruva* ladle, he offers the full *sruc* as the *audgrahaṇa* oblation with the verse: "May every mortal choose the friendship of the divine Leader; everyone seeks wealth from him; let him choose glory so that he may prosper."

At the word "svāhā," he pours out this full vessel within the altar. Then, having carried it around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, he hands it to the sacrificer. Then he asks for the principal fire-pan (*ukhā*); having scattered clods of earth, lumps of cow-dung, and withered grass into it, and having thrown a dipping-spoon (*sruva*) filled with clarified butter into it, he places it upon the outermost embers of the Āhavanīya fire with two verses: "Do not break! Be firm! He then entrusts it to the guardians: "O Mitra, heat this pan; let it not break. I entrust this to you so that it may not break. Now, indeed, there is this [instruction]:

"If it should break, he should join it together with those very potsherds. If it breaks, he grinds these very potsherds into powder, mixes them with that clay which lies set aside for the expiation, and having mixed them, formed [the vessel], baked it, and allowed it to cool, he sets it down. Then he chooses another [vessel]. Now it is said: "For one who desires food, he should take [the powder] from a frying pan (ambarīṣa) and add it. Now it is said: "If he should desire of a sacrificer, 'May I produce a rival for him,' he should take [the powder] from elsewhere and add it. Now it is said:
"One whose prosperity has departed should place [the fire] after churning it; for it is said:
'He who desires prosperity, or whoever is preparing the fire-pan (ukhā), for him that very [fire] should be used.'"

Whatever [fire] is produced from the heating of this fire-pan, into that he places a nest of muñja grass with the mantra: "O Agni, that vigorous body of yours which has entered into the plants—with that I worship you; svāhā! Then he places a piece of krumuka wood soaked in clarified butter with the mantra: "Flowing for us, with its libation of ghee. Then he places two fuel-sticks, one of vikaṅkata wood and one of śamī wood: the vikaṅkata with the mantra "From the highest gathering-place," and the śamī wood with the mantra "From the furthest distance."
Then, with the three verses beginning, "Now sit thou in the lap of this mother," he worships the newborn; then he places five fuel-sticks of Udumbara wood upon the fire.

With the verses, "Whatever, O Agni," "Whatever the upajihvikā eats," "Night after night, never failing," "In the navel of the earth," and "The armies that come on," he then worships him with the five-verse *rakṣoghna* hymn beginning, "Make your strength wide like a net. Then he adds three fuel-sticks from different trees, having anointed them: one of *aśvattha* wood with the verse, "With your two tusks, [slay] the thieves"; one of *vikaṅkata* wood with the verse, "Those who among the people are thieves"; and one of *śamī* wood with the verse, "He who is hostile toward us."

Then, while reciting, "Firm is my sacred power; I have extended their arms," he places the two Audumbara logs on the fire at the end. At this point, he makes the sacrificer recite over the black antelope skin;

he neither forms his fists nor restrains his speech. Then he sets down that stool, with its loops and cords untied, behind the Āhavanīya fire. Upon it, having grasped it with two fingers, he places the fire-pan (*ukhya*).

"As a mother bears her son, so does the earth bear Agni Purīṣya in her own womb; may Prajāpati Viśvakarman, in harmony with all the gods and the seasons, yoke him. Then, seated, he fastens the gold plate (rukma) upon the northern support with the verse, "The gold plate shines forth. Then he fastens the sling-rope with two verses, "The sage assumes all forms" and "Night and Dawn," and silently places the black antelope skin over it. Then he gazes at it with the formula, "Thou art the fair-winged Garuḍa; the Trivṛt is thy head."

"The Gāyatra is the eye, the Stoma is the self, the Vāmadevya Sāman is your body, the Bṛhat and Rathantara are the wings, the Yajñāyajñiya is the tail, the meters are the limbs, the Dhiṣṇiya hearths are the hooves, and the Yajus formulas are the name. Then he lifts it up with the words, "You are the fair-winged Garutman; go to the sky, fly to the light!
Prior to this, these long loops of the sling have been prepared for him; there he either steps forward or he lifts it up.

"Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of the adversary; ascend the Gāyatrī metre; stride along the earth; excluded is he whom we hate"—with these four verses, according to their respective metres, he strides three times, applying the fourth verse to the third stride, but does not stride for a fourth time.

He does not pass by the Āhavanīya fire; then he recites this verse, "Then he cried out. Next, he turns around toward the southern shoulder [of the altar] while reciting these four verses: "O Agni, who turnest hither... O Agni Aṅgiras, return with vigor and wealth. Then, having turned toward the north and unfastened the black antelope skin, he unfastens the loops of the carrying-net while reciting, "O Varuṇa, loosen the highest bond from us. Then he brings it back while reciting two verses: "I have brought thee hither... O Great One, he has stood erect at the head of the dawns.
At this point, if he should desire of a Rājanya, "May he possess a kingdom," he should meditate upon him with his mind; "He indeed becomes possessed of a kingdom," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Then, having carried him back around in the same manner as he was brought, he places him within the altar (antarvedi) with four verses containing the word "sit" (*sīda*), beginning with: "Sit thou in the lap of this mother. At this point, he makes two fist-closures and restrains his speech. Then, intending to give him the vow-food, he either places upon the fire a fuel-stick from the *annapati* (lord of food) or mutters: "O Lord of Food, give us food. Thereafter, he kindles the *ukhya* fire with the verse: "By which light the gods rose upward."

As many times as he intends to grant him the vow, in that same manner he either places upon the fire a fuel-stick dedicated to Annapati or mutters [the relevant formula]; in this way he kindles the fire of the *ukhya*. Then, in the morning when the sun has risen and speech has been released, he worships with the *Vātsapra* hymn consisting of eleven verses beginning, "Agni was first born from heaven. He proceeds in this very same manner on the previous day and worships on the following day. Now, on his fast-day (*upavasatha*), the *Vātsapra* is completed; and now follows the investigation of the departure.

The consecrated one finds security and well-being either elsewhere or he undergoes consecration at the place of sacrifice (*devayajana*). They mix the *vrata* milk; they tie up the calves of the two *vrata*-milking cows; whatever is to be placed [on the fire-altar] is prepared: the Gārhapatya fire in the seat (*nīḍa*), the Āhavanīya fire on the front part (*prauga*). Then they lift up the *ukhya* fire with the verse, "May all the gods lift thee up. Then he places it on the front part of the cart with the verse, "Sit thou in the lap of this mother," using four verses beginning with *saṃsīdasva*. Then they firmly fasten these legs of the stool onto the wooden planks as best as possible.

In the middle part of the pole, they tie the loop of the sling; or else, having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇis*), he departs with the two verses: "Go forth toward better fortune," and "Go forward, O Agni, full of light. Now, if the axle creaks, he recites this verse: "He has cried out. Then, when he has halted, he places upon the fire a fuel-stick anointed with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) with the *gāyatrī* verse for a Brāhmaṇa: "Worship Agni with fuel; awaken the guest with clarified butter; offer the oblations into him, Svāhā! And with the *triṣṭubh* verse for a Rājanya: "This Agni of Bharata has spread abroad; hear [him]."
As many times as he is about to go forth, he performs all this in that very manner.
Now, therefore, follows the consideration regarding the excessive growth of the ashes.
If the ashes grow excessively, he prepares a needle, a pair of forceps, and a piece of iron; having taken these, they go to where there is water. This is the procedure.

Then, having grasped this fire with tongs and placed it in the vessel, he causes the ashes to enter the water with the ladle, reciting three verses in their respective meters: "O divine waters, receive these ashes; O Agni, your seat is in the waters; you are the embryo of the plants. Then he places it back [on the altar] with two verses containing the word "light" (jyotiṣmatī): "Having settled in the womb by means of the ashes, having sat down again in your seat, O Waters... and "Agni has entered the waters... and so on.

Then, with the two verses, "Return again with vigor" and "Together with wealth," he goes up again; then he adds fuel to the *ukhya* fire with the verse, "May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus kindle thee again. Then, having carried it back around in the same manner as it was brought, standing in the sacrificer's station, he worships it with the entire Anuvāka beginning, "Be awake, thou art awake.
As many times as the ashes increase, so does he perform all this. Now, therefore, he lies down until the time for the *saṃbhāra* offerings.
Now, therefore, the day before the purchase (*kraya*) arrives.

He prepares five hundred bricks, an unlimited number of *apasyā* bricks, *nairṛtī* bricks that are black and baked with husks, three measures of ash, loose earth, crucibles, and sand. Then, on the day of the *upavasatha*, he settles upon the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) with the two verses, "We have come to this," and "Away from here. Then he measures out the great altar (*mahāvedī*) by taking these same larger steps; having measured it diagonally and measured it all around, he encloses it with a cord and stretches the *pṛṣṭhyā* line. Then he measures out this fire-altar westward from the peg at the hole for the sacrificial post (*yūpāvaṭīya-śaṅku*) using a bamboo rod one man's length long, so as to be symmetrical in its wings and tail.
The two wings become longer by one *aratni*.

Whether he intends to build it as sixfold, sevenfold, twelvefold, or however many-fold it may be, he then measures it diagonally with a measuring-cord and encloses it all around with a taut cord. Following the cord, he draws a line; then, having removed the cord, they dig the trenches and raise the mounds for water, making them higher on the south and on the west. This much is the ritual work performed on this day.
They pass this night.

Then, at the latter part of the night, the Adhvaryu hastens forward and gives the command: "Milk the three-teated cow for the vow. Then, having gathered that fire and placed it together, they sit to the south keeping it burning. Then he smears that fire-altar site with a lump of dung; upon it, he lays out four bricks facing east—two joined together in front and two joined together behind.

Then he encloses it with thirteen bricks, moving clockwise; for each brick, he draws a line. Having removed the bricks, they dig out the trenches and raise up the *apasyā* bricks; those on the south and west sides they make larger. Then, with two verses, "I take Agni into myself first" and "The Agni who is ours," he takes the fire into himself and mutters the *svayaṃcit* formula: "Those logs of thine, O Agni, those abodes..."

Having touched a white horse, he places this [brick] upon the gravel with the formula: "May Prajāpati settle you; by that deity, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, sit firm. Here he pours down the ritual materials: ashes with "Thou art the ash of Agni"; soil with "Thou art the soil of Agni"; saline earth with "Thou art consciousness, the upholder of desires"; and sand with "May thy upholding of desires be in me. Then he mixes them together with the verse: "Those bodies of yours which are dear, may your hearts be united."

"May you be dear to me; may my bodies be dear to you"—with these words he arranges them: "May Heaven and Earth be in harmony; may the waters and plants be in harmony; may the fires, being of one accord, be in harmony for my preeminence. Then he lays down the upward-facing bricks with the formula: "You are piled, you are piled around, you are piled upward; rest firm with that deity in the manner of the Aṅgirases.

Then he spreads them out: with the *gāyatrī* verse, "Swell up," for a Brāhmaṇa; with the *triṣṭubh* verse, "May your milks unite," for a Rājanya. He spreads them out according to the stones and according to the gravel.

Upon that [altar], he lays down four *prācīr-yājuṣī* bricks: "This Agni is the shoulder of Agni; toward the flood of heaven you go, O Agni" (*ayaṃ so agniragne divo arṇamacchā jigāsi*); "O Agni, that luster of yours which is in heaven and on earth" (*agne yatte divi varcaḥ pṛthivyām*); and two facing forward: "The Agnis of the soil" (*purīṣyāso agnayaḥ*). With "O Agni, the *iḍā*" (*iḍāmagna*), he lays down the southern one; with "This is your seasonal womb" (*ayaṃ te yonirṛtviyaḥ*), the northern one. Two facing backward: with "Thou art consciousness" (*cidasī*), the southern one; with "Thou art all-around consciousness" (*paricidasī*), the northern one.

Then he encloses it on the right with thirteen *lokampṛṇā* bricks, [saying]: "Fill the space, fill the gap; sit down, you who are auspicious. May Indra, Agni, and Bṛhaspati seat you in this womb. With this he performs the *tayādevata* rite, [saying]: "By that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm. Then he performs the *sūdadohas* rite, [saying]: "These dappled ones, yielding milk for him, mix the Soma; the clans of the gods at his birth, in the three bright realms of heaven. Then, having stepped down and touched a black horse, he lays down the *tanūpurīṣa* earth, [saying]: "He is anointed in heaven..."

Having performed the *tayādevatam* formula, he performs the *sūdadohas*. Now, this first layer is completed; in the same way the second is completed, in the same way the third, in the same way the fourth, and in the same way the fifth.

If, while they are piling these, the sun should rise, the sacrificer, restraining his speech, takes hold of the Adhvaryu from behind. The Adhvaryu takes up the fire-pan (*ukhā*), and the Pratiprasthātṛ takes up the fuel for rekindling.
Facing each other from the east, they both pour together [the fires] with the four verses beginning, "United. Then he draws the fire-pan down from the sling.
"As a mother her son, so has the Earth placed Agni Purīṣya in his own womb; may Prajāpati Viśvakarman, in harmony with all the gods and the seasons, release him"—thus [he says].
"One should not look at it," they say, "for it is indeed full of heat."

Looking away from it, he pours drops of curd into it, either with the formula, "I place that pure [substance] for you," or silently. Then, having filled it with sand and covered it on top with curd, he places it in the northern part of the shed. In the same way he fills the second one, and likewise the third. These remain there until the appointed time. Then, with a verse addressed to Vaiśvānara, he takes up the sling: "That bright light which was born beyond this region..."

"May he drive away our enemies from this assembly"—saying this, he then requests: three black *nairṛta* vessels cooked in chaff, a stool, a binding for the gold plate, and a water-pot. Having taken these, he goes out by the southern door and proceeds toward that direction where there is a natural salt-flat or a cleft in the ground.
There he lays down the sling with its loop turned away, saying: "O Agni Vaiśvānara, hail!"

Along the cord of the sling, he lays down the Nairṛta bricks facing away [from the fire], with the formulas: "Homage to thee, O Nirṛti of all forms," and "O Goddess Nirṛti, that which thou hast bound upon me—of this thy cruel mouth I offer oblation. He throws down the stool and the fastening of the gold plate;
then he worships it with two verses: "Seek him who presses no Soma, who does not sacrifice," and "I praise the Goddess Nirṛti.
Then, having poured out water, they go away, casting aside the vessel without looking back.

Having washed their hands and feet, they return by the same way they came and worship the Gārhapatya fire with the mantra: "The dweller, the gatherer of treasures. Some, however, worship the Āhavanīya fire, thinking, "This shall be the Gārhapatya from here on.
Then he proceeds with the Prāyaṇīya offering;
having performed the Prāyaṇīya, he proceeds with the footprint rite.

Having walked with the *pada* [formula], he purchases the King [Soma] and prepares the guest-offering (*ātithya*). Having performed the guest-offering, he proceeds with the first two *pravargya* and *upasad* rites. Then, having gone out, he issues the command: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā; give the three-teat vow-milk. The Subrahmaṇya invokes the Subrahmaṇyā and gives the three-teat vow-milk. He steps four steps westward from the tail-end first, and the fifth step toward the south; there he places the wooden sword (*sphya*).

That is the time for the *uparava* holes. Then, from the *śaṅku* at the northern shoulder of the Great Altar (*mahāvedi*), he strides twelve steps westward along the edge of the altar and a thirteenth step northward; that is the place where the *Āgnīdhra* sits down. That is the time for the rubbish-heap (*utkara*). Then, from the place of the *uparavas*, he carries away the *stambayajus*—this being the well-known procedure of the *Pauroḍāśika* section: three times with the sacrificial formula and the fourth time silently. He performs the first tracing of the altar, mutters the *karaṇa* formula, and after the earth has been dug up, the *Āgnīdhra* carries it away three times.
When the Āgnīdhra has carried [the earth] three times, then, standing in front of the hall, he issues the command: "O preparers of the altar, prepare the altar!"

They act according to the directions. Then they put on sandals made of black antelope skin: the Adhvaryu with "For the piled one (citaye) thee!", the Pratiprasthātṛ with "For the piled-up one (ācitaye) thee!", the Brahman with "For the mind-piled one (manaścite) thee!", and the sacrificer with "For the heat-piled one (tapaścite) thee! Or rather, all of them may do so with "For the piled one, for the piled one thee! or even silently. Then he calls for: a bow with arrows, four stones, an Aindra brick, the Vibhakti brick, a water-vessel, a bunch of Darbha grass, Dūrvā grass, and a vessel of clarified butter with a dipping-spoon (sruva). Having taken these, they set them down together at the northern corner of the altar.
Then, with two verses, he takes the fire into himself: "I take Agni first into myself; that Agni who is ours...
He mutters the *svayaṃcit* formula: "Those logs of thine, O Agni, those abodes...

Having touched a white horse, he places this [brick] within the gravel, saying: "May Prajāpati seat thee; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm. Then he takes up a bow with an arrow and four stones; having taken these, having gone around the fire by the south and behind, and standing before the peg for the sacrificial post-hole, having strung the bow, he shoots an arrow into the gravel.

"Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra, the protector of our bodies, the watcher against [enemies]"—having torn it up with these words, he places a stone [on the altar], saying: "May that stone strike him who seeks to harm us from the east. Then, on the southern side of the right wing, at the point where the wing extends over the body, he drives an arrow into the ground between the pebbles, tears it up, and places a stone [on the altar], saying: "He who seeks to harm us from the south. Then, on the rear part of the tail, at the point where the tail extends over the body, he drives an arrow into the ground between the pebbles, tears it up, and places a stone [on the altar], saying: "He who seeks to harm us..."

Thereafter, on the northern side of the northern wing, when the wing is about to collapse, he drives in an arrow with gravel inside for the sake of future stability; having pulled it out, he lays down a stone while reciting, "He who [is] from the north...

According to the Brāhmaṇa, he lays them down in the quarters. Having performed the *tayādevatam* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* formula. Then he lays down this Aindra brick at the point of crossing over, reciting: "May he protect us—he who is the consumer of the soma-residue (*ṛjīṣin*), the deliverer, the fair-cheeked bull, the lord of hymns; he who is the breaker of the cow-stalls, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the one who stands upon the bay horses—may that Indra pierce through various spoils of war."
Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse; then, to the south, he lays down the *vibhakti* brick with the verse, "O Agni, come hither for the feast."

Having performed the *tayādevatam* formula, he performs the *sūdadohas* recitation. Then, having stepped forward, having pulled out the peg of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, and having poured out a vessel of water, he lays down a clump of *darbha* grass, either with the formula, "May Speech lay thee down in the ocean," or silently. Then he makes offerings over it with five spoonfuls, beginning with, "In harmony with the year, with the days... Then he lays down a blade of *dūrvā* grass with the verse: "At thy coming and at thy going, may flowering *dūrvā* grow; may a spring arise there, or a lake filled with lotuses."

Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he performs the *sūdadohas* verses. Now, for this [ploughing], a pair of ploughs made of *udumbara* wood has already been prepared in front of him, either yoked by six oxen or by twelve. He touches its thongs with two verses: "Lay on the thongs; prepare the trench and the furrow. He yokes them with two verses: "The wise yoke the ploughs; yoke the ploughs."

With the two verses, "He ploughs with the plough, the sharp-pointed one; may our ploughshares be auspicious," he inspects the furrow. With the two verses, "O yielder of desires, milk for us desire; [milk] the furrow with ghee," he ploughs three furrows from the tail-end toward the east, from the northern hip to the southern shoulder, three from the southern hip to the northern shoulder, and three from the southern wing to the northern wing. Then, having unyoked these [oxen], turning them to the right, sprinkling them with water, he releases them toward the north.
These [oxen] belong to the Adhvaryu if he performs a sacrifice accompanied by sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇā).
If, however, it is a sacrificial fire (sattriya), they scatter [the earth] according to the nature of the oxen; where the ox is, there the yoke and plough are.
Then, to the east of this, in a trough made of udumbara wood, there is all kinds of herbs mixed together with curds and clarified butter.

At the very beginning of the question, he sows three furrows toward the east with the three verses beginning, "The plants that have been born. He sows toward the southern shoulder from the northern hip with three verses according to their meters; toward the northern shoulder from the southern hip with three verses; and toward the northern wing from the southern wing with five verses. "He sows with fourteen [verses]," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then he collects clods of earth from the various directions.

Therefore, having first run forward, he takes a clod of earth from outside the gravel and places it inside the gravel with the mantra, "May he who is the progenitor of the earth not harm us. Then, having run along the right wing, he takes a clod of earth from outside the gravel.

He places that [clod] inside the pebbles with the verse, "Turn back, O Earth! Then, having run along the tail, he takes a clod from outside the pebbles and places it inside the pebbles with the verse, "O Agni, that which is thy bright and that which is thy radiant... Then, having run along the northern wing, he takes two clods from outside the pebbles with the formula, "I take from here food and strength.
Of these two, he places one inside the pebbles with the verse, "May it enter into our cows and into the plants."

He throws the other [clod] toward that direction in which he has an enemy, saying, "I cast away this want, this disease. While taking it up, he should direct it toward that very direction; this is one way to transpose the sacrificial formula with the formula. This is another.

Then, from the northern shoulder-mark of the great altar (mahāvedi), he strides three steps westward along the edge of the altar and a fourth step northward; there, following the procedure for the pit (cātvāla), he traces out the pit; following the procedure for the high altar (uttaravedi), he pours out the earth for the high altar; having leveled the northern navel, he pours out sand with the six verses beginning "O Agni, thy fame and vigor," according to their respective meters.

Then he lays down the upward-facing bricks with the formula: "You are layers, you are surrounding layers, you are upward-facing; rest firm through that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras. Then he spreads them out: for a Brāhmaṇa, with the Gāyatrī verse, "Swell up"; for a Rājanya, with the Triṣṭubh verse, "May your milks unite.
He spreads them out according to the stones and according to the gravel.

Then they pile up this great altar (mahāciti) in front of the hall, either on a raised platform or on a skin. There are twenty-two bundles of *darbha* grass, water for sprinkling, clarified butter for sprinkling, the horse, the materials for the high altar (*uttaravedi*), thirteen *bārhaspatya* jars and as many pieces of gold, a jar of water, a lotus leaf, a gold plate, a golden man, two offering-ladles (*sruk*), a serpent’s head, and everything pertaining to the naturally perforated brick (*svayamātṛṇṇā*)—ten [of each].

Having placed upon the sprinkling-milk twenty-two bunches of *darbha* grass—the *skandhyā* plants, the *avakā* plants, and whatever others he intends to place there—along with curds mixed with honey, a tortoise, a mortar and pestle made of *udumbara* wood, all kinds of medicinal herbs, the fire-pans, and the heads of the sacrificial animals; then, with the formula "Agni is kindled by Agni," he sprinkles them with the clarified butter-sprinkling, either with the mantra "I sprinkle you, who are dear to the fires, for the fires," or silently. Then he issues the call: "Recite for the fires being led forward."

If the Hotṛ does not desire [to recite], the sacrificer himself recites this single verse, "The fires of the soil," three times; then they proceed with Agni at their head. Then he drives forward with this horse facing eastward, [reciting]: "He has overcome all hostile armies. As the horse steps upon the southern shoulder, he addresses it with the mantra: "When you first neighed at birth... At the northern hip-end, they cause it to halt.
Then, with two verses—"I take Agni into myself first" and "He who is our Agni"—he takes Agni into himself.

He mutters the *svayaṃcit* formula: "O Agni, those logs of thine, those abodes... Having touched the white horse, he steps upon it with two verses: "This is the gathering-place of the waters; homage to thee... Then, at the junction of the tail and at the junction of the body, he places a hundred [bricks]. Then he pours out the water-pitcher. With his right hand he takes the pitcher and with his left the pot; having filled them from that [pitcher] and having thrown in two chips of gold, they run toward the *svayamātṛṇṇā* from the southern shoulder. At the midpoint, he lays them down along the furrow.

With the two verses, "Golden-hued, pure, purifying, in whose midst King Varuṇa moves," he fills [the pits] in this very manner and pours [the earth] back in this way. Among those which run toward the *svayamātṛṇṇā* at the northern hip, he places them along the furrow on the *viṣuvat* day with the third and fourth verses, filling them in this very manner and pouring [the earth] back in this way. Among those which run toward the *svayamātṛṇṇā* at the southern hip, he places them along the furrow on the *viṣuvat* day with the fifth and sixth verses, filling them in this very manner and pouring [the earth] back in this way. Among those which... [he places them].

From the northern shoulder they approach the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks; upon them, at the *viṣuvat*, he lays them down along the furrows with the seventh and eighth verses, filling them in this manner and casting [the earth] back in this manner. Those which they approach from the southern wing toward the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, upon them, at the *viṣuvat*, he lays them down along the furrows with the ninth and tenth verses, filling them in this manner and casting [the earth] back in this manner. Those which they approach from the northern wing toward the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, upon them, at the *viṣuvat*, he lays them down along the furrows with the eleventh and twelfth verses.

Of those [bricks], he places the one dedicated to Bṛhaspati in the middle, saying: "Rest in the sky, strive in the atmosphere, arise from the earth; thou art spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); for spiritual luster, thee!"—thus says the Brāhmaṇa. Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* formula. Then, according to the procedure for the high altar (*uttaravedi*), he consecrates the high altar. Then, upon the high altar, he places a lotus leaf with the words: "Thou art the back of the waters."

Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he performs the *sūdadohas* recitation. Then, upon the high altar (*uttaravedi*) itself, he places the northern *nirbādha* gold plate with the verse, "The Brahman was first born. Then he sprinkles it crosswise with fivefold-drawn ghee, using the verse, "Make your body wide like a net. Then, to the south, he places a golden man facing eastward with the verse, "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning. Then he touches him with the verse, "The drop has fallen."

Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he performs the *sūdadohas* verses. Then, at the distance of a step to the north, he places two ladles: one made of *kārṣmarya* wood, filled with clarified butter; and one made of *udumbara* wood, filled with curds. The *kārṣmarya* ladle is on the south and the *audumbara* ladle is on the north. With the formula "Thou art this," he addresses the *kārṣmarya* ladle, and with "Thou art that," the *audumbara* ladle. Having performed the *tayādevata* rite for them mentally, he performs the *sūdadohas* verses. Then, on the southern forehead [of the altar], he places a serpent's head with the three verses beginning with "Homage be to the serpents," according to their respective meters.
Alternatively, from whatever direction one perceives that danger arising from the people of the countryside may come, having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he performs the *sūdadohas* formula.

Then he prepares the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone with the *yajus*: "Thou art firm, a supporter, spread out by Viśvakarman, well-fashioned. May the ocean not submerge thee; may the Suparṇa [not harm] thee. Without trembling, do thou steady the earth."

Then, having made the horse sniff it, he runs toward it together with an unlearned Brāhmaṇa and lays it down, so that his vital breaths may be joined with [the vital breaths of] this person and not be closed off. Having recited, "Bhūḥ! May Prajāpati settle you," and having further recited, "May Agni protect you with great well-being, with most peaceful shelter; by that deity, like Aṅgiras, sit firm," he should breathe over it after laying down the first *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick; then he breathes over it, and then this Brāhmaṇa gives a boon; then, over the *sruc*.

Having taken four portions [of clarified butter], he offers it in the space of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone with the formula, "I offer consciousness with mind and ghee. Having caused [the sacrificer] to touch it with both thumbs, he makes him recite the *anvāroha* formula: "I have stepped upon the earth; may my vital breath not forsake me. In the other cavity, he places a gold brick with the formula, "Thou art brilliance; grant me brilliance; grant me the earth; protect me from the earth.
Behind that, at the line of the strides, he places a *maṇḍaleṣṭakā* brick with the formula, "The earth has entered its enclosure with food."
To the south, he lays down the Retahsic brick with the formula: "The earth is the Retahsic; may she bestow seed upon me; may she cause my seed to procreate.
Having performed the tayādevata rite, he pronounces the sūdadohas verse.

Then he lays down these ten *skandhya* bricks facing east: two seasonal (*ṛtavyā*) bricks, two *dviyajus* bricks, the *virāj*, the *viśvajyotis*, the *sayuj*, the *aṣāḍhā*, and two *saṃyānī* bricks. He places two seasonal bricks with the formula, "Madhu and Mādhava. He places an *avakā* plant upon them with the formula, "Thou art the womb of Agni. Then he places two *dviyajus* bricks with the two verses, "Growing up from joint after joint, thou that extendest with a hundred," and [the second verse], "O Dūrvā brick.
Then he places the *hiraṇyamūrdhnī* brick with the formulas, "Those splendors of thine, O Agni, which are in the sun," and "Those splendors of yours, O gods, which are in the sun."

He places the Virāj and the Viśvajyotis; [with the formula] "Bṛhaspati has established thee as the light of the Virāj," he places the Uttara. Then he lays down the Sayuj with [the formula], "I yoke thee as a companion for Indra and Agni.

Then he lays down the Aṣāḍhā, marked with three lines and having its characteristic marks on the upper side, with [the formula], "Thou art the invincible, the overcoming. Then he lays down the two Saṃyānīs with [the formulas], "Thou art the path of Agni," and "Thou art the path of the gods."
Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses.
Then, having sat down to the north of the three-lined brick (*tryālikhitā*), he requests curds mixed with honey and the tortoise;
he anoints it with the curds mixed with honey, reciting the three verses beginning with "The winds are honey for the one who follows the Law," according to their respective meters.
Then, having enveloped it with a load of *avakā* plants, he lays it down in the east facing west with two verses: "May the great Heaven and Earth and the four quarters move forward for us, O Agnis.

Then he fixes it around with stakes on all sides so that it does not slip away. Having performed the *tayādevatam* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* formula. Then, standing right there, he asks for an *audumbara* mortar and pestle and all kinds of herbs.

This mortar is a span in measure, and the pestle is a cubit in measure. Upon it he pounds all kinds of herbs, saying: "Thou art a portion of vigor; thou art the purifier of vigor; thou art vigor, food for the sake of eating. Then he places it to the north at the distance of a step, with the verse, "That highest step of Viṣṇu.
To the north of that, he makes a *lokapṛṇā* brick, and having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the two *sūdadohas* formulas. Then he asks for the principal fire-pan (*ukhā*).

Within that [space], he offers two spoonfuls of oblations that flow inward: he offers into the southern cavity with the verse, "O Agni, yoke those [steeds] which are yours," and into the northern one with, "Yoke, indeed, those who best invoke the gods. Then, to the north of it, at the distance of a step, he lays down [the brick] with the formula, "Thou art the pole, O earth; overcome the enemy. He places the other two *lokapṛṇā* bricks to the north.
Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he performs the *sūdadohas* recitation. Then he asks for the head of that man.

He throws pieces of gold into his vital breaths: with the verse "The drop has fallen," he offers into the mouth; with "This is the vigor of the whole world," into the right nostril; with "Of Agni Vaiśvānara," into the left nostril; with "Agni is radiant with light," into the right eye; with "The golden disk is radiant with splendor," into the left eye; with "For the *ṛc*, thee! into the right ear; and with "For the splendor, thee! into the left. Then, having taken four portions in the *sruc* ladle, he makes an offering into the right eye with the verse beginning "The wonderful... (*citraṃ*).

Having taken another fourfold portion with the verse, "The host of the gods has risen," he offers it into the northern eye; "He offers with the same [verse], 'The bright face of the gods,'" so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Then he fills it with curds mixed with honey, reciting from the beginning of the section until the end of the verse, "The songs flow together like rivers. Then he places it face upwards within the *ukhā* (fire-pan), facing eastward.
Having run after [the verse], "Anointing the solar embryo with milk," he says, "Do not harm this two-footed one among the animals";

then, saying, "I assign the wild animal to thee," he releases the heat upon the forehead and places a golden brick thereon, saying, "Viśvakarman is the lord of the quarters. Then, sitting down in the east facing westward, he places the horse's head within his own self, having run after [the verse], "The speed of Vāta, the navel of Varuṇa," and saying, "Do not harm this one-hoofed one among the animals."

Saying, "I assign the white forest animal to you," he casts away the impurity; he places a golden brick on the forehead with the words, "Prajāpati, lord of the quarters. Then, sitting behind [the altar] facing east, he places the head of the bull within his own self, reciting, "The unceasing drop, the ruddy, the swift one... and continuing with, "This ocean, the hundred-streamed fountain. Saying, "I assign the gayal, the forest animal, to you," he casts away the impurity.

On the forehead, he lays down a golden brick with the formula, "Rudra is the lord of the quarters. Then, sitting to the south facing north, he lays down the head of a ram within the interior with the verse, "The protectress of Tvaṣṭṛ, the navel of Varuṇa," reciting it in its entirety; and with the verses, "This woolly one, the magic of Varuṇa," and "The wild camel I assign to thee," he releases the grief.

On the forehead, he lays down a golden brick with the formula, "Varuṇa, lord of the quarters. Then, sitting to the north facing south, he places the head of the inner self upon him, reciting: "The fire which was born from the heat of Agni... and continuing with "For from the womb of Agni she was born. He releases the heat with the verse, "After the wild Śarabha, I assign [the quarters] to thee. On the forehead, he lays down a golden brick with the formula, "Agni, lord of the quarters. At the corners, he should lay them down after having pushed them aside; so says the Brāhmaṇa. Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses.

Then he lays down the Apasyā bricks with the formula, "I settle thee in the movement of the waters. He lays down five in front facing west, five to the south, five behind facing east, and five to the north as Chandasyā bricks.

Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses; then he lays down the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks. [He recites: "This one here is Bhūvas; his breath is *Bhauvāyana*; the spring is *Prāṇāyana*; the Gāyatrī belongs to the spring; from the Gāyatrī comes the Gāyatra-sāman; from the Gāyatra comes the Upāṃśu-graha; from the Upāṃśu comes the Trivṛt-stoma; from the Trivṛt comes the Rathantara-sāman; from the Rathantara comes the seer Vasiṣṭha. With thee, taken by Prajāpati, I take hold of the breath for the sake of offspring.
He stretches out ten bricks toward the east, reaching as far as the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, with the formula: "This one here is Viśvakarman."
He extends ten [bricks] southward from the *svayamātṛṇṇā* with the formula, "This one behind, all-encompassing";
he extends ten westward from the *svayamātṛṇṇā* with the formula, "This one to the north, heaven"; he extends ten northward from the *svayamātṛṇṇā* with the formula, "This one above, thought."

With ten [bricks] he encloses them from above, turning to the right; "he lays them down crosswise," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse. Then he lays down the *saṃyatas*: "The breath of life, may it continue," twelve in number—three in each of the quarters, but not in the middle. Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse. Then he lays down the *apānabhṛts*: "The east among the quarters, spring among the seasons, Agni the deity, the Brahman the wealth, the *trivṛt* the hymn-form, that same [hymn] with fifteen turns, the *tryavi* the age, the Kṛta the throw of the dice, the easterly wind the wind, Sānaga the seer."

He causes [the priest] to recite, "The fathers, the grandfathers," and lays down ten *prāṇabhṛt* bricks to the south, directed westward, reaching up to the *svayamātṛṇṇā*; "The southern quarter," he says, and lays down ten [bricks] behind the *prāṇabhṛts*, directed northward, reaching up to the *svayamātṛṇṇā*; "The western quarter," he says, and lays down ten [bricks] to the north of the *prāṇabhṛts*, directed eastward, reaching up to the *svayamātṛṇṇā*; "The northern quarter," he says, and lays down ten [bricks] in front of the *prāṇabhṛts*, directed southward, reaching up to the *svayamātṛṇṇā*; "The upward quarter," he says.
With ten external *prāṇabhṛt* bricks he encloses [the altar] from above by moving counter-clockwise;
"he lays down the *viṣūcī*s," so says the Brāhmaṇa; by means of the *apānabhṛt*s, the layer is completed.
Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses; then he piles the fire-altar facing in all directions:
he places a *gāyatrī* verse in the east, a *triṣṭubh* in the south, a *jagatī* in the west, an *anuṣṭubh* in the north, and a *paṅkti* in the middle.

Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse; then he lays down the limbs of Agni: "With the eastern quarter I settle thee, with the Gāyatrī metre, with Agni as the deity; by means of the head of Agni, I lay down the head of Agni. "With the southern quarter I settle thee," "with the western quarter I settle thee," "with the northern quarter I settle thee," "with the upward quarter I settle thee, with the Paṅkti metre.
Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse; then, to the north, he lays down the one belonging to Prajāpati with the formula: "The image of the year."
At the time of stepping forward, he places the bull facing east behind that [brick] with the verse, "Thee, O Agni, the bull, the wise one...

Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he performs the *sūdadohas* formula. Then he lays down the *lokapṛṇā* bricks with the formula: "Fill the space, fill the gap; sit here, thou who art auspicious. Indra, Agni, and Bṛhaspati have seated thee in this womb. He performs the *tayādevata* rite with: "By that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm," and then he performs the *sūdadohas* formula: "These dappled cows, yielding milk for him, mix the Soma; they are the clans of the gods at their birth, in the three luminous realms of heaven."

Here, he consecrates the fire with a *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick facing east; they cover it completely with bricks facing east; once covered, he sweeps around it with a *palāśa* branch, saying, "Fill the world, fill the gap. Then he touches the layer with the *citikḷpti* formula: "May the wise one distinguish between thought and non-thought," and having touched this layer with a *gāyatrī* verse addressed to Agni, he descends with two verses: "May speech be in my mouth, O giver of breath," and so forth. Then he proceeds with the afternoon *pravargya* and *upasad* rites; only this much ritual action is performed on this day, and they dwell for that night.

Then, on the second day, when the sun has risen, he proceeds with the Pravargya and Upasad rites. Now the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer put on shoes made of black antelope skin. Then, with two verses, "I take Agni into myself first" and "He who is our Agni," they take Agni into themselves.
He mutters the *svayaṃcit* formula, "Those logs of thine, O Agni, those abodes...
Having touched the black horse with the verse, "Thou art asked about heaven," he lays down the *tanūpurīṣa* brick.

Having performed the *tayādevatam* formula, he performs the *sūdadohas* verse; then he proceeds with the afternoon *pravargya* and *upasad*. Only this much ritual action is performed on this day, and they dwell for that night.
Then, on the third day, when the sun has risen, he proceeds with the *pravargya* and *upasad*.

All put on sandals made of black antelope skin. Then he asks for the vessel of clarified butter together with the *sruva*-ladle, the *vibhakti* brick, a water-vessel, five *skandhya* bricks, and *avakā* plants;

whatever other [bricks] he is about to lay down, having taken all these together, they set them down at the northern corner of the hip. Then, with two verses, he takes Agni into himself: "I take Agni first into myself... that Agni of ours...
He mutters the *svayaṃcit* formula: "Those logs of thine, O Agni, those abodes..."
Having touched a white horse, he runs up to it with two verses: "This is the descent into the waters; homage to thee!
Then, having run up, he offers the first two *saṃcita* oblations with the verses: "O Agni, from the ocean... and "I go to thee...
On the south side, he lays down the *vibhakti* brick with the verse: "We choose Agni as our messenger."
Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he performs the *sūdadohas* verse.

Then he stretches out these five *skandhyā* bricks toward the east: two *ṛtavyā*s, two *sayuj* bricks, and one *saṃyānī*. He lays down the two *ṛtavyā*s with the formula, "Śukra and Śuci," and he places an *avakā* plant upon them with the formula, "Thou art the womb of Agni. Then he lays down the two *sayuj* bricks with the formulas, "I yoke thee with the two Āghāra-libations as my companion; I yoke thee with splendor as my companion. Then he lays down the *saṃyānī* brick with the formula, "Thou art the path of Vāyu."

Having performed the *tayādevatam* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses; then he lays down the five *āśvinī* bricks—one in each of the four directions and one in the center—with the formulas beginning "A firm dwelling, a firm womb.
Having performed the *tayādevatam* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses;
then he lays down the five *ṛtavyā* bricks—one in each of the four directions and one in the center—with the formulas beginning "In harmony with the seasons, in harmony with the ordainers."

"They have the same beginning and the same end," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Having performed the tayādevata rite, he recites the sūdadohas verses; then he lays down the prāṇabhṛt bricks with the formulas, "Protect my out-breath, protect my in-breath," five in each direction and one in the middle.

Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses; then he lays down the "rain-winning" bricks with the formulas, "Thou art the sweller of waters, quicken the plants," five in each direction and one in the middle. "He sets them down by moving around [the altar]," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses; then he lays down the "head-possessing" bricks with the formulas, "The support, the vigor," four in the east, and the *haṃsapātinī* bricks. Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses; then he lays down the *vasasyā* bricks.

With the formula "The three-year-old bull, strength," he places five [bricks] on the southern hip; with "The four-year-old ox, strength," five on the northern [hip]; with "The ram, strength," he places one on the southern shoulder;
with "The bull, strength," one on the northern [shoulder];
and with "The tiger, strength," he places one on the southern wing.
With "The lion is my vigor" in the north, and "The man is my vigor" in the middle;
by means of the man, the piling is attained.

Having performed the *tayādevatam* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses. Then he piles the fire facing in all directions (*agni-sarvatomukha*). He piles the limbs of Agni, the one for Prajāpati, the bull, and the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks. Here, with the *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick placed toward the north, he pours the libation; they cover the fire with bricks facing northward. Once covered, he sweeps around it with a *palāśa* branch, saying: "Fill the world, fill the gap. Then he touches it with the *citikḷpti* formula: "May the wise one distinguish between thought and non-thought..."

Having touched this layer with a Triṣṭubh verse addressed to Agni, he descends with two verses: "May speech be in my mouth" and "O giver of breath. Then he proceeds with the afternoon Pravargya and Upasad rites; only this much ritual action is performed on this day, and they dwell for that night.
Then, on the fourth day, when the sun has risen, he proceeds with the Pravargya and Upasad rites.
The laying down of the loose earth is the same.

Then, on the fifth day, when the sun has risen, he proceeds with the Pravargya and Upasad rites. All put on sandals made of black antelope skin. Then he asks for the vessel of clarified butter together with the *sruva*-ladle, the *vibhakti* brick, a water-pot, the entire *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick along with its covering, the ten *skandhyā* bricks, *avakā* plants, and whatever other bricks he is about to lay down.
Having taken this up, they place it on the northern hip. Then, with two verses—"I take Agni first in myself; that Agni who is ours"—he takes the fire into himself.
He mutters the *svayaṃcit* formula: "Those logs of thine, O Agni, those abodes...
Having touched the white horse, he mounts it with two verses: "This is the descent-place of the waters; homage to thee... and so forth.

Then, having stepped forward, he offers two *saṃcita* oblations on the second layer with the verses, "O Agni, thou art fierce; I approach thee... and so forth. To the south, he lays down a *vibhakti* brick with the verse, "By Agni Agni is kindled... Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* formula. Then, having caused a horse to smell the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick, he steps forward together with a Brāhmaṇa who is not a learned scholar and lays it down with the verse, "O Bhūḥ, Indra and Agni, [place] this unshakable [brick]... and so forth, followed by, "May Vāyu protect thee with great well-being, with a most peaceful shelter; by that deity, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, sit thou firm."
Having laid down the second [brick] with the formula, "He should breathe out and breathe in," that is the *vyāna*.

Then this Brāhmaṇa gives a boon. Then, having taken four portions of clarified butter in the *sruva* ladle, he offers it in the space of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick with the formula, "I offer consciousness with mind and with ghee. Having caused him to touch [the brick] with his two thumbs, he makes him recite the *anvāroha* formula: "I have stepped into the intermediate space; may offspring not forsake me."
In another cavity, he lays down a gold brick with the formula: "Thou art light; grant me light; grant the intermediate space; protect me from the intermediate space.
Behind that, at the limit of the strides, he lays down a circle-brick with the formula: "The sky above, the intermediate space, entered by means of the holy power (brahman).

To the south, he lays down the Retahsic brick with the formula: "The intermediate space is the Retahsic; may it place seed in me; may it cause that seed of mine to procreate"—this [he does] by means of the mind alone.

Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses; then he lays down these ten *skandhya* bricks facing eastward: four seasonal (*ṛtavyā*) bricks, the *samrāj* and the *viśvajyotis*, two *sayuj* bricks, and two *saṃyānī* bricks. He lays down the two seasonal bricks with the formulas, "Nabha and Nabhasya," and he places an *avakā* plant upon each with the formula, "Thou art the womb of Agni. He lays down [the next two] with "Iṣ and Ūrj," and upon each he places an *avakā* plant with "Thou art the womb of Agni. He lays down the *samrāj* and the *viśvajyotis* with the formula, "The sovereign has established the light; may Viśvakarman settle thee," with the latter [formula] for the northern one.

Then he lays down two *sayuj* bricks with the formulas, "I yoke thee with splendor as a companion," and "I yoke thee with hymns as a companion. Then he lays down two *saṃyāni* bricks with the formulas, "Thou art the path of the gods," and "Thou art the path of Vāyu for this atmosphere. Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse. Then he lays down the *diśyā* bricks with the formulas, "Thou art the queen, the eastern quarter," and so on—five bricks, one in each of the four directions and one in the middle. Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse. Then he lays down the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks in the east, facing eastward, with the ten formulas, "Protect my life-span; protect my breath," and so forth.

Of those [bricks], he lays down the *jyotiṣmatī* as the last; having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse. Then he lays down the *bṛhatī* bricks: twelve to the south with "The *mā* metre," twelve to the west with "The *pṛthivī* metre," and twelve to the north with "Agni the deity";
having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse.
With the formula "Thou art the head, the sovereign," he lays down seven bricks facing westward in the east; with "The restrainer, the sovereign," seven facing eastward in the west.
By means of the *vālakhilyā* bricks, the layer is completed.

Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses. Then he piles the fire-altar facing in all directions: the limbs of Agni, the brick dedicated to Prajāpati, the bull, and the *lokapṛṇā* bricks.

Here, he pours out the first [offering] with a *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick facing east; they cover it completely with bricks facing east; once covered, he draws a line around it with a *palāśa* twig, saying, "Fill the world, fill the gap. Then he touches this layer with the *citikḷpti* formula, "May the wise one distinguish between thought and non-thought," and having touched this layer with a *jagatī* verse addressed to Agni, he descends with two verses: "May speech be in my mouth" and "O giver of breath. Then he proceeds with the afternoon *pravargya* and *upasad* rites; only this much ritual action is performed on this day, and they dwell for that night.
Then, on the sixth day, when the sun has risen, he proceeds with the Pravargya and Upasad rites;
the laying down of the loose earth is the same.
Then, on the seventh day, when the sun has risen, he proceeds with the Pravargya and Upasad rites.

Everyone puts on sandals made of black antelope skin. Then he asks for the vessel of clarified butter with the dipping-spoon, the *vibhakti* brick, a water-vessel, the five *skandhya* bricks, the *avakā* plants, and whatever other bricks he is about to lay down; taking all these together, they set them down at the northern corner of the hip. Then, with two verses—"I take Agni first within me" and "The Agni who is ours"—he takes the fire into himself. He mutters the *svayaṃcit* formula: "Those logs of thine, O Agni, those abodes. Having touched the white horse, he mounts it with two verses: "This is the descent-place of the waters" and "Homage to thee."

Then, having stepped forward, he offers two *saṃcita* oblations on the third layer with the verses, "O Agni, I approach you as a householder" and "Agni shall strike down the Vṛtras. Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* formula. Then he lays down these five *skandhyā* bricks facing eastward: two *ṛtavyā*s, two *sayuj* bricks, and one *saṃyānī*.

He places the two seasonal bricks with the formula, "Saha and Sahasya. He places the Avakā plants upon them with the formula, "Thou art the womb of Agni. Then he places the two Sayuj bricks with the formulas, "I yoke thee with the Stomas as my companion; I yoke thee with the Chandomas as my companion. Then he places the Saṃyānī brick with the formula, "Thou art the aerial path of the gods.
Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse.

Then he places the Akṣṇayāstomīya bricks: "The Swift, the Trivṛt"—he places these in the east; "The Void, the Saptadaśa"—in the south; "The Support, the Ekaviṃśa"—in the west; "The Radiant, the Pañcadaśa"—in the north.

He places [the bricks] with "The rush, eighteen" in the east; with "The turn, twenty" in the south; with "Splendor, twenty-two" in the west; and with "Austerity, nineteen" in the north. He places [the bricks] with "The womb, twenty-four" in the east; with "Embryos, twenty-five" in the south; with "Vigor, twenty-seven" in the west; and with "Maintenance, twenty-three" in the north.

He places [the brick] in front with the words, "The thirty-first is the creative power"; on the south with, "The thirty-fourth is the summit of the ruddy one"; behind with, "The thirty-third is the foundation"; and on the north with, "The thirty-sixth is the vault of heaven. He places [the brick] in front with, "Thou art the portion of Agni"; on the south with, "Thou art the portion of those who watch over men"; behind with, "Thou art the portion of Mitra"; and on the north with, "Thou art the portion of Indra. He places [the brick] in front with, "Thou art the portion of the Vasus"; on the south with, "Thou art the portion of the Ādityas"; behind with, "Thou art the portion of Aditi"; and on the north with, "Thou art the portion of the god Savitṛ."

He places [the brick] in the east with the formula, "The Dhartra is the Catuṣṭoma"; in the south, "Thou art the portion of the Yāvas"; in the west, "Thou art the portion of the Ṛbhus"; and in the north, "The Vivarta is the Aṣṭācatvāriṃśa. Regarding this, the Brāhmaṇa says: "He recites differently and lays down differently. Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse. Then he lays down the *sṛṣṭi* bricks with the formula, "With one [verse] they praised; offspring were produced," and so on. There are seventeen [bricks]; he lays down four on the southern shoulder, then three, then three, then three, and then four, extending them from the southern shoulder to the southern hip.

Having performed the *tayādevatam* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses; then he lays down the *vyuṣṭi* bricks with the formula, "She indeed is she who first shone forth," fifteen in number—three in each of the quarters and three in the middle.
By means of the *vyuṣṭi* bricks, the layer is completed.
Having performed the *tayādevatam* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses;

then he piles the fire facing in all directions—the limbs of Agni, the one for Prajāpati, the bull, and the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks. Here, with the *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick placed toward the north, he pours the libation; they completely cover the fire with bricks facing northward.

He draws it along, covered with a *palāśa* branch, saying, "Fill the world, fill the gap. Then he touches that layer with the *citi-kḷpti* formula, "May the wise one distinguish between thought and lack of thought," using an *anuṣṭubh* verse addressed to Agni. Having touched this layer, he steps down with two verses: "Speech be in my mouth, O giver of breath... Then he proceeds with the afternoon *pravargya* and *upasad* rites; only this much ritual action is performed on this day, and they dwell for that night. Then, on the eighth day, when the sun has risen, he proceeds with the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites.
The laying down of the loose earth (purīṣa) is the same.

Then, on the ninth day, when the sun has risen, he proceeds with the Pravargya and Upasad rites. All put on sandals made of black antelope skin. Then he asks for the vessel of clarified butter together with the dipping-spoon (sruva), the Vibhakti brick, a water-pot, the entire Svayamātṛṇṇā brick, the Nīkta brick, the seven Skandhyā bricks, the Avakā plants, and whatever other bricks he is about to lay down.
Having taken this up, they place it together at the northern end of the hip; then, with two verses—"I take Agni first within me" and "The Agni who is ours"—he takes the fire into himself;
he mutters the *svayaṃcit* formula, "Those logs of thine, O Agni, those abodes";
having touched the white horse, he mounts it with two verses: "This is the descent-place of the waters" and "Homage to thee."
Then, having stepped forward, he offers two *saṃcita* oblations on the fourth layer with the verses "O Agni, from the *kiṃśila* tree... and "I approach you...";
he then places the *vibhakti* brick on the south side with the verse "O Agni, we meditate upon the hymn of praise..."

Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he performs the *sūdadohas* recitation; then he lays down these seven *skandhyā* bricks facing east: two *ṛtavyā*s, the *svarāj*, and the *viśvajyotis*; one *ekāsa-yuj*; two *saṃyānī*s; and two *ṛtavyā*s. He lays them down with the formulas: "Tapa and Tapasya," and he places an *avakā* plant upon each with the formula, "Thou art the womb of Agni. [He lays down] the *svarāj* and the *viśvajyotis* with the formula, "Svarāj has established the light; may Prajāpati settle thee," for the northern one.

Then he lays down the *sayuj* brick with the formula: "For wealth, for prosperity, for preeminence among my kinsmen; with thee as my companion and ally, I yoke thee. Then he lays down the two *saṃyānī* bricks with the formulas: "Thou art the atmosphere; for the atmosphere, thee! Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse.

Then he lays down the *asapatnā* bricks: with "O Agni, drive away our born enemies," he lays one down in the east; with "the born [by] force," he lays one down in the west; with "the forty-fourfold hymn-form (*stoma*)," he lays one down in the south; and with "the sixteenfold hymn-form," he lays one down in the north.

In the middle of those [bricks], he lays down the *purīṣavatī* brick with the formula, "Thou art the soil of the earth; thy name is Apso. Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse. Then he lays down the *virāj* bricks with the formulas, "The *eva* metre; the *varivas* metre," forty in number—ten in each direction, but not in the middle—as the Brāhmaṇa states: "He lays them down crosswise. Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse. Then he lays down the *stomabhāga* bricks with the formulas, "Thou art a ray; for dwelling thee, quicken the dwelling," thirty-one in number—seven in each direction and three in the middle.

Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse. Then he lays down the five *nākasad* bricks: "Thou art the queen; the eastern quarter; the Vasus are thy gods; [Indra] is the overlord," and so on. He lays them down one by one in each of the quarters and one in the middle.

Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse. Then he lays down the five *coḍā* bricks above the *nākasads*: "This one in front is the golden-haired, with sun-like rays," and so on. He lays them down one by one in each of the quarters and one in the middle.
Behind these, he lays down the last one facing eastward; there, he meditates in his mind upon whomsoever the sacrificer hates.

Having performed the *tayādevatam* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses; then he lays down the meters. From the section beginning with "Agni is the head of heaven," he lays down three *gāyatrīs* from each [verse] as prescribed: the *gāyatrīs* in front, the *triṣṭubhs* on the south, the *jagatīs* on the west, and the *anuṣṭubhs* on the north. He lays down the *bṛhatīs* in the middle. He lays down the *uṣṇih*s in front, the *paṅktīs* on the south, the *akṣarapaṅktīs* on the west, and the *aticchandas* on the north. The *dvipadās* are in the middle; alternatively, the *aticchandas* is in the middle and the *dvipadās* on the north.

Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse. Then, on the southern shoulder, he lays down seven bricks made in clusters, beginning with "Thou art Ambā by name, thou art Dulā by name," and having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse. Then he lays down the rain-winning bricks (*vṛṣṭisani*) with the formulas, "Thou art the winner of the east wind, thou art the winner of the clouds," and so on—five in total. He places them one in each of the four directions and one in the middle, moving around them in order; for thus it is said in the Brāhmaṇa. Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse. Then he lays down the Aditya bricks with the formulas, "For the ocean thee, for the flowing one thee," and so on—eight in total, two in each direction, but not in the middle.

Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses; then he lays down the *ghṛteṣṭakā*s with the formulas, "Thee for Ṛc, thee for Ruc," five in number—one in each of the quarters and one in the middle. Regarding this, the Brāhmaṇa says: "Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses. Then he lays down the *yaśodā*s with the formula, "Thee, the giver of glory, I settle in glory," five in number—one in each of the quarters and one in the middle.
Then he lays down the *bhūyaskṛt*s with the formulas, "Thou art the maker of abundance, thou art the maker of wide space," five in number—one in each of the quarters and one in the middle.

Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse. Then he lays down the five *apsuṣad* bricks—one in each of the four directions and one in the middle—with the formulas, "Thou art seated in the waters; thou art seated in the hawk. Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse. Then he lays down the five *draviṇodas* bricks—one in each of the four directions and one in the middle—with the formulas, "I seat thee in the wealth of the earth. Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse. Then he lays down the seven *āyuṣya* bricks—one in each of the four directions and three in the middle—with the formulas, "Protect my out-breath; protect my in-breath," and so on.

Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he performs the *sūdadohas* verses; then he lays down the bricks named after the seasons with the formula "yāvā ayāvā," seven in each of the directions and three in the middle;
having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he performs the *sūdadohas* verses;
then he lays down the twenty-two *indratanu* bricks with the formula "agninā viśvāṣāṭ," five in each of the directions and two in the middle.

Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses; then he lays down the bricks of the body of the sacrifice (*yajñatanū*) with the formula, "Prajāpati, blind, sought with his mind..."—thirty-three in total, eight in each of the quarters and one in the middle.

Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses; then he lays down the *jyotiṣmatī* bricks with the formula, "I settle thee, the luminous one"—twelve in total, three in each of the quarters, but not in the middle.

Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses; then he lays down the *bhūteṣṭakā* bricks with the formula, "Svāhā to the earth! Svāhā to the atmosphere!"—twelve in total, three in each of the quarters, but not in the middle.

Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse; then he lays down the *ājyānī* bricks with the verses beginning "To him of a hundred weapons, of a hundred powers," five in number—one in each of the four directions and one in the middle. Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse. Then he lays down the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* bricks with the verses beginning "O Agni, glorious one, endow this man with glory," four in number—one in each of the four directions, but not in the middle. Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse. Then, on the southern shoulder, he lays down the *paurṇamāsī* brick with the verse "Full behind."

Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse; then, on the southern shoulder itself, he lays down the *nakṣatra*-bricks, beginning with: "Kṛttikā is the constellation, Agni is the deity. He then causes them to shine with the formula: "O lights, you are the radiance of Prajāpati, Dhātṛ, Soma, and Agni; for luster you, for radiance you, for splendor you, for brilliance you, for light you! Then he extends that path of the constellations from Rohiṇī up to Viśākhā.

From the right shoulder he extends [the line] to the right hip; then he lays down the two *Amāvāsyā* bricks at the junction of the tail and the junction of the body with the words, "The portion which the gods assigned to thee. Then he extends this path of the constellations from Anurādhā to Apabharaṇī; from the northern hip he extends it to the northern shoulder. Then he lays down the *Paurṇamāsī* brick on the northern shoulder itself with the words, "Full behind. He lays them down so that they do not touch one another; thus says the Brāhmaṇa. By means of the *Nakṣatra*-bricks, the layer is completed.

Having performed the *tayādevatam* formula, he recites the *sūdadohas* verse; then, having descended and touched the black horse, he places the *tanūpurīṣa* (body-filler) with the verse, "Thou art asked about in heaven.
