Having performed the *tayādevatam* formula, he recites the *sūdadohas* verse. Here he piles the sixth layer (*citi*), consisting of five bricks with the formulas beginning "The Restrainer" (*saṃyat*) and "The Wise One" (*pracetās*), one in each of the four directions and one in the middle.

Having performed the *tayādevatam* formula, he recites the *sūdadohas* verses. Then he piles the fire-altar facing all directions (*sarvatomukha*), including the limbs of Agni, the one dedicated to Prajāpati (*prājāpatyā*), the bull (*ṛṣabha*), and the *lokapṛṇā* bricks.

Here, he emits the fire toward the east with the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks; they cover it completely with those facing east, and then with those facing north; however, they finally complete it with those facing east. He piles as much as he intends to pile, and then it remains untouched by the *citikḷpti* formula.

He asks for these four *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks; he places them in the quarters [of the altar] with the formulas: "For out-breathing (*prāṇa*), for sight, thee—with that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! For diffused breathing (*vyāna*), for sight, thee—with that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! For in-breathing (*apāna*), for sight, thee—with that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! For speech, for sight, thee—with that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! Then, having caused a horse to sniff the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, he hastens forward together with an unlearned Brāhmaṇa and lays it down with the formula: "In the seat of heaven and earth, thee."

Having recited "I settle thee," [he says] "May Sūrya protect thee with great well-being, with a hundredfold shelter; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm. Having settled the third [brick], he breathes out through the lower opening. Then this Brāhmaṇa gives a boon. Then, having taken four portions of ghee in the ladle, he offers it in the space of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* [brick] with the words, "I offer consciousness with mind and ghee. Having touched it with both thumbs, he makes him recite the ascent: "I have ascended to heaven; we have gone to the light-world," at the rear cavity.
He lays down a golden brick with the formula: "Thou art the heavenly light; grant me the heavenly light; uphold the sky; protect me from the sky.
Behind that, at the line of the steps, he lays down a circular brick with the formula: "The sky, unconquered, entered with immortality.
To the south, he lays down the *retahsic* brick with the formula: "The sky is the *retahsic*; may she bestow seed upon me; may she cause my seed to procreate."

Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he performs the *sūdadohas* formula; then, to the north at the point of the step, he lays down the *vikarṇī* brick with the verse: "Like a neighing horse eager for pasture..."

Having performed the *tayādevatam* formula, he performs the *sūdadohas* verse; then he lays down the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks with the formula, "Fill the space, fill the gap. Then he touches this layer with the *citikḷpti* formula, "May the wise one distinguish between thought and lack of thought," using a *paṅkti* verse addressed to Agni. Having touched this layer, he descends with two verses: "Speech is in my mouth, O giver of breath... Then he proceeds with the afternoon *pravargya* and *upasad* rites. Only this much ritual action is performed on this day; they dwell for that night.
Then, on this very ninth day, for the tenth day, he prepares a thousand pieces of gold.
Some say that beyond three there are an unlimited number;
if there are a thousand, these two hundred each are located in the leaf-veins. Then, on the tenth day when the sun has risen, he proceeds with the Pravargya and Upasad rites;
the laying down of the loose earth is the same.

Then, having poured water into a vessel and scattered pieces of gold, he sprinkles [the earth] with two hundred each: with "Thou art the measure of a thousand" over that which is to the east of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*; with "Thou art the image of a thousand" over that which is to the south of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*; with "Thou art the span of a thousand" over that which is to the west of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*; with "Thou art the height of a thousand" over that which is to the north of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*; and then he sprinkles the center with two hundred.

With the formula, "Thou art a thousandfold; for a thousand thee," he then stands at the northern end of the buttock [of the altar] and performs the *iṣṭakā-dhenu* rite with the entire section beginning, "O Agni, may these bricks of mine be cows," until the end of the *anuvāka*. Then he proceeds with the afternoon *pravargya* and *upasad* rites. Only this much ritual action is performed on this day; they pass the night remaining there.

Now, on this very tenth day, for the eleventh day, he prepares a leaf of the *arka* tree, goat’s milk, a pap of *gāvīdhuka* seeds, a stone with three notches, a water-pot, a frog, *avakā* plants, a branch of reed, a bunch of *darbha* grass, a vessel for clarified butter together with a dipping-spoon (*sruva*), and a long bamboo pole—making twelve items in all. Then, on the eleventh day, when the sun has risen, he proceeds with the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites. Having fastened the dipping-spoon onto the long bamboo pole, he offers the two final *saṃcita* oblations with the verse: "O Agni, you who are of the forest, to you I go... (RV 10.8.6).

While the Adhvaryu is occupied there, the Pratiprasthātṛ stops at the last brick of the northern wing, which has been covered with loose earth (purīṣa). Then, having made a funnel from this Arka-leaf so that it filters through the interior, he stands facing north, holding it at the height of his mouth, and says, "Bring it here!

When he reaches the Dhareṣṭakā brick, he begins there; having recited this entire Anuvāka beginning with "Homage to thee, O Rudra, to thy wrath," he recites the second and the third [sections], and at the fourth, where he recognizes the words "Homage to the doorkeepers," he utters "Svāhā."

Therefore, turning toward the east and holding [the fire] at the height of the navel, he begins with "To the gatherers... and recites the remainder of the section; when he reaches the fifth, sixth, and seventh [sections], specifically where he recognizes the words "Homage to the one of the rain-clouds," he utters *svāhā*.

Turning from there toward the south and holding [the fire] at the height of the knee, he begins with "To the one not of the rain-clouds... and recites the remainder of the section; when he reaches the eighth, ninth, tenth, and eleventh [sections], specifically where he recognizes the words "Those who are as many and more than that," he utters *svāhā*.

Therefore, having turned toward the west, while holding [the vessel] at the height of the ankles, he causes the sacrificer to recite: "Obeisance to the Rudras who are on the earth. While holding it at the height of the navel, he causes the sacrificer to recite: "Obeisance to the Rudras who are in the intermediate space.

While holding it at the height of the neck, he causes the sacrificer to recite: "Obeisance to the Rudras who are in heaven. At this point, he throws that Arka leaf in the path of the cattle of one whom he hates.

If, however, he does not hate anyone, he deposits it in a hole dug by a rat; there, upon the final brick, he places this *gavīdhuka* porridge with the formula: "To that Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who is in the plants—to that Rudra who has entered all beings, let there be homage. Then he asks for this bow with three arrows.

Standing at the northern corner of the altar, or else moving around it, he offers worship: "O Rudra, may the wind blow after that bow of yours which is in the east; to that [bow] of yours, O Rudra, I pay homage for a year. "O Rudra, that bow of yours which is in the south," "that bow of yours, O Rudra, which is in the west," "that bow of yours, O Rudra, which is in the north," "that bow of yours, O Rudra, which is all around"—having said this, he gives it to a Brāhmaṇa without asking for anything in return. Then this water-pot of his lies touched by a stone at the northern corner of the altar.
He who is strong, he says to him, "Go around three times to the right, sprinkling with this water-pitcher in a continuous stream.
He does so.

While being sprinkled, he causes the sacrificer to recite: "O Maruts, bestowing favor upon us, bestow upon us that food and vigor which has been gathered from the rock, from the mountain, from the wind, from Parjanya, from the strength of Varuṇa, from the waters, from the plants, and from the trees. Then he sets down this pitcher so that it touches the stone, saying: "O stone, let hunger be yours; let the pain reach him whom we hate."
Having set down the pitcher as it was brought, he goes around it three times again in the opposite direction;

then, upon this very long bamboo pole, he fastens a frog, an *avakā* plant, a branch of cane, and a clump of *darbha* grass. With that, he drags [the earth] over the area east of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone, with the formula: "Thee with the *avakā* of the ocean; thee with the afterbirth of the snow."

"Two in front, two to the south, two behind, and two to the north—with eight [spokes] he draws it," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Then, having cut these very black antelope-skin sandals and this long bamboo pole, they throw them into the *cātvāla* pit. Now, thinking "the fire is appeased," taking the clarified-butter vessel together with the *sruva* ladle, he hastens forward and, dipping the *sruva* into the butter-vessel, offers the serpent-oblations (*sarpāhuti*), sitting behind for the first oblation in the eastern hole with the formula: "Thou art Samīcī by name, the eastern quarter. Sitting to the north for the second oblation in the southern hole, he offers it with: "Thou art Ojasvinī by name, the southern quarter."

Sitting in the east, he offers into the western hole with the formula: "Thou art the eastern one by name, the western direction. Sitting in the south, he offers into the northern hole with the formula: "Thou art the one with a firm foundation by name, the northern direction. Then, having returned by the same way he came, he offers two oblations at the very place where he first offered, with the formulas: "Thou art the overlord by name" and "Thou art the controller by name. Then, having descended, he worships the fire with Sāman chants.

He worships from the front with the Gāyatra; the right wing-tip with the "Heart of Agni" (Agnihṛdaya); the right wing with the Rathantara; the right hip with the Vāravantīya; the tail with the Ṛtusthā-Yajñāyajñiya; the left hip with the Śyaita; the left wing with the Bṛhat; the left wing-tip with the "House of Prajāpati" (Prajāpatigṛha); and the center with the Vāmadevya. Then he says, "O Hotṛ, recite the praise for Agni according to the Uktha."

If the Hotṛ does not desire [to recite], the sacrificer himself, having spread grass behind the tail and sat down upon it, recites the *anuśaṃsa* for Agni with the *uktha*: "Father Mātariśvan has established flawless steps; the eager ones have fashioned flawless steps. Soma, the all-knowing leader, shall lead us; Bṛhaspati shall recite the *ukthas* and *madās*. Om!"—either once or thrice—and then he causes him to recite the *doha* (milking) of the *stotra* and *śastra*: "The sacrifice has been offered by the Bhṛgus; may there be a blessing from the Vasus. Of that which has been offered and enjoyed, may there be wealth here for you."
Having said, "May I partake," he then proceeds with the afternoon Pravargya and Upasad rites; this much alone is the ritual performed on this day, and they remain for that night.

Then, on this very eleventh day, for the twelfth day, he prepares: a ladle (*sruva*) made of *udumbara* wood, a wooden trough (*droṇa*) made of *udumbara*, a pouring-vessel (*praseka*) made of *udumbara*, and a *vitaṣṭi* (a small vessel) made of *udumbara*; in it there is clarified butter taken in five portions; a cup of *udumbara* wood filled with curds; three fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *udumbara* wood; three fuel-sticks of various trees; a faggot (*idhma*) of various trees; curds mixed with honey; a handful of *grumuṣṭi* grass; a bundle of *avakā* plants; a spotted stone; a sprinkling of clarified butter; and a second *hotṛ* priest who will recite the *Apratiratha* hymn.

Having melted and purified the clarified butter, he prepares two or three jars for the *brāhmaudana* rice, as well as *vrīhi* rice, all kinds of herbs, a red bull’s hide, an iron chariot, the *caṣāla* for the *homīya* wood, and chips for the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). Then, on the twelfth day, when the sun has risen, he proceeds with the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites. Having gone out, he issues the call: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā; give the half-milk vow.
The Subrahmaṇya then invokes the Subrahmaṇyā.

He offers the vow of the half-breast; then, having taken five portions of clarified butter, curds mixed with honey, a handful of *grumuṣṭi* grass, and a load of *avakā* plants, he runs forward and sprinkles the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone crosswise with the five-portioned butter, saying: "To the one seated among men, vaṭ! To the one seated in the waters, vaṭ! To the one seated in the forest, vaṭ! To the one seated on the sacrificial grass, vaṭ! To the winner of heaven, vaṭ! With that same ladle, dipping it out, he offers the Gandharva-oblations with curds mixed with honey, sitting behind [the altar] and offering into the eastern cavity, saying: "You are the weapons by name; may your houses be in front."
"You are the *nilimpas*; your dwellings are to the south"—sitting to the north, he offers into the southern hole.

"You are the *vajrins*; your dwellings are behind"—sitting to the east, he offers into the western hole. "You are the *avasthāvanas*; your dwellings are to the north"—sitting to the south, he offers into the northern hole. Then, having returned by the same way he came, he offers two oblations at the very place where he first offered: "You are the *adhipatis* (overlords); you are the *kravyads* (flesh-eaters). Then he says, "O Pratiprasthātṛ, make this fire spotted with tortoises."
He makes it marked with the back of a tortoise;

he does not step upon it unless it has been sprinkled. Then, taking a handful of loose earth, he sprinkles it with curds mixed with honey, using two verses: "Those gods who [are] of the gods... and "Those gods who among the gods attained divinity...
He sprinkles first with these two, then from the south with these two, then from the west with these two, and then from the north with these two, sprinkling around it in order—so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Then, having covered it with a load of *avakā* plants and appointed a guardian, he hastens back and performs the afternoon *pravargya* and *upasad* rites. Then, having gone out, he issues the call: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā; O Āgnīdh, prepare the Vaiśvānara and the Marut offerings; O Pratiprasthātṛ, set down the *pravargya* according to the procedure for the *pravargya*, for the purpose of pouring it out.
They then divide this footprint into three parts.

He places one third [of the offering] on the *gārhapatya* fire, one third in the *upacamanī* waters, and deposits the third [portion]. Then, having raised the *pravargya* vessel according to the procedure for the *pravargya*, he places it on the fire. He prepares a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara and cakes on seven potsherds for the Maruts.

Then, having melted the clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* and purified it, and having taken four portions into the ladle, he offers the *anīkavant* oblation in the *āhavanīya* fire. Having recited "Agni with his sharp flame," he offers it with the verse, "May he, the bountiful giver, [protect us] with that host. Having taken another four portions, he offers the *vaiśvakarmanī* oblations in the *āhavanīya* itself.

Having recited "He who, offering up all these worlds... and so on, he offers with "For Viśvakarman has been born as a god. Having taken another fourfold-drawn portion of ghee and having recited "The father of the eye... and so on, he offers with "O Viśvakarman, with the strengthening oblation...
The Brāhmaṇa says: "He offers with two separate hymns; he thus bestows the power of the two hymns separately.

Then he places three fuel-sticks of Udumbara wood, [reciting]: "Lead him upward, O Indra; make our fame more extensive; for whose house we prepare the oblation. Then he places the faggot to be led forward.

They prepare the *upaprayamanī* verses from the *cātvāla* pit; then he issues the formal command: "Recite for Agni as he is being led forward! O *Āgnīdh*, follow along with the single wooden sword (*ekasphya*)! Let the second *Hotṛ* recite the *Apratiratha* hymn!
This second *Hotṛ* begins the *Apratiratha* hymn with "The swift one, sharpening [his weapons]...
which consists of ten verses; thus says the Brāhmaṇa.

Then, with this very [formula], they take up the fire, the speckled stone, the ghee for sprinkling, and the wooden chips for the enclosing-sticks; then he lifts it up with the verse, "May all the gods lift thee up," and carries it with six [verses], for so says the Brāhmaṇa. Of those [six verses], two contain the word "encompassing. Then, at the midpoint, in the place of the Āgnīdhra, he sets down the speckled stone with two verses: "This measurer of heaven, the bull... and "The ocean... (RV 10.123.8).
Then, with four verses beginning with "ā puccha," he goes as far as the tail; [the priests] maintain this fire with the verse "indraṃ viśvā avīvṛdhan.
Then, once it has been piled up, he sprinkles it with the sprinkling of clarified butter.

"May the Vasus with the Rudras protect you from the east," [he says] as he goes to the east; "May the Fathers, whose king is Yama, with the Pitṛs protect you from the south," [he says] as he goes to the south; "May the Ādityas with all the gods protect you from the west," [he says] as he goes to the west; "May Dyutāna Māruta with the Maruts protect you from the north," [he says] as he goes to the north; "May the gods, with Indra as their chief and Varuṇa as their king, protect you from below and from above," [he says] as he goes above. Then, together with this very fire, he hastens forward, saying: "Go forth along the eastern quarter."

"O wise ones, step forward with Agni toward the highest vault of heaven; from the earth I have ascended to the intermediate space. Those going to the world of light do not look back. With these five verses, beginning with "O Agni, go forward as the first of those seeking the gods," they hold up this fire.

Then, he offers a ladle full of curd upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick made of udumbara wood, reciting the invitatory verse "Night and Dawn," and then he offers with the verse "O Agni, thousand-eyed one. Then, having turned clockwise, he establishes the fuel-bundle with the verse "Thou art the fair-winged Garuḍa."

"He settles it with three [verses]," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Then, having untied it and made it capable of bearing the oblations, he makes offerings over it with the *adhvara* oblations: "May Agni, knowing, lead the sacrifice; may those who destroy the sacrifice not find him; announce the sacrifice to the gods; further the sacrifice, further the lord of the sacrifice—Svāhā! May Vāyu, knowing, lead the sacrifice; may Sūrya, knowing, lead the sacrifice; may the Sacrifice itself, knowing, lead the sacrifice; may those who destroy the sacrifice not find him; announce the sacrifice to the gods; further the sacrifice, further the lord of the sacrifice—Svāhā! Then, having descended, he performs the subsequent rite on the fire-altar (*agnivat*).

Having taken hold of the enclosing sticks and having smoothed them, and having fixed the crosswise *sphya* in place, he issues the call: "Set down the sprinkling waters; place the fuel and the sacrificial grass! Then, having stepped up and laid the chips of wood as the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), and having anointed the fuel of various trees and placed it on the fire with the utterance of *svāhā*, he lays three fuel-sticks of various trees upon it: one of *udumbara* wood with the verse, "O Agni, shine forth, well-enkindled, before us"; one of *vaikaṅkata* wood with the verse, "We would worship thee in thy highest birth, O Agni"; and one of *śamī* wood with the verse, "That wonderful [splendor] of Savitṛ, the most excellent."

Then he offers two *suvāhuti* oblations with the verses, "I offer thought, O Agni; that today... and so on. Then, having taken four portions of clarified butter into the *sruc* ladle, he offers the full *sruc* with the verse, "Seven are thy kindling-sticks, O Agni, seven thy tongues... While offering here, he should meditate upon the quarters with his mind; thus he wins them from the very quarters. He offers curds first and clarified butter afterwards; "He thereby bestows brilliance and power upon him in combination," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then, standing right there, he asks for a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara and cakes on seven potsherds for the Maruts.
Having spread a layer of clarified butter [in the offering ladle], while depositing the entire Vaiśvānara cake [into the fire], he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni Vaiśvānara.
He pours clarified butter over it twice, steps across, causes the announcement to be made, and says, "Recite the offering verse for Agni Vaiśvānara."

When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers in the middle; then he makes offerings over it with ladle-offerings (*sruvāhuti*) using five [formulas], beginning with "The Gharma is light, svāhā! Then he proceeds with the Maruts, in the manner of a *darvihoma* with a base-layer of butter, reciting "Such-like and other-like," and having recited "Śukrajyotis and Citrajyotis," he offers;

having recited "Śukrajyotis and Citrajyotis," he offers "Ṛtajit and Satyajit"; having recited "Ṛtajit and Satyajit," he offers "Ṛta and Satya"; having recited "Ṛta and Satya," he offers the group that is to be recited in the forest, and having recited that, he offers.

Having recited the group of verses that are to be recited in the forest, he offers the oblation with the words, "Such as these, such as these"; having recited, "Such as these, such as these," he offers the oblation with the words, "Measured ones and commensurate ones, not [so]";
having recited, "Measured ones and commensurate ones, not [so]," he offers the oblation with the words, "The one of this form and the one of another form";
he thus piles them around Vaiśvānara on all sides.

"One offers by following one group with another; he causes the announcement for Vaiśvānara loudly, but offers the oblations to the Maruts in a low voice," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Then he places this pouring-vessel upon the fire, either to the south facing north, or behind facing east. Its front half is like a *sruk* ladle, its middle part likewise, and its base is like a *camasa* cup. While spreading four [portions] into it, he says: "Be careful; bring the stream of wealth continuously; I shall recite the *Vasordhārā*."
When he reaches the stream of fire, he enters it with the verse, "O Agni and Viṣṇu, being of one accord. He pours out the entire stream of wealth (vasordhārā) until its end;

at this point, he throws the sprinkling-vessel into the fire and then makes an offering over it with the residue of the oblation. Then, whatever clarified butter remains, in that he cooks the *brahmaudana* (the rice for the Brahmins);
four Brahmins consume it.
"One should give four cows to them," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, previously for him, there is a wooden trough made of Udumbara wood containing all kinds of herbs, mixed together with curds and clarified butter.

With a dipping-spoon (*sruva*) made of Udumbara wood, he offers the *Vājaprasavīya* oblations, drawing from that mixture: "The impulse of strength (*vāja*) has brought forth this [sacrifice] in the beginning; may strength [impel] us in the seven directions"—with these fourteen spoonfuls. He leaves over a remnant for the consecration. Then, having covered it, he sets it down in a known place. Then he offers the milk of a black cow that has a white calf, with the verse, "Night and Dawn... (RV 1.72.1).
Then he offers the six *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations with the verses beginning, "Obeisance to Ṛtāṣāṭ, obeisance to Ṛtadhām.

At the front of the chariot, he offers five oblations with the verse, "O Lord of the World. Then he offers three *ruc* oblations with the verses: "Those splendors of yours, O Agni, which are in the sun; those splendors of yours, O gods, which are in the sun; bestow splendor upon us among the Brāhmaṇas. Then, having poured clarified butter into a vessel, he offers the names of the winds, dipping his joined palms each time: "Thou art the ocean, full of mist, moist, a wind, auspicious, and refreshing; blow toward me, svāhā! Thou art the Marut, the host of the Maruts, auspicious and refreshing; blow toward me, svāhā! Thou art the seeker of favor..."

"O you who are swift, who bring happiness, who bring bliss, blow toward me, Svāhā!"—some indeed think that they are offering oblations to the wind; at this point he throws these wooden splinters as enclosing-sticks (paridhis) into the fire;
thus ends the section concerning the wooden splinters.
Then he erects the Sadas and the Havirdhāna sheds; having erected the Sadas and the Havirdhāna sheds, he pours out the fires for the Adhvara altars.

Upon them, he lays down the fire-hearths (*dhiṣṇiyas*). At the Āgnīdhra hearth, he lays down one *yājuṣī* brick with the formula, "O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations," and seven *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks. Then, at the Hotṛ's hearth, he lays down one *yājuṣī* brick and eleven *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks. Then, at the others, he lays down one *yājuṣī* brick and seven *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks each. Then, at the Mārjālīya hearth, he lays down one *yājuṣī* brick and five *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks. Then he leads forward Agni and Soma; having led forward Agni and Soma, he raises the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) according to the procedure for the post, and having equipped the post with a *svaru*, he dedicates the animal victim to Agni and Soma.

Having performed the rite with its well-known omentum and having cast the two omentum-spits into the fire, he takes up the *vasatīvarī* waters; then he offers the sacrificial cake for the animal victim (*paśupuroḍāśa*).
Following that, eight *devasū* oblations are offered, beginning with "To Agni Gṛhapati"; these they prepare separately.
They cook [the offerings] separately, for there are various grains.

For the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa), the call is "Recite! and "Sacrifice!"; for the other oblations, it is as follows: when he is cutting portions from the offering to Varuṇa, he says, "Recite for Varuṇa, the Lord of Law (dharmapati)! At that moment, he cuts once from the northern half of each of all the offerings into the *upabhṛt* ladle for the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice.
He pours the clarified butter over [the oblation] twice, but does not smear it back. Having stepped across and caused the announcement to be made, he says, "Sacrifice to Varuṇa, the lord of dharma.
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers the oblation. Now, it is indeed said: "Varuṇa becomes sacrificed for him, but Sviṣṭakṛt remains unsacrificed"; then the Brahman priest takes his hand.
When Varuṇa has become the iṣṭa and Sviṣṭakṛt has become the aniṣṭa, then the Brahman takes his hand.

"May Savitṛ impel you among those who impel; Agni among householders; Soma among lords of the forest; Rudra among cattle; Bṛhaspati among speeches; Indra among the eldest; Mitra among the truthful; Varuṇa among the lords of dharma—thus all this comes to pass. O gods who are the impellers of the gods, impel this man, the son of such-and-such, toward freedom from enemies, toward great sovereignty, toward great overlordship, and toward great rule over the people. Then, while he stands in the sacrificer’s place, he addresses him: "This one is your king," [saying this] to those for whom he has become the chief.

"May Soma be the king of us Brāhmaṇas," the others reply. Then he releases his speech with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. He wipes his mouth with two [verses]: "That name of yours has been established as sovereignty; all the hosts have become Varuṇa's. He strides the Viṣṇu-strides with Gāyatrī verses: "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu, thou art the step of Viṣṇu, thou art the wide-stride of Viṣṇu. Then he proceeds with the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.
He does not cut off the *iḍā* from the *raudra* [oblation]; they consume it with water.
The sacrificial cakes conclude with the *iḍā*.

The animal sacrifice concludes with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, or according to some, with the heart-spit (*hṛdayaśūla*). Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and set aside the milks, they fast.
Then, at the very dead of night, they awaken;
the ritual procedure is the same up to the placing of the offering-spoons (*sruc*).

Having placed the spoons, he yokes the fire with the "yoking" formula: "I yoke the fire; these two are thy wings; thou art thought, ocean-born," with these three verses. Then, having brought down King Soma, he begins the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*).

When the morning litany (prātaranuvāka) has been recited, he goes toward the water; having emerged from the water, he enters that ritual resolve (kratu), and the pressing (abhiṣava) proceeds according to the established rule.
The cups are taken in the established manner. The ritual procedure is the same up to the Āśvina cup. Having taken the Āśvina cup and having taken eleven cords, he approaches the sacrificial post.

Having set aside the post provided with a wooden chip (svaru), he dedicates the animals of the set of eleven: a black-necked animal for Agni; a ewe for Sarasvatī; a brown one for Soma; a dark-grey one for Pūṣan; a white-backed one for Bṛhaspati; a speckled one for Viśve Devas; a ruddy one for Indra; a dappled one for the Maruts; a composite one for Indra-Agni; a dark-red one for Savitṛ; and a long-haired ram for Varuṇa.
Having performed the ritual for them with the omenta as is well known, they proceed to the morning pressing;
that concludes in the regular manner, and they proceed to the midday pressing.
Whenever it is midday, he fills this golden vessel with honey, looks at it with a bright verse addressed to Sūrya, makes the horse smell it, and gives it to the Brahman priest.
The pressing of the Soma is performed in the established manner,
and the cups are drawn in the established manner.

The ritual procedure is the same up to the offerings for the *dakṣiṇās*. Having offered the *dakṣiṇā* oblations, he proceeds with three *marutvatīya* offerings. The *nārāśaṃsa* cups, having been replenished, are set down. Below the rear support of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, they sit for the *māhendra* cup. Prior to the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), he offers six *pārtha* oblations: "To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! and so forth. Then, on the sacrificer's seat, he spreads a black antelope skin with the neck pointing eastward and the hair side upward. Having seated the sacrificer there facing east and having placed gold and silver plates around him, he sprinkles him from the front toward the west with a mixture of all herbs.
He sprinkles [the water] from the head down to the mouth, pouring it over [the face]. With the formula:

"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech—with the sovereignty of Agni I sprinkle you; with the sovereignty of Indra I sprinkle you; with the sovereignty of Bṛhaspati I sprinkle you"—as he is wiped clean, they shout out together: "This one has been consecrated, the son of so-and-so, the grandson of so-and-so, the great-grandson of so-and-so, by means of the Agni-consecration. Then, with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he releases his speech.
He wipes his face with two [verses].
He takes the steps of Viṣṇu accompanied by Gāyatrī verses. Then, after the consecration, he offers six Pārtha oblations with the formulas:
"To Indra, svāhā! To Ghoṣa, svāhā! and so forth.

He offers twelve *aveṣṭi* oblations for the elements with the formulas, "To Earth, svāhā! To the Atmosphere, svāhā! and so forth. The midday pressing concludes in the regular manner. They proceed to the third pressing.
Having performed the rite with the *ādityagraha* in the established way, he draws the *āgrayaṇa* cup.
The ritual action is the same; having performed the Pavamāna rite with the Pavamāna cup, he proceeds with the animal sacrifices in their own place.

For these, there are separate *manotā* hymns, separate deities, separate touchings [of the victim], and separate *vasā-homa* offerings. The *vanaspati* offering is common, as is the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering accompanied by the *praisha* call. The *iḍā* is common, and the directions are common; however, some say the directions are separate.

The ritual procedure is the same up to the *yajñāyajñiya* stotra. At the *yajñāyajñiya* stotra, when it has been commenced with a single verse, he touches the fire with two verses: "Homage be to thee; do not harm me; give us water; break open the ocean. The ritual procedure is the same up to the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.

Having performed the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, having gone forward to the east, having replenished the *dhruvā* ladle, and having offered the *sam-iṣṭayajus* oblations belonging to the *adhvara*, he offers ten oblations pertaining to the fire-altar (*agni*) with the verse: "From the intention [of the heart] it flowed forth... and so on.

The ritual procedure up to the *avabhṛtha* bath is the same; then, at this *avabhṛtha*, he offers a second *avabhṛtha* oblation with the formula: "To the ocean, for the discernment of the rivers, to the lord of the streams, obeisance!
The *avabhṛtha* bath is performed in the established manner. Having sacrificed the *udayanīyā* offering, he dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa.
For that cow, there is curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) belonging to Mitra and Varuṇa from which the portions are to be cut.

They perform all the formalities for the animal sacrifice. Then, having melted the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire and purified it, and having taken four portions of the butter into the ladle, he offers the full ladle as the "unloosing" (vimoka) oblation of the fire with the verse: "Suck this breast, rich in strength, of the waters. Then he worships it with the verse: "The fires that belong to the soil... Then he worships it with the nine "attainment" (āpti) verses, beginning with "I have attained thee, O Agni, with my mind," according to their respective meters. Then he performs the Udavasānīyā sacrifice; then he sacrifices with the Devikā offerings; then he sacrifices with the Traidhātavīyā; then he sacrifices with the Sautrāmaṇī.
For a year he does not descend [to a lower level] toward anyone;

he does not eat the flesh of the head, nor the flesh of birds; having piled the fire-altar, he should not approach a woman; one who has piled the fire-altar should not run while it is raining; if he should run, he should turn back, for "he thus turns toward food," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

One who is about to perform the Vājapeya sacrifice prepares the following: a black antelope skin, two gold plates—one of gold and one of silver—a goat-skin, a piece of gold weighing a hundred mānas, seventeen gold *kṛṣṇalas*, a golden vessel filled with honey, a chariot wheel made of *udumbara* wood with seventeen spokes, a wooden frame consisting of seventeen planks, a sacrificial post that is hornless, four-cornered, and seventeen cubits long, a bundle of wheat, a turban, and seventeen *śarāva*-measures of wild rice (*nīvāra*).

Seventeen bundles of herbs, seventeen vessels for the wind, seventeen broad-based *upayāma* cups, a hundred and seven locks of hair, seventeen gold neck-ornaments (*niṣka*), seventeen garments, seventeen loads of clothing, seventeen chariots, seventeen drums, seventeen elephants, seventeen female slaves, seventeen wagons yoked with oxen, and seventeen hundred cattle—or of each kind of bird, seventeen thousand; for in this [sacrifice] all kinds of birds are present.
Twenty-four animals, fifty-one horses, and a split pole made of khadira wood bound with thongs; the well-known materials for the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice are prepared.
He undergoes initiation during the final days of summer, prior to the full moon of Āṣāḍha.

For him, there are thirteen initiation days and three *upasads*, and he performs the *prasava* (the pressing) on the seventeenth day. Alternatively, there may be seventeen initiation days and three *upasads*, and he performs the *prasava* on the twenty-first day. Or again, there may be exactly three initiation days and three *upasads*, and he performs the *prasava* on the seventh day.
Now it is indeed said: "One offers the Sāvitra oblation before each and every ritual act.

When about to pour out the oblation for the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* [initiatory] sacrifice, he offers the Sāvitra oblation with the mantra: "O God Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice; impel the lord of the sacrifice for his portion. May the divine Gandharva, the purifier of intentions, purify our intention. May the Lord of Speech make our speech sweet today. Svāhā!"
When about to offer the initiation oblations, he offers to Savitṛ;
when about to pour out the Prāyaṇīyā oblation, he offers to Savitṛ; when about to offer while holding gold between [his fingers], he offers to Savitṛ;
he proceeds with the footprint.
Having moved about with the foot and having purchased the King Soma, the Adhvaryu, intending to perform the guest-offering (*ātithya*), offers the *sāvitra* oblation;

when about to proceed with the first two *pravargya* and *upasad* rites, he offers the *sāvitra* oblation. At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having caused a pit to be dug in the southern section of the hall, prepares the *vājapeya* surā-liquor.
When about to perform the first tracing of the great altar (*mahāvedi*), he offers the *sāvitra* oblation; when about to lead forward the Āhavanīya fire, he offers the *sāvitra* oblation.

When about to direct [the attendants] to the Rathavāhana, the Sadas, and the Havirdhāna sheds, he offers the Sāvitra oblation; when about to lead forward Agni and Soma, he offers the Sāvitra oblation—thus he has offered ten times within the hall; now he will offer in the Āgnīdhra shed itself;
and when about to erect the sacrificial post, he offers the Sāvitra oblation.

When the Adhvaryu and the Sacrificer move forward from the east toward the west, rubbing [the post], then the Pratiprasthātṛ moves up from behind toward the east, wrapping it with cloths or tying on strips of cloth with their fringes pointing northward, or he wraps it with bow-strings. At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having made a sheaf of wheat equal at both ends, ties it with a turban;

they perform upon that what is done at the top of the sacrificial post when one has set up the post provided with a wooden ring (svaru) and is about to bring forward the animal for Agni and Soma—he offers the oblation to Savitṛ.
Having performed the rite with its omentum in the established manner, when about to take up the *vasatīvarī* waters, he offers an oblation to Savitṛ;
when about to offer the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), he offers an oblation to Savitṛ.
These [three] are offered at each pressing, making seventeen [oblations] in total; or alternatively, he may offer them at each pressing individually—this is another view.
Then he offers the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) for Paśupati;
following that are the eight oblations of the Devasū, beginning with "To Agni Gṛhapati. Their performance has been explained as being according to the procedure for Agni.
The sacrificial cakes conclude with the Iḍā-portion.
"The animal sacrifice ends with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings;

some say it ends with the heart-spit (*hṛdayaśūla*)," so it is said. At this point, he fastens these drums in every direction: five on the southern hip, five on the northern, four on the right shoulder, and three on the left shoulder. "In this way, they obtain speech from the quarters for him," Baudhāyana used to say. Āñjīgavi says they should be fastened in clusters in front of the *āgnīdhra* shed; Kātya says they should be around the *sadas*.
Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and having set aside the various milks, they observe the fast.
Thereupon, at the very dead of night, they wake up; having taken the morning clarified butters and having brought down King Soma, he begins the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*).

When the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*) has been concluded, the Adhvaryu goes toward the waters; at this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having purified the *vājapeya* surā and taken it along with the vessel, brings it out through the southern door, goes around the south of the *sadas*, carries it around the south of the Mārjālīya hearth, and having brought it in through the western door, sets it down behind the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart. Then the Adhvaryu comes up from the waters and enters all the ritual sessions; the pressing (*abhiṣava*) is performed in the established manner.
The cups are drawn according to the established rule;
the ritual procedure is the same up to the Āgrayaṇa cup.
Having drawn the Āgrayaṇa, he draws five *natigrāhya* cups for Indra with these five [verses]: "Thou art taken with a support; thee, the man-seated, the tree-seated... and so forth.
Then he places them, arranged in clusters, on the eastern half of the southern half of the mound;

while the Adhvaryu is occupied there, the Pratiprasthātṛ purifies the *surā* with a woolen filter whose fringes point northward, [reciting]: "May the daughter of the Sun purify for you the flowing *soma* through the eternal fleece."

The Adhvaryu takes the Vāyu-vessel, and the Pratiprasthātṛ takes the Upayāma-vessel; the Adhvaryu, being first, draws the Soma-cups from the Droṇakalaśa with the Vāyu-vessel, reciting the verse, "Impelling these powers, generating deeds," and then, having run through the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Prajāpati," he wipes it and sets it down with, "This is thy womb; for Prajāpati thee. Then the Pratiprasthātṛ draws the Surā-cups from the Sat vessel with the Upayāma-vessel, reciting the verse, "O friend, like those who possess barley," and then, having run through the formula, he draws them with, "Thou art taken with a support; for Prajāpati thee."

With "To Prajāpati thee," he deposits [the cup]; he neither makes it "pleasing" (juṣṭam) nor [assigns] a womb (yoni). In this very manner, the two of them draw the cups in an interlocking fashion: one draws seventeen, the other seventeen.
The Adhvaryu extends the Soma-cups in two rows or three rows toward the north, in front of the axle.

The Pratiprasthātṛ extends the line for the Surā-graha toward the north, either in two rows or three rows. Then he draws the Ṣoḍaśin cup, running forward with the formula, "Mount the chariot, O slayer of Vṛtra! He then says, "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Indra for the Ṣoḍaśin," and having wiped it around, he sets it down with, "This is thy womb; [I set thee down] acceptable to Indra for the Ṣoḍaśin. Then he draws the Ukthya cup; the ritual procedure is the same up to the Āśvina cup. Having drawn the Āśvina cup and having taken six cords, he approaches the sacrificial post.

Having set up the sacrificial post provided with a *svark* (top-ring), he then dedicates these animals: one for Agni, one for Indra-Agni, one for Indra, a barren cow for the Maruts, seventeen for Prajāpati—black and of uniform color—and finally one for Sarasvatī.
Then, according to the procedure for the fire-drilled (*nirmanthya*) fire, he proceeds with the fire-drilling;

having struck the fire and offered the oblation, he fastens these animals dedicated to various deities separately with double-stranded cords and binds them individually to triple-stranded cords. Then, having fastened these animals dedicated to the same deity separately with double-stranded cords, he binds them together on a single post-hole, or else he attaches each animal to another animal.
Having finally assigned the *sārasvatī* [verse], he then sprinkles them, makes them drink [the water], sprinkles [the ground] around them, and pours out [the remainder];
then, taking a fuel-stick from the faggot while saying, "Recite for the fire being kindled," he places the faggot [on the altar] and leaves one fuel-stick remaining;
he fans it with the *vedā* grass-bundle, and when the *sāmidhenī* verses have been recited, he pours the *āghāra* libation with the *sruva* spoon.

Having wiped the two offering-ladles (*sruk*) with the *uttara* formula, then stepping across toward the north without letting the two ladles touch each other, having anointed the victims with the *juhū* and set down the two ladles, he chooses the *pravara*;
he chooses the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) in the established manner.
The Hotṛ sits down and awaits the impulse;
once impelled, he takes up the two offering-spoons, steps across, calls for the *āśrāvaṇa*, and says, "Prompt [the Āgnīdhra] for the kindling-sticks! (*samidbhyaḥ preṣya*).
He offers when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered; he says "Prompt! Prompt!
at the fourth and eighth [pressings], drawing together [the butter] at each, and at the eighth he draws it all together;
he leaves behind a residue for the *svāhākṛti* offerings.
Having performed the ten *prayāja* offerings, he steps northward and anoints the animals with the *svaru* and the splinter-shavings.
These animals have different deities, different *svarus*, and different splinter-shavings; whereas these other animals have the same deity, the same *svaru*, and different splinter-shavings.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the carrying of fire around them (*paryagnikaraṇa*). Then, they proceed northward with the animals that have been carried around by fire.

Among them, the one for Sarasvatī is in the northern half; the one for Agni is by way of proximity. The Adhvaryu takes hold of the two omentum-roasting spits belonging to the victim for Agni alone. They lead the other attendants separately toward the north, one after another without jostling.
The Adhvaryu throws down sacrificial grass for the victim for Agni as it is being slaughtered, but separately for the others.

Then he strikes down the others, whether they face east or north, saying, "Kill them! Make them motionless! Render them senseless! Having returned by the same way he came, they sit near the *pṛṣadājya* (spotted butter) with the verse: "May offspring of every form rejoice here in this sacrifice, all-knowing and dripping with ghee; dwelling together in Agni as their home, may they favor us with milk and ghee.

When they announce that the animals have been rendered senseless, he offers the *saṃjñaptāhuti* (oblation for the senseless) with the formula: "Since the animals have made no sound. Then he approaches, saying, "O slaughterers, come hither! and consecrates the animals as they are being released from the nooses with the mantra: "May Aditi release these nooses."
He casts this direction away with separate *aviśākhā* branches, saying: "I cast down the one who acts as an enemy; upon him whom we hate, I fasten my snares.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ leads the wife forward, having caused her to lift up the water-jar.

He successively causes the vital breaths of the animals to swell. Following him, as the Adhvaryu goes about extracting the omenta, he begins with the omentum of the animal dedicated to Agni; they bring the others in succession. While the omentum of the animal for Agni is being heated, he throws the tip of a blade of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) into it; they hold the others near. He makes an offering over the omentum of the animal for Agni with a spoonful of clarified butter; they hold the others near. Then, having proceeded according to the *svāhākṛti* call, he sprinkles the clotted butter (*pṛṣadājya*) with the residue and [offers] that of the animal for Agni.

He bastes the omentum; they bring the other [omentum] forward. Then, having offered a spoonful of oblation with the *svāhā*-utterance in front, he says, "Recite for these animals dedicated to various deities; give the command! and proceeds with the omenta. Then, while gathering together the omentum of the principal animal among those dedicated to the same deity, he says in a low voice, "For Prajāpati," and loudly, "Recite for the fat of the goats' omenta as it is being cut off. As many [portions] as can be contained in the ladle, so many he takes; the others he holds up either in a vessel or with the *veḍasūna* [ladle].

He pours clarified butter over [the portions] twice; having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says in a low voice, "For Prajāpati," and aloud, "Prompt [the Hotṛ] regarding the fat of the goat's omentum that has been set forth.

At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers the omentum. He proceeds with the omentum of Sarasvatī in a low voice. Then, having offered a spoonful with the *svāhākṛti* formula after [the omentum], and having thrown the omentum-spits into the fire and stepped out, they purify themselves at the *cātvāla* pit. Then he gives instructions regarding the animals, saying, "O *śamitr*, cook that which is not to be cut from the portion for the Maruts on one side. Then, having offered the oblation to Savitṛ, they proceed to the morning pressing.
It concludes in this straightforward manner.

Then, having offered the oblation to Savitṛ, they proceed to the midday pressing. Having recognized that the officiants have proceeded from the very place where [the doors were opened] with the words "O divine doors," the Adhvaryu, moving forward, says: "Fix the chariot-wheel in the Cātvāla pit; place the chariot on the chariot-stand; wash the horses; whatever you intend to give as a gift, place that to the south; O Soma-pressers, summon him; O Grāvastut, come; O Sacrificer, come. The pressing is performed in the established manner.
The cups are drawn according to the established rule; the ritual procedure is the same up to the Āgrayaṇa cup.

Having drawn the Āgrayaṇa, he draws the Ṣoḍaśin, reciting: "Indra, the two bay steeds carry thee," and then, "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Indra for the Ṣoḍaśin. Having wiped it around, he deposits it with: "This is thy womb; [I place thee] acceptable to Indra for the Ṣoḍaśin."
Then he draws the Ukthya cup;
the ritual procedure is the same up to the offerings for the Dakṣiṇās.
Intending to offer the Dakṣiṇā oblations, he asks for the vessel of clarified butter together with the dipping-spoon and the ladle, and a cloth.

When the fringe of this very garment has reached its final state, a cord without a noose is fastened to it; taking hold of this, he says, "Come, O Sacrificer," and having gone around to the north of the Āgnīdhrīya fire and having gone around to the north of the Sadas, he stands before the hall and hands over these ritual implements to the Pratiprasthātṛ. Then he says, "Come, O Sacrificer";
here on the southern hip of the chariot-stand, the chariot is placed upon the chariot-stand.

He brings it down [from the cart] with the formula: "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra; through thee may this man slay Vṛtra. Then, while the horse is still held by the neck, they lead it into the interior of the sacrificial ground (antarvedi) with the verse: "In the impulse of strength, we celebrate with our speech the great Mother, named Aditi, in whom this entire world has entered; may the god Savitṛ impel for us the sacred law within her. Then he causes the horses to wash themselves in the waters with the formula: "Within the waters is immortality, in the waters is healing; and in the praises of the waters, O horses, become swift-winners. Then...

He yokes the right-hand horse with the formula: "Vāyu has yoked you, or Manu has yoked you, or the twenty-seven Gandharvas; they first yoked the horse, they placed speed in him. Then he rubs its back with the formula: "O Son of the Waters, swift impeller, whose wave is humped, the over-leaping one, best winner of booty—by that may this [horse] win the prize. In the same way, he yokes the left-hand horse. To its left, he yokes the side-horse (*praṣṭi*). In the same way, he rubs the backs of these two. Following the yoking of this [central horse], all living beings are yoked. They make the elephants wear extra girth-bands.
They cause loads of garments to be brought in; they tie cords for the fringe of the clothes in bundles.

Then he bestows the sacrificial fees. Next, he offers oblations on the Gārhapatya fire with two verses addressed to Sūrya, and he offers on the Āgnīdhra fire with a verse containing the word "lead" (naya).
The sacrificial gifts are created by way of the southern path;

whatever he gives, he gives beginning with gold. Then there are garments, old ones that have been worn out, as well as cattle, horses, elephants, and men—at the very end, even these chariots pass by without being given away;
they do not run the race while belonging to anyone else.
With the mind alone he gives his own chariot to the Adhvaryu; having mentally assigned the sacrificial gifts, he proceeds with the three Marutvatīya offerings;
the Nārāśaṃsa cups, having been replenished, sit down; below the rear support of the southern Havirdhāna cart are the Māhendras.
Then he asks for seventeen bowls of wild rice; this is cooked in milk, and with it he performs the offering. He says, "Recite for Bṛhaspati," and "Sacrifice to Bṛhaspati.

Having covered that [offering] before the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation has been made, he sets it aside in a known place. Now, previously, in a wooden trough (*droṇa*) made of *udumbara* wood, there is all kinds of herbs mixed together with curds and clarified butter.

With a dipping-spoon (*sruva*) made of *udumbara* wood, he offers seven oblations of food, each preceded by a dipping, with the mantra: "This impulse of strength was born first... He leaves over a remnant for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), then, having covered it, he sets it down in a known place. Then, prior to the consecration, he offers six oblations to the quarters with the formulas: "To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! and so forth. Then, upon the sacrificer's seat, he spreads out a black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and the hair upward.

Having seated the sacrificer facing eastward and having placed gold and silver plates on both sides of him, he sprinkles him from the front toward the west with all-herbs, sprinkling from the head down to the mouth, while pouring the liquid down along [the body] with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech—with the sovereignty of Agni I sprinkle you; with the sovereignty of Indra I sprinkle you; with the sovereignty of Bṛhaspati I sprinkle you."

When he has been wiped clean, they cry out, "This one, the son of such-and-such, the grandson of such-and-such, the great-grandson of such-and-such, is being consecrated with the Vājapeya! Then, saying "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he releases his speech;

he wipes his face with two verses and strides the Viṣṇu-strides following the Gāyatrī verses. Then, after the consecration, he offers six Pārtha oblations: "To Indra, svāhā! To Ghoṣa, svāhā! and so forth.

He offers twelve oblations to the elements with the formula, "To the earth, svāhā! To the intermediate space, svāhā! and so forth; at this point, he performs the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering for this oblation to Bṛhaspati. Then, taking it [the vessel], he goes out toward the north between the *cātvāla* pit and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*). To the north, these chariots stand harnessed.

He causes these yoke-horses to smell the *ājya* with the formula: "O swift ones, winners of the prize, about to run for the prize, about to win the prize, smell the portion of Bṛhaspati! Then, having covered it, he sets it down in a known place. Then he approaches the chariot with the formula: "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu; thou art the step of Viṣṇu; thou art the wide-stride of Viṣṇu. Then he touches the two sides of the chariot with the formula: "The two hooks, the two side-hooks, on both sides of the chariot..."

"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, may I win the prize through Bṛhaspati, the winner of the prize"—at this moment, the Brahman ascends the chariot wheel that has been marked. He consecrates him right there with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, may I ascend the highest firmament through Bṛhaspati, the winner of the prize. Then, having mounted after the sacrificer, he causes him to recite the *ujjitī* verses: "Agni won speech by means of the one-syllable [word]," and so on, seventeen verses. Then he hands him the horse-whip: "O horse-whip, winner of the prize, rich in prizes, win the horses for us in the contests!"
With that [formula], he urges the horses according to their respective positions: "O courser, run! for the right horse; "O steed, run! for the middle one; and "O racer, run! for the left one.

Then he causes those who have entered the racecourse to look on, saying: "O racers, run for the prize! Conquer in the impulse of the Maruts! Measure out the distances! Steady yourselves upon the paths! Reach the goal! This is a post made of Udumbara wood, fixed at seventeen throws of the yoke-pin.

They call it "the wood. Those who run the race, do not pass it; do not turn back without reaching it. Having made it level with the inner wings and having grasped it from the left, you should turn around with the right hands, saying, "Do not creep away before you have brought forth [the fruit].

Then he says, "Come hither, O sacrificer; I shall draw the cup for Mahendra. While the sacrificer holds on to him, he draws the cup for Mahendra, reciting: "Great is Indra, who by his might... and continuing, "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Mahendra. Having wiped it around, he deposits it, saying, "This is thy womb; [I place thee] acceptable to Mahendra."

Then he sets down these five *atigrāhya* cups dedicated to Indra together. Having touched water and taken two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), restraining his speech, he runs westward and introduces the chant.

When they chant the *stotra* for Mahendra and the *prastāva* of the Sāman has been intoned, he issues the direction: "O Brahman, sing the *Sāman* of the racers! O charioteers, run the race! Beat the drums! Pressers, press the Soma! Āgnīdh, pour out the milk-mixture (*āśira*); cause the mortar to resound! Pratiprasthātṛ, offer the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) to Varuṇa; take note of the offering for Soma!"
They perform their duties according to the directions;
the Brahman priest sings the Vājina-sāman, while anyone who serves as an attendant wraps him [the horse] around.
The arrow-shooters run, they strike the drums,
and voices cry out together.

When the voices have risen up, he recites the consecration formulas: "O Indra, speak with speech; make Indra win the prize; Indra has won the prize. Then he recites over the chariots as they race: "In every contest, O prize-winners, protect us," with four verses according to their meters. The noises subside for the sake of the *śastra* recitation by the Hotṛ; "This is the last," they say. At the moment of the Hotṛ's call, the Adhvaryu turns away, and the Hotṛ calls out to him.
The Adhvaryu calls out; when there is "śam," he responds with "pratigṛṇāti."
Having responded with the well-known recitation, he goes forward and lifts up this Māhendra cup;
while they lift up the others,
they lift up the Nārāśaṃsa goblets.
Then, having caused the announcement to be made with "Ośrāvaya! Let it be heard! Oṣaṭ!", [the Adhvaryu] says, "Recite the offering prayer for the Soma of the Uktha-praiser!
and when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering; thus they offer these five *atigrāhya* cups dedicated to Indra together.
He offers twice, at the *vaṣaṭ* call and at the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ* call;
likewise, they shake the *nārāśaṃsa* cups twice each time.
The *māhendra* cup, having been offered twice, remains as a remnant.
The chariots come;

having seen the chariots arrived, he asks for a vessel of clarified butter together with the *sruva*-ladle. If they report to him that there has been a mishap with the chariot, the *āgnīdhra* offers this oblation with the verse, "And as he runs and hastens...
He offers the *rathavimocanīya* (chariot-unloosing) oblation with both [verses], ending with, "May the impulse of strength come to me."

Then he asks for seventeen śarāva-measures of wild rice, seventeen gold kṛṣṇala-weights, and a golden vessel filled with honey; having taken these, he goes out northward between the cātvāla and the utkarī-pile, where these chariots stand yoked to the north.

Then he causes these yoke-horses to smell the barley with the formula: "O prize-winning horses, having run for the prize, having won the prize, roll yourselves in the portion of Bṛhaspati. Then, having covered it, he sets it down in a known place. Then he addresses the chariots as they are being unyoked: "This was that true compact of yours which you made with Indra.
He addresses the drums as they are being silenced: "O trees, you have caused Indra to win; now be unyoked!"

Then he unyokes this chariot yoked with a *yajus*-formula; they turn the other [chariots] back as they were given. These race-runners approach him, and to each one of them he distributes a single *kṛṣṇala* weight of gold.
Taking those together with a golden vessel filled with honey, he presents it all at once to the Brahman priest.

Having accepted that [cup], the Brahman descends; then he says: "O race-horses, having passed along the southern path, take your station at the southern buttock; O Maruts, having gone around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, take your station at the southern shoulder. Then they strike them with the two sheds. Then he says, "Come, O sacrificer," and having led the sacrificer into the Havirdhāna shed by the eastern door, he causes him to stand near the Soma-cups.
"You are mingled; mingle me with what is auspicious," he says; "you are separated;
separate me from evil. Having taken this surā with its dregs and these cups of surā, they offer them to the race-winners (*ājisṛt*).

Drinking it, rejoicing, and exalting themselves, they sit there. Whatever portion of the *mārutyā* offering is not to be cut off, he places that between the two [other portions] upon branches of the *parṇa* tree; they then cry out and tear it apart. Then he asks for the vessel of clarified butter together with the dipping-spoon (*sruc*), as well as a garment of silk (*tārpya*) made of *darbha* grass. Having taken these, he says, "Come, O sacrificer! The sacrificer follows behind him, and the wife follows after the sacrificer. He offers twelve spoonfuls of oblations in the *āhavanīya* fire while the sacrificer maintains contact [with him], reciting: "Vāja and Prasava... and so on. Then he causes the sacrificer to put on the silk garment with the formula: "Thou art the caul of the ruling power (*kṣatra*)."
With the formula, "Thou art the womb of the Kṣatra," he takes a girdle made of *darbha* grass for the wife;
then he leads her from the sacrificer’s place toward the sacrificial post, either eastward or northward. Then he addresses his wife: "O wife, come! Let us two ascend to heaven (*suvar*).
The other replies, "Let us two indeed ascend to heaven. The sacrificer says, "I shall cause both of us to ascend to heaven."

"You, O *Suvar*, mount both of us," he says; she, the wife, mounts it with ten formulas: "May life prosper through sacrifice," and so on until the end. Then he raises his arms, saying: "We have gone to the heavenly world (*suvar*); we have become immortal; we have become the offspring of Prajāpati. Then he looks back toward this world, saying: "May I be united with offspring, and may offspring be united with me; may I be united with the increase of wealth, and may the increase of wealth be united with me. Then he descends from it at such a distance as he thinks he will not fall from. There they strike him with handfuls of grass.

With "For food, thee! the Adhvaryu strikes from the east; with "For the eating of food, thee! the Brahman from the south; with "For strength, thee! the Hotṛ from the west; and with "For the winning of strength, thee! the Udgātṛ from the north.
Or, if these do not so desire, the Adhvaryu alone strikes from the east, the Pratiprasthātṛ from the south, the Āgnīdhra from the west, and the Unnetṛ from the north;
their division [of duties] is according to that of the drums.
At this point, he places a stool for him to descend upon;
on it he spreads a goat-skin, and on the goat-skin he places a hundred-māna weight of gold.
Then he steps down with his right foot onto the gold, saying, "Thou art immortality."

"Thou art nourishment; thou art procreation," [he says] as he places the left foreleg on the goat-skin. Then they bring him to his seat with this stool, or they carry him there. These goblets follow after him. At this point, he invokes the *iḍā* of this offering to Bṛhaspati.
Once the *iḍā* has been invoked, the Hotṛ and the Adhvaryu together consume the portion for Mahendra. With the remnants of the Narāśaṃsa-drink, they consume the Narāśaṃsa cups.

In this regard, having poured together the remnants of these *atigrāhya* cups into the principal vessel, the sacrificer himself consumes them directly; or alternatively, they may pour them all out into the goblets and consume them—this is another option. Then these three, having invited one another, consume from the *hotṛ*-goblet alone.
They touch themselves with the formula, "Impel the goblets according to their respective owners; impel me."
They do not swell the cups;
having consumed the entire contents, they perform the *mārjana* purification. Then, with the three rounds of the *ukthya*—"O Indra, O Indra"—he proceeds.
Thus the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdinaṃ savanam*) is concluded.

Then, having offered the *sāvitra* oblation, they proceed to the third pressing. Having performed the established ritual with the *āditya-graha*, he draws the *āgrayaṇa*. Then he draws the *ṣoḍaśin*: having recited "The Soma has been pressed for thee, O Indra," and "Thou art taken with a base; I take thee, acceptable to Indra for the *ṣoḍaśin*," he wipes it around and sets it down with, "This is thy womb; [I set thee down] acceptable to Indra for the *ṣoḍaśin*. Then he draws the *ukthya*; the ritual procedure is the same up to the *pavamāna* chant.
Having performed the Pavamāna rite, he proceeds with the animal sacrifices in their own place.

For these, there are separate *manotās*, separate deities, separate touchings of the victim, and separate offerings of the omentum-fat (*vasāhoma*). The *vanaspati* offering is common; the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, accompanied by the *praisha* call, is common; the *iḍā* is common; the directions are common, though some say they are separate.

Having performed the ritual with the *dhruva*-like cups in the same manner as for the *dhruva*-like cups, he proceeds with the three *ukthya* rounds: for Indra and Varuṇa, for Indra and Bṛhaspati, and for Indra and Viṣṇu. Then he proceeds with the *ṣoḍaśin* cup. Then, moving forward, he says: "Fill the Hotṛ’s cup after [filling] yours; O Unnetṛ, draw up the King Soma entirely so that nothing remains over. They fill the Hotṛ’s cup first, and the others as they come along.
Having raised the King Soma in every respect, they place him upon the high altar;
thus they place these [cups] belonging to Prajāpati together. Then, having touched water and taken two blades of sacrificial grass, he, restraining his speech, runs westward and introduces the chant;
they chant.
They perform this Bṛhat-sāman on the twenty-one-fold stoma with verses addressed to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa;
"This is the last [verse] for the Hotṛ," they say. After the time of the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu turns away from him, and the Hotṛ calls out to him.
The Adhvaryu calls out in response;
when there is the word "śam," he utters the response.
Having responded to the well-known hymn, he goes forward and lifts up this Hotṛ’s cup;
while they lift up the others in succession, they lift up the cups.
Then, having caused [the Hotṛ] to announce, "O announce! Let there be hearing! Ukthaśas, recite the offering-verse for the Soma-libations!"—at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the oblation;
thus they offer these Prājāpatya cups together.

He offers twice—at the *vaṣaṭ* call and at the subsequent *anu-vaṣaṭ* call—and likewise, they offer their respective *camasa*s twice each. Then, they move westward with the portions for consumption (*bhakṣa*). The formula for consumption at each pressing is: "Of that which has been drunk by Prajāpati... At this point, having poured the residues from these vessels dedicated to Prajāpati into the principal cup, the sacrificer himself consumes them directly; or alternatively, they may pour them all out into the *camasa*s and consume them—this is another option.
Here, whatever portion of the offering to the Maruts is not to be cut off, he presents that to the officiating priests.

Having divided this [portion] into equal shares, they consume it; these three, having invited one another, consume from the *hotṛ*’s cup alone, while the others consume from their respective cups according to their vessels.
With the words "Impel me," they touch themselves; they do not swell the cups;

having consumed the entire contents, they perform the purification (mārjana). Then he issues the call: "O Āgnīdh, bring the embers for the after-offerings; O Upayaṣṭṛ, sit down; O Brahman, we shall set forth; having placed the fuel-stick, O Āgnīdh, cleanse the fires once each. They bring these embers for the after-offerings from the Āgnīdhra shed; the Hotṛ pours them down in front of himself, and the Upayaṣṭṛ sits down with the third portions of the entrails (guda-tṛtīya).
Then, having divided these eleven portions, each containing a third part of the rectum, the *upayaṣṭṛ* priest performs the *upayaja* offerings.
From this point onward, the procedure is the same; the *Vājapeya* sacrifice concludes.
Having sacrificed with the *Vājapeya*, one should perform the *pratyavarohaṇīya Agniṣṭoma*.
The Vājapeya is concluded; the Vājapeya is concluded.
One who is about to sacrifice with the Rājasūya performs the New Moon oblation before the full moon of Phālguna or Caitra, and then undergoes initiation.
He has three initiation days (dīkṣā) and three Upasad days; on the seventh day the Soma-pressing concludes.
This Prāyaṇīya Agniṣṭoma is a Catuṣṭoma sacrifice with a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), ending with the Udavasānīyā offering. Then, on the eighth day, he offers the Ānumata oblation;
at the call for the preparer of the oblation (haviṣkṛt), he releases his speech.

The ritual procedure up to the pouring of the grain is the same; having poured it out, he places eight potsherds on the southern half of the Gārhapatya fire, while the Pratiprasthātṛ places one to the north.
As he hands over the oblation for Nirṛti to be ground, he says: "Crush it, making it fine, both lengthwise and crosswise."

Those [grains] which fall to the east of the *śamyā* peg, the Adhvaryu, having gathered them together and mixed them, cooks as the portion for Anumati. Then those which fall to the west of the *śamyā*, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having gathered them together and mixed them, cooks as the portion for Nirṛti. He takes this cooked portion for Nirṛti, over which butter has been spread beneath and poured upon; a black garment with a black fringe, a firebrand from the innermost part of the house, and a vessel of water—having taken all this, he offers a spoonful in the Gārhapatya fire with the formula, "Vīhi svāhā! May he enjoy the oblation. Then, by way of the south...
Having gone out through the door, they go in that direction where his own-made barren spot or a cleft is clearly visible.

Having kindled this single firebrand and strewn grass around it, he takes hold of it with both thumbs and offers it to Nirṛti, saying: "This is your portion, O Nirṛti; you are possessed of the oblation among the beings; release this man from distress, Svāhā! At this point, he gives away a black garment with a black fringe. Then, having poured out water and cast aside the vessel without looking back, they return; having washed their hands and feet, they come back by the same way they went and offer a spoonful on the Gārhapatya fire, saying: "Svāhā! Homage to him who did this! Then, with the permission of Anumati, he completes the rite and gives a cow as a gift.

Then, on the ninth day, he offers a *caru* oblation to Āditya and gives a choice boon as a gift. Then, on the tenth day, [he offers] a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu and gives a small draft-ox as a gift. Then, on the eleventh day, [he offers] a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Soma and gives gold as a gift. Then, on the twelfth day, [he offers] a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and gives a bull that draws a cart as a gift.

Then, on the thirteenth day, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and curds to Indra; he gives a bull as the sacrificial fee. Then, having passed over the Āgrayaṇa oblations, on the fourteenth day he offers a pap to Sarasvatī and gives a heifer that has not yet calved as the fee. Then, on the fifteenth day, he offers a pap to Sarasvant and gives a steer as the fee.

Now, if the fast-day (upavasatha) happens to fall on the fourteenth day itself, then on that very day he should sacrifice with these two offerings using separate sets of sacrificial grass. On this day, moreover, the calves are driven away for the Viśve Devas.

Having caused the milk for the Vaiśvadeva offering to be milked, he observes the fast according to the procedure for the Sāṃnāyya, or silently. Then, on the following day, having sacrificed with the Vaiśvadeva oblations and having sacrificed with the Paurṇamāsa and Vaimṛdha offerings, he proceeds in the established manner. Then, on the following day, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Sutrāman. A chariot is brought forward, covered with armor, yoked either with mares that are pregnant or with stallions; it is to be driven around, and he gives away a gold ornament (niṣka) as the sacrificial fee. Then, on the following day, [he offers] to Indra... *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.*

On the day before [the full moon], he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni Mucukunda. He gives away a chariot that has not been driven, equipped with a breastplate and yoked either with mares that have not yet brought forth or with horses that are eight years old, along with a smooth necklace;
these two rites are called the *saṃtanī*. Then, on the following day, he proceeds with the two *saṃtanī* offerings themselves.

In this very manner, sacrificing alternately day by day with the two *saṃtanī* offerings, he proceeds for four months—performing at will an *iṣṭi*, at will a *paśubandha*, and at will the *yavāgrayaṇa*. Then, when the four months have elapsed, having sacrificed with the *saṃtanī* offerings, having sacrificed with the *varuṇapraghāsa* oblations, and having sacrificed with the *paurṇamāsa* and *vaimṛdha* sacrifices, he concludes the procedure in the established manner. Then, on the following day, he begins again with the two *saṃtanī* offerings.

In this very manner, sacrificing alternately with the two *saṃtanī* offerings day after day, he passes another four months—sacrificing at will with the *kāmyeṣṭi*, at will with the *paśubandha*, and at will with the *śyāmākāgrayaṇa*. Then, when those four months have elapsed, having sacrificed with the *saṃtanyā iṣṭi*, having sacrificed with the *sākamedha* oblations, and having sacrificed with the *paurṇamāsa* and *vaimṛdha* offerings, he concludes the procedure in the established manner. Then, on the following day, he begins again with the two *saṃtanī* offerings.

In this very manner, performing the *saṃtanī* sacrifices day after day in alternation, he passes four further months—at will with an *iṣṭi*, at will with an animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), and at will with the *vrīhyāgrayaṇa*. Then, when those four months have elapsed, having performed the *saṃtany-eṣṭi*, having sacrificed with the *śunāsīrīya* oblations, and having sacrificed with the *paurṇamāsa* and *vaimṛdha* offerings, he concludes the procedure in the established manner. Then, on the following day, he begins again with the two *saṃtanī* sacrifices.

In this very manner, performing the sacrifice alternately day by day with the two *saṃtanī* offerings, he proceeds for seven days—performing at will the *iṣṭi* and at will the *paśubandha*. Then, on the eighth day, he offers an eight-potherd cake for Agni, a *gāvīdhuka* pap for Rudra, curds for Indra, and a barley pap for Varuṇa.
Having set out the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives a milch-cow that has recently calved as a gift.
Then, at that very moment, he begins the ritual with the five-fold fuel-wood offering (*pañcedhmīya*).

Having drawn out five glowing coals, he places five fuel-sticks upon them: one made of *parṇa* wood in the east, one of *nyagrodha* in the south, one of *aśvattha* in the west, one of *udumbara* in the north, and one of *plakṣa* in the middle; then he sprinkles them with clarified butter, saying: "The gods who sit in the east, led by Agni, slayers of demons—may they protect us, may they help us, homage to them, svāhā! The gods who sit in the south... the gods who sit in the west... the gods who sit in the north... the gods who sit above... and so forth.

Then, with the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick), he sweeps away the embers, saying: "The *rakṣas* is swept away; the *rakṣas* is burnt up; here I burn the *rakṣas* away. Then he makes offerings over them with oblations from the *sruva*-ladle, saying: "To Agni, the slayer of *rakṣases*, svāhā!"—with these five [formulas]. At this point, he gives away a chariot drawn by a *praṣṭi* horse. Then he asks for a *sruva*-ladle made of *parṇa* wood, groats of *apāmārga* plants, a garment to be worn as a lower cloth, a firebrand from the edge of the house, and a vessel of water. Having taken all this, they go out toward the north and proceed in that direction to where there is a natural salt-flat (*iriṇa*) or a cleft in the ground belonging to him.

Having kindled this single firebrand and strewn it all around, he offers groats of *apāmārga* with a ladle made of *parṇa* wood, saying: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I offer the slayer of the Rakṣas; svāhā!"

Saying, "The Rakṣas is slain," he throws the dipping-spoon (sruva) after [the oblation]; saying, "We have struck down the Rakṣas," he stands in worship. Here, he gives whatever belongs to them. Then, having poured out the waters alternately, they cast away the vessel without looking back and return; having washed their hands and feet, they go back by the same way they came. With the fourth [portion] of Indra, he completes the rite. Then, on the ninth day, he offers the previously mentioned Devikā oblations: a pap for Anumati, a pap for Rākā, and a cake on twelve potsherds for Dhātṛ. Having set down the Anvāhārya rice, he gives a heifer as a gift.
