Then, on the tenth day, he offers the subsequent Devikā oblations: a pap for Sinīvālī, a pap for Kuhū, and a cake on twelve potsherds for Dhātṛ. Having set aside the Anvāhārya rice, he gives away a young bull as a gift. Then, on the eleventh day, he proceeds with the Triṣaṃyukta offerings: he offers a cake to Agni and Viṣṇu, a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Viṣṇu, and a cake on three potsherds to Viṣṇu. He gives away a dwarf, draft-worthy bull as a gift. Then, on the twelfth day, [he offers] a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma.

He offers an oblation on eleven potsherds for Indra and Soma, a pap for Soma, and gives a brown horse as a gift; then, on the thirteenth day, he offers a pap for Soma and Pūṣan, a pap for Indra and Pūṣan, and a pap for Pūṣan, and gives a black horse as a gift; then, on the fourteenth day, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara and gives gold as a gift; then, on the fifteenth day, he offers a barley pap for Varuṇa and gives a horse as a gift.
Then, while he is performing the New Moon sacrifice, those possessing ritual treasures (ratnin) attend upon him from the south, facing north, or from behind, facing east.
Among them, once they have settled down, the Brahman priest stands either at the southern or the western end.

Whatever sacrificial utensils there may be, they remain in the house of the Brahman alone. Then, having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods (araṇis), having settled in the house of the Brahman, and having churned out the fires and spread them out, he offers a pap (caru) for Bṛhaspati in the house of the Brahman.
He gives away a white-backed [bull], then, having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods, he departs toward his own fire-places.

As he is departing, he addresses him with the mantra: "May this king, the slayer of Vṛtra, having become king, slay Vṛtra. Then, having settled upon his own fire-places, churned the fires, and distributed the fires, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Sutrāman. Now, on that day, having caused the milk to be milked from a white cow with a white calf and having mixed it together, he sets it aside. Then, on the following day, having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods, having settled upon the house of the Rājanya, churned the fires, and distributed the fires, he gives a bull at the house of the Rājanya as an offering for the cake on eleven potsherds for Indra.
Likewise, having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*), he sets out toward his own fire-places. As he is traveling, he consecrates him with the mantra;

in whichever house he performs the sacrifice, there he consecrates him with the mantra: "This king, the slayer of Vṛtra—having invoked the king, may he slay Vṛtra. Then, having settled at his own fire-places, having churned the fire and spread the fires, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra for the sake of release from distress (*homuc*).

On this very day of his birth, having caused milk to be milked from a white cow with a white calf and having mixed it together, he sets it aside. Then, on the third day, he gives a *caru* offering to Āditya in the house of the chief queen (*mahiṣī*), and a milch-cow that has miscarried in the house of the favorite wife (*vāvātā*).

Then, on the fourth day, he gives a *caru* offering to Bhaga in the house of the favorite wife, and a cow that has miscarried in the house of the discarded wife (*parivṛktī*). Then, on the fifth day, he gives a *caru* offering to Nirṛti in the house of the discarded wife, made of black rice grains split by fingernails.
On the sixth day, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni in the house of the commander of the army; he gives a black ewe as a gift and gold.
On the seventh day, he offers a cake on ten potsherds to Varuṇa in the house of the charioteer;
he gives a castrated bull as a gift. On the eighth day, he offers a cake on seven potsherds to the Maruts in the house of the village headman.

On the ninth day, he gives a speckled cow; at the house of the *kṣattṛ*, he gives a cake on twelve potsherds for Savity, together with a discarded horse. On the tenth day, he gives a cake on two potsherds for the Aśvins at the house of the *saṃgrahītṛ*; he gives two horses of the same age.

On the eleventh day, he gives an oblation of cooked rice for Pūṣan at the house of the *bhāgadugha*; he gives a dark-colored bull. On the twelfth day, he gives an oblation of *gavīdhuka* grain for Rudra at the house of the *akṣāvāpa*.
He offers a mixture of milk;

this day of his is indeed well-known. Having caused the milk to be milked from a white cow with a white calf and having curdled it together, he sets it aside. Then, on the thirteenth day, there is an offering to Mitra and Bṛhaspati; and indeed, it is so stated.

One should separate the husks and the non-husks and the grains from rice cooked in the milk of a white cow with a white calf, using clarified butter that has solidified by itself and been churned by itself, in a four-cornered vessel made of *aśvattha* wood from a branch that has fallen of its own accord. Now it is said:
"The altar is self-made, the sacrificial grass is self-cut, and the fuel is self-prepared";
for this king indeed becomes honored by his own deeds.

He himself prepares the altar; he himself binds together the sacrificial fuel and the grass; he himself fashions a four-cornered vessel from *aśvattha* wood; he himself separates the husked grains and the unhusked grains from a branch that has fallen of its own accord. Now it is said: "Those that are husked are for Bṛhaspati in the milk; those that are unhusked are for Mitra in the clarified butter. Then, having drawn out embers mixed with ash toward the north, he places a new vessel upon them, pours clarified butter across the strainer, and having placed the unhusked grains across the strainer, he covers the portion for Bṛhaspati with it.
He places that [offering] likewise covered within the altar; the ritual procedure is the same up to the *prayāja* offerings.
Having performed five *prayāja* offerings, having stepped northward, and having sprinkled the [oblation] for Bṛhaspati with the residue of the butter, he sprinkles the [oblation] for Mitra.

He proceeds first with the offering to Bṛhaspati and then with that to Mitra. He cuts the portion for the Sviṣṭakṛt from the earlier offering to Bṛhaspati, and then from that to Mitra. He cuts the Iḍā-portion from the earlier offering to Bṛhaspati, and then from that to Mitra. Having set down the Anvāhārya mess, he gives away this very white cow with a white calf.
The oblation to Mitra and Bṛhaspati is concluded;
then, in this very same bright fortnight, he undergoes initiation for the Ukthya consecration sacrifice,
for which there are an unlimited number of initiation days and six Upasad days.

He purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks, "My Soma-pressing will coincide with the new moon day, the day of sacrifice"; for him, it so happens accordingly. Then he performs the Prāyaṇīya offering;
having performed the Prāyaṇīya, he proceeds with the footprint ritual.

Having proceeded with the *pada* rite, having purchased the king [Soma] on a red hide and carried him away, he performs the guest-offering (*ātithya*). Having performed the guest-offering, he then proceeds daily with the *upasad* rites. Then he leads forward the Āhavanīya fire; having led forward the Āhavanīya, he erects the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds upon the chariot-stand. Having erected the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds upon the chariot-stand, he leads forward Agni and Soma. Having led forward Agni and Soma, he raises the sacrificial post according to the procedure for the post; having set up the post provided with a wooden cup (*svaru*), he dedicates the animal victim to Agni and Soma.
Having performed the offering with its omentum in the established manner, he takes up the *vasatīvarī* waters; then he offers the sacrificial cake for the animal victim.
Eight oblations for the *devasū* deities follow it, beginning with "To Agni Gṛhapati";
the procedure for these has been explained as that of the *agni-vidhā*.
The cake-offerings conclude with the *iḍā*-portion;

the animal sacrifice concludes with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, though some say it concludes with the heart-spit. At this point, he hangs these drums in every direction. Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and set aside the milks, they remain in attendance. Thereupon, at the very dead of night, they wake up; having taken the morning clarified butters and brought down King Soma, he begins the *prātaranuvāka* recitation.
When the *prātaranuvāka* has been concluded, he goes toward the waters, emerges from the water, and enters upon the *ukthya* ritual.
The pressing is well-known;
the cups are drawn in the established manner.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the Āśvina cup: having drawn the Āśvina cup and taken two ropes, he approaches the sacrificial post.
Having set up the sacrificial post provided with a *svarkā* (top-ring), he dedicates an animal for Agni;
for that [animal], one for Indra-Agni is to be seized as a secondary victim. Having proceeded with the two omenta in the established manner, they move forward for the morning pressing.
That concludes in a straightforward manner;
they proceed for the midday pressing, and the pressing of the Soma is well-established.

The cups are taken up as prescribed; the ritual procedure is the same up to the offerings for the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). Intending to offer the *dakṣiṇā* oblations, he asks for a vessel of clarified butter together with a *sruva*-ladle and a *sruk*-ladle, and a garment.

At the end of this garment, at the fringe, a cord for a gold ornament (*niṣka*) is tied. Taking all this, he says, "Come, O sacrificer! Having gone around the north of the *Āgnīdhrīya* fire and having gone around the north of the *Sadas*, he stands in front of the hall and hands over these implements to the *Pratiprasthātṛ*. Then he says, "Come, O sacrificer!"
This chariot has been placed upon the chariot-stand at the right hip [of the altar];

he brings it down with the formula: "Thou art the thunderbolt of Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra; through thee may this man slay Vṛtra. Then they turn it toward the interior of the altar while it is still held by the yoke-pole, silently.
Then he causes the horses to bathe in the waters, silently.
Then he yokes the southern team with the formula, "By the command of Mitra and Varuna, the directors, I yoke you for the harnessing of the sacrifice. Then he strokes its back silently.
In the same manner, he yokes the northern team; in the same manner, he attaches the side-horse to its north.
In this very manner, they groomed the backs of those two [horses]; following their yoking, everything down to the smallest atom was prepared; they made the elephants wear additional girth-bands;
they caused loads of clothing to be brought in; and they tied cords for the untying of garments to the fringes of the cloths.
He causes the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) to be brought in groups; then he offers two verses addressed to Sūrya into the Gārhapatya fire;
he offers a verse containing the word "lead" (naya) into the Āgnīdhra fire;
the sacrificial gifts are released along the southern path.

Whatever he gives, he gives beginning with gold; then garments, then yoked cattle, horses, elephants, and men; even at the very end, these chariots do not run in the race as if they were already given to another, for he gives his own chariot to the Adhvaryu by means of his mind alone.
With his mind, he assigns the four-footed field to Brahmā;
having assigned it with his mind, he proceeds with three Marutvatīya offerings as the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās).
The Nārāśaṃsa cups, having been replenished, sit down below the rear support of the southern Havirdhāna cart for Mahendra.

Then he asks for a trough made of cane, sixteen Vāyavya cups, and those waters of his previously collected from the quarters for the *Ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice; they lie placed behind the axle and in front of the support-pole of the southern *havirdhāna* cart.
Of these, the flowing waters are in the eastern half, and the waters of the Sarasvatī are in the western half.

He offers oblations into the flowing waters with the verse: "O divine Waters, you who are honey-sweet, grasping the strength-bestowing, gathered for the Rājasūya; you with which they consecrated Mitra and Varuṇa, and with which they led Indra beyond his enemies—granters of kingship, grant us kingship, Svāhā! He takes [the water] with a vessel made of *parṇa* wood. With the formula, "Granters of kingship, grant kingship to so-and-so, the son of so-and-so, the grandson of so-and-so," he takes water from a male-named well or from the ocean with the formula, "Thou art the lord of waters."

With the formula "The wave of the bull," [he takes] those from a river; with "Thou art Vṛṣasena," those from a pond; with "Thou dwellest in the fold," those from a well; with "Thou art the vigor of the Maruts," those from a pool;
with "Thou art sun-bright," those that are visible from afar;
with "Thou art sun-skinned," those that rain during sunshine; with "Thou art the giver of water," hailstones; and with "Thou art the lowing one," those that are frothy.

"Thou art the Śakvarī; thou art the womb of the cow. "Thou art the sustainer of the universe; thou art the milk. "Thou art the sustainer of the people; thou art the curd. "Thou art the brilliance of Agni; thou art the clarified butter. "Thou art the essence of the waters and the plants; thou art the honey. Then he offers the Sarasvatī oblations: "The divine waters, rich in sweetness, have been taken up—full of vigor, prepared for the Rājasūya. With them they consecrated Mitra and Varuṇa, and with them they led Indra beyond his enemies. Thou art the givers of kingship; grant us the kingdom, Svāhā!"

He takes [the water] with a vessel made of *parṇa* wood, saying: "You are the givers of sovereignty; grant sovereignty to so-and-so, the son of so-and-so, the grandson of so-and-so. Then he pours them together into a wooden tub (*droṇakalaśa*) made of cane, saying: "O divine waters, unite with the honeyed ones, you who are honeyed, winning great splendor for the Kṣatriya. Then he places them between the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths of the Hotṛ and the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, saying: "Sit down, unassailable and full of vigor, bestowing great splendor upon the Kṣatriya. At this point—
Those stalks of the *adhvaryu* that are usable they carry to the dwelling; then those that are unusable they throw into the water.
They set aside the *sārasvata* waters for the *daśapeya*, which have not yet been offered as libations.

Then, remaining right there, he asks for a stalk of *darbha* grass, a piece of gold weighing a hundred *mānas*, four vessels made of different kinds of wood, a linen garment and a turban, one hundred and one tufts of *darbha* grass, curds, an *udumbara* branch, young grass shoots, a bow, and arrows.

He ties a hundred-māna weight of gold onto a stalk of *darbha* grass with the formula: "Thou art uncrushed, the bond of speech, born of heat. Then he places it into a wooden trough (*droṇakalaśa*) made of *veta* wood with the formula: "Thou art the gift of Soma. He purifies [the water] with the gold using the formula:

"The bright ones, I purify you with the bright; the radiant ones with the radiant; the immortal ones with the immortal; Svāhā! For the Rājasūya, for those who are gathered. He draws [the water] with a cup made of *parṇa* wood, with the verse: "These glorious, vigorous, uncrushed, active ones, dwelling in their abodes—Varuṇa has made his seat among them, the child of the waters within the most motherly of waters."

Having taken it with this same formula, he hands it to the Brahman seated in the east; having taken it with this same formula, he hands it to the Rājanya seated in the south with a staff of Udumbara wood; having taken it with this same formula, he hands it to the Vaiśya seated in the west with a staff of Aśvattha wood; having taken it with this same formula, he hands it to the Janya seated in the north with a staff of Nyagrodha wood. Then, having carried that *prareka* (filter) to the Āgnīdhra and covered it, he sets it down in a known place. Then he causes the sacrificer to put on a *tārpya* garment with the formula, "Thou art the caul of the Kṣatra"; he fastens the *tārpya* with the formula, "Thou art the womb of the Kṣatra."

As if drawing the navel toward the crown of the head, he turns it around; then he purifies him with one hundred and one tufts of *darbha* grass using the regular purification formula. Then, wiping him, he causes him to eat curd, an *udumbara* fruit, and young grass. Then he leads him eastward with the *āvida* formulas: "Agni, the lord of the house, has found us," and so on, with seven verses according to their meter.
Then, as he stands in the sacrificer’s station, he addresses those for whom he is the chief: "O Bharatas, this is your king!"

"May Soma be the king of us Brāhmaṇas," the others reply. Then he hands him a bow with the formula: "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra; with thee may this man slay Vṛtra. With the words, "Be thou a repeller of enemies," the other receives the arrows with the formula: "Repel my enemies from behind, repel me from the side, protect me from all destructive powers. Then, with the Triṣṭubh verse, "The two golden-hued ones at the dawning of the Dawns," he raises his arms. Then he instructs him by means of the mind alone.

"Proceed through the quarters; soar upward with the mind," he says. Then he makes him recite: "Stand firm on the fuel-stick; stand firm on the fierce one; stand firm on the Virāj; stand firm on the northern quarter; stand firm on the upward direction. Then, standing right there, he causes [the offerings] to be brought: a cake on twenty-one potsherds for the Maruts and a curd-mixture (āmikṣā) for the Viśve Devas. Of that [cake], the middle potsherds are placed with the group of verses to be recited in the forest (araṇye'nuvākyo gaṇaḥ), while the others are placed with the two groups [of verses] from the Rājasūya.

He proceeds with those two [oblations]: "Recite for the Maruts," "Sacrifice to the Maruts"; "Recite for the Viśvedevas," "Sacrifice to the Viśvedevas. Having thus covered these two oblations for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, he sets them aside in their designated places. Then he asks for a tiger skin, a gold and silver plate, boar-skin sandals, lead, and red iron.

A eunuch sits to the south, and then, prior to the consecration, he offers six oblations for the sake of the quarters, saying: "To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! Then, on the sacrificer’s seat, he spreads out a tiger skin with its neck to the east and its hair upwards, saying: "Thou art the splendor of Soma; may my splendor be like thine. Having seated the sacrificer there facing eastward, he places gold and silver plates upon him, saying: "Thou art immortality; protect me from death! He places the silver plate underneath, saying: "Protect me from lightning! and the gold plate above, which is perforated by a hundred holes.
Then, with the verse, "Now the biting serpents are bound," he pierces a eunuch sitting to the south with lead;
with his left foot he casts away an object of red iron, saying, "The head of Namuci is cast away. At this point, they collect the consecration waters for him, and he gazes upon them.

"May King Soma, Varuṇa, and the gods who are the impellers of dharma, may they inspire your speech; may they inspire your breath; may they inspire your sight; may they inspire your hearing. Then, taking the vessel of the Brahman, the Adhvaryu alone pours the water over him while muttering the sacrificial formula, while the others pour as well: "With the splendor of Soma, with the brilliance of Agni, with the luster of Sūrya, with the power of Indra, with the heroism of Mitra and Varuṇa, with the force of the Maruts—[I sprinkle] you, the chief of the ruling powers."

"The Lord of the Kṣatras casts forth the drink of heaven, O Sūrya; then the upward streams are wiped away, and they flow together from below toward the north, moving along the bottomless Ahi. Like ships on the back of the bull-like mountain, they move about, self-pouring as they go."

Here, having poured together the remnants of these consecrations into the principal vessel, he goes to the house of the deputy (pratihita). Then, while the deputy and the queen consort (mahiṣī) hold on to him from behind, he offers an oblation with the verse: "O Prajāpati, none other than you... At this point, the deputy gives a gift to him. Then, handing the vessel to the deputy, he says: "This vessel is your inheritance; when I consecrate you, may it be yours. Then, returning by the same way he came, he offers the *prareka* oblation in the Āgnīdhra fire with the verse: "O Rudra, that which is yours..."
"O buyer, you are the supreme name; for him you are offered, you are sacrificed to, svāhā!"—at this point, he hands him the bow, if it has not already been handed over previously.

When he has been wiped clean, they shout out together: "This one is being consecrated—the descendant of such-and-such, the son of such-and-such, the grandson of such-and-such, the great-grandson of such-and-such, by means of the Rājasūya! Then, with the words "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ," he releases his speech;
he wipes his face with two [mantras].

He steps the *gāyatrān* and *viṣṇukrama* steps; then, after the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), he offers the six *pārtha* oblations with the formulas, "To Indra, svāhā! To Ghoṣa, svāhā! and so forth. He offers the twelve *bhūtānām aveṣṭi* oblations with the formulas, "To Earth, svāhā! To Atmosphere, svāhā! and so forth. At this point, he performs the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering for these two oblations. Then, having covered them, he sets them down in their known places. Then he puts on two boar-skin sandals with the formula, "Thou art the wrath of cattle," on the right foot, and with "May my wrath be like thine," on the left. Then he touches this earth with the formula, "Homage to Mother Earth."

He lowers his right foot onto it with the formula, "May I not harm mother Earth," and his left foot with, "May mother Earth not harm me. Then, between the *cātvāla* pit and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), he goes out toward the north with the formulas, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s stride; thou art Viṣṇu’s step; thou art Viṣṇu’s wide-stride. To the north, these yoked chariots stand ready; as soon as he sees them, the attendant stops. Then, taking the attendant’s bow and stringing it, he mounts the chariot with the formula, "In the impulse of the Maruts may I conquer. With the words, "The mind has reached its goal," he leans over the pole of the chariot.
At that very moment, the deputy stands by him; [the Brāhmaṇa says]: "With the Triṣṭubh verse, 'O much-invoked one, you have overcome the enemies,' he takes hold [of the king].

Then, handing the bow to the deputy, he says: "This Rājanya has been stationed at thirty-six throws of the *śamyā* with a prize of a thousand [cows]; shoot an arrow at him and pierce him through; having conquered him, lead him away by the southern path."
"The nobleman alone is instructed; the prince shall shoot the arrow and he will miss you. Therefore, let him wipe [the cup] with the *uttaravargya* formula and hand over the arrow.

He does so. Then he says, "Approach, O sacrificer! I shall draw the *māhendra* cup. While the sacrificer has taken hold of him, he draws the *māhendra* cup, reciting: "Great is Indra who by his might... and continuing, "Thou art taken with a base; I take thee, acceptable to Mahendra."

Having wiped it clean, he sets it down with the formula, "This is thy womb; for Mahendra thee! Then he asks for these beads—a silver one, a figwood one, and a golden one—and they are strung upon separate threads.

Having tied them to the middle beam of the northern *havirdhāna* cart, and having touched water and taken two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he, restraining his speech, runs westward and introduces the chant.

When the *māhendra* cup is being praised and the *sāman* has been chanted, he issues the formal command: "O race-riders, run the race! Beat the drums! Pressers, press the soma! Agnīdh, pour out the milk-mixture! Make the mortar resound! Pratiprasthātṛ, offer the cake on one potsherd to Varuṇa! Inquire about the *saumya* offering!
They act according to these commands.
The runners who have set out with their spears strike the drums; voices cry out together, and he consecrates those voices as they resound.
The sounds subside;
"This is the best for the Hotṛ's offering," they say. At the time of the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu turns away, and the Hotṛ calls out to him;
the Adhvaryu responds with a call.
When there is the *śaṃ* [utterance],
he responds; having responded with the well-known hymn (*uktha*), he goes forward and lifts up that cup for Mahendra.
While raising the others, they raise the *nārāśaṃsa* cups;
then he causes the announcement: "Ośrāvaya! Astu śrauṣaṭ! O reciter of the hymn (*ukthashā*), offer the oblation of Soma!"
He offers twice, at the *vaṣaṭ* call and at the subsequent *anu-vaṣaṭ* call;
likewise, they shake the *nārāśaṃsa* cups twice each time.

When the *māhendra* cup has been offered twice and remains, they approach with the chariots. Having seen the chariots that have arrived, he mutters: "May I be united with power and vigor; may power and vigor be united with me."
Then he goes out northward between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*. To the north, these chariots stand with their horses harnessed;

as soon as he sees them, the attendant stands by. Then, taking the attendant's bow and stringing it, he mounts the chariot, saying, "May I conquer at the impulse of the Maruts. He leans against the pole of the chariot, saying, "The mind has reached its goal," while the attendant immediately follows behind him, saying, "O much-invoked one, you have overcome the enemies."
"He takes hold with a *triṣṭubh* verse," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Then, handing the bow to the deputy, he says: "This bow is your inheritance; when I consecrate you, let it be yours. Then, returning by the same way he came, having passed between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, and having caused him to enter the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door, he turns the chariot facing eastward and stands still.
Thereupon, he asks for these three amulets: one of silver, one of udumbara wood, and one of gold.

He fastens a silver [ring] on his left hand with the formula, "This is life; bestow life upon me"; a [ring] of Udumbara wood on his right hand with, "This is vigor; bestow vigor upon me"; and a golden one on his right hand with, "Thou art a yoke-mate, thou art splendor; bestow splendor upon me. At this point, he brings up for him the *āmikṣā* (curdled milk). He lowers his right hand into it with the formula, "Thou art Mitra," and his left hand with, "Thou art Varuṇa.
Then he touches it with, "May I be united with all the gods," and having covered it, he sets it down in a known place.
He strings these jewels onto a single cord, placing the one made of *udumbara* wood in the middle.
Having fastened them to his neck, he returns by the same way he came, turns the chariot eastward in front of the *Āgnīdhra* shed, and stands there.

Then, at the *Āgnīdhra*, he offers the "chariot-unloosing" oblations with four spoonfuls, saying: "To Agni Gṛhapati, svāhā! and so forth. Now, prior to this, the chariot-stand has already been brought forward in front of the *Āgnīdhra*, with its pole facing east and its yoke prepared.
Upon that chariot-stand, together with the charioteer, he places the chariot;
thus he separates him from the heavenly world.
He places it with the verse, "He is the swan, dwelling in purity... and so forth.
"By means of the Brahman he brings it down; by means of the Brahman he places it; he places it with an Aticchandas [verse]," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, for him, a shed has already been prepared to the rear of the Āgnīdhra fire, measuring four or eight steps.
In its center, he erects a throne made of Udumbara wood with the formula: "Thou art the navel of the Kṣatra."

Upon it, he spreads a northern woolen cloth with its fleece upward, saying, "Thou art the womb of the Kṣatra. Then he sits down upon it; as he is sitting down, [the Adhvaryu] addresses him: "Sit on what is pleasant; sit on what is comfortable; do not harm me.
The other replies, "Do not harm me. He then consecrates the one who has sat down, saying, "Varuṇa, whose law is firm, has sat down in his dwellings for sovereign rule, he the wise one.
Then the officiating priests sit down around him.
The Adhvaryu sits in the east, the Brahman in the south, the Hotṛ in the west, and the Udgātṛ in the north;
then the Ratnins [sit] facing either east or north,
and he addresses the Adhvaryu.
"O King, you are the Brahman," says the Adhvaryu; "You are Savitṛ of true impulse," [says] the Brahman. "O King, you are the Brahman," he says; "You are Indra of true vigor," [says] the Brahman.

"O King, you are the Brahman," he says to the Hotṛ; "You are Mitra, the kindly one," says the Hotṛ to the Brahman. "O King, you are the Brahman," he says to the Udgātṛ; "You are Varuṇa, whose law is truth," says the Udgātṛ to the Brahman.
"O King, you are Suśloka," he says to the Kṣattṛ; "You are Suśloka," says the Kṣattṛ.

"To the gatherer he says, 'O King, you are Sumaṅgala! To the gatherer he replies, 'O King, I am Satyarāja. To the distributor of portions he says, 'O King, you are Satyarāja! To the distributor of portions he replies, 'O King, I am Sumaṅgala.
Having approached seven persons of auspicious names, he hands him the wooden sword (sphya), saying: 'You are the thunderbolt of Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra; with it, may you prosper for me.'"

"May I succeed through that," says the other, and he hands it over to the charioteer, to the head of the charioteers, to the kinsman, to the head of the kinsmen, to the charioteer of the chariot-pole, and finally to the two, Akṣāvāpa and Govyaccha.

Then, having cleared the gaming board from the center, those two pour out three fifties of golden dice; then, having set aside five dice for himself, he gives them to him, saying, "This king has conquered the quarters."

At that very moment, he casts those [dice] onto the dice-board. Then they announce this rice-porridge: "The two *nānāṃśinas*, the Brahman and the sacrificer; the two *samānaṃśinas*, the charioteer and the village headman; the two *samānaṃśinas*, the attendant and the chariot-driver.
Now, whoever is like one skilled at dice, having sat upon the king's seat and broken off four hundred dice, says, "The king has won! (udbhinnaṃ rājñaḥ).
Having treated them as if they were slightly on all sides, he says, "It is done for the Brahmin. Then they announce this rice:
"The Brahmin and the sacrificer are sharers in what is common; the charioteer and the village headman are sharers in what is distinct; the steward and the collector are sharers in what is distinct.
He who is defeated, for him the steward cooks this [rice] in his own household."
While this rice is being cooked, the Hotṛ priest causes the Śunaḥśepa narrative to be recited while seated upon a golden cushion;
the Adhvaryu priest responds to him while seated upon a golden mat, saying:
"Oṃ, Hotṛ! So be it, Hotṛ! Truly, Hotṛ! We have succeeded, Hotṛ!"
If the Hotṛ does not recite, and another person recites the *hotrāśaṃsī*, the Pratiprasthātṛ responds for him;
"it becomes more than a hundred," so says the Brāhmaṇa. When this rice-porridge is cooked, he then draws it out all at once and offers it to the Brahman.
Therefore, he gives these very jewels: a hundred [cows], a carriage, and a four-footed animal to the Brahman;
then he gives a hundred [cows], a carriage, and a golden pillow to the Hotṛ; and he gives a hundred [cows] and a carriage to the Udgātṛ.

Then he gives to the Adhvaryu a hundred oxen, a carriage with a by-path, a self-yoked chariot, fifty golden dice, and a golden mat; having divided this thousandfold wealth into four parts, they give it to them right here. Then they bring him to the Sadas on this very seat, or they go there together, and these goblets follow after him. At this point, he invokes the *iḍā* for these two oblations. The Hotṛ and the Adhvaryu both consume the *māhendra* portion when the *iḍā* has been invoked. With the *narāśaṃsa*-portioned drink, these three—the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, and the Pratiprasthātṛ—consume the *hotṛ-camasa* after having invited one another.
With the words, "Impel the cups according to their respective vessels; impel me," they touch themselves,
but they do not cause the cups to swell.
The *sarvabhakṣas* purify themselves, saying "O Indra, O Indra," and thus he proceeds with the three *ukthya* rounds;
the midday pressing is concluded. They proceed to the third pressing. Having performed the rite with the *āditya-graha* in the established manner, he draws the *āgrayaṇa* cup.
Then he draws the Ukthya cup;
the ritual procedure is the same up to the Pavamāna laud.
Having performed the rite with the Pavamāna, he proceeds with the two animals in their own place.

Their two *manotā*-invocations are separate, their two deities are separate, their two touchings [of the victim] are separate, their two *vasā-homa* offerings are separate; their *vanaspati* offering is common, as is the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering accompanied by the *praisha*, the *iḍā* is common, and the directions are common—though some say the directions are separate.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the *avabhṛtha*. Then, at this *avabhṛtha*, they take up two leather-winged sandals;
having washed them, he steps out with the two leather-winged sandals made of boar-skin.
He offers at the edge of the waters with the formula, "Svāhā to the grandson of the waters!
At the midpoint, he offers upon a clump of darbha grass with the formula, "Svāhā to the grandson of strength!
Having returned, he offers on the gārhapatya fire with the formula, "Svāhā to Agni, the lord of the house!"

The *avabhṛtha* rite is well-known. Having performed the *udayanīyā* sacrifice, he dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa. Having proceeded with its omentum in the established manner, he neither shaves his beard nor his hair;
thus concludes this *ukthya* consecration sacrifice (*abhiṣecanīya*), which has thirty-four *pavamāna* stotras, a sacrificial fee of a thousand, and ends with the *udavānīyā* rite.
Now, for him, a hall has already been constructed on a chosen sacrificial ground (devayajana) at a distance of seven throws of the yoke-pin (śamyā);
right there he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and gives gold as the sacrificial gift.
Having moved away at the placement of the yoke-pins, he dwells there; he offers a pap of cooked rice to Sarasvatī and gives a heifer as a gift.
Having moved away at the second placement of the yoke-pins, he dwells there.
He gives a cake on twelve potsherds dedicated to Savitṛ, being one that has been trampled;
having moved away at the third throw of the yoke-pin, he dwells there.
He gives a dark-colored *caru* to Pūṣan;
having moved away at the fourth throw of the yoke-pin, he dwells there and offers a white-backed *caru* to Bṛhaspati.
On the fifth day, having moved away at the placing of the yoke-pin, he dwells; he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and gives a bull as a gift.
On the sixth day, having moved away at the placing of the yoke-pin, he dwells.
He gives a cake on ten potsherds to Varuṇa and presents a large castrated bull. Then, on the seventh day, he settles in the sacrificial hall;

on this very day he undergoes initiation. Now it is said: "They initiate him immediately, they purchase the Soma immediately, and they present him with a lotus-garland. Having brought him from the bathing-place and purified him, and having brought forward the one wearing the lotus-garland, he performs the initiatory offering (*dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi*).
When that offering has been completed, he neither closes his fists nor restrains his speech.
They set aside for him this remnant of the oblation as his portion of the vow; then he performs the Prāyaṇīyā offering,
and having released his speech with the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), they give him here this remnant of the oblation as his portion of the vow.

Then he performs the Prāyaṇīya offering; having performed the Prāyaṇīya, he proceeds with the footprint (pada); having proceeded with the footprint, he purchases the King Soma with ten castrated young bulls and carries him away. He prepares the Ātithya offering; having performed the Ātithya, before the Upasads, he offers a pap of cooked rice to Soma and gives a brown horse as a gift. Then, between the two middle Upasads, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Tvaṣṭṛ and gives a white-spotted horse as a gift. Then, after the [last] Upasads, he offers a cake on three potsherds to Viṣṇu and gives a dwarf horse as a gift. Then he leads forward the Āhavanīya fire.

Having led forward the Āhavanīya fire, he erects the Sadas and the Havirdhāna sheds; having erected the Sadas and the Havirdhāna sheds, he leads forward Agni and Soma; having led forward Agni and Soma, he raises the sacrificial post according to the procedure for the post, and having set up the post provided with a wooden chip (svaru), he dedicates the animal victim to Agni and Soma.

Having performed the ritual with its well-known omentum, he takes up the *sārasvata* *vasatīvarī* waters; then he offers the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*). The animal-cake concludes with the *iḍā* offering, the animal sacrifice concludes with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, or according to some, with the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*). Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and set aside the milks, they remain in attendance. Thereupon, at the very dead of night, they awaken; having taken the morning clarified butters and brought down King Soma, he begins the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*).

When the morning litany (prātaranuvāka) has been concluded, he goes toward the waters; he emerges from the waters and enters upon the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; the pressing of the Soma is performed in the established manner.
The cups are taken in the established manner;
the ritual procedure is the same up to the Āśvina cup. Having taken the Āśvina cup and having taken two ropes, he approaches the sacrificial post.
Having set aside the sacrificial post provided with a wooden chip (svaru), he dedicates the animal victim to Agni.
For that [sacrifice], a hornless goat dedicated to Prajāpati is to be offered.
Having proceeded with the two omenta of those [animals] in the established manner, they move forward for the morning pressing.
At the eastern door, the charioteer and the village headman stand ready; at the western door, the attendant and the collector of taxes.

As he moves forward and asks, "Who is your mother? Who is your maternal grandmother? they let him pass if he can trace his lineage back ten generations; but if he cannot trace it, they drive him away with a long bamboo pole.

He who says, "A Vaiśya woman is my mother; Sāvitrī [is my mother]," they release him, saying, "The people shall be the protectors of his marriages. Here, ten by ten, they agree upon the cup. The morning pressing concludes in a straightforward manner. They proceed to the midday pressing; the pressing of the Soma is well-established.
The cups are taken as prescribed;

the ritual procedure up to the offerings for the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) is the same. Having offered the *dakṣiṇā* oblations, he gives two mirrors to the Adhvaryu, a garland to the Udgātṛ, a gold plate to the Hotṛ, a horse to the Prastotṛ and Pratihartṛ, twelve heifers to the Brahman, a barren cow to the Maitrāvaruṇa, a bull to the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, two garments to the Neṣṭṛ and Potṛ, a single-horse chariot laden with barley to the Acchāvāka, and an ox to the Agnīdh.
The Hotṛ is a descendant of Bhṛgu.
The Śrāyantīya is the Brahman’s chant; the Vāravantīya is the Agniṣṭoma chant.
The midday pressing concludes in the regular manner;
they proceed to the third pressing.
Having performed the rite with the Āditya cup as prescribed, he draws the Āgrayaṇa;
the ritual procedure up to the Pavamāna laud is the same.
Having performed the rite with the Pavamāna laud, he proceeds with the two animal offerings in their own place.

For these two, there are separate mental intentions (*manotā*), separate deities, separate touchings, and separate *vasā-homa* offerings; the *vanaspati* offering is common, as is the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering accompanied by the *praisha*, the *iḍā* portion, and the directions. Regarding the directions, some say they are separate, while others say they are common.
The ritual procedure up to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) is standard; having performed the *udayanīya* sacrifice, he dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa.
Having performed the rite with its well-known omentum, he shaves only his beard at the southern edge of the altar, not his hair;
this Agniṣṭoma, the Daśapeya, is completed as a seventeen-fold sacrifice with a thousand-fold sacrificial fee, ending with the Udavasānīyā offering.

Then he performs the Diśām Aveṣṭi sacrifice consisting of five oblations: he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra, a pap to the Viśve Devas, curdled milk (āmikṣā) to Mitra and Varuṇa, and a pap to Bṛhaspati. Now, it is indeed said:

Having offered each oblation, he pours clarified butter over the offering to Bṛhaspati; thus, having offered each oblation, he pours clarified butter over the offering to Bṛhaspati. Having placed the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives these prescribed sacrificial fees. Then he performs the animal sacrifice with two animals: he immolates a pregnant, long-uddered ewe for Āditi, and a spotted, four-year-old cow that is pregnant for the Maruts. The one for Āditi is without a fetus, while the one for the Maruts is pregnant. He proceeds first with the offering to Āditi and then with the one to the Maruts. He causes the call for the *āśrāvaṇa* to be made loudly for the offering to Āditi, but in a low voice for the offering to the Maruts.

It concludes just as the animal sacrifice for two animals does; then he performs the sacrifice with the oblations of the Sātyadūtas. He offers a cake on twelve potsherds to the Aśvins and Pūṣan, a pap to Sarasvatī of true speech, and a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ of true impulse.
Having set down the Anvāhārya rice, he gives away a bow with three arrows and a dried leather water-bag;
he sends this off to rival kings.

He knows him who accepts [the gift], thinking, "He is my friend," and he knows him who does not accept it, thinking, "He is my enemy. Then, having sacrificed with the former *prayuja* oblations, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, a pap to Soma, a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ, a pap to Bṛhaspati, a cake on eight potsherds to Tvaṣṭṛ, and a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara.

Having set out the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives as a sacrificial fee the right-hand ox that draws the chariot-stand. Then, having performed the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha sacrifices, he sacrifices with the latter *prayuja* oblations.
He offers a *caru* for Sarasvatī, a *caru* for Pūṣan, a *caru* for Mitra, a *caru* for Varuṇa, a *caru* for Kṣetrapati, and a *caru* for Āditya.
Having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives away the northern ox of the chariot-pole.
At this point, he observes the vow for twelve days and anoints himself.

He does not wash his teeth, he does not anoint himself, he does not rejoice, and he does not fight when battle has arrived; or rather, the sacrificer undertakes the vow of consuming only the remnants of the *agnihotra*.
His wife brings the cooked food; then, on this very site where the gods have already been pleased, three halls have been constructed for him.
Having settled in the southern hall, kindled the fires, and spread them out, he undergoes initiation for the Atirātra sacrifice known as the Keśavapanīya, which features reversed Stomas.
Its period of initiation is unlimited, and there are twelve Upasad days.
He purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks, "My Soma-pressing will coincide with the day of sacrifice on the full moon";
for him, it happens exactly so.

Having proceeded through the established ritual up to the Upavasatha day, and having carried around the Vasatīvarī waters and set aside the milks, they observe the fast. Then, at the very dead of night, they awaken.
Having taken up the morning libations and brought the King Soma down, he begins the Prātaranuvāka;
when the Prātaranuvāka is concluded, he goes toward the waters and enters upon the Atirātra sacrifice; the pressing of the Soma is performed in the established manner.
The planets are taken up in the established manner;
the ritual procedure is the same up to the *avabhṛtha* bath;
the *avabhṛtha* is performed in the established manner; having sacrificed with the *udayanīya* offering, he dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa.

Having performed the rite with the omentum of that [cow] in the prescribed manner, he has his hair shaved at whatever spots on the southern edge of the altar there may be. This concludes the *pratīcīnastoma* *keśavapanīya* *atirātra* sacrifice, which involves a thousand sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) and ends with the *udavasānīyā* offering. Then, having settled in the middle hall, churned the fire, and spread out the sacred fires, he undergoes initiation for the *vyuṣṭi*-day *dvirātra* sacrifice.
For this, the number of initiation days is unlimited, and there are twelve *upasads*.

He purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks: "Since this is for me a two-night sacrifice, the first day shall coincide with the Upavasatha day of the new moon, and the second day on the following day. Thus concludes the Vyūṣṭi-dvirātra. Then, having settled in the northern hall, churned the fire, and spread out the fires, he undergoes initiation for the Udayanīya Agniṣṭoma.
For that sacrifice, there are three initiation days and three Upasad days; the Soma-pressing takes place on the seventh day.

This Udayanīya Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, consisting of four stomas and involving a thousand-fold sacrificial fee, concludes with the Udavasānīyā offering; then he sacrifices with the Devikā oblations, then he sacrifices with the Traidhātavīyā, and then he sacrifices with the Sautrāmaṇī.
Thus the Rājasūya is completed; the Rājasūya is completed in six and a half months; the Rājasūya is completed.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the *iṣṭis*.

For them, the procedure (*tantra*) pertaining to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dārśapaurṇamāsika*) is prescribed once and for all; the preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) is that of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

All [the *iṣṭis*] are first, all are middle, and all are last. One should offer them at the proper time on the parvan day. Those whose place is specified, and those whose place is not specified—those auspicious days (*puṇyāha*) of the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*) are the points of access (*tīrtha*). Those which are non-urgent *iṣṭis*, and those which are urgent *iṣṭis*, have times determined by specific circumstances.

Just as it has been stated that the *agnyanvādhāna* (the adding of fuel to the fires) is performed for the [sacrifices] beginning with the *abhyuddhṛta*, the *abhyudita*, the *abhinimrukta*, and the *avijāta*, so too should one constantly perform the undertaking of the vow (*vratopāyana*) until its completion, following the sacrificer’s duties, except for the deities of the *āvāpa* (insertion). Among those [deities],
those which have secondary names (*sopanāman*) are recited in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), while the others are recited loudly (*uccaiḥ*), precisely because of their designation.

One should know that there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses; as for this, one should make two verses of Manu the *dhāyyās*, two *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* verses the *dhāyyās*, and two *triṣṭubh* verses the *saṃyājyās*.

The two *ājyabhāga* offerings should have the *vārtraghna* verses in the first fortnight and the *vṛdhanvat* verses in the second fortnight—thus says Aupamanyava. As for those oblations which are separated by either a specific desire or a sacrificial fee, one should know that they indeed require separate layers of sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

By direct injunction alone, the *barhis* grass is common [to all offerings] even when separated by the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), as in the case of the *Diśām Aveṣṭi*. One follows the *iṣṭis* and the *upāṃśuyāja*. For whichever deity the oblation is intended, the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses belong to that same deity. The *upahoma*s are performed before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; those for which specific *upahoma*s have been mentioned, or for which no such *upahoma*s are stated, have garments as their sacrificial fees. These are the optional *iṣṭis*. Those for which no fee is specifically prescribed have a cow as the fee. The animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) has a cow as its fee, and the regular *anvāhārya* rice is also included. Thus, these *iṣṭis* have been explained.
Now, indeed, there is this [injunction]: "One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni.

For that [offering], these two are the verses: "Both of you, O Indra and Agni... and "I have heard of you two, O Indra and Agni... One who is contending for land or among his kinsmen should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni;

for that, these two are the verses: "O Indra and Agni, the luminous realms of heaven... and "He pierced Vṛtra... One who is about to set out for battle should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni.

For this [offering], these two [verses] belong to it: "O Indra and Agni, the ninety forts... and "The pure hymn of praise... One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni after having won a battle;

for this [offering], these two [verses] belong to it: "Both of you, O Indra and Agni... and "I have heard of you both, O Indra and Agni... One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni when about to go among the people;
for this [offering], these two [verses] belong to it: "O Indra and Agni, the luminous realms of heaven... and "He pierced Vṛtra..."
"One should subsequently offer a pap for Pūṣan";
these two [verses] belong to it: "O Lord of the Path, we [follow] thee on every path," and "One should offer a pap for Kṣetrapati when one has come among the people."
For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "We [are yours], O Lord of the Field" and "O Lord of the Field. One should subsequently offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra-Agni;
for this [offering], these two [verses] are used, which belong to those who have won a battle.

"One who, being a regular performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, should omit either the new moon day or the full moon day, shall offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt. Intending to perform this sacrifice, he procures sacrificial grass from near a path and a draft-ox; for this [sacrifice], these two [verses] are used: "O Agni, lead us to the gods... Having placed the *Anvāhārya* rice, he gives away the draft-ox. "One who, having established the sacred fires, should act as if violating his vow, shall offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati."

Regarding this, these two verses occur: "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows; when we violate our vows... One for whom the *rakṣas* demons might pursue [his sacrifice] should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Rakṣohan.

Now it is said: "He should offer at the onset of night; he should cause him to sacrifice within an enclosed space. Having risen during the deep of night, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Rakṣohan.
He causes the sacrifice to be performed in an enclosed space.
He recites fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses from this section beginning with "Make thy strength wide-spreading like a net" (*kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ prasitiṃ na pṛthvīm*), proceeding straight through them;

for him, these two [verses] occur: "The Rakṣas-slayer" (*rakṣohaṇam*) and "With light" (*vi jyotiṣā*). Then, before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers an oblation with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), [reciting]: "And let the roaring ones be in heaven of Agni" (*uta svānāso divi ṣantu agneḥ*).

"One performing sorcery should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni accompanied by Rudra"—for this [offering], these two are the verses: "O Agni, you who are Rudra... and "To you, the King... One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Surabhimat (the Fragrant) if one's cattle or men have died, or if one is afraid;

for this [offering], these two are the verses: "Agni is the Hotṛ... and "The virtuous path... One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kṣāmavat (the Earth-possessing) when a battle is joined.
For him, these two [verses] occur: "Agni has cried out for you" (*akrandad agnis tve vasūni*) and "Now indeed it occurs": "Verily, he overcomes those whose earlier members die in succession;
for the human offering is most dear to him. He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kṣāmavat."

For this [offering], these two [verses] are used; moreover, there is also [the following]: "He indeed approaches the house of that man whose house they consecrate with fire; he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kṣāmavat"—for this [offering], these two [verses] are used. Furthermore, there is also [the following]: "He whose desire does not come to pass should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kāma."

For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "To you, O most Aṅgiras-like... and "May we attain that desire, O Agni..."; one who is contending for land or among kinsmen should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Yaviṣṭha; for this, these two [verses] are used: "O most excellent, O youngest, O Bhārata... and "He, shining forth..."; one against whom witchcraft is being practiced should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Yaviṣṭha;
for this, these two [verses] are used; one who desires, "May I reach a full lifespan," should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Āyuṣmat.

For this [offering], these two verses belong to it: "O Agni, you are life" and "O Agni, giver of life"—one desiring prosperity should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jātavedas; for this [offering], these two verses belong to it: "For him from heaven..."—one desiring radiance should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Rukmat;
for this [offering], these two verses belong to it: "Pure, purifying, appearing like a golden ornament"—one desiring splendor should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tejasvat.

For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "When he seeks the lord of men... and "May that more brilliant [one]... One who is seeking [victory] should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Sāhantya;

for this, these two [verses] are used: "O Agni, bring the victorious one... and "That wealth, O Agni, which conquers in battle... One who desires, "May I be possessed of food," should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Annavat.

For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "For the bull-eating, for the cow-eating... and "For you, O Son..."; one who desires, "May I be an eater of food," should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, the eater of food—for him, these two [verses] are used. One who desires, "May I be a lord of food," should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, the lord of food.

For this [sacrifice], these [verses] are used: "One who has been ill for a long time should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pavamāna, to Agni Pāvaka, and to Agni Śuci. One intending to perform this sacrifice prepares gold. For this [sacrifice], these [verses] are used: "O Agni, you purify our lives," "O Agni, purify," "O Agni Pāvaka," "May that Agni Pāvaka [purify us]," "O Agni, most pure in your vows," and "O Agni, your [flames] are bright. Having placed the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives the gold as a gift. One desiring sight should likewise offer this same [sacrifice]; for this [sacrifice], these [verses] are used.

"One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Putravat, and a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Putrin," it is said. For this [offering], these are the verses: "He who, thinking of thee with a longing heart... (RV 10.70.1), "For which well-doer, O Jātavedas... (RV 3.2.5), "O thou with good sons, in strength... (RV 8.96.20), "At every hymn, O Soma, thou didst exhilarate Indra" (RV 8.91.2). One who desires, "May I be full of essence," should offer a pap cooked in goat's milk to Agni Rasavat.

For one who desires, "May I be possessed of wealth," he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vasumat; for him these two [verses] are used: "I have followed the waters with the juice of this [plant], O Agni...

and "Thou art the Vasu, the lord of wealth, O Agni, the lord of riches among the Vasus... When a battle is joined, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vājasṛt; for him these two [verses] are used: "Thee, O Agni, the best winner of booty... and "This Agni of ours...
One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Agnimat for one from whose fire they might take out another fire. For him these two [verses] are used: "Ayaṃ no agniḥ... and so forth.
These two verses belong to it: "By fire is fire kindled; for you, O Agni, are [kindled] by fire.

One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jyotiṣmat (the Luminous). Regarding one whose fire, having been taken out, goes out before the Agnihotra has been offered, they say: "One should take another fire and carry it forth"—but that should not be done. For when the former fire was taken out for its own specific portion, why should another be taken out?
Rather, having placed those very same embers together, one should churn [a new fire].

Having set down those very embers, he churns: "From here Agni was first born; Jātavedas [was born] from his own womb. May he, knowing, carry the oblation to the gods by means of the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, and the Jagatī"—thus, by means of the meters, he causes him to be born from his own womb; so says the Brāhmaṇa. "He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jyotiṣmat."

For this [offering], these two [verses] belong to it: "O Agni, thy pure [flames]... and "Thy light shines forth...". Now, indeed, it is said: "One who is being accused should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara, a pap to Varuṇa, and a pap to Dadhikrāvan. One who is about to perform this sacrifice prepares gold. For this [sacrifice], these [verses] belong to it: "Vaiśvānara with his aid...", "Thou, O Agni, with thy flame, shining brightly...", "Away from us thy wrath...", "Up the highest [step]...", "I have performed the praise of Dadhikrāvan...", and "Dadhikrā has come...". Having placed the *anvāhārya* rice in its position, he gives the gold as a gift. "One desiring offspring should perform this very same [offering]," so it is said.
For her, these [verses] are used: "One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when a son is born";
for that [offering], these two [verses] belong to Vaiśvānara: "This is the birthplace of the kinsman" and "Great is he who has been born, O Agni."
"One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara if one has omitted either the new-moon or the full-moon sacrifice.

For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Vaiśvānara with his aid... and "He who is praised in heaven...". "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when one intends to extinguish the sacred fires.
For this [offering], these [verses] are used: "Agni is the head of the world...", "Vaiśvānara with his aid...", and "O Agni, shining brightly with your flame...".

"One desiring a village should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara and one on seven potsherds to the Maruts. Now, it is said: "He places the offering for Vaiśvānara over the Āhavanīya fire and that for the Maruts over the Gārhapatya; he sets them down while the Sāmidhenī verses are being recited. At the proper time, he sets down the Vaiśvānara oblation facing westward while the Sāmidhenīs are being recited, and the Māruta oblation [is set down] while the Sāmidhenīs are being recited. For this [rite], these are the verses: "Vaiśvānara with his aid," "Pṛṣṭo divi," "Maruto yaddha vo divaḥ," and "Yā vaḥ śarma."

"One who is about to set out for battle should offer a *caru* oblation to Āditya"; for this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "May Aditi protect us" and "The great mother. "Having reached the camp, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara."
For this [offering], these two [verses] belong to it: "Vaiśvānara, for our aid... and "O Agni, maintain us among the liberal patrons.
Having eaten the food of two people who are at enmity with one another, he should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara;
for this [offering], these two [verses] belong to it: "Vaiśvānara, for our aid... and "The righteous one..."
"One who first commits an offense against two people of equal status should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara;
for him, these same two [verses] are used. One who has accepted a sheep as a gift should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara;
for him, these two [verses] are used: 'Vaiśvānara with his protection' and 'Thou, O Agni, shining brightly with thy flame.'"
"One who has accepted [as a gift] either a horse or a human being that is bi-dentate should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara.
For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "One desiring gain should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara.
For this [offering], these two are used: "May Vaiśvānara [come] to our aid; may we be in the good favor of Vaiśvānara."
Now it is indeed said: "He who, having yoked the year-long [rite], does not release it, becomes without a firm foundation; therefore, having returned, one should offer this very Vaiśvānara.
So, having returned, he offers this very Vaiśvānara.

"Whomever he employs, him he releases by means of his allotted portion for the sake of stability," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is further said: "With whatever rope one should drive away the best cow, that one should send to his rival."
"Having sent away the rope with which he drives the best cow toward his rival, he casts it into the rival's pen;
thus he sends Destruction itself against him," so says the Brāhmaṇa. These two [verses] belong to that [rite].
Now, indeed, it is said: "One desiring cattle should offer a caru-oblation to Indra."

For that [offering], these two are the invitatory and offering verses: "Indra for you from every side... and "O men, Indra... For one desiring cattle, he should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Indriyāvat;

for that [offering], these two are the verses: "The powers, O Śatakratu... and "May he grant to thee... For one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), he should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Gharma-vat;

for that [offering], these two are the verses: "In whom the seven Vasus... and "Into the raw [cows] thou hast placed the cooked... For one desiring food, he should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Arkavat.

For this [offering], these two [verses] belong to him: "O Indra, the Midgāthins sing loudly to you," and "The Gāyatrins sing to you. One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Āyāsyagharma-vat; one to Indra Indriyāvat; and one to Indra Arkavat for one who desires prosperity.

For that [offering], these verses belong to him: "In whom the seven Vasus... and "The raw within the cooked you have set in motion, O Śatakratu"; "Your gifts, O Indra, the Midgāthins sing loudly to you," and "The Gāyatrins sing to you.
One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Homuc for one who is seized by evil.

For this [offering], these two [verses] belong to it: "Viveṣa yanme" and "Indrā yā vaimṛdhāya. One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Vaimṛdha for one whom enemies cause to tremble, or against whom rival kingdoms have risen up;
for this [offering], these two [verses] belong to it: "Vi na indra mṛdho jahi" and "Mṛgo na bhīmaḥ. One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Trātṛ for one who is either bound or besieged.

For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Indra, our protector... and "O powerful one, do not [forsake] us in this... Indra. One who desires that the Great Sacrifice (*mahāyajña*) may come to him should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra-Arkāśvamedhavant;
for this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Your chariot for the bull... and "That which for the vigorous one... Indra.
One who desires a village should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra-Vṛjivant.

For her, these [oblations] occur every day: "The months follow thee; may he give to thee. For one whose army is as if sharpened, one should offer a *caru* oblation to Indrāṇī. Now it is also said: "One should bind *balbaja* grass to the fuel-bundle;
one should place them on the fire together with the fuel."
He places those [two kindling-sticks] on the fire together with the fuel-wood;

for this [offering], these two are the verses: "O Indra, among these women... and "I, O Indra, have not rejoiced...". One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Manyumat Manasvat when a battle has been joined;

for this [offering], these two are the verses: "He who, as soon as born... and "Great is thy power, O Indra, exceedingly fierce...". One should offer this very same [oblation] if one should be as if depressed in spirit.
For this [offering], these two [verses] belong; one who feels as if he himself were evil should offer this very [oblation].
For that [offering], these same two [verses] belong.
He who desires, "May my offspring be desirous of giving," should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Dātṛ.

For this [offering], these two [verses] belong to it: "Do not neglect us; bring hither... and "O Indra, for the giver... One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Pradātṛ (the Giver) for one to whom something has been given as if it were already bestowed, yet it is not being delivered;

for this [offering], these two [verses] belong to it: "We invoke the Giver" and "The wielder of the thunderbolt, the Giver... One who has been expelled or is being expelled should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Sutrāman (the Good Protector);
for this [offering], these two [verses] belong to it: "Indra Sutrāman" and "In the favor of that worshipful one, we [dwell]..."
"One who is worthy of prosperity, yet is on equal footing with those who are his equals—on his behalf, one should offer this cake on eleven potsherds to Indra. Now, it is further said:

"The *puro'nuvākyā* is a *revatī* [verse], for the sake of peace and to prevent burning; the *yājyā* is a *śakvarī* [verse]. These two belong to that [offering]: "The wealthy ones for us... and "Forward for him, the chariot..."

Now, it is indeed said: "One who practices sorcery should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu; Sarasvatī should have a portion of clarified butter, and there should be a pap for Bṛhaspati.

Now, it is further said: "Those who practice sorcery against one who is already practicing sorcery from afar strike back at him; he should therefore employ two invitatory verses (*puro'nuvākyā*) each, for the sake of overreaching [the enemy]."
He recites the invitatory verse twice each time;
he cuts portions of the oblations three times each.

For this [offering], these are the verses: "O Agni and Viṣṇu," "O Agni and Viṣṇu," "Forward for us," "O Goddess," "From heaven for us," "O Bṛhaspati," and "Thus, O Father. With this very [offering], one who is being subjected to malevolent magic should sacrifice.

For her, these very same [verses] are used: "He for whom the sacrifice does not come to him should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu"—for him, these two [verses] are used; "O Agni and Viṣṇu, O Agni and Viṣṇu! He who desires sight should offer a caru-oblation of ghee to Agni and Viṣṇu—for him, these very same two [verses] are used.

Now, indeed, it happens that an enemy who does not sacrifice seizes the sensory power and vigor of the sacrificer. When an enemy is sacrificing, one should offer a substitute *adhvarakalpa* sacrifice;
thus, he does not seize his sensory power and vigor.
One should offer it before the voice has been uttered.
Before the breaking forth of speech, having risen in the dead of night, he should offer an eight-potherd cake to Agni and Viṣṇu at the time of the morning pressing;
Sarasvatī should have a portion of clarified butter, and there should be a pap for Bṛhaspati.
For this sacrifice, these are the verses: "O Agni and Viṣṇu," "O Agni and Viṣṇu," "Forward for us," "The goddess," "From heaven for us," "O Bṛhaspati," and "Thus, O father."
At the time of the midday pressing, one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu;
Sarasvatī should have a portion of clarified butter, and there should be a pap for Bṛhaspati.
For this [offering], these same [verses] are used. At the time of the third pressing, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu.
"Sarasvatī should have the portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), and there should be a pap (caru) for Bṛhaspati"— for her, these same [offerings] are prescribed;
one should offer a cake on one potsherd (ekakapāla) to Mitra and Varuṇa at the time of the barren cow (vaśā).
"These two [verses], 'ā no mitrāvaruṇā' and 'pra bāhavā,' belong to it.
For one who should desire spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), he should offer this *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra on the full moon of the month of Tiṣya.
Thus, whoever should desire spiritual luster, he offers the *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra on the full moon of the month of Tiṣya.

He causes the sacrifice to be performed in an enclosed space. Now, it is indeed said: "Clarified butter produced from the milk of a white cow with a white calf is used; the sprinkling is done with clarified butter, and they purify themselves with clarified butter."

"Whatever constitutes spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), he produces all of that; yet they say, 'Excessive spiritual luster is being produced, and [the sacrificer] is liable to become afflicted with skin disease.
He should therefore employ two *ṛc*s of Manu as *dhāyyā*s.
By doing so, he places two of these verses—'Swift is the chariot of the god-favored one'—in the position of the *dhāyyā*s."
For this [offering], these two [verses] belong to it: "O Soma and Rudra, tear asunder in all directions... and "O Soma and Rudra, you two [have performed] these [deeds]...

If one should fear, "I shall become afflicted with skin disease," he should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Pūṣan; for this [offering], these two [verses] belong to it: "O Soma and Pūṣan, these two gods... and so forth.

"One desiring offspring should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra"—for this [rite], these two [verses] are used: "O Soma and Rudra, tear asunder in all directions... and "O Soma and Rudra, you two [take] these...";
"One practicing exorcism should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra."
For this [offering], these same two [verses] are used.

One who is afflicted by a chronic illness should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra; one intending to perform this sacrifice prepares a bull for the Hotṛ. For this [sacrifice], these same two [verses] are used. Having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, the Hotṛ gives the bull as a gift.
One who desires, "May I produce a rival for him in his own abode," should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra.
Having settled upon the boundary of another’s field, having churned the fires and distributed them, he offers a *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra.

Now it is said: "Having enclosed the altar, he should dig up half and not the other half; he should strew half of the sacrificial grass and not the other half; he should place half of the fuel on the fire and not the other half.
Thus he produces a rival for him in his own abode"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. For this [rite], these two [verses] are used.

Now, indeed, there is this [injunction]: "One desiring a village should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and one on seven potsherds to the Maruts. Now, indeed, there is this [instruction]: "He places the offering for Indra over the Āhavanīya fire and that for the Maruts over the Gārhapatya; he sets them down while the *sāmidhenī* verses are being recited. At the proper time, he sets down the offering for Indra facing westward, and the offering for the Maruts while the *sāmidhenī* verses are being recited. For this [offering], these [verses] are used: "Indra, you who encompass all," "The men [invoke] Indra," "O Maruts, when from heaven," and "Whatever protection of yours."

One who desires, "May I cause strife between the nobility (*kṣatra*) and the common people (*viś*)," should offer this very same sacrifice. While cutting off portions for the Indra-oblation, he should say, "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra! He recites, "O Indra, [protect] you from all sides... Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering verse for the Maruts!
He offers with, "That which is your protection... While cutting off portions for the Marut-oblation, he should say, "Recite the invitatory verse for the Maruts!"
When he recites, "O Maruts, since you from heaven... and having stepped forward and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to Indra," and sacrifices with the verse, "Indra, O heroes...

He thus establishes a conflict among them regarding their own respective shares. "They stand as if splitting asunder," so says the Brāhmaṇa. One who desires, "May they be reconciled," should offer this very same oblation.
Having cut off portions according to the respective deities, one should sacrifice according to the respective deities; thus, by means of their own shares, he arranges them each in its proper place.
"They indeed become arranged," so says the Brāhmaṇa. For this [offering], these same [verses] which belong to the preceding [offering] are used.

"One desiring a village should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and one on twelve potsherds to the Viśve Devas. One who is about to perform this sacrifice prepares a garment that has never before been worn by a teacher. Now it is said: "Having taken a portion from the offering for Indra, he should take a portion from the offering for the Viśve Devas; then, after the portion for Indra. Thus, having taken a portion from the Indra-offering, he takes two portions from the Vaiśvadeva-offering, and then [another] from the Indra-offering. "By means of his own power (*indriya*), he thus encompasses his kinsmen on both sides," so says the Brāhmaṇa. For this sacrifice, these two [verses] are used.
Having placed the *anvāhārya* rice mess down with the verse, "O Indra, may he exhilarate us in battles," he gives a garment that has been previously worn by his teacher (*upādhyāya*).

Then [the injunction]: "One desiring a village should offer a *caru* of millet cooked in the milk of a spotted cow to the Maruts"; and furthermore, "The *yājyā* and *anuṣākyā* verses should contain the word 'dear' (*priya*)."
These two [verses] belong to it: "I invoke the beloved name of you, the swift ones" and "for glory, with your splendors.
With this *saṃjñānī* (reconciliatory) sacrifice, one should cause him to sacrifice who might be at variance with his peers.
When those with whom he wishes to reconcile have assembled, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vasumat.
"One should offer a *caru* to Soma accompanied by Rudra, a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra accompanied by the Maruts, and a *caru* to Varuṇa accompanied by the Ādityas.
For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "May Agni, the first, protect us with the Vasus; may the god [Soma] unite us with the Vasus.
"One desiring prosperity should offer a *caru* to the Ādityas who are associated with the earth (*bhuvadvat*)."
For him, these two [verses] are used: "The sacrifice of the gods" and "The pure waters.

One who has been expelled or is being expelled should offer a *caru* oblation to the Ādityas, the sustainers (*dhārayadvat*). Then, saying "O Aditi, give your consent," he takes a clod of earth from the footprint of the one who is expelling him while he is being expelled. Having taken these, he brings them forward, saying, "Come hither, O Maruts, givers of good gifts, together with this lord of the people, toward that king. Then he pours them into the hollowed palms of the sacrificer, saying "May the blessing be true. He holds them there, saying "Here is the mind. At this point, he throws those clods of earth onto the path of the cattle-track; there, he meditates in his mind upon whomsoever the sacrificer hates.
Of this [verse], these two parts occur: "The Ādityas uphold the three earths.
One should fetch rice from the house of whoever might be a speaker of vulgar speech beyond [the proper bounds]; he should separate the white and the black grains. Now it is said:
"Those which are white, with those one should offer a *caru* oblation to Āditya."

For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Do not lead away the Kṣatriyas as a sacrificial fee," and so on; for the Brāhmaṇa says, "The people (viś) are indeed the Ādityas by deity; he thus approaches the people. Now, it is further said: "If his people have been won over but the kingdom has not been won over, they say, 'He should offer a *caru* oblation to Varuṇa for those [cows] that are black.
For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Hear this my cry, O Varuṇa," and "To thee, according to the truth, I go."
"The kingdom belongs to Varuṇa;
verily, he attains both the people and the kingdom," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is also said:

"If he should not obtain [the consent], he should offer this portion to the Ādityas, thinking: 'I offer this to the Ādityas so that such-and-such a person from such-and-such a clan may obtain [consent].
Having offered it, he desists; then, when he obtains [consent], he brings the portions together.

For him, these two [verses] are used: 'The sacrifice of the gods, with the newest protection of the Ādityas... and so forth. The Brāhmaṇa says: 'The Ādityas themselves, seeking their own share, cause him to obtain the consent of the clan.'"
Now, it is indeed said: "If he should not succeed, he should drive seven stakes of *aśvattha* wood into the middle shaft.
Having stationed the cart with its pole facing east, he drives seven stakes of *aśvattha* wood into the middle shaft.

Having struck the middle one, he stretches out three towards the west and three towards the east, saying, "Here I bind the Ādityas so that they may go down to such-and-such a clan for the sake of such-and-such a person. Regarding this, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "The Ādityas themselves, having their heroes bound, cause him to go down to the clan. Now, it is further said: "If he should not succeed in making them go down, he should offer this very same oblation of cooked rice (caru) to the Ādityas; he should also bind the pegs to the sacrificial fuel (idhma)."
"One should place them on the fire together with the fuel-wood"—thus he places them on the fire together with the fuel-wood; "he approaches [the fire] without being excluded," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is further said: "They are made of *aśvattha* wood."
