This is indeed the vigor of the Maruts, namely the *aśvattha* tree; by means of its vigor, he approaches the people (*viś*).
There are seven [verses], for the Maruts consist of seven groups; thus, group by group, he approaches the people—so says the Brāhmaṇa. For this [offering], these very two [verses] are used.
Now, it is indeed said:

"He who fears death should offer this oblation of a hundred *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces to Prajāpati. One who is about to sacrifice with this *iṣṭi* prepares a hundred golden *kṛṣṇalas*, a new vessel, and abundant clarified butter. Then, having performed the introductory formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he pours out four handfuls of *kṛṣṇalas* with the words, "I pour out what is pleasing to Prajāpati."

Having released his speech at the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviskṛt*), he places a new vessel over the *gārhapatya* fire, pours clarified butter across the strainer, and throws the black grains (*kṛṣṇala*) across the strainer;
then he pours out the clarified butter, heats it over the fire, carries fire around both of them, and sets them down within the altar (*antarvedi*). Now, there is this [instruction]:

He cuts four *kṛṣṇala* seeds each, for the attainment of the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*). Thus he cuts eight portions for the deity, four for the *Sviṣṭakṛt*, eight for the *iḍā*, four for the intermediate *iḍā*, one for the *prāśitra*, and one for the sacrificer. While offering, they offer only clarified butter; while consuming, they consume only clarified butter. Then, having taken these [portions] up together as one, he presents them to the Brahman priest.
For this [priest], there are these two [verses]: "Hiraṇyagarbha" and "Prajāpati."

"For one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), he should offer this *caru* oblation to Sūrya. Intending to sacrifice with this offering, he prepares five *kṛṣṇalas* of gold, as well as a golden and a silver plate. Having cooked this *caru*, poured clarified butter over it, and moved it toward the north, he takes hold of it with the golden and silver plates and places it within the altar (*antarvedi*).
The ritual procedure is the same up to the *prayāja* offerings. Now, it is indeed said: "At each *prayāja* offering, he offers a *kṛṣṇala*."

At each *prayāja* offering, he places a piece of gold and offers it; for this [sacrifice], these two [verses] are used: "Upwards that" (*udu tyam*) and "The bright one" (*citram*). Having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives two plates, one of gold and one of silver. "One who desires, 'May I find gold; may gold come to me,' should perform this sacrifice: he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ, and a pap to Bhūmi. One intending to perform this sacrifice prepares gold. For this [sacrifice], these [verses] are used: "As of old, the poetic wisdom... (*sa pratnavat*), "The golden-handed for protection... (*hiraṇyapāṇim*), "O Savitṛ, today the lovely thing... (*vāmam adya savitar*), and "Thus indeed among the mountains... (*baḍitthā parvatānām*). "Hymns [praise] you... (*stomāsas tvā*).
Regarding the [offering] called *vicāriṇī*, having placed the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives gold; one should offer this very same [oblation] after having found lost gold.
For that [offering], these same [verses] are used. One should offer this very same [oblation] for one whose gold has been lost.
For her, these same [verses] are used:
"He who is a consumer of Soma—for him one should offer this Śyāmāka rice-oblation to Soma and Indra.
For that [offering], these two [verses] are used: "With the soft-bellied one," and "The wrathful one has drunk."
"One is a Soma-drinker, while another is one who has over-indulged in Soma;
for him who has over-indulged in Soma, one should offer this oblation of millet (śyāmāka) to Soma and Indra."

For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "pra suvānaḥ sabādhas taḥ" (VS 28.1). One desiring cattle, intending to sacrifice with this *iṣṭi*, should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Dātṛ and a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Pradātṛ. He prepares curd, honey, ghee, water, and barley. Then, having performed the introductory formula "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he pours out four handfuls of rice with the words "I pour out what is pleasing to Agni Dātṛ. Having performed that same introductory formula, he pours out exactly four handfuls of rice with the words "I pour out what is pleasing to Indra Pradātṛ."

Having performed this very same procedure, [he says] "I offer what is pleasing to Prajāpati," and pours out four grains of barley; he causes the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*) to be raised over those [barley grains] while they are still among the rice grains. They lift up the barley grains, and with the call to the preparer of the oblation, he releases his speech.
The ritual action is the same up until the pouring [of the grains].

Having poured [the grain] out, he places eight potsherds on the southern half of the Gārhapatya fire and eleven on the northern half. Then, having crushed these [grains] with a mortar and pestle, he places the single-potsherd cake on the Gārhapatya fire and roasts the parched grains (*dhānā*). When he spreads these two sacrificial offerings (*havis*) over the fire, then he sprinkles those parched grains with four substances: with curd, honey, clarified butter, and water. For this [rite], these [verses] are used: "O Agni, give wealth to the donor; O Agni, give us hundreds. "We invoke the giver, the wielder of the thunderbolt. "Like purified clarified butter. "O you who are bright with both [worlds], with the melted butter."

For one who has failed in a sacrifice, he should offer this *iṣṭi*: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, and a pap for Soma. Now it is said: "He should join together the portions of the offering for Agni and that for Soma in the offering for Indra.
He joins together the portions of the offering for Agni and that for Soma in the offering for Indra;

thus he bestows upon him both splendor and spiritual luster in a unified manner—so says the Brāhmaṇa. For this sacrifice, these are the verses: "As of old," "O poets," "Indra for you from all sides," "Indra, the men," "Thou art ours, O Soma," and "What are thy abodes."

"One whose desire does not come to pass should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma"—for him these two [verses] are used: "O Agni and Soma, you who possess common wealth" and "You two have performed these [deeds]. "One desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should offer an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni and Soma"—he who desires spiritual luster offers an oblation of *śyāmāka* grains on eight potsherds to Agni and Soma.
For this [offering], these two [verses] belong to Agni and Soma: "Agni and Soma, this... and "O Agni and Soma, of the oblation set forth...";
one who fears impotence should offer a *caru* of millet (*śyāmāka*) to Soma Vājin; for this [offering], these two [verses] belong to it: "Swell up... and "Unite with...".
"One desiring a village should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Bṛhaspati. Now it is said:
"The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses should contain the word 'host' (*gaṇa*).

For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "We invoke thee, the lord of hosts, of all hosts," and "He, with his people... One who desires, "May I destroy the subjects through the power of the *brahman*," should perform this very same offering.
"One should use the two verses addressed to the Maruts as the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*";
these two belong to her: "O Maruts, whatever [you have] from heaven" and "Whatever protection is yours.
"One desiring the heavenly world should offer a *caru* oblation to Aryaman."
These two [verses] belong to her: "O Aryaman... and "Come to us, O Aryaman... One who desires, "May my subjects be desirous of giving," should offer a *caru* oblation to Aryaman;
these two [verses] belong to him. One who desires, "May I go safely to the assembly," should offer a *caru* oblation to Aryaman;
these same two [verses] belong to him. If there be a *rājanya* who is inferior in rank, for him one should offer this eleven-potherd oblation to Indra-Anuṣūka; thus it is indeed said.
"The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are 'possessing a base' (*budhnavatī*) and 'possessing a summit' (*agravatī*).
These two belong to her: "Being praised by the Aṅgirases from the base to the summit," and "From the base he measured out the summit with measures.
"If there be a Brāhmaṇa who is younger than his brothers, for him one should offer this *ānuṣūka* rice-pap dedicated to Bṛhaspati"—thus it is said. And then indeed it occurs:

"The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are 'possessing a base' (*budhnavatī*) and 'possessing a summit' (*agravatī*). Of that [offering], these two [verses] are used: "The Great One, having propped up the earth from its base, reached the summit with his might," and so forth.
Now, indeed, it is said:

"For one who is seized by *pāpayakṣman*, he should offer this *caru* oblation to Āditya on the new moon day. For that [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Being born, he becomes ever new," and "O Ādityas, you cause his rays to swell."

If he should desire of someone, "May he be an eater of food," for him he should offer this three-layered oblation: "To Indra the King, a cake on eleven potsherds; to Indra the Overlord; to Indra the Self-Ruler. Then, having performed the introductory formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he offers four handfuls of rice with the words, "I offer what is pleasing to Indra the King. Having performed that same introductory formula, he offers four handfuls each for [Indra] the Overlord and [Indra] the Self-Ruler.
He releases his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*).

The ritual procedure up to the pouring of the grain is the same; having poured it, he places eleven potsherds face upwards on the Gārhapatya fire. Now it is said: "He places [the dough] upon the potsherds while they are face upwards, for the sake of non-exhaustion.
There are three sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*);
these worlds are three, [and this is] for the attainment of these worlds. Each subsequent one becomes larger."
He makes each subsequent portion larger than the preceding one, cutting off while causing all of them to be presented.
While cutting, he says: "Recite for Indra, the King!"

Having recited, "In the eastern direction you are Indra, the King," he offers the sacrifice with, "Indra conquers; he is not conquered. While cutting the portion, he says, "For Indra, the Overlord, recite the invitatory verse! Having recited, "Indra conquers; he is not conquered," he offers the sacrifice with, "Truly, his greatness has surpassed all. While cutting the portion, he says, "For Indra, the Sovereign, recite the invitatory verse! Having recited, "Truly, his greatness has surpassed all," he offers the sacrifice with, "In the eastern direction you are Indra, the King."
"The reversal of the sequence of the invitatory and offering verses is for the sake of non-burning," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

"He who desires sensory power and vigor, him one should cause to sacrifice with this Sarvapṛṣṭhā [offering]. One who is about to perform this sacrifice prepares a horse, a bull, a ram, and a goat. Then, having performed the introductory formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he pours out four handfuls of rice with the formula, "I pour out what is pleasing to Indra associated with the Rathantara."

Having followed this very procedure, [the Adhvaryu] offers four handfuls each for the deities—Indra of the Bṛhat-sāman, Indra of the Vairūpa-sāman, Indra of the Vairāja-sāman, Indra of the Śakvara-sāman, and Indra of the Raivata-sāman—and releases his speech after the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*). The ritual procedure is the same up to the pouring [of the grain]; having poured it, he places twelve potsherds with their faces upward on the Gārhapatya fire. Now it is said: "He places [the vessel] upon the potsherds with their faces upward, so that there may be no loss of potency."
There is a cake on twelve potsherds for the sake of its being dedicated to the Viśvedevas; he cuts portions from all sides.

While cutting, he says, "Recite for Indra, the one associated with the *Rathantara*! Having recited the verse, "To thee, O hero, we sing aloud," he performs the offering with the verse, "For we invoke thee indeed."
While cutting the portion, he says, "Recite for Indra the Bṛhatī verse";
having recited, "For we invoke thee indeed," he offers with, "O Indra, as many as are thy heavens. While cutting the portion, he says, "Recite for Indra the Vairūpa verse."
Having recited, "O Indra, as much as you [desire]," he performs the offering with, "Drink the Soma, O Indra; let it exhilarate you.

While cutting off the portion, he says, "For Indra Vairāja, recite the invitatory verse. Having recited, "Drink the Soma, O Indra; let it exhilarate you," he performs the offering with, "Never indeed art thou barren."

While cutting the portion, he says: "Recite for Indra the Śākvara [offering]! Having recited the verse, "Never art thou barren," he performs the offering with the verse, "O wealthy ones, rejoice with us.
While cutting the portion, he says: "Recite for Indra the Raivata [offering]!"
Having recited "The Revatīs, our common feast," he offers the oblation with "O Hero, we cry out to thee.

He recites them in alternation, for the Brāhmaṇa says, "lest there be burning. Having placed the Anvāhārya rice, he gives away a horse, a bull, a ram, and a goat; and with this very rite one who is being falsely accused should sacrifice.

This very sacrifice which was previously mentioned is this one: for one who desires sight, he should offer this oblation—namely, a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Bhrājasvat, a pap of cooked rice for Sūrya, and a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Bhrājasvat.

For this [offering], these [verses] belong to it: "Up, O Agni, thy pure [flames]," "With light," "Up that wonderful one," "Up, O Agni, thy pure [flames]," "With light"—these are used when the *iḍā* has been invoked. The portion not placed [on the *iḍā*] remains for the *agnīdh*. Then he gives three balls (*piṇḍas*) to the sacrificer. He gives the balls with the verses, "Up that Jātavedas," "Seven bay mares are on thy chariot," and "The wonderful face of the gods has risen.
Verily, he bestows sight upon him; "Whatever belongs to him, that he gives," so says the Brāhmaṇa. "One desiring a village should offer the *sāṃgrahaṇī* oblation dedicated to the Viśve Devas."

They cook the *vaiśvadeva* oblation of rice-porridge as if gathering it together; then he lays the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) around with the formula, "Thou art firm; may I be firm among my kinsmen. For this sacrifice, these two [verses] belong to him: "O All-Gods" and "All-Gods. Then, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers three spoonfuls with the formula, "O gods, of the mind, of the mind... Then indeed it is said: "The body of such a person goes to Agni, his sap to Soma, Varuṇa seizes him with the noose of Varuṇa, Sarasvatī [seizes] his speech, and Agni-Viṣṇu [seize] his self, for one who has been long ill."

"For one who has been long ill, or for one who desires, 'May I live my full span of life,' he should offer this sacrifice. One intending to perform this sacrifice prepares a new vessel made of *khadira* wood, fresh butter as the clarified butter, and a *pravarta* (a gold disk) of such a measure as he thinks he will live for in years.

Then, having performed the introductory formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he offers an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni, a pap to Soma, a cake on ten potsherds to Varuṇa, a pap to Sarasvatī, and a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the inspection of the clarified butter.
He causes [the sacrificer] to look at the clarified butter with the verse, "That which was fresh became fresh butter.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the placing of the ladles;
having placed the ladles, he then places this Pravarta stone—prepared in a new Khadira vessel, with an under-layer of ghee and sprinkled over—with the sacrificial oblations within the altar.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the *prayāja* offerings;
having performed the *prayāja*s, he proceeds with the oblations (*havir*).

For this [offering], these are the verses: "O Agni, give us life," "O Agni, grant us life," "Swell up," "May thy wrath depart," "Loosen the highest [knot]," "Lead us forward," "From heaven to us," "O Agni and Viṣṇu," and "O Agni and Viṣṇu. Then, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers additional oblations with the *sruva*-ladle.

"You are the breath of the Aśvins; may they two grant it to you, whose breath you are—svāhā! You are the breath of Indra; may he grant it to you, whose breath you are—svāhā! You are the breath of Mitra and Varuṇa; may they two grant it to you, whose breath you are—svāhā! You are the breath of the Viśvedevas; may they grant it to you, whose breath you are—svāhā!"

Having offered oblation after oblation, he pours clarified butter over the turning ladle with the formulas: "Thou art the ruler (rāṭ), thou art the far-ruler (virāṭ), thou art the sovereign ruler (samrāṭ), thou art the self-ruler (svarāṭ). Then, having carried this turning ladle around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, he places it to the south. Then he causes the sacrificer to look at the clarified butter with the verse: "The stream of ghee, the path of immortality, given by Indra and the Maruts, extended forth."

Viṣṇu surveyed the principles; with the principle, Iḍā drove the cows. Then, having taken hold of the hand of the Brahman priest, the officiating priests (ṛtvij) went around him, saying: "With the *pāvamāna* hymn, with the course of the *gāyatrī*, with the power of the *upāṃśu* cup—may the god Savitṛ release you for life, for the sake of living! With the hymn of the *bṛhat* and *rathantara*, with the course of the *triṣṭubh*, with the power of the *śukra* cup—may the god Savitṛ release you for life, for the sake of living! With the measure of Agni, with the *jagatī*..."
"By the power of the Agrayaṇa vessel, may the god Savitṛ release you for life, for the sake of living"— saying this,
he then drinks the clarified butter from the gold.

While he is drinking it out, [the teacher] recites over him: "O Agni, make this [boy] long-lived and radiant; O King Soma Varuṇa, make his seed dear. O Aditi, grant him protection as a mother; O All-Gods, may he reach old age. Then, having washed this ear-ring with water, he ties it on his right ear, reciting: "Bestowing life upon you from all sides. Then he turns it around him, reciting: "You are life; you are all-encompassing life; you are complete life; you are total life. Then the *brahmā* takes his hand, reciting the *anuvāka* beginning with "Agni is long-lived" until its conclusion.
"For as many horses as he may accept, so many four-potherd cakes to Varuṇa should he offer, with one in excess.
For this [sacrifice], these two [verses] belong to it: "Hear this my call, O Varuṇa" and "That I implore of thee.
If he should be a recipient of further [gifts], he should subsequently offer a cake on one potsherd to Sūrya.

For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "ud u tyam" and "citram. Then he goes down for the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath). Now it is said: "Having returned, he should offer a *caru* oblation to Aponaptr.
For this [oblation], these two [verses] are used: "apāṃ napāt" and "samanyā yanti."

"For one who has been seized by evil, he should offer this curd-mixture (payasyā) dedicated to Indra and Varuṇa. Intending to sacrifice with this offering, he prepares curds, milk, and the curd-mixture (āmikṣā). Then, having performed the introductory formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he pours out four handfuls of rice, saying, "I pour out what is pleasing to Indra and Varuṇa.

He releases his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (haviṣkṛt). The ritual procedure is the same up to the pouring [of the grains]; having poured them, he places eleven potsherds on the southern half of the Gārhapatya fire.

When he places this cake upon the fire, then he cooks this *āmikṣā* on the *gārhapatya* fire; then, having taken out that cake after it has been spread with a base of butter and sprinkled over with butter, and having covered it completely with the *āmikṣā*, he sets it down within the altar.
Now, indeed, it is said:
"He places the cake upon the *payasyā*; thus he makes it possessed of a self, and moreover, possessed of a proper abode."
He arranges them in four ways, establishes them in the very directions, and then gathers them together again.

Having divided the *āmikṣā* into four parts from the *puroḍāśa*, he spreads them out with the verses: "O Indra and Varuṇa, whatever body of yours is worthy of being restrained, with that release this man from sin; O Indra and Varuṇa, whatever body of yours is powerful, protective, and brilliant, with that release this man from sin. He brings them together again and, having brought them together, he cuts portions.

For this [rite], these two [verses] belong to him: "Of Indra and Varuṇa... and "O Indra and Varuṇa, you two for our sacrifice... Then, before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers eight spoonfuls with the formula: "O Indra and Varuṇa, whatever damage there is in your fire, that we expiate for you with this. These are the eight.

Now, it is indeed said: "He who has rivals and is contending with them should sacrifice with this offering. He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni the Impetuous (pravat), to Agni the Overpowering (vibādhat), and to Agni the Facing (pratīkavat).

For this sacrifice, these are the verses: "This Agni has gone forth... (praprāyam agniḥ); "I worship for thee, I send forth my thought for thee... (pra te yakṣi pra ta iyarmi manma); "Thou hast become great by thy brilliance, by thy light... (bhuvo vi pājasā vi jyotiṣā); "O Agni, thou with thy face... (sa tvam agne pratīkena); "Him who is fair-faced, fair-looking, and well-moving... (taṃ supratīkaṃ sudṛśaṃ sv-añcam).

He who has rivals and is contending with them should sacrifice with this offering. He should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Vimuc, to Indra Vaimṛdha, and to Indra Indriyāvat. Now, it is also said: "He offers a cake on thirty-three potsherds.
Those very three cakes on eleven potsherds are what these [thirty-three] are said to be.
These are its [verses]: "tasyā etā bhavanti," "aṃhomuce," "viveṣa yanmā," "vi na indre," "indra kṣatram," "indriyāṇi," "śatakrato," and "anu te dāyi.
He who has rivals should, while contending, sacrifice with this *iṣṭi*. He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Saṃvarga;
when it is cooked and placed in position, he should touch it with this *yajus*.

When it has been cooked and is ready, he touches it with this *yajus*: "Thou art vigor; thou art might; thou art strength; thou art splendor; thou art the abode of the gods by name; thou art the universe; thou art all life; thou art everything; thou art all life. May I, having overcome that rival by means of this oblation, be victorious.
He recites seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses from the section beginning with "Worship the best invokers of the gods" (*yakṣvā hi devahūtamān*), specifically these two:
"O friends, [unite] you together" (*sakhāyaḥ saṃ vaḥ*) and "O bull, thou enkindlest them together" (*saṃsamidyuvase vṛṣan*).

"For one who desires offspring, he should offer this *gārmuta* oblation to Prajāpati"—for him these two [verses] are used: "O Prajāpati, he knows... and so forth. "For one who desires cattle, he should offer this *gārmuta* oblation to Soma and Pūṣan."
For this [offering], these two [verses] belong to Soma and Pūṣan. "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā at the divine assembly.

On the day before the Citrā, he observes the fast; then, on the following morning, he offers an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni, a pap to Soma, an oblation on eight potsherds to Tvaṣṭṛ, a pap to Sarasvatī, a pap to Sarasvant, a pap to Sinīvālī, and an oblation on eleven potsherds to Indra.

For this [offering], these [verses] are used: *agninā rāyamaśnavat*, *gomāṃ agne āpyāyasva*, *saṃ ta iha*, *tvaṣṭāramagriyam*, *tannasturīpam*, *pra ṇo devyā*, *divo naḥ pīpivāṃsam*, *sarasvataḥ*, *ye te sarasva ūrmayaḥ*, *sinīvāli yā supāṇiḥ*, *indram vo viśvataspari*, and *indram naraḥ*. Then, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers oblations with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) using five verses and two *yajus*-formulas beginning with *agne gobhirna āgahi*.
He is one who is about to perform the *kārīrī* sacrifice.

He prepares a black garment with a black fringe, a black horse, a black halter, a black antelope skin, black honey, groats of *karīra* fruit, a black unbaked jar, a black *anastrigadha*, a black ewe, a clump of *varṣāhū* grass, and *vetasa* wood for fuel and sacrificial grass. Then, at the sacrificer’s station, he places the black garment with the black fringe. Then, having tethered the black horse with the black halter in front of the Āhavanīya fire, he pours out the black honey and the groats of *karīra* fruit upon the black antelope skin within the altar.

He fixes a jar in the rubbish-heap (utkara). Then, having placed a cart with its pole pointing east in front of the rubbish-heap, he ties a black sheep in front of it as a support. To the north of the Āhavanīya fire, he places a clump of *varṣāhū* grass, a cane branch, and the sacrificial fuel and grass (*idhmā-barhis*). Then the sacrificer puts on a black garment with a black fringe, saying:
"Thou art of the Maruts, the vigor of the Maruts; pierce the stream of water! He then restrains the wind from behind, saying: "O Maruts, let the swift falcon rest!"
"He generates the east wind for the sake of obstructing the rain," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then, having released this horse from its tether, he makes it leap about with the Uttaravargya formula: "Bellow! Thunder! Deposit the embryo!"

If he shakes himself, if he urinates, or if he voids excrement, one should know: "It will rain. Then he offers oblations with the names of the winds: "The east wind, raining, has turned toward us—Svāhā! and so on, up to eight. Then, within the sacrificial altar, he mixes honey with the flour of *karīra* fruits upon a black antelope skin: "The gladdening ones, the lowing ones, the purifying ones, the swift ones; the luminous ones, the dispelling darkness, the encompassing ones, the well-foaming ones; the supporters of friends, the supporters of the ruling power, the ones with good realms—protect me here!"

Having made three balls and gathered them together, he fastens them to the ends of the black antelope skin with a cord, saying: "Thou art the fastening of the vigorous horse; for rain I fasten thee. Then he binds them to the first notch of the cart-pole, saying:
"O gods who possess wealth, O Agni, Soma, and Sūrya! He halts at day and night. He binds them to the second notch, saying: "O gods who grant protection, O Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman!"
He ceases at the end of the day and night;
he fixes [the fire] on the third [layer] with the verse, "O gods who drink together, O son of the waters, swift-coursing. He ceases at the end of the day and night.
Now it is said: "If it should rain, one should sacrifice for only that long."

Whether it rains or not, he offers the *piṇḍī* oblations, spread with butter and sprinkled with butter from the *sruva*-ladle, with the verse: "O Maruts, you who create light in the day, whom men raise up like the ocean. Then he gazes at their smoke with the verse: "The dark-colored, tawny, well-winged ones.

If it does not rain, on the following day he should offer the oblation; he should offer a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Dhāmacchat, a cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts, and a cake on one potsherd for Sūrya.

For this [offering], these are the verses: "O Agni, you [are] even those unshakable ones," "Many are yours, O Jātavedas," "Grant us rain from heaven, O Maruts," "The bounteous Maruts swell the waters," and "Upwards that bright [sun]. Then, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers three spoonfuls with the verses beginning, "Like Aurva and Bhṛgu, like Śuci and Āpnavāna, we invoke. Then he fills this pot with water, saying: "Release the rain from heaven; fill the ocean with waters."

If it tears or breaks, one should know that it will indeed rain; then he offers an oblation upon it with the words, "Thou art born of the waters, the first-born; thou art strength, belonging to the ocean.
If it shakes, or if it urinates, or if it voids dung, one should know that it will indeed rain; then he offers an oblation upon a clump of *varṣāhū* grass.

"Make the earth swell; cleave this divine sky; give us of the divine water; O Lord, release the leather bag," he says. Then he throws it after [the fire] into the Āhavanīya fire with the verse, "The golden-haired one, the spreader of the region. Then, looking at its smoke, he recites, "Thy well-winged ones have measured out their courses. Then, standing within the altar (antarvedi), he shakes the black antelope skin while reciting the rest of the section, beginning with, "O gods who have your share in heaven. The Kārīrī sacrifice concludes there. Now follows the Añjaḥsava Kārīrī: he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni; having cooked it, he places it upon the altar.

For this [offering], there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, five *prayāja*s, and two *ājyabhāga*s belonging to the *vārtraghna* class; furthermore, the two *saṃyājyā*s for the oblation are the two *triṣṭubh* verses beginning with "Agni is the head" (*agnirmūrdhā*) and "From the earth" (*bhuvaḥ*).
Those [verses] by which he ties the lumps of clay together, those by which he offers the oblations, and those with which he gazes at the smoke—all these become successful.
The Añjas-savakārīrī sacrifice is concluded. Now, indeed, it is said:

"One should perform the Traidhātavīya sacrifice when practicing sorcery, or being practiced against by another; or when about to sacrifice with a thousand [cows], or having sacrificed with a thousand; or one who, having said 'I shall sacrifice,' does not sacrifice. One intending to sacrifice with this offering prepares a thousand pieces of gold, a garment of *tārpya* silk, and a milch-cow. Then, having performed the introductory formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he pours out four handfuls of rice with the formula, "I pour out what is pleasing to Indra and Viṣṇu. Having performed that same introductory formula, [he pours out] for Indra...

Having performed this same introductory formula, "I offer what is pleasing to Viṣṇu," he pours out four grains of barley; then, having performed the same introductory formula, "I offer what is pleasing to Indra and Viṣṇu," he pours out four grains of rice. He causes the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*) to be raised over those very rice grains;
they lift up the barley grains.

He releases his speech at the call for the preparer of the oblation; the ritual procedure is the same up to the pouring [of the grain]. Having poured it, he places twelve potsherds on the Gārhapatya fire. Now, indeed, it is said: "The sacrificial cake is one of twelve potsherds."
Those three cakes on four potsherds each become three sacrificial cakes for the sake of attaining triple prosperity.
"These three worlds—of these worlds, each succeeding one is greater than the preceding.
Thus, he makes each succeeding layer greater. There is barley in the middle; for it is said: "All the meters (*chandas*) are to be recited in connection with this sacrifice."

"The *kakud* is indeed the vigor of the *triṣṭubh*, and the *uṣṇih* is that of the *jagatī*. In that he recites the *uṣṇih* and the *kakud* consecutively, by that very means he secures all the meters.

"O Agni, with thy aids..."—in these [verses], he places two *dhāyyā*s in their proper place; then, with the verse containing the word "three," "O Agni, three are thy strengths, three thy stations," he concludes the section. "Because of its similarity of form," says the Brāhmaṇa; "cutting off [the portions] while causing them to reach all [the gods]."

For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Together you both have conquered through your deed," and "O Indra and Bṛhaspati, do not abandon us. Having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives a thousand pieces of gold, a garment of silk (*tārpya*), and a cow. If he should desire of a Rājanya: "May he be born unsubdued and may he go about slaying his enemies," for him he should offer this oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) to Indra and Bṛhaspati. One who is about to perform this sacrifice prepares a golden cord. For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "O Indra and Bṛhaspati, be with us," and "May Bṛhaspati protect us from behind. Having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives the golden cord.

One who has eaten new grain without having performed the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, or one who should sacrifice in the fires of another, or for whom another should sacrifice in his fires, must consign the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*), move away, churn out the fires, spread them out, and offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. For this [sacrifice], these two verses belong to it: "Vaiśvānara with his aid... and "Heaven-backed...". One whose *Agnihotra* has been interrupted should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tantumat if he desires, "May the thread of my progeny not be severed."

"Having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods, having descended from the sacrificial ground, having churned out the fires, and having spread them out, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tantumant. For this [offering], these two are the verses: "You are our thread and also our bridge, O Agni; you are the path that leads to the gods. By you, O Agni, may we ascend to the high ridge, and then may we rejoice in the common banquet with the gods. Making for himself an easy path that does not fail, the sharp-horned bull, shining brightly, looking back upon his ancient dwelling place, Agni has stretched out the divine thread."

The two *saṃyājyā* verses for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering are: "We invoke Agni Sviṣṭakṛt—the bearer of oblations, the subduer of adversaries, the slayer of Rākṣasas, victorious in battles, luminous, shining, and the possessor of abundant wisdom. "O Agni, make that well-offered; O God, overcome all hostile armies. Show us a wide path and shine forth; bestow upon us a long, undecaying life full of light. One who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and sheds tears should offer a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) to Agni Vratapati (the Upholder of Vows).

For this [rite], these two [verses] belong to him: "O Agni, you who bear the vows, the pure one, seat the gods here; O Agni, for the carrying of the oblation. "Now bearing the vows, the protector of vows, undeceivable, sacrificing to the gods, ageless, possessing excellent heroes—bestowing treasures, easy to find, O Agni Jātavedas, protect us that we may live.

Now, if one's fires should be mixed with other fires—either with each other or with the fires of another—he should cause the fires to ascend into the two kindling woods (*araṇis*), move away, churn out the fires, spread them out, and offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vivici and to Agni Vratapati.

For this [offering], these are the verses: "Thy flames, O Agni, driven by the wind, spread in all directions"; "Thee, O Agni, the human clans praise"; "O Agni, thou art the guardian of vows"; and "Whatever vows of yours we may violate. Thus the sacrifices conclude;
thus the sacrifices conclude. Now, indeed, it is said:
Prajāpati desired, "May I create offspring.
He performed austerity;
he created the serpents.
He desired, "May I procreate offspring. He performed fervent penance a second time; he created the birds.
He desired, "May I create offspring.
He performed austerity for a third time;
he saw this speech of the consecrated.

He said to him: "From that, indeed, he created progeny. Regarding this they ask: "Which was that austerity which, having performed that austerity, he uttered the speech of one consecrated? Now it is also said: "The Aṅgirases, when going to the heavenly world, caused the consecration and the austerity to enter into the waters;
he bathes in the waters; verily, he directly wins for himself the consecration and the austerity. Thus one should say. Now it is also said:
If one who is consecrated sees something impure, the consecration departs from him and his dark-blue luster fades away.
Therefore, having seen something impure, he mutters: "The mind is unbound, the eye is poor; Sūrya is the best of lights. O Consecration, do not abandon me! Thus he says.
"Initiation does not depart from him,
nor does his dark-blue or tawny color fade away," so says the Brāhmaṇa; and now, indeed, it occurs as follows.
"If it rains upon one who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*), the divine waters, being unappeased, destroy his vigor (*ojas*), strength (*bala*), consecration, and ascetic heat (*tapas*).

While being rained upon, he mutters: "O flowing ones, bestow strength; bestow vigor; bestow strength; do not destroy my consecration or my ascetic heat. He says this, and thus he places all of that within himself;
neither his vigor, nor his strength, nor his consecration, nor his ascetic heat are destroyed—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said: "Agni is the deity of the consecrated one;
he becomes as if hidden from him at the moment when [the sacrificer] goes forth.
Thus, having ascended [into Agni], he becomes as if hidden from him.
Having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods, he proceeds with the verse addressed to Bṛhaspati:
"Go forth to better fortune from here; may Bṛhaspati be your leader.
He says this because Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman among the gods.

"He takes hold of that very one; he carries him across," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Regarding the journeying together of the waters and the settling, it has been stated. Now, furthermore, it is said: "He who purchases King Soma after having caused him to go to the world of sovereignty (*sāmrājya*) attains sovereignty among his own people."
"Verily, the world of sovereignty belongs to King Soma through the *chandāṃsi*;
one should thus address him before the purchase of Soma. Thus he addresses him before the purchase of Soma.

"Announce this to Soma for me: 'This is your Gāyatra portion'; announce this to Soma for me: 'This is your Triṣṭubh portion'; announce this to Soma for me: 'This is your Jagatī portion'; announce this to Soma for me: 'May he attain sovereignty over the Chandomas. Having caused him to go to that very world of sovereignty, he purchases [him];
"he attains sovereignty among his own people," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said: "He who knows the foundation of the *tānūnaptra* stands firm.
The exponents of the Veda say: "They do not consume it, nor do they offer it as a libation; where, then, does the *tānūnaptra* find its foundation?"
"Over Prajāpati, in the mind," he should say;
"let him smell [the butter] three times," so he smells it three times, saying, "I offer you over Prajāpati, in the mind. This indeed is the foundation of the *tānūnaptra* rite.
"He who knows thus stands firm"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is also said: "He who knows the foundation of the Adhvaryu stands firm."

"From whatever point he thinks, 'Standing here, I shall offer,' from that point he should cause the announcement to be made. From whatever point he thinks, "Standing here, I shall offer," from that point he causes the announcement to be made. "This indeed is the firm foundation of the Adhvaryu;
he who knows thus stands firmly"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said: "If one were to offer while stepping forward, he would depart from his firm foundation;
therefore, the offering should be made by one standing in the same place, for the sake of stability."

This [practice] occurs elsewhere than in the *havis*-sacrifices, for it is said, "He offers while stepping forward" in the *havis*-sacrifices. Now, furthermore, it is said: "Whoever knows the property of the Adhvaryu becomes possessed of property; the ladle (*sruc*) is his property, the *vāyavya* cup is his property, and the *camasa* vessel is his property."
"If one were to cause the announcement (*āśrāvayet*) without holding onto either the vessel for Vāyu (*vāyavya*) or the cup (*camasa*), he would depart from his own [nature]";
therefore, he causes the announcement while holding onto both the vessel for Vāyu and the cup, so that he does not depart from his own [nature]. Thus says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said:

"He who introduces the *stotra* without having established the *soma*, his *soma* becomes unestablished, the *stoma* becomes unestablished, the *ukthas* become unestablished, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) becomes unestablished, and the *adhvaryu* becomes unestablished. The wind-deity (*vāyavya*) is the support of the *soma*, and the cup (*camasa*) is its support; the *stoma* is the support of the *stoma*, and the *graha* is the support of the *ukthas*. Having either drawn a *graha* or poured out the contents of the cup, he should introduce the *stotra*; for pouring out is indeed the drawing of the cup. Thus, having either drawn a *graha* or poured out the contents of the cup, he introduces the *stotra*.
"He establishes the Soma toward [the sacrificer], toward the Stoma, toward the Ukthas,
and the Adhvaryu stands toward the sacrificer"— so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, indeed, it is said:
They indeed prepare the sacrifice when they take the footprint of the Soma-purchase cow; the two Havirdhāna sheds are the mouth of the sacrifice.
Therefore, at the moment they move the two Havirdhāna sheds forward, he should then smear an axle with that [clay].
When he moves the two *havirdhāna* carts eastward, then with that third footprint he anoints the axle-end for the wife;
"He thus extends the sacrifice from the very mouth of the sacrifice," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, moreover, it is said:

They carry the fire forward; they lead the wife away; they let the sacrificial utensils follow after. Now, this hearth-fire of his is left behind; it broods and, becoming Rudra, is capable of destroying the offspring and cattle of the sacrificer. "When they lead the animal, once it has been consecrated with the *āprī* verses, toward the north, then one should take its *paśuśrapaṇa* (animal-cooking) fire," so it is said. When they lead the animal, once it has been consecrated with the *āprī* verses, toward the north, then he takes its *paśuśrapaṇa* fire;
by that very means, he makes it a sharer [in the sacrifice]. Thus says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now it is indeed said:
"The Āhavanīya fire is the sacrificer; they tear the sacrificer asunder when they carry the animal-cooking fire from the Āhavanīya.
Therefore, that [fire] itself should be used, or one should produce it by friction."
If he intends to perform it for him, he does not bring the firewood after him; rather, that very fire remains burning there continuously.
But if he does bring it after him, then at the time of the animal sacrifice, having taken a firebrand and grasped the two kindling woods (*araṇī*), he goes before the animal;
they cook the animal here by means of the fire produced by friction.
"They bring the omentum together with the firebrand for the sake of the sacrificer’s integrity," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is further said: "If a portion of the victim should be lost, one should cut from clarified butter as a substitute."
"As many portions as of the victim's meat are lost, so many times does he cut off [portions] of clarified butter in their stead;
that indeed is the expiation for it," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, moreover, it is said:

If those who have seized an animal should desire, "May they meet with misfortune," he should offer an oblation in the Āgnīdhra fire with the verse beginning "kuvidaṅga" that contains the word "namas. He offers it in the Āgnīdhra fire with the verse beginning "kuvidaṅga" that contains the word "namas"; thus he appropriates their very act of homage.
"They go toward the slaughter," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, if he slaughters a solitary animal, he offers this at the Śāmitra fire;
the procedure for the dedication is well known as it has been stated. The performance of the Apāvya offerings is explained in the subsequent Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it occurs thus:
He who performs a sacrifice not according to its respective deity is cut off from the deities and becomes worse off;

he who performs it according to the respective deity is not cut off from the deities and becomes more prosperous. One should touch the *Āgnīdhra* shed with a verse addressed to Agni, the *Havirdhāna* shed with one addressed to Viṣṇu, the ladles with one addressed to Agni, the *Vāyavya* cups with one addressed to Vāyu, and the *Sadas* with one addressed to Indra.

Thus, by touching the *Āgnīdhra* with a verse addressed to Agni, the *Havirdhāna* with one addressed to Viṣṇu, the ladles with one addressed to Agni, the *Vāyavya* cups with one addressed to Vāyu, and the *Sadas* with one addressed to Indra, he performs the sacrifice according to its respective deity.
"He is not cut off from the deities; he becomes more prosperous"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
The laying of the great enclosing-sticks made of Udumbara wood has been explained, as has the placing of the offering-spoons.
The touching of the vessels has been explained. Now, it is said:

"The Adhvaryu is indeed the one who desires success for the sacrificer; surely, he who desires success first perishes from his mouth. One should offer [an oblation] before the Prātaranuvāka with the words: "Protect me from the mantra in my mouth, from every curse!

Rising at the dead of night before the Prātaranuvāka, the Āgnīdhra offers in the mouth [of the fire] with: "Protect me from the mantra in my mouth, from every curse! Svāhā! Thus, the Adhvaryu binds protection upon himself beforehand so as not to suffer injury; so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now it is indeed said: "He who overcomes by means of the meters overcomes both those who press the Soma.

Therefore, having risen during the great night while the two [sacrificers] are pressing the Soma, he offers three oblations for overcoming in the Āgnīdhra fire, saying: "For settling thee, for entering thee, for the overcoming of the Gāyatrī, svāhā! For settling thee, for entering thee, for the overcoming of the Triṣṭubh, svāhā! For settling thee, for entering thee, for the overcoming of the Jagatī, svāhā! Then he offers two breath-oblations, saying: "O Prāṇa and Apāna, protect me from death; O Prāṇa and Apāna, do not abandon me! Now it is indeed said:
"Those for whom the Soma comes together strive against the deities regarding the out-breath and the in-breath.
'For settling thee, for sitting down thee,' he says; the meters are indeed the settling and the sitting down. 'By means of the meters he appropriates his meters,' so says the Brāhmaṇa."

Now, indeed, it is said: "Of him who has more sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*), they say that he appropriates the deities. If there should be a *soma* sacrifice of the *agniṣṭoma* type further on, one should perform the *ukthya*; thus he enters upon the *ukthya* rite.
"If it should be an Ukthya, one should perform an Atirātra"—thus he enters the Atirātra sacrifice;
"by means of the sacrificial rites (yajñakratu), he appropriates the deities for himself and becomes more prosperous," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
This is from the perspective of the Adhvaryu; now, from the perspective of the Chandoga.

The *ājya* verses are both *pretivant* and *caitivant* for the sake of victory; the *pratipad* verses contain [the word] "Marutvat" for the sake of conquest. Both the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara* are used. Now, according to the *Chandoga* tradition, there is the *Sajanīya* to be recited by the Hotṛ, the *Vihavya* to be recited, and Agastya’s *Kayāśubhīya* to be recited. Now, this is for those performing a one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*); but for those performing a sacrificial session (*sattra*), the rising at the end of the night is the same. There are five *abhibhūti* verses and two *prāṇāhuti* offerings.

They proceed according to their resolve; they undertake the days as they have been assigned. The recitation over the *nigrābhya* waters has already been explained. Now, indeed, it is said: "The plants are the subjects (*viś*) of Soma. The subjects, indeed, are capable of bestowing [sovereignty] upon a king. Soma belongs to Indra."

Having pressed [the Soma], he begs the King from the plants, saying: "O well-born ones, born of Truth, I have increased you with my mind; may we be sharers in your portion. O divine plants, in harmony with Indra, may you permit the Soma for the pressing. Regarding this, the Brāhmaṇa says: "Verily, having begged him from the plants, from his own people, and from his own deity, he presses him. Now it is said: "If the first shoot of the Soma being pressed should fall, it is capable of destroying the sensory power, vigor, progeny, and cattle of the sacrificer; one should address that [shoot] with a mantra."

When the first drop of the Soma being pressed falls, he should address it with the mantra: "Do not fall away from me, together with offspring and together with abundance of wealth; do not destroy my sensory power and my vigor. This is indeed a benediction he invokes for the sake of the non-destruction of his sensory power, vigor, offspring, and cattle—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Herein is this *drapsānumantraṇīyā* (the mantra for addressing the fallen drops);
we shall recite it along with the others. Now, it is also said:

He who indeed endows the gods with the glory of the gods and men with the glory of men becomes possessed of the glory of the gods among the gods and possessed of the glory of men among men. Those cups which he should draw prior to the Āgrayaṇa, those he should draw with the *upāṃśu* [whispered] formula; those which are subsequent, those he should draw with the *upabdimat* [resounding] formula. Thus, those cups which he draws prior to the Āgrayaṇa, those he draws with the *upāṃśu* formula.
Those chants which are recited loudly and accompanied by responsive responses (*upabdimat*), he thereby endows the gods with divine glory and men with human glory;

thus he becomes possessed of divine glory among the gods and possessed of human glory among men—so says the Brāhmaṇa. When they are about to chant the *bahiṣpavamāna*, while they have all taken hold of one another, he offers a spoonful of oblation in the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra: "May Agni Vaiśvānara, who is beneficial to all, protect us at the morning pressing by his greatness. May he, the purifier, bestow wealth upon us. May we be long-lived, sharing in the draught together, Svāhā!"

During the midday *pavamāna*, when they have likewise taken hold of one another, he offers a spoonful (*sruvāhuti*) into the *āhavanīya* fire with the mantra: "May the Viśve Devas, the Maruts, and Indra not abandon us at this second pressing; may we, long-lived and speaking what is pleasing to them, abide in the good favor of the gods, svāhā! During the *ārbhava-pavamāna*, when they have likewise taken hold of one another, he offers a spoonful into the *āhavanīya* fire with the mantra: "This is the third pressing of the seers (*kavīnām*), those who by means of the Eternal Law (*ṛta*) set the chalice (*camasa*) in motion."

"May those sons of Sudhanvan, having attained heaven, lead our well-offered sacrifice toward greater prosperity—Svāhā! Now, it is indeed said: "Some oblations are offered with a proper foundation (*āyatana*), while others are without a foundation. Those which possess the *āghāra* libation have a foundation; those belonging to Soma are without a foundation. Having taken the cup for Indra and Vāyu, one should perform the *āghāra* libation. Thus, having taken the cup for Indra and Vāyu, he performs the *āghāra* libation: "O gods, may this sacrifice be a peaceful rite (*adhvara*) for the plants, for our cattle, and for our people. For all beings you are the peaceful rite; swell, O divine Soma, with ghee—Svāhā!"
"He thus makes the oblations gentle and provided with a dwelling-place; he who knows this becomes possessed of a dwelling-place. Moreover, he anoints heaven and earth with ghee;
when they are anointed, they become sources of sustenance, and he who knows this becomes a source of sustenance," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Then the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the residue of the Manthin cup on the northern half of the Āhavanīya fire with the formula: "O Rudra, this is your portion which you requested; enjoy it! May we obtain lordship over cattle, abundance of wealth, and excellent heroic strength for a full year—Svāhā! Now, it is indeed said:
"Manu divided his inheritance among his sons;
he excluded Nābhānediṣṭha, who was living as a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī)."
He arrived;
he said, "Why have you excluded me?
[The others] replied, "We have not excluded you. These Aṅgirases are performing a sacrificial session."
They do not know the world of heaven;
speak this Brāhmaṇa to them,
for as they go to the world of heaven, those who are their cattle will give them [the way].

"He told this to them"—this they ask: "What did he tell them? [The answer is: the *apāvyas*, the *santanīs*, the *drapsānumantraṇīyas*, the *acchāvākīyās*, the *stotrīyās*, and the *śastrīyās*; "Speak the truth; let not faith depart from you"—this is what he told them. Then, as he was moving about with the sacrificial animals on the sacrificial ground, Rudra approached him; this is a restatement of that ritual action already mentioned. Then he offers two *pravṛtāhuti* oblations.

"May I be one who delights in speech; may I perfect the hymn with the *ṛc*," [he says]. Regarding this third [verse], we shall speak of it later. Then he consecrates the drops with the formulas: "The drop has fallen," "Thy drop which [has fallen]," and "The drop which is thy drop. Now it is indeed said: "The Adhvaryu is the first of the officiating priests to be yoked; by him the *stoma* must be yoked.
Therefore, when they proceed to the *bahiṣpavamāna*, the Adhvaryu proceeds first, bowing low and holding two blades of *barhis* grass.
"May speech, going at the head, go at the head; going straight, bestowing glory upon me from the gods, [bestowing] vital breaths upon the cattle, and offspring upon me and the sacrificer," he says.
"Thus he yokes speech itself at the mouth of the sacrifice," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it occurs as follows:
Indeed, this very thing is performed as a foundation for the sacrifice: that having drawn the cups, they proceed to the *bahis-pavamāna* chant;
for they go away from here, and they chant with verses directed away.
"Having returned, he worships with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu.
He indeed returns and worships with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu;

for Viṣṇu is the sacrifice, and thus he has made it the sacrifice. "O Viṣṇu, you who are nearest to us, grant us protection, O victorious one! Your streams, dripping with honey, milk out an inexhaustible spring," so he says.

"Whatever of him dries up while he is lying down, that very thing he causes to swell by means of this," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is also said: "He who, knowing the ascents of the Pavamāna chants, performs the sacrifice, truly ascends after the Pavamānas."

"One is not separated from the Pavamāna [laud]," it is said. At the Bahiṣpavamāna, when the fifth [verse] has been commenced, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite: "Thou art a falcon, having the Gāyatrī metre; I take hold of thee; lead me safely across.

At the Mādhyandina-pavamāna, when the eighth [verse] has been commenced, he causes him to recite: "Thou art a well-winged bird, having the Triṣṭubh metre; I take hold of thee; lead me safely across. At the Ārbhava-pavamāna, when the ninth [verse] has been commenced, he causes him to recite: "Thou art a steed, having the Jagatī metre; I take hold of thee; lead me safely across. These, indeed, are the "ascents" (anvārohas) of the Pavamāna lauds.
"One who, knowing them thus, performs the sacrifice, ascends after the Pavamāna chants and is not cut off from the Pavamānas," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it occurs:
He who indeed knows the continuity of the Pavamāna reaches a full lifespan;
he does not die before his time,
and he becomes possessed of cattle.

One obtains offspring through the *pavamāna* cups; these are the cups drawn for him. Now, if these were not drawn—the *droṇakalaśa*, the *ādhavanīya*, and the *pūtabhṛt*—and one were to proceed without having drawn them, he would sever the *pavamāna*.

If that *pavamāna* were severed, the breath of the *adhvaryu* would follow after it and be severed. Therefore, one should touch the *droṇakalaśa* with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; for Prajāpati, thee!"
With "For Prajāpati thee," he touches the *droṇakalaśa*; with "For Indra thee," the *ādhavanīya*;
and with "For the Viśvedevas thee," the *pūtabhṛt*.
Thus, he maintains the continuity of the *pavamāna* [soma].
He attains a full lifespan;
he does not die before his time;
he becomes possessed of cattle.

"He obtains offspring," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is indeed said: "There are three pressings; yet they omit the third pressing, making it incomplete. Having offered the Upāṃśu [libation], having placed the *aṃśu* stalk in the Upāṃśu vessel, one should mix it with that [stalk] at the third pressing and press it."
"That *aṃśu* which has been set aside in the *upāṃśu* vessel, he pours into the *ṛjīṣa* of the midday pressing and presses it.
In that he causes it to swell, by that it becomes *aṃśumat*; in that he presses it, by that it becomes *ṛjīṣin*.
Thus he makes all the pressings *aṃśumat*, *śukravat*, and of equal strength," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, therefore, follows the investigation concerning those [Soma vessels] that have burst or leaked.

If the *droṇakalaśa* has burst or leaked, having taken four portions with the dipping-spoon (*pātrī*), he offers them into the *āhavanīya* fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, reciting: "The grey-haired one has swallowed the bright, darting youth who was in the midst of many. Behold the poetic power of the god through his greatness; he who died today was here yesterday, O living one! Svāhā! Then, having poured water from the *vasatīvarī* waters into the *hotṛcamasa*, he collects its essence, reciting: "May prosperity increase through Soma; may the wealth of this [Soma] which has been sacrificed and consumed come to me."
He consecrates the spilled [soma] with the mantra: "To the Lord of the Earth, svāhā! To the Lord of the World, svāhā! To the Lord of Beings, svāhā!"

If it is cracked, he smears it; if, however, it has leaked, having lifted it up and placed two blades of *barhis* grass between, he pours the *svadhā* offering into it. Having removed the two blades of *barhis*, he causes a portion to spill from the *āgrayaṇa* vessel into the *ādhavanīya* jar, whether it is cracked or has leaked. In that same manner, having taken four spoonfuls into a vessel, he offers it into the *āhavanīya* fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, [reciting]: "Two oceans, vast and undecaying, revolve like feet within the belly."

Beholding one of the two, they pass over it; not beholding the other, they pass over it with the cry, "Svāhā! Then, having poured water from the *vasatīvarī* vessels into the *hotṛ*'s cup, he collects its dregs in the same manner as before, saying: "May prosperity increase through Soma; may wealth come to me from that which has been sacrificed and enjoyed. He consecrates what has been spilled with: "To the Lord of the Earth, Svāhā! To the Lord of the World, Svāhā! To the Lord of Beings, Svāhā!"

If it (the *pūtabhṛt* vessel) is cracked, he smears it; if, however, it is leaking, having lifted it up and placed two blades of *barhis* grass in between, he pours the *svadhā* offering into it. Having removed the two blades of *barhis*, he causes the *āpyāyana* (supplementary libation) to flow from the *āgrayaṇa* vessel into the *pūtabhṛt*, whether it be cracked or leaking. In that same manner, having taken four portions into a ladle, he offers it into the *āhavanīya* fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, [reciting]: "The one with long hair, knowing all beings, clothes himself in two continuous garments; covering himself in black, he takes up the bright [milk] for his aged mother, Svāhā!"

Then, having poured out water from the *vasatīvarī* waters into the *hotṛ*-cup, he collects its essence in the same manner as before with the formula: "May prosperity increase through Soma; may wealth come to me from that which has been offered and consumed.
He consecrates what has been spilled with the formula: "To the Lord of the Earth, Svāhā! To the Lord of the World, Svāhā! To the Lord of Beings, Svāhā!"

If it indeed breaks, he smears it [with the sediment]; if, however, it leaks, having lifted it up and placed two blades of *barhis* grass in between, he pours the *svadhā* offering into it; then, removing the two blades of *barhis*, he causes the sediment to flow back from the *āgrayaṇa* vessel. If the *āgrayaṇa* itself breaks or leaks, having offered with its *puroruc* verse and lifted it up, he places two blades of *barhis* grass in between and pours the *svadhā* offering into it; then, removing the two blades of *barhis*, he causes the sediment to flow back from the *droṇakalaśa*.

Now, if another cup has been split or has begun to leak, one offers with a verse addressed to that very deity, raises it up, places two blades of *barhis* grass between [it and the vessel], and pours the *svadhā* offering. Having removed the two blades of *barhis*, he causes the liquid to flow out from the *Āgrayaṇa* vessel itself.
Now, it is indeed said:
"Whatever the gods did at the sacrifice, the Asuras did likewise."
Those gods perceived this great sacrifice; they performed it.
They made the *agnihotra* their vow;
therefore, one should observe two vows, for twice they offer the *agnihotra*.
They made the Full Moon sacrifice the animal sacrifice for Agni and Soma; they made the New Moon sacrifice the animal sacrifice for Agni;
and they made the Vaiśvadeva the morning pressing.
They made the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings the midday pressing, the Sākamedha offerings the third pressing, and the Pitṛyajña and Tryambaka offerings the third pressing;
regarding this they ask, "Which is that great sacrifice? It is said that this very Cāturmāsya is the Soma sacrifice; moreover, whatever Soma-sacrifice there may be, that is the great sacrifice.
The Asuras once sought to attack that sacrifice of theirs.
They did not follow him;
they said, "These gods have indeed become those who are not to be served (adhvartavya). That is the reason for the name of the *adhvara* sacrifice.
"Then the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated; he who, knowing thus, sacrifices with Soma, prospers in himself and his rival is defeated"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Then he worships the entire King [Soma] with the verse: "Encompassing Agni, encompassing Indra, encompassing all the gods, encompass me with spiritual luster! Flow for us as a blessing for our cattle, a blessing for our people, a blessing for our horses; O King, a blessing for the plants! O Lord of Wealth, may we be givers of your unbroken, heroic, and increasing riches. Grant me of that; may I partake of that which is yours; cleanse this for me from that. There are four desires fulfilled by the Brāhmaṇas; whichever desire he wishes for among them, he should specify it when the cleansing is performed. Then he proceeds with the *avakāśa* (invocations).

With the words, "For my out-breath, O giver of splendor, flow pure for splendor," he looks at the Upāṃśu cup; with "for the in-breath," the Antaryāma cup; with "for the diffused breath," the Upāṃśusavana stone; with "for speech," the Aindravāyava cup; with "for skill and will," the Maitrāvaruṇa cup; with "for hearing," the Āśvina cup; with "for the two eyes," the Śukra and Manthin cups; with "for the self," the Āgrayaṇa cup;
with "for the limbs," the Ukthya cup; and with "for life," the Dhruva cup; and with "for stability," the two Ṛtu cups at the midday pressing.
At the morning pressing, he does not gaze at either the *atigrāhya* cup or the *ṣoḍaśin* cup with the formula "For valor.
He gazes at the *droṇakalaśa* with "Thou art the belly of Viṣṇu," at the *ādhavanīya* with "Thou art the belly of Indra," and at the *pūtabhṛt* with "Thou art the belly of the All-gods."

Then he worships the entire King [Soma] with: "Who art thou? What is thy name? For whom thee? To whom thee? Him thee whom I have satiated with Soma; him thee whom I have gladdened with Soma—may I be rich in good offspring through offspring, rich in heroes through heroes, rich in splendor through splendor, rich in nourishment through nourishments! O giver of splendor, for all my forms, flow for splendor! Grant me of that! May I partake of that which is thine! Of that which is thine, cleanse this!"

There are four desires fulfilled by one perfected as a Brahmin; whichever desire he may wish for, he declares: "I wipe away life; I wipe away prosperity; I wipe away spiritual luster; I wipe away the breath of so-and-so; I wipe away this!

Whomever he thus satisfies, that person—being satisfied—departs from him through his out-breath and in-breath, his speech and his skillful resolve, his two eyes and his two ears, and from his very self and its limbs, taking away his life.
"The Brahmana has stated that 'they run forward quickly'; the worship of the *sphyavighana* stones has been stated;
and the recitation for the consumption of the soma during the *saṃprasarpaṇa* has been stated."
The taking of the unmixed *pṛṣadājya* has been stated; the *dadhigharma* has been stated. Now, it is said:

"If a black bird should touch the *pṛṣadājya*, his *śūdras* would be liable to die; if a dog should touch it, his four-footed cattle would be liable to die; if it should spill, the sacrificer would be liable to die. Now, it is further said:
"The speckled butter is indeed cattle; cattle indeed spill away for him whose speckled butter spills.
In that he takes up the speckled butter again, he recovers the cattle for him—so says the Brāhmaṇa."
Now it is indeed said:
"The speckled butter is indeed the vital breath; the vital breath of that person indeed spills away whose speckled butter spills."
In that he takes up the speckled butter again, he thereby recovers his breath for him;
he takes it after placing gold within.
When the speckled butter has been spilled, he asks for either a vessel or a cup.
Having placed it within the altar, he gathers its essence with the formula: "May prosperity increase through curds and ghee; may the wealth of that which has been offered and consumed come to me."

He consecrates the spilled [soma] with the formula: "To the Lord of the Earth, Svāhā! To the Lord of the World, Svāhā! To the Lord of Beings, Svāhā! Then he places a gold piece weighing a hundred mānas into this ladle; at the regular drawing [of the soma], he recites the verse addressed to Viṣṇu: "O Viṣṇu, you are our nearest... Having removed the gold and made the horse smell [the offering], he sets it down. Now, regarding that which has become impure—such as what has been smelled by a dog, wiped by a crow, or infested by insects, or whatever else he considers impure.

Having entirely immersed this ladle into the water, he then places a piece of gold weighing a hundred mānas into another ladle; at the regular drawing of the portion, he recites the verse addressed to Viṣṇu: "O Viṣṇu, you are our closest [kinsman]. Having removed the gold and caused the horse to smell it, he sets it down. Now it is said: "The sacrifice of him whose *pṛṣadājya* spills is indeed torn asunder;
he takes it up again with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu."

He takes it up again with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu; "Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; by means of the sacrifice he continues the sacrifice," so says the Brāhmaṇa. When they are about to proceed within the hall, he says: "O Brahman, we shall proceed; O Hotṛ, recite for the Gharma!

Then the Brahman gives the impulse: "O God Savitṛ, he has declared this to you; impel it and perform the sacrifice! Bṛhaspati is the Brahman; protect the sacrifice, protect the lord of the sacrifice, protect me! Om! Proceed! Thus it stands in the Haviryajñas.

When [the Hotṛ] says, "O Brahman, we shall praise; O Praśāstṛ," then the Brahman gives the impulse: "O God Savitṛ, he has told this to you; impel it and perform the sacrifice! Bṛhaspati is the Brahman. Do not depart from the long-lived Ṛc, nor from the body-protecting Sāman; may your blessings be true, may your intentions be true; speak Ṛta and Satya! Praise at the impulse of the god Savitṛ: 'bhūr, praised with Indra!'—thus at the morning pressing; 'bhuvaḥ, praised with Indra!'—thus at the midday pressing;
'suvar, praised with Indra!'—thus at the third pressing."

At the *stotra*, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite the "milking" of the *stotra*: "Thou art the *stotra* of the *stotra*; may the *stotra* milk strength for me; may the *stotra* of the *stotra* not depart from me. At the *śastra*, he causes him to recite the "milking" of the *śastra*: "Thou art the *śastra* of the *śastra*; may the *śastra* milk strength for me; may the *śastra* of the *śastra* not depart from me."

He causes both of them to recite the practice: "As many as we choose, may we milk offspring and food; may this my true blessing be among the gods; may spiritual luster come to me. Then he mutters the re-attainment of the sacrifice: "The sacrifice came into being; it has come into being; it was born; it grew; it became the overlord of the gods; may it make us overlords; may we be masters of riches. Now it is indeed said:
"Either the sacrifice milks the lord of the sacrifice, or the lord of the sacrifice milks the sacrifice."
If one performs a sacrifice without knowing the milking of the Stotra and Śastra, the sacrifice milks him;
having sacrificed, he becomes worse off.
But if one performs a sacrifice knowing the milking of these two, he milks the sacrifice.
"Having sacrificed, he becomes more prosperous.

'The praise of the praised is yours; may the praised yield me strength; may the praise of the praised not pass me by! The recitation of the recited is yours; may the recitation yield me strength; may the recitation of the recitation not pass me by! Thus he says. This indeed is the milking of the praise and the recitation.
He who, knowing this, sacrifices, truly milks the sacrifice."
"By sacrificing, one becomes more prosperous"— so it is stated in the Brāhmaṇa; the satiation of the *hotṛ*-priests has been described,
the *vaiśvakarman* offerings have been described, and the pouring of the *āśiras* mixture has been described.

The ritual procedure for the *dhruva* cup has been declared. Now, when the *hotṛ* calls out to the *adhvaryu*, he hurls a thunderbolt at him. He says, "O reciter of hymns (*ukthaśas*)"; having responded to the morning pressing, he says, "O reciter of hymns. Having responded to each hymn, or to each pressing, he says, "The hymn is uttered. Having responded to the midday pressing, he says, "The hymn is uttered; O Indra, come! Having responded to the third pressing...
"These seven syllables are the seven-footed Śakvarī;
the Śakvarī is the thunderbolt. By means of the thunderbolt itself, he places the thunderbolt between [the earth and the sky] at the third pressing," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it is so:
the exponents of sacred knowledge say, "He would be a true *adhvaryu* who, in the response (*pratigara*), should bring the meters into correspondence with each pressing:

he should place brilliance within himself at the morning pressing, sensory power at the midday pressing, and cattle at the third pressing. Having responded to the morning pressing, he says, "The reciter (*ukthaśas*)"; having responded to the midday pressing, he says, "The hymn is in speech (*ukthaṃ vāci*)"; and having responded to the third pressing, he says, "To Indra, O Vāc! (*ukthaṃ vācīndrāya*).
These are seven syllables;
the Śakvarī consists of seven feet; cattle are connected with the Śakvarī; and the third pressing belongs to the Jagatī.
"Only at the third pressing does he accomplish the meters in the response; moreover, the Jagatī is indeed cattle, and the third pressing is cattle;
thus he places cattle within himself at the third pressing," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now it is indeed said:
"In that the Hotṛ calls out toward the Adhvaryu, he places a blemish in him;
therefore, lest they should be afflicted in his house before the year is out, he should respond with 'Oṃ! Soma! Modīva! (ŚB 3.5.2.10).
When he is called out, he responds with "Śom̐ sā modīva," for by that very means it is struck away; thus says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, there is this [further teaching]:

Just as one awaits a long-distance runner, so does the Adhvaryu await the response (*pratigara*). If he were to respond prematurely, it would be just as if he were to collide with the runner; if he were to omit [the response] at the half-verse (*ardharca*), it would be just as if he were left behind by those who are running. Regarding this they say: "One should not be a responder who anticipates the call. For such an anticipatory responder either responds too early or omits [the response] at the half-verse.

"One should respond with 'praṇau' as if one were breathing out, and one should respond with 'apāni' as if one were breathing in. He who, knowing thus, responds, becomes an eater of food, and a vigorous son is born among his offspring," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is further said: "This [earth] indeed is the Hotṛ, and that [sky] is the Adhvaryu. When the Hotṛ sits, he does not depart from this very earth; for she, as it were, sits.
Moreover, by this means the sacrificer milks this very earth."
In that the Adhvaryu responds while standing, he does not depart from that very [world] of yonder sun; for yonder sun stands, as it were. Moreover, by that means the sacrificer milks yonder sun.
In that [the Hotṛ] recites while sitting, therefore the gods subsist upon what is offered from here.
Because he responds while standing, therefore humans live upon what is given from above;

because he responds while sitting facing east and [the sacrificer] standing facing west, therefore seed is deposited in the eastward direction and offspring are born facing westward— so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now it is indeed said: "When the Hotṛ calls out toward the Adhvaryu, he hurls a thunderbolt at him; therefore, he should turn away."
"When he is thus summoned, he turns away;
he thereby strikes down the thunderbolt," so says the Brāhmaṇa regarding the taking of the *pratinirgrāhya* cups.
The covering of the residue has been stated;
the consecration of the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups has been stated;
the procedure for the dual-deity offerings has been stated.
Now, therefore, follows the drawing of the *atigrāhya* cups. Whether there be one or many, having drawn them from the *āgrayaṇa* vessel itself, he draws them;
they are offered following the offering of the *māhendra* cup.
He draws the cup for Agni, reciting: "O Agni, you purify our lives... and then: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the radiant Agni."

Having wiped [the ladle], he sets it down with: "This is thy womb; for Agni, the radiant, thee. Then, about to offer it, he gazes at it: "O Agni, thou art radiant; mayest thou be radiant among the gods; make me radiant, long-lived, and full of luster among men. He offers with: "I offer thee for the consecration and for the luster of austerity.
Having offered, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite: "Thou art the knower of luster; may luster not forsake me; may I not forsake luster; may luster not forsake me."

"May he consume my wisdom, my progeny; may Agni bestow splendor upon me"—thus [he says]. Then he draws the draught for Indra, running forward with the mantra, "Rising up together with vigor," and having murmured, "Thou art taken with a base;
I take thee, acceptable to Indra the vigorous," he wipes it around and sets it down with, "This is thy womb;
for Indra the vigorous. Then, about to offer it, he gazes at it, saying: "O Indra, the vigorous one, mayest thou become vigorous among the gods; make me vigorous, long-lived, and radiant among men."
Having offered the oblation, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite: "O possessor of vigor, let vigor not forsake me; may I not forsake vigor; may vigor not forsake me.

He then consumes [the remnant] with the formula: "In me may wisdom, in me progeny, and in me may Indra bestow sensory power. Then, with a verse addressed to Sūrya, he draws the draught for Sūrya, reciting: "The swift one, visible to all," and continuing: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to radiant Sūrya."

Having wiped it around, he sets it down with the formula: "This is thy womb; for the radiant Sūrya, thee! Then, about to offer it, he gazes at it with the formula: "O radiant Sūrya, mayest thou be radiant among the gods; make me radiant, long-lived, and full of luster among men.
He offers it with the formula: "I offer thee for the radiance of Vāyu and of the Waters.
Having offered, he makes [the sacrificer] recite: "Thou art the finder of light; do not abandon me, the finder of light; may I not abandon the light; may the light not abandon me."

"May he consume wisdom in me, offspring in me; may Sūrya bestow radiance upon me"—these indeed are the [Soma] cups drawn on the latter days of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*: they are to be drawn at the twenty-one-fold, the twenty-seven-fold, the thirty-three-fold, and the *viśvajit* which consists of all the *pṛṣṭha*-stotras, for the sake of the sacrifice's possession of vigor. "They are also to be drawn at the *agniṣṭoma* for the sake of the sacrifice's continuity," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Then he mutters the introductory formula: "Vāyu is the *hiṃ*-singer. One who is about to perform the office of a priest (*ārtvijya*) or is about to respond to a recitation (*śastra*) mutters this *yajus*. With the words "Iḍā is the invoker of the gods," he becomes dear indeed to the office of the priest.
When about to explain a question, he enters the assembly hall while muttering this *yajus*; he surely triumphs over that question.

Now, therefore, follows the drawing of the Aṃśu and Adābhya cups. One who is about to draw the Aṃśu and Adābhya cups prepares two new vessels made of Udumbara wood; of these, the Aṃśu vessel has four corners, while the Adābhya vessel is smooth; they are both encircled by gold and silver plates, and there is also a piece of gold weighing a hundred mānas.

Then, from the king [Soma] who has been bound, he draws out three shoots with the formulas: "May the Vasus draw thee forth with the Gāyatrī metre; go to the beloved path of Agni! May the Rudras draw thee forth with the Triṣṭubh metre; go to the beloved path of Indra! May the Ādityas draw thee forth with the Jagatī metre; go to the beloved path of the Viśve Devas! Then, having poured water from the *vasatīvarī* vessels into the *hotṛ*-cup, he shakes it with twelve purifications, saying: "O bright one, in the *māndā* waters for thee..."
