Having begun with "I shake the bright," he then, having gathered the stalks into this Adābhya vessel, draws [the juice] with: "O bright one, I draw your bright [juice] with the bright, by the form of the day, with the rays of the sun."

"In this [vessel], the fierce, unceasing streams from heaven have flowed forth"—having said this, he takes it up and stands; "The lofty form of the bull shines brightly"—having said this, he goes; "Soma is the precursor of Soma, the bright one is the precursor of the bright"—having said this, he offers it in the Āhavanīya fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, saying: "O Soma, that invincible, wakeful name of yours—unto that, O Soma, for Soma, svāhā! Then, having turned to the right, he pours the swollen King [Soma] back into the [filtering] skin, saying: "O divine Soma, you have been sprinkled by means of the Gāyatrī metre for Agni."

"Go to the beloved abode, O divine Soma, you who have mastery; with the *triṣṭubh* metre, go to the beloved abode of Indra. You are our friend, O divine Soma; with the *jagatī* metre, go to the beloved abode of all the gods.
Then he says, "O Pratiprasthātṛ, receive [the water] from behind the Āhavanīya fire with either a vessel for water or a cup for joy."

He does so; then, having washed this gold with water, he ties it on his middle finger or fastens it upon his nose. Then, while mentally singing the *vāmadevya* Sāman without pausing, he takes a stalk (*aṃśu*) from the King [Soma] that has been pressed once, saying, "For Prajāpati, thee! He takes it saying, "For Prajāpati, thee! and offers it saying, "For Prajāpati, thee! Then, covering the gold, he recites: "May breath come to us from afar, from the intermediate space, and from heaven."

"Thou art the life-span of the earth; thou art immortality. For breath, thee! Then, within the altar (antarvedi), he purifies himself with water: "May Indra and Agni grant me splendor; may Soma and Bṛhaspati grant me splendor; may all the gods grant me splendor; O Aśvins, bestow splendor upon me."

"Or when he has run after it, he shall proclaim the sacred utterances (brahmāṇi); you indeed know that. "He has encompassed all poetic wisdoms as the felly encompasses the wheel"—this is the gold of the Adhvaryu;
the Brāhmaṇa portion follows.

Now, therefore, follows the drawing of the Pṛśni cups: having divided the King Soma, which has been fully satiated, into ten parts, he touches them with ten formulas, saying, "You are Vāyu, named Prāṇa," and so on for each of the ten.
These [cups] are indeed drawn on the days that do not decrease in the year;
"wherever one might draw them," this is another [view].

Now, therefore, follows the drawing of the *paraḥsāman* cups. These *paraḥsāman* cups are drawn day by day for three days prior to the *vaiṣuvata* day, proceeding from here outward; then on the *vaiṣuvata* day itself, they are drawn both outward and inward; and thereafter, for three days above the *vaiṣuvata*, he draws them only in reverse order.

"Prajāpati created the gods and the asuras," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, there is also this [text]: "The sacrificer is indeed cut off from the two fires when, having prepared what is cooked for them, he goes elsewhere for the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha). One who is about to go to the avabhṛtha should offer an oblation with the words: 'O Agni, giver of life, enjoying the oblation.'"

Intending to perform the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), he offers the tenth oblation, the "Life-giver" (*āyurdā*). [The mantra: "O Agni, giver of life, enjoying the oblation, with ghee as your face and ghee as your womb, come! Having drunk the ghee and the sweet, pleasant product of the cow, protect this person like a father protects his son; Svāhā! By means of this offering, he indeed pacifies these two; the sacrificer does not meet with misfortune—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
The procedure for the burning of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) has been stated, and the procedure for the offering of parched grain flour (*saktu-homa*) has been stated. Now, it is further said:
"If one should act as if mixed [with the fire], he should offer groats with his cupped hands into a forest fire," so it is said.

A *snātaka* who considers himself a man of merit, having approached a forest fire burning in the wilderness, offers groats—previously spread out and sprinkled with clarified butter—into that forest fire with his cupped hands, saying: "O Viśvālopa, I offer thee into the mouth of Viśvadāva, svāhā! Then he rubs his hands together, saying: "One has eaten, one has not offered, one has gathered together; may they provide us with healing, a dwelling, strength, and what is excellent. Then he purifies him with three bunches of *darbha* grass using this eight-verse hymn beginning: "The purifying one, the winner of heaven..."

He indeed becomes pure, clean, purified, and fit for sacrifice. Now, regarding the rule for the days: on the Ekāṣṭakā day, having baked a cake of four śarāvas of grain, one should burn the brushwood with it in the morning.

Desiring to know the year, he rises during the dead of night; on the Ekāṣṭakā day, according to the rule for the days, having baked a cake of four śarāvas of grain, when the sun has risen and its rays have scattered, he takes this cake—smeared with butter below and above—and grasps it with two palāśa leaves.
Together with that, there are putrid grasses; having taken a single firebrand from the end of the house and a vessel of water, they go toward that direction where his thicket is visible.
Having kindled that single firebrand and set it ablaze, he holds it with two leaves and twigs;
together with that, there are putrid grasses.
With that he heats the armpit; then he lifts it up. Here one attains a sign of knowledge:
if it burns, it is equal to merit; if it does not burn, it is equal to evil.
"By means of this very sign of knowledge, the seers of old used to enter upon long sacrificial sessions," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Having eaten this cake and sipped water, he goes home; the bull grows old among the cows, and by that he becomes one who is about to sacrifice.

That which is prepared for one about to sacrifice with an animal is now prepared for him. Then, if he is going to release it, he strikes its right ear and mutters over it the two verses, "O Tvaṣṭṛ, be auspicious" and "Of tawny form.
Thereafter, he releases it among the cows.

With the verse, "This youth I give over to you," he addresses him as he departs: "The cows chose you for kingship; the Maruts, the singers of fair hymns, call upon you. Standing at the height, at the peak of dominion, from there, O fierce one, distribute wealth to us. Then he sacrifices another animal to Tvaṣṭṛ, or to Indra, or to Prajāpati; for these are the deities of the castrated bull.

He follows the two introductory offerings with the verses, "Homage to the Greatness and to the Eye" and "Thine is this. Then he offers its omentum with the verse, "This was the bond of the gods. Then he offers its sacrificial oblation with the verse, "Father of calves, lord of the inviolable cows.
The subsequent ritual procedure for the animal sacrifice is the same.
When about to sacrifice with a cow that has a calf, he says, "Look at the embryo!"

If they see the embryo, they cover it over and offer the omentum of the barren cow; then he offers its omentum with the formula: "May the god Sūrya for those dwelling in heaven, Dhātṛ for the kṣatra, Vāyu for the subjects, and Bṛhaspati offer you, full of light, to Prajāpati—svāhā!"

He addresses the barren cow with the mantra: "Her embryo is tawny, and her womb is golden; her limbs are uninjured—her I have brought together with the gods. Then he asks for gold weighing eight *prasthas*, a chest and an inner chest, a garment, and a turban. Having washed this gold with water, bound it in the garment, and tied it with the turban, he places it in the small chest and then deposits it in the large chest.
He says: "Turn the embryo backward between the two thighs."

As it is being turned back, he addresses it with the mantra: "O turning one, turn hither; O turning-back one, turn back! Indra, Nardabuda, by the four quarters of the earth, turn it back again. He addresses the embryo as it is being released from the membrane with the mantra: "I split open thy caul, I split open the womb, I split open the two sides, the mother and the son, the embryo and the afterbirth; let thy hair be outside, O Bāli! Then, having grasped this embryo with the *ṛsadaṃśa* (a pair of tongs), and having sprinkled it with water, he heats it over the *śāmitra* fire.

From its belly he causes the fat-offering to drip. Then, having drawn out that embryo between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, between the sacrificial post and the *āhavanīya* fire, and having moved it southward facing east, he deposits it with the *pañcahotṛ* formula. Then he proceeds with the oblation of the barren cow (*vaśā*). Then, while cutting off portions of the embryo before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he says, "Recite for Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa!
Now it is said: "One should cut one portion from below the navel, and another from above."
He cuts one portion from in front of the navel and another from behind; he pours clarified butter over them twice. Having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa!

At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers the oblation with the verse: "The wide-striding, omniform drop, the purifying sage, has anointed the embryo. May she—of one foot, two feet, three feet, four feet, five feet, six feet, seven feet, eight feet—expand through the worlds, Svāhā!"

Then he proceeds with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; then, having carried that embryo back in the same manner it was brought, and having moved it westward on the northern half of the Āhavanīya fire, he covers it with ashes, saying: "May the great Heaven and Earth sprinkle this sacrifice for us; may they nourish us with their blessings. This becomes the Adhvaryu’s mixing-vessel; the Brāhmaṇa passage follows.
He is about to sacrifice with the *ajavaśā*.
On those days which he considers to be cloudless, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni.

Of those deities prescribed in the Brāhmaṇa, he sacrifices this one animal to a single deity; he follows it with the two introductory verses: "O Vāyu, come hither, O drinker of the pure," and so forth.
While she is being led forward, he follows with the formula: "For intention thee, for desire thee, for prosperity thee!

While the fire is being carried around her, he offers five *kikkiṭākāra* oblations: "Kikkiṭā! Thy mind to Prajāpati, svāhā! Kikkiṭā! Thy breath to Vāyu, svāhā! Kikkiṭā! Thy eye to Sūrya, svāhā! Kikkiṭā! Thy hearing to Heaven and Earth, svāhā! Kikkiṭā! Thy speech to Sarasvatī, svāhā! Then, as she is being led northward between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, he addresses her with the mantra: "Thou art the fourth, the all-pervading, the barren cow; when the embryo entered thee once with the mind."

"Go to the gods as a barren cow; may the desires of the sacrificer come true"—with these words he directs [the cow] toward the fire-wood. "Thou art a goat, established in wealth; sit upon the earth; stand upright in the mid-air; in heaven be thy great light"—with these words he offers its omentum, saying, "Stretching the thread, follow the radiance of the region. Then he offers its sacrificial portion, saying, "Thou art the oblation of the mind, the color of Prajāpati. Then he eats of its portions, saying, "May we become sharers of thy limbs. Now, indeed, it so happens:
For this very [cow], there is indeed one non-sacrificial ground (*adevayajana*): when it has been seized and a cloud appears.

If a cloud should appear when it has been seized, one should either cast it into the waters or consume it entirely. Regarding this, Baudhāyana says that casting it into the waters is a lost rite; rather, having consumed the portions (*avadāna*) with this same mantra for her, one should throw the remainder into the fire. Āñjīgavi, however, says that one should eat it after placing it down. Now, it is also said:
This [offering] is indeed appropriated by only three: those who sit for the year-long sacrifice, those who perform the thousand-fold sacrifice, and householders;
they alone should sacrifice with it, for it is attained only by them.

Indeed, one of these [priests] performs this sacrifice for them; now follows the oblation of the *jayas*. One intending to offer the *jayas* prepares a *bādhaka* wooden spoon and ladle, *bādhaka* enclosing-sticks (*paridhis*), sacrificial grass (*barhis*) made of *śara* reeds, and fuel (*idhma*) of *vaibhītaka* wood. Then, having kindled a common fire, strewn the *śara* grass, laid the *bādhaka* enclosing-sticks, and anointed the *vaibhītaka* fuel before adding it with the utterance "Svāhā!", he offers the oblations by dipping the *bādhaka* spoon, saying: "Consciousness, Svāhā! Perception, Svāhā!"—thus thirteen spoonfuls, or alternatively, [the full set].

Having taken four portions of clarified butter with the *bādhaka* dipping-spoon (*sruva*) into the *bādhakī* offering-ladle (*sruc*), and having recited all the mantras in succession, he offers [the oblation] with: "Thought and thinking, intention and intending, what is known and knowledge, mind and the Śakvarī verses, the new moon and the full moon, the Bṛhat and the Rathantara; Prajāpati gave these victories to Indra, the fierce one, in the battles for booty. To him all the people bowed down; he became fierce and worthy of invocation, Svāhā! Now, it is indeed said:
The gods and the asuras were arrayed for battle; Indra, having run to Prajāpati,
he gave him these Jaya oblations, and he offered them.

"Then indeed the gods conquered the Asuras; because they conquered, this is the victory of the victors. These [oblations] should be offered by one who is contending; he surely conquers that host," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it further occurs:
"One should offer into that fire for whatever rite one desires.

Therefore, for whatever rite one desires, thinking "May this be successful for me," one should offer the *abhyātāna* oblations. When about to offer the *abhyātāna* oblations, he prepares a ladle (*sruva*) and a large spoon (*sruk*) made of *parṇa* wood, enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) made of *parṇa*, sacrificial grass (*barhis*) made of *kuśa*, and fuel (*idhma*) made of *parṇa*. Then, having kindled a common fire, spread the *kuśa* sacrificial grass, laid the *parṇa* enclosing sticks around, and anointed the *parṇa* fuel, he places it on the fire with the utterance of "svāhā" and, using the *parṇa* ladle, makes the offerings by dipping.

Having offered seventeen spoonfuls with the formula, "Agni is the lord of beings; may he protect me," he makes [the sacrificer] recite, "O fathers, O grandfathers... Alternatively, having taken four portions of clarified butter with a ladle made of *parṇa* wood into a *sruc* made of *parṇa* wood, and having offered while reciting all the mantras together, he finally makes [the sacrificer] recite, "O fathers, O grandfathers... Now, the oblation for all [the ancestors] together: one should first offer the *abhyātāna* formulas, then the *jaya* formulas, then the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* formulas; the subsequent portion is for the Brāhmaṇa priest. Now, indeed, it is said: "They should be offered for one who desires a kingdom."

One who intends to offer for one desiring a kingdom prepares yoke-pin enclosures. Then, having established a common fire and laid the yoke-pin enclosures around it, he offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations at night with two *svāhā* utterances over each yoke-pin enclosure, using the formulas beginning "The upholder of Truth, whose abode is Truth.
The *rāṣṭrabhṛts* are indeed the kingdom; by means of the kingdom, he wins the kingdom for him, and he becomes the very kingdom—so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Now, indeed, there is this [text]: "They are to be offered for oneself. When about to offer for oneself, having kindled a fire in vain (without ritual purpose), he offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations at night with two *svāhā* utterances while using a wooden pin as the enclosing sticks.

For the *rāṣṭrabhṛts* are the kingdom; the kingdom is the progeny, the kingdom is the cattle, and the kingdom is that which one becomes when one is the most excellent. By means of the kingdom, he wins the kingdom;
he becomes the most excellent among his equals—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said:
"They are to be offered for one who desires a village.

One about to offer them for one desiring a village, having kindled a common fire on the gambling-ground, offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations at night with two *svāhā* utterances, using a wooden pin as the enclosing-stick.
The *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings are indeed the kingdom; the kinsmen are the kingdom. By means of the kingdom, he secures for him the kingdom and his kinsmen;
"he becomes possessed of a village," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now it is further said: "He offers on the gambling-ground; verily on the gambling-ground itself he secures for him his kinsmen."
"The *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings are to be made on the front of the chariot by one desiring vigor," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it is said:

"One desiring vigor, about to offer, should hold the front of the chariot over the fire at night and offer the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations twice with the utterance of *svāhā* upon the yoke-pin used as an enclosing stick (*paridhi*). For the *rāṣṭrabhṛts* are vigor, and the chariot is vigor; by means of vigor he wins vigor for himself, and he becomes possessed of vigor. So says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said:
"For one who has been expelled from his kingdom, these [oblations] should be offered. He should say to as many chariots as he possesses, 'Yoke them!
Thus, he yokes the kingdom for him"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now it is indeed said: "The oblations of him whose kingdom is not in order are unestablished; having removed the right wheel of his own chariot, he should offer upon the axle-rod.

Having thus removed the right wheel of his own chariot and held the chariot-axle over the fire at night, he offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* (kingdom-sustaining) oblations twice with the utterance of *svāhā* upon the yoke-pin as the enclosing-stick. Thus he establishes the oblations for him.
"Those [oblations] of his, when being prepared, prepare the kingdom accordingly," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said:
"When a battle is joined, they are to be offered."

When he is about to sacrifice in a battle that has been joined, he prepares fuel of *māndhuka* wood. Then, having established the fire against his enemy and having anointed the *māndhuka* fuel, he places it on the fire with the utterance of "svāhā. At night, using the yoke-pins as enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations twice with the utterance of "svāhā. "The embers, turning back, turn back the army of his enemies," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, there is this [further teaching]:

"If one should go mad, for him they are to be offered. Intending to offer for a madman, he prepares [wood] from the Nyagrodha, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Plakṣa trees. Then, having established a common fire and having anointed this fuel-stick, he places it on the fire with the utterance "Svāhā! At night, using the yoke-pins as enclosing sticks (paridhi), he offers the Rāṣṭrabhṛt oblations twice with the utterance "Svāhā. "These indeed are the dwellings of the Gandharvas and Apsarases; he thus pacifies them in their own abode," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Now, it is indeed said: "By one practicing sorcery, the oblations should be offered in reverse order. One who is about to practice sorcery, having established a fire at will in a self-made salt-flat or a cleft, at night, with the *śamyā* as the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations twice with the exclamation *svāhā*.
With whatever is cruel in speech, he utters the *vaṣaṭ*; by means of that cruelty of speech, he cuts him down.
"He incurs swift pain," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Now, it is further said: "If he should desire to take away the food of someone, let him lie down on his back in that person's assembly hall and gather blades of grass while reciting, 'O Lord of the World...

Thus, for whomever he should desire to take away the food, he lies down on his back in that person's assembly hall and gathers blades of grass while reciting, "O Lord of the World... Then, taking them up, he carries them away while saying, "Here I take away the food of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so. Verily, he takes away that person's food.
"He takes it away with six [verses]," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then he bestows these upon his own assembly or upon his own ministers;
"Having taken his food from him by means of Prajāpati, the seasons hand it over to him," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said: "If one's eldest kinsman should be unsuccessful, having settled him on dry ground and having cooked a *brahmaudana* of four *śarāva*-measures, one should offer it to him.

Therefore, if one's eldest kinsman should be unsuccessful, having settled him on dry ground and having cooked a *brahmaudana* of four *śarāva*-measures, he offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations at night upon a yoke-pin used as a sacrificial enclosure, twice with the utterance of *svāhā*.
"The *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings are indeed height; the high ground is height.
By means of height, he causes him to attain height among his equals," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, there is also this [text]: "It truly comes to pass."
It consists of four measures; thus one finds firm footing in the quarters. It is prepared with milk.
He bestows relish upon him; he takes it out for the sake of being cooked; it contains clarified butter for the sake of purity;
four who are descendants of seers consume it.
"One offers in the light of the quarters themselves," so says the Brāhmaṇa; now, it is further said: "One desiring offspring should offer the Devikās."
First he makes the Dhātṛ for one desiring offspring; first for one desiring cattle;
in the middle for one desiring a village.
In the middle for one who has been long ill;
first for one about to sacrifice; last for one who has already sacrificed; first for one desiring wisdom.
They are placed in the middle of the cart-pole;
these indeed are cooked in milk.
If he were to offer all of them together, they would be liable to burn him up; therefore, having offered two at the first stage, he should offer the third at the third stage.
"In the same way one should offer it in the northern part;
thus they do not burn him, and furthermore, he attains whatever desire for which it is offered"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, indeed, there is this [further teaching]:

In that he offers the Agnihotra in the evening and in the morning, the sacrificer lays down those very oblations as bricks. For one who has established the sacred fires, the days and nights are indeed his bricks; in that he offers in the evening and in the morning, having obtained the days and nights, he makes them into bricks and lays them down. He offers ten times in the same place;
the Virāj consists of ten syllables.
Having obtained the Virāj itself and made it into a brick, he lays it down; thus he obtains the sacrifice within the Virāj, and his altar becomes both built and unbuilt.
Therefore, when he departs after staying for ten nights, that is the site of the sacrifice; and whatever is prior to that, that is indeed not the site.

When, having stayed for ten nights, he is about to depart, they collect together on the cart standing nearest the fire whatever of his is to be collected; for that which is less than that is indeed not a dwelling-place (*avāstva*). Since Rudra is indeed Vāstoṣpati, if one were to depart without having offered the oblation to Vāstoṣpati, Agni would rise up after him as Rudra and destroy him. He offers the oblation to Vāstoṣpati;
thus he pacifies him with his own portion, and the sacrificer does not come to ruin—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said:

"If one were to offer while [the chariot] is yoked, it would be just as if one were to offer an oblation at a dwelling already set out on its journey; and if one were to offer while it is unyoked, it would be just as if one were to offer an oblation while at rest. Thus, his offering to Vāstoṣpati would be as if unoffered. Therefore, the right [ox] is yoked and the left is unyoked, and then he offers the oblation to Vāstoṣpati."

When the right [ox] is yoked and the left is unyoked, he should take four spoonfuls in a ladle made of *parṇa* wood and offer the oblation to Vāstoṣpati in the Āhavanīya fire. Having recited "O Vāstoṣpati, acknowledge us," and then "O Vāstoṣpati, with thy auspicious dwelling, sit down with us," he makes the offering. Having set down this ladle there and yoked the left [ox], he departs. "He thus pacifies it entirely, leaving no part behind," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it is said:
"If one were to offer with a single [verse], he would perform a *darvihoma*;
having recited the *puro'nuvākyā*, he offers with the *yājyā*—this ensures the presence of the deities," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, furthermore, it is said:

If he were to take up the fire that has been shaken out, he would cause Rudra to mount after his house; if he were to depart without having completely extinguished the embers, it would be just like a sacrificial ruin or a conflagration. Therefore, with the words, "This is your seasonal womb," he causes the fire to mount into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*).

This, indeed, is the womb of Agni; he thus causes it to mount into its own womb. Now, however, they say: "If [the fire] mounted in the two kindling woods should be lost, the fire would perish from him; it would have to be established again. [To this, one should reply:
"With the words, 'That body of yours, O Agni, which is worthy of sacrifice—come, mount here,' he causes it to mount into himself."

He causes [the fire] to ascend himself with the mantra: "O Agni, that body of yours which is worthy of sacrifice—come, ascend it! Entering yourself into yourself, bestowing upon us many human riches; having become the sacrifice, sit upon the sacrifice, your own womb, O Jātavedas, being born again; come to your dwelling! Then he causes him to descend with: "Descend again, O Jātavedas; carry our oblation to the gods, knowing them well. Bestow upon us long life, progeny, and wealth; shine forever within our home. For the sacrificer is the womb of Agni;
thus he causes him to ascend into his own womb—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
The ritual of following (anvārambha) has been explained. Now, it is said that the sages did not perceive Indra directly, but Vasiṣṭha perceived him directly.
He said, "I shall tell you the Brāhmaṇa [explanation] so that people will be born with you as their domestic priest; but do not speak of me to the other sages."
Therefore, he spoke these *stomabhāga* formulas;
from that, creatures with Vasiṣṭha as their priest were born. Therefore they say, "The office of the Brahman priest belongs to a descendant of Vasiṣṭha."

When he says, "O Brahman, we shall chant praises; O Praśāstṛ, [give the command]," then the Brahman gives the impulse. Having made "O God Savitṛ" the introductory formula, he impels by taking up one by one from this section beginning with "Thou art a ray; for dwelling thee; quicken the dwelling.

Impelling in this very manner, he impels the Agniṣṭoma with twelve [verses], the Vājapeya with thirteen, the Atirātra with twenty-nine, and the Aptoryāma with all [of them]. When they proceed toward the Rathantara-sandhi, then he says: "Thou art Vasuku; thou art Veṣaśri; thou art Vasyaṣṭi."

He thus consecrates himself for the Āptoryāma sacrifice. Now, therefore, one who is practicing sorcery, being beset by rivals and contending with them, should perform the ritual arts of sorcery and step with these strides throughout the year: "With Agni as my god, I conquer the hostile armies; with the Gāyatrī metre, the Trivṛt Stoma, the Rathantara Sāman, the Vaṣaṭ-call as my thunderbolt, I cast down my previously born rivals; I press them down, I drive them back—to this dwelling, to this world of earth—whosoever hates us and whomsoever we hate."

We hate them; by the stride of Viṣṇu I step over them. With Indra as my god I conquer the hostile armies. By means of the Triṣṭubh metre, the fifteenfold Stoma, the Bṛhat Sāman, and the Vaṣaṭ-call as a thunderbolt, I cast down my co-born rivals; I press them down, I thrust them back. In this abode, in this world of earth, him who hates us and him whom we hate—by the stride of Viṣṇu I step over them.

With all the gods, I conquer the battles; with the *jagatī* metre, with the seventeen-fold hymn-form (*saptadaśa-stoma*), with the *vāmadevya* chant, and with the *vaṣaṭ*-call as my thunderbolt, I cast down my younger rivals, my enemies. I press them down, I drive them back, into this dwelling, into this world of earth—him who hates us and whom we hate. By the stride of Viṣṇu, I step over them. Or rather, these [formulas] may follow along in the rites intended for malevolent magic. Or else, one should omit the other steps and take these steps for a year. Thus has been declared the mounting upon the *śukra* and *manthin* vessels. Now, therefore, regarding the *atīmokṣa* formulas themselves.

Having offered the Vaiśvakarman oblations, having melted clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire and purified it, and having taken four portions into the offering-spoon, he makes an offering on the Gārhapatya while the sacrificer maintains contact with him.

"O gods who, as destroyers of the sacrifice, dwell upon the earth—may Agni protect me from them; may we go to the world of those who have performed good deeds, svāhā! Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers it in the *gārhapatya* fire itself: "O gods who, as stealers of the sacrifice, dwell upon the earth—may Agni protect me from them; may we go to the world of those who have performed good deeds, svāhā! Then he proceeds toward the *āgnīdhra* shed, saying: "We have come, O Mitra and Varuṇa, to that which is desirable; yours is the portion of the nights."

"Seizing the firmament in the world of the well-done, upon the third back in the luminous realm of heaven"—having thus run to the Āgnīdhra fire, having taken four portions in the ladle, he offers it in the Āgnīdhra while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, saying: "Those gods who, slayers of the sacrifice, dwell in the intermediate space—may Vāyu protect me from them; may we, the doers of good, go to [the world of] heaven, svāhā!"

Having taken another fourfold portion, the Āgnīdhra himself offers it with the mantra: "O gods who steal the sacrifice and dwell in the intermediate space—may Vāyu protect me from them; may we, the doers of good deeds, go [to heaven], svāhā! Then he proceeds toward the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra: "O Savitṛ, those nights of yours which travel between heaven and earth along the paths of the gods..."

"May we ascend with all our houses and progeny to the world of light, crossing over the regions," he says. Then, having hastened to the Āhavanīya fire and taken four portions of clarified butter in the ladle, he offers it into the Āhavanīya while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, saying: "O gods who destroy the sacrifice and dwell in heaven, may Sūrya protect me from them; may we, the doers of good deeds, go to the world of light, Svāhā! Having again taken four portions in the ladle, he offers it into the Āhavanīya itself, saying: "O gods who steal the sacrifice and dwell in heaven..."

"May Sūrya protect me from them; may we go as doers of good deeds, Svāhā!"—with these words he worships the Āhavanīya fire: "O Jātavedas, with that most excellent oblation wherewith you, O Indra, gathered the waters, with that, O Agni, cause this man to prosper; bestow upon him preeminence among his kinsmen. Indeed, there are gods who destroy the sacrifice and those who steal the sacrifice; they dwell in these worlds, seizing and plundering the property of whoever gives and whoever sacrifices.

"The gods who, as destroyers of the sacrifice, dwell upon the earth, those in the intermediate space, and those in heaven—having thus strewn these very worlds, he goes to the heavenly world with his house and his cattle," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Or rather, he offers three oblations on the Gārhapatya fire, three on the Āgnīdhra fire, and three on the Āhavanīya fire. Or else, muttering [the formulas] from the Gārhapatya, he follows them up to the Āhavanīya. Regarding the Udavasānīyā sacrifice which has been described, at this point he offers this third *pravṛtāhuti* (offering of the ladle): "May the god Sūrya protect me from the gods; may Vāyu protect me from the intermediate space; may the sacrificer and Agni protect me from sight, Svāhā!"

Now, one practicing exorcism offers milk with a vessel made of *kārṣmarya* wood to a brown cow that has brown calves, [reciting]: "O Soma, you who are powerful and impetuous, O you who belong to all people; with these names, O Soma, we shall worship you; with these names, O Soma, we shall worship you—svāhā!
Having thus directly pierced his heart and caused his intestines to be scattered, he surely lays low that rival.
Now, if he should have a rivalry with any of his officiating priests (ṛtvij), he says to him: "Let him not approach my cup; I shall perform the touching.
With this very mantra, he should offer that man's cup.
Whether standing upright or bent over, the King (Soma) flows through him. The mixing of the Pātnīvata [cup] has been explained.
The scooping out for the Āditya-graha has been stated;
the spoon-offering for the Prāyaṇīya has been stated; the offering for the Udayanīya has been stated; the attendance upon the sacrificial post has been stated;
the Patnīsaṃyāja-formulas have been stated—in this very manner these spoons [are used], according to this Brāhmaṇa.
The *dadhigraha* has been explained. Now, indeed, it is said: "One desirous of splendor should take the *ājyagraha*";
placing two blades of *barhis* grass in between, he takes the *ājyagraha*.

"One desirous of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should take the *somagraha*"; grasping the [stalks] at their bases, he takes the *somagraha*. Then, on the day of the *mahāvrata*, he takes this *atigrāhya* cup for Prajāpati, reciting: "All encompass thy will," and then: "Thou art taken with a base; I take thee, acceptable to Prajāpati."

Having wiped it, he sets it down with: "This is thy womb; for Prajāpati thee! Now follows the taking of the Prāṇagrahas themselves. Having gathered the King (Soma) who has been fully satiated and formed into a heap, he stretches out nine shoots toward the east: "This one is Purobhū; his breath is Bhauvāyana; the spring is Prāṇāyana; the Gāyatrī belongs to the spring; from the Gāyatrī comes the Gāyatra [chant]; from the Gāyatra comes the Upāṃśu cup; from the Upāṃśu comes the Trivṛt [stoma]; from the Trivṛt comes the Rathantara [sāman]; from the Rathantara comes the seer Vasiṣṭha. With thee, taken by Prajāpati, I take the breath."
With "For the subjects," he extends nine [lines] to the south;

with "Viśvakarman," he extends nine to the west; with "This from the north, the light," he extends nine to the north; with "This above, the thought," he extends nine from above, moving clockwise around.

He drives them away with those who carry water and food, saying: "The eastern direction of the quarters; spring of the seasons; Agni the deity; the Brahman the wealth; the Trivṛt Stoma; he is the fifteen-fold path; the Tryavi the age; the Kṛta of the ages; the east wind the wind; Sānaga the seer"—thus he causes [the sacrificer] to recite. "The fathers, the grandfathers, the further and the nearer"—thus for those who are in the east.
"The southern direction"—thus for those who are in the south.

"Those who are behind [say], 'The western direction!'; those who are to the north, 'The northern direction!'; and those who are above, 'The upward direction! Thus they proceed, moving clockwise around.

These [libations] are indeed employed at the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* offerings on the tenth day; they may also be taken during the *rātrisattra*s, or by one who is ill, or by one who has been seized by disease, at the *agniṣṭoma*. He indeed becomes free from illness."

Now, indeed, there is the Brāhmaṇa passage: "Both these were created from Prajāpati," namely, "O Aśvins, you two [drank] the surā. This occurs specifically in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice. Furthermore, there is the [Brāhmaṇa] passage: "This earth is indeed the Agnihotrī cow; she sits down for him whose Agnihotrī cow sits down; he should make her rise up."

If his *agnihotrī* cow sits down, he makes her rise with the verse: "The divine Aditi, of all forms, has risen; she has bestowed life upon the lord of the sacrifice, making a portion for Indra, Mitra, and Varuṇa. Now it is said: "She sits down having perceived the misfortune or the evil of him whose *agnihotrī*, though set free, sits down.
Having milked her, one should give her to a Brāhmaṇa whose food one would not eat.
Thus, when his *agnihotrī* sits down after being set free, he milks her right there and gives her to a Brāhmaṇa.
And from that time on, he does not eat food;
indeed, the milk enters the earth of him whose *agnihotra* spills while being milked.
He should consecrate it with this mantra: "..."

If his *agnihotra* milk spills while it is being milked, he consecrates it with the mantra: "Whatever milk today has clung to the earth, whatever has flowed into the plants, whatever into the waters—let there be milk for me in my houses, milk in my cows, milk in my calves; let that be mine. He says this so that he places milk within himself, in his house, and among his cattle. He pours water [over it]; "He recovers it by means of water," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now it is said:

"Whoever releases an unstruck verse of the sacrifice that has been struck, both [the sacrificer and the verse] then come to harm; indeed, this Agnihotra comes to harm when, while being milked, it spills. Therefore, if one's Agnihotra spills while being milked, he does not milk over it again.
"In whatever manner and of whatever kind it may be, that very [milk] should be offered; then, having milked another cow, one should offer again.
'By means of the unafflicted, he repairs the afflicted part of the sacrifice,' so says the Brāhmaṇa."
Now, it is indeed said:

"If [the oblation] of one who has hastened should spill, if he were to go back without having offered it from that point, he would cut off the sacrifice; therefore, wherever it spills, having sat down there, he should take it up again.
Thus, right where it spills, he should set down the vessel, pour the remainder into it, and having poured more over it, he should offer it exactly as it is, in whatever state it may be.
"Then, having milked another [cow], he should offer again;
by means of the unafflicted, he repairs the afflicted part of the sacrifice," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it is said:
The sacrifice of one whose dog runs between while the *āgnihotra* oblation has been placed on the fire is indeed torn asunder.

This Agni is indeed Rudra; if he were to turn back toward the cow, Rudra would strike down his cattle, and the sacrificer would become destitute of cattle. If he were to sprinkle water [on the path], since water is not food for Agni, he would deprive these two of food. Therefore, taking ashes from the *gārhapatya* fire, he should run out toward the *āhavanīya* fire with the verse addressed to Viṣṇu, "Viṣṇu strode across this," while scattering the ashes. Thus, with the verse addressed to Viṣṇu, he runs out toward the *āhavanīya* fire while scattering the ashes.
"Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; by means of the sacrifice he continues the sacrifice," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then he fills even the dog's footprint with ashes, "for the sake of peace," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is indeed said:
The Āhavanīya fire does not desire the Gārhapatya, nor does the Gārhapatya desire the Āhavanīya, of him whose fire has not been lifted when the sun sets upon it;
therefore, having tied gold with a blade of Darbha grass, one should first carry that, then the fire, and then the Agnihotra offering.

If the sun sets while his fire has not been taken out, an attendant, having tied gold to a blade of *darbha* grass, goes forward first; behind him follows a *brāhmaṇa* of the *ṛṣi*-lineage, followed by the fuel, followed by himself, and followed by the *agnihotra* oblation. Then, having placed this gold in the place of the *āhavanīya* fire and removed it, he turns to the right and establishes the fuel. Now it is said: "Having set down the *agnihotra*, one should sit until the [sun] has risen."

"One who dies while his vow is still unfulfilled indeed goes to the end of himself; he reaches the very end of the sacrifice whose fire, not yet lifted, the sun sets upon. Having kindled it again, he offers an oblation;
by means of that very [act], he repairs the end of the sacrifice—so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, moreover, it is said:"
"Varuṇa seizes the sacrifice of him for whom the sun sets while the fire has not yet been carried forward;
he should offer a *caru* oblation to Varuṇa;
by that very act, he ransoms the sacrifice"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said:
"The Āhavanīya fire of one whose fire has not been taken out desires the Gārhapatya, and the Gārhapatya desires the Āhavanīya, when the sun rises over him;
[therefore] one should first carry forth clarified butter taken in four ladlings, then the fire, and then the Agnihotra."

If the sun rises upon one whose fire has not been taken out, the assistant first proceeds with ghee taken in four ladlings; following him comes a Brāhmaṇa of Ṛṣi-descent with the fuel, and following him the sacrificer himself with the Agnihotra-oblation. Then, having placed this ghee in the location of the Āhavanīya fire and having removed the ghee, he establishes the fuel. Now, indeed, it is so stated:

"The dawn indeed dawns turned away from him for whom the sun rises while the fire has not yet been lifted up. [He should offer] with the formula: 'May Uṣas with her banner, together with the gods, favor this sacrifice accompanied by the gods; to the gods, the most honey-sweet, Svāhā! Sitting facing west, he should offer with clarified butter. Thus he causes the dawn to shine toward him again—so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now it is said: 'Having set down the Agnihotra, he should remain seated until the breath ceases. He who faints follows after his own broken vow. He who faints goes to the end of himself; he for whom the sun rises while the fire has not yet been lifted up goes to the end of the sacrifice.'"
"Furthermore, by performing the *samanya* oblation until the very end, he completes the conclusion of the sacrifice," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is indeed said:
"Mitra seizes the sacrifice of him whose fire has not been lifted when the sun rises over it."
"One should offer a *caru* oblation to Mitra;
by that very means one redeems the sacrifice," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it occurs [in the text]:

If the Gārhapatya fire should go out while the Āhavanīya has not yet gone out, if one were to churn the Gārhapatya without having extinguished the Āhavanīya, he would cut the sacrifice in two and produce a rival for himself. For Rudra follows whatever part of the sacrifice is performed in a desecrated manner (*vāstavya*).

If he were to settle [the fires] with the former [Gārhapatya], he would worship a desecrated fire, and Rudra would be likely to destroy his cattle. Therefore, one should churn the Gārhapatya after having extinguished the Āhavanīya.

Having extinguished the Āhavanīya fire, he churns the Gārhapatya with [the verse]: "From here Agni Jātavedas was first born from his own womb; may he, knowing [his way], carry the oblation to the gods by means of the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, and the Jagatī. Thus, by means of the meters, he procreates him from his own womb—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, furthermore, it is said:
He churns the *gārhapatya* fire;
for cattle attend upon the one who has established the *āhavanīya* fire with the *gārhapatya*.

If that [fire] goes out, cattle depart following it. Therefore, he worships it [with the mantra]: "Delight in food, in wealth, in power, in splendor, in vigor, and in lordship. Then he kindles it [with the mantra]: "May the two springs of Sarasvatī kindle thee; thou art the sovereign (*samrāj*), thou art the radiant ruler (*virāj*)."
Now it is indeed said:
"The discus is a thunderbolt;
the thunderbolt cuts through the sacrifice of him between whose two fires a wagon or a chariot passes. Having extinguished the Āhavanīya fire, he should draw it out from the Gārhapatya."

Having extinguished the Āhavanīya fire, he takes up the fuel for the Gārhapatya and other fires with the verse: "O Agni, that former foot which was set down by thee has indeed extended along the rays of the sun; bring hither that which stands in wealth, and unite us with favor and with booty. Thus, by means of his former sacrifice, he continues the sacrifice; so says the Brāhmaṇa. Then he worships it with the verse: "Thou, O Agni, art far-extending, the beloved, excellent Hotṛ; through thee they extend the sacrifice. "Agni is all the deities; verily by means of the deities he continues the sacrifice," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt;
having set down the Anvāhārya mess, he gives an ox as a gift.
That well-known sacrifice is completed. Now, it is indeed said:
If the Soma at the morning pressing overflows, desiring the midday pressing, it overflows further;
when the Soma has overflowed at the morning pressing, he, walking eastward, says: "Fill the Hotṛ’s cup after [the others]; O Unnetṛ, draw up the King (Soma) entirely so that nothing remains over.
They fill the Hotṛ’s cup first, and the others as they come along.

Having raised the King [Soma] in every respect, they place him upon the *uttaravedi*. Then, having touched water and taken two blades of *barhis* grass, he, restraining his speech, runs westward and introduces the chant;
they chant it.
This is the *Gāyatra* *sāman*, the fifteenfold; they perform it with verses containing the word "suckles," beginning with: "The cow suckles for the Maruts."
"This is the highest *hotrā*," they say;
from this point upward it is the same.
Now, indeed, it so happens:

When the Soma was left over at his midday pressing—having been left over because he desired the third pressing for the Ādityas—he, while the Soma was still overflowing at the midday pressing, stepped forward and said: "Fill the Hotṛ’s cup after [the others]; O Unnetṛ, draw up the King [Soma] entirely so that nothing remains over. They fill the Hotṛ’s cup first, and the others as they come along.

Having raised the King Soma in every respect, they place him upon the high altar (uttaravedi). Then, having touched water and taken two blades of sacrificial grass (barhis), he restrains his speech, runs westward, and introduces the chant (stotra).
They chant for him; this is the Gaurīvīta Sāman, a seventeen-versed hymn, which they perform on the verses beginning with "baṇ mahām̐ asi sūrya."
"This is the highest oblation," they say;
from this point upward it is the same.
Now, indeed, it comes to pass:
If at the third pressing one's Soma should be left over, one should perform the Ukthya;
if it should be left over at the Ukthya, one should perform the Atirātra;

if it should be left over at the Atirātra, that indeed is difficult to determine. When it is left over at the Atirātra, as he goes forward, he says: "Draw out the Hotṛ’s cup after [the others]; O Unnetṛ, draw out the King [Soma] in its entirety so that nothing is left over."
They draw the Hotṛ’s cup first, and the others as they come;

having drawn the King Soma entirely, they place it upon the northern altar. Then, having touched water and taken two blades of sacrificial grass, he, restraining his speech, runs westward and introduces the chant;
they chant the Stotra.
They perform this Bṛhat-sāman on twenty-one verses addressed to Viṣṇu containing the word *śipiviṣṭa*;
"This is the last [verse] for the Hotṛ," they say;
from here upwards, it is the same.
Thus, when the Chandogas and Bahvṛcas desire [the draught],

if they do not so desire, then at the morning pressing, from the vessel which he considers to have been left over for the King [Soma] who has exceeded [his share], he pours the Āgrayaṇa upon it and catches it below;
he causes it to overflow three times.
As it overflows, it becomes entirely the Āgrayaṇa;

having uttered the *abhihiṅkāra* over it three times and wiped it around, he sets it down at the midday pressing when [the Soma] is in excess. In the same manner, whichever vessel he considers to have been left over for the King (Soma), having poured the Āgrayaṇa over that vessel, he catches it from below.
He causes it to overflow three times;
as it overflows, it becomes entirely the Āgrayaṇa vessel.
Having likewise performed the *abhihiṅkāra* over it three times and wiped it around, he sets it down.
At the third pressing, when [the Soma] has been exhausted, one causes the Hāriyojana cup alone to overflow here;

for there is no further drawing [of Soma]. Now, therefore, regarding the Dhruva cup that has been depleted: having enclosed it with these two ṛg-verses addressed to Indra and Agni, one should offer it. For Indra and Agni are the gods among the gods whom we worship again and again; this is one [view].

Having grasped it with two *ṛc*-verses addressed to the Aśvins, he should offer it; for the Aśvins are the physicians of the gods—it is through them that he provides medicine for him. This is one way. Having grasped it with two *ṛc*-verses addressed to Viṣṇu, he should offer it; for whatever is redundant in the sacrifice, that is redundant for Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa—this is another way.

"One should throw it into the water along with the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) vessel, thinking: 'Just as my other vessels smeared with Soma [were disposed of], so shall this one be for me'—this is one way. Or, he should burn it up together with a single blade of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), thinking: 'The wild forest fire is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara; this [Soma] is taken for Vaiśvānara, so it will have been offered into Agni Vaiśvānara in the *dhruva* [vessel]'—this is another way. Then he undergoes initiation again."

"The sacrifice itself is indeed the expiation for the sacrifice"—this applies to those who perform a one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*). Now, for those performing a sacrificial session (*sattra*), having prepared a flowing pool with an overflow at the *mārjālīya* shed, they pour it out there.
For on the following day, they are about to press the Soma.
The *saṃsava* has been explained. Now, moreover, it is said: "Verily, those among the consecrated (*dīkṣita*) who die undergo affliction."
If they were to reject him, his world would become like that of those who commit cruel deeds; one should say, "Bring it! Burn it!
If he should find something that afflicts the consecrated one, there is indeed a bed at the Āgnīdhrīya fire.
They bring him food portions as much as he deems sufficient for eating. If he recovers, he returns;

but if he indeed passes away, they should draw out embers from all the fires, consign the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇīs*), carry them out between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, and cremate him with them.

Having cooled it for three nights, they should pile it up; having done so, they may wait for the completion of the six-day period. Then, when the six-day period has concluded, he asks for a jar for the bones.

Having placed the piled-up material into that jar and set it down to the south of the altar, they should chant the praises with the verses of the Serpent Queen (*sarparājñī*). For she is indeed the queen of all that creeps; thus they entrust him to her.
"They say that it is unsuccessful when a hymn has been chanted but not followed by a recitation," they say.
"The Hotṛ, as the first, should go around the Mārjālīya fire with his sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), reciting the *yājyās* and mentioning the *Sarparājñīs*.

When they have thus gone around, the Adhvaryu goes around last; then, having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavīta), they all three go back around again in the same manner as they came.

When they have thus been reduced in number, the Adhvaryu goes around first; then, taking him [the deceased], he places him between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, as well as between the stone and the jar of bones, and sprinkles him with water, reciting: "May the sin be burnt away from us. In that [jar], they draw the cups beginning with the Maitrāvaruṇa cup. Then, what remains, they sit for the sacrificial session (*sattra*).

At the time of the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of that session, having placed the jar of bones there, he sprinkles it with water; this indeed constitutes his purificatory bath. Or else, he should initiate in the place of the deceased one who is his own nearest relative.
In the course of a year they cause his bones to perform the sacrifice. Now it is said: "The cattle and the virility depart from him who makes the sacrificial post sprout;
he should offer an animal of many forms to Tvaṣṭṛ."

If the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of those performing a *sattra* should sprout, they should cut off its top-ring (*caṣāla*). They should then offer a victim for Tvaṣṭṛ as part of the *savanīya* animal sacrifice. Alternatively, having cooked a *brahmaudana* (rice-mess for the Brahmins) for Tvaṣṭṛ, they should cut down these branches or plane them down. Or else, having offered two spoonfuls (*sruvāhuti*) to Tvaṣṭṛ, they should cut down these branches or plane them down. Or again, one should simply say, "To Tvaṣṭṛ, to Tvaṣṭṛ. Now, it is indeed said: "Those initiated ones whose fire goes out meet with misfortune."

If the Āhavanīya fire should go out, if one were to churn it [from scratch], he would cut it off and produce a rival for himself. If the Āhavanīya should go out, one should take it from the Āgnīdhra fire; if the Āgnīdhra should go out, one should take it from the Gārhapatya fire; if the Gārhapatya should go out, one should churn it again from that very place. For it is indeed there that it settles down.
When people see what has settled down as being most excellent, then they desire it.
One should make the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) from the same log from which the fire went out.
"One should also make a *krumuka* [churning stick].

Having made the two fire-drills (*araṇī*) from whatever wood he fells, and having placed a piece of *krumuka* wood upon them, and having set down those very embers that have been extinguished, he should churn.

Thus, having set down those very embers, he churns: "From here Agni was first born, Jātavedas from his own womb; may he, knowing, carry the oblation to the gods by means of the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, and the Jagatī."
"By means of the meters he procreates him from his own womb," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Now, if both the Āhavanīya and Gārhapatya fires should go out, one should churn the Gārhapatya fire and then draw the Āgnīdhrīya fire from it to serve as the Āhavanīya. If both the Āgnīdhrīya and Gārhapatya fires should go out, one should churn the Gārhapatya fire and then draw the Āgnīdhrīya fire from it. If both the Āgnīdhrīya and Āhavanīya fires should go out, one should draw the Āgnīdhrīya fire from the Gārhapatya and then draw the Āhavanīya fire from that. And if all of them should go out, one should churn the Gārhapatya fire, draw the Āgnīdhrīya fire from it, and then [draw the others].
"One should draw out the Āhavanīya fire," it is said; now, it also occurs that one churns the Gārhapatya fire,
for the Gārhapatya is indeed the womb of Agni.
"He generates him from his own womb; he does not generate a rival for him," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, there is also this [text]:

"If one's *soma* should run out, he should divide a piece of gold into two parts; shaking one part over the *arjiṣa*, he should offer the other. This is the rule for one whose *soma* runs out: he divides that piece of gold into two parts, shakes one over the *arjiṣa*, places the other into the principal cup (*mukhya-camasa*), and offers it.
"He presses *soma* itself; he offers *soma*," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, there is this Brāhmaṇa: "When Soma was being pressed, his beloved body went forth; it became gold. In that they fashion gold, they endow him with his very own beloved body."
Now it is indeed said in the Brāhmaṇa: "If they should carry off one's un-purchased Soma, he should simply purchase it again; that itself is the expiation for that."
Now, it is indeed said:
"If they should steal what has been purchased, one should press *ādāra* and *phālguṇa* plants. The *ādāras* are small grasses; the *phālguṇas* are those from the Himalayas.
In the absence of those white ones, a substitute is prescribed:
"Soma was in the third heaven from here;
Gāyatrī brought him down."
Its leaf was cut off; that became the Parṇa tree;
that is the reason for the name "Parṇa" of the Parṇa tree.
Therefore, the pressing should be performed using only the parṇa- and saru-sticks; thus, one should mix [the soma] with boiled milk at the morning pressing,
for this becomes "boiled" (śṛta).
"With curds at midday"— this refers to curds that have been brought forward;
"with mixed [curds] at the third pressing."
They say that [butter] which has been churned together with curds and extracted before it reaches the state of fresh butter is the Agniṣṭoma Soma sacrifice, having the Rathantara as its sāman.

Those very priests who have been chosen should perform this sacrifice for him; they indeed perform it for him. "He should give one cow as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)"—here he gives one cow as the sacrificial fee.
"What he intends to give here, he gives there again;
he should purchase Soma [again], for by means of the sacrifice itself he seeks the sacrifice— this indeed is the expiation from that," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Now it is said: "He who pledges himself for a sacrificial session (*sattra*) pledges himself to all deities, to all desires, to all hymn-forms (*stoma*), to all meters (*chandas*), and to all *pṛṣṭha* chants. Man is indeed as great as his wealth; he should sacrifice with his entire property. Thus they perform the *Atirātra* Viśvajit, and at this point he gives away his entire property;
his Soma-sacrifice should consist of all the *pṛṣṭha* chants.
"One ransoms oneself from all the deities, from all desires, from all hymns of praise, from all meters, and from all *pṛṣṭha* chants," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"The *pavamāna* [verse] beginning with 'pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ' occurs at the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice; this is the subsequent Brāhmaṇa."
Now, indeed, it is said: "Therefore, the sacrificer performing the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice should pray, 'May I obtain well-being for a year,' and so he should pray.
Therefore, the sacrificer performing the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices should pray, "May I obtain well-being for a year," and so he should pray.
Therefore, when sacrificing with the Sākamedha offerings, the sacrificer should pray: "May I obtain well-being for the coming year";

therefore, when sacrificing with the Śunāsīrīya offering, the sacrificer should pray: "May I obtain well-being for the following year. Now, it is indeed said: "The Kṛttikās belong to Agni; the bright [light] is above, the light is below"—thus they say that one may optionally use the Nakṣatra-bricks.
Furthermore, it is indeed said: "On whichever auspicious lunar mansion (nakṣatra) [the moon is], he should perform the rite before sunrise."
One should perform it in the morning, one should perform it at the time of the Sangava, one should perform it at midday, and one should perform it in the afternoon.

One should perform it in the evening for as long as the sun remains there; one should perform it for as long as one can still see the lowest part [of the horizon]. Whatever one performs in this way, one performs on an auspicious day. Thus it is said.
A Brāhmaṇa, a Brāhmaṇa;
a king who is victorious and sovereign over the whole earth is about to perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
He chooses this sacrificial ground: one part facing the east, one facing the south, one facing the west, and one facing the north.
They cut down trees, break up the high ground, fill in the depressions, and cast away the thorny shrubs.

They create river fords, springs everywhere, and ponds. Then, they select two lakes in the middle of the sacrificial site—those that flow together, do not dry up, and have auspicious names—if they find such;
or, if they do not find such, they dig these two and fill them with water brought from elsewhere or carried by hand.

However, so that the two [fires] may be leak-proof, non-consumptive, and bear auspicious names, he causes them to be chosen from the western side of the middle of the sacrificial ground (devayajana). They construct the hall for the fire-altar (agni) twice as large as the space for the fire itself; it has its ridge-pole facing east, openings toward the quarters, and is wider on the south side. To the south of that, they construct the horse-stable.

Then they construct a horse-pen with *aśvattha* wood, its planks having their tips pointing downward. Now these materials are prepared for him: a horse that is most excellent among his fine steeds; other than that, an unlimited number of worn-out, castrated horses; a black four-eyed dog; two slaves, one for the junior wife and one for the secondary wife; an old reed mat; a pestle made of *saidhraka* wood; a winnowing basket made of *palāśa* wood; four hundred guards; and one hundred attendants who sleep in the same quarters as the king.

A hundred princes of non-royal status, a hundred fierce men, a hundred charioteers and village chiefs, a hundred chamberlains and collectors, and four great officiating priests— others accompany them,
bringing them along on foot at the appropriate time.

Until the Subrahmaṇyā call, he waits for Citrā as it approaches, having prepared four sets of water collected from the quarters, four thousand gold coins, two ornaments of gold and silver, two other pieces of gold, two lute-players, a Brāhmaṇa and a Rājanya, two cords—one of muñja grass and one of kuśa grass—both thirteen cubits long. Then, with the thought "O Citrā," having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods, he proceeds toward the hall with the verse: "O Savitṛ, those paths of yours which are ancient, dustless, and far-extending..."

"In the intermediate space. "By those easy paths, protect us today and speak for us, O God," he says. Having gone around the north of the hall, having entered the hall by the eastern door, having churned the fire in the place of the *gārhapatya* and having spread the fires, he worships the *gārhapatya*: "Homage to Agni, who dwells on earth, the winner of the world; grant a world to this sacrificer!
"Homage to Vāyu, who dwells in the intermediate space, the winner of the world; grant a world to this sacrificer! [He worships] the *anvāhāryapacana*.

"Obeisance to Sūrya, who dwells in heaven, the protector of the world; grant a world to this sacrificer," he says, [referring] to the Āhavanīya fire. Now, to the east of that, behind the horse-stable, a shed with a single outlet has been constructed for him. Having kindled a common fire there, he offers ninety oblations with the formula, "To Mṛtyu, svāhā! To Mṛtyu, svāhā! and eleven oblations with "To Prayāsa, svāhā! and so forth.

"A man has a lifespan of a hundred years and a strength of a hundred; the self is the one hundred and first. To the extent that a man is [constituted], from that he wards off death," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Then, having had his hair and beard shaved, having clipped his body hair, having trimmed his nails, and having cleansed his teeth, both bathe and put on two unwashed garments. Adorned with human ornaments and wearing new clothes, he causes the food for the commencement of the vow to be cooked for them both.

On the day before that [sacrifice], he eats [food] mixed with clarified butter and mixed with milk; then, in the afternoon, two pieces of gold are placed upon his two mouths—the sacrificer holds a piece of gold and the wife a piece of silver, or silver if there are many wives. Then, while he maintains silence, he offers the evening Agnihotra sacrifice. These royal attendants approach him: the charioteers, the village overseers, the door-keepers, the collectors, and the artisans;
to them he gives a four-year-old cow that has not yet calved.

Cooking that [food] for you, they sit keeping it warm and remaining awake; then in the morning, while sipping water for rinsing the mouth, they strike against two pieces of gold. He takes up two small wooden spoons. Then they worship the rising sun with the formula: "Homage to the seer, homage to the one who sees nearby, homage to the one who sees from afar, homage to the one who makes known, homage to the one who makes known nearby, homage to the one who makes known from afar, homage to the one who hears, homage to the one who hears nearby, homage to the one who hears from afar, homage to the existent, homage to the non-existent, homage to what has been born, homage to what is to be born, homage to what has come into being, homage to what is to come into being."
Then he offers the Vaiśvadevī Sāṃgrahaṇī; that sacrifice concludes in the well-known manner.

While the Adhvaryu is occupied here, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having cooked the Brahmaudana in fourfold waters, pours clarified butter over it and carries it out toward the north. Then, having washed this vessel and spread a layer of ghee within it, he places this washed silver disk into it.

Without striking it, he draws this [horse] out from that [spot], having made a vessel for pouring ghee and having brought a large quantity of clarified butter; then he places a washed golden plate upon it. Then, having seated those great officiating priests to the north, each in his respective direction, and having caused them to sip water in succession, he pushes this [horse] toward them while touching the ground, as if without breaking the continuity.
He says: "O Brāhmaṇas and kings, may you bring me safely to completion through this horse fit for sacrifice, for the attainment of the status of Brahman."

The others reply to him, "So be it; with this sacrificial horse we shall bring you safely to the state of being the Brahman. Then they agree with him regarding his status as the Brahman. Then he instructs them: "Having each eaten once, hold [the food] without touching it again. Then, having soaked the two reins in the vessel for pouring ghee, he hands them to the attendant. Having eaten a second time, he says, "Your Brahma-rice is prepared."

To them he gives four thousand gold coins, as well as golden and silver ornaments and garments. Those who are to consecrate the Kṣatriya consecrate the Adhvaryu. He says: "O Brāhmaṇas and kings, the Adhvaryu and these two shall be king for these two years; serve him. Whoever does not serve him, they shall deprive him of all his property. Then the Adhvaryu becomes king for these two years, while the other is called the sacrificer (yajamāna).
He says, "O Brahman, I shall bind the sacrificial horse for the gods and for Prajāpati; may I prosper through it.
The other replies, "Bind it; may you prosper through it for the gods and for Prajāpati.

Then he takes up the halter with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee. Having taken it, he consecrates it with the verse, "They took hold of this halter of the Eternal Order."

With that [rope] he ties the horse: "Thou art the tie; thou art the world; thou art the controller; thou art the sustainer. Go to Agni Vaiśvānara, the far-extending; consecrated by Svāhā, on earth, a controller, a king! Thou art the controller, the restrainer; thou art the sustainer, the support. In this very same way he takes up the second rope, and with that he ties the horse in the same manner.

At this time, he fills the back of the horse; the son of the junior wife and the son of the woman who has been provided with a dowry tie the dog to two dog-tethers. Then this Pauṃścaleya, having wrapped his left knee with an old garment, stands behind the dog with a pestle made of Sidhraka wood. Then the Adhvaryu steps forward from the front together with a hundred princes fit for the couch; the Brahman from the south together with a hundred fierce men who are not kings; the Hotṛ from the west together with a hundred charioteers and village headmen.

The Udgātṛ stands to the north together with a hundred attendants, charioteers, and collectors; in their midst are the horse and the dog. Then they proceed toward the southern lake, making the horse run up to its chest with three sections of the text beginning, "Heaven is thy back; the steed has stepped over with his strides; the steed has stepped with his strides. Standing to the east facing west, the Adhvaryu sprinkles it, saying: "Having sacrificed with this pure horse, may this king slay Vṛtra."
Following that, a hundred princes entitled to the royal bed sprinkle him;

the Brahman priest, standing to the south facing north, sprinkles him with the formula: "Having sacrificed with this horse worthy of sacrifice, may this king be invincible. Following that sprinkling, a hundred fierce non-kings (arājānaḥ) sprinkle him.

Standing behind [the horse] facing eastward, the Hotṛ sprinkles it with this formula: "Having sacrificed with this pure horse, may this man be king over this people—[a people] possessing many cattle, many horses, many goats and sheep, much rice and barley, much mung beans and sesame, much gold, many elephants, many male and female slaves, wealthy, prosperous, possessing abundant increase of wealth, and possessing all kinds of riches in abundance—may he be king!"

Following its sprinkling, a hundred charioteers and village headmen sprinkle it; the Udgātṛ, standing to the north facing south, sprinkles it with the formula: "Having sacrificed with this horse worthy of sacrifice, may this king attain a full lifespan.
Following its sprinkling, a hundred attendants and collectors sprinkle it; "They sprinkle the horse from all directions," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then, when this sacrificial cake of *paumsya* remains for him as a remnant, and when Upamīva says,
"Strike the dog," he strikes the dog with that *paumsya* cake using a mace of *sīdhraka* wood from the side of Upamīva;
he consecrates it with a mantra right there.

"Whoever intends to strike down the courser, Varuṇa strikes him down"—saying this, he places his foot upon the horse's hindquarters and washes it away toward the south with the verse, "Away, O mortal! Away, O dog! Then the Brahman priest takes hold of his hand, or the sacrificer takes hold of the Brahman's hand, with the verse: "I and you, O slayer of Vṛtra, have come together for the sake of gains; even the enemy, O stone-caster, shall submit to us. O Hero, may your gifts be auspicious for us; Indra’s gifts are indeed auspicious. At this point, he places a reed-stalk (*aiṣīka*) against [the horse], fastening it at both ends with two ropes of muñja grass, which is further bound together with a cane-shoot (*vetasa-śākhā*).
By this, one hundred princes entitled to a couch are selected;
following their selection, the others take one hundred each from either of the two remaining ends.

Then he instructs them: "With this reed-mat, as if pushing from the front, you two shall drive the horse toward the west with a wave. While it is being driven, the Adhvaryu makes the sacrificer recite: "O Indra, by your power you have become great; your majesty has pervaded the worlds."

"By your own power indeed you struck down Vṛtra; no enemy found the end of you with his weapon"—having said this, he wraps him up and washes him toward the south. Then, having turned this horse clockwise, he leads it into the shed: "When the wind has gone to the waters, O Indra, [protect] his dear body; by this path, O singer, bring the horse back again."

The Adhvaryu follows that [horse] with the first *stokīyā* verses, reciting this Anuvāka—"To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā!"—repeating the introductory call again and again until its drops cease. Then, having stationed the horse facing east in front of the hall and entered it, he offers the *sāvitra* oblations for the horse: "To Agni, svāhā! To Vāyu, svāhā! and so on, seven times. Then, in the morning, he prepares a cake on eight potsherds for Savitṛ; having set it down, he offers the fore-portion: "To Agni, svāhā! Svāhā to Indra and Agni! and so on, five times.

Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers eighty-three oblations of horse-entrails with the formulas, "To the *iṅkāra*, svāhā! To the one made by *iṅkāra*, svāhā! and so on, until thirteen *pradrāvins* have been offered. This well-known sacrifice concludes. Then, having turned the horse to the right, having led it into the hall through the eastern door, and having stationed it facing east within the altar, he says:

"As for what they say here—that at every step the Adhvaryu indeed makes an offering for the sacrificial horse—we shall make that offering right here, so that for us it will be as if an offering has been made at every step."

He offers the *dhṛti* oblations at his feet, either straight across or in a circumambulatory manner: "To this world, *dhṛti*, svāhā! To this world, *vidhṛti*, svāhā! To this world, *ratni*, svāhā! To this world, *ramati*, svāhā! Then, having made him step forward facing east, he sprinkles him: with "For Prajāpati, thee" in front; with "For Indra and Agni, thee" from the south; with "For Vāyu, thee" from behind; with "For the Viśve Devas, thee" from the north; with "For the Devas, thee" from below; and with "For all the Devas, thee" from above. Then he sprinkles him with the extra water.

"For cultivation thee, for security thee, for wealth thee, for prosperity thee; for the earth thee, for the intermediate space thee, for the sky thee; for what exists thee, for what does not exist thee; for the waters thee, for the plants thee; for all beings thee"—thus [he says]. Then he offers oblations of its forms with these two sections: "To the one with ointment, svāhā! To the one with ointment on the thighs, svāhā! To the black one, svāhā! To the white one, svāhā! and so forth.

Then, having risen up after it, he murmurs the names of horses into its right ear: "Abundant with thy mother, powerful with thy father; thou art a horse, thou art a steed, thou art a racer, thou art a man, thou art a courser, thou art a swift runner, thou art a stallion, thou art one whose mind is on men, thou art the one named Yayu. Then he stands over it, saying, "Go along the flight-path of the Ādityas. Then he releases it from the two reins, saying, "Thou art the earth; for the past thee, for the present thee, for the future thee; for all beings thee. Then he entrusts it to the deities, saying, "O gods, guardians of the quarters..."

"Guard this horse, sprinkled for sacrifice to the gods"—at this point, they release for him these unlimited draught-oxen, castrated and eight-year-old; here they harness these four hundred guardians for him, with their armor fastened and their protective fenders spread out, as if for battle.
He gives them permission to eat cooked food.
He says: "O Brahmins and kings, those for whom these cooked foods shall be brought, being authorized by me, do not speak ill of one another."

He said: "O Brahmins and kings, drive away your vehicles from outside the sacrificial ground; whoever this stallion is joined with, he shall seize their entire property. They drove away their vehicles from outside the sacrificial ground; they moved about with stallions and mules, but not with mares nor with female mules.

Then these two lute-players take hold [of the horse]; then this Brahmin lute-player sings: "You have given," "you have sacrificed," "you have cooked"—thus he sings three mixed verses; there is freedom of movement for the horse.

And they protect him from bathing and from the vehicle; furthermore, if the horse falls ill, there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, a cake on eight potsherds for Savitṛ, a pap for Pūṣan, and a pap for Rudra. Now, if he does not come back, there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Agni Vaiśvānara and a wild donkey. And if a mare is joined with him, there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Amhomuc, milk for Sūrya, and a portion of clarified butter for Vāyu. If he smells [the smoke], there is an offering to Rudra; if there is a discharge, one to Pūṣan; if [he dies] in the waters...

If the horse dedicated to Varuṇa is one-eyed and that dedicated to Sūrya is [normal], whichever of these two misfortunes occurs, there is a single expiation. Then, he releases the best of his well-bred horses; thereafter, he proceeds with the two reins alone.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the formal entrustment.
Having released the horse, they immolate the animals dedicated to the Viśvedevas; the Vaiśvadeva oblations follow their animal-cake offerings (paśupuroḍāśas), or rather,
their animal-cake offerings themselves become the Vaiśvadeva oblations.
The Madhyamā Sāvitrī follows them; the well-known animal sacrifices are completed. Then, in the afternoon, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ Āsavitṛ;

that well-known iṣṭi is completed. Then, having performed the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha sacrifices, he proceeds with the well-known [rites]. Then these two lute-players take up their positions. Then this Rājanya, the lute-player, sings songs: "Thus you fought," "Thus you conquered," "Thus you slew such-and-such a battle"—in this way, three mixed songs.

When the morning Agnihotra has been offered, a Brāhmaṇa who is a lute-player sings; when the evening Agnihotra has been offered, a Rājanya sings. These two sing in this very manner for a year. Then, in the morning, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Savitṛ Prasavitṛ. Having placed it, he first offers the portions (bhāgas); before the sun has risen, he offers the *dhṛtis* and the *pradrās*. That sacrifice concludes in the established manner. Then, at midday, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Savitṛ Prasavitṛ.

That well-known sacrifice is completed; then, in the afternoon, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ Āsavitr; that well-known sacrifice is completed. Then, on the next day, he begins with the rites dedicated to Savitṛ.

In this very manner, the sacrificer proceeds day by day for four months with the rites dedicated to Savitṛ—either by means of an *iṣṭi*, or by means of an animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), or by means of the first-fruits offering of barley (*yavāgrayaṇa*). When the four months have elapsed, having performed the *Sāvitrī* sacrifice, they immolate the animals for the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings.
The Varuṇapraghāsa oblations follow their animal-cake offerings;
indeed, for them, the Varuṇapraghāsa oblations themselves become the animal-cake offerings,
and the middle Sāvitrī follows those.
The animal sacrifices conclude according to the established procedure; then, in the afternoon, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ Āsavitṛ;

that sacrifice concludes according to the established procedure; then, having performed the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha sacrifices, he proceeds with the well-known rites; then, on the following day, he begins again with the offerings to Savitṛ.
