In this very manner, performing the *sāvitrī* offerings day after day, he passes four further months—at will with an *iṣṭi*, at will with a *paśubandha*, or at will with the *śyāmākāgrayaṇa*. Then, when those four months have elapsed, on the fast-day (*upavasatha*) of the full moon, he immolates an animal for *Ānīkavata*.

Following the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) of that animal is the oblation for *Ānīkavata*; indeed, his sacrificial cake for the animal belongs to *Ānīkavata*, and following it comes the first *sāvitrī* offering.
The animal sacrifice is concluded in the established manner; then, at midday, he immolates the Saṃtapana animal.
The oblation of cooked rice (havir) for the Saṃtapana follows its animal cake (paśupuroḍāśa);
indeed, its animal cake becomes the Saṃtapana itself.

The Madhyama Sāvitrī follows that; the well-known animal sacrifice concludes. Then, in the afternoon, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ Āsavitṛ; that well-known iṣṭi concludes. Then, in the evening, he performs the Gṛhamedhīya rite; then, in the latter part of the night, he performs the Pūrṇadarvya rite; then, in the morning, the Kraiḍina oblation.
The animal sacrifice for Paśupati belongs to Kraiḍina Vaivāsya;
it follows that first Sāvitrī offering. The animal sacrifice is completed in the established manner, and then at midday they immolate the animals of the Sākamedha offerings.
The great oblations follow their animal-cake offerings;
indeed, for them, the animal-cake offerings become the great oblations,
and the middle Sāvitrī follows those.
The animal sacrifices are completed according to the established ritual procedure; then, in the afternoon, he performs the Pitṛyajña;
having performed the Pitṛyajña, he performs the Traiyambaka offerings;
having performed the Traiyambaka offerings, he immolates the animal for Āditya.

The offering to Aditi follows the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) of that [animal sacrifice]; indeed, the cake for Aditi becomes his animal-cake. It follows that [cake], and the final oblation to Savitṛ follows it.

The animal sacrifice concludes in the established manner. Then, having performed the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha sacrifices, he returns to the established procedure. Then, on the next day, he begins again with the [oblations] to Savitṛ.

In this very manner, performing sacrifices daily with the Sāvitrī offerings, he passes three and a half months—performing at will an *iṣṭi*, at will a *paśubandha*, and at will the *vrīhyāgrayaṇa*. Then, on the day of the fast (*upavasathīya*) of the new moon, having performed the *sāvitrī-iṣṭi*, having offered the *agnikāni* and *sāvitrāṇi* oblations, and having collected the fire-pans (*ukhāḥ*) and the heads of the sacrificial animals, he immolates an animal for Vāyu. For that sacrifice, a hornless goat dedicated to Prajāpati is to be immolated as a secondary victim. Having proceeded in the established manner with the omenta of these two, he offers the two *paśupuroḍāśa* cakes.
The Madhyama Sāvitrī continues for that long; the two animal sacrifices are completed as established. Then, in the afternoon, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ Āsavitṛ.
That well-known sacrifice is completed; then, on the following day, he begins again with the Sāvitrī offerings.

In this very manner, the sacrificer proceeds for half a month with the Sāvitrī offerings at will—either with an *iṣṭi* or with an animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*). Then, when four months have elapsed, having performed the Sāvitrī sacrifice, they immolate the animals dedicated to Śuna and Sīra.
The Śunāsīrīya oblations follow after their animal-cake offerings; indeed,
their animal-cake offerings become the Śunāsīrīya oblations,
and the middle Sāvitrī follows after them.
The animal sacrifices for the Cāturmāsya rites are concluded. Then, in the afternoon, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ Āsavitṛ;

that well-known sacrifice is completed. Then, having performed the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha sacrifices, he sits down in the sacrificer’s place and, with a three-striped porcupine quill and a razor of red iron, he has his hair cut and shaved—first in front, then on the south, then on the west, then on the north, and finally on top.
The Cāturmāsya animal sacrifices are concluded; the rites dedicated to Savitṛ are concluded.
Then, having tethered the horse in the stable and having brought it from the bathing-place and purified it, he performs the three-oblation *agnidīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice.

For her, as many [oblations] are exhausted as there were for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice. Then the Adhvaryu, having turned to the right and hastened westward, having performed the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, goes eastward, replenishes the *dhruvā* ladle, and offers the three first *vaiśvadeva* oblations with "Svāhā to the kindled fire! Svāhā! Then he offers the seven *prāṇāhuti* oblations with "To the out-breath, svāhā! To the diffused breath, svāhā! He offers the twenty-one-fold *dīkṣā* oblation with "To the earth, svāhā! To the intermediate space, svāhā!
He offers five *adhvara-dīkṣā* oblations and six *agni-dīkṣā* oblations, and one *ṛtu-dīkṣā* oblation with "Bhuvo devānāṃ karmaṇe."
"He sacrifices with this offering for seven days.

He offers three *vaiśvadeva* oblations each time, and each subsequent one corresponds to a subsequent seasonal initiation (*ṛtudīkṣā*). At the end, he offers two seasonal initiations. On the very day [of the sacrifice], he undergoes the initiation with the verse "The great, well-protecting... He carries the fire in the pan for a year.
There are twelve *upasads*; here these people settle around him as prescribed:
carpenters, chariot-makers, mat-makers, potters, and two kinds of smiths—those who work with nails being the seventh. Then he instructs these carpenters.

"Cut one hundred and one pieces of *bilva* wood, bound with wood; having split them into sections, pile them up. Cut twenty-one sacrificial posts (*yūpa*), each twenty-one cubits long: one made of *rājjudāla* wood for the central post, two made of *pūtudru* for the side-posts, six of *bilva*, six of *khadira*, and six of *pālāśa*. Let there be a *pālāśa* post for the resting-place, a *pālāśa* for the *pātnīvata* offering, and a broad *pālāśa* post. Make wooden vessels of a single type. Make thirty-six *sruva* ladles with long handles."

"Have one hundred long-shafted chariots with four or eight poles; have four-wheeled, large-wheeled chariots that are level with the tops of the sacrificial posts; and prepare an unlimited number of platforms and kitchens. Prepare one mat of reeds for the horse's bedding. Then he instructs the chariot-makers: "Construct a chariot for yourself, and construct an unlimited number of chariots."

Then he instructs these workers in clay: "Prepare an unlimited amount of leather. Then he instructs the potters: "Make bricks according to the twenty-onefold fire-altar; make three large jars; cook these—the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal—along with their limbs; and prepare an unlimited number of cooking pots."

Then he instructs these made of black iron: "Make an arrow with a white shaft, a black one with a black shaft, a golden one with a golden shaft, four of black iron with copper shafts, four of copper with black-iron shafts, thirty-six golden ones with silver shafts, thirty-six silver ones with golden shafts, three hundred and thirty-three golden needles, and three hundred and thirty-three [silver ones]."

"Make three hundred and thirty-three vessels of silver and one water-pot of black iron for the cooking of the *aśvatejanī* [horse-wool]. Then he instructs the goldsmiths: "Make more than a hundred *niṣkas* weighing a hundred *palas* each; make two bowls of gold and silver for the *mahiman* cups; make golden vessels with single-folded rims; and make as many golden *upaśayas* as there are wives, with silver knots, or silver ones with golden knots. As many as...

Have that many golden water-pots with lids made, with silver pegs, or silver ones with golden pegs; have as many golden water-jars made as there are wives, with silver bands, or silver ones with golden bands; make one golden fan; make three golden whisks with silver handles, or silver ones with golden handles; make a thousand glass beads of gold, a thousand of silver, and a thousand [of copper].
The ocean has a golden mattress, a golden sixfold halter, and a golden tethering rope.

Then he instructs those who have worked with the nails: "Make them in unlimited numbers, [but] eight of each. Now, other things are prepared for him: a hundred skins of ghee, a hundred skins of honey, a hundred skins of rice, a hundred skins of *pṛthuka* (flat rice), a hundred skins of parched grain, a hundred skins of groats, a hundred skins of fried grains, a hundred skins of flour, a hundred skins of *masūṣya* (lentils), and a hundred skins of *priyaṅgu* rice-grains. Then there are these twenty-one Pratiprasthātṛs standing ready together with him, making twenty-two including himself.
They collect animals from various regions—those of such and such a form, and those of other forms; they know them:

they guard the domestic animals in the villages, the wild animals in the forest, the mountain-dwellers on the mountains, the river-dwellers in the rivers, the birds in cages, and the reptiles in jars; such is the well-known manner of gathering them. Then he proceeds with the *prāyaṇīya* offering.
Having performed the *prāyaṇīya* offering, he proceeds with the *pada* ritual;
having performed the *pada* ritual, having purchased the King [Soma] for a thousand [cows] on a bull's hide, he brings it home and performs the *ātithya* offering;
having performed the *ātithya*, he then proceeds day by day with the *pravargya* and the *upasad* rites.

This twenty-one-fold Agnicayana is completed in twelve days. Its *sadas* has twenty-one roofs; then he carries forward the Āhavanīya fire. Having carried forward the Āhavanīya, he erects the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds.
Having erected the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna*, he carries forward Agni and Soma. Having carried forward Agni and Soma, he raises the sacrificial post according to the procedure for the post.
Having set aside the Agniṣṭha post made of *rājjudāla* wood which possesses a wooden ring (*svaru*), he dedicates the animal for Agni-Soma.
Having performed the well-known ritual with its omentum (*vapā*), he takes up the *vasatīvarī* waters; then he offers the sacrificial cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) for the animal.

Following that, eight oblations for the Devasū deities are offered—namely, those beginning with "To Agni Gṛhapati"—and this tenth oblation, "To Agni Gāyatra"; thus concludes the sacrifice of ten offerings.
For this [sacrifice], these are the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses: "The kindled one, the hope of the quarters, the finder of light for us... The animal-cake offerings conclude with the *iḍā*;

the animal sacrifice concludes with the *patnīsaṃyāja*s, or according to some, with the *hṛdayaśūla* rite. Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and set aside the milks, they fast. Thereafter, at the very dead of night, they wake up;
the ritual procedure is the same up until the laying down of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).

He moves along the enclosing-sticks [with the formula]: "Who yokes thee? May he yoke thee. Six times on the middle stick, six times on the southern one, and five times on the northern one. Then, having brought down King Soma, he begins the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*).
When the morning litany is concluded, he goes towards the waters; he emerges from the waters and enters the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice.
The pressing of the Soma juice is performed in the established manner.
The planets (grahas) are taken in the established manner;
the ritual procedure up to the *pavamāna* is the same.

Intending to press the *pavamāna*, he asks for sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and a hundred-pala gold ornament. Then he says, "O Udgātṛ, let the horse sing the *udgītha* for me with both the sacrificial grass and the hundred-pala ornament."

They take hold of the horse's tail [with the words]: "O Vājina, Agni is yoked for thee; I take hold of thee from behind; convey me safely across. O Vājina, Vāyu is yoked for thee; I take hold of thee from behind; convey me safely across. O Vājina, Āditya is yoked for thee; I take hold of thee from behind; convey me safely across. Then they move northward toward the *pavamāna* [laud]. To the north, this stall for the mares has been raised and enclosed; they open it, and the mares neigh toward the horse, and the horse neighs toward the mares; that is the *udgītha* of the horse.

Then auspicious voices cry out: "This sacrificial horse has risen! Life-force has risen! Prosperity has risen! Spiritual luster has risen! This has risen! This has risen! Auspicious voices cry out; they release the mares in the stable and tie up the horse. There they scatter for him food for this world and for the next. Then he says: "O Udgātṛ, a hundred cows and a hundred palas of gold are yours; you have sung the Udgītha for me. For him, the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant is performed on four verses, and the *ājya* chants on eight verses each.
The midday Pavamāna is twelvefold; the Pṛṣṭhas are sixteenfold; the Ārbhava Pavamāna is twenty-onefold.
The Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the twenty-fourfold;
they call that the Catuṣṭoma.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the Āśvina cup: having drawn the Āśvina cup and taken eleven cords, he approaches the sacrificial post.

Having released the eleven animals, beginning with the one made of *rājjudāla* wood that has a hornless goat (*svarvat*) as the first for Agni, he dedicates them. Having performed the ritual with their omenta in the established manner, they proceed to the morning pressing; that concludes in the regular way.
They proceed for the midday pressing;
the pressing is well-established,
and the cups are drawn in the established manner.
The ritual procedure for the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) is the same: having offered the *dakṣiṇā* oblations, he offers eight *saṃvarga* oblations with the formula, "May the sacrifice come hither.
He gives the third portion of the sacrificial gifts.
Having offered the *vaiśvakarmaṇa* oblations, he offers nine *paryāpti* oblations with the formula, "The past, the present, and the future."

In this case, the consecration with fire does not effect a continuous lineage; the midday pressing concludes in the regular manner. They proceed to the third pressing. Having performed the rite with the Āditya cup in the established way, he draws the Āgrayaṇa cup.
The ritual action is the same; having performed the Pavamāna rite with the Pavamāna cup, he proceeds with the animal sacrifices in their own place.

For these, there are separate *manotā* hymns, separate deities, separate touchings, and separate *vasā-homa* offerings. The *vanaspati* offering is the same, as is the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering accompanied by the *praisha* call, the *iḍā* portion is the same, and the directions are the same; however, some say the directions are different.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings; this Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, characterized by four stomas, concludes with the Patnīsaṃyājas.

Then, these one hundred ox-hides are spread out for him, placed along the northern buttock and the northern wing. Then, having removed twenty or twenty-four of those butter-skins, they mix the foods with the others. Then, having piled twenty or twenty-four of those wood-filled skins in the middle of the fire-altar, they cut up the others and scatter them all around.

He extends this square [shed] from the middle of the divine city toward himself, or he constructs wings and a tail so that it may be level with the tops of the sacrificial posts; then, having raised it, they enclose it, making its door facing north.
They then set up these *indrāṇasā* pillars: four in each of the cardinal directions and the others in the intermediate directions, if there are eight.

Four of them mount each of these [chariots], and ten others are night-walkers; then they bring clarified butter in bowls for them, and food with the eighth [portion]. Then the Adhvaryu takes a long-handled *sruva* ladle and a long-handled *darvī* spoon; twenty-one Pratiprasthātṛs take [the spoons], and ten others are night-walkers. Then the Adhvaryu, having dipped the *sruva* into the clarified butter, offers the first three Vaiśvadeva oblations.

With "Svāhā to the one who has meditated upon the meditation," they offer oblations of clarified butter with the *sruva* ladles; with "Svāhā to the toothed one," they offer oblations of food with the *darvī* spoons; and with "Svāhā to the toothless one.
In this very manner, when they reach the end of this section (*anuvāka*), he then interposes this section:

first the *stokīyā* verses, then this section, then the *diśyā* verses, then this section, then the *ekaviṃśinī* initiation, then this section, then the seasonal initiations (*ṛtudīkṣā*), then this section, then the *sāvitrāṇi* formulas of the horse, and then this section.
In this very way, they proceed through these sections with this very section;

when they reach the end of these sections, they then enter these [subsequent] sections: those dedicated to the All-Gods (*vaiśvadeva*), the limbs of the horse, two for the forms of horses, two for plants and trees, two for the confluences of waters and their names, one for the *saṃplava* [section], and the *khārī-homa*. In this very way, they proceed through these sections with this very section.
When they reach the end of these sections (anuvākas), they then turn back to these very sections, offering [oblations] with: "Svāhā to one! Svāhā to two!

In this very manner, they repeatedly offer these sections, reciting them again and again with this same section; then, at the time of carrying around the Vasatīvarī waters, they run toward [the fire].
When the *vasatīvarī* waters have been carried around, when the *subrahmaṇyā* has been invoked, they run back up again;
in this very same way, they complete these recitations by offering oblations while repeatedly beginning them with this same *anuvāka*.
These, indeed, are called the "full lifespans of the horse."

"‘They are for the sake of completion,’ so some say; for with these [oblations] they offer throughout the night. Then, as the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ are about to commence the Prātaranuvāka, two others who have been busy with the night-rites run forward. Having brought down King Soma, he commences the Prātaranuvāka. When the Prātaranuvāka has been concluded, he goes toward the waters; having emerged from the water, he enters upon the Ukthya sacrifice."

The ritual procedure up to the offering of the Upāṃśu cup is the same. Intending to offer [the subsequent libations], Indra, having hastened toward us, offers four spoonfuls with the formulas: "Svāhā to the Dawn! Svāhā to the Breaking of Dawn! Svāhā to the One about to Rise! Svāhā to the Rising! The pressing of the Soma is performed in the established manner; the ritual procedure up to the Antaryāma cup is the same.

When about to offer the Antaryāma cup, he hastens toward Indra and offers four spoonfuls with the formulas: "To the one arisen, svāhā! To heaven, svāhā! To the world, svāhā! To all, svāhā! At this point, when the sun has risen, those performing the night-rites cease; they do not dismantle the enclosures, but turn back the *indrāṇāsas*. The cups are drawn in the usual manner with golden vessels.

The ritual procedure is the same up to the Āgrayaṇa cup; having drawn the Āgrayaṇa, he draws two Mahiman cups with gold and silver [spoons], using the verses "He who from breathing... and "He who gives the self...". Then he draws the Ukthya cup. The ritual procedure is the same up to the Āśvina cup; having drawn the Āśvina cup and taken twenty-four cords, they proceed toward the sacrificial posts. The other assistants take four cords each. Having set aside the Rājjudāla post for the Agniṣṭha which is fitted with a wooden ring (svaru), he first raises the Pautudrava post to its south as the Upasthāvāna.

Then, three on the north, three on the south made of *bilva* wood; three on the north, three on the south made of *khadira* wood; three on the north, three on the south made of *pālāśa* wood. Here, he places that *pālāśa* resting-post (*upaśaya*) silently on the south. Having set out the sacrificial posts provided with *svaru*s, the Adhvaryu then dedicates the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal—these three animals belonging to Prajāpati—at the post nearest the fire.

Then he dedicates the animals tied to the sacrificial post: a black-spotted bull for Agni-Indra; a goat for Indra-Pūṣan; two goats with black necks for Agni; two woolly-thighed ones for Tvaṣṭṛ; two white-backed ones for Bṛhaspati; a spotted-bellied one for Dhātṛ; and a white-footed ram for Sūrya. Then the Adhvaryu dedicates at the very post nearest the fire eleven animals: "A red-marked ox for Agni Anīkavant," and so on. Then the Adhvaryu dedicates at the very post nearest the fire two pairs: "Two oxen that draw carts for Soma Svarāj. Then the Adhvaryu dedicates at the very post nearest the fire eleven wild animals: "A boar for Indra Rājanyabandhu," and so on.
This very [set] consists of sixty animals for the central post. Then there are the ten *anu-vākas* of eighteen [animals each], beginning with "The ruddy one, the smoke-colored ruddy one.

Of these, they station nine on the southern posts and nine on the northern posts. For those on the south, the *āgnendra* ones are the principal; for those on the north, the *aindra* ones are the principal.
Then there are the ten *anu-vākas* of ten [animals each], beginning with "The *mayu* belonging to Prajāpati."
They station five of those [animals] on the southern sacrificial posts and five others on the northern ones;
of the former, the one dedicated to Soma and Pūṣan is the first, and of the latter, the one dedicated to Indra and Pūṣan is the first.
Then, upon this spare post (upaśaya), he mentally dedicates whichever person he hates.

If he does not hate anyone, he assigns him [the victim] with the formula, "The whole animal is yours. At this time, he offers a spoonful of oblation in the Āhavanīya fire with the words, "Svāhā to the one consecrated!

Then he yokes that horse to the chariot in front of the axle with the verse, "They yoke the ruddy, bright one as he moves around those who stand still. Then he strokes its back with the verse, "The luminaries shine in heaven. In the same manner, he yokes the second horse; he yokes the side-horse to its left in exactly the same way.
He cleanses the backs of the two [horses]. He yokes the two beloved bay horses to the chariot on opposite sides—“the red, bold ones that carry the hero,” he says.

Then, saying “making a banner for those without banners,” he fastens the standard. Then he equips the sacrificer with the verses for binding the armor. With the fourteen verses beginning, “Like a cloud, his face appears,” according to their form, he then stands near the chariot with the three verses beginning, “O Lord of the Forest, may you be strong-limbed,” each in its proper meter.

Then he causes the drum to be silenced with three verses in their proper meters: "Silence the earth and the sky. Then he proceeds toward the southern pool with three sections [of the Veda]: "The sky is your back; the steed has stepped across with his strides; the prize-winner has won the prize. They cause the horses to run up to the chests [of the sacrificer]. Then, having turned this chariot clockwise, he brings it to the hall with [the verse]: "Since the wind has gone to the waters, the dear body of Indra—by this path, O singer, bring the horse back to us again."

The Adhvaryu follows them with the subsequent *stokīyā* verses, namely the Anuvāka beginning with "To Agni, Svāhā! To Soma, Svāhā!", reciting it again and again with repeated intonation until these drops cease. Then, having unyoked that horse from its own chariot in front of the sacrificial posts and bound it with a golden tether, they lead it twice around to the Adhvaryu’s dwelling. Then the Mahiṣī, the Vāvātā, and the Parivṛktī—these women approach him, bringing perfumes, aromatic powders, and amulets for the horse.

That which is before the chest, he anoints with the wife of the Pautudrava [priests] together with their wives, saying: "May the Vasus anoint you with the Gāyatrī metre. Then that which is behind the chest up to the navel, he anoints with the wife of the Gaulgulava [priests] together with their wives, saying: "May the Rudras anoint you with the Triṣṭubh metre.

Then that which is behind the navel up to the tail, he anoints with the wife of the Parivṛkti [priests] together with their wives, saying: "May the Ādityas anoint you with the Jagatī metre," using [ointment] from Musta grass for the wives of the Sūtas, Grāmaṇīs, Kṣattṛs, and Saṃgrahītṛs.

Of his hair that flows forward, the chief queen (*mahiṣī*) fastens a thousand golden beads with the word "Bhūḥ," together with the wives of those who have been appointed as deputies. Then, of the hair that flows backward, the favorite wife (*vāvātā*) fastens a thousand silver beads with the word "Bhuvaḥ," together with the wives of those who are not kings. Then this discarded wife (*parivṛktī*) fastens a thousand beads from the sea with the word "Svaḥ," together with the wives of the charioteers, the village headmen, the attendants, and the collectors.

As they go away in this manner, the wives—the chief queen (*mahiṣī*), the favorite (*vāvātā*), the discarded one (*parivṛktī*), the kitchen-maid (*māhānasī*), and the slave-girl (*dāsī*)—scatter for him parched grains mixed with honey, saying:
"O Lājī, O Śācī, eat this food, O God; eat this food, O Prajāpati, for the sake of glory, for the sake of long life, for the sake of cattle."

"It is known from scripture: 'The offspring of her whose food he eats shall indeed be prosperous. Then, having released this horse from its tether, he proceeds with the fire-drilling according to the ritual for fire-drilling; having cast the fire-sticks and made the oblation, the Adhvaryu then binds the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal to the post nearest the fire. Then he binds to it the animals to be distributed around it: a black-spotted one for Agni-Indra, one for Indra-Pūṣan, and one for Pūṣan;
these three on the forehead; two for Agni with black necks on the necks; and two for Tvaṣṭṛ with hairy thighs on the thighs."
Two white-backed animals for Bṛhaspati are tied to the back; a speckled-bellied one for Dhātṛ is tied to the belly;

a white-spotted ram for Sūrya is tied to the tail. Then the Adhvaryu ties to the post standing nearest the fire-altar a red-marked bull for Agni Anīkavant; then the Adhvaryu ties to the same post two oxen that draw carts for Soma Svarāj; then the Adhvaryu ties to the same post a boar for Indra Rājā.

He follows all the wild animals by means of the very act of tethering them; those domestic animals which he intends to release, as well as the wild ones, he then has the Pratiprasthātṛs tether for the sacrificial gifts—first the southern ones, then the northern ones.

Then, having sprinkled this horse with the regular sprinkling, he sprinkles it with the "over-sprinkling" (atiprokṣa) while reciting, "Born is the seed," but he sprinkles the other animals with the regular sprinkling alone.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛs sprinkle the southern [posts], then the northern ones;
then he causes this horse to smell the sprinkling waters in front of the sacrificial posts [with the formulas]:
"Agni was the victim; with him they sacrificed; he won this world in which Agni is. That is your world; you shall win it—smell it! Vāyu was the victim; Āditya was the victim."

If he does not smell it, he makes him smell it again, saying: "Agni was the sacrificial animal; with him they sacrificed. He won this world in which Agni dwells. That is your world; therefore, I shall exclude you from it if you do not smell it. "Agni was the sacrificial animal; with him they sacrificed. He won this world in which Agni dwells. That is your world; you shall win it if you smell it. "Vāyu was the sacrificial animal... Āditya was the sacrificial animal... If he does not smell it, he makes him smell it again, saying: "Agni was the sacrificial animal; with him they sacrificed. He won this world in which Agni dwells. That is your world; you shall win it if you smell it. "Vāyu was the sacrificial animal... Āditya was the sacrificial animal..."
At this time, he offers a spoonful of oblation into the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "To the one seized, svāhā!
Then, taking a fuel-stick from the faggot, he says, "Recite for the fire being kindled," and he places the faggot on the fire, leaving one stick aside;
he fans it with the *vedā* grass-bundle, and when the *sāmidhenī* verses have been recited, he pours the *āghāra* libation with the *sruva* spoon.
Having wiped the two offering-spoons, he then,
without letting them touch each other, steps northward and anoints the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal with the *juhū* spoon; then the animals tied to the limbs,
and then the others.
Then, having placed the two offering-spoons first to the south, then to the north, and then in their proper places, he chooses the *pravara*.
He chooses the well-known officiating priests;
the Hotṛ priest sits down and awaits the impulse.
Having been born [from the fire], he takes up the two offering-spoons, steps across, causes the announcement to be made, and says, "Prompt for the kindling-sticks!
The verses beginning with "The well-kindled one, anointing the navel of prayers" constitute the *apri* hymns of the horse.
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering. Saying "Prompt! Prompt!", he pours together the butter at the fourth and eighth [oblations]; at the eighth, he pours out the entire remainder.
He leaves over the remnants for the *svāhākṛti* offerings.
Having performed ten *prayāja* offerings and stepped across toward the north, he asks for a golden arrow;
having smeared those two [the arrow and the gold] on the *juhū* ladle, he anoints the horse, the hornless goat, and the wild ox with them.
The animals tied to the middle post are made of black iron, those to the others of common iron; the sacrificial fees for the southern posts are gold, and for the northern ones, silver.
Then, having set down the two offering-spoons (*srucau*) in their respective places, he says, "Recite for the fire being carried around.

During the regular fire-circumambulation (*paryagnikaraṇa*), he continues the formula: "May the ram protect thee with cooked offerings, the red-necked one with goats, and the *śalmali* tree [with its products]."

When these animals have been encircled by fire, they release two ewes, two cows born on earth, for the quarters; two mares, two cows born on earth, for the Vairāja; two women, two cows born on earth, for Indra; and a boar for King Varuṇa—thus all the wild animals are released here. Then, with the animals having been encircled by fire, they proceed toward the north; among them, the bulls for Indra are those at the northern end, and the horse follows in its proper order. The Adhvaryu takes hold of the horse itself with the two omentum-roasting spits.

The other attendants lead the horse northward one after another, without letting them touch each other. Then he calls for sacrificial grass (*barhis*), a hundred-pala weight of gold, a skin, an upper garment, a mattress, and a linen cloth (*tārpya*). To the north, this is spread out in abundance;

he throws these—the sacrificial grass, the hundred-pala weight, the skin, the upper garment, and the mattress—down for the horse as it is being slaughtered. This fivefold set, while the horse is being slain with the *tārpya* cloth, the Prastotṛ priest attends upon it from behind with the *yāma-sāman*.
He does so separately for each of the others.

Then, having said, "Strike down the others who do not make the sounds *māyu*, whether they face east or north; make them senseless," he returns by the same way he came and sits at the place for the clotted butter (*pṛṣadājya*). Then the Hotṛ and the Brahman engage in a theological debate (*brahmodya*); the Brahman stands to the south between the sacrificial post and the Āhavanīya fire, and the Hotṛ to the north.
The Hotṛ asks the Brahman a question.
"What was the first thought? What was the great winged one? What was the devourer? What was the *pilippila*?
To him the other replied: "The sky was the first thought; the horse was the great winged one; the night was the devourer; the sheep was the *pilippila*.
To him the other asks: "Who indeed wanders alone? Who indeed is born again? What is the remedy for cold? What is the great receptacle?"
The other replied to him: "The sun moves alone; the moon is born again. Fire is the remedy for cold; the earth is the great receptacle. The other asked him:

"I ask you about the furthest limit of the earth; I ask you about the navel of the world; I ask you about the seed of the stallion; I ask you about the highest heaven of speech. The other replied to him: "They call the altar the furthest limit of the earth; they call the sacrifice the navel of the world; they call Soma the seed of the stallion; and Brahman indeed is the highest heaven of speech."

He says, "They have been quieted," and offers the oblation for those quieted with the verse, "When the animals did not cry out. Then he offers seven breath-oblations with, "To Prāṇa, svāhā! To Vyāna, svāhā!

He offers one hundred and thirty-three oblations related to the Aśvastoma with the verses beginning, "When you first cried out as you were being born," "May Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman [protect us]," "Those who look upon the steed when cooked," and "And indeed, of him as he runs and hastens. Then the immolators approach;
with the words, "Come hither," he consecrates the animals as they are being released from their bonds with the verse, "May Aditi release these bonds."

"Along with the individual Viśākhās, they cast this direction away; I make the one who acts as an enemy low; upon him whom we hate, I fasten the nooses. Then these wives go forth with golden water-vessels, following along the back of the horse while causing its vital breaths to swell; they proceed in the same manner for the other animals in succession.

Then this chief queen, having cast off her hair and put on a garment, shaking it with a golden fan, goes three times around the horse counter-clockwise, saying: "May the protectors protect you; may the protectors protect you. We invoke you, the beloved of the beloved, the most excellent of the dear ones; we invoke you, the lord of treasures, the treasure of treasures—O Vasu, mine! Having gone around three times, she stands to the north together with the wives of the appointed attendants. In the same way, [the other queens stand] with the wives of the favorite queens; in the same way, the discarded queens [stand] with the wives of the charioteers, the village leaders, the chamberlains, and the collectors.

As the wives go forth in this manner, they then decorate this horse with all its ornaments and enclose it; they make a door for it facing the north. Then, having decorated this chief queen with all her ornaments, the Adhvaryu leads her forward while she hides herself and reproaches [the horse], saying: "O Mother, O little Mother, O dear Mother, no one is leading me away; the little horse has fallen asleep. Having lain down to the north of the horse, she places a cloth over his head.

Then the Adhvaryu covers her with a garment, saying: "O fortunate one, dweller in Kāmpīla, may you two cover yourselves together in the heavenly world. Then the chief queen places her vulva over [the sacrificer's] penis, saying: "I have conceived a child; you have conceived a child. May we two together extend our four feet. The Adhvaryu addresses her with the mantra: "May the bull, the placer of seed, place seed in you," beginning with the verse: "He who, upon their dark mark, struck down the destroyer of the dwelling. Thereafter, the wife reproaches him.
"O Amba, O Ambālī, O Ambikā, let no one have intercourse with me; my little horse has fallen asleep"—
thus the sacrificer addresses her mockingly, [thinking], "Lift her up, make her stand upright," yet she reproaches him in that very same way.
The favorite wife mocks her, saying, "She who is a doe eating barley"; she, in turn, reproaches her; then the neglected wife mocks her, saying, "This little bird."
She reproaches them in that very manner,
but all the members of the group revile her, saying, "Your mother and your father [do this]," and thus she does not reproach them here.

Having lain down beside the horse for a moment, or having risen and put on his garment, he purifies himself with water using the three verses beginning "O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss," according to their respective meters; the fourth verse, "I have celebrated Dadhikrāvan," they all recite, as do those who speak what is impure at the sacrifice.
They lead away the wife and dismantle the enclosure.

They carry the horse's ornaments and the Adhvaryu’s dwelling-place away; then, having mixed powdered *śalmali* wood with sour curds, they smear it over the horse in the direction of its hair. Then the chief queen (*mahiṣī*), the favorite wife (*vāvātā*), and the discarded wife (*parivṛktī*)—these women, taking needles and bundles of wool, approach the horse. Upon that part of him which is before the chest, the chief queen fashions incisions with golden needles while reciting two verses: "The *gāyatrī*, the *triṣṭubh*, the *dvipadā*, and the *catuṣpadā*," together with the wives of those who have been appointed as attendants. Then...

That which is behind the chest up to the navel, in that part, the Vāvātā wives of the kings [anoint] with silver needles using the next two verses; then that which is behind the navel up to the tail, in that part, the Parivṛktī wives of the charioteers, village headmen, chamberlains, and collectors [anoint] with lead needles using the next two verses.

The wives go back as they came to the Adhvaryu’s dwelling; they take the needles, and then he asks for a golden arrow and a bronze arrow, and with those two he scrapes the chest of the horse, saying, "Thus dissect the horse."
"Who flays you? Who dissects you?"—with these six verses he causes the sacrificer to recite.
When he reaches the end of this hymn, the Adhvaryu then scrapes the flesh from the horse's breast, saying, "Thus one should dissect the horse, thus," for there is no omentum (vapā) of the horse.
The fat of the horse is like the moon, surrounded by fat; the omentum of the hornless goat, and likewise that of the Gomṛga.

The entrails of those animals tied to the limbs are held with iron hooks; those of the others with copper ones; those of the southern animals with golden ones, and those of the northern ones with silver ones.

The Adhvaryu begins with the omentum of the horse first; they bring the other omenta following in succession. While the omentum of the horse is being heated, he throws the tip of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) into it; they hold the others over it. To the north, they cook the omenta of the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal; to the south, those of the other animals.

He makes an offering of the horse's omentum with a spoon-oblation; they hold the other [omentum] back. Then, having proceeded with the *svāhākṛti* call and the *praisha*, he sprinkles the clotted butter (*pṛṣadājya*) with the residue of the oblation and sprinkles the horse's omentum itself. They hold the other [omentum] back. Then, having offered a spoon-oblation before the *svāhākṛti* call, he offers the *mahiman* cup with a golden vessel, saying, "The sky is thy greatness. Then, having spread an underlayer of butter twice with the spoon while cutting off the horse's omentum, he says, "To Prajāpati," and he smells it.

"Recite for the omentum and fat of the goat and the ox as they are being cut off," he says loudly. As many offering-spoons as there are, he takes them up; then the others are lifted with a vessel or a *veḍasūna* ladle. He pours clarified butter over them twice. Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says in a low voice, "To Prajāpati," and then loudly, "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the omentum and fat of the goat and the ox that have been set forth. When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers the omentum. Then, from above, he offers the *mahiman* cup with silver. "Of thee, that great one, the earth... he recites. Then he proceeds with the omenta of the animals tied to the limbs (*paryaṅgya*), and then those of the others.

Then the Pratiprasthātṛs proceed with the omenta of those on the south; then [they proceed] with those on the north. For those domestic animals which he has released and for the wild ones, he offers spoonfuls (sruvāhuti) in place of their omenta. They proceed with the omenta of these various classes of animals: those dedicated to Prajāpati, to Savitṛ, to Sarasvatī, to Pūṣan, to Yama, to the Pitṛ-deities, to Dyāvāpṛthivī, to Vāyu, to Sūrya, and to Viśvakarman. Then follows the offering with the *svāhā*-utterance.

Having offered the oblation with the *sruva* ladle and having thrown the two *vapā-śrapaṇī* spits into the fire, they step out and purify themselves at the *cātvāla* pit. Then he gives instructions regarding the animals, saying to the *śamitr*: "Do not cut away the hair of the horse; do not crush the bone of the horse. Having dissected it limb by limb, place it together in a pot on the *śāmitra* fire. Do the same for the hornless goat and the *gomṛga*. Furthermore, cook the right horse-hoof and the neck of the *gomṛga* on the *śāmitra* fire. Cook the horse-whip in an iron vessel. Then, having offered the *sāvitra* oblation, they proceed to the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*); thus the rite concludes directly.
Then, having offered the Sāvitra oblation, they proceed to the midday pressing; the pressing is performed in the established manner,
and the cups are drawn in the established manner.

The ritual action is the same for the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*). Having offered the offerings pertaining to the sacrificial gifts, he offers eight *saṃvarga* oblations with the formula, "May the sacrifice come hither.
He gives the sacrificial gifts as he desires.
Having offered the *vaiśvakarmaṇa* oblations, he offers nine *paryāpti* oblations with the formula, "The past, the present, the future."

The consecration with fire is well-known; it effects the continuity of the Ahīna sacrifice. The midday pressing concludes in the regular manner. Then, having offered the Sāvitra oblation, they proceed to the third pressing.
Having proceeded in the established manner with the Āditya cup, he draws the Āgrayaṇa cup; then he draws the Ukthya cup. The ritual procedure up to the Pavamāna chant is the same.

Having performed the Pavamāna rite, he then calls for these animals: the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal; then the animals bound to the limbs (paryaṅgyas); then the others; then those on the south side and those on the north side.
They set down the sacrificial oblations to the east of the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal, and to the south of the other animals.
Then, having placed the heart of the horse upon a mat of reeds (vaitasa), while cutting off portions from its front with both gold and an arrow, he says:

"Recite for the *manotā* as the oblation is being cut off," he says; thus he cuts off eleven portions. He does so for the hornless goat (*tūpara*) in this manner, and for the gayal (*gomṛga*) in this manner. For the animals tied to the limbs, [he uses] iron [knives]; for the others, copper ones. For those on the right side, golden ones; for those on the left, silver ones. He does not [cut portions] for the horse, nor for the hornless goat, nor for the gayal, when cutting for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; he does not cut portions from the other animals either. He does not cut portions for the *iḍā* offering for the horse, nor for the hornless goat, nor for the gayal; he does not cut portions from the other animals either.
Then he arranges this horse limb by limb on a mat of reeds: he stretches out a hornless goat facing west in front [of the horse],
and a wild ox facing east behind it.

Then, taking up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, he says in a low voice, "For Prajāpati," and loudly, "Recite the invitatory verse for the oblation of the goat, the bull, and the ox. Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says in a low voice, "For Prajāpati," and loudly, "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the oblation of the goat, the bull, and the ox, which has been set forth. When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he throws them together with the mat into the fire, reciting the three sections beginning with, "The sky is your back; you have stepped across with strides, the steed has stepped with vigor. Then he proceeds with the oblations of the animals tied to the limbs (*paryaṅgya*), and then those of the others.

Then the Pratiprasthātṛs perform the offerings with the oblations for those on the south; then for those on the north. For those domestic animals which he has released and for the wild ones, he offers in exchange with spoon-oblations from their respective oblations. It has already been stated that they perform the offerings with the oblations for those species of white animals. Then, prior to the Vanaspati offering, he sacrifices to the common quarters. Then he proceeds with the Vanaspati offering. Then, prior to the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, [he offers] with the neck of a Gomṛga.

He offers the first oblation with the *aśvatejanī* verse; then he proceeds with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. At this time, he offers a spoonful into the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "To the offered, svāhā!

Then he places that pouring-vessel (*praseka*) upon the fire—either to the south facing north, or behind facing east. Its front half is like a *sruk* ladle, its middle part is exactly like that, and its base is like a *camasa* cup.
Into it, spreading four portions of butter, he says: "Bring [the ghee] continuously without being careless; I shall recite the *stega* verses."

When he reaches the *dhārāgni* (the stream-fire), he enters it with the fourteen *anuvākas* beginning, "The steers with their tusks, the frogs with their jaws," and the fifteenth with "To Prayāsa, svāhā!

Then he offers two oblations: "To the young bull, svāhā! To the draft-ox, svāhā! He recites the thirty-sixth verse dedicated to the *Aśvastomīya*, three *dvipadā* verses, and the verses "May we establish these worlds," "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss," and "May we find a friend. At this point, he throws the sprinkling-vessel into the fire and then pours the residue over it.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the after-offerings (*anūyāja*s). Then, prior to the final after-offering, he offers the horse-tackling cord (*aśvatejanī*) with a horse-hoof.

The ritual procedure is the same up to the offerings to the wives (*patnīsaṃyāja*s). Then, prior to the final offering to the wives, he offers the horse-tackling cord with an iron water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). The Ukthya sacrifice, consisting of twenty-one [stotras] and performed in a straight manner, concludes with the offerings to the wives. Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and set aside the milks, they fast. Thereafter, they wake up at the dead of night.
Having taken the morning clarified butter offerings and having brought the King Soma down, he begins the Prātaranuvāka recitation;

when the Prātaranuvāka is concluded, he goes toward the waters and emerges from the waters, and thus enters upon the Atirātra sacrifice; the pressing of the Soma is performed in the established manner.
The cups (grahas) are taken as established by tradition;
the ritual procedure is the same up to the Āśvina cup. Having drawn the Āśvina cup and having taken eleven cords, he approaches the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
Having set aside the one with a wooden ring (*svaru*) made of *rājjudāla* wood which stands nearest the fire, he dedicates in the morning eleven bovine animals consecrated to Prajāpati.
Having performed the ritual for them with the omenta as is well known, they proceed to the morning pressing;
that concludes in the regular manner, and they proceed to the midday pressing.
The pressing is well-known;
the cups are drawn in the established manner.

The ritual procedure up to the offerings for the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) is the same. Having offered the offerings pertaining to the sacrificial gifts, he offers the eight *saṃvarga* oblations with the formula, "May the sacrifice turn hither. He gives away the remainder of the sacrificial gifts.

Having offered the Vaiśvakarman oblations, he offers nine *paryāpti* offerings with the formulas, "The past, the present, the future... The consecration of the fires is omitted; he does not here effect the continuity of the *ahīna* sacrifice. The midday pressing concludes in the regular manner.
They proceed to the third pressing.
Having performed the rite with the Āditya cup in the established way, he draws the Āgrayaṇa cup, and then he draws the Ukthya cup.
The ritual action is common; having performed the Pavamāna rite with the Pavamāna [laud], he proceeds with the animal offerings in their own place.

For these, the Manotā hymn is common, the deity is common, the touching [of the victim] is common, the offering of the fat (vasāhoma) is common, the Vanaspati offering is common, the Sviṣṭakṛt offering accompanied by the formal summons is common, the Iḍā portion is common, and the directions are common.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.

Having performed the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings and having gone forward to the east, he replenishes the *dhruvā* ladle and offers the *abhūtis* and *anubhūtis* with these two sections: "May my houses be [prosperous]... and "By means of Agni, he experienced the heat... Then he offers the two oblations for the past and the future with "To the past, svāhā! To the future, svāhā! Then, having offered the *samiṣṭayajus* formulas belonging to the *adhvara*, he offers the ten oblations pertaining to the fire-altar (*agni*).

The ritual procedure is the same up to the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath). Then, having offered the second *avabhṛtha* oblation at this *avabhṛtha*, he offers ten *vāruṇa* oblations with the formula, "Homage to the King! Homage to Varuṇa! He then offers ninety oblations with the formula, "To Death, svāhā! To Death, svāhā! and eleven oblations with the formula, "To Prayāsa, svāhā! To Ayāsa, svāhā! A man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundred powers; the self is the one hundred and first. As great as man is, from that much he sacrifices away death—so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Now, this Ātreya—emaciated, pale, leprous, covered in moles, with reddish-brown eyes, bald, deformed, with deformed nails, hunchbacked, afflicted with skin disease, and naked—submerges himself [in water]. Into his head he offers an oblation with the words, "To Jumbaka, svāhā! At this point, they give him a hundred-wheeled chariot. Then they blow him away from the place where the arrows were won, saying, "May you not dwell in my kingdom! The purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) is performed in the usual manner. Having sacrificed the concluding offering (udayanīyā), he dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa.

For this [offering], nine white barren cows dedicated to Sūrya are to be seized as victims. Having performed the ritual with their omenta in the established manner, and having raised the Pātnīvata offering in front of the Gārhapatya fire, he dedicates to Tvaṣṭṛ the animals—a speckled goat, a *kikidīvi* bird, and a *vidīgaya*—at that [fire]. Having carried fire around them and released them, he completes the rite with clarified butter. Then he offers the animal-cake oblations; or rather, two animal-cake oblations. Or else, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of the animal-cake, he offers ten barley-grain oblations with the formulas: "Homage to the King! Homage to Varuṇa! and so forth.

Then, before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of the animal sacrifice, he offers ten oblations of clarified butter with the verses beginning, "May the wind blow pleasantly toward the cows. The animal rites conclude in the established manner. Then, having performed the *udavasānīyā* sacrifice and having erected a wide sacrificial post in front of the *āhavanīya* fire, he dedicates these animals to it: one for Agni, one for Indra-Agni, and one for the Aśvins.
Having proceeded with their omenta in the established manner, he offers the sacrificial cakes (*paśupuroḍāśa*) for them.

They follow these with the eight oblations for the gods’ instigation (*devasū*), beginning with "To Agni, the deliverer from distress, a cake on eight potsherds"; this is the sacrifice of ten offerings, and these are its *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses: "I meditate upon Agni, the first, the wise one... Then, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of the animal-cake, he offers ten oblations for spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) with the formula: "O Brahman, may a Brāhmaṇa be born endowed with spiritual luster. Then, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of the animal victim, he offers ten *saṃnati* oblations with the formulas: "He has bowed down to Agni; he has bowed down to the Earth," and so forth.
The animals are well-known; they conclude here. With these twelve *brahmaudana* offerings he performs daily.

Their performance has been explained as it was for the one [offering] elsewhere, except for the two girdles. Here, for these [offerings], he gives more than a hundred gold coins (*niṣka*), each weighing a hundred *pala*.
He gives two vessels of gold and silver; he gives vessels made entirely of gold—a golden cushion, a golden foot-rope, and a golden tethering-cord.

Then he gives a hundred cows to the two lute-players; then he sacrifices with the seasonal victims (*ṛtu-paśu*). Or rather, he performs them according to the sequence of seasons, or in a single year within the same fire-altars: three tawny ones for spring, three dappled ones for summer, three spotted ones for the rainy season, three speckled ones for autumn, three speckled-thighed ones for winter, and three anointed ones for the cool season—these are for the year. Then he sacrifices with the Devikā offerings, then he sacrifices with the Traidhātavīya, then he sacrifices with the Sautrāmaṇī;
thus the Aśvamedha is completed in three years.
The Aśvamedha is concluded; the Aśvamedha is concluded.
One who is about to sacrifice with the Dvādaśāha may be either one person or many; for even a single person sacrifices with that which possesses sacrificial fees.
Whether it be one or many, they undergo initiation after the New Moon day by means of the six-day period.
They agree on the two araṇis of the householder; or, if they do not agree on the two araṇis of the householder, having churned [the fire], they carry forth the Gārhapatya and the Āhavanīya,
and they bring the Vrata-offering from the village.
If, however, they act separately, the householder churns first;
then the others sit around him and, having churned each time, they together pour the Gārhapatya fire into one place.
From that which has thus become a single entity, they draw out the Āhavanīya fire.

Having brought the sacrificial food for the vow from the village, they pour it together. Now, if another person arrives later, he churns fire and pours half [of the food] onto the Gārhapatya and half onto the Āhavanīya; having brought the sacrificial food for the vow from the village, he also offers it. They summon him to participate in the previous rites. Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the purification.

The Adhvaryu purifies first the householder, then the Hotṛ, then the Brahman, then the Udgātṛ; the Pratiprasthātṛ purifies the Adhvaryu, the Prastotṛ, the Praśāstṛ, and the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; the Āgnīdhra purifies the Pratiprasthātṛ, the Acchāvāka, the Neṣṭṛ, the Potṛ, and the Sadasya; the Unnetṛ purifies the Āgnīdhra, the Grāvastut, the Subrahmaṇya, and the Pratihartṛ; and finally, he purifies himself.
If they should say, "The Adhvaryu alone is the purifier of all; let him purify us all," then he indeed purifies them all. Or rather, they purify one another if they are students.
For them, the well-known Dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi sacrifice is performed.

When it has been announced once, wherever he says "like Bharata," he first chooses the ancestral lineage (*ārṣeya*) of the *gṛhapati*, then that of the *hotṛ*, then his own, then that of the *brahman*, then the *udgātṛ*, then the *pratiprasthātṛ*, then the *prastotṛ*, then the *praśāstṛ*, then the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*, the *acchāvāka*, the *sadasya*, the *agnīdh*, the *potṛ*, the *neṣṭṛ*, the *grāvastut*, the *unnetṛ*, the *subrahmaṇya*, and finally the *pratihartṛ*; at the end, [he chooses] "possessing the *brahman*. All of them together touch him during the *dīkṣā*-oblations;
the *adhvaryu* makes only the *gṛhapati* recite loudly while on the black antelope skin.
The others follow after him, or they cause one another to recite if they are learned;
they approach the cow that yields the milk for the vow according to their enthusiasm—either one by one or several at once.
For them, just as there is a sequence for the *pravara* ancestors, so it is with the remnants of the *gharma*, the consumption of the *atigrāhya* cups, and the *ṣoḍaśin*.

On the sixth day, at the Upasad, they pile up the *uttaravedi* altar if it is a sacrifice without piling the fire-altar (*agni-citi*); but if it is one with piling the fire-altar, they pile up the *uttaravedi* on the very first Upasad day.

For them, there are twelve initiation days (*dīkṣā*), twelve Upasad days, and the Soma-pressing lasts for twelve days. Regarding this, some say, "One should not pile the fire-altar during the twelve-day sacrifice," while others indeed pile it; they proceed to the Upavasatha day by means of the established ritual procedure.
For them, the Jyotiṣṭoma Vaiśvānara Atirātra is performed as the introductory sacrifice.

When, at the midday pressing, he pours [the water] from the Vasatīvarīs for the third pressing, he then runs to the Āgnīdhra shed and, leaving just enough remaining in the Vasatīvarī jar, draws [the water] at the junction of shade and sunlight with the mantra: "These waters are rich in oblation; the divine sacrifice is rich in oblation; he desires to worship rich in oblation; may Sūrya be rich in oblation. Saying, "This is the continuity of the Ahīna sacrifice; we shall urge this very one again and again," they proceed.
Thereupon, he mutters the *punarālambha* formula for the sacrifice, either at the *yajñāyajñiya* chant, or at the *śaṃyuvāka*.
For them, the Jyotiṣṭoma Vaiśvānara opening *atirātra* sacrifice comes to a conclusion; when that has concluded, they remove the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
They throw the *prastara* grass-bundle [into the fire], and the ritual concludes with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. By means of the *atipraiṣa* call, the *brahmán* restrains his speech.
Once the *vasatīvarī* waters have been carried around and the *subrahmaṇyā* has been invoked, the *brahmán* releases his speech.

He proceeds with the *prātaranuvāka* recitation for the day, moving forward through the day. The *hotṛ* recites the meters; the *adhvaryu*, closing his eyes, offers the *upāṃśu* oblation, saying, "This is the form of night."

The Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma with the Rathantara-sāman is performed; at the Māhendra-stotra, a yoked chariot rushes forward, and by the sound of the chariot, one introduces the Māhendra-stotra. This much artistry is performed on this day; he thus maintains the continuity of the Ahīna sacrifice. Then, when tomorrow comes, the Pañcadaśa Ukthya with the Bṛhat-sāman is performed.

On this day, the Adhvaryu introduces the *stotra* for Mahendra with the *dundubhi* drum; this much is the artistic skill (*śilpa*) performed on this day, and he thereby effects the continuity of the *ahīna* sacrifice. Then, on the following day, the *ukthya* sacrifice is performed with seventeen verses and the *vairūpa* *sāman*. On this day, the Adhvaryu introduces the *stotra* for Mahendra [with the *dundubhi*]; this much is the artistic skill performed on this day, and he thereby effects the continuity of the *ahīna* sacrifice. Then, on the following day, the *ukthya* sacrifice is performed with twenty-one verses and the *vairāja* *sāman*, and there is also the *ṣoḍaśin* cup dedicated to Agni.
Some say that the *ṣoḍaśin* is not to be chanted with the *nyūṅkha*, because it possesses the *atigrāhya* cups; on this day, the *ekaviṃśa* [stoma] is to be chanted with the *nyūṅkha*.
They chant the *nyūṅkha* either at the beginning of the *virāj* verses or during the recitation (*śastra*); this is one view.
Now, another: they chant the *nyūṅkha* during the *prātaranuvāka*, at the call for the *haviṣkṛt*, when both [sets of vessels] have been set forth, and at the call for the *māhendra* cup.
They do not chant the *nyūṅkha* beyond that point. On this day, while holding the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) in his hands, the Adhvaryu introduces the *stotra* for Mahendra.
He rubs [the fire] on the right thigh of the Udgātṛ;
when it has been produced, they all together utter the sound *hiṅ* over it.
One who desires stability should throw its marrow into the Gārhapatya fire;
one who desires offspring, into the Āgnīdhra fire; and one who desires cattle, into the Śāmitra fire.

Disregarding the rule that [the offering] for those desiring heaven is in the Āhavanīya fire, he nevertheless throws [the two spoons] into that very Āhavanīya with the formula, "May you two be of one mind for us.

Having thrown them, he makes an offering over them with the verse, "Fire moves within fire, having entered it. This much alone is the artistic performance (*śilpa*) performed on this day; he thereby effects the continuity of the *Ahīna* sacrifice. Then, on the following day, the *Triṇava Ukthya* is performed. There is an *Atigrāhya* cup for Indra accompanied by the *Śākvara Sāman*. On this day, the Adhvaryu introduces the chant for Mahendra with water mixed with *Avakā* plants; such is the deliberation regarding them.

"One should pour them out into the *cātvāla* pit, pour them into the *āstāva*, prepare the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling waters, and knead the flour for the sacrificial cakes"—disregarding this, one should instead place them under the control of the *udgātṛ*s;
for the *udgātṛ*s believe that by means of these [waters], they pacify the impurity (*śuc*) of the *sāmans* to be sung in the forest (*araṇyegeya*).

If they should announce this to the Adhvaryu, he should simply say, "Carry them down to the water. This much alone is the artistic performance (*śilpa*) performed on this day; he thereby ensures the continuity of the *Ahīna* sacrifice. Then, on the following day, the *Trayastrimśa Ukthya* is performed with the *Raivata Sāman*. There is a *Saura Atigrāhya* cup. On this very day, the Adhvaryu introduces the chant for the *Māhendra* cup with water mixed with *dūrvā* grass. Regarding these waters, the deliberation has already been stated.
On this day, the *Ṛtu-yāja* (seasonal offerings) indeed take place spontaneously.
On this day, one does not perform the *ṛtuyāja* for the other. When the Adhvaryus say, "Sacrifice!

(*yajataṃ*), then the two Adhvaryus, sitting behind the *havirdhāna* sheds, themselves perform the *ṛtuyāja*: "We who sacrifice to the Aśvins, the two Adhvaryus—drink the Soma with the *ṛtu* from the office of the Adhvaryu! Yoke today your hither-turning chariot that carries heroes; here is your place of unyoking. Mix the oblations with honey; come quickly, and then drink the Soma, O you who possess wealth in horses! Drink the Soma with the *ṛtu*—*vauṣaṭ*!"*

When he says, "Householder, sacrifice," then the householder, sitting behind the *gārhapatya* fire, himself performs the *ṛtuyāja*: "We who sacrifice to Agni Gṛhapati from the *gārhapatya*—may these Soma-pressing sacrificers be good householders through you, O Agni; may you be a good householder with these Soma-pressing sacrificers. May Agni Gṛhapati drink the Soma with the season from the *gārhapatya*. O Agni, enjoy the fuel-stick; enjoy the oblation; enjoy the prayer of the people; enjoy the fair praise."

"O Vasu, with all [the gods] and according to the season, do thou, the great one, desiring [them], cause the desiring gods to drink the oblation; according to the season, let him drink the Soma—*vauṣaṭ*!

On this day there is a lowing together (*saṃvāśana*). They hold the calves to the north and the mothers to the south. At the *stotra* for Mahendra, having caused the calves to low together between the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna*, they release the calves to their mothers and tie up the calves.

They release the mothers; he introduces the hymn of Māhendra. Then, in the afternoon, during the Ukthya rounds, the artistic performances (*śilpa*) are performed, and the Hotṛ recites the verses of Parucchepa.
The Maitrāvaruṇa recites the Vālakhilyas;
the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin recites the Vṛṣākapi; the Acchāvāka recites the Śaṃsa Satyevayāmarut.
Thus the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha concludes, and he effects the continuity of the Ahīna sacrifice.

Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and having set aside the milks, they fast. Then, on the following day, they perform the *caturviṃśa* *chandoma*, which has the *bṛhat* as its *sāman*.
Then, on the following day, they perform the *catuścatvāriṃśa* *chandoma*, which has the *rathantara* as its *sāman*.
Then, on the following day, they perform the Aṣṭācatvāriṃśa Chandoma sacrifice with the Bṛhat Sāman;
then, on the following day, they perform the Caturviṃśa Agniṣṭoma sacrifice with the Rathantara Sāman;
this day is one on which no dispute (avivākya) is permitted.
"One should not recite this to another who has been struck down, nor should one explain it to him with a *gāthā* or a *nārāśaṃsa* verse"— so they say;
but they also say, "The sacrifice does not truly conclude if one does not explain it," for our *Brāhmaṇa* states that one should indeed explain it.
"One should not pay heed to this, one should not pay heed"— this is the established rule; on this day, there is no *anuṣṭubh* [verse],
nor do they recite *anuṣṭubh* verses.

If they should extract the *anuṣṭubh* verses, the Adhvaryu should extract the *anuṣṭubh*s with the verse, "Those [waters] which are near the sun, or those with which the sun is together—may they impel our sacrifice. With this *gāyatrī* addressed to Sūrya, he should take the *vasatīvarī* waters.

Having removed the formula, "For the heart thee, for the mind thee," he should bring down the King (Soma) with another *gāyatrī* addressed to Soma: "O Viṣṇu, you are our nearest... Having removed that [verse], he should worship the King with another *gāyatrī* addressed to Viṣṇu.
If he, being ignorant, utters an *anuṣṭubh*, he says to the Hotṛ, "I have overstepped."
The Hotṛ is the one who causes the unattained to be attained;
he weaves this [sacrifice] together with the syllables.
Now, if he should think, "I am indeed possessed of such-and-such a desire; let the two Vedas, consisting of Ṛc and consisting of Yajus, accomplish that for me," he should not pay heed to this.
"One should not pay heed"—this is the established rule.
This twenty-fourth Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, having the Rathantara as its Sāman, concludes;
when it has concluded, the fuel-bearers go forth, and having brought the fuel-sticks, they deposit them on the Āgnīdhrīya fire.

When they have taken hold of them, he offers a spoonful in the Āhavanīya fire with the formula "To Prajāpati, svāhā! mentally; then they proceed silently to the Sadas. Having perceived that they have proceeded for the Stoma, the Adhvaryu, having rushed forward to the east mentally and having made this [earth] the vessel mentally, takes another draught for Prajāpati mentally with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Prajāpati."

Having mentally reflected on "What is that? and set it down with the words, "This is your womb; for Prajāpati, you," he then touches water, takes two blades of *barhis* grass, restrains his speech, runs back toward the west, and with the mind alone introduces the *stotra*, with the mind gives the impulse, and with the mind performs the *prastāva*.
He chants the udgītha with the mind,
he responds with the pratihāra with the mind; "This is the highest Hotr-portion," they say, and the Hotṛ invokes with the mind.
The Adhvaryu calls back mentally; "Śaṃsati" [is uttered] mentally; he responds mentally.
When he has reached the end of this mental weapon, then the Hotṛ recites the Caturhotṛ formulas aloud; for him, the Adhvaryu responds:
"Oṃ! Hotṛ! So be it, Hotṛ! Truly, Hotṛ! We have succeeded, Hotṛ!"
If the Hotṛ does not recite, and another person performs the duties of the Hotṛ,
the Pratiprasthātṛ utters the response for him.
When they reach the end of these [recitations], the Adhvaryu, having hastened eastward by mind alone, lifts up that cup by mind alone.
He causes the announcement to be made mentally;
he responds mentally;
having offered at the *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*, he carries away [the remains]; having invited one another mentally, they consume the portion.
Having cleansed the vessel with his mind, he hands it over;

this Tūṣṇīṃstoma comes to a conclusion. Then he asks the officiating priests: "Will you release your speech when the sun is above the trees, or under the stars? "When the sun is above the trees," is our Brāhmaṇa text.
They release their speech when the sun is indeed above the trees.

While they remain seated right there, they enclose the wives in the *patnīśālā*. Then, without stepping across, the two *adhvaryu*s, holding two bundles of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), take hold of the *audumbarī* post together, saying: "Here is support, here is separation, here is delight, here is enjoyment.
They release their speech as they have agreed upon.
Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the creeping:
they should creep beneath the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart;
for by this means, indeed, the serpents crept away.
"Then indeed they cast off that worn-out body.
Regarding this, they say: "He who proceeds by a wrong path either strikes against a stump, falls into a pit, or meets with disaster;
therefore, they should proceed by the path of the *vaṣaṭ*-call. For this path of the *vaṣaṭ*-call is indeed the path leading to heaven."

Regarding this, they say: "Truly, this path of the *vaṣaṭ*-call is like one that turns away and is unappeased; they should proceed by the path of the *adhvaryu* alone, for this path of the *adhvaryu* leads both hitherward and thitherward and is conducive to heaven. Thus, they proceed by the path of the *adhvaryu*.

While they have taken hold of one another, he offers a spoonful in the *āhavanīya* fire with the mantra: "Releasing the calf to its mother, supporting it while it sucks, may he bestow upon us abundance of wealth, food, and strength—*svāhā*!"

Having stepped out to the site of the *cātvāla*, they mutter: "May speech come; may speech approach; may speech come to us. That which we have done, that which we have not done; that which we have passed beyond, that which we have not passed beyond; that which we have exceeded, that which we have not exceeded—let all that go unto Prajāpati, the Father.
Thus, in the end, they find firm support in Speech.
For them, that very *Atirātra* sacrifice which is the opening one (*prāyaṇīya*) is also the concluding one (*udayanīya*).

Having concluded the sacrificial session (*sattra*) with the *jyotiṣṭoma* consisting of the *agniṣṭoma* form, the fourfold stoma, and the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya*, with a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), each individual should perform the sacrifice.
Now follows the deliberation regarding the arrangement of the cups (*graha*): on the first day, the cup for Indra and Vāyu comes first;
on the second day, the cup for Śukra comes first.
The third and fourth days have the Āgrayaṇa cup first; the fifth day has the Aindravāyava cup first;
the sixth and seventh days have the Śukra cup first; the eighth day has the Āgrayaṇa cup first;
and the ninth and tenth days have the Aindravāyava cup first.
Thus, indeed, from the perspective of the Adhvaryu: the first three-night rite has the Gāyatrī at the morning pressing, the Triṣṭubh at the midday pressing, and the Jagatī at the third pressing;
the second three-night rite has the Jagatī at the morning pressing, the Gāyatrī at the midday pressing, and the Triṣṭubh at the third pressing;
the third three-night rite has the Triṣṭubh at the morning pressing, the Jagatī at the midday pressing, and the Gāyatrī at the third pressing. Thus [it is said] by the Chandogas and Bahvṛcas.
Therefore, they approach with the *sac* verses.

Now, therefore, follows the investigation regarding the preparation of the sacrificial animals (*paśuklpti*). "The animals should belong to Indra and Agni," say some; "this world belongs to Agni, the intermediate space to Vāyu, and that [heavenly] world to Indra."

When there is an animal sacrifice for Indra and Agni, and the fat-oblation is for Vāyu, they proceed while gratifying these very worlds and establishing themselves in these worlds. Now, those who undertake sacrifices not for Indra and Agni—just as one might bring [wealth] for a superior person without first bringing it for an inferior—it is exactly like that.
Therefore, the animals should be for Indra and Agni; this is one view.
Furthermore, the Atirātra animals are on both sides with the Indra-Agni animals in the middle, and the Ekādaśinī animals are on both sides with the Indra-Agni animals in the middle.

"One view is that they should all be dedicated to Agni; another is that they should all be dedicated to Indra; another is that they should all be dedicated to Prajāpati; and yet another is that they should all be of the *ekādaśinī* (sets of eleven) type. Regarding those who follow the *sarvaikādaśinī* method, it is well-established that on the first day they immolate the first *ekādaśinī*. They perform the secondary immolation (*upālambhya*) for Varuṇa instead of the one for Agni;
in this way, these ten middle days proceed without the sacrificial animals being exceeded."
It is well known that on the final day they immolate the highest set of eleven victims; having offered one for Agni or for Varuṇa, they perform the Vaiśvadeva as the victim to be immolated last.

Regarding this, they say: "Since there are twelve initiations, twelve Upasad days, and the Soma-pressings last for twelve days, how do these days of his become characterized by sacrifices, propitiated, and accompanied by animal offerings? [The answer is: there are three sets of eleven victims—the Agnīṣomīya, the Vaiśvadeva, and the Anūbandhyā.

"These are thirty-six animals; these are thirty-six days. Thus, these days of his become sacrificed, propitiated, and possessed of animals. Regarding this, they say: "There are twelve initiations (*dīkṣā*), twelve *upasad*s, and the Soma-pressings last for twelve days. How, then, is the year obtained through the twelve-day rite?
There are twelve full-moon days, twelve *aṣṭakā* days, and twelve new-moon days. These indeed are the most excellent days of the year; it is by means of these that the year is obtained.
The twelve-day rite is completed;
the year-long desire is fulfilled. In this way, the year is attained through the twelve-day rite.
Those who are about to undergo initiation for the sake of the year settle together.

In this regard, it is said that in former times, having gathered together for a year, they sat [in session], desiring to understand one another's recited texts and their human affairs; for indeed, there might be one who was the maker of a peaceful chariot for them.
They undergo initiation four days before the full moon of Māgha;
for them, the purchase of the Soma is completed on the Ekāṣṭakā day—this is the case if they undergo initiation after having ascertained the year.

Or, if they desire to know the year in this very Ekāṣṭakā, they undergo initiation four days before the full moon of Phālguna or Caitra; for them, the purchase of the Soma falls on the eighth day of the waning fortnight,
and thus they do not leave the Ekāṣṭakā empty.
For them, the Soma-pressing is accomplished in the first fortnight; the months are completed in the first fortnight;

the initiation (prasava) is in the first fortnight; the Viṣuvat day is in the first fortnight; and the rising from the sacrifice is in the first fortnight; the ritual procedure is the same as that of the twelve-day sacrifice.

In the same way, on the sixth day, having approached the Upasad rites, they pile up the Uttaravedi if it is a rite without piling the fire-altar (anagnicitya); but if it is a rite with piling the fire-altar (sāgnicitya), they pile up the Uttaravedi on the very first Upasad day. For them, there are twelve initiation days (dīkṣā) and twelve Upasad days; they press the Soma for a year. Regarding this, some say, "One should not pile the fire-altar during the year," while others indeed do pile it, proceeding to the Upavasatha day by means of the established ritual procedure.

For them, the well-known Vaiśvānara Jyotiṣṭoma Atirātra serves as the introductory sacrifice (*prāyaṇīya*). When that has been completed, they enter upon the twenty-four-fold Ukthya, the *ārambhaṇīya*, which possesses both *sāmans*. Then they enter upon the six-day period of the *abhiplava*:
the Jyotis Agniṣṭoma, the Gauḥ Ukthya, the Āyuḥ Ukthya, the Gauḥ Ukthya, the Āyuḥ Ukthya, and the Jyotis Agniṣṭoma.
They mount that chariot in four ways: the Rathantara, the Bṛhat, the Rathantara, and the Bṛhat; these two, alternating, serve as the Pṛṣṭhas for the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha.
That month, when completed in this manner, makes five months; then they prepare this sixth month: three *abhiplava* six-day periods constitute eighteen days.
The Prāyaṇīya and Ārambhaṇīya [offerings], those thirty days,
the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, the Abhijit, and the three Paraḥsāman [days].
That month is the Vaiṣuvata;

then, on this Vaiṣuvata day, they perform the twenty-first Agniṣṭoma sacrifice with the Bṛhat-sāman. For that sacrifice, there is an *atigrāhya* cup for Sūrya, and an animal victim for Sūrya is to be immolated.

Regarding this, some begin this very day while it is still daylight, saying, "The Divākīrtya day [begins] when the sun has risen. Maudgalya says that one should commence it just as one does for the other days.

For that [sacrifice], the Mahādivākīrtya is the *pṛṣṭha* chant for the *hotṛ*, the Vikarṇa is the *brahmasāman*, and the *agniṣṭoma* is the *bhāsa*. Then, after the *vaiṣuvata*, they proceed with three reversed *svarasāmans*; then they proceed with the *viśvajit*; then they proceed with the reversed *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*. Starting from the thirty-third day, this day has the *āgrayaṇa* as its opening cup; then they proceed with the reversed *abhiplava-ṣaḍaha*: the *jyotis* *agniṣṭoma*, the *āyus* *ukthya*, the *go* *ukthya*, the *āyus* *ukthya*, the *go* *ukthya*, and the *jyotis* *agniṣṭoma* again.
They approach that very same [sacrifice] in the same manner; however, the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] occur in reverse order for the Pṛṣṭha laud,
while the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha precedes it.
That month is thus completed;
then, having completed five months, they perform that sixth month by collecting the materials,
consisting of two *abhiplava* six-day periods— those are twelve days.
Those [days] up to the *go* and *āyus* are fourteen;
