four above the *vaiṣuvata* make eighteen;
then there is the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*), the *mahāvrata*, and the *atirātra*.
That month is this Māsipṛṣṭha Gavāmayana;
it is performed without interruption, and in the final month they should perform the Pṛṣṭha-stotras once with both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara.

The second [form] of the Gavām Ayana consists of ten months; the third consists of Abhiplava and Atyagniṣṭoma days—that is the Aṅgirasām Ayana. It consists of Pṛṣṭhya and Atyagniṣṭoma days—that is the Ādityānām Ayana. It consists of Agniṣṭomas on both sides with the Prāyaṇīya and Udayanīya at the center—that is the Prajāpateḥ Ayana. There is a second form of the Prajāpateḥ Ayana where all the days would be Agniṣṭomas; that is the third form of the Prajāpateḥ Ayana.
Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the preparation of the cups (graha).

Regarding this, some take two cups for Sarasvatī and Viṣṇu from the very beginning—either from the Prāyaṇīya or up to the Udayanīya. Sarasvatī is Speech and Viṣṇu is the Sacrifice; they say, "By encompassing both Speech and the Sacrifice in the middle, we shall proceed to the conclusion without harm.

But concerning this they also say: "Insofar as the sacrifice is performed by means of Speech, Sarasvatī is thereby obtained; and insofar as it is the Sacrifice, Viṣṇu is thereby obtained. Yet, our Brāhmaṇa-text does not so state."
"One should draw the Sārasvata and Vaiṣṇava cups"—one should not pay heed to this; "one should not pay heed to it"—this is the settled rule.

Now, therefore, follows the drawing of the Aṃśu and Adābhya cups: one should draw the Adābhya at the Prāyaṇīya [day], the Aṃśu at the Viṣuvat, and the Adābhya at the Mahāvrata; both at the Prāyaṇīya, both at the Viṣuvat, and both at the Mahāvrata.

"Wherever one might take these two"—this is another [view]. Now, therefore, follows the taking of the *paraḥsāman* cups. These *paraḥsāman* cups are indeed taken day by day for three days prior to the *vaiṣuvata* day, moving away from here in a forward direction: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the waters and the plants. "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the plants and the offspring. "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the offspring and Prajāpati.
Then, on the *vaiṣuvata* day, the cups are taken beginning with the *śukra*.

The ritual procedure is the same up to the Āgrayaṇa cup. Having drawn the Āgrayaṇa, he draws three Paraḥsāman cups with the formulas: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the waters and the plants. "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the plants and to offspring. "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to offspring and to Prajāpati. Then, with a verse addressed to Sūrya, he draws the Atigrāhya cup for Sūrya, reciting: "Swift, visible to all," and then: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to radiant Sūrya."

Having wiped [the vessel], he sets it down with the formula: "This is thy womb; for Sūrya, the radiant, thee! Then he draws the cups in reverse order: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the creatures, to Prajāpati. Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the plants, to the creatures. Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the waters, to the plants. "These seven *atigrāhya* cups are drawn on this day," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Thereafter, from the *vaiṣuvata* day onwards, for three days he draws them every day in reverse order, alternating with the cups for Viśvakarman and Āditya.

"You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to Prajāpati, for the sake of creatures. Then [he takes] the Vaiśvakarman [cup]: having recited, "O Viśvakarman, increasing by the oblation," he says, "You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to the plants and to creatures. Then [he takes] the Āditya [cup]: having recited, "May Aditi protect us," he says, "You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to the waters and to the plants. Then [he takes] the Vaiśvakarman, and then the Āditya.
Then, after three days from the Vaiśvakarman [offering], having proceeded with the reversal of those very two, the Vaiśvakarman and Āditya [cups], up until the Mahāvrata;
both of them are taken together at the Mahāvrata.
Then, on this day of the Mahāvrata, he takes the Prājāpatya Atigrāhya cup.

Having recited, "All indeed turn toward you for wisdom," and having said, "You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to Prajāpati," he wipes [the vessel] and sets it down with, "This is your womb; for Prajāpati, you.

Now, therefore, follows the investigation regarding the preparation of the animals: the Sāttrāgni sacrifices have the Aindrāgna animals on both sides with the Sātirātra animals in the middle; the Ekādaśina sacrifices have the Aindrāgna animals on both sides with the Aindrāgna animals in the middle.

"One view is that all [the offerings] should belong to Agni; another is that all should belong to Indra and Agni; another is that all should belong to Prajāpati; and yet another is that all should consist of sets of eleven [animals]. Among these, according to those who follow the system of all sets of eleven, it is well known that on the third day of the final ten-night period (*daśarātra*), the *ukthya* sacrifice with seventeen animals is reached through the set of eleven; thus, nine days remain without animals."

Among these, they immolate these nine Brāhmaṇavat animals, beginning with the dwarf (vāmana) dedicated to Viṣṇu. For those who proceed in this manner, the animal sacrifice at the Vaiṣuvat day becomes one dedicated to Bṛhaspati;
for that, they perform an additional immolation dedicated to Sūrya.
However, if they do not find these nine Brāhmaṇavat animals, they perform the animal sacrifices dedicated to Indra and Agni on these nine intermediate days of the year-long rite.
For them who proceed in this manner, at the Vaiṣuvata day, the Savanīya animal sacrifice belongs to Indra and Agni;
for that, they perform a victim for Sūrya as the Upālambhya,
and one for Savitṛ at the Mahāvrata.
For that [rite], a hornless goat dedicated to Prajāpati and a bull dedicated to Indra are to be offered;

"Tomorrow is the Mahāvrata," he prepares an unlimited number of chariots and an unlimited number of drums, as many as there are horse-racers, as well as a skin for the *iḍā*-song, a *saṃvarta* drum, a bull-hide with its tail, a Brāhmaṇa and a Śūdra, a fresh hide-cutter, a *pleṅkha* swing, two *kūrca* grass-mats for the Hotṛ, seats (*bṛsī*) for the Hotrakas, and the Udgātṛ prepares a seat (*āsandi*) made of Udumbara wood.
He also prepares a lute (*vāṇa*) with a hundred strings, *āghāṭī* cymbals, *piñcholā* flutes, and *karkarīkā* rattles; these are for the wives.
There is a matting enclosure, two couples, and countless female slaves, as many as there are water-jars.

Then, on the day of the Mahāvrata, they perform the Pañcaviṃśa Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, having the Rathantara as its Sāman. The ritual procedure is the same up to the drawing of the Māhendra cup; having drawn the Māhendra cup, he then brings these materials together.
Having caused a pit to be dug behind the Āgnīdhra shed, they cover it with the hide of a bull, rough and with the hair turned upward.
Having torn out its tail, the slayers stand behind it; at this point, he fastens these drums to the various quarters.
Without striking them with beaters, these slayers stand behind [the drums]. Then these chariots, having gone around the sacrificial ground on all sides, stand to the north.
Among them, the prince is the chief, possessing three bows.
Therefore, in front of the Āgnīdhra shed, he spreads out a piece of leather at the *iḍasaṃvarta* spot;

at that very moment, he cuts it with a knife. Then the Brāhmaṇa and the Śūdra stand between the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds, taking up the moist piece of leather; the Hotṛ priest fixes the *pleṅkha* (wooden seat) upon it.
The Adhvaryu spreads out two bundles of grass; the Hotrakas spread out mats; the Udgātṛ ascends a throne made of Udumbara wood and takes up a lute with a hundred strings.

The wives sit down around the Udgātṛ with clappers, flutes, and small drums. Then, at the southern edge of the altar, enclosed by mats, a married couple plays together. Then these female slaves, having set down water-pitchers, sit down around the Mārjālīya fire-altar. Then the Adhvaryu, seated upon the two bundles of grass, introduces the chant for the Mahendra hymn; they chant the praise for Mahendra.

When the *sāman* has been introduced, he issues the command: "O race-runners, run the race! Beat the drums! O pressers, press the juice! O *Āgnīdh*, pour out the *āśira* mixture! Make the mortar resound! O *Pratiprasthātṛ*, attend to the *Saumya* offering!
They act according to the command:
the race-runners run, and they beat the drums.

They speak aloud with clappers, flutes, and lutes; thus the wives sing in accompaniment to the Udgātṛ. There is a Sāman named Bhadra, and it is sung in accompaniment with speech. Then this prince, armed with three bows, pierces the hide.
The Brāhmaṇa stands behind it, saying, "May you not fail; may you not overstep.

Thus, with three [verses], he pierces that which was hidden. Then the Brāhmaṇa and the Śūdra strive together over the hide-cutter, saying, "These have succeeded; these have done well," says the Brāhmaṇa; "These have failed; these have done ill," says the Vṛṣala (the Śūdra). The Brāhmaṇa wins; the Vṛṣala perishes.

These slave-girls, acting in pairs, place water-jars down and dance around the Mārjālīya fire; striking their breasts and stamping their right feet while singing, "This is honey. When they have completed one circuit, he makes her recite the first verse: "The cows are fragrant, the cows have the scent of bdellium; the cows are the mothers of clarified butter—may they be here in abundance! This is our honey! Having struck their breasts, they stamp their right feet.

For the second [offering], he causes those who are present to recite only the first verse: "Did not the cows of Maṅkīra drink the water of the Gaṅgā? They drank for the river Sarasvatī; they have gone forth toward the east. Having approached with the verse, "O golden one, this honey," they strike their right feet.

On the third day, he causes those who are present to recite the first verse: "When Rākaṇdyu and Maṅkīra-Dāśaka speak of village matters, and settle for peace in the village, the ox does not suffer while drawing; we have drunk this honey. Then, while standing to the north of the Mārjālīya fire, he causes them to recite: "This very honey is from the bee-hive; this is the Soma pressed out, the great one. Indra, you have fully satisfied yourself with it; we have drunk this honey. From that point upward, they proceed saying, "This honey! This honey! This honey! For them, the *atirātra* sacrifice which serves as the opening (*prāyaṇīya*) is also the concluding (*udayanīya*).

Having concluded the *sattra*, one who desires heaven should perform the *jyotiṣṭoma* as an *agniṣṭoma* with four stomas, concluding with the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* and giving a thousand-fold sacrificial fee; each individual should sacrifice thus. One undergoes initiation for the two-night rite (*dvirātra*);
its initiation period is unlimited, and there are twelve *upasad* days.

He purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks: "Since my sacrifice is a Dvirātra, may the first day fall on the Upavasatha day of the new moon, and the second day on the following one. For him it happens accordingly: the Abhiplava becomes the first day and the Gati the second; the Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma becomes the first day; by that, he wins brilliance.
The Atirātra sacrifice with all the Stomas is performed on the latter day for the attainment of everything and for the securing of everything;
on the first day the Sāman is Gāyatra,
and on the second day it is Traiṣṭubha.
The Rathantara is the Sāman on the first day, and the Bṛhat on the latter;
the Vaikhānasa is the Sāman on the first day.

In the sixteenth [night], the *haviṣmat* finale belongs to the first day and the *haviṣkṛt* finale to the second; they belong to different fortnights and possess different powers—so says the Brāhmaṇa. Thus the two-night rite is completed.

Intending to sacrifice with the Trirātra, he prepares a thousand [cows]; among them there are a humpbacked one, a long-horned one, and a dwarf. Now, his "thousandth" cow is a speckled one that has been scratched and prepared;
he undergoes initiation.
He purchases Soma with a reddish-brown, one-year-old cow;
twelve Upasad days are performed, and on the first day, an Agniṣṭoma is celebrated.

For him, the morning pressing is the *trivṛt*, the midday pressing is the *pañcadaśa*, and the third pressing is the *saptadaśa*. Having offered the oblations for the sacrificial gifts (*dākṣiṇāni*), he offers a spoonful (*sruvāhuti*) in the *āgnīdhra* fire with the verse: "O Unnata, bring a thousand! O Unnata, pierce the skin of the waterless one! Grant me a share of a thousand, together with offspring and cattle; may wealth return to me again! Among these three sets of three hundred [cows], the first is led away; he thus effects the continuity of the *ahīna* sacrifice. On the second day, the *ukthya* sacrifice is performed.

Its morning pressing has fifteen stotras, its midday pressing seventeen, and its third pressing twenty-one. Having offered the oblations for the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*), he offers a spoonful in the *Āgnīdhra* fire with the mantra: "Thou art vigor, belonging to Aṅgiras; soft as wool; grant me vigor; protect me; do not harm me; may she share me in a thousandfold [blessing] together with offspring and cattle; may wealth enter me again. Of these three sets of three hundred [cows], the *vehat* (barren cow) is led first; she effects the continuity of the *Ahīna* sacrifice, and on the third day the *Atirātra* is performed.

For this [sacrifice], the morning pressing has seventeen verses; the midday pressing has twenty-one; the *ārbhava-pavamāna* has twenty-nine; the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* has thirty-three; the *uktha* chants have twenty-one each, including the *ṣoḍaśin*;
the first night-chant (*rātri-sāman*) has sixteen verses, while the others have fifteen; the *sandhi-stotra* is the *trivṛt* with the *rathantara* melody.

Having offered the *dakṣiṇā* gifts, he offers a spoonful of oblation in the *āgnīdhra* fire with the mantra: "Thou art the foundation of a thousand, thou art the dwarf belonging to Viṣṇu. Grant me a share in a thousand, together with offspring and cattle; let wealth enter me again."
O Vāmana, of these three hundred and forty [cows], the first is led forward;
he does not break the continuity here.

Then, having led this thousandth cow around the north of the Āgnīdhra fire, he should cause her to smell the *droṇakalaśa* at the edge of the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra: "Smell the jar, O great one; may the milk-stream be abundant. May the drops enter thee as rivers enter the ocean. Grant me a share in the thousandfold [reward] together with offspring and cattle; may wealth enter me again."
"He endows him with offspring, cattle, and wealth; he becomes possessed of offspring, cattle, and wealth, who knows thus"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is further said: "Having gone together with her to the Āgnīdhra shed, one should offer while she stands in front, facing westward."

Having gone with her to the Āgnīdhra shed, he offers while she stands in front facing westward, [with the verse]: "Both of you have conquered; you two are not defeated; neither of these two has been defeated. O Indra and Viṣṇu, when you strove together, you divided the thousand threefold.
For in the three-night sacrifice, a thousand is indeed divided threefold; thus he makes her thousandfold, for he makes her the measure of a thousand—so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Then he offers oblations to her forms, saying: "To the speckled one, svāhā! To the black one, svāhā! To the white one, svāhā! Then, having risen toward her, he whispers these names into her right ear: "O Iḍā, Rantī, Aditi, Sarasvatī, Priyā, Preyasī, Mahī, Viśrutī—these, O inviolable one, are your names. May you announce me as a doer of good deeds among the gods.
Thus he announces him to the gods; "The gods take notice of him," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Then, as this thousandth cow is being led northward between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, he addresses her with the mantra: "May she lead me to the heavenly world; may she lead me to the luminous world; may she lead me to all auspicious worlds; may she lead me to a firm foundation. May she enter back into me along with progeny, cattle, and wealth.
He thus establishes him upon a foundation of progeny, cattle, and wealth; "He who knows thus becomes possessed of progeny, cattle, and wealth," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it is said in the Brāhmaṇa: "One should give her to the Āgnīdhra, or to the Brahman, or to the Hotṛ, or to the Udgātṛ, or to the Adhvaryu;
thus a thousand have been given by him, and a thousand have been received by him."
Now, it is indeed said:

"He who accepts her without knowing this—let him accept her with [the formula]: 'Thou art one, not a thousand; I accept thee as one, not as a thousand; enter me as one, not as a thousand. Thus, he who knows this accepts her as one, not as a thousand. This is the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is indeed said:
"Thou art pleasant, well-seated, and very gracious; enter me as one who is pleasant, enter me as one who is well-seated, enter me as one who is very gracious," he says.
"Verily, having become pleasant, well-seated, and very gracious, she enters him and does not harm him," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it comes to pass:
The exponents of Brahman say: "A thousand follows the thousandth; the thousandth follows the thousand.
If he were to release [the horse] facing eastward, the thousand would follow the thousandth, and that thousand, lacking discernment, would not know the heavenly world.
He releases it toward the west; he turns around it a thousand times;
knowing the way, it goes to the heavenly world.
"He releases it toward the sacrificer.
He releases it from the front toward the west, facing the sacrificer.

"Quickly a thousand offspring are produced; as the last, it is led forth, yet as the first, it goes to the gods," so says the Brāhmaṇa. With this very [rite], Rauhiṇeya Krothuni, Kaulāśva Yāska, and Ājamīḍha Maśaka Gārgya—the latter being a pupil of Āruṇi—performed the sacrifice at the beginnings of the seasons using the *vihṛta* (expanded) form.
Having seen the *saṃsthā*, he said, "Is it not, then, my one-day sacrifice? He replied to him, "No," and he went up to him.
Therefore, he said this to him;
with that [sacrifice] in its entirety, he indeed used to sacrifice.
This very [sacrifice] they call the Gargatrirātra.
Desiring to win the four heroes, he undergoes initiation for the Catūrātra sacrifice;
its initiation period is unlimited, there are twelve Upasad days,
and its days are Agniṣṭomas with twenty-four-fold Pavamāna-stotras that have rising stomas— this is one view.

There is one Agniṣṭoma, two Ukthyas, and then an Atirātra; the Chandogas should ask about the alternative arrangement of the Sāmans. This is another [view]: for a sacrificer who is faithful to Atri, four powers do not come to him—splendor, sensory power, Vedic luster, and food; desiring to obtain these desires, he undergoes initiation for the four-night sacrifice.
For that, the period of initiation is unlimited, and there are twelve Upasad days.

On its days, these fourfold-stoma sacrifices should be Agniṣṭomas; this is one view. Alternatively, there may be one Agniṣṭoma, two Ukthyas, and then an Atirātra; regarding this, one should ask the Chāndogas about the variation of the Sāmans—this is another view. One desiring prosperity undergoes initiation for the four-night sacrifice;
its initiation period is unlimited, and there are twelve Upasad days. Now, indeed, it is so stated.
"The Upasad days are characterized by sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśin).
On the first four-night period, having placed an oblation of clarified butter for Agni and a cake on eight potsherds for Agni into the fire both evening and morning, he offers them;
on the second four-night period, having placed an oblation of clarified butter for Soma and a cake on four potsherds for Soma into the fire both evening and morning, he offers them.
On the third four-night period, having placed a Vaiṣṇava oblation of clarified butter and a Vaiṣṇava cake on three potsherds alternately at evening and morning, he offers them;
for that sacrifice, the Trivṛt and Saptadaśa Stomas alternate,
and the Trivṛt is indeed breath while the Saptadaśa is food and Prajāpati.
For indeed, having grasped both the vital breath and the food, Prajāpati procreated;
and having grasped both the vital breath and the food, the sacrificer likewise procreates.
On those days, these [sacrifices] should be Agniṣṭomas with thirty-four-fold Pavamāna-stotras; this is one view.
There is one Agniṣṭoma, two Ukthyas, and then an Atirātra; the Chhandogas may ask for a variation of the Sāmans—this is another [option].
One who desires offspring, or distinction, or cattle, or wishing to reach the end of speech, undergoes initiation for the Pañcarātra sacrifice;
its initiation period is unlimited, and there are twelve Upasad days.

Its days consist of a *trivṛt* *agniṣṭoma*, a *pañcadaśa* *ukthya*, a *saptadaśa* *ukthya*, a *pañcaviṃśa* *agniṣṭoma* with the *mahāvrata*, and a *viśvajit* *atirātra* with all the *pṛṣṭhas*. Those intending to proceed by the Sarasvata *ayanam* prepare two sets of cows: one set consisting of ten cows and a bull as the eleventh, and another set consisting of ninety-nine cows and a bull as the hundredth. For them, the *havirdhāna* and the *āgnīdhra* sheds are made of *aśvattha* wood.
For that is conducive to heaven; they have two [sacrificial posts] with rings, and their sacrificial post has a mortar-base;
they undergo initiation at the lower waters of the Sarasvatī;
for them, this very Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma comes to a conclusion.

When that has been completed, they carry [the materials] toward the sacrificial post and toward the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths; they settle whatever of theirs is to be settled upon the cart standing nearest the *agniṣṭha*. They proceed by means of this very *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*, day after day, at each placement of the *śamyā*-measures, the sacrificers shouting and desiring non-defeat. When they make ten into a hundred, that is one *utthāna*; when they make a hundred into a thousand, that is one *utthāna*. When someone among them dies, or when they are defeated, that is one *utthāna*; or at the Plakṣa spring.
Now, therefore, they call this the "Course of the Sage" (munyayana).

A wandering ascetic (śramaṇa) carrying a load of a khārī on a pole performs the offering of a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati at the Sarasvatī where its waters are lowest. That well-known sacrifice is completed; then he performs this Savana-offering: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, and a cake on twelve potsherds for the Viśve Devas.

He proceeds with that [sacrifice] performed either in its entirety or in parts, day after day at each throw of the sacrificial pin (*śamyā*), the sacrificer crying out, desiring no failure. When they overcome him, or when they cut off this *khārīvivadha* (the load of grain) from him, then there is one rising. One who desires cattle should undergo initiation for seven nights at a spring of the *plakṣa* tree;
his initiation period is unlimited, and there are twelve *upasad* days.

Its days are: a *trivṛt* *agniṣṭoma*, a *pañcadaśa* *ukthya*, a *saptadaśa* *ukthya*, an *ekaviṃśa* *ukthya*, a *triṇava* *ukthya*, a *pañcaviṃśa* *agniṣṭoma* accompanied by the *mahāvrata*, and a *viśvajit* *atirātra* with all the *pṛṣṭha* stotras. Having approached the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [samans] in the preceding days, they perform the *pṛṣṭha* stotras explicitly in the *viśvajit*. One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) undergoes initiation for the eight-night sacrifice;
its initiation period is unlimited, and there are twelve *upasads*.

Its days consist of a *trivṛt* *agniṣṭoma*, a *pañcadaśa* *ukthya*, a *saptadaśa* *ukthya*, an *ekaviṃśa* *ukthya*, a *triṇava* *ukthya*, a *trayastrim̐śa* *ukthya*, a *pañcaviṃśa* *agniṣṭoma* with the *mahāvrata*, and a *viśvajit* *atirātra* with all the *pṛṣṭha* stotras.
One who is afflicted by hunger among his subjects, or one who has been long ill, undergoes initiation for the nine-night sacrifice;
its initiation period is unlimited, and there are twelve *upasad* days.
Their days consist of Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyuḥ; they perform this very three-day period three times.
For them, the Āyus Atirātra becomes the final day.

One who desires offspring, or one who desires distinction, or one practicing sorcery, or one being subjected to sorcery, or one about to undergo initiation for the ten-night rite, should offer the Daśahotṛ oblation and then undergo initiation for the ten-night rite.
Its initiation is unlimited; it has twelve *upasads*.
Its days consist of a *trivṛt* *agniṣṭoma*, which is an *agniṣṭut* performed with verses addressed to Agni;
and a *pañcadaśa* *ukthya*, performed with verses addressed to Indra.
The Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma is performed with verses addressed to the Viśvedevas;
the Saptadaśa Agniṣṭoma is performed with verses addressed to Prajāpati; the Tīvrasoma Ekaviṃśa Ukthya is performed with verses addressed to Sūrya;
and the Saptadaśa Agniṣṭoma is the Upahavya sacrifice with verses addressed to Prajāpati.

On both sides are two Agniṣṭomas with the Triṇava stoma; the Ukthya sacrifice with the Trayastriṃśa stoma is performed on verses addressed to Indra; and the Viśvajit Atirātra, comprising all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras, is performed on verses addressed to the Viśvedevas.
Those desiring offspring undergo initiation for the eleven-night sacrifice;
its initiation days are unlimited, there are twelve Upasad days, and its days consist of the Jyotis and the Atirātra.
The Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha, three Chandomas, then an Atirātra; then the procedure for the Ahīna: the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha, three Chandomas, and the tenth day.

Then there is the Atirātra, and then this Pauṇḍarīka, an eleven-night sacrifice with a fee of ten thousand [cows] and a fee of a thousand horses; its consecrations (dīkṣās) are unlimited, it has twelve Upasad days,
and its days consist of the Abhyāsaṅgya six-day period.

There are three *Chandoma* days, then the tenth day, and then the *Atirātra*; he gives a thousand [cows] every day, and on the final day he gives a thousand horses. Now, they call this the "Jyotirayana"; some say it is the "Bharata-dvādaśāha," and one undergoes initiation for it.

Its initiation is unlimited; it has twelve *upasads*. Its days consist of a *jyotis-atirātra*, a *jyotis-agniṣṭoma*, eight *jyotiṣ-ukthya*s, a *jyotis-agniṣṭoma*, and a *jyotis-atirātra*. The twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) has been described; he interposes the tenth day and the *atirātra* with the *mahāvrata*. That, indeed, is the thirteen-night rite (*trayodaśarātra*).
Now follows the first fourteen-night rite:
an Atirātra, a Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, a reverse (pratyañc) Ṣaḍaha, and then an Atirātra; then the second fourteen-night rite: an Atirātra and a three-day period consisting of Jyotis, Go, and Āyus.

The *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, then three days facing westward, then an *atirātra*; then the first fifteen-night period, an *atirātra*, and a three-day period consisting of the *jyotis*, *go*, and *āyus*; then a ten-night period, an *atirātra*, and the tenth day; he interposes the *mahāvrata* between the *atirātra* and the [next] day.
That indeed is the sixteen-night period without a *brāhmaṇa* explanation; then the subsequent fifteen-night period and an *atirātra*.
The Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma; the three-day period consisting of Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus;

the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha; the three-day period in reverse order; then an Atirātra; then the Saptadaśarātra; then an Atirātra; then a Pañcāha; then a Daśarātra; then an Atirātra; and he interposes the Mahāvrata between the tenth day and the Atirātra.

That indeed is the eighteen-night sacrifice for one who is not a Brāhmaṇa; then the twenty-one-night sacrifice consists of an Atirātra, three three-day periods—namely Jyotis, Go, and Āyus—a Pṛṣṭhya ṣaḍaha, a three-day period in reverse order, and then an Atirātra; then the twenty-one-night sacrifice begins with an Atirātra.
The Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha and these seven middle days of the year-long sacrifice constitute the six-day period directed westward, followed by the Atirātra.

Now, the first twenty-four-night period consists of an *atirātra*, four three-day periods beginning with the *jyotis*, the *go*, and the *āyus*, a ten-night period, and then an *atirātra*. He separates the tenth day and the *atirātra* by means of the *mahāvrata*. That same [period] is also called the twenty-five-night period, though it lacks a *brāhmaṇa* explanation. Then follows the subsequent twenty-four-night period, consisting of a *jyotis-ati-rātra* and a *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*.
From the Trayastriṃśa they go to the Trayastriṃśa; then they enter upon the undefined Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha.

In the place of the Trivṛt, they enter upon the Trayastriṃśa Ukthya, which has the Rathantara as its Sāman; its Pavamāna stotras consist of the Caturviṃśa stoma. In the place of the Pañcadaśa, they enter upon the Triṇava Ukthya, which has the Bṛhat as its Sāman.

For that [sacrifice], there are thirty-eight *pavamāna* stotras; they proceed to the *ukthya* with the twenty-one-fold chant as its basis, having the *vairūpa* as its *sāman*. For that, there are thirty-two *pavamāna* stotras;
they proceed to the *ukthya* with the twenty-one-fold chant in its own proper place, having the *vairāja* as its *sāman*. For that, there are thirty-six *pavamāna* stotras.

In its own place, they proceed to the Triṇava Ukthya with the Śākvara Sāman; its Pavamāna stotras consist of forty verses. In its own place, they proceed to the Trayastriṃśa Ukthya with the Raivata Sāman; its Pavamāna stotras consist of forty-four verses.
From the Trayastriṃśa, they proceed to the Trayastriṃśa.
For him there are forty-eight Pavamāna stotras; then they proceed with the reversed Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha,
going from the Trivṛt up to the Trivṛt for the attainment and mastery of the Stomas.
They enter upon the Jyotis Agniṣṭoma, then the Atirātra, then the Triṃśadrātra, then the Jyotis Atirātra,
the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha,
and they enter upon the Trayastriṃśa from the Trayastriṃśa.
They perform the twenty-sevenfold [stoma]; they perform the twenty-onefold;
they perform the threefold Agniṣṭut; they perform the fifteenfold Indra-stoma.
They resort to the seventeenfold [stoma], they resort to the twenty-onefold,
they resort to the twenty-fourfold;
from the twenty-fourfold they resort to the pṛṣṭha [stotras].
They go from the thirty-three-fold to the thirty-three-fold; they go to the twenty-seven-fold; they go to two twenty-one-fold stomas.
They perform four sets of the Catuṣṭoma stomas; then an Atirātra; then an Atirātra consisting of the thirty-two-fold stoma; then nine three-day periods—the Jyotis, Go, and Āyus;
then a three-day period in reverse order; then an Atirātra; then an Atirātra consisting of the thirty-three-fold stoma;
and three five-day periods.

The Viśvajit, with all the *pṛṣṭha* chants, is an *atirātra*; then there is one five-day period (*pañcāha*), a ten-night period (*daśarātra*), and then an *atirātra*. He interposes the *mahāvrata* between the tenth day and the *atirātra*. Now, that which is not accompanied by a Brāhmaṇa explanation is the thirty-four-night sacrifice. Then there is the thirty-six-night sacrifice: an *atirātra*, four four-day *abhiplava* periods, a ten-night period, and then an *atirātra*. He interposes the *mahāvrata* between the tenth day and the *atirātra*.

Now, that same [sacrificial session] is indeed for non-Brāhmaṇas: thirty-seven days consisting of *rātris*, then one day consisting of forty-nine *rātris*, an *atirātra*, three *agniṣṭomas* with the *trivṛt* stoma, then a three-night period consisting of ten *ukthya*s with the *pañcadaśa* stoma, and then an *atirātra*;
for these, the tenth day is provided with the *ṣoḍaśin*.
There are twelve Ukthya days of seventeen [stomas], then an Atirātra;

then a Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, then an Atirātra; then twelve Ukthya days of twenty-one [stomas], then an Atirātra; then the Saṃvatsara-kḷpta consisting of forty-nine nights: an Atirātra, the introductory day (Ārambhaṇīyamahaḥ), three Abhiplava Ṣaḍahas.
Those eighteen days,
together with the Prāyaṇīya and Ārambhaṇīya [days], make twenty.

The Abhijit, three Paraḥsāman days, then the Vaiṣuvat day, three Arvāksāman days, then the Viśvajit; returning, there is the Abhiplava six-day period, the Go and Āyus days, the ten-night period, the Mahāvrata, and the Atirātra; then there is the sixty-one-night sacrifice, which, being thus constituted, adds two Pṛṣṭhya six-day periods on both sides of the nine-night period.

For those two, the *uttara* is reversed; then there is a *śatarātra*, an *atirātra*, and a three-day period consisting of *jyotis*, *go*, and *āyus*; fourteen *abhiplava* six-day periods; a ten-night period (*daśarātra*); the *mahāvrata* and an *atirātra*; then a *sahasrarātra*, an *atirātra*, ninety-nine *trivṛt* *agniṣṭomas*; one hundred *pañcadaśa* *ukthyas*; one hundred *saptadaśa* *ukthyas*; one hundred *ekaviṃśa* *ukthyas*; one hundred *triṇava* *ukthyas*; one hundred *trayastrim̐śa* *ukthyas*; one hundred *caturviṃśa* *ukthyas*; one hundred *catuścatvārim̐śa*...
There are one hundred Ukthya sacrifices—eighty-four Ukthyas and ninety-nine Trivṛt Agniṣṭomas—and then the Atirātra.

One intending to perform the Atirātra procures four Atirātra animals: a reddish-brown horse, a vessel for the Ṣoḍaśin made of Udumbara wood with four corners, larger Āmraṇa cups, and larger Ekadhana vessels; he then undergoes initiation.
He purchases Soma with a reddish-brown, one-year-old cow.
There are twelve Upasad days.

He proceeds from the Upavasatha day according to the established ritual procedure. Then, having carried around the Vasatīvarī waters and set aside the milks, they observe the fast. Then, at the very dead of night, they wake up.
Having taken the morning butter-portions and having brought the King [Soma] down, he begins the morning litany (prātaranuvāka).
When the morning litany has been concluded, he goes toward the waters and comes up out of them; he enters the Atirātra sacrifice.
The pressing of the Soma is well-known [as performed in the standard manner].
The cups are taken as is well known.

The ritual procedure up to the Āgrayaṇa cup is the same; having taken the Āgrayaṇa cup, he takes the Ṣoḍaśin cup, running forward with the verse, "Mount the chariot, O slayer of Vṛtra," and then, having murmured, "Thou art taken with a support;
I take thee, acceptable to Indra for the Ṣoḍaśin," he wipes it around and sets it down with, "This is thy womb; [I set thee down] acceptable to Indra for the Ṣoḍaśin. Then he takes the Ukthya cup.
The ritual procedure up to the Āśvina cup is the same; having drawn the Āśvina cup from the [Soma] vessel, having taken four cords, he approaches the sacrificial post.

Having set aside the post provided with a wooden chip (svaru), he dedicates four animals for the Atirātra: one for Agni, one for Indra-Agni, one for Indra, and a ewe for Sarasvatī. Having performed the offering of their omenta in the established manner, they proceed to the morning pressing.
That concludes in a straightforward manner;
they proceed for the midday pressing,
and the pressing is well-established.

The cups are drawn as prescribed. The ritual procedure up to the Āgrayaṇa cup is the same; having drawn the Āgrayaṇa, he draws the Ṣoḍaśin. Having recited "Indra, the two bay steeds carry thee," and then "Thou art taken with a support;

I take thee, acceptable to Indra for the Ṣoḍaśin," he wipes it around and sets it down with "This is thy womb; [acceptable] to Indra for the Ṣoḍaśin. Then he draws the Ukthya; thus the midday pressing concludes in the regular manner.
They proceed for the third pressing.

Having performed the ritual with the Āditya cup in the established manner, he draws the Āgrayaṇa; then he draws the Ṣoḍaśin. Having recited "Pressed is the Soma, O Indra, for thee," he says, "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Indra for the Ṣoḍaśin. Having wiped it around, he sets it down with, "This is thy womb; [I take thee] acceptable to Indra for the Ṣoḍaśin. Then he draws the Ukthya.
The ritual action is common up to the *pavamāna* [laud];
having performed the *pavamāna* with the *pavamāna*, he proceeds with the animal sacrifices in their own place.

For these, there are separate *manotās*, separate deities, separate touchings, and separate *vasā-homas*; the *vanaspati* offering is common, as is the *sviṣṭakṛt* accompanied by the *praisha* call; the *iḍā* is common, and the directions are common, though some say the directions are separate.

Having performed the ritual with the *dhruva*-like goblets in the same manner as for those who possess the *dhruva*, he proceeds with the three *ukthya* rounds: for Indra and Varuṇa, for Indra and Bṛhaspati, and for Indra and Viṣṇu.
Then, intending to proceed with the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, while moving forward, he says: "Fill the goblets following the Hotṛ’s goblet; O Unnetṛ, prepare the Soma!
They fill the Hotṛ’s goblet first.
Having raised the other [vessels] as they are brought forward, they set them down on the Uttaravedi;
they set down this Ṣoḍaśin together with them, and then he worships it.

Since there is no other born who is superior, who has entered into all beings—Prajāpati, in harmony with his offspring, he dwells with the three lights; he is the Ṣoḍaśin. This is the Brahman priest who is timely; he is renowned by the name Indra in the troop. For your great assembly, I have prepared the two bay steeds; I win for you that which is timely, the desirable exhilaration of the one who desires it. He who is renowned by the name Indra, who pours out what is beautiful like clarified butter with his bay steeds—he, the famous troop, may enter into you.

Having recited the *harivarpasaṃ giraḥ*, he touches water, takes two blades of *barhis* grass, and, restraining his speech, runs westward. When the sun has reached the meridian, he introduces the *ṣoḍaśin* chant with gold.
To the east, they hold a reddish-brown horse facing westward, or a dark one; having handed over the gold, they chant the praise.
"This is the final *hotrā*," they say; at the time of the *hotṛ*, the *adhvaryu* turns away, the *hotṛ* calls out to him,
and the *adhvaryu* responds with the call "śaṃsati."

He responds; then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ’s [verse] beginning with "May the bay steeds carry thee hither," he responds with the *ubhayatomoda* (joy on both sides): "Othā moda iva made madā moda ivoma-theti.
Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ’s [verse] beginning with "Forward for you the Triṣṭubh," having responded to that well-known hymn (*uktha*), he goes forward and lifts up this Ṣoḍaśin cup;
the goblets are lifted up after it.
Then he causes [the Hotṛ] to announce: "O announce! Let it be heard! *Astu śrauṣaṭ*! O reciter of the *uktha*, sacrifice the *soma*s!

At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers the *ṣoḍaśin*. [With the formula: "O Indra, lord of lords, you are the lord of the gods; make me, long-lived and radiant among men," he offers twice at the *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *vaṣaṭ* utterance.

In the same manner, they offer the cups together with their respective portions twice each; then they turn back toward the west with the portions for consumption. The formula for the portion at each pressing is: "Of that which was drunk by Indra with the Ṣoḍaśin...
Its distribution of the portion depends on the sacrificer, for it belongs to the sacrificer, or on the Hotṛ, for it belongs to the Hotṛ.
If those two should inform the Adhvaryu, he should simply say: "The portion belongs to the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ*."
In this way, he does not exclude himself from the portion;

his portion is Indra the Sovereign and Varuṇa the King—those two made this their portion first. Following their portion, I consume it: may Speech, being pleased, be satisfied with the Soma. Of that which has been drunk by Indra with the Ṣoḍaśin cup, which is honeyed and for which I have been invited, I, being invited, consume thee.
Having washed the vessel, he hands it over; at this point, he gives away this horse, which is reddish-brown or dark-colored.
They consume the *hotṛ*’s cup itself, and these three, having invited one another, consume the other cups according to their respective vessels.
With the words "Impel me," they touch themselves; they do not swell the cups;

they consume the entire contents and perform the ritual purification (mārjana). Then he issues the direction: "O Pratiprasthātṛ, guard the third portion of the Āgrayaṇa, the third portions of the entrails, the tail-ends, and the speckled butter. O Agnīdh, let the Aśvin cup on two potsherds remain cooked even for the latter part of the night."
They perform their duties according to the directions; then, having gone out, they proceed for the night session.
Having ascertained that they have all proceeded, the Adhvaryu, moving forward, says: "Fill the cups following the Hotṛ's cup; O Unnetṛ, cause the Soma to flow forth."

They draw the Hotṛ’s cup first; having drawn the others as they come, they set them down on the Uttaravedi. Then, having touched water and taken two blades of sacrificial grass, he, restraining his speech, runs westward and introduces the Stotra;
they chant the hymn.
"This is the best oblation," they say; the Adhvaryu turns away from the time of the Hotṛ's duty, the Hotṛ calls out to him,
and the Adhvaryu responds with "Śam".
He responds with the well-known *uktha*; having responded, he goes forward and lifts up this *hotṛ*-cup,
and the other cups are lifted up after it.
Then he causes [the announcement] to be heard: "O announce! Let it be heard! *Astu śrauṣaṭ*! O reciter of the *uktha*, sacrifice the *soma*s!

At the *vaṣaṭ* call and the subsequent *anu-vaṣaṭ* call, he offers twice; in the same way, they offer each of the *camasa*s twice. Then, with the portions for consumption (*bhakṣa*), they move westward; the formula for consumption at each pressing is: "Of that which was drunk by Indra..."

Having invoked these three together in the same manner as the Hotṛ’s cup, they consume them; then, according to their respective cups, they touch themselves with the formula: "Impel the cups; impel me."
They do not fill the cups;
having consumed all the portions, they perform the *mārjana* purification. Then, moving eastward, he says:
"O Unnetṛ, cause the Soma to flow forth; fill the cup of the Maitrāvaruṇa in succession."
They first draw the cup belonging to Mitrāvaruṇa;

having drawn the others as they come, they set them down on the high altar (uttaravedi). Then, having touched water and taken two blades of sacrificial grass (barhis), he, restraining his speech, runs westward and introduces the chant (stotra).

They chant the praise for the Maitrāvaruṇa; "This is the last," they say. From the time of the Maitrāvaruṇa’s turn, the Adhvaryu turns away; the Maitrāvaruṇa calls out to him, and the Adhvaryu responds.
When the *śaṃs* has been uttered, he responds; having responded with the well-known *uktha*, he goes forward and lifts up this cup of Maitrāvaruṇa.
The goblets are lifted up;
then he causes the announcement to be made: "Ośrāvaya! Astu Śrauṣaṭ! O reciter of the hymns (ukthaśas), sacrifice the Soma-cups!
At the utterance of Vaṣaṭ and the subsequent Vaṣaṭ-utterance, he offers twice.

In the same manner, they offer the cups together with their respective owners twice each; then, turning westward, they proceed with the consumption. At each pressing, they consume [the Soma] with the formula, "Of that which was drunk by Indra. These three, having invited one another, consume the cup of the Maitrāvaruṇa; the others consume their respective cups according to their vessels.
With the words "Impel me," they touch themselves; they do not cause the cups to swell;
having consumed the entire contents, they perform the ritual purification. Then he says, "O Pratiprasthātṛ, proceed with your two sets of cups."
Having heard that, the Pratiprasthātṛ, stepping forward to the east, says: "O Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, fill your cup after [the others]; O Unnetṛ, cause the Soma to flow forth.
They fill the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin's cup first.
Having raised the other [bricks] as they arise,
they place them on the high altar; then, having touched water and taken two blades of sacrificial grass, he, restraining his speech, runs westward and introduces the chant for the priests to sing.
"This is the last [cup] for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin," they say; at the time of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the Pratiprasthātṛ turns away; he calls out to him; the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin responds;
"Śaṃsati! says the Pratiprasthātṛ.
He responds with the well-known *uktha*. Having responded, he goes forward and raises this cup of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin;
they raise the other cups after it.
Then he causes [the Hotṛ] to announce: "Oṃ śrāvaya! Let it be heard! Oṣaṭ! Recite the offering-verse for the Soma-libations!
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ* and at the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ*, he offers twice;

likewise, they offer the cups of Soma twice each. Then they turn back with the portions, consuming according to the formula for the consumption at each pressing: "Of that which was drunk by Indra... and so forth.
These three—the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin and the others—having invited one another, consume [the Soma] from their respective cups; they touch themselves with the formula, "Impel the cups; impel me."
They do not fill the cups;

having consumed all [the Soma], they perform the *mārjana* purification. Then, moving eastward, he says: "Fill the cup of the Acchāvāka; O Unnetṛ, cause the Soma to flow forth. They fill the cup of the Acchāvāka first.

Having raised the other [soma vessels] as they were brought forward, they place them upon the Uttaravedi; then, having touched water and taken two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he restrains his speech, runs westward, and introduces the chant.
They say, "It is for the Acchāvāka; this is the last [verse]. At the time of the Acchāvāka, the Pratiprasthātṛ turns away from him, and the Acchāvāka calls out to him.
The Pratiprasthātṛ calls out in response; when it is "śam," he utters the *pratigara*.
Having responded to the well-known *uktha*, he goes forward and lifts up this cup of the Acchāvāka;
the other cups are lifted up after it.
Then he causes the announcement to be made: "O Śrauṣaṭ! Let it be heard! O reciter of the *uktha*, sacrifice to the Soma-draughts!"
He offers twice, at the *vaṣaṭ* call and at the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ* call;

likewise, they offer the cups for the *soma*-drinkers twice each. Then, turning westward with the portions for consumption, they proceed according to the consumption formula for each pressing: "Of that which was drunk by Indra... These three, having invited one another, consume the cup of the *acchāvāka*; the others consume their respective cups according to the cup-assignment.
With the words "Impel me," they touch themselves; they do not cause the cups to swell;
they consume the entire contents and perform the ritual purification.

First, the Hotṛ praises; then the Maitrāvaruṇa; then the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; then the Acchāvāka. The Adhvaryu proceeds with the two preceding groups of cups, and the Pratiprasthātṛ with the two subsequent ones. All the draughts and the groups of cups belong to Indra. Thus indeed this first fourfold round is completed; in the same way the second is completed, and likewise the third. During the middle round, they proceed as if possessed of artistic skill. Then, having gone out, they move forward for the Rathantara Saṃdhi ceremony.

Having perceived that they have all moved forward, the Adhvaryu, stepping forward toward the east, says: "Fill the cups following the Hotṛ’s cup; O Unnetṛ, draw up the King Soma in its entirety so that nothing remains over.
They fill the Hotṛ’s cup first, and the others as they come to hand.
Having lifted up the King Soma in every respect, they set him down upon the Uttaravedi;

then they set down this cup for the Aśvins together with it, having spread a base of ghee and poured an oblation over it. Then, having touched water and taken two blades of sacrificial grass, restraining his speech, he hastens westward and introduces the Stotra;
they chant the hymn.
"This is the final offering," they say. After the time of the *hotṛ*, the *adhvaryu* turns away;
the *hotṛ* calls out to him, and the *adhvaryu* responds with the *pratigara*.
When it is "śaṃ," [the ritual continues].

He responds up to the *mahāhava* call; the *āśvina-śastra* consists of more than a thousand verses—this is the well-known Brāhmaṇa teaching. Having responded to the *uktha*, walking eastward, he says: "Recite for the Aśvins the Soma-draughts of the *tiroahnya* [day]. Having gone forward, he lifts up this cup of the Hotṛ.
While raising the *āśvina* cup, they raise the goblets;
then he causes the announcement to be made: "O Śrauṣaṭ! Let it be heard! For the Aśvins, for the Soma-draughts belonging to the day before yesterday that have been set forth—proclaim the *praisha*!"
When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers;
then they offer this oblation for the Aśvins together— both the one with the under-layered butter and the one sprinkled over—
at the *vaṣaṭ* and at the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*, offering twice.

In the same manner, they offer the cups together with their respective portions twice each; then they turn westward with the portions for consumption. The formula for the portion at each pressing is: "Of that which was drunk by the Aśvins...

The formula for its consumption, for the entire group, is: "Of thee, who art drunk by the Aśvins, belonging to the entire group, of the Soma of yesterday, well-pressed, honeyed, being invited—I, invited, consume.
These three, having invited one another, consume the Hotṛ’s cup alone.
With the words, "Impel the cups according to their respective vessels; impel me," they touch themselves,
but they do not cause the cups to swell.

Having consumed all [the portions], they cleanse themselves. Then he issues the command: "O Āgnīdh, bring the embers for the supplementary offerings (aupayaja); O Upayaṣṭṛ, sit down; O Brahman, we shall set forth; having placed the fuel-stick, O Āgnīdh, cleanse the fires once each. They bring these embers for the supplementary offerings from the Āgnīdhra fire-chamber; the Hotṛ pours them down in front of himself, and the Upayaṣṭṛ sits down. With the third portions of the entrails, the Upayaṣṭṛ performs the supplementary offerings here, having divided these third portions of the entrails into eleven parts.
From this point onward, the procedure is the same; thus the Atirātra sacrifice concludes.

One who is about to perform the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice, having offered the oblation for the sacrificial post (*yūpa-āhuti*), goes toward that direction where he intends to find thirteen sacrificial posts. Having cut them—including the one lying on the ground as the twelfth and the one for the *pātnīvata* as the thirteenth—he causes them to be brought, or they are brought to him; once brought, he prepares them. He fashions the *svaru*-chips from the very wood used for planing. Now, on the previous day, his altar has already been measured out eleven times by means of a chariot axle. When he traces around the hole for the central sacrificial post (*agniṣṭha-yūpa*), he asks for that chariot axle.

With that [cord], he measures to the south and traces around the sacrificial post-hole (yūpāvaṭa) so as to be level with the top; then he measures to the north and traces around the sacrificial post-hole so as to be level with the top.
In this very same way, measuring to the south and then to the north, he traces around eight sacrificial post-holes.
Regarding this, some raise these posts on the very day of the Upavasatha, saying, "The sacrificer is the central post among the limbs, while the others are its form."
If someone should say of him there, while he is not yet erecting it, "This sacrificer will surely become limbless," so indeed would it be.

However, they also say: "If these sacrificial posts were to stand like non-animals, like mere stakes, it would be like a desecration of the sacrificial site, like a ruin of the sacrifice; therefore, one should erect these sacrificial posts on the very next day."
On the following day, they raise them; having girt the eleven cords around the sacrificial post standing nearest the fire (the *agniṣṭha*), they let them remain.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the cup for the Aśvins. Having taken the cup for the Aśvins and having taken the eleven cords, he approaches the sacrificial post.
Then these posts—washed, brought forward, and fitted with their head-rings (*caṣāla*)—lie down before the pits.

Having set aside the central post which possesses a ring, he first erects the southern attendant post, then the northern one; in this same manner, he erects eight posts, alternating between southern and northern. Now, it is said: "One should erect them level with the top-ring for one who desires the world of the fathers"—they are all equal at the base-rings.
"Level with the girdles for one who desires the world of men"—they are all equal at the girdles. "Level with the top-pieces for one who desires power"—they are all equal at the top-pieces.
"For one desiring a firm foundation, he makes all equal"—thus he makes them equal for one desiring a firm foundation.
"Those three which are in the middle, for one desiring cattle, he makes them equal"—thus he makes those equal for one desiring cattle.
"He should interweave the others"—thus he interweaves them.

In this very manner, he interlinks eight sacrificial posts, [namely] the southern and the northern. Now it is said: "If he should desire of someone, 'May he be liable to die,' he should set up a post for him that has been dug into a pit; the one on the northern side should be the tallest, and the one on the southern side shorter. In this case, he sets up the tallest on the northern side and the shorter one on the southern side.

"Indeed, he who erects [the posts] in this manner for one who digs a pit (*gartamit*) will quickly perish," so says the Brāhmaṇa. One desiring heaven should erect the southernmost post as the tallest; then, the others should be successively shorter.
Here, he erects the southernmost as the tallest and the northernmost as the shortest.
"In this way, the sacrificer constructs a staircase and a bridge for the attainment of the heavenly world," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said in the Brāhmaṇa: "Because he winds two girdles around one single sacrificial post, therefore one man finds two wives;
because he does not wind a single girdle around two posts, therefore one woman does not find two husbands."

Now, it is indeed said: "If he should desire of someone, 'May a female be born to him,' he should intertwine [the verses] at its end for that person. He intertwines them at its end for him; "Thus a female is born to him," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Now, it is indeed said in the Brāhmaṇa: "If he should desire of someone, 'May a male be born to him,' he should cause [the garment] to be wrapped up to its end for that person. He causes it to be wrapped up to its end; thus a male is born to him. So says the Brāhmaṇa.
He spreads out this resting-place to the south silently. Having set out the sacrificial posts provided with *svaru*-blades, he dedicates the animal for Agni at the central post;

the one for Sarasvatī to the north, the one for Soma to the south, the one for Pūṣan to the north, the one for Bṛhaspati to the south, the one for the Viśvedevas to the north, the one for Indra to the south, the one for the Maruts to the north, the one for Indra-Agni to the south, the one for Savitṛ to the north, and the one for Varuṇa to the south. Now it is said: "If he should desire, 'May he who has fallen into misfortune be excluded, and may he who is excluded regain his position,' he should dedicate the animal for Varuṇa in the place of the one for Indra, and the one for Indra in the place of the one for Varuṇa."
"He who has understood is excluded; he who is excluded understands," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is further said: "If he should desire, 'May the subjects become bewildered,' he should intermingle the cattle."
"He interlinks the animals here;
he confuses the progeny," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it occurs:

If one were to sacrifice an animal dedicated to Varuṇa with the flow of the waters, Varuṇa would seize his offspring; therefore, he sacrifices it from the south, facing north, against the flow of the waters, so that Varuṇa shall not seize his offspring—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, upon this secondary sacrificial post (upaśaya), he dedicates with his mind alone whomsoever he hates;
and if indeed he does not hate anyone, he assigns it, saying, "The dog is your victim."
The ritual procedure is the same up to the carrying of fire around the victims (*paryagnikaraṇa*).

Having brought these animals to the fire, he stations five of them on the southern side and leads two of them forward; then he interlinks them with the others. Then they proceed northward with the animals for which the fire has been carried around. Among them, the one dedicated to Varuṇa is on the northern side, while the one dedicated to Agni is by way of proximity. The Adhvaryu takes hold of the animal for Agni with the two omentum-roasting spits (*vapāśrapaṇī*), while the assistants lead the others separately toward the north, one after another, without interlinking them.

Having performed the ritual for them with the omenta as is well known, they proceed to the morning pressing; that concludes in a straightforward manner. Now it is indeed said: "The offering with the omentum is completed, but the offering with the *vaśā* cow is not yet completed; then one proceeds with the *pātnīvata* offering."

When he has offered the omentum of the animal to be bound at the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice, but not yet the animal itself, he carries the *stambayajus* from behind the *gārhapatya* fire onto the sacrificial altar prepared for the *aupasadā* rites.
This is the well-known procedure according to the *pauroḍāśika* ritual: he performs it three times with the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) and a fourth time silently.
He performs the first tracing of the altar, mutters the *karaṇa* formula, digs up the earth, and from what has been dug up, the *āgnīdhra* carries away the earth three times.
When the Āgnīdhra has carried [the coals] three times, he then traces around the pit for the *pātnīvata* sacrificial post in front of the *gārhapatya* fire.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the placing of the offering-spoons (*sruk*).
Having placed the spoons, he erects the *pātnīvata* post in front of the *gārhapatya* fire; upon it, he dedicates a one-year-old ram with testicles as the animal victim for Tvaṣṭṛ.

Having released that [animal] after the fire has been carried around it, he completes the rite with clarified butter (*ājya*). Then, taking four portions of clarified butter, he says loudly, "For Tvaṣṭṛ—recite the invitatory verse (*anuvācya*) in a low voice. Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "For Tvaṣṭṛ—recite the offering verse (*yājyā*) in a low voice," and when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers the oblation. Thus he performs the ritual response for the omentum (*vapā*). Taking four portions of clarified butter, he says loudly, "For Tvaṣṭṛ—recite the invitatory verse in a low voice. Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "For Tvaṣṭṛ—recite the offering verse in a low voice," and when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers the oblation. Thus he performs the ritual response for the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*).

Taking four portions of clarified butter, he says, "For Agni," in a low voice; "Recite the invitatory verse," loudly; having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "For Agni," in a low voice; "Recite the offering verse," loudly; and when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering in the eastern half of the northern half, passing over the previous offerings—this is how he performs the *sviṣṭakṛt* of the animal-cake. Taking four portions of clarified butter, he says, "For Tvaṣṭṛ," in a low voice; "Recite the invitatory verse," loudly; having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "For Tvaṣṭṛ," in a low voice; "Recite the offering verse," loudly; and when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering—this is how he performs the offering of the oblation. He offers to the quarters with clarified butter.
He cuts off the portion for Vanaspati from the speckled butter,
the portion for Sviṣṭakṛt from the clarified butter,
and the iḍā-portion from the clarified butter.
He performs the after-offerings with speckled butter;
having performed the offerings to the wives right here, he offers the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations right here; thus the offering to the wives (*pātnīvata*) is concluded.
Now, it is indeed said:

"He who does not prosper after the establishment of the fires (agnyādheya) performs the re-establishment (punarādheya); he who does not prosper after piling the fire-altar (agni-citi) piles the altar again. Having piled the fire-altar and being in decline, he prepares twelve bricks: eight *yājuṣī* bricks and four *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks.

When the high altar (*uttaravedi*) has been sprinkled with butter and the *saṃbhāra* materials have been scattered upon it, he then takes the fire into himself with two verses: "I take Agni first within me" and "That Agni of ours..."
He himself mutters the *svayaṃcit* formula: "O Agni, those logs of thine, those abodes...
Having touched the white horse, he lays down eight bricks with the *yājuṣī* formulas: "By which the seers sat for the sacrificial session through austerity...

Then he lays four *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks with the formula: "Fill the space, fill the gap... Then he touches the layer with the *citiklpti* formula: "May the wise one distinguish between thought and non-thought... With this *gāyatrī* verse addressed to Agni, having touched this layer, he descends with two verses: "May speech be in my mouth, may it grant breath..."
It is either a Paśubandha or an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; it is completed in a well-known manner.

Jarvara is the Gṛhapati; Dhṛtarāṣṭra Airāvata is the Brahman; Datta Tāpasa is the Hotṛ; Pṛthuśravas Dūreśravas is the Udgātṛ; Glāva and Ajagāva are the Prastotṛ and Pratihartṛ; Śitipṛṣṭha is the Maitrāvaruṇa; Takṣaka Vaiśāleya is the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; Upariti Tarkṣya is the Sadasya; Śikha and Atiśikha are the Neṣṭṛ and Potṛ; Aruṇa Ahiya is the Acchāvāka; Cakra and Piśaṅga are the Āgnīdhra; Ajira Māheya is the Subrahmaṇya; Arbuda is the Grāvastut; Sāṇḍa is the Unnetṛ; and Paśukra is the assistant.

Dhruvagopa and Kautu were the two *adhvaryu* priests; Arimejaya and Janamejaya were the kings and princes of the serpents. These, desiring poison, performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*) at Khāṇḍava-prastha in human form.

For them, some days consisted of ten-fold hymns (*daśastoma*), while others consisted of twelve-fold hymns (*dvādaśastoma*). Because they [chanted] "ten, ten," therefore the serpents are *damśukas*, and they possess ten-fold strength.
This is a sacrificial session (sattra) belonging to the world of men, pertaining to grandsons, and conducive to cattle;
serpents do not harm those who undertake it.

Austerity is the householder; Food is the wife; the Veda is the Brahman priest; Truth is the Hotṛ; Immortality is the Udgātṛ; the past and the future are the Prastotṛ and Pratihartṛ; Order is the Maitrāvaruṇa; the seasons are the Sadasyas; the seasonal periods are the Upagātṛs; Splendor is the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; Glory is the Acchāvāka; Radiance and Honor are the Neṣṭṛ and Potṛ; Fire itself is the Agnīdhra; Speech is the Subrahmaṇya; Fortune is the Grāvastut; Vitality is the Unnetṛ; Strength is the Dhruvagopa; Mind is the Adhvaryu; and Sight is the Pratiprasthātṛ; while Exhaustion and Hunger are the two assistants.
Cedhmavāha was the *diṣṭṛ*, Viśas was the *viśastṛ*, and Mṛtyu was the *śamitṛ*. These were indeed the first creators of the universe (*viśvasṛj*); they performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*).

For them, there were a hundred years of consecration (*dīkṣā*), a hundred *upasads*, and a thousand *prasutas*. This [verse] speaks of that: "The first creators of the universe performed a sacrificial session, proceeding for a thousand years with the *prasuta*; from that, the blinking and the non-blinking came into being; from that, the guardian of the world was born. It was indeed by means of *agniṣṭomas* that they then proceeded.
This is the prosperous course, the means of procreation, which consists of Agniṣṭomas.
Those who are about to undertake the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana undergo initiation; there are five *dhurs* on all sides.

For them, this very one is the known year-long consecration (*saṃvatsara-dīkṣā*). The ritual procedure is the same up to the *ārambhaṇīyā* [offering]. Having performed the *ārambhaṇīyā*, he causes the milk for Indra to be milked according to the procedure for the *saṃnāyya*, or silently. Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and without leaving behind any of the milk, they fast. Then, on the following day, they sacrifice with the new-moon oblation (*āmāvāsya-havis*). By means of that, they proceed for eighty-eight days.
The month [begins] with the Prāyaṇīya and Ārambhaṇīya offerings;

they proceed for a month with the Vaiśvadeva oblations, for a month with the Varuṇapraghāsa oblations, for a month with the Sākamedha oblations, and for a month with the Śunāsīrīya oblations; there are thirty-six days, including the Abhijit and the three Para-sāmans.
That month is the Vaiṣuvat; then there are three Arvāksāman days, and then the Viśvajit.

They proceed for a month with the Triṃśa-stoma, they proceed for a month with the Triṇava-stoma, they proceed for a month with the Ekaviṃśa-stoma, they proceed for a month with the Saptadaśa-stoma, they proceed for a month with the Pañcadaśa-stoma, they proceed for a month with the Trivṛt-stoma, and [they perform] twelve days of the Dvādaśāha.
Those fourteen [months] are the *go* and *āyus*;
four are above the *vaiṣuvata*.
Those eighteen [days],
the Daśarātra, the Mahāvrata, and the Atirātra constitute that month.
Now, their "pits" (kuṇḍas) are this: in that they are all possessed of the three Vedas, that is their pit;
and in that they cause one another to sacrifice by moving around in succession, that is their pit.

Now, as for the fact that they consume [the soma] from cups with handles, their *kuṇḍa* [is formed thus]: he who is the *brahmán* is the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsín*, he is the *potṛ*; and he who is the *hotṛ* is the *maitrāvaruṇa*, he is the *acchāvāka*; and he who is the *udgātṛ* is the *prastotṛ*, he is the *pratihartṛ*; and he who is the *adhvaryu* is the *pratiprasthātṛ*, he is the *neṣṭṛ*; and he who is the *āgnīdhra* is the *grāvastut*, he is the *subrahmaṇyá*, he is the *unnetṛ*. Furthermore, the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) is: Agni is the *caturhotṛ*, Vāyu is the *pañcahotṛ*, and the Moon is the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ*.

Prajāpati is the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ; yonder Āditya is the Saptahotṛ; and these [other] deities are the Navahotṛ. By this very course (ayana) they went forth, and thereupon they prospered and went to the heavenly world.
Those who, knowing thus, go by this course, indeed prosper and go to the heavenly world.
Those who intend to perform the *utsargiṇām ayana* undergo initiation;
for them, this very well-known initiation lasts for a year, and the ritual procedure is the same up to the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*.

Having sacrificed with the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite, he causes the milk for Indra to be milked either according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya* or silently. Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and set aside the milk, they fast. Then, on the next morning, having released the day's ritual, they immolate an animal for Prajāpati at the place of the *jyotis* [stotra].

Following the animal cake (paśupuroḍāśa) for that [animal sacrifice], they offer an eight-potherd cake to Agni Vasumat at the midday pressing; they offer an eleven-potherd cake to Indra Marutvat and the Sāṃnāyya oblation to Indra—that is the two-oblation sacrifice which concludes here. Having invited one another, they consume this Sāṃnāyya belonging to Indra. Then, in the afternoon, they offer a twelve-potherd cake to the Viśve Devas and a pap (caru) to the Viśve Devas; they proceed with these two offerings, beginning from the deities and ending with the Iḍā.

Then he proceeds with the animal sacrifice, beginning with the *manotā* and ending with the *iḍā*. Then, having performed the after-offerings (*anūyāja*), turning to the right, hastening westward, and having offered the oblations for the wives, he goes eastward, replenishes the *dhruvā* ladle, and having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters, they wait while the milk is being set apart. Then, on the next day, they begin with the cow-sacrifice.

Proceeding in this very manner, omitting one month each time, they omit five *jyotiḥ* sacrifices; then from there they turn back and omit four *trayastrim̐śa* stomas and one *jyotis*. Then, on the next day, they begin again with the *āyus* sacrifice.
Desiring to attain the accumulation of austerity through this [sacrifice], they undergo initiation;
for them, this very initiation of the fires is well-known, and the ritual procedure is the same up to the pouring together of the grains.
The preparation of the materials is well-known. Then he performs the Prāyaṇīyā offering;

having performed the Prāyaṇīyā, he proceeds with the footprint-rite; having performed the footprint-rite, he purchases the King Soma and carries him away; he offers the Ātithya oblation; having performed the Ātithya, he then offers this sacrifice consisting of five oblations: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, a cake on twelve potsherds for the Viśve Devas, a pap for Bṛhaspati, and a cake on three potsherds for Viṣṇu.
Some say that having sacrificed with her only once, they should not pay further heed; others say they should sacrifice with her every day for a year;

others say on the first day with all [the formulas], on each subsequent day with one each; others say on the sixth day with all [the formulas], on each subsequent day with one each; and some say one should pile the fire-altar on the first twelve-day period (dvādaśāha).
Regarding this, they say: "Agni is indeed Rudra; he is born now when he is completely piled up.
Just as a newborn calf seeks the udder, so does he now seek his portion."

"Verily, the year itself is his portion from this; one should not go beyond even its hope. Thus he should pile the fire-altar on the last day of the twelve-day period (*dvādaśāha*); this is another [view].
Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the daily piling:
they complete the piling in a single day, and then, laying down the space-filling bricks (*lokaṃpṛṇā*), they reach a month.
In the first month, he performs the *tayādevata* rite; in the second month, there is the piling of the soil (*purīṣaciti*).
They complete the immediate piling (*sadyaściti*), and then the month passes while following the manner of the handfuls (*muṣṭi*).
In the first month he performs the Tayādevata rite; in the third month is the Vaṇḍa layer; in the fourth month is the Purīṣa layer;
in the fifth month is the middle layer.
In the sixth month there is a layer of loose soil;

in the seventh month a layer of bricks with projections; in the eighth month a layer of loose soil; in the ninth month he lays down the seven *skandhya* bricks up to the *nakṣatra* bricks; in the tenth month a layer of loose soil; in the eleventh month he lays down these [bricks] with the formulas beginning "He who is self-restraining and wise" up to the *vikarṇī*; in the twelfth month there are twenty-eight days of loose soil; in the twenty-ninth [day] the *Śatarudrīya*; on the following day the *Vasordhārā*.
Now, they say that [the rite] lasts for a month above [that].

On the first day of the month, they complete the *sadyaś-citi* (the immediate piling), including the *satya-devata* and the *sasūdadohas*. They proceed with the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites for the duration of the month.
On the first day of the second month, there is the *purīṣa-citi* (the piling of earth).
They complete the Sadyaś-citi with the Satadēvata and Sasūdadohas formulas. They proceed with the Pravargya and Upasad rites for the second month.
On the first day of the third month is the Vaṇḍa-citi; on the first day of the fourth month is the Purīṣa-citi;
on the first day of the fifth month is the middle layer (Madhyama-citi).
On the first day of the sixth month is the layer of loose soil (*purīṣaciti*);

on the first day of the seventh month is the layer of the egg (*aṇḍaciti*); on the first day of the eighth month is the layer of loose soil; on the first day of the ninth month he lays down the seven *skandhyā* bricks up to the *nakṣatra-iṣṭakā*s; on the first day of the tenth month is the layer of loose soil; on the first day of the eleventh month he lays down these [bricks] beginning with "Saṃyac and Pracetas" up to the *vikarṇī*; on the first day of the twelfth month is the layer of loose soil; and on the twenty-ninth day, the *Śatarudrīya* is to be performed on the following day.
Then follows the Vasordhārā for the beings; they say that for a month [they perform] the Pravargya and Upasad rites.

On the final day of the first month, they complete the *sadyaś-citi* (the immediate layering), which belongs to the deity Satya and includes the *sūdadohas* verse. For the second month, they proceed with the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites.
On the final day of the second month, there is a *purīṣa-citi* (filling of earth);

they complete the *sadyaś-citi*, which belongs to the deity Satya and includes the *sūdadohas* verse. On the final day of the third month, there is a *vaṇḍa-citi* (layer of bricks). On the final day of the fourth month, there is a *purīṣa-citi*.

On the last day of the fifth month is the middle layer; on the last day of the sixth month is the layer of loose earth (*purīṣaciti*); on the last day of the seventh month is the layer of bricks with projections (*vaṇḍaciti*); on the last day of the eighth month is the layer of loose earth; on the last day of the ninth month he lays down the seven *skandhyā* bricks up to the *nakṣatra*-bricks; on the last day of the tenth month is the layer of loose earth; on the last day of the eleventh month he lays down these [bricks] beginning with "Saṃyac and Pracetas" up to the *vikarṇī*; on the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month is the layer of loose earth.
On the twenty-ninth day, the Śatarudrīya; on the following day, the Vasordhārā.
Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the rites for rising from the sacrifice: "Having sacrificed with the Abhijit, they should rise"—this is established by the Brāhmaṇa.

Or rather, having sacrificed with the Abhijit, they then perform this Savaneṣṭi: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, and a cake on twelve potsherds for the Viśvedevas.

Whether they proceed with all [the Vasatīvarī waters] together or having distributed them, they place a lump of clay within the Vasatīvarī waters and go about carrying the Vasatīvarī waters around day by day. Now, that which is completed in a year is called "the course of the Brahman";
they spend four months in consecrations (*dīkṣā*), four months in the *upasad* rites, and four months in the *prasuta* (pressing) ceremonies.

Regarding this they say: "Who, having performed such austerity, would make it common to others? Or would he seek an invitation among his pupils? They should rather cause him to sacrifice with a sacrificial fee.
He indeed seeks an invitation among his pupils, and they cause him to sacrifice with a sacrificial fee.
Now, moreover, it is said:
"One desiring cattle should pile the Chandaścit.

Wherever an oblation reaches, he offers it there; but whatever else besides the oblations there is, that is like the body—he merely mutters the *yajus* there. There is *yajus* for the two girdles, *yajus* for the horse and the donkey, and *yajus* for the preparation of the fire-pan (*ukhā*).
He performs the sacrifice with an animal dedicated to Vāyu.
He undergoes initiation.
Having measured out the fire-altar and dug a trench, he mutters the *yajus* in the place of the waters; he offers the *yajus* at the laying down of all the bricks.
He performs the *Śatarudrīya* and the *Vasordhārā*. "One desiring heaven should pile the *Śyenacit* (Falcon-pile)"—this very altar is the *Śyenacit*.

One who desires, "May I be possessed of a head in that world," should pile the Kaṅkacit; from this very [altar], he projects it forward by a span as if it were headed, and it is thus measured out so that the sacrificial post (yūpa) shall not be outside the altar. One who desires a firm foundation should pile the Alajicit, which has four furrows; from this very [altar], he projects the tips of the wings by a span each, and the two wings are made wider by that same measure.
When those two [altars] have receded slightly, the other two become smaller than them; he ploughs each furrow with a single verse.

"One who has rivals should pile the *prauga*-altar"—of this very [altar], having drawn out the two shoulders (*aṃsau*) together, he extends them eastward. It is measured out in such a way that the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) shall not be outside the altar. "One who desires, 'May I drive away my rivals already born and those yet to be born,' should pile the *ubhayataḥ-prauga* altar"—of this very [altar], having drawn out the two hips (*śroṇī*) together, he extends them westward.

It is measured in such a way that the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) would not be outside the altar-ground. It is known from scripture: "One who has rivals should pile it in the form of a chariot wheel. This is a modification of the shape due to the connection with the specific term. Having made a circular area of ground as large as the fire-altar itself—measuring one *aratni* and one *prādeśa*—he piles the bricks around it, first along the pebbles on the outside, then further inward; in this very manner, he places the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick so that it is surrounded by them, like a navel in the center.
He lays down bricks for it toward the cardinal and intermediate directions, like spokes around a rim.

This is the chariot-wheel-shaped altar (*rathacakracit*); it is to be drawn around by one who has enemies. One desiring food should build the trough-shaped altar (*droṇacit*). While this very same altar exists, he raises it up toward the east by a span’s measure, as if it were a manger, and then makes it hollow in the middle.
This is the trough-shaped altar (*droṇacit*) for one desiring food; it is to be drawn around.
"One who desires cattle should pile the *samūhya*," so it is known.
"A lotus leaf, a gold disk, a golden man, and two offering-spoons—these they call the characteristic marks.
He indeed prepares them; furthermore, he causes the bricks of the loose soil (*purīṣa*) to be brought together.
