This is the *samūhya* altar for one desiring cattle;

the *parikṛṣya* altar is for one desiring a village. One should pile the *paricāyya* altar. He piles the bricks around the pebbles, first on the outside, then inside, and then again inside; in this very manner, he piles the bricks around the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone, surrounding it on all sides.
This is the *paricāyya* altar for one desiring a village, which is the *parikṛṣya*.
One who desires, "May I prosper in the world of the fathers," should pile the Śmaśānacit altar.

There are six persons facing east; three are transverse in front, two are transverse behind, and two are transverse [at the sides]. That is the body (ātman). Its measurement is: if it is neck-deep in front, it is navel-deep behind; if navel-deep in front, it is knee-deep behind; if knee-deep in front, it is ankle-deep behind; if ankle-deep in front, it is level with the ground behind.

This very [altar] piled in the cremation ground is for one who desires the world of the fathers; now, this [altar] piled in the form of a tortoise is for a Brāhmaṇa—one that is raised in the middle with its back curved away. Having drawn it around, he raises it up as if with its head toward the east by a span's measure from that very same [central point].
He extends the bricks as its feet toward the intermediate directions.
This very [altar] piled in the form of a tortoise is for a Brāhmaṇa—one that is raised in the middle with its back curved away, having been drawn around.
One who is about to perform the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice procures the following:

the hide of a red bull, lead, a eunuch, young grass, sprouts of grain, rice, flour made from the *agnihotra* oblation, three vessels made of different kinds of wood, three types of groats, hair from three different animals, a sacrificial post, a hawk’s wing-feather, a pregnant mare, a stool, a *iṇḍva*-shaped vessel, a jar, a *kārotara* filter, two *viśākha* poles, a long bamboo pole, a sling, a hundred-holed sieve, a gold coin weighing a *śatamāna*, a hundred hairs, and a Brāhmaṇa for the portion of the remnant of the oblation.
If he does not find a Brāhmaṇa to drink [the Soma],
then, having sacrificed with the New Moon oblation or under a lunar mansion, the Surā-Soma lies prepared in front of the hall on a red hide;
a eunuch sits beside it to the south.
With lead he buys the shoots from a eunuch, saying, "This is yours, this is mine;

the *surā* and the *soma* have been bought. Then, taking them and having entered the hall by the eastern door, he places them down behind the *gārhapatya* fire. Then they thresh half of these rice grains, while the others, having placed a cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) upon the *gārhapatya*, they roast.

Of these, those that ripen become *lāja* grains; those that do not ripen are *tarya*. Having placed a new pot on the *gārhapatya* fire, they cook the rice with plenty of water. Then, having drained it, they attach it to either a wooden board or a mat. They then pound them until they are crushed. Of these, whatever small fragments and *tarya* there are, they pour into the overflow;

this they call *māsara*. Then, taking a measure, he measures it out: one part of young grass (*śaṣpa*), two parts of sprouts (*tokman*), three parts of *lāja* grains, and four parts of *nagnahu* (unhusked barley).

Then, while strewing this cooked rice with flour and sprinkling it with *māsara*, he prepares it, saying: "I mix thee, the sweet, with the sweet; the strong, with the strong; the immortal, with the immortal; I unite thee with Soma. Then, having carried this stool around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, he places it to the south. Upon the stool he places a mat (*iṇḍvā*), upon the mat a jar (*kumbha*), and upon the jar a strainer (*kārotara*). Then he scatters the cooked rice all around the strainer. Having covered it, he touches it, saying: "O Soma, be cooked for the Aśvins; be cooked for Sarasvatī; be cooked for Indra the Good Protector."
"Three nights does he dwell when the [Soma] has been pressed; three nights does the purchased Soma dwell," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Then, when three nights have dawned, the animal sacrifice (Paśubandha) consisting of either three or four animals is performed. Now, on the previous day, this sacrificial altar for the Sautrāmaṇī is measured out for him.

Having strewn it around, he performs the *stambayajus* rite in this well-known manner according to the *pauroḍāśika* rules: three times with the sacrificial formula and the fourth time silently. He performs the first tracing of the altar, mutters the *karaṇa* formula, digs up the earth, and from the dug-up spot, the *āgnīdhra* carries away the earth three times.

When the Āgnīdhra carries [the earth] three times, then he traces around the *cātvāla* with the procedure for the *cātvāla*; he pours out the *uttaravedi* with the procedure for the *uttaravedi*; having leveled the *uttaranābhi* and dug the post-hole, he leads forward two fires with the procedure for the fire—the Adhvaryu from the Āhavanīya and the Pratiprasthātṛ from the Anvāhāryapacana. Having performed the second tracing with the fire already present, having leveled [the ground] and fixed the wooden sword (*sphya*) crosswise, he issues the call: "Set down the sprinkling waters; place the fuel and the sacrificial grass; bring the *sruva* ladle."

"Cleanse the knife and the offering-spoons; silently [cleanse] the vessel for the clotted butter; gird the wife; bring the clarified butter and the curds; O Pratiprasthātṛ, attend to the Surā-Soma!"—thus the Adhvaryu alone performs the well-known ritual actions pertaining to the animal sacrifice. Then the Pratiprasthātṛ, having purified the Surā and taken it along with the filter, carries it out by the eastern door and places it within the altar.

While the Adhvaryu is occupied here, the Pratiprasthātṛ purifies the *surā* with a sheep’s tail-hair whose fringe points northward, [reciting]: "May the daughter of the Sun purify thy flowing *soma* with her eternal fleece.

If he has over-purified the *soma*, he then takes up a vessel made of *parṇa*-wood and draws [the *surā*] from it, reciting the verse, "O friend, those who possess barley... and then, "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the Aśvins."

Having placed two blades of *barhis* grass in between, he mixes [the soma] with flour of *kvala* beans and with the hair of a porcupine; having removed the two blades of *barhis*, he wipes [the vessel] with a hawk’s wing-feather and sets it down, saying, "This is thy womb; for the Aśvins, thee! Then he takes a vessel made of *nyagrodha* wood; with that he draws [the soma], reciting the verse, "O, surely, they who possess barley... and then [the formula], "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Sarasvatī."

Having placed two blades of *barhis* grass in between, he mixes [the soma] with *badara* flour and tiger hair; having removed the two blades of *barhis*, he wipes it with a hawk’s wing-feather and sets it down, saying, "This is thy womb; for Sarasvatī, thee! Then he takes an *āśvattha* vessel and draws [the soma] into it, reciting the verse, "O friend, those who possess barley... and the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Indra Sutrāman."

Having placed two blades of *barhis* grass in between, he mixes [the mixture] with *karkandhu*-berry flour and the hair of a *vṛka* wolf; having removed the two blades of *barhis*, he wipes it with a hawk’s wing-feather and sets it down, saying: "This is thy womb; for Indra Sutrāman thee!
He causes it to extend behind the handles of the ladles, either towards the east or towards the north. Then, taking this *surā* liquor together with its dregs, he approaches the southern fire;
he has two pits dug on both sides of it.

He places near [the fire] two *viśākhā* branches, a long bamboo pole, a sling, a hundred-holed sieve, a hundred-measure weight of gold, and a hundred hairs. Then, in front of the southern fire, he prepares a mound from old ashes;
upon it he places a Brāhmaṇa who is to drink the remnants of the oblation. If he does not find a Brāhmaṇa, he places a termite-mound instead.
Then, having touched water, he raises the sacrificial post according to the procedure for the post.

Having erected the sacrificial post provided with a *svaḥ*-shaft, he then drives up these animals: a smoke-colored one for the Aśvins, a ram for Sarasvatī, a bull for Indra, and a fourth animal for Bṛhaspati, if he has been a Soma-offender (*somātipavita*).

Having performed the ritual with their omenta in the established manner, the Adhvaryu takes the portions for the Aśvins and Sarasvatī, and the Pratiprasthātṛ takes the portions for Indra; then, rising up while holding the two cups, he says: "Recite the invitatory verses for the Aśvins, for Sarasvatī, and for Indra Sutraman, for the *surā* Soma!"

He recites this verse: "O Aśvins, [you two] drank the *surā*... Having stepped forward and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "Prompt the Hotṛ to recite the offering prayer (*praṣya*) for the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra the Good Protector (*Sutrāman*), for the *surā* Soma that has been set forth.
The Maitrāvaruṇa says: "Let the Hotṛ worship the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra the Good Protector.

He offers the sacrifice with the words: "Like parents [protecting] a son, O Aśvins, come hither! At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering with the verse: "O Agni, the oblation is placed in your mouth."

When the second *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered—with the verse, "In whom the horses, the bulls, the oxen..."—having offered the libation, he pours the residue of the *āśvina* cup into the *sārasvata* cup, and the residue of the *sārasvata* cup into the *aindra* cup. A Brāhmaṇa shall consume that; with the two verses, "For yours, O gods, is the ordained place here... and "Different indeed are you two...," if he does not find a Brāhmaṇa, he pours it into an anthill mound with this same mantra. Then, having filled these vessels with bark-shavings, he hides a hawk's feather in one made of *parṇa*-wood.

Having raised those two Viśākhas with their tips pointing southward, he pushes forward the *vam̐śa* with the formula "vam̐ śam"; he hangs the sling upon the *vam̐śa*, the hundred-holed sieve (*śatātṛṇṇā*) upon the sling, the horse-tail brush (*vāla*) upon the hundred-holed sieve, and the gold weighing a hundred *mānas* upon the horse-tail brush.
Then, taking this *surā* together with its dregs, he pours it into the hundred-holed sieve with the formula: "O Fathers, whose faces are Soma, be satisfied!"

They stand over [the vessel] with the verse, "It leaks through a hundred holes," and with this eight-verse hymn beginning, "Pavamāna, [thou art] the world of light. Now, if one has exceeded the Soma [limit], they stand over [him] with the invitatory and offering verses for the ancestors: "May the lower ones rise up, and the higher ones; I have found the well-finding ancestors; let there be homage today to the ancestors"—thus the Adhvaryu, the Hotṛ, and the Brahman stand over him.

"Wherever he holds the Śatātṛṇṇā, there he deposits it for the sake of stability," so says the Brāhmaṇa; having thus deposited it, he places it to the south. Then he sets these vessels on a mound of old ashes, saying:

"To the fathers who receive the *svadhā*, *svadhā*! Homage! To the grandfathers who receive the *svadhā*, *svadhā*! Homage! To the great-grandfathers who receive the *svadhā*, *svadhā*! Homage! At this point, he gives a pregnant mare as a gift. Then, having touched water, he asks for the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) dedicated to Bṛhaspati.

He proceeds with [the offerings] beginning with the *devatā-praiṣas* and ending with the *iḍā*; then he proceeds with the animal sacrifices beginning with the *manotā* and ending with the *iḍā*; then he asks for these sacrificial cakes: "An eleven-potherd cake for Indra, a twelve-potherd cake for Savitṛ, and a ten-potherd cake for Varuṇa."

Having performed the rites with those [offerings] beginning with the deities and ending with the *iḍā*, and having performed the after-offerings (*anūyāja*), he turns to the right, hastens westward, and performs the offerings for the wives (*patnīsaṃyāja*). Having gone eastward and replenished the *dhruvā* ladle, he offers the three *samiṣṭayajus* oblations pertaining to the animal sacrifice with the formulas: "O Sacrifice, go to the Sacrifice; this is thy sacrifice, O Lord of Sacrifice; O gods who know the way. At this point, they set down this *avabhṛtha* (purificatory bath) vessel. Whatever has been smeared with *surā* liquor, along with the heart-spikes (*hṛdayaśūla*), they take all this and go out toward the north between the *cātvāla* pit and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*).
I have heard of two paths for the fathers, for the gods, and for mortals; by these two, this entire world comes together between the eastern and the western signs.

Having performed the rite with the well-known "Heart-piercing" formulas, he then places these vessels turned away from him on the edge of the water: "O divine Varuṇa, that bond of thine which is established in the Brahmin and has the Gāyatrī metre—by this [wood] I release it for thee. [He places] the one made of *parṇa* wood. "O divine Varuṇa, that bond of thine which is established in the Kṣatriya and has the Triṣṭubh metre—by this [wood] I release it for thee. [He places] the one made of *nyagrodha* wood. "O divine Varuṇa, that bond of thine which is established among the common people and has the Jagatī metre—" [He places] the one made of *aśvattha* wood.

"By this, I expiate that [noose] of yours"—with these words he offers the *āśvattha* (fig-wood) chip; "O God Varuṇa, that noose of yours which is of the *anuṣṭubh* metre and rests upon the cattle—by this, I expiate that [noose] of yours"—with these words he offers the *śatātṛṇṇā* (the hundred-holed stone). He offers the *sata* and the *vāla* silently.

The *avabhṛtha* (concluding purificatory bath) proceeds in the established manner, except that he does not recite the *Sāman* nor the verse, "O divine Waters, this is your embryo. Then they proceed without looking back, for the sake of escaping from Varuṇa.

While on the journey, he prepares fuel sticks, saying, "Thou art fuel; may we prosper through thee," and having arrived, he places them on the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "Thou art a fuel stick; thou art brilliance; bestow brilliance upon me. Then they stand in worship before the Āhavanīya, saying, "I have followed the waters; we have united with their essence. O Agni, rich in milk, I have come; unite me with splendor. Then he performs the Kusīda sacrifice with an offering of groats. Having worshipped the deities, he stands in worship before the sacrificial post. Thus the Sautrāmaṇī is concluded.

Having studied the Veda and being about to perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*), he should prepare these materials: a grass mat (*erakā*) and a pillow (*upabarhaṇa*), a barber, a razor, pieces of wood for a seat (*upastaraṇa*), a brush (*vṛkalā*), a tooth-stick, warm water and cold water, powder of all fragrant substances, collyrium, a garland, a mirror, an unwashed garment, an upper robe, another inner garment, a jujube-seed amulet (*bādara-maṇi*) with a gold setting, a cord, two ear-rings (*pravarta*), a staff, sandals, an umbrella, and the skin of a bull entirely red;
these are his prepared requisites.

Regarding the investigation of bathing: "One should bathe under Rohiṇī"—this is one view. This constellation belongs to Prajāpati; thus, his bath is performed under a constellation belonging to Prajāpati. Furthermore, thinking "May I ascend all ascents," one should bathe under Tiṣya—this is another view. This constellation belongs to Bṛhaspati; thus, his bath is performed under a constellation belonging to Bṛhaspati. Furthermore, thinking "May I be impelled by Bṛhaspati," one should bathe under the two Uttarā-Phalgunīs—this is another view. This constellation is auspicious; thus, his bath is performed under an auspicious constellation.

"Furthermore, one should bathe when the moon is in Hasta, thinking, 'May I be fortunate'—this is one view; for this lunar mansion belongs to Savitṛ, so he has bathed under the very asterism of Savitṛ. Furthermore, one should bathe when the moon is in Citrā, thinking, 'May I be impelled by Savitṛ'—this is another view."
This lunar mansion belongs to Indra; therefore, he bathes under this very mansion of Indra. Furthermore, thinking "May I be distinguished," he should bathe under the Viśākhās—this is one view.

This lunar mansion belongs to Indra and Agni; therefore, he bathes under this very mansion of Indra and Agni. Furthermore, thinking "May I be distinguished by offspring and cattle," he enters the cow-pen before sunrise during one of these [lunar mansions] while the moon is waxing.
On this day the sun shall not scorch him; for on that day he indeed shines with the splendor and glory of those who have bathed. They enclose a pen with a skin whose hair is turned inward.
Having kindled the fire in the middle of the eastern half of the pen and strewn grass around it, they bring all these ritual materials at once.

From the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "Whatever [is done] together with all men," a Brāhmaṇa sits to the south, and to the north he places a vessel of water and a fuel-stick of *palāśa* wood. To the west of the fire, having spread out *eraka* grass with its tips directed toward the north and covered with a fine cloth, he sits upon it facing east. To the north sits the barber; to the north is a cushion. One should give alms until midday. He may also cook a cow here if he possesses one that is barren. At this point, having anointed this *palāśa* fuel-stick with clarified butter, he places it on the fire at midday.

"Let us fashion this hymn for the worthy Jātavedas with our inspired thought, as one fashions a chariot; for his providence toward us is auspicious. O Agni, may we never suffer harm in your friendship—svāhā! Then, on the *airaka* grass, he lies down facing northward and consecrates the rising [sun] with the mantra: "The triple life-span of Jamadagni, the triple life-span of Kaśyapa, the triple life-span of Agastya, the triple life-span of the Ṛṣis, the triple life-span which belongs to the gods—may that triple life-span be mine. And he says: "Be auspicious to me when you touch me."

He consecrates the razor with the mantra: "Thou art named Razor; the axe is thy father; homage be to thee; do not harm me. He follows the one being shaved with the mantra: "When thou shavest with the razor, O shaver, thou shavest the hair and beard; make my face bright; do not rob me of my life. He shaves the beard first, then the armpits, then the hair, and then the other limbs down to the feet; for it is from this [shaving] that they depart in old age before their full span of life, yet those who, knowing this, have their body hair shaved, become eaters of food before their full span of life.

If he is about to have his body hair shaved, having had his hair and beard shaven and his body hair gathered together, he should have his nails clipped. Then, collecting these [clippings], while handing them to a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*), he says: "Having taken these, deposit them on a clump of *darbha* grass or at the root of an *udumbara* tree. He deposits them there. Sitting behind the fire facing east, he loosens his girdle, saying: "I loosen this bond of Varuṇa."
To whoever there is the son of that patron, or a pupil, he says while giving it to him: "Having taken this away, deposit it at the foot of a *nyagrodha* tree or at the root of an *udumbara* tree.
He then deposits it there, saying: "Here I bury the sorrow and the evil of such-and-such a person, the descendant of such-and-such, for the sake of his future enemies."

Having run with *vṛkala* plants, he cleanses his teeth for the sake of eating food, [reciting]: "Drive away, O Bhaga; this king has arrived. May he flow forth upon my face for splendor and for fortune. He pours together both kinds of water—hot and cold—for the sake of distinguishing between the divine and the human. Having taken some of that water with his joined palms, he sprinkles him with the three verses beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss," and with the three verses beginning with "The golden-colored, pure, and purifying ones."
"Man is indeed composed of six parts"—from this *brāhmaṇa* passage [it follows that]. Then, having mixed together all fragrant powders, he sprinkles them three times [with water], saying:

"Homage to Śāka and Jañjabha; homage to those deities who are the seizers. He then anoints himself, saying: "Whatever fragrance is among the Apsarases, whatever glory is among the Gandharvas, whatever divine and human fragrance there is—may it enter into me here! Then he puts on a new garment, saying: "May my own body enter me; may my auspicious body enter me. In the same way he puts on the upper garment, and in the same way from this point onward.

Then, having strung this jujube bead (*bādara-maṇi*) set in gold upon a thread, having placed it in a ladle, and having wound the thread around the handle of the ladle, he offers [the oblation] with the mantra: "O herb, thou art the protecting, the conquering, the powerful one. May she make me possessed of the luster of Soma, possessed of the luster of the Sun, endowed with the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*), and a consumer of food; Svāhā! Then he causes it to float away in a vessel of water with the verse: "And through thee may we overcome all [enemies], like streams of water."

Saying, "May we overcome our enemies," and "Thou art the loosener," he passes [the cord] across [the head of the horse]. For they fasten what is to be slain facing backward for the sake of turning away; this is according to the Brāhmaṇa. Then, having strung these two ear-rings (*pravartau*) on a thread, placed them in a ladle (*darvī*), and wound the thread around the handle of the ladle, he offers [an oblation], saying: "Granting long life, bestowing splendor, providing excellent strength, yielding abundance of wealth, and breaking forth—may this gold enter this [horse] for splendor and victory, bringing this prosperity, Svāhā!"

He offers the second oblation with: "Like a dog, I have seized the name of gold as if it were my father's; may that make me resplendent with Soma, resplendent with Sūrya; may it make me one possessed of the splendor of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcas) and an eater of food, Svāhā! He offers the third oblation with: "O powerful one, conqueror of armies, subduer of assemblies, winner of wealth—whatever prosperities and successes are gathered within gold, [grant them], Svāhā! He offers the fourth oblation with: "The sovereign power (virāj) and the self-ruling power (svarāj), the blessing that is in our house, and the fortune (lakṣmī) that is at the head of the kingdom—with that we unite thee, Svāhā!"

He offers the fifth oblation with the verse: "Bestow glory upon the Brāhmaṇas; bestow glory upon the Kṣatriyas; bestow glory upon the Vaiśyas and the Śūdras. I am the glory, and you are the glory—Svāhā! Then he causes the two of them to float together in a vessel of water with the verse: "And through you, may we overcome all [enemies]. Taking one of the two, he ties it to the right ear with these five verses beginning: "Life-giving, glorious... Then he turns him around with the formula: "With the seasons, with the seasonal periods, with the nourishment of the year, I follow along with those. In the same way, he ties the other turban on the left side. Then he puts on a garland.

O auspicious one, ascend my head, adorning my face; adorn my face indeed, and may you grant me good fortune. You whom Jamadagni took away for faith, for desire, and for another—her, this very one, I now fasten upon myself for splendor and for good fortune.

When he applies collyrium made from the *traikakuda* plant—collyrium produced upon the Himavat mountains—with the formula, "With that I anoint you both; may there be mountain-like luster in me," he gazes into a mirror with the formula, "That mind of mine which has gone away, as I gaze into the mirror—this I behold within myself; may it be conducive to long life and luster for me. Then he puts on his two sandals with the formula, "Thou art the sky" on the right foot, and "Thou art the earth" on the left. Then he takes up his staff with the formula, "Friend, protect me," and he takes up his umbrella with the formula, "Thou art divine, a fair-winged bird; protect me from the intermediate space."

He remains right there until the rising of the stars; then, when the stars have risen, he goes outside and worships the quarters with the mantra: "O six divine, wide-spreading ones, make room for us! O all you gods, display your heroism here!
With the words, "May we not be abandoned by our offspring nor by our bodies," he worships the stars;
and with the words, "O King Soma, may we not be delivered over to our enemy," he worships the moon.
Having performed the ritual attendance, he goes wherever he desires; this is the *samāvartana*.
Now, as for the other [rites]:

having bathed silently at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) and emerged from the water, if he obtains a chariot, he touches the right wheel with the words, "Thou art the *Rathantara*"; the left with, "Thou art the *Bṛhat*"; and the middle one with, "Thou art the *Vāmadevya*."

Then he consecrates the starting chariot with the mantra: "O Aśvins, may this chariot of yours not suffer harm in either sorrow or joy. Now, if he intends to prepare a couch for rest, he touches water and then touches this [earth] with the formula: "Here is support; here is separation; here is delight; here is enjoyment; may it find rest here. Then the teacher causes a grass mat (kūrca) to be brought for him; having turned it around clockwise and returned toward the north, he sits down. He pushes it from the east toward himself with the formula: "Thou art the kingdom-sustaining seat of the teacher; may I not abandon thee. Then he causes water to be brought for him.

With that [water], he washes his feet; he wipes the hands of the one who washed them, touching water while reciting: "In me be splendor, in me fortune, in me radiance, in me glory. Then, touching himself on the chest while reciting, "In me be sensory power and vigor," he causes another [gift] to be brought to him. He accepts it, saying: "It has come to me with luster and glory; unite me with milk and brilliance! Make me dear to the people, a lord of cattle"—thus says a Brāhmaṇa; "Make me dear to cattle, a lord of the people"—thus says a Rājanya.

Having touched that [water] with the words "May he sprinkle eastward," he consecrates the announced *madhuparka* with the mantra: "May he protect me; may he guard me; may he be pleased with me. He receives it with both hands, [reciting]:
"He has come to me with splendor and glory; unite me with milk and brilliance! Make me dear to all creatures, the lord of cattle!"—thus says the Brāhmaṇa.
"Making the beloved lord of cattle and of subjects"—this is for a Kṣatriya.

If anything has happened to him, he takes it with his thumb and his ring finger and throws it out in this direction (the south), saying: "I cut away what has struck thee; with that terrible body of thine, enter him who hates us and whom we hate. Then, having touched water and gathered [the remainder], he eats it three times, saying: "O Breath, I bring this offering to thee; make me the best and the lord. "Thou art Soma; make me a drinker of Soma," he says a second time.

Saying, "Make me an eater of food, [you who are] food," he drinks the third portion three times and gives the remainder to one whom he desires to be superior to himself; he should give the rest to that person. He consecrates the cow brought for the initiation with the mantra, "Strike away my evil, [and that of] the initiator";
they either perform this rite with her or release her.

If he intends to perform the sacrifice, he says, "Do it! But if he intends to release her, he consecrates her with the mantra: "The cow, who is to become a milch-cow, is the mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, and the navel of immortality. I declare this to the discerning people: do not slay the cow, the sinless Aditi! Let her drink water, let her eat grass; release her!
Then he causes rice-milk (odana) to be brought for him, which he eats with the words:
"May the Brahman eat you; may the Brahman eat you."
The *arghya* consists of those four: curds, honey, clarified butter, and water;
some say it consists of five, namely curds, milk, honey, clarified butter, and water.
A Brāhmaṇa, who was the intended recipient of the Soma, encountered [the king] on the road—he was fair-complexioned, with reddish-brown eyes, and with his head split open and oozing.
He said to him, "How shall I know you, O Venerable One?
He replied to him, "I am King Soma.

[The other said,] "A certain Adhvaryu priest, ignorant of the *naiṣṭyayana* rites, squeezed me; because that Adhvaryu, ignorant of the *naiṣṭyayana* rites, squeezed me, I have become leaky here and there. That Brahmin over there knows the *naiṣṭyayana* rites."
"I shall go to him;
he will cause these colors to grow for me.

When they descend for the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), they offer oblations over the *niṣṭyā* and the *ṛjīṣa* with a branch of *udumbara* or a branch of *palāśa*, or with a *sruva* ladle not smeared with clarified butter, using curds, milk, or honey-mixed [liquids].

With the section beginning "O King Soma, that which they have cut from you with the pressing-stones," and with the verse "Whatever of this [sacrifice] is deficient for us," and with fourteen [verses], they offer oblations upon the *ṛjīṣa*.

He should say to those who would perform the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*): "Those who, having pierced the skin of the King, having committed a cruel act here with the pressing-stones, and without having appeased it with the *naiṣṭyayana* rites, go away—even though their offense has been thus committed."
Those who, having set aside the Soma, sit together with water as their Soma, come back to us saying "We have finished"; he destroys them in the world beyond.
They pierce with swords and spears in the abode of Yama that man who, without having pacified his senses through the final ascetic practices, ascends to the celestial realm.
Becoming the wind, he blows through the third heaven, the highest firmament; having stilled [the senses] by means of the final rites, he then ascends to the celestial realm.
Of the Adhvaryu, the Sacrificer, the Pratiprasthātṛ, the Agnīdh, the Brahman, the Hotṛ, and the Udgātṛ—he seizes their world; and they did not offer the oblation—fourteen [in total].
Those who offer these fourteen spoonfuls of curds as oblations—the King does not take away their world, nor their progeny, nor their strength.
"Strengthening the King with the pressing-stones, the fierce officiating priests, pacifying him with milk, offer indeed—thus [it is] fourteen. Now, it is said:
"The exponents of sacred knowledge say, 'He indeed should sacrifice the New and Full Moon offerings who sacrifices them as accompanied by Indra.'"
The Vaimṛdha cake is to be offered subsequently at the full moon;
by that, the full moon sacrifice becomes possessed of Indra. One should offer curds for Indra on the new moon day; by that, the new moon sacrifice becomes possessed of Indra.

"By what means, indeed, do both Indra and Agni become well-disposed toward one who does not know? "One should say: 'By means of a cake for Indra and Agni. Now, it is also said: "Whatever the gods did at the sacrifice, the Asuras did likewise.
Those gods saw this oblation: a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Viṣṇu, a pap for Sarasvatī, and a pap for Sarasvant."
Having completed the Full Moon sacrifice, they offered this subsequent oblation;
then the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. He who has a rival should, having completed the Full Moon sacrifice, offer this subsequent *iṣṭi*.

By means of the Full Moon sacrifice itself, he hurls the thunderbolt at his rival; and by means of the offering to Agni and Viṣṇu, he seizes both the deities and the sacrifice of his rival—so says the Brāhmaṇa. This is the application for one who has a rival according to his desire: [he offers] pairs of animals to Sarasvatī and Sarasvant.
"Whatever he possesses, all that he seizes," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is further said:
"One who has enemies should sacrifice only at the full moon, not at the new moon."

One who has enemies should sacrifice only at each full moon, not at the new moon; for by slaying the enemy at the full moon, he does not allow him to swell—so says the Brāhmaṇa. This [offering] is either for the purpose of spreading [the grass] or for the purpose of excluding the enemy.

Now it is said: "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Sākaṃprasthāyīya. One who is about to perform this sacrifice should prepare a large vessel made of Udumbara wood and an abundant quantity of clarified butter. Then, having performed the introductory formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra, and the Sāṃnāyya offering to Indra.

Having performed the well-known *āgneya* oblation, he then takes portions from the other two sacrificial offerings into a large *audumbara* vessel and says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra," or "for Mahendra," if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra. [The Adhvaryu] thinks, "It is to be offered with a full [ladle]. Having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Recite the offering verse for Indra," or "for Mahendra," if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra.
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers the oblation together with the vessel itself.
"Indra indeed satisfies him with offspring and cattle; he satisfies him," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is further said:
"He offers with a wooden vessel."

"For one does not consume an offering made of clay; it becomes *udumbara* wood, for the *udumbara* is strength (*ūrj*), and cattle are strength; by means of strength he wins strength and cattle for him"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. This [wood] is either obtainable or unobtainable, or else it is obtained through despair. Now it is said: "One who has not attained prosperity should not sacrifice to Mahendra. There are indeed three who have attained prosperity: the learned scholar (*śuśruvān*), the village headman (*grāmaṇī*), and the noble warrior (*rājanya*); for them, Mahendra is the deity."

If anyone other than these [priests] should desire to sacrifice to Mahendra, he, having sacrificed to Indra for a year, offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati; that well-known sacrifice is completed. Then, when the new moon arrives, he sacrifices to Mahendra on that day;
from then on, he indeed becomes a sacrificer to Mahendra. Now, it is also said:
"One should sacrifice to Indra for a year,
for one does not transcend the vow for a year; thus the deity being worshipped kindles him with prosperity, and he becomes more wealthy," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now it is indeed said: "After a year has passed, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati;
thus Agni Vratapati causes him, who has slain the enemy Vṛtra for a year, to regain his vow."
"Thereafter he should sacrifice according to his desire," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now it is indeed said:
"One who has not sacrificed with Soma should not offer the *saṃnayya* (curdled milk offering); for the milk of one who has not sacrificed with Soma has not yet arrived."
If one who has not performed the Soma sacrifice should perform the *sāṃnāyya* offering, that is merely a theft; he commits a falsehood, and moreover, it is poured away for another.
Only one who has performed the Soma sacrifice should perform the *sāṃnāyya*.
Soma is indeed milk, and the *sāṃnāyya* is milk.
"By means of milk itself, he places milk within himself," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is indeed said:
"He deprives of offspring and cattle that man for whom, after the sacrificial oblation has been set out, the moon rises in the east; he causes his rival to prosper."

One should divide the rice grains into three parts: those that are of medium size, from them one should prepare a cake on eight potsherds (*puroḍāśa*) for Agni Dātṛ; those that are the largest, from them a pap (*caru*) of boiled milk for Indra Pradātṛ;
and those that are the smallest, from them a pap of boiled milk for Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa. For this sacrifice, these are the verses:

"O Agni, give wealth to the donor," "Give us, O Agni, a generous giver," "We invoke the generous giver, the wielder of the thunderbolt," "That [gift] of thine today," and "What, O Viṣṇu, is to be blamed in thee? By the first of these two verses, he sacrifices with the intention of avoiding failure; by the latter, with the intention of non-failure.

One should not sacrifice with two [offerings]. If one were to sacrifice immediately with the first, he would make the second redundant; if he were to sacrifice immediately with the second, he would make the first redundant. The sacrifice is not successful, nor is the rite; consequently, a son is born who is bashful and lacking in confidence. One should sacrifice with only one; a confident son is born to him. Nevertheless, disregarding that, one should indeed sacrifice with two.
With the first [verse] he obtains the very mouth of the sacrifice when he sacrifices; with the second,
he secures the deities by the first and Indra’s power by the second.
"By the first [offering] he conquers the world of the gods, and by the second the world of men;

he attains many sacrificial rites," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now it is further said: "This sacrifice is indeed named Sumanā; for him who has sacrificed and the moon rises in the west, there is prosperity in this very world," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Dākṣāyaṇayajña;

he should offer the *saṃnāya* at the full moon and sacrifice with the *āmikṣā* for Mitra and Varuṇa at the new moon. One who is about to perform this sacrifice prepares an unwashed garment. Then, on the day of preparation (*upavasatha*) for the full moon, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati.

That well-known sacrifice is completed. Then, on this day, when the calves have been driven away for Indra, he causes the milk for Indra to be milked and observes the fast according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya*, either with the prescribed formulas or silently. Then in the morning, he offers a cake on eight potsherds for Agni and the *sāṃnāyya* for Indra; thus that sacrifice of two oblations is concluded. At this point, having invited one another, they consume this *sāṃnāyya* for Indra. Then, having put on a new garment, he observes the vow during the waning fortnight.

His vow is this: he speaks no untruth, he does not eat meat, he does not approach a woman, and they do not wash his garment with lye. Then, on the day of the new moon, on its fast-day (upavasatha), he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati; that sacrifice concludes in the well-known manner. Now, on this day, the calves are driven away for Mitra and Varuṇa; having caused the milk for Mitra and Varuṇa to be milked, he observes the fast according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya* offering, either silently or [with the prescribed formulas]. Then, in the morning, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and a clotted curd (*āmikṣā*) to Mitra and Varuṇa.
That sacrifice of two oblations is completed;

at the time for the *vājina*, he proceeds with the *vājina* offering, lays aside the garment, and releases his vow. Having released his vow, he remains during this first fortnight. Then he comes to the full moon day; the Lord of Vows (*vratapati*) is set aside, and he proceeds by means of that which follows the Lord of Vows.
This very [period] lasting for a year is called the *soma-saṃsthā*, and then the *iḍā-dadha*; the procedure for the garment and for the *vratapati* is the same.

In the same manner, having caused the milk for Indra to be milked according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya*—either with the prescribed ritual formula or silently—he then offers in the morning a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Soma, and the *sāṃnāyya* for Indra; thus this sacrifice consisting of three oblations is completed. At this point, having invited one another, they consume this *sāṃnāyya* for Indra.
Then, having put on a new garment, he observes the vow during the waning fortnight until the new moon arrives.
On the day of preparation (*upavasatha*) for that [new moon], he performs the sacrifice.

In the same manner, having caused the milk for Mitra-Varuṇa to be milked according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya*—either with the prescribed ritual formula or silently—he then, on the following morning, offers a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, and curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) for Mitra-Varuṇa; this sacrifice consisting of three oblations is completed.

At the time of the whey (*vājina*), he proceeds with the whey, lays aside the garment, and releases his vow. Having released his vow, he remains thus during this first fortnight. Then, at the full moon, he arrives; the Lord of Vows (*vratapati*) departs.
That which is above the Vratapati [cup], by that one proceeds;
this is the Soma-station extending for a year.
Now, the sacrifice of one who has rivals consists of four wheels.

The procedure for the garment and for the Vratapati [offering] is the same; likewise, having caused the milk for Indra to be milked according to the ritual rule for the *sāṃnāyya*—either with the prescribed formula or silently—he offers in the morning an oblation on eight potsherds for Agni, an *upāṃśuyāja* for Sarasvat, and a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Soma, as well as the *sāṃnāyya* for Indra. This sacrifice consisting of four offerings is thus completed. At this point, they partake of this *sāṃnāyya* for Indra after having invited one another. Then, having put on the unwashed garment, he observes the vow during the dark fortnight until the new moon arrives.
He does not sacrifice on the day of preparation (*upavasatha*).

In the same manner, having caused the milk for Mitra and Varuṇa to be milked—either according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya* or silently—he then, in the morning, offers a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a *vaiśvadeva* oblation for Sarasvatī, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, and curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) for Mitra and Varuṇa; thus this sacrifice of four offerings is completed.
At the time of the whey (*vājina*), he proceeds with the whey.

He puts on the garment and releases the vow; having released the vow, he remains during this first fortnight. Then he comes to the full moon day; the Lord of the Vow (Vratapati) rises up. He proceeds by means of that which is above the Lord of the Vow.
This is the Soma-station that descends into the year.
This is the four-wheeled sacrifice for one who has enemies.
Just as here on earth this [chariot] comes along, striking down its enemies, so indeed does he, having sacrificed with this sacrificial rite, come along, striking down evil and his rival.

This is the sacrifice of Vasiṣṭha, the sacrifice of Keśin, the sacrifice of Sārvaseni. For when Vasiṣṭha performed sorcery against the Saudāsas, he struck them down in this very manner; and when Keśin performed sorcery against Khāṇḍika, he struck him down in this very manner.

Sārvaseni, indeed, once performed an incantation against his rivals; in that same manner he now performs it against them. He who is about to sacrifice with the Cāturmāsya Soma offerings prepares two sets of materials: those for the Agniṣṭoma and those for the Vaiśvadeva.
Before the full moon of Phālguna or Caitra, having sacrificed with the *āmāvāsya* oblation, he undergoes initiation;
his period of initiation is unlimited, and there are three *upasads*.
He purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks, "My Soma-pressing will coincide with the full-moon day, which is the day of sacrifice."
It happens for him accordingly:
having emerged from the fast-day with the well-known ritual procedure, on this day the calves are driven away for the Viśvedevas;

he causes the milk for the Vaiśvadeva to be milked according to the procedure for the Sāṃnāyya, either silently or [with the prescribed formulas]. Then, having carried around the Vasatīvarī waters, they wait in attendance after setting aside the milks. Then, in the morning, there is the threefold sacrificial grass.
He strews [the sacrificial grass] in that same single layer; then he dedicates the animal victim for Agni.
For that [victim], one dedicated to the Viśvedevas is to be immolated as a secondary victim.
The oblations for the Viśvedevas follow after the morning *savana* offerings of that [victim].
The *savanīya* offerings are accompanied by *praiṣa*-calls; for the other oblations, one recites the invitatory verses and says "recite the offering verse" (*anubrūhi yaja*).
The *trivṛt-agniṣṭoma* concludes in the regular manner;
before the *dhānāsoma* offerings, he proceeds with the *vājina*.
The ritual procedure up to the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) is the same;

the avabhṛtha is performed in the established manner. Having sacrificed the Udayanīya offering, he dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa; for that [cow], one to be offered to Heaven and Earth is to be seized as an additional victim.
Having performed the ritual with the omenta of those two in the well-known manner, he offers the two animal-cake oblations;
it concludes just as a double-animal sacrifice does. Then, having sacrificed with the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha offerings—this has already been stated—thereafter, after four months have passed...
One who is about to sacrifice with the Varuṇapraghāsa and the two Soma offerings undergoes initiation;
for that [sacrifice], the initiation period is unlimited and there are twelve Upasad days.
He purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks, "On the sacrificial day of the full moon, my second day will be accomplished";
for him it is accomplished accordingly.
He proceeds from the Upavasatha with the well-known ritual; then, on this day, the calves are driven away from their mothers for the Maruts.

He causes the milk for the Maruts to be milked according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya*, or silently; then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and having set aside the milks, they fast. Then in the morning, he dedicates the animal victim to Agni; for that, there is one to be immolated for the Maruts. The seven *Varuṇapraghāsa* offerings follow the morning pressing sacrifices.
When he distributes the fires for the Dhiṣṇiya hearths at the morning pressing, he makes the Mārjālīya fire perpetual.

When the oblations have been set down, having carried fire around the Karambha vessels at the Gārhapatya, he proceeds with them at the Mārjālīya. For the Savanīya offerings, there are calls such as "Recite! and "Sacrifice!"; for the other oblations, [the calls are] "Recite! and "Sacrifice! respectively.
In the straightforward manner, the Ukthya sacrifice concludes with fifteen [stotras]; thus he ensures the continuity of the Ahīna rite.
Now, on this day, the calves are driven away for Varuṇa;

he causes the milk for Varuṇa to be milked according to the procedure for the Sāṃnāyya, either silently or according to the established rule. Then, having carried around the Vasatīvarī waters and having set aside the various portions of milk, they remain in attendance. Then, in the morning, he dedicates the animal victim to Agni.
For this sacrifice, an animal dedicated to Varuṇa is to be immolated;
following the morning pressing-offerings (prātaḥsavanīya) are the offerings to Varuṇa and to Ka.

The offering-formulas (praiṣas) for the pressing-offerings include the calls "Recite! and "Sacrifice! for the other two oblations. In the straightforward manner, the Ukthya sacrifice concludes with seventeen verses.
Before the *dhānāsoma* offerings, he proceeds with the two *vājina* oblations;
the ritual procedure is the same up to the *avabhṛtha*. Then, at this *avabhṛtha*, they take the scrapings of the *vāruṇī* and the husks.
The scrapings of the *vāruṇa* [cake] serve as the portion to be cut from the *vāruṇī āmikṣā*; together with the *ṛjīṣa*, they scatter the husks.
The *avabhṛtha* bath is well known. Having performed the *udayanīyā* sacrifice, he dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa;
for that cow, a ewe is to be seized as a supplementary victim. Having proceeded with the two omenta in the established manner, he offers the two animal-cake oblations.
The animal sacrifice for a pair of animals is concluded just as [the standard] animal sacrifice is; then it has been said, "having sacrificed with the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha offerings," and now,
after four months, one is about to perform the Soma sacrifices known as the Sākamedhas.
He undergoes initiation;
his initiation is of unlimited duration, with twelve *upasads*.
He purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks: "On the full-moon day, on my sacrificial day, the third day will be completed."
For him, it is accomplished in this manner:

having emerged from the Upavasatha with the well-known ritual procedure, and having carried around the Vasatīvarī waters and set aside the milks, they remain in attendance; then, in the morning, he dedicates the animal victim to Agni, for which the Anīkavant is to be immolated.
The *ānīkavata* [offering] follows the morning *savanīya* offerings;
the *savanīya* offerings for the *ānīkavata* are accompanied by *praiṣa* calls, with the formulas "Recite! and "Sacrifice! The *sāṃtapana* [offering] follows the midday *savanīya* offerings.

The *savanīya* offerings are accompanied by *praiṣa* calls; [the Adhvaryu] says, "Recite the invitatory verse," and "Sacrifice! The *ukthya* sacrifice of the *Sāṃtapana* rite concludes with the twenty-first [stotra]. He performs the *ahīna-saṃsati* rite; then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters, they set aside the milks and remain in fast. Then, in the evening, he proceeds with the *Gṛhamedhīya* offering; then, in the latter part of the night, he proceeds with the *pūrṇadarvya* offering; then, in the morning, he dedicates the animal victim for Agni.
For that [victim], one belonging to Krīḍin is to be immolated as an additional offering (*upālambhya*). The *krauḍina* offering follows the morning *savanīya* offerings.

The *savanīya* offerings are accompanied by the *praiṣa* calls: "Recite! and "Sacrifice! The *ukthya* sacrifice of Kraiḍina, consisting of twenty-seven verses, concludes in a straight manner; it effects the continuity of the *ahīna* rite. Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and set aside the milks, they fast. Then, in the morning, he dedicates the animal victim for Agni; for that, a hornless goat dedicated to Prajāpati is to be immolated.
For that [victim], the *mahāhavīṃṣi* oblations follow the morning *savana* offerings.

The *savanīya* offerings are accompanied by *praiṣa*-calls, with the instructions "recite" (*anubrūhi*) and "sacrifice" (*yajeti*) for the other oblations; the oblations of the *mahāpitṛyajña* follow the *tṛtīyasavanīya* offerings.
When he distributes the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths at the third pressing, he makes the *mārjālīya* hearth perpetual.
Once the oblations have been set down, having cooked the oblations of the *mahāpitṛyajña* on the *gārhapatya*, he proceeds with them at the *mārjālīya*.
The *savanīya* offerings are accompanied by *praiṣa* calls; for the other oblations, one says "recite" and "sacrifice" directly.
The *ukthya* sacrifice consisting of thirty-three [verses] concludes;
prior to the *dhānāsoma* offerings, he performs the *traiyambaka* rites.
The ritual procedure up to the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) is the same;
the avabhṛtha is performed in the established manner. Having sacrificed with the Udayanīya offering, he dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa;
for that [cow], one to be offered to Viśvakarman is to be seized as an additional victim.
Having performed the rite with the omenta of those two in the established manner, he offers the two animal-cake oblations (paśupuroḍāśa);
he follows them [with the recitation], and for the Aditya [oblation], the calls are "Recite the invitatory verse for the Aditya cake" and "Sacrifice! (praiṣavantau).
The animal sacrifice for two animals concludes just as the Paśubandha does; it has been stated that one should perform the Paurṇamāsa and Vaimṛdha sacrifices [at that point].
Now, therefore, after four months, one becomes intent on sacrificing with the Śunāsīrīya Soma.
He undergoes initiation;
his initiatory days are unlimited, and there are three *upasads*.
He purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks, "My Soma-pressing will coincide with a full-moon day suitable for sacrifice."
For him it is accomplished in this manner:

having emerged from the fast-day with the well-known ritual procedure, and having carried around the Vasatīvarī waters, they remain fasting after having set aside the milk. Then, on this night, the calves are driven away for Vāyu;
in the morning, he causes the milk for Vāyu to be milked according to the procedure for the Sāṃnāyya, either silently or [with the prescribed formulas]. Then he dedicates the animal victim to Agni.
For this [sacrifice], a bull dedicated to Indra is to be immolated;
the oblations of Śunāsīra follow the morning *savana* offerings.
For the other oblations, the calls are "Recite for the *savanīya* offerings! and "Sacrifice! respectively.
The Agniṣṭoma sacrifice concludes in a straightforward manner;
the ritual procedure up to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) is standard, and having performed the established avabhṛtha and the Udayanīyā offering, he dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa.
For that [sacrifice], a victim for Sūrya is to be immolated. Having performed the ritual with their two omenta in the established manner, he offers the two animal-cake oblations (*paśupuroḍāśa*).
It concludes just as a double-animal sacrifice (*dvipaśu-paśubandha*) does; then, having sacrificed with the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha offerings—this has already been explained.
Now, therefore, they call this the "Luminous Year" (*jyotirayana*).

One is about to sacrifice with the *vaiśvadeva* *soma* sacrifice; the introductory verses (*pratipad*) are the same, only this much is different: there is a threefold (*trivṛt*) *agniṣṭoma* "light" (*jyotis*) there, but here [it is] the opposite. Then, after four months, one is about to sacrifice with the *varuṇapraghāsa* *soma* sacrifice.
He undergoes initiation;
his initiations are unlimited, and there are six *upasads*.
He purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks, "My Soma-pressing will coincide with the full-moon day, the day fit for sacrifice."
For him it is accomplished in this manner:

having emerged from the Upavasatha with the established ritual procedure, on this day the calves are driven away in two groups; he causes two milks to be milked for the Maruts and for Varuṇa, either according to the procedure for the Sāṃnāyya or silently. Then, having carried around the Vasatīvarī waters and set aside the milks, they remain fasting. Then, in the morning, he dedicates the animal victim to Agni.
For this sacrifice, there are two animals to be immolated, one for Māruta and one for Vāruṇa;
the seven Varuṇapraghāsa oblations follow the morning libations.
At the point where he distributes the Dhiṣṇiya hearths at the morning libation, he makes the Mārjālīya fire-pile perpetual.

When the oblations have been brought near, having performed the *paryagnikaraṇa* rite around the *karambha* vessels at the *gārhapatya* fire, he proceeds with them at the *mārjālīya* fire. For the *savanīya* offerings, the calls are given as "Recite! and "Sacrifice!"; for the other oblations, the *vāruṇī* and *kāya* offerings follow the midday rites.
For the two remaining oblations, the calls are given as "Recite! and "Sacrifice!"; thus the *Jyotiṣṭoma Ukthya* sacrifice is concluded in the regular manner.
The subsequent ritual procedure is the same as that for the Dvirātra sacrifice; then, after four months,
he becomes one who intends to sacrifice with the Sākamedha Soma and undergoes initiation.
His consecrations (*dīkṣā*) are unlimited; there are six preparatory rites (*upasada*).
He purchases the King (Soma) in such a way that he thinks, "My Soma-pressing will coincide with the full-moon day, the day of sacrifice";
for him, it so happens accordingly.

Having emerged from the Upavasatha day by means of the well-known ritual procedure, and having carried around the Vasatīvarī waters and set aside the milks, they remain in retreat. Then, in the morning, he dedicates the animal victim for Agni; for that [day], the Anīkavat, the Kraiḍina, and the hornless goat for Prajāpati are the animals to be immolated. The Anīkavat sacrifice follows the morning libation offerings (prātaḥsavanīya).
The *savanīya* offerings for the *Ānīkavata* [rite] follow the midday [pressing] with the calls "Recite! and "Sacrifice!";
the *savanīya* offerings for the *Sāṃtapana* [rite] follow with the calls "Recite! and "Sacrifice! for the *Sāṃtapana*.
The Great Oblations (mahāhavīṃṣi), beginning with the Gṛhamedhīya, follow the [rites] of the third pressing.
When he distributes the fires upon the Dhiṣṇiya hearths at the third pressing, he makes the Mārjālīya fire perpetual.
Having performed the Great Oblations and having cooked the oblations for the Mahāpitṛyajña on the Gārhapatya fire, he proceeds with them on the Mārjālīya.
The *savanīya* offerings are accompanied by *praiṣa* formulas; for the other oblations, one says "recite" (*anubrūhi*) and "sacrifice" (*yajeti*).
The *jyotir-ukthya* concludes in the regular manner.
The subsequent ritual procedure is the same as that of the three-night sacrifice (*trirātra*).
That indeed is the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice;
now, therefore, they call it the Mahāyajña; some say it is the Jyotir-atirātra; he undergoes initiation.
His initiation lasts for an unlimited number of days, with twelve *upasads*;
he purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks, "My Soma-pressing will coincide with the full-moon day, a day fit for sacrifice," and for him it so happens.

Having approached from the Upavasatha day by the well-known sequence, on this day three calves are driven away for him; he causes the milk to be milked for the Viśve Devas, the Maruts, and Varuṇa—three portions—either according to the procedure for the Sāṃnāyya or silently. Then, having carried around the Vasatīvarī waters and having set aside the milks, they remain fasting. Then, in the morning, he spreads the sacrificial grass (barhis) in a triple-layered manner, but spreads it as a single unit; then he dedicates the animal victim to Agni.

For this sacrifice, there are animals to be immolated: a hornless goat for the Viśvedevas, one for the Maruts, one for Varuṇa, one for Ānīkavant, one for Kraiḍin, one for Prajāpati (a hornless goat), and a bull for Indra.
The Vaiśvadeva oblations follow the morning *savanīya* offerings with their respective *praisha*-calls;
for the other oblations, one says, "Recite the invitatory verse" and "Sacrifice," and all the Varuṇapraghāsa oblations follow the midday *savanīya* offerings.
When he distributes the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths at the midday pressing, he makes the *mārjālīya* hearth perpetual.

When the oblations have been set down, having carried fire around the *karambha* vessels at the *gārhapatya*, he proceeds with them at the *mārjālīya*. The *savanīya* offerings are accompanied by calls (*praiṣa*): "Recite the invitatory verse! and "Offer! For the other oblations, the *mahāhavīṃṣi* beginning with the *ānīkavata* follow the *tṛtīyasavanīya* offerings.
When he distributes the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths at the third pressing, he makes the *mārjālīya* hearth permanent.

Having performed the *mahāhavis* offerings and having cooked the oblations for the *mahāpitṛyajña* on the *gārhapatya*, he proceeds with them at the *mārjālīya*. For the *savanīya* offerings, there are calls for "Recite! and "Sacrifice!"; for the other oblations, [the calls are] as follows.
The Atirātra sacrifice concludes directly with light.
Having performed the Vājina offerings prior to the Dhānāsoma offerings, he performs the Traiyambaka rites.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the Avabhṛtha bath; then, at this Avabhṛtha, they take up the scrapings for Varuṇa and the husks.
For the Vāruṇa [offering], there is a portion of the curd-mixture (āmikṣā) to be cut off; they scatter the husks together with the *ṛjīṣa*.
The purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) is well-known. Having performed the concluding offering (*udayanīyā-iṣṭi*), he dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa.
For that [cow], there are animals to be seized for the sake of Heaven and Earth, for Ka, for Viśvakarman, and for Sūrya.
Having performed the ritual with their omenta as is well known, he offers the animal-cake oblations;
following those are the Śunāsīrīya offerings beginning with that for Āditya.

The animal-cake offerings (paśupuroḍāśas) are accompanied by *praiṣa* calls; for the other oblations, [the procedure] concludes with the calls "Recite! (*anubrūhi*) and "Sacrifice! (*yajeti*). As the five-animal sacrifice (*pañcapaśu*) in the animal-binding rite (*paśubandha*), so it is here. Then, having performed the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha sacrifices, he sits down in the sacrificer’s station and, with a three-striped porcupine quill and a razor of red iron, he trims his hair and shaves his beard—first in front, then on the right, then behind, then on the left, and finally on top. The Cāturmāsya Soma sacrifices are concluded; the Cāturmāsya Soma sacrifices are concluded.
One who is about to perform the Bṛhaspatisava becomes [prepared].

He prepares thirty-four horses as the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), a black antelope skin, two gold and silver plates, a vessel made of *parṇa* wood, and clarified butter for the consecration. Now, indeed, the Brāhmaṇa says: "The Hotṛ priest is one wearing a garland, ruddy, mirmira, and triśukra. He who is bald and has hair all around his head is indeed the one wearing a garland; he who is white, moist-skinned, marked with spots, and yellow-eyed is the mirmira; and he who is learned in the three Vedas when he undergoes initiation is the triśukra. For him who has fasted for one night, they purchase the Soma.
It is performed with three *upasads*;

it is a *trivṛt* *agniṣṭoma* with the *rathantara* as its *sāman*, accompanied by the *pravargya* ceremony, and having a single *stoma* in *gāyatrī* verses; the preparation of the *devasū* oblations is well-known; for this sacrifice, there is an *atigrāhya* cup for Bṛhaspati, and an animal victim for Bṛhaspati is to be immolated.
Up to the time of the consecration, it is the same; at the time of the consecration, he spreads a black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and the hair upward upon the sacrificer’s seat.

Having seated the sacrificer there facing east and having placed gold and silver plates on both sides of him, he pours clarified butter into a vessel made of *parṇa* wood and consecrates him, [reciting]: "Bṛhaspati, being born first from the great light in the highest heaven, seven-mouthed and born with power, with his roar he blew away the darkness with his seven rays."
"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech, I consecrate you with the Bṛhaspatisava.

When he has been wiped clean, they cry out together; this is the same procedure up to the wiping of the face. At his morning pressing, when the Nārāśaṃsa cups have been set down, eleven sacrificial gifts are led forth; at the midday pressing, when the Nārāśaṃsa cups have been set down, eleven; at the third pressing, when the Nārāśaṃsa cups have been set down, twelve including a horse.
"One should give the horse at the midday pressing alone," so said Maudgalya.
Indeed, this is the Naimārjana sacrifice;
just as this river from the mountains sweeps away [impurities], even so does one who has performed this sacrificial rite go forth, sweeping away evil and his rival.
On this very same occasion, during the first fortnight of the month, he should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma consisting of four stomas for the sake of peace before any mishap occurs.
A king who has performed the Rājasūya desires to be consecrated by means of the Bṛhaspatisava, thinking, "May I be consecrated.

Regarding this, they say: "One who has been consecrated by the Rājasūya should not be consecrated by another sacrificial rite, for he would then be unable to descend [from his status]. He should indeed be consecrated; he should be consecrated by both the Brahman and the Kṣatra. Thus he should be consecrated.
He undergoes initiation;

for him there are three initiation days and three *upasads*, identical [in procedure] up to the time of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*). At the time of the consecration, the cups belonging to the midday pressing approach him while wiping [the vessels].
This [section] consists of twenty-four [verses].

A king, intending to sacrifice with the Rājasūya, reflects upon being consecrated among the three castes—the domestic priest (purohita), the charioteer (sthapati), and the herald (sūta)—and thinks, "May I be consecrated.
Thereupon, the domestic priest undergoes initiation.

He has three *dīkṣā*s and three *upasads*, which are the same up to the time of the consecration; at the time of the consecration, he sprinkles him with the residue of the *śukra* and *manthin* cups. This sacrifice consists of the *catuṣṭoma*.
A *sthapati* who is about to sacrifice with the *Sthapatisava* procures the following: a bull’s hide, two gold and silver plates, and a vessel made of *udumbara* wood for the consecration with curds.
He undergoes initiation;
his initiation lasts for three days and there are three *upasads*. A speckled heifer dedicated to the Maruts is to be offered as a sacrificial animal along with the one dedicated to Agni.

Seven oblations follow the offerings of the morning pressing; since there is an offering to Agni, prosperity indeed proceeds from the mouth of Agni—these [details] are the same up to the time of the consecration. At the time of the consecration, he spreads a bull’s hide on the sacrificer’s seat with the neck pointing eastward and the hair side up.

Having seated the sacrificer facing east and having placed gold and silver plates on both sides of him, he pours curd into a vessel made of Udumbara wood and consecrates him with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech, I consecrate you with the Sthapatisava.
When he has been wiped clean, they shout out together; this is the same procedure up to the wiping of the face.
This is the Saptadaśa Agniṣṭoma Sthapatisava; it was with this that they performed the sacrifice previously.
The Sūta, being about to sacrifice with the Sūtasava, prepares a black antelope skin, two gold and silver plates, a vessel made of *parṇa* wood, gold, and clarified butter for the consecration.
He undergoes initiation;

he has three initiation days and three *upasads*. There are eight oblations which follow the morning pressing offerings. As for the fact that there is an offering to Agni: "The Brāhmaṇa indeed belongs to Agni"—these are the [details].

Up to the time of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), it is the same; at the time of the consecration, he spreads a black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and the hair upward upon the sacrificer’s seat.

Having seated the sacrificer there facing east and having placed gold and silver plates on both sides of him, he pours clarified butter into a vessel made of *parṇa* wood, purifies it with gold, and consecrates him, saying: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech, I consecrate you with the *sūtasava*. When he has been wiped clean, they cry out together; this continues up to the wiping of his face.

This very Sūtasava is a seventeen-fold Agniṣṭoma; it is indeed the Sūtasava, it is the Grāmaṇīsava, it is the Ṛtusava—for by means of this, the seasons sacrificed previously. One who is about to perform the Somasava prepares a barren cow for Soma, a black antelope skin, two gold and silver plates, a vessel made of Palāśa wood for the consecration with milk; then, indeed, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "Whatever belongs to the Rājasūya, except for the Soma sacrifice, all that takes place here."

Having performed the New Moon sacrifice (*āmāvāsya-havis*), he proceeds for eight days with the *ānumat* and subsequent offerings; for a year he performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, for seven days the *indraturīya* and subsequent offerings; then he sacrifices with the oblations of the Ratnins, then he sacrifices with the oblations of the Devasū; then he immolates this Soma-cow that has calved for the first time; before the sun has risen, he spreads a black antelope skin upon the sacrificer’s seat, with the neck pointing eastward and the hair side up.

Then, having seated the sacrificer facing eastward and having placed gold and silver plates on both sides of him, he pours milk into a vessel made of *parṇa* wood and consecrates him with the verse: "Unconquered in battles, the furtherer in conflicts, the winner of light, dwelling in the waters, the guardian of the enclosure, born for the fray, providing good habitation and great renown—may we rejoice after you as you conquer, O Soma!"
"On the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech, I consecrate you with the Soma-pressing."

When he has wiped [the face], they cry out together; this is the same up until the wiping of the mouth. Then he sacrifices with the *saṃsṛp* oblations; then he sacrifices with the five-oblation *diśām aveṣṭi*; then he sacrifices with the animal sacrifice of two animals; then he sacrifices with the oblations of the Sātyadūtas; then he sacrifices with the former oblations of the *prayujas*; then, having sacrificed with the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha offerings, he sacrifices with the latter oblations of the *prayujas*; then he sacrifices with the oblations of the Devikās; then he sacrifices with the Traidhātavīya offering; then he sacrifices with the Sautrāmaṇī.
The Soma-sacrifice concludes in thirteen and a half months.

One who is about to perform the Pṛthisava procures a red bull's hide, two gold and silver plates, a four-cornered wooden trough made of Udumbara wood, and four kinds of water collected from the various quarters. Now, indeed, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage which says: "Whatever belongs to the Rājasūya that does not require a high altar (uttaravedī), all that is performed here."

Having performed the New Moon sacrifice, he proceeds for eight days with the offerings beginning with the *Ānumata*; for seven days with those beginning with the *Indra-turīya*; then he sacrifices with the oblations of the *Ratnins*, then he sacrifices with the oblations of the *Devasū*s; then he offers this four-oblation sacrifice: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, a cake on twelve potsherds for the Viśve Devas, and a pap for Bṛhaspati.
While that [sacrifice] is still uncommenced, he spreads out a red bull’s hide on the sacrificer’s seat, with the neck toward the east and the hair side up.

Then, having seated the sacrificer facing eastward and having placed him upon two gold and silver plates, he pours together four kinds of water into a wooden trough made of Udumbara wood and consecrates him with [the verse]: "They who have given me fifty horses in joint praise—O Agni, immortal one, bestow upon these wealthy patrons great, brilliant, and lofty glory, like that of heroes."
"On the impulse of God Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech, I consecrate you with the broad consecration."

When he has been wiped clean, they cry out together; this is the same [procedure] up to the wiping of the face. Then he sacrifices with the *saṃsṛp* oblations. Then he sacrifices with the five-oblation *diśām aveṣṭi*. Then, having passed over it, he sacrifices with the animal sacrifice of two animals and with the oblations of the Sātyadūtas. Then he sacrifices with the former *prayuja* oblations. Then, having sacrificed with the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha offerings, he sacrifices with the latter *prayuja* oblations. Then he sacrifices with the Devikā oblations. Then he sacrifices with the Traidhātavīyā. Then he sacrifices with the Sautrāmaṇī.
The Pṛthisavas are completed in one and a half months.

One who is about to sacrifice with the Gosava prepares ten thousand cows as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), two plates— one of gold and one of silver— a vessel made of parṇa wood for the mixing of the *pratidhuk* milk for the consecration,
and undergoes the initiation (*dīkṣā*).
For him there are six days of initiation and six days of preparatory rites (*upasad*).

Everything up to the time of the consecration is the same as for the [Soma] consecration. At the time of the consecration, a portion of the sacrificial ground equal to the size of a black antelope skin remains unexcavated at the sacrificer’s station.

Having seated the sacrificer there facing eastward, having placed gold and silver plates on both sides of him, and having brought the *pratidhuk* milk in a vessel made of *parṇa*-wood, he consecrates him in response to the *Bṛhat* Stotra with the verse: "Born wealthy, increased by strength, the best sustainer of dominion among dominions, the bestower of vigor; great, established in greatness, watch over the dominion and the kingdom! I consecrate you with the self-sovereignty of Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin."
"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech, I consecrate you with the Gosava.
When he has been wiped clean, they cry out together; this is the same [ritual] up to the wiping of the face.
This very Gosava is a thirty-six-fold sacrifice, complete, an Ukthya with both Sāmans, and one for which the sacrificial fee consists of ten thousand [cows].
While the *pavamāna* [laud] is being chanted, they perform the *Kaṇvarathantara*.

One who is about to sacrifice with the *odanasava* procures the following: the skin of a red bull, two gold and silver disks (*rukma*), a *pravarta* ornament weighing one hundred *mānas*, four men of the four castes—a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra—four liquids—honey, *surā* liquor, milk, and water—four vessels made of gold, silver, bronze, and clay, four sacrificial fees—a piece of gold weighing one hundred *mānas*, a bow with three arrows, a goad, and a water-pot filled with beans—and four sets of small sticks.

Two vessels made of *parṇa* wood from a banyan tree, two from *aśvattha* wood ripened in the month of Phālguna, four vessels made of various trees, groats, three bunches of *darbha* grass, a four-cornered wooden trough (*droṇa*) made of *udumbara* wood, and six hundred pots of water collected from the various directions; with these prepared, he awaits the approaching Rohiṇī constellation. Then, saying "Rohiṇī has arrived," he settles by the eastern fire. A householder who maintains the sacred fires establishes the *uttapanīya* fire, while one who has already established his fires establishes the *ānvāhāryapacana*. Then, toward the end of the night, the Adhvaryu, having hastened there, gives the command: "Cook the single-rice mess."
They cook it in such a way that it is cooked before sunrise, for the Brāhmaṇa says, "The work must be done by the rising sun.

Then, having cooked this rice-mess and poured clarified butter over it, he removes it toward the north. Having washed this vessel and spread a layer of ghee in it, he draws out the rice into it as if without striking it. Having made a hollow for pouring the ghee and having brought a large quantity of clarified butter, he then seats these four castes to the south, facing north. Then, while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, he offers four spoonfuls with the verses: "In the lion, in the tiger, and in the viper... and so forth.

Having offered oblation after oblation, he pours clarified butter over the turning ladle with the formulas: "Thou art the ruler (rāj), thou art the far-ruler (virāj), thou art the sovereign ruler (samrāj), thou art the self-ruler (svarāj). Then, having carried this turning ladle around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, he places it to the south.
Then he asks for that golden vessel;
having poured honey into it across the strainer and added barley meal, he stirs it with two sticks made of *parṇa* wood, saying: "O Indra, I mix thee, the radiant one, for the radiant [Indra]."
With the words, "Thou art splendor," he hands it to the Brāhmaṇa;

with the words, "I give this to thee," the Brāhmaṇa receives it. Then the sacrificer wipes his face, saying: "May my face be full of splendor, may my head be full of splendor; may I be full of splendor on every side; do thou endow me with splendor.
Having sipped water three times, he praises himself.
Therefore, he gives him this very vessel and a hundred-measure weight of gold.
Then he asks for that silver vessel;

having poured surā over a strainer placed within it and having added barley meal, he stirs it with two sticks made of *nyagrodha* wood, saying, "O Indra, I mix thee, who art powerful, with power. Saying, "Thou art power," he hands it to the Rājanya.

"I give this to you," says the Kṣatriya as he accepts it. Then the sacrificer wipes his mouth, reciting: "May my face be full of vigor; may my head be full of vigor; may I be full of vigor from every side; do thou endow me with vigor.
Having sipped water three times, he praises him and gives him this very vessel along with a bow and three arrows, and then he asks for this bronze vessel.

Having poured milk across the strainer into that [vessel] and added barley meal, he stirs it with two sticks of *aśvattha* wood, saying: "O Indra, I mix thee, who art rich in milk, with what is rich in milk.

He hands it to the Vaiśya, saying: "Thou art milk. The Vaiśya receives it, saying: "I accept this from thee. Then the sacrificer wipes his mouth, saying: "May my mouth be rich in milk; may my head be rich in milk. May I be rich in milk on every side; do thou satiate me with milk."
Having rinsed his mouth three times, he praises him;

then he gives him that very vessel and a knife. Then he asks for a clay vessel; having poured water into it across a strainer and having added barley meal, he stirs it with two *phālguna-pācī* sticks, saying, "O Indra, I mix you, the long-lived one, for the long-lived [guest]—you are life," and he hands it to the Śūdra woman.

"I give this to you," [saying] thus, the Śūdra accepts it. Then the sacrificer, having wiped his mouth, recites: "May my face be endowed with long life; may my head be endowed with long life. May I be endowed with long life from every side; do thou unite me with long life.
Having sipped water three times, he praises [the gift].
