To him, he gives that very vessel and a water-pot filled with beans.
Then, having reached out and taken a portion of this boiled rice, he eats it;
whatever he cannot endure, he causes to enter into the water, and then he drinks ghee from a golden vessel.

While he is drinking it out, one should address him with the mantra: "O Agni, make this [child] for life and splendor; O King Soma and Varuṇa, make him beloved as seed. Like a mother, O Aditi, grant him protection, so that he may reach old age, O All-Gods. Then, having washed this amulet with water, one should tie it on his right ear with the mantra: "Bestowing life upon you from every side. Then one turns it around him with the mantra: "Thou art life, thou art all-encompassing life, thou art complete life, thou art total life. Then one purifies him with three tufts of *darbha* grass, from which...

"The wind is as swift as thought, from which the rivers flow; with the luster of all of them, I sprinkle you for splendor. Then he touches his right temple with [the formula]: "Like the ocean in depth, like Soma you are inviolable; like Agni you face in every direction, like the sun you are pervasive with light."

While the Adhvaryu is occupied here, the Pratiprasthātṛ pours together four kinds of water into a wooden trough made of Udumbara wood and draws four cups: with a cup of Parṇa wood, he says, "I take that which is the essence of the waters in their flowing for this [sacrificer], the son of such-and-such, for luster and spiritual splendor"; with a cup of Nyagrodha wood, he says, "I take that which is the essence of the waters in their waves for this [sacrificer], the son of such-and-such, for vigor and heroism"; and with a cup of Aśvattha wood, he says, "I take that which is the essence of the waters in their midst for this [sacrificer], the son of such-and-such, for prosperity and procreation."

With a cup made of *aśvattha* wood, he says, "I take that which is the sacrificial essence of the waters; I take it for this [person], the son of such-and-such, for the sake of life and long-livedness. Then, with a cup made of *udumbara* wood, he spreads out a red bull's hide with its neck to the east and the hair side up.

Then, having seated the sacrificer facing eastward and having placed him between two plates of gold and silver, he sprinkles him with water from a vessel made of *parṇa* wood, saying: "With that essence which is in the flow of the waters, with that I sprinkle this [son] of such-and-such lineage for splendor and for holy luster (*brahmavarcasa*). With a vessel made of *nyagrodha* wood, he says: "With that essence which is in the wave of the waters, with that I sprinkle this [son] of such-and-such lineage for vigor and for heroism. With a vessel made of *aśvattha* wood, he says: "With that essence which is in the midst of the waters, with that I sprinkle this [son] of such-and-such lineage for nourishment and for procreation. With a vessel made of *udumbara* wood... [the essence] of the waters which is fit for sacrifice...
"By means of this essence, I consecrate this son of such-and-such a lineage for life, for long-livedness," he says as he wipes [the boy] with a piece of udumbara wood.
They cry out together; [the ritual] is the same up to the wiping of the face. To the north stands a hundred [pieces of wood] that have been fumigated, and a chariot;

he approaches it [with the verse]: "Go forward, show your heroism; be fierce, a watcher, a slayer of rivals. Ascend, O increaser of friends; the gods have spoken in favor of you. Then he touches the two sides of the chariot [with the verse]: "The two hooks, the two side-hooks on both sides of the chariot..."

He mounts the chariot with the verse, "Mount, O slayer of Vṛtra! Having begun with "May this one fill the two worlds and the lap," he then goes around it three times to the right, keeping it to his front, and returns;
he gives that [chariot] to the Adhvaryu.
This is the Odanasava sacrifice, a sacrifice for a king, a Brāhmaṇa, or a Vaiśya who desires prosperity.

One who is about to perform the Pañcaśāradīya sacrifice prepares seventeen castrated yearling heifers. Having sacrificed with the New Moon oblation prior to the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa, he seizes seventeen spotted heifers dedicated to the Maruts. After having the heifers stand for the sprinkling, they release them; then they complete the ritual with the remaining [animals].

When the year has elapsed, he sacrifices seventeen spotted heifers to the Sāṃtapana Maruts; having set the heifers aside after the sprinkling, they release them, and then they complete the ritual with the other animals. When the second year has elapsed, he sacrifices seventeen speckled heifers to the Gṛhamedhin Maruts; having set the heifers aside after the sprinkling, they release them, and then they complete the ritual with the other animals.

When the third year has elapsed, he immolates seventeen unanointed heifers for the Maruts who sport; having set aside the heifers from the point of sprinkling, they release them, and they complete the ritual with the others alone.

When the fourth year has elapsed, he immolates seventeen spotted heifers for the Maruts who possess their own wealth; having set aside the heifers from the point of sprinkling, they release them, and they complete the ritual with the others alone. On this very day he undergoes initiation and carries the fire-drill (ukhā) for a year.
There are twelve *upasads*.

Its days consist of a *trivṛt* *agniṣṭoma*, a *pañcadaśa* *ukthya*, a *saptadaśa* *ukthya*, a *pañcadaśa* *ukthya*, and a *saptadaśa* *atirātra*; for this [last], there is a *māruta-stoma*. Now, of these animals, on the first day three bulls dedicated to Indra and the Maruts are offered as *savanīya* victims; likewise on the second, likewise on the third, and likewise on the fourth.
"On the fifth day, the best [animals] are seized, for they consider this day to be the most excellent; 'He becomes the most excellent among his peers,' so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Now, if any of these animals is lost or dies, having performed that expiation which is prescribed in the Aśvamedha, they then seize another animal of the same deity, the same form, and the same species."
This is the Pañcaśāradīya sacrifice, belonging either to a king or to a Brāhmaṇa;
he who should desire, "May I become greater than the great," should sacrifice with the Pañcaśāradīya sacrificial rite;
he indeed becomes greater than the great.
One is about to sacrifice with the Agniṣṭut;
for that [sacrifice], everything is indeed the same, except for the *puroruc* verses: "O Agni, you are ageless" is that of the cup for Indra and Vāyu;
"Sacrifice for us to Mitra and Varuṇa" is that of the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa; and "O Aśvins, drink the pressed [juice]" is that of the cup for the Aśvins.
"Two of different forms move about; they move one after the other by means of illusion—these are the Śukra and Manthin cups.
With these words, he assigns three hundred and three thousand [bricks] to the fire-altar for the Āgrayaṇa cup and for the Ukthya.

The *nityā* verses are: "By fire Agni is kindled" for the [offering] to Indra-Agni; "Agni is the belly of the gods" for the Vaiśvadeva; "I praise Agni, the most excellent, the well-protecting" and the three [verses] beginning with "I praise Agni, the well-protecting" for the Marutvatīya offerings; "Hear us, O you of hearing ears, together with the carriers" for the Māhendra;
"Aditi is of all those worthy of sacrifice" for the Āditya cup; and "Thee, O Agni, thee, O Agni"—these three—for the Āditya cup; and "Thee, the accomplisher of the sacrifice" for the Sāvitra.
He performs the immolation for the Pātnīvata cup and for the Hāriyojana cup;

this Agniṣṭut Pavitra sacrifice is threefold. Just as these plants here, having been burnt by a forest fire and then rained upon, rise up again renewed, even so does he, having sacrificed with this sacrificial rite, become pure, cleansed, and fit for the sacrifice.

If he should consider himself a doer of evil through his mouth, he should perform the *trivṛt* [stoma]; for he indeed commits evil with his mouth who understands what is difficult to understand from one who has studied the Vedas or from a sage.
If [he considers himself a doer of evil] through his arms, he should perform the *pañcadaśa*; for he indeed commits evil with his arms who makes a violent assault upon a Brahmin.
If [he considers himself a doer of evil] through his belly, he should perform the *saptadaśa*; for he indeed commits evil with his belly who eats the food of one whose food ought not to be eaten.

If one should perform the twenty-one-fold [Stoma] with the feet— since it is indeed with the feet that he commits evil who goes to the Āraṭṭas, the Gāndhāras, the Sauvīras, the Karaskaras, or the Kaliṅgas—
if he should consider himself an evildoer in every respect, he should sacrifice with the fourfold Agniṣṭoma.
With this very [sacrifice], Ṛtuparṇa Bhāṅgāśvina, the king of the Śaphālās, performed a sacrifice. Having sacrificed with it, he set out on a hunt.
Indra, having observed him, looked upon him [with the thought]: "I shall indeed pursue you for that, since you have interrupted my sacrificial rite."
Being perspired, he went down into the water;
there he made a woman of himself.
She was named Sudevalā, and she ascended that very kingdom.
That woman, though being virtuous, gave birth to sons;
against them Indra provoked a conflict, and they, slain and shattered, lay prostrate.
While she was weeping between those two, Indra came there;
he approached her and said, "O Sudevalā!"
"Venerable sir," [he said], "this is dear to you.

[The father replied,] "What will be dear to me, venerable sir? [The son said,] "That very thing was indeed unpleasant to me—that you chose me as an obstacle to the sacrifice. Now, choose whichever of your sons shall live."
"O Blessed One, I have understood the truth regarding women," he said.
Therefore they say, "Sons are dearer than a woman.
He should perform the Catuṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma sacrifice during this very first fortnight for the sake of peace before any failure occurs.
When one who is about to sacrifice has been praised by Indra, everything for him is the same; however, the *puroruc* verses are different:

"Stand up, O Lord of the two bay horses" (*tiṣṭhā harī*) for the draught for Indra and Vāyu; "Whose bull at the pressed juice? (*kasya vṛṣā sute*) for the draught for Indra and Vāyu; and "O Indra, we [invoke] thee in the great contest" (*indraṃ vayaṃ mahādhane*) for the draught for Mitra and Varuṇa.
"dvitā yo vṛtrahantama" for the Āśvina cup;
"sa sūra ājanayañ jyotir indra uta tyad āśvaśviyam" for the Śukrāmanthin cups; and "bhareṣv indra" for the Āgrayaṇa cup, which is the standard formula for the Ukthya.
He joins [the verses]:
"The great field of Dhruva, shining much"—this belongs to Indra and Agni; "O Knower, lead us to wide space"—this belongs to the Viśvedevas.

The verses for the Marutvatīya offerings are fixed; those for the Māhendra offering are fixed. "With all your protections, O Indra, never be a barren cow to us," "O Indra, the cows [bring] the milk-mixture"—these three belong to the Āditya cup; "This prayer of yours"—this belongs to Sāvitra.
He joins [the verses] for the Pātnīvata cup;
those for the Hāriyojana cup are constant.
This fifteen-fold hymn to Indra is for one who desires power.
Or, whoever may be deprived of his seniority, he should sacrifice with this sacrificial rite; indeed, he attains seniority.
One who is about to sacrifice with the Aptoryāma undergoes initiation.

Its initiation is unlimited; there are twelve *upasads*; the *bahiṣpavamāna* is the *trivṛt*; the *ājya* of the Hotṛ is the *pañcadaśa*; that of the Maitrāvaruṇa is the *saptadaśa*; that of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin is the *ekaviṃśa*; that of the Acchāvāka is the *triṇava*;
the *mādhyamdina-pavamāna* is the *trayastriṃśa*; the *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ is the *caturviṃśa*; and the two *sāmans*, the *rathantara* and the *vairāja*, they chant around one with the other.

The Maitrāvaruṇa [recites] the forty-four-versed hymn; the Vāmadevya and Śakvara Sāmans are used, with one or the other being chanted as a response (pariṣṭuti). The Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin [recites] the forty-eight-versed hymn; the Naudhasa and Vairūpa Sāmans are used, with one or the other being chanted as a response. The Acchāvāka [recites] the twenty-one-versed hymn; the Kāleya and Raivata Sāmans are used, with one or the other being chanted as a response. This very [rite] the Chandogas call "the eight-fold back-chant" (aṣṭapṛṣṭha).

The *ārbhava-pavamāna* has twenty-seven verses; the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* is the thirty-three-fold; the *ukthya* chants are twenty-one-fold along with the *ṣoḍaśin*; the others are fifteen-fold; the *sandhi-stotra* is the nine-fold *rathaṃtara*. Thereby the small cattle surpassed [the large ones]. Indeed, Soma went forth being left over; the gods said, "This one has exceeded the *aptoryāma*; what is its course?"

That is why the Aptoryāma is called "Aptoryāma. For it, they prepared these additional *stotras*: the *Trivṛt* for the Hotṛ, the *Jarābodhīya*; the *Pañcadaśa* for the Maitrāvaruṇa, the *Sauhaviṣa*; the *Saptadaśa* for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the *Udvaṃśīya*; and the *Ekaviṃśa* for the Acchāvāka, the *Vāravantīya*. Regarding this, they say: "If the sacrifice were to conclude following the cup of the Acchāvāka, one would bring the sacrifice to its end, and the sacrificer would be liable to perish at the end. Therefore, they should chant the *stotra* for the Hotṛ alone, and the Hotṛ should recite the *śastra*; in this way, the sacrifice is restored from the middle.

Regarding this, they say: "All the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns should belong to the Aśvins; for whatever exceeds the night, all that belongs to the Aśvins"—this is one view. Then there is another: [the stomas] are the *trivṛt*, the *pañcadaśa*, the *saptadaśa*, and the *ekaviṃśa*.
Now, their deities are Agni, Indra, the Viśve Devās, and Viṣṇu.

Intending to sacrifice with the Mṛtyusava, he prepares the following: a tiger skin, two golden and silver ornaments, sandals made of tiger skin, sandals made of leather, a garment of ram's wool, a linen garment, a tripod-stool with three arrows, a stool with a coverlet, a drum, a shed, a wooden trough of Udumbara wood, four-cornered, containing water collected from the four quarters, a hundred [cows], and a chariot. With these materials prepared, he waits for the Citrā constellation to appear; then, when the Citrā has appeared, he settles by the eastern fire and establishes the *uttapanīya* fire.

The sacrificer, being modest and having established the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, then, while the [Adhvaryu] maintains contact with him, offers six oblations with the *sruva* ladle, saying: "This tiger moves about, entered into the fire. Then, on the sacrificer's seat, he spreads out a tiger skin with its neck toward the east and its hair upward, saying: "O Kaśyapa, that artifice of yours which is radiant, powerful, abundant, and of wondrous luster..."

"In that [chariot] upon which the seven suns are fixed together—upon that let us establish this king. Then he puts on two tiger-skin sandals with the formula, "Thou art heaven" on the right foot, and "Thou art earth" on the left. Then, bending his right knee, he mounts [the chariot] with the formula: "O tiger, mount upon the tiger-skin; may the great quarters and all the people desire thee; may the kingdom not fall away from thee. Then he hands him a bow, just as it is done at the Rājasūya sacrifice.

Then, having seated the sacrificer facing east and having placed him upon two gold and silver plates, he pours together four kinds of water into a wooden trough made of *udumbara* wood and consecrates him with the formula:
"The celestial waters which have come together with milk, those which are in the intermediate space and those which are on earth—with the luster of all those, I consecrate you with splendor."
I have sprinkled you with splendor along with divine milk; may Savitṛ make you such that you are the increaser of the kingdom.
All songs have magnified Indra, who is as vast as the ocean, the best of charioteers among charioteers, the true lord and master of spoils.

"May the Vasus consecrate you from the east with the Gāyatrī metre,"—having recited these same three [verses], [he does so] from the east. "May the Rudras consecrate you from the south with the Triṣṭubh metre,"—having recited these same three [verses], [he does so] from the south. "May the Ādityas consecrate you from the west with the Jagatī metre,"—having recited these same three [verses], [he does so] from the west. "May the Viśve Devas consecrate you from the north with the Anuṣṭubh metre,"—having recited these same three [verses], [he does so] from the north.

"May Bṛhaspati sprinkle you from above with the Pāṅkta metre," he says as he sprinkles him from above. Then his chest is wiped upward with the verse, "The ruddy one, the fierce wolf, the self-born, the doer. Then he strokes his two arms with the verse, "Stretch forth your two arms that we may live. Then he brings them down with the formula, "I bring down your two arms, which perform Indra’s heroic deeds. At this point, if it has not already been handed over, he gives him a bow.
When he has been completely wiped, they all cry out together; the procedure is the same up to the wiping of the face. To the north, a hundred fumes stand ready, as does a chariot.

"Intend that, intend it; be valiant, O fierce one, the protector, the slayer of rivals! Ascend the best of Vṛtra-slayers; the gods have spoken in favor of you. Then he touches both sides of the chariot: "The two hooks, the two side-hooks, which are on both sides of the chariot and move along with the darkness at the edge of the wind."

"May the far-shooting Indrāyudha, the winged one, and our fires carry us across; may they ferry us over. Then he stands by the chariot, saying: "Homage to thee, O Seer, at thy coming. Then he takes up the reins, saying: "O Brahman, let this be known to thee; mount upon the chariot, thou who art thunderbolt-handed. O God, thou yokest the reins with thy noble horses.

He mounts the chariot, saying: "Mount the chariot, O slayer of Vṛtra! "May Indra rejoice after him as he mounts the chariot; all have magnified Indra. At this point, he strings his bow, saying these two verses: "May the shouts of the army pass me by; may Anumati grant her approval to me."
Then, having circumambulated this hundred [of cows] three times from left to right and placed them in front, he approaches; here, for him, he sets down the throne-seat (*āsandī*) for the descent.
He descends upon it in the same manner as in the *rājasūya*.
While the Adhvaryu is occupied with his duties here, the Pratiprasthātṛ ceases his work with the cooked offering to Varuṇa (*vāruṇa-śṛta*).
There are two Vāruṇī offerings for the Sviṣṭakṛt sacrifice, containing the word "well-sacrificed" (sviṣṭavat). He gives him this hundred [of cows]. Then they enclose him within a measured shed.
On its northern half, he fixes a drum;
as the sun sets, they beat it. Then he instructs him: "O Sacrificer, restrain your speech and remain watchful over the kingdom."
From that point onward, he remains silent;

whatever he speaks, he speaks only "I give. These royal households—the charioteers, the village headmen, the chariot-attendants, and the artisans—approach him, and to them he gives a four-year-old cow and a barren cow.

While cooking it, they sit there delighting and keeping watch over it; then, at the end of the night, the Adhvaryu hastens forward, stirs the mash in the overflow of the fourfold waters, and having either smelled it or not smelled it, hands it to him;
he consumes it silently.

Then he anoints him with fresh butter [with the verse]: "Embracing this tiger... Then he worships the rising sun [with the verses]: "May Sūrya send up this word of mine; may it go up, O divine Sūrya, together with my voice. May I be the one who causes speech to be uttered; may speech be a firm foundation within me. He consecrates the kings as they depart for their residences [with the verse]: "May the rivers flow, may the rain-clouds pour, may the plants be rich in fruit. May I become the king of these [people] who possess food, who possess cooked rice, and who possess curds. At this point, he observes this vow for twelve days.

If he goes out toward the east or the north, wearing linen garments and shoes of leather; or if he goes toward the south or the west, wearing garments of bull-hide and shoes of tiger-skin; then, after twelve nights have dawned, he offers two spoonfuls of oblations with the two verses beginning, "Those long-haired ones who dance...

Then he mounts a wagon-seat with the verse, "Mount the seat, overcome the enemies..."; then he loosens his hair with the verse, "When the comb marked the parting of thy hair..."; then he shaves his hair with the verse, "With the razor wherewith Savitṛ shaved..."

As he shaves, he recites the consecration formula: "May this luster not follow after thy hair. Then, having gathered them together, he places them upon a bunch of *darbha* grass with the verse: "For them they sought a dwelling in many ways. Then he washes him with warm water with the formula: "May Savitṛ bestow strength upon thy two arms. With that very [rite], Mṛtyu performed a sacrifice, thinking: "May I attain sovereignty, overlordship, and kingship over all creatures."

Then indeed, he attained sovereignty, overlordship, and kingship over his subjects. He who should desire, "May I attain sovereignty, overlordship, and kingship over my equals," let him sacrifice with this sacrificial rite;
he attains sovereignty, overlordship, and kingship over his equals. Now, Suratha Śaivya sacrificed with this [rite] called Ātiṣṭhya, thinking, "May I reach the highest point.
Then indeed, he reached the highest point. He who should desire, "May I reach the highest point," let him sacrifice with this sacrificial rite; he surely reaches the highest point.

One who is about to perform the *sadyaskrī* sacrifice fells both a tree suitable for a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and a tree suitable for a plough-handle (*lāṅgalya*). He has a sacrificial post fashioned from the former and a plough from the latter;

having joined these two together, they either consume them or set them aside. Now, prior to this, a shed equal in size to the altar (*vedi*) has already been caused to be constructed for him on a chosen place of sacrifice.
With this plough he ploughs around that area which is to be avoided;

having sown inferior seeds in that [area], he causes it to be trampled. Then these chariots are prepared for him: one yoked with four horses, one drawn by side-horses (*praṣṭivāhī*), and a two-yoked heavy chariot (*sthūri*).
At the proper time, they fasten curds and reeds to them.

During the final days of summer, when the barley has been harvested, he causes the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) to summon him by foot, saying, "Will you perform a sacrifice for me, or shall I provide you with food?

When they have assembled, at the very time [of the ritual], he offers the morning *agnihotra* oblation; these officiating priests approach him, and then he says to them, "Perform for me a sacrifice of the same-day type (*sadyaskrī*.
They reply to him, "So be it."
At that very moment, they prepare for him the hall for the *sadyaskāra* rite;
having brought him from the *tīrtha* and purified him at that same time, he performs the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice.
When that sacrifice has been completed, he neither closes his fists nor restrains his speech.
They set aside for him this remnant of the oblation as his portion of the vow;

then he performs the Prāyaṇīyā sacrifice, and having called for the preparer of the oblation (haviskṛt), he releases his speech; at this point they give him this remnant of the oblation as his portion of the vow.

As soon as they are born, these chariots run the race: one yojana with four yoked horses facing forward; one tripada as the sacrificial fee with a side-horse; one gavyūti from behind with two horses unyoked.

"A cry of 'A shout from the water!'—whomever they encounter, to him they announce: 'This one is sacrificing; he is the son of so-and-so, the grandson of so-and-so, the great-grandson of so-and-so, performing the Sadyaskrī sacrifice. Thus they come with chariots. When the chariots have arrived, whatever fresh butter settles on the axle-trees, having melted that and purified it, he pours it into the jar of clarified butter, saying, 'For the immediate performance. Then he proceeds with the Prāyaṇīya offering."
Having performed the *prāyaṇīya* offering, he proceeds with the *pada* ritual;

having proceeded with the *pada*, he purchases the King (Soma) for a three-year-old castrated steer that is still a calf, and having conveyed it, he offers the *ātithya*. Having performed the *ātithya*, the *upasads* consist of single groups.

Having performed the middle *upasad*, at the time for the high altar (*uttaravedi*), he causes the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*) to be measured out. Then, having yoked oxen and having scattered barley, they thresh it.

The high altar (uttaravedi) consists of barley husks. Then, having yoked oxen in the middle, they go forward while grasping barley grains, so that this great altar becomes one with a barley-strewn sacrificial grass (barhis). Having brought forward the Āhavanīya fire, and having established the Sadas and the two Havirdhāna sheds, he erects the Sadas and the two Havirdhāna sheds. Having erected the Sadas and the two Havirdhāna sheds, he brings forward Agni and Soma. Having brought forward Agni and Soma, he takes up the Vasatīvarī waters.
Having set those aside at that very moment, he begins the morning litany (prātaranuvāka).
When the morning litany has been concluded, he goes toward the waters; having emerged from the water, he enters the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
The pressing of the Soma is performed in the established manner.
The cups are taken in the established manner.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the Āśvina cup; having taken the Āśvina cup and having taken three ropes, he goes toward the plow.
On its mat, there is a vessel for the *caṣāla* as if it were the upper part.
Having cast away the *lāṅgalī* plant ending with its fragments, he then dedicates these animals— the one for Agni-Soma, the one for Agni, and the *anūbandhya*—
and they proceed toward them in succession with their omenta;
the Adhvaryu enters first with the omentum of the animal for Agni-Soma, while the others bring theirs in succession.
When the *stokīya* verses have been recited and the omenta of the Agniṣomīya animal have been cooked, he proceeds with the omentum of the Agniṣomīya;
they cause the other [omentum] to lie around [the fire],
and among the morning-pressing offerings, the sacrificial cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) of the Agniṣomīya becomes the principal one.
At the midday *pavamāna* laud, he proceeds with the offering to Agni-Soma; immediately following that, he proceeds with the omentum of the animal for Agni;
at its own place, he proceeds with the offering to Agni; and immediately following that, he proceeds with the omentum of the *anūbandhya* victim.
Among the offerings of the third *savana*, the sacrificial cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) of the *anūbandhya* is the principal one; he proceeds with the *anūbandhya* before the [main] pressing has concluded.
The Sadyaskrī sacrifice is completed;

whatever in it is not performed as a Sadyaskrī is indeed a failure for him, yet that is [restored] within the sacrifice itself. Now, the Ādityas and the Aṅgirases were contending for the world of heaven.
Those Aṅgirases approached the Ādityas with Agni as their messenger, saying, "We shall perform the Soma-pressing tomorrow."
Then the Ādityas said, "Today is our Soma-pressing;
you shall be our Hotṛ."

They led forth this horse, the white one that had become [the sun], as the sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā), with a golden girth-band; therefore, for the Sadyaskrī sacrifice, the sacrificial gift is a white horse with a golden girth-band. That which is the white horse is the form of Āditya; and that it has a golden girth-band is the form of his rays. Of that [sacrifice] which is threefold, the midday and afternoon *pṛṣṭha* chants are twenty-four-fold, the *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ is forty-four-fold, and the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* is twenty-four-fold.

Everything else is threefold; he gives a white horse as a gift. Intending to sacrifice by imitation, he undergoes initiation among rice grains; it concludes in two days: one day for the Upavasatha and one day for the Soma-pressing. Although it is a Trivṛt [stoma], the Mādhyandina and Ārbhava [Pavamāna stotras] consist of forty-four verses; the Hotṛ’s Pṛṣṭha-stotra consists of forty-four verses, and the Agniṣṭoma-sāman consists of forty-four verses.
Everything else is threefold; he gives a white mare as the purchase price.
One who is about to perform the sacrifice undergoes initiation among beans.
It concludes in three days: one day for the preparatory rites (*kraya*), one day for the fast-day (*aupavasathya*), and one day for the pressing-day (*sutyā*).
Although it is indeed threefold, its Mādhyandina- and Ārbhava-pavamāna-stotras consist of forty-eight verses; the Hotṛ’s *pṛṣṭha* consists of forty-eight verses;
the Agniṣṭoma-sāman consists of forty-eight verses;
and everything else is threefold. He gives according to his faith as an act of exceeding ritual performance. One who is about to sacrifice undergoes initiation (*dīkṣā*) with sesame seeds.

It concludes in four days: one day up to the purchase of the Soma, one day for the high altar (uttaravedi), one day for the Upavasatha, and one day for the pressing (sutyā). This is the Catuṣṭoma sacrifice;
he who is about to perform the Vrātyastoma [proceeds as follows]:
they seek a gift from a king or a Brāhmaṇa for a month or for a year.
Whomever they recognize, him they appoint as their chief;
he performs their religious observances for them, and he becomes one who sleeps on the ground, eats meat, and approaches women.
For that is indeed the vow of the consecrated one.
Now, as for the black garment with a black fringe that he puts on, that is the form of the garment of the consecrated one;
and as for the two black and white skins that he wears, that is the form of the two black antelope skins.
Now, when he wears the two plates of gold and silver, that is the form of the two *parigharmya* vessels;
when he wears the black turban, that is the form of the turban of the consecrated one (*dīkṣita*);
and when he carries the triple-bow with arrows made of leather, that is the form of the staff of the consecrated one.
Now, when he utters the speech of a Vrātya, that is the form of the speech of one consecrated for sacrifice (dīkṣita).
And as for the fact that he wears shoes with wooden heels, it is so that being consecrated, he may not stand upon anything impure;
thus, for this very form of sacrifice, the whip-handle itself is the sacrificial post (yūpa).

The driving-goad is the *caṣāla*; the front of the chariot is the *āhavanīya* fire; the two shafts are the altar (*vedī*); the yoke is the *uttaravedī*; the upper yoke is the *uttaranābhi*; the bow is the two *havirdhāna* sheds;
the two sides are the *āgnīdhrīya* and *mārjālīya* altars; and the pole is the *sadas*.
The *kiṃkaras* are the sacrificial hearths (*dhiṣṇiyas*);
the *patnīśāla* is the chariot-seat; the *gārhapatya* fire is the base; and the ancient *gārhapatya* is their place of origin.

They cook the *yamaja* offering, which is their sacrificial animal; and the cake (*apūpa*), the pot-offering (*sthālīpāka*), the cooked rice (*caru*), and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) are their sacrificial portions.
That which he calls upon as the attendant is the *puro'nuvākyā*; what he utters is the *yājyā*;
what they eat is the *vaṣaṭkāra*; and the jar that he measures out is the *puro'nuvākyā*.
That which is the address to the gods is the *yājyā*;
that which he calls out as a summons is the *pratigara* of the *śastra*; and that which they shout out is the *udgītha*.
Those who, having approached this sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*) indirectly, do not approach it directly—[for them this is prescribed].

Just as those who have been initiated (*dīkṣita*), have broken their vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*), or whose Soma-drinking has been interrupted (*vicchinna-somapītha*) are not to eat the food [of others], so it would be for one who remains a *vrātya* without having performed the *vrātyastoma*.

Therefore, for one who remains a *vrātya* without having sacrificed with the *vrātyastoma*, his food is not to be eaten; for he is like one whose Soma-drinking has been interrupted, and his food is not to be eaten by them. Among them, those who have not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) go back to their respective homes, establish the fires, and then approach the *sthapati* (chief) with thirty-three sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) each.

Among them, the *brahmabandhu* is one who speaks like a Magadha, and the *brahmabandhu* is an unchaste woman who speaks like an unchaste woman; Jaratkadratha is joined with two who are aged and perform [ritual] acts. The *brahmabandhu* is an unchaste woman who speaks like an unchaste woman, and Jaratkadratha is joined with two who are aged and perform [ritual] acts. By means of that which is failed (*vyṛddha*), he expiates the failure. This is the wealth of the *vrātya*, which has been fully pacified: a staff, sandals, and a deer-skin from a black antelope. Standing upon the chariot, the *subrahmaṇya* priest invokes the *subrahmaṇyā*.

At the time of the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), this very thing occurs for him: the priests distribute the fees, and his [offerings] follow those of the morning pressing. There are the Saṃjñānya oblations; for those who practice as Vrātyas act as if they were without mutual recognition, and these [oblations] cause them to recognize one another.

It follows the offerings of the midday pressing: there is a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra and the Maruts; for Indra is the Vrātya and the Maruts are the village; verily, by means of the village, he makes them harmonious.

It follows the offerings of the third pressing: there is a pap for the Ādityas who are becoming; for those who live as Vrātyas move as if they have not yet come into being; verily, he leads them to prosperity.
It follows the animal-cake of the Anūbandhya sacrifice: there is a pap for Aditi.
Those who practice the *vrātya* walk as if they were without a firm foundation; this [earth] is indeed Aditi, and it is upon her that they find support.
This is the *agniṣṭoma* of the eldest [priests];
it has four *ṣoḍaśin* chants, two *pavamāna* chants, and both [the *ṣoḍaśin* and *pavamāna*] belong to the *acchāvāka*'s hymns.
This very Ukthya is the most precarious; it has six Ṣoḍaśin cups, all its Pavamāna lauds, and all the Stotras of the Acchāvāka.
By means of this very sacrifice, the Maruts performed the sacrifice.

Viṣṇu was their *sthapati* (architect/priest), and moreover, by means of this [sacrifice], the divine *vrātyas* sacrificed; Budha Saumya was their *sthapati*, and moreover, by means of this, the sons of the Kuru-Brahmans sacrificed;
Aupoditi Gaupālāyana Vaiyāghrapadya was their *sthapati*.
Having looked down upon the Pañcālas, the Vrātyas set out toward them.
Their fathers said to them, "My sons, do not go to the Pañcālas; the Pañcālas are indeed revilers, and they will revile you. But disregarding them, they nevertheless set out.

The Keśins came to the sacrificial retreat of Dālbhya; on the following day, as they were proceeding with the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant, they took hold of them from behind, saying, "The *bahiṣpavamāna* is indeed a means of purification; we shall purify ourselves. Now, among the Pañcālas there was a learned man named Vāleya Āgniveśya of the Gandharvāyaṇa lineage; he asked those who were proceeding together, "Who are these that are proceeding?"
"We are the Maruts"—
"Who among you is the architect?"— "I am Viṣṇu," replied Aupoditi Gaupālāyana Vaiyāghrapadya.
"Whatever you have done, who has performed it?"— thus he pointed out the vow in its hidden form.
He said to them, "I have censured you who are ignorant; we shall exclude you.
They said to him, "It was the father who has censured his sons; your offspring will become more wretched. And so it came to pass.
Now, among the Pañcālas, there were the Gandharvāyaṇas, the Vāleyas, and the Āgniveśyas, who were as if fallen into sin; yet formerly, that was indeed a great family.
Whoever would revile a Vrātya should revile him in this very manner; and whoever Vrātya is capable of responding should respond to him in this very manner.
Now, therefore, they call them the Bhāllavi-stomas:
the Trivṛt is repeated, the Pañcadaśa is the Agniṣṭoma-sāman, and all the Pavamānas are Ṣoḍaśas;
the Pañcadaśa is repeated, the Saptadaśa is the Agniṣṭoma-sāman, and all the Pavamānas are Ṣoḍaśas.

Repeating the seventeenth [stoma], the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the twenty-onefold; all the Pavamāna-stotras are sixteenfold; repeating the twenty-onefold, the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the twenty-sevenfold; all the Pavamāna-stotras are sixteenfold; repeating the twenty-sevenfold, the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the thirty-threefold; all the Pavamāna-stotras are sixteenfold;
repeating the thirty-threefold, the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the twenty-sevenfold; all the Pavamāna-stotras are sixteenfold.

Repeating the Triṇava [stoma], the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the Ekaviṃśa; all the Pavamāna [laud] stotras are Ṣoḍaśa, and the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the Ekaviṃśa repeated. Repeating the Saptadaśa, the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the Saptadaśa; all the Pavamāna stotras are Ṣoḍaśa, and the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the Saptadaśa repeated. Repeating the Pañcadaśa, the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the Pañcadaśa; all the Pavamāna stotras are Ṣoḍaśa, and the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the Pañcadaśa repeated. Repeating the Trivṛt, the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the Trivṛt; all the Pavamāna stotras are Ṣoḍaśa.
Now, it is indeed said: "Whatever the gods did at the sacrifice, the Asuras did that too. Thereupon, Prajāpati reflected: "How now might I cause the gods to turn away from the Asuras?"
He saw this undefined sacrificial rite, the Upahavya; he invited them into it, saying, "Enter into this!"

When he says, "To the gods who move at dawn," he means "to the Maruts who move at dawn"; when he says, "Soma purifies itself," he means "Indu purifies itself"; when he says, "For Indra, of the sacrificial cakes," he means "for Śakra, of the sacrificial cakes"; when he says, "O Vāyu, for Indra and Vāyu," he means "for Niyutvat, for Śakra and his team, the Niyuts"; when he says, "For Mitra and Varuṇa," he means "for the two seekers of Truth (Ṛtāyus)"; and when he says, "For the Aśvins."

Regarding "to the Nāsatyas," he says there; then, where he says "O Indra, for the Soma-draughts," he says there "to Śakra, for the Indus"; then, where he says "to Indra and Agni," he says there "to Śakra and Jātavedas"; then, where he says "to the Viśvedevas," he says there "to the Maruts, to the Viśvedevas"; then, where he says "to Indra accompanied by the Maruts," he says there "to Śakra, who possesses a host"; then, where he says "to Mahendra," he says there "to the Great Śakra"; then, where he says "to the great Ādityas."

When he says, "To the Ādityas," he says there; then when he says, "To the Vanaspatis," he says, "To the lords of the forest"; then when he says, "To the god Savitṛ," he says, "To the great god Savitṛ"; then when he says, "To the Viśve Devas," he says, "To the great Viśve Devas"; then when he says, "To the wives of the gods," he says, "To the great wives of the gods"; then when he says, "To Indra, the lord of bay horses," he says, "To Śakra, the bountiful one";
and regarding "The parched grains for the drops," some indeed prescribe this [formula].
This occurred right before the chanting of the *yajñāyajñiya* stotra; indeed, it was during the *yajñāyajñiya* stotra that he uttered that [formula].
The Asuras merely looked on at him, wondering, "What is he doing? Or what is he not doing?
When he realized, "These [Asuras] no longer have power over good and evil," he then uttered this [formula]: "The god who bestows wealth (*draviṇodā*) for you."
"Prajāpati, the divine Draviṇodas, desires a full ladle," he says;
thus he pours out the full ladle. "Pour it out, or fill it up"—this means, "fulfill every single desire of his. "Then indeed, O God, you have been honored."
Prajāpati bestows every desire upon the deities who are to be propitiated;
the Stoma becomes seventeenfold, for Prajāpati is seventeenfold.
The horse with black knees is the sacrificial fee for the attainment of Prajāpati;
for the horse belongs to Prajāpati, and it serves to conform to Prajāpati.
He who wishes to separate himself from evil and from his rival should sacrifice with this sacrificial rite;
he indeed separates himself from evil and from his rival. Having slain Vṛtra, Indra went to the furthest distance, thinking, "I have failed.
The gods sought him out by means of the sacrifice.
They made him milk out a hundred *āśira* offerings, saying, "He will return with a greater share and greater affection.
But he did not come at the morning pressing;
they all, however, consumed the portion of the morning pressing.
"Who indeed shall drink of this Soma, O Indra?

While that [Soma-pressing] was concluding at the morning libation, all the *camasādhvaryu*s, being joyful, resolved to wake up for the recitation of the *acchāvāka*’s *śastra*. They waited expectantly for the *acchāvāka*’s *śastra*.
For they consider themselves as being with Indra;
therefore, at the *tīvrasoma* sacrifice, all the *camasādhvaryu*s rejoice and respond to the recitation (*śastra*) of the *acchāvāka*,
for they consider themselves as being with Indra.
Then indeed that was so;
and regarding this they say, "Now the sacrifice is complete with Indra," and so they pressed it out for him.

"Come here! Come here! Come here!"—thus indeed they said to him; "Great! Great! Great!"—thus indeed they said to him, "This great food of yours, come back to that! This, indeed, was what they said regarding the midday pressing. That is also the underlying principle for other [vessels] at the midday pressing: he should pour down a vessel of boiled [milk] from the *ekadhana* waters at the morning pressing, curd at the midday pressing, and churned [milk] at the third pressing.
This is its intensity:
there is a seventeen-fold chant; Prajāpati is seventeenfold.
A pregnant mare with a white spot on her forehead is the sacrificial fee for the attainment of Prajāpati; for the embryo is power (*indriya*) and the white spot is power,
[given] for the sake of possessing power.
Whoever has been brought to emaciation by old age or by illness should sacrifice with this sacrificial rite; he indeed attains vigor.
Indra desired, "May I strike away evil and attain preeminence among the gods";
he beheld this sacrificial rite.
He brought it; with it he sacrificed.

Thereby, indeed, he struck away evil and attained preeminence among the gods. He who should desire, "May I strike away evil and attain preeminence among my equals," let him sacrifice with this sacrificial rite.
Verily he strikes away evil and attains preeminence among his peers.

For him there is an *atigrāhya* cup [with the mantra]: "O Indra, scatter our enemies; strike down those who attack us; cast him beneath our feet who seeks to harm us. You are taken with a base; I take you, acceptable to Indra Vaimṛdha.
Having wiped it around, he sets it down with: "This is your womb; for Indra Vaimṛdha, you!"
For him, the Trivṛt and Pañcadaśa stomas are reversed;
these are six Gāyatrīs. Indeed, among the meters, the Gāyatrī struck away evil; by means of the Gāyatrī, the sacrificer likewise strikes away evil.
Indra desired, "May I attain preeminence among the gods by breaking through [the obstacles].
He perceived this sacrificial rite;
he performed it.
With that he sacrificed;

thereby, indeed, he attained preeminence among the gods by breaking through [the obstacles]. He who desires, "May I attain preeminence among my equals by breaking through," should sacrifice with this sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*); verily, he attains preeminence among his equals by breaking through.

Its *atigrāhya* cup is: "This Soma, the all-conquering, the breaker-through, the seer, the sage, by his poetic wisdom, taken with a support—O Indra, I take thee, acceptable for the sake of breaking through."
Having wiped it around, he sets it down with the formula: "This is thy womb; for Indra thee, the piercer!
For this [sāman], the fifteenfold and twenty-onefold stomas alternate.

These are six *bṛhatī*s; the *bṛhatī* indeed pierced through among the meters. By means of the *bṛhatī*, the sacrificer thus pierces through. Indra desired: "May I pierce Vala and release the cattle."
He perceived this sacrificial rite; he took it up and sacrificed with it.
From that, having indeed split Vala, he released the cattle.
He who should desire, "May I, having split Vala, release the cattle," let him sacrifice with this sacrificial rite; verily, having split Vala, he releases the cattle.

Its *atigrāhya* draught is Indra. He won the plants; he won the waters and the trees; he split Vala and drove out the contending voices; then he became the subduer of those who were arrogant in their own power. "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Indra, the slayer of Vala"—having wiped it around, he deposits it with the words, "This is thy womb; for Indra, the slayer of Vala. For this draught, the seventeenfold and the twenty-onefold *stomas* alternate.

These six are *gāyatrīs*; for the *gāyatrī* indeed split open the strength (*vala*) among the meters. By means of the *gāyatrī* itself, the sacrificer, having split open the strength, releases the cattle. One is about to perform the *ṛtapeya* sacrifice; whatever food he desires, having eaten thereof, he undergoes initiation (*dīkṣate*), or whatever he obtains.
He does not eat for one day, then he eats; he does not eat for two days, then he eats; he does not eat for three days, then he eats.
Thus he attains the Virāj right here;
having purchased and brought home the King Soma, he performs the guest-offering (ātithya).
Or, if he passes over this [offering], he does not eat for four days, and then he eats.
He does not eat for five days, then he eats;
he does not eat for six days, then he eats; there are three *upasads*.
They amount to thirty;

the Virāj consists of thirty syllables, and the Virāj is food. By means of the Virāj, he obtains food. Now, those which are eleven are her udder; by that he milks her. And those which are thirty-one are also her udder.
By that very means he milks her out for him; during the Upasad days, his vow consists of clarified butter: he takes it with three fingers of cold ghee, then with two, and then with one.
Or else, with three joints of cold clarified butter he strikes [the fire], then with two, then with one;

or when the clarified butter has melted, he places three joints, then two, then one—these being the forms of the vow consisting of three, two, and one teat. He turns away from the sun by day, and not from the fire by night.
The Soma-vessel is made of Udumbara wood, four-cornered; the Brahman priest possesses the three Vedas and belongs to the same lineage;
the Stoma is seventeenfold, for Prajāpati is seventeenfold.
Prajāpati did not yield his food. The gods sought him through *ṛta* and *satya*.

When he eats, it is for the sake of securing that which is secured by eating; and when he does not eat, it is for the sake of securing that which is secured by fasting. Furthermore, when during the *upasad*s he observes the clarified-butter vow (*ājyavrata*), it is because clarified butter is the dear abode of the gods; thus he secures the dear abode of the gods. Furthermore, when he does not turn away from the sun by day, nor from the fire by night—it is these two, *ṛta* and *satya*, that belong to the gods.

"May I not turn my back on the nectar and truth of the gods"—this is why it is made of udumbara wood; for the udumbara is strength and food, and it is for the attainment of strength and food. And as for the fact that it is a soma-cup: soma is indeed the supreme food of the gods.

"By means of this very highest food, one secures lower food"—this is why it is so. Now, as to why it has four corners: it is for the securing of that food which entered the quarters. And as to why it consists of three Vedas: for one who knows only a single Veda is not fit to offer this sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*). And as to why he belongs to the same lineage (*sagotra*): the *sagotra* is indeed the self; thus, "I shall establish the glory and the food of the sacrifice within my own self"—this is why it is so. Having drawn it up together with the cups of the midday pressing, they offer it. When it has been offered, the priests assign it to the Brahman at the time of the sacrificial gifts.

Sitting around him as he was [partaking of] that *brahman*, they ate; because they thought it was truth (*ṛta*), by means of that truth they ate. That is why the drinking of this [sacrifice] is called *ṛtapeya*. The quarters desired: "May we be possessors of food, may we obtain food, may food be established within us.
They perceived this sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*).
They brought it and sacrificed with it;

then indeed they became eaters of food and obtained food. Food was established in them. He who desires, "May my offspring be eaters of food, may they obtain food, and may food be established in them," should sacrifice with this sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*). His offspring becomes eaters of food, he obtains food, and food is established in him.

In that [sacrifice], there are four *bahispavamānas*, eight *ājyas* each on eight verses, the midday *pavamāna* has twelve verses, the *pṛṣṭhas* have sixteen verses, the *ārbhavapavamāna* has twenty verses, and the *agniṣṭomasāman* has twenty-four verses;
they call this the *diśāṃ catuṣṭoma*.
The *chandas* desired: "May we attain glory, may we secure glory, may glory be established within us."
They saw this sacrificial rite; they took it up and sacrificed with it.

Then indeed they attained glory, they won glory, and glory became established in them. He who should desire, "May I attain glory, may I win glory, may glory be established in me," let him sacrifice with this sacrificial rite;
he attains glory, he wins glory, and glory becomes established in him.
His hymns of praise were: on one [verse], then on three, on one, and then on three.
This very thing they call the "Three-ones of the Chandomas. Regarding the statement, "The Stomas desired," the introductory praise is the same.
Its Stomas are: first, three Trivṛts; then three Pañcadaśas; then three Saptadaśas; then three Ekaviṃśas.
This very [chant] they call the "Ekatrika" among the Stomas;
for Indra and Agni once desired, "May we be in the same world, may we go to the same world."

The two of them saw this sacrificial rite (yajñakratu); they took it up and performed it with it. Thereupon, indeed, they came to share the same world; they attained the same world. Even so, if a king and a domestic priest (purohita) should desire, "May we be of the same world; may we go to the same world," let those two perform this sacrificial rite. They will indeed become sharers of the same world; they will go to the same world. A horse-chariot equipped with sacrificial implements and a wooden cup suspended from it—this is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the Brāhmaṇa; a mule-chariot [is that for the Kṣatriya].
The sacrificial fee for the Rājanya consists of a bow with all its weapons, a quiver made of bronze, and a leather case;
for this sacrifice, the Trivṛt and Pañcadaśa Stomas are used in alternation;
indeed, the Trivṛt belongs to the Brāhmaṇa and the Pañcadaśa to the Rājanya.

This very [sacrifice] is called "the nest of Indra and Agni"; being this very thing, it is the sacrifice of father and son, of two friends, and of two brothers. One who is about to perform the *abhicaraṇīya* Soma sacrifices prepares two kinds of sacrificial implements: those that are obstructive and those made of *tailvaka* wood; two pressing-boards from a corpse-cart, and two testicles from a human bone.

When the Adhvaryu, intending to draw the Upāṃśu cup, presses the King Soma, whatever shoot (*aṃśu*) falls away from it, he places that into this vessel, holds it close, and then says: "Kill so-and-so; then I shall offer you. He remains seated until the sound has ceased, and then he throws that broken piece (*bhaṅga*) into the Āhavanīya fire, saying: "With this whirling fragment, I pierce so-and-so, the son of such-and-such. At this point, he meditates in his mind upon whomsoever the sacrificer hates.
Then he sets down this vessel on the mound (*khara*) in its proper place, saying: "I set you down in the breath of so-and-so."
Whatever cup he draws, he draws it in this very manner; whatever vessel he sets down, he sets it down in this very manner.
This is the Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma, having a single stoma and a single havirdhāna cart.
They call that the hawk; then the arrow—this is the common craft for the purpose of sorcery. They chant in three triplets;
the chariot is the oblation-holder.
Now, as for the *saṃdaṃśa* (the "tongs" rite):
the ritual procedure for exorcism is the same; there are two *triṣṭubh* stomas of thirty-three verses each in the middle, two *havirdhāna* sheds, and then the *indra-vajra*.
The ritual procedure for the malevolent rite (*abhicāra*) is the same; this [sacrifice] consists of fifteen [stomas].

One who is about to perform it with the *durāśa* [offering] prepares sixty *śatamāna* weights of gold—thirty of gold and thirty of silver—and a large quantity of other gold. Having sacrificed with the new-moon oblation (*āmāvāsya-havis*), he offers a pap (*caru*) to Sūrya.

In that [first sacrifice], he gives a gold *śatamāna* as a gift; then, when the evening *agnihotra* has been offered, he prepares a *caru* of *cāndramasa* rice and gives a silver *śatamāna* as a gift in that [second sacrifice].
In this very manner, the sacrificer performs these two sacrifices day after day for a month, and then he undergoes initiation (*dīkṣā*).
At the *dīkṣaṇīyā* he gives gold weighing twelve *mānas*;
at the *prāyaṇīyā* he gives [gold] weighing twenty-four *mānas*; at the *ātithyā* he gives two [pieces of gold] weighing twenty-four *mānas* each;
at the first *upasad* he gives four [pieces].
On the second *upasad* day he gives eight;
on the third *upasad* day he gives sixteen;
on the fourth *upasad* day he gives thirty-two.
On the fifth *upasad* day, he gives sixty-four;

on the sixth *upasad* day, he gives one hundred and twenty-eight, consisting of twenty-four measures. Now, therefore, there is a count of one hundred for the *agnīṣomīya* animal: when the omentum has been offered, he gives two hundred; when the omentum of the *āgneya* animal has been offered, he gives four;
and at the morning pressings (*prātaḥsavana*), he gives eight.
At the time of the midday libations, he gives sixteen as sacrificial fees;
at the time of the afternoon libations, he gives thirty-two;
at the third pressing, he gives sixty-four; and when the omentum of the Anūbandhya animal has been offered, he gives one hundred and twenty-eight.
When he sacrifices day by day with these two offerings, he attains union with and residence in the same world as the Sun and the Moon.
Now, in that the sacrificial fee consists of gold, the sacrificer thereby refines his own self into a golden form:
that which is above his navel is gold, and that which is below is silver. Indeed, when he becomes golden, he becomes immortal.
The gods are indeed golden;
therefore they are immortal.
The Stoma consists of seventeen parts.

Prajāpati is seventeenfold; for the attainment of Prajāpati, both Sāmans come into being, consisting of the meters. These two wings, made of meters, the sacrificer prepares for himself for the conquest of this world. When he performs this sacrificial rite, he wins union with and residence in the same world as the sun and the moon.

Therefore, it is called *duraśas*, for the world of these two deities is indeed difficult to attain. Now, one who is about to sacrifice with the *durṇāśa* procures a hundred oxen and thirty-three gold coins; by this very rite he wins the world of oxen, and by this very rite he wins the luminous world.
By means of this very [stotra], one conquers the heavenly world from the light;
it consists of the seventeen-fold chant, for Prajāpati is seventeenfold.
There are two *sāmans* belonging to Prajāpati; these two wings consist of the *chandases*. By this, the sacrificer prepares his own self for the conquest of this world.
Because one does not perish after having performed this sacrificial rite, it is called *durṇāśa*;
that is the reason for the name *durṇāśa*. Keśin Dālbhya, desiring honor, performed the *apaciti* sacrifice; they avoided using those two names [of the *sāmans*].
Therefore, indeed, they avoid pronouncing the names of the Pañcāla kings;
they call their hair "śīrṣaṇyās" and their sacrificial grass "kuśās."
"The two rivers"—thus [it is said regarding] the two Gaireyaka Vimatyas.
Therefore, he who desires, "May I be possessed of honor," should sacrifice with this sacrificial rite; he indeed becomes possessed of honor.
For this rite, the Bahiṣpavamāna is the twenty-four-fold stoma, and the Ājya-stotras are the threefold and fifteen-fold stomas.
Those three [verses] are *gāyatrīs*; the midday *pavamāna* consists of twenty-four; the *pṛṣṭha* stotras consist of fifteen and seventeen;
those two are *triṣṭubhs*; the *ārbhava-pavamāna* consists of twenty-seven; and the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* consists of twenty-one.
These are indeed the most honored among the meters; he who knows this becomes truly honored. That Sun desired, "May I be radiant.
He perceived this sacrificial rite, he took it up, and he sacrificed with it.
Thereupon, he indeed became radiant. He who desires, "May I be radiant," should sacrifice with this sacrificial rite.
He becomes possessed of splendor alone; for him there is a *atigrāhya* cup for Sūrya, a victim for Sūrya is to be immolated, and this [stoma] is the twenty-one-fold.
Indra desired: "May I attain sovereignty, lordship, and kingship over the gods, like a bull among cattle.
He perceived this sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*), he took it up, and he sacrificed with it.

Then indeed he attained sovereignty, lordship, and kingship over the gods, like a bull among cattle. Whoever should desire: "May I attain sovereignty, lordship, and kingship over my equals, like a bull among cattle," let him sacrifice with this sacrificial rite; he will attain sovereignty, lordship, and kingship over his equals, like a bull among cattle.

His *atigrāhya* cup is the bull; he flows as the *aṃśu*, rich in oblation, Soma, the portion for Indra, seeking the *ṛta*, possessing a hundredfold life. May he make me a bull, a steer, dear to the people, possessed of all heroes and excellent heroes. "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Indra, the Bull.
Having wiped it around, he sets it down with: "This is thy womb; [I take thee] acceptable to Indra, the Bull.
Of that [cup] which consists of fifteen [verses], the twenty-first is the form of the Hotṛ’s *praṣṭha-kakud*.

In former times, those desiring to come together with Indra used to sacrifice with the *vaniṣṭhu-sava* (the offering of the rectum), saying, "Indra, being satisfied, will appear to us; we shall declare our desires to him.

One who is about to sacrifice with the *vaniṣṭhu-sava* prepares a hundred uncastrated oxen, a hundred bundles of wood, a hundred vessels of clarified butter, a hundred vessels of milk, a hundred vessels of curd, and a hundred vessels of fat; he also prepares a boat made of *udumbara* wood, capable of being steered from both sides and provided with oars, as well as the boatmen.

With this prepared [oblation], he ceases from the *citrā* sacrifice; then, with the words "O Citrā," he settles down by the eastern fire. A householder takes the *utpavanīya* fire, while one who has established the sacred fires takes the *anvāhāryapacana* fire. Then, at the very onset of night, he places these wood-faggots upon the fire. When they have been kindled, they strike the oxen that are lowing. Then, on the near side of them, they cook the *vaniṣṭhu* (rectum) and the fat. Then, when the sun has risen, he causes [the boat] to move: an udumbara-wood boat, capable of being rowed from both sides, held together by the oarsmen.

Upon it he spreads fifty vessels of clarified butter, fifty vessels of milk, fifty vessels of curds, and fifty vessels of fat. Having scattered the omentum and the fat upon it, he then pours over it fifty vessels of fat, fifty vessels of curds, fifty vessels of milk, and fifty vessels of clarified butter. Then he recites the invitatory verse (*puro’nuvākyā*):

"Indra is the king of what has been settled and of the horned beast; he whose arm wields the thunderbolt. He, the king, dwells among the people; like a felly around the spokes, he encompasses them all."

Indra, the king of the moving world and of men, bestows from above the earth whatever exists in manifold forms. From that, may he grant riches to the donor; may he, being praised, impel the gifts hitherward. With the cry "Svāhā!", Indra indeed becomes manifest to him when satisfied;
to him they declare their desires.
Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa once officiated as the priest for Kānva Andha Vādhryaśva.
On the day preceding the Soma sacrifice, his faith departed from him.
He said, "Adhvaryu, my faith has indeed gone away; restore my sacrifice for me."
He said to him, "That is indeed another matter; tomorrow is the fast-day, and your sacrifice will be completed tomorrow.
He replied, "Let it remain exactly as it is for me.

Having understood this, he placed the *ulūkhala* mortar and *musala* pestle upon a hide in front of the two *havirdhāna* carts and began to pound the rice grains together, saying: "O little mortar, though you are joined in every house, here speak most brilliantly, like the drum of the victors!"

Then, having poured water from the *vasatīvarī* jars into the *hotṛ*-cup and having mixed it together, he offered the oblation with [the verse]: "As people gather together, so do their vows; who would disturb the vow of those observing a vow? O Indra, hear the pressed juice of Kānāndha, the strong draught of Vadhryaśva; enjoy it, Svāhā!

This is the sacrifice of one who is mad, or one whose faith has departed, or one who is led astray. When that [sacrifice] has been completed, he should then perform the *catuṣṭoma-agniṣṭoma* for the sake of pacifying any prior failure.
Manu Vaivasvata desired: "May I create offspring; may I obtain offspring; may I find offspring; may they recognize me through my offspring.

He perceived this sacrificial rite (yajñakratu); he took it up and performed it with it. Then indeed he created offspring, he obtained offspring, he found offspring, and they recognized him through his offspring.
He who should desire, "May I create offspring, may I obtain offspring, may I find offspring, and may they recognize me by my offspring," should sacrifice with this sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*).
Verily he creates offspring, he obtains offspring, he finds offspring, and they recognize him by his offspring.
For that [sacrifice], there are three *prācīnastoma* days, each consisting of three *trivṛt* stomas, three *pañcadaśa* stomas, three *saptadaśa* stomas, and three *ekaviṃśa* stomas.
He desired, "May my offspring be eaters of food; may they obtain food; may they be established in food.

He saw this sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*), he took it up, and he sacrificed with it. Then indeed his offspring became eaters of food, they obtained food, and they were established in food. Whoever should desire, "May my offspring be eaters of food; may they obtain food; may they be established in food," let him sacrifice with this sacrificial rite. His offspring will become eaters of food, he will obtain food, and he will be established in food.
Its stomas are ten; they chant in ten [verses] upon ten [stomas], which is the form of the Virāj. Vāc Āmbhṛṇī desired, "May I attain unlimited glory.
She saw this sacrificial rite, she took it, and she sacrificed with it. Thereupon, indeed, she attained unlimited glory.
He who should desire, "May I attain immeasurable fame," should sacrifice with this sacrificial rite; he indeed attains immeasurable fame.

Its *bahiṣpavamāna* chant consists of ten verses, then a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, a million, ten million, a hundred million, a billion, ten billion, a hundred billion, a trillion, ten trillion, a quadrillion, and finally a quintillion.
Yama Vaivasvata desired, "May I attain sovereignty, overlordship, and kingship over the fathers."
He saw this sacrificial rite; he took it up and performed it with it.

Thereupon, he indeed attained sovereignty, overlordship, and kingship over the ancestors. Whoever should desire, "May I attain sovereignty, overlordship, and kingship over my equals," let him sacrifice with this sacrificial rite;
he attains sovereignty, overlordship, and kingship over his equals.

Having spoken of it constantly in a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, a million, ten million, a hundred million, a billion, ten billion, a hundred billion, a trillion, a quadrillion, a quintillion, and so on up to a parārdha, or even in a padva, a palva— praising with the mind alone— he thinks, "My praise extends this far. Then, having performed the Pravargya once and having proceeded with the Ātithya rite, he prepares the Pravargya on the Gārhapatya fire and performs the ritual with it on the Āhavanīya fire.
At that time he causes it to be removed;
for the guest-offering (ātithya) is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and the Pravargya is glory;
thus he places glory upon the very head of the sacrifice—this is the case for the single-performance of the Pravargya. Now, as for the Pravargya at the Soma-pressing:
Having performed the Pavamāna rite, he sets up the Pravargya in the Āgnīdhra shed;
with that, he proceeds at the Āhavanīya fire itself,
and he removes it at that very time.
"The Pravargya is glory;

verily, he places glory in the head of the sacrifice"—thus [is said regarding] the Sutyā-Pravargya. Now, there is the once-only Pravargya, then the Pravargya at the pressing, and then the Sutyā-Pravargya.
Formerly, Purūravas, the son of Iḍā, was a most excellent king.
The Apsaras Hovraśī set her mind upon him;
desiring him for a full year, she followed after him. For in this way indeed the ancients used to exert themselves, yet she thought that it was too long a time.
As he was running, a hollowed-out chariot appeared before him;
having seen it, the king stopped,
but having stopped, he did not see it, and so he mounted it once again.
Having descended from his chariot, he looked at it and asked the charioteer, "Charioteer, what do you see? "I see you, sir," he replied, "as well as the chariot, the horses, and the road."
He thought to himself, "I am indeed becoming arrogant.
Then a voice addressed him: "You are not to be arrogant; it was I who caused you to look upon this [woman]. Who are you? He replied, "I am Urvaśī, an Apsaras.
She said, "Desiring you for a year, I have followed after you; take me as your wife."
"The gods are indeed difficult to serve," he said. "How are they to be served? [He replied: "I should have a hundred *upasads*."
"Let a hundred jars of clarified butter come to me every day, and let me eat thereof,
but do not look upon me naked"— "All this is quite easy for you, O Blessed One," he said.
Kathā said, "Even a wife does not look upon her husband naked; therefore, you should wear an undergarment. He replied, "Be not naked. He lived with her wearing an undergarment.
She, however, used to cast away each son as soon as he was born.
The king said to her, "O Blessed One, we are indeed human beings who desire sons, yet you cast away each one as soon as they are born.
She replied, "The nights pass away; others have their lifespans exhausted.
Let us both do what is more pleasing."
She gave birth to Āyu and Amāvasu. She said, "Let these two support [us]; they shall reach a full lifespan.
Thus, Āyu departed toward the east.
Of him these Kurupañcālas, Kāśis, and Videhas are the eastern offspring; Āvasu was his western offspring, of whom these Gandhāris, Sparśavas, and Arāṭṭas are the descendants;
and furthermore, Pūrvacitti the Apsaras became his sister.

She reflected: "For a long time indeed my sister has lived among humans; come now, I shall go to her. Having approached her, she was unable to have union with her. Moreover, her herd had strayed away, and she herself had become exhausted. Such indeed was the appearance of former queens;
having assumed the form of a wolf, she sought to seize her. Furthermore, a ewe that was nursing its young was tied to a leg of her throne.
She crushed him; as he was being carried away, he cried out, "I am not a coward!
Hearing this, the king sprang up.
He pursued her and approached her;
she, having become a female mongoose (*nakulī*), went toward him and tore out his inner garment. Then she produced lightning.

She saw him naked in the lightning. Then the king arrived and said, "I have indeed mounted my own chariot, O unconquered one; I have truly mounted a wide expanse. She replied, "I shall send you forth [to the enemy]," and he asked, "What has happened?
She said, "I saw you naked."
When she had gone forth as a renunciant, he wandered about pierced by grief and lamenting.
Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa said to him: "Come, I will cause you to sacrifice with the *śada* [offering]; having caused you to prosper, I will restore you to life.
Then Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa caused him to sacrifice with the *śada*.
Having emerged from the very place of the final offering (avabhṛtha), she beheld him.
Her two sons approached her and said, "Take us there where your destination is; your father is powerful and is grieving for you.
She said, "I shall give birth to both of you, my little sons; I will stay here for exactly three nights, so that the word of a Brahmin may not be in vain."
He dwelt with her for exactly three nights, wearing an inner garment;
he discharged his semen into her,
and she said, "How can this be?"
"How indeed [was this]? the king replied.
She said, "Bring a new pitcher.
He poured it out into that [pitcher]. Now, at Kurukṣetra, there are lotus-pools named Bisavatī.
Of those [sacrificial pits], the northernmost was the Suvarṇasavanī;

into it he cast this [seed], and from that the Aśvattha tree was born. Enclosed by the Śamī wood, the Aśvattha arose from the seed, and the Śamī from the womb; this indeed is the creation of the Śamī-garbha, this is its origin.
Now it is indeed said:
"By means of everything, the gods went to the heavenly world. When this sacrifice descended from the gods to men, it descended specifically onto the *aśvattha* tree.

They made this [Aśvattha tree] his fire-drill, thinking, "This indeed is that sacrifice. Furthermore, whatever Aśvattha tree contains the heartwood of Śamī, when he says, "O Urvaśī, you are Āyu; you are Purūravas," he thereby utters the names of these very father and sons. Alternatively, one may transpose this commonality. When she had departed, he wandered about again, pierced by grief and mourning.
Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa said to him, "Come, I shall officiate for you with the Upaśada; indeed, your misfortune shall surely depart.
Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa then officiated for him with the Upaśada, and thus he removed his misfortune.
These two, indeed, are named Śada and Aupaśada, the descendants of Purūravas.
If one should desire to acquire wealth, one should cause him to sacrifice with the Śada;

for him, ten [verses] are added one by one to the Bahiṣpavamāna, and he presses [the Soma] for the sake of the twenty-one-fold chant. And if one should desire to bestow wealth upon another, one should cause him to sacrifice with the Aupaśada.
In that [twenty-one-fold stoma], during the *bahiṣpavamāna*, one brick is added at each step until ten; then there are two bricks named *prājāpatya*, namely the *śada* and the *upaśada*.
In that [thirty-three-fold stoma], during the *bahiṣpavamāna*, three bricks are added at each step until thirty-six.
In the thirty-six-fold [stoma], three triplets are left over after the *bahiṣpavamāna*; then there are the *śada* and *upaśada* of Kaśyapa Naidhruva;

in his case, four [verses] are added to each of the four [triplets] during the *bahiṣpavamāna*, until reaching forty-eight; in the forty-eight-fold [stoma], four [verses] are left over from each of the four [triplets] after the *bahiṣpavamāna*, until reaching four [remaining].
When the gods and the asuras engaged in a great battle, all these beings divided themselves into two parties: some sided with the gods, and others with the asuras.

Bṛhaspati was the domestic priest (*purohita*) of the gods, and Uśanas Kāvya was that of the asuras. The gods were possessed of sacred knowledge (*brahma*), and the asuras were also possessed of sacred knowledge.
As they could not gain the upper hand in many battles, they took counsel together.
Neither of them knew what would happen in the future; only the Gandharva Sūryavarcas knew it.
Indra was jealous of his wife, so he said to her, "O lady with unblown limbs, ask this Gandharva: 'For what reason do the gods and the Asuras not prevail?'"
He said to him, "So be it; you too should come tomorrow.
Then, within the ocean, he prepared his own wedding with the maiden Hiraṇyakeśī on a golden boat. Now Indra arrived, having become a golden water-bird, and perched upon the rim of the boat.
Knowing that he had indeed arrived, he asked him with joyful limbs, "Tell me this: for what reason do neither the gods nor the asuras achieve victory?
He replied loudly, "Because the boat is hollow.
"The gods possess the *brahman*," he said. "The asuras also possess the *brahman*," [the other] replied.
Having heard that, Indra assumed the form of a tawny boar and sprang up;
as soon as he saw him, [Uśanas] said, "O Maghavan! Whose tawny ones shall conquer? He went and entreated Uśanas Kāvya with his daughter Jayantī and with four wish-fulfilling cows.
Having been thus commanded, he went from among the Asuras to the gods;
then, indeed, the gods won a great battle against the Asuras. He, however, felt as if burdened, as if he had swallowed poison, having accepted much wealth from the Asuras.

He said, "I am like one who has swallowed poison; having accepted much wealth from the Asuras, come, perform a sacrifice for me. Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa performed the sacrifice for him with the twelve-stoma Agniṣṭoma;
having sacrificed with it, he vomited up gold.
Having seen that, he reflected: "Come now, let me carry this away from the Asuras.
Indra, perceiving his intention, turned it into a stone.
These are indeed those stones known as the Auśanasas, located on the mountains in Kurukṣetra.

He acted as if he were light, being without a firm foundation. He said, "I am indeed as if light, being without a foundation; come, perform the sacrifice for me. Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa performed the sacrifice for him with the Agniṣṭoma consisting of the twenty-one-fold Stoma.
Thereupon he indeed stood firm; then Indra won the wish-fulfilling cows.
She said to him in the evening, "It is this [cow] in the morning," and she said to him in the morning, "It is that [cow] in the evening."
In this very manner he led him about for a year.
He said, "In the morning you said 'this'; in the evening you said 'that'."
"Do not speak at dawn! Who is this that comes? Which one is this that comes? O Maghavan, whom do you call 'this'? Having said this, he departed. Then Indra made the hymns (ukthas) yield all desires.
He gave them to Varuṇa, saying, "This is yours, this is mine, and this belongs to both of us together.

[He gave them] to Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa, saying, "I have declared this to both of us; maintain it for us, do not mock this of ours. [And he gave them] to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa. This indeed is the creation of the hymns; this is their foundation.
Then Manu Vaivasvata, feeling himself empty, became his friend; he gave him his fourth daughter,
and he deposited her within him.
This is indeed cultivation; this is the creation of cultivation; this is the root cause. These two *punastoma* sacrifices are called the "Aushanasa" (belonging to Uśanas).

He who might consider himself heavy—as if having swallowed poison, or having officiated at a sacrifice for one for whom he should not have done so, or having accepted what should not have been accepted—him one should cause to sacrifice with the twelve-fold-stoma *agniṣṭoma*; he indeed attains lightness.
Then, he who might act as if light but remains unstable, him one should cause to sacrifice with the twenty-one-fold-stoma *agniṣṭoma*.
It stands facing [the enemy]; then follows the expulsion (*praṇoda*).
The rite for malevolent purposes (*abhicaraṇīya*) is the same; it follows the morning-offering cakes (*prātaḥsavanīya*): a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) for Agni Pravat.

This [offering] consists of the *trivṛt* stoma; then follows the *vibādha*, which is a common ritual art for exorcism (*abhicaraṇīya*) following the midday libations. There is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Vibādhavat;
this too consists of the *trivṛt* stoma; then follows the *pratinoda*.
The ritual art pertaining to the practice of sorcery is common [to all]; it follows the cakes offered at the third pressing. There is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Pratīkāvat;
this indeed becomes the Trivṛt-stoma. Then follows the piercing of Agni; the ritual art pertaining to the practice of sorcery is common.
The animal-cake offering (paśupuroḍāśa) of the Anūbandhya sacrifice follows [the model]. There is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Vasumat;

this indeed becomes threefold (trivṛt). Then there is the Indra-vajra; the ritual artifice (śilpa) pertaining to the practice of sorcery is the same; this [Indra-vajra] becomes fifteenfold (pañcadaśa).
Śunaḥśepa Śaivya was indeed a king who performed meritorious deeds and had many patrons for his sacrifices.

Once, having perceived that his subjects were turning against him, he asked his officiating priests (ṛtvij): "Is there such a sacrificial rite by which, having sacrificed with it, I might depart [in safety]? The priests replied to him, "There is one.
Thereupon, the Adhvaryu priest drew the cups (grahas) accompanied by *puroruks* that were not born from a womb.
The Udgātṛ chanted the Sāmans with the *svaras*, without the *nidhanas* and without the *iḍās*;
the Hotṛ recited the *arghya* verses facing away;
he died immediately after emerging from the *avabhṛtha*.
If one should hate someone, he should perform a sacrifice for that person, or he should officiate at a sacrifice for one who has approached him;
indeed, he quickly departs from this world. Now, they speak of "the heap and the non-heap": at the Catuṣṭoma, he gives grain made into a heap;

that is the "heap" (rāśi), and the Catuṣṭoma itself is the "non-heap" (marāya). Then they speak of "the ointment and the salve": the officiating priests proceed with their eyes anointed and themselves adorned.

That sacrifice belongs to one who has applied ointment, who is anointed, who wears garments of deerskin, and whose sacrificial shed faces in various directions; it is the sacrifice of one who has rivals.
