He chooses the place for the sacrifice in such a way that it slopes toward the east from the Āhavanīya fire and toward the west from the Gārhapatya fire.
Therefore, they measure out these two sheds facing opposite directions; they perform the rites moving eastward and westward;
the Gārhapatya fire is situated in the middle.

They bring the portions of food to him as he sits in the middle; "there should be two *stomas* for each direction"—this is one view; "there should be two *ekaviṃśas*"—this is another view; disregarding that, they perform only the *catuṣṭoma*.

When the gods and the Asuras engaged in a great battle, Śibi Auśīnara won the Asuras from the ranks of the gods. Indra granted him a boon for his victory, and he said, "May no fear ever come upon me while I am in my house."

He caused him to sacrifice with the Sarvatomukha on the Varṣiṣṭhīya plateau. Therefore, indeed, that fear which is called the "Shibi-Naiṣṭhya" does not come upon him whom he desires should conquer unconquerably; one should cause such a person to sacrifice with the Sarvatomukha on the Varṣiṣṭhīya plateau, and he conquers unconquerably.
Thus, they measure out these four halls according to the cardinal directions.
They proceed toward the east, they proceed toward the south, they proceed toward the west, and they proceed toward the north;
the Gārhapatya fire is in the middle.

While seated in the middle, they carry the portions for consumption on mules and mule-carts according to the directions, thinking, "May the Stomas be in accordance with the quarters"—this is one view.
Disregarding the statement that "there should be twenty-one-fold [stomas]," the Pārthas perform only those [sacrifices] with four stomas.
Pārtha, the carpenter, desired the gods;
he pressed Soma for those who give a thousand-fold dakṣiṇā, and he pressed it a thousand times; thus he attained the gods.

Intending to fetch these Soma plants, he prepares a thousand halls, a thousand [other] halls, and a thousand chariots drawn by mules; they measure out these halls according to the directions: two hundred and fifty to the east, likewise to the south, likewise to the west, and likewise to the north. They proceed forward, they proceed to the south, they proceed to the west, and they proceed to the north;
in the center stands the Gārhapatya fire.

While she is seated in the middle, they carry food in chariots drawn by mules; "the Stomas should be [in] every direction"—this is one view; "they should be twenty-one-fold"—this is another; disregarding those two views, they perform only the Catuṣṭoma.
When one is about to perform the sacrifice with the two Yamastomas,
he selects a sacrificial ground (devayajana) such that there would be a path for movement to the north between the Cātvāla pit and the Utkara heap;
thus they measure out these two sheds side by side.
Having settled upon the southern shed, having churned the fire and distributed the fires, he performs the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering;
then, having settled upon the northern shed, having churned the fire and distributed the fires, he performs the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering.
Having performed it here, he then performs it there; here he offers the *dīkṣā* oblations, and then there. Here he performs the *prāyaṇīyā* offering, and then there.
Having performed [the rites] here, one performs them there; having moved here by means of a footstep, having purchased and carried away the King, one offers hospitality there.

Therefore, having performed [the rites] here, he performs them there; first, he performs the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites here, then there; in the middle, he performs the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites here, then there; here, he performs the first tracing-out of the *mahāvedi*, then there; here, he performs the final *pravargya* and *upasad* rites, then there; here, he brings forward the *āhavanīya* fire, then there; here, he erects the *sadas* and *havirdhāna* sheds, then there; here, he brings forward Agni and Soma, then there.
He erects the sacrificial post according to the procedure for the post; having set up the post with its wooden cupola, he dedicates the animal for Agni and Soma.

Then, as there [in the Soma sacrifice], so here: having proceeded with the omentum in the established manner, he takes the Vasatīvarī waters; then, as there, so here: he offers the animal-cake. Then, as there...

Having performed [the rites] here, he performs them there; having performed with the Agniṣomīya [animal sacrifice] here, he performs it there. Having carried the Vasatīvarī waters around here, they remain fasting after setting aside the milks; then, having settled down here, they settle down there. Having brought down the King [Soma] here, he begins the Prātaranuvāka; then, the pressings (savana) are completed here in successive order until the conclusion, and likewise in the northern hall the pressings are completed until the conclusion. Here he performs the Avabhṛtha bath; then there he offers the Udayanīyā iṣṭi. Then there...
Having performed [the rites] here, he performs them there; then, right here, he dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa, and having performed [the rites] there, he performs them here again.

The *udavasānīyā* sacrifice is the same in both cases. Now, as for the fact that the interconnected rituals are performed prior to the pressings (*savana*), it is therefore that the two Yamas lie together, intertwined within the belly.
Now, because the pressings (savana) are completed in successive order, therefore they are born in succession;

and because after the pressings the rites are performed in an interwoven manner, therefore they lie down together, suckle together, and move about together; and because the kindling-wood (araṇi) is common, therefore their origin is the same.

Agni and Āditya, desiring to win the same world, perceived this sacrificial rite; they took it up and sacrificed with it. Thereupon, indeed, those two came to possess the same world; they attained a common world. He who should desire, "May I go to the same world as Agni and Āditya," should sacrifice with this sacrificial rite; he surely goes to the same world as Agni and Āditya.

One is indeed a sacrificer of the *vāja* (strength/oblation), while another is a sacrificer of the *vājapeya*. He is truly a sacrificer of the *vāja* who, without having sacrificed with the *peyas*, then sacrifices with the *vāja*; and he is a sacrificer of the *vājapeya* who, having sacrificed with the *peyas*, then sacrifices with the *vāja*.
Therefore, one should sacrifice with the *vāja* only after having sacrificed with the *peyas*;
for one becomes [fit] to sacrifice with the *peyas* [only after that].
Without having performed the Full Moon sacrifice, he undergoes initiation;
his period of initiation is unlimited, and there are twelve Upasad days.
He purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks, "My Soma-pressing will coincide with the New Moon day, which is fit for sacrifice."
For him, it is accomplished in this manner:

having emerged from the fast-day (upavasatha) with the well-known ritual procedure, and having carried around the Vasatīvarī waters and set aside the milks, they remain in retreat. Then he offers this Savaneṣṭi sacrifice: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, one on eleven potsherds for Indra, and one on twelve potsherds for the Viśve Devas; with that he sacrifices for twelve days. Then, on the thirteenth day, he sacrifices with the Full-moon oblation which has not yet been offered by him. Then, on the fourteenth day, he sacrifices with the New-moon oblation which has not yet been offered by him. Then, of these...
He performs one of the sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*), and then he undergoes initiation again;
in this very manner he sacrifices for a year.

Its days are: the *trivṛt*, the *pañcadaśa*, then the *trivṛt*, the *saptadaśa*, then the *trivṛt*, the *ekaviṃśa*, then the *trivṛt*, the *triṇava*, then the *trivṛt*, the *trayastriṃśa*, and then the *trivṛt* with the *catuṣṭoma*; these are the forms of the months, which are to be drunk.

Vāja is the form of the year; thus this year of his is sought after and thus becomes attained. Now follows the rule for the Ahīna sacrifice: its days are the Trivṛt, Pañcadaśa, Saptadaśa, and Catuṣṭoma, and then again a Trivṛt; then the Ekaviṃśa, then the Triṇava, then the Catuṣṭoma, and then again a Trivṛt; then the Trayastriṃśa, then the Catuṣṭoma, and then again a Trivṛt; then the Catuścatvāriṃśa, then the Catuṣṭoma, and then the Atirātra. There are twelve months and seventeen sacrifices. In nine months he goes through nine sacrifices, and there remain three months and eight sacrifices.
He performs two three-night rites and one two-night rite; however, if he should exceed this, he should sacrifice with the fourfold Agniṣṭoma.

The Stomas and Śastras are the form of the months; the Agniṣṭoma is the form of the year, and the Vāja is likewise [the form] of this year. Thus, this year is sought after and thus becomes attained. Now, therefore, regarding the odd and the even: they chant on one verse, then on three—this is for the odd; then they chant on four, then on eight—this is for the even. Those who proceed by this path, and those who know it thus, attain union and co-residence with both the odd and the even.
Now, therefore, regarding the quarters: the Trivṛt belongs to the eastern quarter.
The fifteenfold [stoma] is for the south;
the seventeenfold for the west; the twenty-onefold for the north; and the twenty-sevenfold for that which is above this.
The Trayastrimsha is from this world downward;
for all the quarters, they attain union and co-residence with the Catustoma. Those who proceed by this path and those who know it thus [attain this]. Now, therefore, regarding the seasons:
the Trivrt belongs to spring.
The fifteenfold [stoma] belongs to summer,
the seventeenfold to the rainy season, and the twenty-onefold to autumn.
The Triṇava belongs to the winter, the Trayastriṃśa to the cool season;

the Catuṣṭoma belongs to all the seasons. Those who proceed by this course, and those who know it thus, attain union with and residence in the same world as the seasons. Now, therefore, [concerning] the seers themselves—
The Trivṛt belongs to Vasiṣṭha, the Pañcadaśa to Bharadvāja,
the Saptadaśa to Viśvāmitra, and the Ekaviṃśa to Jamadagni.
The Triṇava belongs to Kaśyapa;
the Trayastriṃśa to Gautama; the Catuṣṭoma to Agastya.
All indeed attain union with and residence in the same world as the Ṛṣis who proceed by this path and those who know it thus. Now, therefore, [concerning] the deities themselves—
The threefold [stoma] belongs to Agni, the fifteenfold to Indra,
the seventeenfold to Prajāpati, and the twenty-onefold to yonder burning sun.
The Triṇava belongs to the Moon;

the Trayastriṃśa belongs to the Viśvedevas. All those who proceed by this course, as well as those who know it thus, attain union with and residence in the same world as all the deities of the Catuṣṭoma.
Now, therefore, they speak of the course of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
Some say that the course of the sun and the moon is [the sacrifice];
one who is about to sacrifice with the Soma of the Full Moon undergoes initiation.
His consecrations (dīkṣās) are unlimited; there are six preparatory days (upasads).
He purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks, "My Soma-pressing will coincide with the full-moon day, the sacrificial day";
for him, it happens accordingly.

Having emerged from the Upavasatha day by means of the well-known ritual procedure, and having carried around the Vasatīvarī waters and set aside the milks, they remain in residence. Then, in the morning, he dedicates the animal victim to Agni;
for that sacrifice, one dedicated to Agni-Soma is to be seized as an additional victim.
For this [Agni] sacrifice, the Full-moon oblations follow the morning Soma-pressing offerings.
The *savanīya* offerings are accompanied by *praiṣa*-calls; for the other oblations, one should recite the invitatory verses and offer with the *yajyā* directly.
The *jyotir-ukthya* sacrifice concludes. One who intends to perform the *soma* sacrifice with the *āmāvāsya* [rite] undergoes initiation (*dīkṣate*).
His initiation lasts for an unlimited number of days, with twelve Upasad days;
he purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks, "My Soma-pressing will coincide with the new moon day, the day sacred to sacrifice," and for him it happens accordingly.

He proceeds from the Upavasatha day by means of the well-known ritual procedure. On this day, the calves belonging to Indra have been driven away; he causes the milk for Indra to be milked according to the procedure for the *saṃnāyya*, or silently. Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and set aside the various portions of milk, they remain in attendance. Then, in the morning, he dedicates the animal victim to Agni; for that, a bull belonging to Indra is to be seized as an additional offering. Following the morning libations of that [bull], the oblations of the New Moon sacrifice take place.
The *savanīya* offerings are accompanied by *praiṣa* formulas; for the other oblations, one should recite the invitatory verses and say, "Recite the offering verse.
Thus, the *jyotis-atirātra* sacrifice is concluded in its direct form.
Those who proceed by this path and those who know it thus attain union with and residence in the same world as the sun and the moon—those who know it thus, and those who know it thus.
"One desiring heaven should pile the Sāvitra [fire-altar].
If it is piled at a Paśubandha sacrifice, one should offer the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ-oblation, offer the Yūpāhuti-oblation, prepare the sacrificial post with its formula, and measure out the altar;
it is known that one should sacrifice on a third of the altar."

Its measurement is like that of the *saumika* [sacrifice], with this much difference: from the *saumika* *prakrama*, one-third part shall be the *prakrama*. With that, he measures the altar (*vedi*). Alternatively, the diagonal side-measure is a *pada*, and the cross-measure is a *pada*; of these two, that *prakrama* which is equal to the corner (diagonal) is intended.

Or, from that [central] point, the ninth step toward the southeast—whichever of those two is measured by the distance of the ear—that is the measure for the *prakrama*; by that, the Soma-altar is to be measured. He should add the fires, enter upon the vow, prepare the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and perform the *stambayajus* rite. This very procedure is well-established according to the *Pauroḍāśika* [Kalpa]: three times with the formula and the fourth time silently; he performs the first tracing of the altar, mutters the *karaṇa* formula, digs up the earth, and from what has been dug up, the Āgnīdhra carries it away three times.
When the Āgnīdhra has carried it away three times, then he measures this fire-altar westward from the peg at the hole for the sacrificial post (*yūpāvaṭīya-śaṅku*).

"The altar should be measured according to its side," it is said; thus, this [measurement] is declared to be merely the size of a chariot wheel. Furthermore, they cite: "The first wheel is two *aratnis* [in diameter], the middle one is two and a half, and the uppermost is three less one-third.

Having made a cord of any one of these lengths with loops at both ends, having driven a peg into the center of the site for the *uttaravedi*, and having fastened the two loops to that [peg], he throws another peg at the end [of the cord] and traces a circle around it clockwise.

Having removed the cord, they dig the furrows and raise the *apasyā* trenches, making them wider toward the south and the west. Then he asks for the vessel of clarified butter together with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), the wooden sword (*sphya*), a bunch of *darbha* grass, a water-pot, the materials for the high altar (*uttaravedi*), curds mixed with honey, gold, pebbles, sand, and *darbha* grass; having taken all this, they place it together on the northern half [of the altar]. Then, with two verses—"I take Agni first within me" and "The Agni who is ours"—he takes the fire into himself and mutters the *svayaṃcit* formula: "Those logs of thine, O Agni, those abodes... and so forth.

Having touched a white horse, he places this [brick] upon the gravel with the formula: "May Prajāpati settle you; by that deity, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, sit firm! Then, having pulled up the peg and poured out a vessel of water, he places a bunch of Darbha grass, either with the formula "May Vāc settle you in the ocean," or silently. Then he makes offerings over it with five spoonfuls using the verses beginning with "In harmony with the year, with the days...
Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse.

Then, according to the procedure for the *cātvāla*, he traces around the *cātvāla*; according to the procedure for the *uttaravedi*, he pours out the earth for the *uttaravedi*. Having leveled the *uttaranābhi* and dug the post-hole (*yūpāvaṭa*), having sprinkled it and poured the libation over it, and having adorned it, he pours sand upon it with the six verses in their respective meters beginning with "O Agni, yours is glory and vigor.

Then he lays down the upward-facing bricks (*ūrdhvacit*) with the formula: "You are piled; you are piled around; as upward-piling ones, take your place! By that deity, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, sit firm! Then he spreads them over with the *Gāyatrī* verse "Swell up" for a Brāhmaṇa, and with the *Triṣṭubh* verse "May your milk-masses unite" for a Rājanya.
He arranges it as smoothly as possible, as evenly as sugar-grains.

Upon it, he draws nine circular lines. Then, having mixed the sugar-grains with curds and honey and sprinkled them [over the ground], he performs the evening *agnihotra* sacrifice, strews grass around the fires, and observes the fast. Then, after the morning *agnihotra* has been offered, he asks for a water-pot, ashes, loose soil, crucibles, sand, and one hundred and eighty-five gold bricks—or sugar-grains—smeared with ghee, each measuring as much as the highest joint of the finger, which is commensurate with the "joint of the sacrifice" (*yajñaparu*). There are an equal number of *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks, or an unlimited number, as well as four *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks.
"One should offer a thousand pieces of gold; some say that after three [pieces], they are unlimited.

If there are a thousand, two hundred each are placed upon the leaf-veins. Then, when the sun has risen, he takes the fire into himself with two verses: "I first take Agni into myself," and "The Agni who is ours... He mutters the *svayaṃcit* formula: "O Agni, those logs of thine, those abodes of thine... and so forth.
Having touched the white horse, he mutters over the mounting-block with two verses: "This is the descent-place of the waters; homage to thee," and so forth.
Then, in the rear half, he places a vessel of water with the formula: "Speech, I place thee as the ocean, bestowing good progeny, bestowing abundance of wealth, for me, the sacrificer."

Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse; then he pours down the ritual materials (*saṃbhāra*s): "Thou art the ash of Agni," for the ash; "Thou art the soil of Agni," for the soil; "Thou art consciousness, the upholder of desires," for the saline earth (*ūṣa*); "May thy upholding of desires be in me," for the sand. Then he mixes them together with the verse: "Those bodies of yours which are dear, may your hearts be united."

"May you be dear to me; may my bodies be dear to you"—with these words he then arranges them, saying: "May heaven and earth be in harmony; may the waters and plants be in harmony; may the fires be in harmony separately for my preeminence, being of one vow.
He arranges them in such a way that the lines do not overlap, or else everything is performed at once in a single session.

Then, on the innermost line, he lays down fifteen *iṣṭakā*s for the days of the bright fortnight with the formulas: "With that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm as *saṃjñāna* (unification); with that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm as *vijñāna* (discernment).

In the intervals between them, he lays down fifteen *muhūrta*-bricks for these very days with the formulas: "With that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm as *citra* (the bright one); with that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm as *ketu* (the banner)."

Beyond all [the bricks] he places the *sūdadohas* verses. Then, on the inner line, he lays down fifteen *kṣapā*-bricks of the bright fortnight with the formulas: "The *darśā*, by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras; the *dṛṣṭā*, by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras," and so on.

In the intervals between them, he lays down fifteen *muhūrta*-bricks of those very nights with the formulas: "The *dātā*, by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras; the *pradātā*, by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras," and so on.

Beyond all [the bricks] he places the *sūdadohas* verse. Then, within the inner line, he lays down the bricks of the waning fortnight on their respective days, with the formulas: "Established by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm; praised by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm"—fifteen [in number].

In the intervals between them, he lays down the *muhūrta*-bricks of these very days, with the formulas: "Savitṛ, by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm; Prasavitṛ, by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm"—fifteen [in number].

On the far side of all [the lines] he places the *sūdadohas* verse; then, on the inner line, he lays down fifteen bricks for the nights of the waning fortnight with the formulas: "The pressed one—with that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm! The pressing one—with that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm!

In the intervals between these, he lays down fifteen *muhūrta*-bricks belonging to those very nights with the formulas: "The accuser—with that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm! The consent-giver—with that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm! and so forth.

At the end of all [the bricks], he performs the *sūdadohas* verse. Then, on the inner line, he lays down the bricks of the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the formulas: "By that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm; for the purpose of purifying, by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm"—twelve [bricks].

At the end of all [these], he performs the *sūdadohas* verse. Then, on the inner line, he lays down the bricks of the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) with the formulas: "The victorious one, by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm; the more victorious one, by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm"—twelve [bricks].

At the end of all [the bricks], he pronounces the *sūdadohas* formula. Then, on the inner line, he lays down the month-bricks (*māseṣṭakā*) with the formulas: "With that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm; Aruṇarajas, with that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm"—thus thirteen [bricks].
At the end of all [these], he pronounces the *sūdadohas* formula. Now, some here pour sand into the intervals between the lines with the verses beginning, "The moving ones, the living ones..."

Then, on the inner line, he lays down the Muhūrta-bricks, fifteen in number, with the formulas: "At this time, by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras; at that time, by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras."

Beyond all of them, he places the *sūdadohas* verse. Then, within the inner line, he lays down the *kratviṣṭakā*s and the *artviṣṭakā*s with the formulas: "The *agniṣṭoma*—by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! The *ukthya*—by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm!"—these six; and [the formulas]: "Agni is the season—by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! Sūrya is the season—by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm!"—these three.

At the end of all [the bricks], he performs the *sūdadohas* verse; then, in the middle at the navel, he lays down the *saṃvatsara*-bricks with the formulas: "By that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! and "The year, by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm!"—thus four [bricks].
At the end of all [these], he performs the *sūdadohas* verse;
then he asks for these four *svayamātṛṇṇā* stones.

He places those [bricks] in the quarters: "Bhūḥ! Agni and the earth," in the east; "Bhuvaḥ! Vāyu and the intermediate space," in the south; "Svaḥ! Āditya and the sky," in the west; "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! Candramas and the quarters," in the north. At the end of all [these formulas], he recites the *sūdadohas* verse. Then he lays down the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks with the formula: "Fill the space, fill the gap; sit down, you who are auspicious. May Indra, Agni, and Bṛhaspati settle you in this womb."

He performs the *tayādevata* formula: "By that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm. Then he performs the *sūdadohas* verse: "These dappled ones, yielding milk for him, mix the Soma; the clans of the gods at his birth in the three luminous realms of heaven. Here, with the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks facing eastward, he pours forth [the earth]; they cover Agni completely with the eastward-facing bricks. Once covered, he draws around it with a *palāśa* branch, saying: "Fill the space, fill the gap. Then it remains untouched by the *citikḷpti* formula. Then he touches Agni with two verses: "That part of thee which is unheaped, O Agni, and that which is heaped... (and so on).

Here, he touches this layer with the verse addressed to Agni, "The wise one discerns thought and non-thought," and with the Gāyatrī verse beginning, "O Agni, bring the gods here. Having touched this layer, he mutters the two formulas for descending: "May speech be in my mouth" and "Giver of breath. Then, having touched a black horse, he lays down the body-filler (tanūpurīṣa) with the verse, "He who is praised in heaven."

Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he performs the *sūdadohas* recitation. Then, having poured water into a vessel and scattered pieces of gold therein, he sprinkles them two by two with the formulas: "Thou art the measure of a thousand" in the east; "Thou art the image of a thousand" in the south; "Thou art the counterpart of a thousand" in the west; and "Thou art the counter-measure of a thousand" in the north. Then he sprinkles the center with two hundred [pieces] with the formula: "Thou art thousandfold; for a thousand thee. Then, standing on the northern half, [he addresses] the bricks that are cows.

"Make these bricks of mine, O Agni, into milch-cows," he says, up to the end of the section. At this point, some offer goat's milk with an *arka*-leaf upon the final brick. Now, if he intends to perform this rite, he then makes a hollow in that *arka*-leaf so that it drips through the middle; standing facing north, holding it at the level of his mouth, he calls out, "Bring it here! When the stream reaches the brick, he begins the recitation with the verse, "Thou, O Agni, art Rudra," up to the end of the section. At this point, he throws that *arka*-leaf onto the path where the cattle pass by of the person whom he hates.

If, however, he does not hate anyone, he deposits [the fire] in a hole dug by a rat and then worships it with the anuvāka: "Thou alone knowest thyself; who thou art, that thou art. Then he worships it with the *saṃhāra* and *vihāra* formulas, with the anuvāka: "Thou art the *saṃvatsara*; thou art the *parivatsara*. Then he says, "O Hotṛ, recite the *uktha* for Agni," and the Hotṛ should recite the *uktha* for Agni. If the Hotṛ does not desire to do so, the sacrificer himself, having spread grass behind the fire and sat down upon it, should recite the *uktha* for Agni.

He recites each of these verses—"bhūr," "bhuvaḥ," and "svar"—three times over with the *praṇava* (the syllable *om*) at the end. In this manner, wherever there is a connection between *ṛc*-verses, the connection is made by means of the *praṇava* alone. Regarding this, if one does not bring sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) for those Brahmins who are learned in many [Vedic branches], the sacrifice would be ill-performed and they might seize his fire;
therefore, he should give to them according to his faith.
"Thus this is performed as a well-offered sacrifice; 'they do not exclude his fire,' so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then, beginning with the placing of the fuel, the ritual pertaining to the animal sacrifice (paśubandha) is carried out."

Having performed the rites up to the carrying forward of the fire (praṇayana), having carried forward the fire and kindled it, and having offered the oblations of the Adhvara, he offers these following oblations with separate fourfold-drawn portions:
"O Agni, you are Rudra" is the form of the Śatarudriya;
"O Agni and Viṣṇu" is for the Vasordhārā; and "O Lord of Waters" is the oblation of food (annahoma).

With the verses, "Seven are thy fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven thy tongues," and "The one who pleases all," he then offers twenty-one oblations with the dipping-spoon (sruva), striking it each time, saying, "To Asu, svāhā! To Vasu, svāhā!
Having offered them one by one, he pours the remnants from the ladles into the joined palms of the sacrificer.

With those remnants, the sacrificer wipes his face. Then, with the section beginning, "Rājñī, Virājñī," the ritual procedure pertaining to the animal sacrifice (paśubandha) is performed, starting from the second tracing of the altar.

Having performed the *siddham* rite up to the *manotā*, having recited the *manotā* hymn and touched the portions of the victim, he takes the *mṛtyugraha* (the cup for Death) of the broth in a vessel made of *udumbara* wood, reciting: "Sing to the wise Pavamāna," followed by: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Death."

Having wiped it around with *darbha* grass, he places it upon the northern altar with the formula: "This is thy womb; for Death thee! Then he proceeds with the animal sacrifice, then he proceeds with the *vanaspati* offering, and then, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, when about to offer this cup, he touches water with the formula: "Thou art lightning; strike away my evil. Then he offers: "Strike away death, strike away hunger, strike away this curse; then, O Agni, bring hither to us thousandfold abundance of wealth."

"O Death, those thousand and ten-thousand nooses of yours intended for the slaying of mortal man—those we all expiate with the power of the sacrifice, svāhā! Having offered thus, he should touch water, saying, "Thou art the rain; rain down my evil. Then he proceeds with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. When the *iḍā* is being invoked, they take hold of the cup. The sacrificer consumes the invoked cup, saying: "Thou art the food, the drink of immortality. Of thee, who hast been drunk by Death, who art possessed of immortality, who hast been made 'well-said' (*svagākṛta*), who art honey-sweet, and who art invoked—I, being invoked, partake."

Having consumed [the portion] for himself, he touches himself with the mantra beginning, "Mandrābhibhūtiḥ keturyajñānām," up to the end of the section. From the *anūyāja* offerings onwards, the ritual procedure pertaining to the animal sacrifice (*pāśubandhika*) is performed;
it is established [to proceed] until the time for the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). At the time of the sacrificial fees, having given a cow, a bull, and an ox, he gives twenty-one sacrificial fees;
he gives a hundred.
He gives a thousand; he gives bricks as the sacrificial fee.
If he cannot find them, he should give as many stirred-drinks (mantha) or boiled-rice portions (odana); or he should give a pregnant heifer; he gives gold.
"He gives clothing;

thereby he extends his life," so says the Brāhmaṇa. If one should pile [the fire-altar] during the Soma sacrifice, [one should perform] the preparation of the site during the first Upasad, the laying down of the bricks between the middle and the last Upasads, the carrying forward of the fire at the proper time, and the giving of the sacrificial fees at the time for the fees.
[There is] the cup for Mṛtyu from the broth of the Savanīya animal.

If one should pile that [Agni] in a sacrificial session (*sattra*) that is not deficient (*ahīna*), the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are on the first day; on the first day there is the cup for Mṛtyu from the broth, but in a *sattra* no sacrificial fees are led forth;
the cup for Mṛtyu should belong to the Nāciketa fire alone—this is another view.
Having piled the fire-altar, one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī or with the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa.
When the evening *agnihotra* has been offered, the evening milking takes place; when the morning *agnihotra* has been offered, the morning milking takes place;
it is cooked together with the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), and the ritual performance occurs before the sun has risen.
The Sāvitra [fire-altar] is completed; now,
the preparation of the site for the Nāciketa [fire-altar] is well-known, being exactly the same as that of the Sāvitra, with this much difference alone.

There are no lines here; then he lays down the Yajus-formulas with his joined palms, saying, "Thou art the world, thou art the heavenly world," and he lays down twenty-one [bricks] wherever they fall.

This same principle applies elsewhere as well for the placement of scattered materials: if it is fivefold (pāṅkta), there are five in the east, five in the south, five in the west, five in the north, and one in the middle; or if it is threefold (trivṛt), there are seven in the east, three in the south, seven in the west, three in the north, and one in the middle; or if they are directed upwards, starting from the rear corner up to the space of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick; or if they are directed eastward, starting from the space of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick.

From the naturally perforated stones (*svayamātṛṇṇā*) onwards, the procedure is established; from this point forward, if he should desire, "May I be radiant, glorious, and endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*)," he should step forward toward the *hotṛ*'s hearth from the vicinity of the *āhavanīya* fire, saying: "She who has gone forth eastward, she who is glorious—may she cover me with radiance, glory, and spiritual luster."

"He becomes resplendent, glorious, and endowed with the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*). Now, if he should desire, "May they have the greatest faith in me; may they bring the most abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*s)," then while the fees are being led forth, he should take a portion with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) and offer it into the *āhavanīya* fire with the formula: "O East, come! O East, come! May the East, enjoying it, partake of the clarified butter, svāhā!
Thus, they have the greatest faith in him and they bring the most abundant sacrificial fees—so says the Brāhmaṇa. The Nāciketa [fire-altar] is concluded.
Now, the preparation of the site for the Brahmacit is well-known, being exactly the same as that for the Sāvitra, with this much difference.

No lines are drawn here; then, in front, he lays down ten *daśahotṛ* bricks facing northward with the formulas: "Thought is the ladle; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! Thought is the clarified butter; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm!"—thus ten. Then he lays down the *hṛdayeṣṭakā* (heart-brick), reciting: "He knows the golden heat, the longing one," and continuing: "The mental self of men, together with the gods"—thus far. Then he lays down two *yajuriṣṭakā* (formula-bricks) with: "Agni with the *yajus*-formulas; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm!"

"Savitṛ [is established] with hymns; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! Then he places two Patnī bricks: "The army of Indra; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! The speech of Bṛhaspati; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm!"

On the far side of all [the bricks], he performs the *sūdadohas* formula; then, to the south, he lays down four *caturhotṛ*-bricks facing eastward with the formulas: "The earth is the Hotṛ; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! Heaven is the Adhvaryu; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! Thus he lays down four. Then he lays down the *hṛdayeṣṭakā*, reciting: "Brahman is Indra, Agni... and so on, up to "...the seers have perceived this sacrifice of the *caturhotṛ*s as their own self. Thereafter, he lays down two *yajus*-bricks with the formula: "Indra with the hymns of praise (*ukthāmadaiḥ*)... and so on.
"By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras; by the blessing of Mitra and Varuṇa, by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras."

Then he lays down two Patnīṣṭakā bricks with the formulas: "Thou art Pathyā Svasti, of Pūṣan; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm! and "Thou art Vāk, of Vāyu; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm! At the end of all these, he performs the Sūdadohas rite. Then, behind [the altar], he lays down five Pañcahotṛ bricks facing north with the formulas: "Agni is the Hotṛ; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm! and "The Aśvins are the Adhvaryus; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm! Or rather, he lays down four bricks, or even two bricks sharing the same deity, using only this mantra: "The Aśvins are the Adhvaryus."

He modifies the mantra: "With that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras. Then he lays down the Heart-brick, reciting: "A hundred teams attend thee," followed by: "The breath is the caul; by it I am fashioned out of immortality. Then he lays down two Yajus-bricks: "O Aṅgiras, with the Dhiṣṇiya fires, with that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras"; "O Maruts, with the Sadas and the Havirdhāna, with that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras. Then he lays down the Patnī-bricks: "Dīkṣā..."

"By that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm; by the deity Agni, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm"—with these words, at the end of all [the formulas], he performs the *sūdadohas* verse. Then, on the north side, facing eastward, he lays down six *ṣaḍdhota*-bricks with the formulas: "Vāc is the Hotṛ; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm; Dīkṣā is the wife; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm. Having recited the verse, "The golden vessel encompassed by the dust," he then lays down the *hṛdayeṣṭakā* (heart-brick), which is the very self of Indra.

With the verse beginning "Moving in a hundred ways," he then lays down two Yajus-bricks: "The waters with the sprinkling-waters; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! The plants with the sacrificial grass; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! Then he lays down two Patnī-bricks: "The Gāyatrī of the Vasus; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! The Triṣṭubh of the Rudras; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! At the end of all these, he pronounces the Sūdadohas verse. Then, above them, he lays down seven Hotṛ-bricks facing eastward.

He lays down [the bricks] with the formulas: "The Mahāhavis Hotṛ; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm! The Satyahavis Adhvaryu; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm! Or rather, he lays down two bricks having the same deity with this mantra: "Anādhṛṣya and Apratidhṛṣya, the protectors of the sacrifice. He adapts the mantra to: "By that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit ye both firm! Then he lays down the Hṛdayeṣṭakā with the verse: "Indra, the king, who is the lord of the moving world..."

Thus, up to the end of the section, he then lays down the *yajus*-bricks with thirteen formulas: "Aditi by the altar; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras! Soma by consecration; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras! Then he lays down the *patnī*-bricks with eighteen formulas: "The *jagatī* of the Ādityas; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras! The *anuṣṭubh* of Viṣṇu; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras!"

At the end of all [these formulas], he performs the *sūdadohas* verse; then, according to the available space, he lays down the *graha*-bricks: with "O Lord of Speech, ordainer, by name," [he lays one] of the *daśahotṛ*; with "O Lord of Speech, by the power of speech," [one] of the *caturhotṛ*; with "Soma is the precursor of Soma," [one] of the *pañcahotṛ*; with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar," [one] of the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ*; and with "O Lord of Speech, ordainer of the heart, by name," [one] of the *saptahotṛ*. At the end of all [these], he performs the *sūdadohas* verse; then, according to the available space, he likewise lays down the *pratigraha*-bricks.
Having recited "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he places nineteen bricks with the formula "This is thy right-hand [gift], O Kāma; may Aṅgiras take thee upturned.

Or alternatively, he places two bricks dedicated to the same deity with the formula "To the Gandharvas and Apsarases, the garland and ornaments," and modifies the mantra by adding "With that deity, like Aṅgiras, sit ye firm."
From the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stones onwards, it is established; from that point upward, the *brahmacit* remains completed. Now follows the [ritual] for the whole.
The preparation of the sacrificial site is well known; as for Sāvitra, it is just this much that is different:
the first layer is the Sāvitra fire-altar, the second is the Lokampṛṇā, and the third is the Nāciketa.
The *lokaṃpṛṇā* is the fourth layer; the *brahmacit* is the fifth;
in all layers, there is a naturally perforated stone (*svayamātṛṇṇā*).
With the verses, "The layers end in soil; O Agni, bring the gods here," he touches the five layers.

If he should pile [the fire-altar] on the final day of the Soma sacrifice, he should worship with the *divaḥ śyenī* verses before the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering, and with the *apāghā* verses after the *udavasānīyā* offering;
having performed them once, he combines them.
It remains complete; now,
the preparation of the site for the Vaiśvasṛja sacrifice is well-known, being exactly the same as that of the Sāvitra, with this much difference.

There are three lines; then he places [the bricks] upon the innermost line with the eighteen verses beginning, "That which is immortal and that which is mortal," and at the end of all of them he performs the *sūdadohas* rite. Then he places [the bricks] upon the next inner line with the fifteen verses beginning, "All the quarters, in the quarters," and at the end of all of them he performs the *sūdadohas* rite. Then he places [the bricks] upon the next inner line with the nine verses beginning, "All the heavens, all the gods in heaven."
At the conclusion of all [the verses], he performs the *sūdadohas* formula.

From the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stones onwards, the procedure is established as already described. If one should pile [the fire-altar] during an *ahīna* or a *sattra* sacrifice—such as the hundred-night *viśvajit* with all the *pṛṣṭha* stotras—at the time for the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), the Brahman priest, seated in the *sadasya* shed, recites the *vaiśvasṛja* formulas: "The eastern direction of the verses is called the Great One," and so on, verse by quarter, half-verse by half-verse, and sentence by sentence according to the Brāhmaṇa.
To him, the Adhvaryu responds: "Om! The Great Truth, the Great Reality, we have accomplished the Great! Thus he concludes.
In its highest form, it succeeds; it becomes great and is completed as the Vaiśvasṛja.
By this, the Āruṇaketuka is explained: [it consists of] the mantras, the bricks, the *lokaṃpṛṇās*, and the *svayamātṛṇṇās*, and water alone.

At the time of pouring out the earth for the *uttaravedi*, one digs a knee-deep pit silently and pours the soil elsewhere; [the items] such as the lotus leaf, gold, the golden man, and the tortoise are not placed there. The formula "rainy waters" (*varṣyāḥ*) is used in the manner prescribed in the text, meaning that they are not to be dried up (*aviśoṣyāḥ*).
The formulas beginning with "Agni knows" (*videragniḥ*) are omitted, and one proceeds with the formula "Thou art firm" (*dhruvāsi*).

Having performed the *śānti* rite with the two verses beginning "Hastagrāham abīṣṭakā upadadhyād bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ," he places them with those two. With the five *Mahānāmnī* verses beginning "Āpam āpām," he [offers] warm water. With the verse "Śivā naḥ śaṃtamā," he gives the water and the herbs to the Adhvaryu.
Having accepted them, the Adhvaryu places them with the verse "Śivā naḥ. He should place the *bhūmivatī* brick with the verse "Sumṛḍīkā. These [bricks] are placed first.

"Smṛtiḥ pratyakṣam" (Smṛti and perception), these eight; "madhye śukraṃ te anyat" (In the middle is your white seed, another); "sākaṃjānām" (Of those born together), this one; eleven [verses] before; "purastāddakṣiṇato'kṣiduḥkhōtthitasyaiva" (To the east and south of the eye-pain-risen one), these six; "iheha vaḥ svatapasaḥ" (Here, here, O you of good penance) and "atitāmrāṇi" (The very copper-red ones), these four; having performed the pacification at the beginning and end with the *Madantī* waters heated like the *Pravargya* rite; "atyūrdhvākṣaḥ" (With eyes turned far upward), these three; the seasonal circles; "ava drapsaḥ" (Down the drop), this one; "arogaḥ" (Free from disease), these eight; [recited] word by word with the names of the Sun; and "yatte śilpam" (That which is your craft).
Having muttered the *vyāhṛtis*, the sacrificer worships with the verse "apo vaḥ" (RV 10.9.1). In the same manner, he performs the subsequent worship after muttering the *vyāhṛtis*:

four verses addressed to Sūrya—"sapta sūryāḥ," "sapta diśo nānāsūryāḥ," "asyadyāvaḥ," and "citraṃ devānām"—and one verse beginning with "kvedamabhram" (RV 5.63.5) before [the last], and the verse "ardhamāsāḥ" (RV 10.88.16) afterwards.
"Black ones enter into the waters," [this is] from the south;
"What indeed is here?"—these five are addressed to Viṣṇu;
"I ask you about death beyond"—these four concern death.

"I ask you, O doer of evil"—these four [verses] belong to Nirṛti; "In which fire, O Agni, lead [us]"—these two belong to Agni; "And Agni Jātavedas"—these eight belong to the Quarters; "The quarters indeed"—the sacrificer [recites];
"The brilliantly shining ones"—these eleven belong to Rudra.
"Prabhrājamānyaḥ"—these are the eleven Rudrāṇīs, word by word, in the middle;
"Rūpāṇi vaḥ"—the sacrificer [recites this];

"Svānabhrāṭ"—these are the eleven Gandharva hosts (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, Taittirīya Saṃhitā), word by word, in the west; "Gaurī mimāya"—this is one [verse]; "Varāhavaḥ svatapasaḥ"—these are the seven Vātas, word by word.
"This is common" refers to the syllable containing *vṛṣṭi*;
"the world, Jamadagni" refers to that which has been nourished;
"śaṃyoḥ" refers to Śaṃyu.
The eight verses beginning with *sahasravṛd* are the *saṃyānī*s; the two beginning with *sa saṃgrāmaḥ*;

the four verses containing the word *pavitra*, beginning with *pavitravantaḥ pavitraṃ te brahmā devānām asataḥ sadyaḥ*, are the *pavitravatī*s on the north side; the seven verses beginning with *amī ya ṛkṣāḥ* are in the middle; and the five verses addressed to the Viśvedevas, beginning with *andho maṇim*, are on the north.

The sacrificer should lay down: "O Agni, up to that chariot" (three verses); "Stretch out" (four verses); "To the delightful ones" (one verse); "With the small ones" (two verses); "Subrahmaṇyom" (one verse);

"The ruddy-horsed ones" (four verses); "The wealthy ones"; "Thou art the rising of the Brahman" (four verses for the seats of the Brahman); and the lotus leaf, the gold plate, the golden man, and the tortoise—just as in the Mahāgni ritual.
Having laid those down, he places two *dūrohaṇa* verses on both sides of the man: "tāny upadhāya haṃ saḥ śuciṣat" and "tadit padam.

In the middle, he places two [verses]: "vasūnāṃ rudrāṇām. To the north, he places eight [verses] beginning with "raśmayo vasu. The sacrificer [recites] "ārogasya. Above, he places eight [verses] beginning with "āpo va," and the sacrificer [recites the final one].

There are eleven bricks called *prabhrājamānāḥ* and eleven called *prabhrājamānīḥ*; the sacrificer places these forms in the middle. With the formula "The forms of Agni," the sacrificer places eight *diśyā* bricks in the eastern direction; with the formula "The quarters indeed," the sacrificer places four *narakavatī* bricks in the south-eastern direction, according to their respective characteristics (*liṅga*).

"Ā yasminn indriyāṇi śatakrato" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka)—these two [verses] on the right; "indra ghoṣā vaḥ saṃjñānam"—these six regional verses; "āditya sarva"—these five regional verses; "evā hy eva"—these six regional verses; "āpam āpām"—these nine [verses] above; "apāṃ rasam"—this one verse; "kāmas tad agre"—this verse containing the word *saṃkalpa*; "āpo ha yat"—this verse containing the word *ogha*; "vidhāya lokān"—this verse containing the word *stambhana*; "ketavaḥ"—this one verse; "imā nu kam"—these three verses; "āplavasva"—these seventeen verses; "viśīrṣṇīm"—these two verses.

He recites the three verses beginning with "parjanyāya" and the three verses beginning with "punarmām aitv"; the subsequent procedure, starting from the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick, is the same as that for the *sāvitra* rite.
The *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks and the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks—these constitute the five layers.

There is a covering of the layers in each direction with lotus leaves (*puṣkaraparṇa*) and other materials, as in the first layer; however, there are no lotus leaves and so forth here. To the north, the conclusion is made with a *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick. Having constructed a platform with long wooden beams, the scattering of the loose earth (*purīṣa*) is performed with the verse "pṛṣṭo divi.

At the final brick, the *śatarudrīya* oblation is offered. At the end of the recitation, the leading forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*) takes place. While the offering is being made, the sacrifice to Vaiśravaṇa is explained by the Brāhmaṇa for one desiring food or all desires; this sacrifice to Vaiśravaṇa is to be performed on every festival day (*parvan*).

"One should pile [the fire-altar] in sacrifices with an upper altar," according to the Brāhmaṇa; "this is his vow," according to the Brāhmaṇa. The prescribed combinations of vows are as stated in the Brāhmaṇa: "One should not loathe water. According to the Brāhmaṇa, one may desire a single object or all objects, for it is known from the Brāhmaṇa: "Water indeed is this entire universe. Water is indeed Brahman; when water is piled [into the altar], one places Brahman within oneself. "He who piles this Agni attains union with and residence in the same world as Brahman"—thus concludes the Āruṇaketuka; thus concludes the Āruṇaketuka.
"The Upavasatha."

"How indeed should one know the fast-day? Is it when the junction [of day and night] has actually arrived, or when it is not yet full and has not appeared? It is indeed good that the junction has arrived; it is good to bring about the junction. But surely the junction is easy to bring about for everyone, as if it were already present. Thus they say regarding the fast-day.

Baudhāyana used to say: "If, while they are fasting on the Upavasatha day, the moon should rise in the east appearing as if reddened after the sun has set, one should recognize that too as an Upavasatha.
Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "This [lunar conjunction] is indeed already passed; one should either bring about the junction (*saṃdhyā*) itself or perform the sacrifice when the moon is full."
If, while he is fasting, the moon should rise in the east appearing as if reddened after the sun has set, he should say, "I have desisted from the Agnihotra," and proceed with the Pārvaṇa rite;
when the Pārvaṇa is completed, he should offer the Agnihotra. This indeed applies to the full moon day;
now, regarding the new moon day: [the same procedure applies].
Baudhāyana used to say: "One should fast while [the moon] is not yet visible, not when it is visible; and indeed, one should act in this very manner. Śālīki, however, says:

"There is also a fast when [the moon] is visible—namely, when the moon has become thin after three nights and the constellation has passed, and at dawn it is no longer seen on the following day; one should recognize that too as a fast-day (upavasatha)."
Regarding the adding of fuel to the fires: "agnīnām anvādhānaḥ."

Regarding the son of Aupamanyava’s Sūtra, Baudhāyana used to say: "One should add fuel to the fires with the *vihavyā* verses—three for each fire if one should recite nine; or, if there are eight, one should repeat either the first or the last verse twice; or, if there are ten, having added fuel three for each, one should recite the tenth while standing to the north of the Āhavanīya. Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "Indeed, that which has been added once becomes the Gārhapatya fire."

"The Anvāhāryapacana fire has its source in the village; one should add fuel to the Āhavanīya alone with the *vihavyā* verses, and then, standing to the north of the Āhavanīya, recite the remaining verses. Regarding this, Upamanyu used to say: "One should add fuel to the fires with the *vihavyā* verses—one verse for each fire—and then, standing to the north of the Āhavanīya, recite the remaining verses. Regarding this, Maudgalya used to say: "One should add fuel to the Āhavanīya alone [with the words]: 'I seize Agni, the good chariot, who is blissful, who ascends the rising sun for the sake of the day.'"
May Āditya, the supreme light among lights, delight tomorrow for the sake of the sacrifice and for the deities.
The Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, and the deities together with Indra—these I first encompass within my own abode through my inspired wisdom.

"I first embrace those gods who have entered this fifteenfold nourishment; let Agni, the bearer of oblations, bring them hither; 'this is their full-moon offering, may it be in me,'" [he says] at the full moon; "this is their new-moon offering, may it be in me," [he says] at the new moon. Regarding this, Maitreya used to say: "One should add fuel to the Āhavanīya fire alone with the *vihavya* verses, the other two silently; then, standing to the north of the Āhavanīya, one should recite the remaining formulas.
Rāthītara, however, said: "One should add fuel to the fires with the *vyāhṛtis* alone."
Regarding the phrase "in the curdling agents" (ātañcaneṣu).

Baudhāyana used to say, "These are the substances for curdling the oblation. Regarding this, Śālīki used to say, "Indeed, curd is seen as the substance for curdling; if that is not available, one should curdle it with any one of these."
Regarding the phrase "in the undertaking of the vow":

Baudhāyana used to say that one should undertake the vow (vratam) either at the time of *saṃgava* (when the cows are gathered), or while the cows are being milked, or when the *praṇītā* waters have been brought forward, or when the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) are about to be brought forward, or when they have already been set down. Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "The undertaking of the vow indeed takes place at the time of the previous day; for the Brāhmaṇa states, 'On the full moon day he undertakes the vow with the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and on the new moon day with the calves'. Therefore, one should undertake the vow precisely at the *saṃgava* time. Aupamanyava, however, says it should be from the time of the *anvādhāna* (the preliminary placing of fuel) onwards.
"In the case of the *abhyuditeṣṭi* sacrifice."

Baudhāyana used to say: "Having performed the New Moon sacrifice with the established oblations, having fasted again, on the following day one should sacrifice at the proper time with an offering that has not been overtaken by sunrise and is unimpaired. Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "One should perform that sacrifice which is the 'Brāhmaṇa-sacrifice' for the sake of distinction; having sacrificed with it, having fasted again, on the following day one should sacrifice at the proper time with an offering that has not been overtaken by sunrise and is unimpaired. This applies indeed to one who performs the *saṃnayana* (the mixing of curds), but now as for one who does not perform the *saṃnayana*.

The ritual procedure is the same for Baudhāyana; however, regarding this point, Śālīki used to say that one should cook these oblations in water, fast again, and on the following day, when the moon has not risen and the time is auspicious, one should sacrifice without any lapse; or else, one may extend the fast-day itself.
Regarding the term "ācchāyana": it means "one who covers."

Baudhāyana used to say: "One should cut the branch while restraining one's speech, and one should bring it back while restraining one's speech; indeed, one should act in this very manner. Śālīki, however, says that according to the Brāhmaṇa, one should converse with a Brāhmaṇa while remaining screened from view, but not with a non-Brāhmaṇa.
Regarding the cutting off of the branch.

Regarding this, Baudhāyana used to say: "One should cut the branch with the formula 'For food, thee!'; one should stroke it with 'For strength, thee!'; or one should gaze at it. Śālīki says: "One should indeed gaze at it."
Regarding the driving away of the calves.

Baudhāyana used to say: "With 'To the winds! one should set aside a male; with 'To the downward winds! a female. Now, if there should be only one or the other, Śālīki says that one should not abandon the mantra, but rather [proceed] with the combined formula, for this is the path of movement for the branch.

"One should move it along the front of the Āhavanīya," says Baudhāyana; "along the rear of the Gārhapatya," says Śālīki. This is the movement for the branch in all ritual procedures, as well as for the milks, except for those belonging to the Prāvargya rite. Aupamanyava says that one should move the Prāvargya along the rear of both fires.
"The duties of the sacrificer apply to one who is away on a journey."
Baudhāyana used to say: "The sacrificer indeed travels while accompanied by his sacrificial formulas;

wherever he may be, he should meditate upon him mentally. If he should arrive while the sacrifice is still in progress, he should consecrate what has been performed and proceed with the remainder of the ritual. Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "If he has a son or a pupil who is capable of performing the ritual, he should send him there."
If he should come while standing apart, or if he should depart from the presence of Kṛtānta, or if he should not look [at him], both of them indeed should consume the sacrificer’s portion.
Regarding the preparation of the sacrificial fuel and the sacrificial grass.

Āñjīgavi says that one should bind the fuel and sacrificial grass after giving [the offerings] to the ancestors in the afternoon for both teachers; Aupamanyava says [it should be done] on the following day, ending with the call to the preparer of the oblation.
"The heating of the sacrificial knife."

Baudhāyana used to say: "One should indeed heat the knife and likewise the horse-rib for the purpose of striking away the Rakṣas. Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "One should not heat brilliance against brilliance; for these mantras are seen to be intended for the horse-rib.
Therefore, one should heat only the horse-rib, and not the knife for the purpose of striking away what is cruel."
Regarding the phrase "in the steps."

Baudhāyana used to say: "Having first taken three or four steps eastward from the Āhavanīya fire, one should then proceed toward that direction where one thinks one will find the sacrificial grass (barhis). Śālīki said: "One should go directly to the place as required from the Āhavanīya itself, but not by way of the southern door."
Regarding the term *pariṣavaṇa*: [it refers to] the act of sipping around.

Baudhāyana used to say: "One should recite the mantra three times and perform the ritual action three times—thus for the tracing around the sacrificial post-hole, thus for the footprint of the Soma-purchase cow, thus for the hole for the Audumbarī post, and thus for the sounding-holes.
Śālīki, however, says: "One should recite the mantra only once and perform the ritual action three times."
Regarding the phrase "in cases of deprivation":

According to Baudhāyana, the Sūtra states that this mantra is indeed seen as having a benediction directed toward oneself; however, Śālīki maintains that it should rather be a ritual touching performed with the mantra.
Regarding the binding of the sacrificial grass-bundle (prastara).

Baudhāyana used to say that one should gird this [grass-bundle] at its midpoint and elsewhere besides this, and one should perform the *nidhana* chants in uneven pairs; regarding this, Śālīki used to say that because the *prastara* receives the mantra, the entire sacrificial grass (*barhis*) receives the mantra, and therefore one should not gird it at its midpoint, and this [bundle] itself should be the final odd one.
Regarding the making of the cord.
Baudhāyana says that the *adhikaraṇa* (the fourth section) belongs to Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, while Śālīki says that the *adhikaraṇa* itself is the third.
"Of the covering of the sacrificial grass."

Baudhāyana used to say: "Having gathered with a mantra those other *nidhana* formulas belonging to the Yajurveda that come first, one should then gather the subsequent Yajurvedic formula with a mantra. Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "Having silently gathered those other *nidhana* formulas belonging to the Yajurveda that come first, one should then gather the subsequent Yajurvedic formula with a mantra. Regarding this, Aupamanyava used to say: "Whatever [formula] was used at the beginning for the cutting and the gathering, having first gathered that very Yajurvedic formula with a mantra, one should then gather the others silently, and having shifted them around, one should tie the knot."
Regarding "the making of knots":
Śālīki says that one should mutter this mantra while actually joining the thread of the Sūtra according to Baudhāyana.
"Afterwards, she embraces him from behind while he faces forward."
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana;
Śālīki says it should be from east to west.
Regarding the placement of the sacrificial grass (barhis).

Baudhāyana used to say: "Having placed either the wooden sword (sphya) or a wood-chip within the altar (antarvedi), and having established it there with the mantra, one should then place [the other items] as best as possible.
Śālīki says: "One should place them with that very same mantra at the exact spot where one intends to place them."
Regarding the making of the enclosing-sticks (paridhis).
Baudhāyana used to say that the middle [post] should be equal in height to the chest, while the other two should be the length of an arm;
Śālīki, however, says that all of them should indeed be the length of an arm.
Regarding the preparation of the sacrificial fuel.
"One should prepare the fuel for the *samidhenī* verses," says Baudhāyana; "an unlimited amount," says Śālīki.
Regarding the "composition of the Veda."
"One should make it calf-knee-shaped," says Baudhāyana; "it should be made like a *mūta* (a bundle)," says Śālīki;
"it should be threefold," says Aupamanyava; "with its tip pointing upwards," says Aupamanyavīputra.
Regarding the sacrificial grass for the ancestral sacrifice: "pitṛyajñabarhiṣī."
"This sacrificial grass (barhis) has its roots," says Baudhāyana, "because of its similarity to the Pitṛyajña;
this is seen specifically in the Mahāpitṛyajña. Śālīki, however, maintains that this sacrificial grass should indeed be rootless.
The convergence of sacrifices.

Baudhāyana used to say: "Whatever sacrifices should coincide on the same day, the cutting of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for them should proceed according to each individual ritual sequence (*tantra*); or, having cut it, one should set it aside for each sequence. Having entered upon the vow (*vrata*) for each sequence, one should release the vow at the conclusion of that sequence. Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "Whatever sacrifices should coincide on the same day, the cutting of the sacrificial grass for all of them together should take place only once; or, having cut it, one should set it aside. Having entered upon the vow for them at the beginning, one should release the vow at the completion of all of them."
The sowing of the *parṇatsaru* [leaves].

Regarding the *sūtra*, Śālīkei used to say that Baudhāyana stated: "One should throw one-third [of the soil] into the fire-hall (*agnyagāra*), one-third within the altar (*antarvedi*), and with one-third one should perform the shaking of the calves; for in this way, it becomes closer to the cattle."
On the full moon day, the preparation of the upaveṣa [is performed].
"One should perform it," says Baudhāyana; "one should not perform it," says Śālīki.
Regarding the making of the milk-purifier for milking.

Baudhāyana used to say: "Having tied the roots together at the base and having stretched out a double-fold rope, one should tie it at the tip; thus its tip becomes joined with the tips. Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "Having tied the roots together at the base and having stretched out a double-fold rope, one should pass it around the base, stretch out a triple-fold rope, and then tie it at the tip; thus its tip becomes joined with the tips.
This concerns the preparation of the remains of the Agnihotra.

Baudhāyana used to say: "If one's [Agnihotra] has already commenced with clarified butter or with vegetable substances, one should offer milk for that night; one should likewise make the remnant of the Agnihotra consist of milk. Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "One should not turn back from a rite before it is completed. If one's [Agnihotra] has already commenced with clarified butter or with vegetable substances, having offered that [milk], one should make the remnant of the Agnihotra consist of that very same substance."
Regarding the sprinkling of the vessels for the *sāṃnāyya* offering.
Baudhāyana says that one should sprinkle with water consecrated in silence; Śālīki says that one should use water contained in a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
Then, having sat down behind the Gārhapatya fire, he draws out the embers toward the north with the upaveṣa.
Regarding this, Śālīke said; however, Baudhāyana said that one should remove the embers silently, and that this entire mantra should be used for the act of placing [the oblation] upon the fire.
Regarding the placement of the strainer for milking: thus it is said.

"One should prepare it with the mantra and place it in the pot with the mantra," says Baudhāyana; "one should prepare it silently and place it in the pot with the mantra," says Śālīki; "one should prepare half with the mantra and place the other half in the pot," says Aupamanyava.
Regarding the consecration of the cows with mantras:

Baudhāyana used to say: "One should consecrate each one of these with its respective formula, and then one should milk each one of them. Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "One should consecrate all of them together with a single formula, and then one should milk each one of them. Regarding this, Aupamanyava used to say: "One should consecrate all of them together with a single formula and milk them all at once; and right there one should finish the drops. Aupamanyavīputra said: "One should finish each one of them with the entire ritual procedure."
Regarding the consecration of small quantities: |||

The *sūtra* has been explained by Śālīki for Aupamanyava; regarding this, Baudhāyana used to say that one should indeed consecrate the drops after they have been milked, for it is at this very point that the end of the drops occurs.
"The milking of the Uttarās."

"Baudhāyana says that one should release the speech and milk the subsequent [cows] without holding onto [the previous one]; Kātya says that one should hold onto it while it is being brought forward and restrain one's speech."
"For one who obtains milk."
"One should perform the mantras beginning with the driving away of the calves," says Baudhāyana; "beginning with the pouring [of water]," says Śālīki.
Regarding the term "ātañcana": it means the act of curdling [milk].

Baudhāyana says that one should pour into the dipping-spoon (sruva) on the fourth [turning] as much as one thinks will cause it to coagulate; Śālīki says that one should pour into the dipping-spoon on the third [turning] as much as one thinks will cause it to coagulate.
"He consecrates it with the remnants of the Agnihotra."

Regarding this, Śālīke said; however, Baudhāyana used to say that one should bring the remains of the Agnihotra and use them for the curdling of the oblation; in this way, both [the Agnihotra and the oblation] become consecrated with the curd.
"He covers it with the watery [ocean]," so it is said.
"One should cause [the vessel] to remain overnight covered with water," says Baudhāyana; "having poured water and covered it with water," says Śālīki.
Regarding the strewing around the fires.

Regarding this, Sūtra says that Ācārya Aupamanyava used to say: "On the very day of the fast (upavasatha), one should strew around the fires as they have been produced; for there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: 'The deities dwell in him who, knowing this, strews around the fire on the eve of the sacrifice.'"
"Eating and not eating."
"One should eat forest food and water," says Baudhāyana; "only water," says Śālīki; "neither forest food nor water," says Aupamanyava, adding that there is also the touching of the hands.
Baudhāyana says that one should rub the hands while standing to the north of the Āhavanīya fire; Śālīki says [one should do so] to the north of the Gārhapatya fire.
Regarding the strewing around the fires: |||

This was declared by Śālīki in the Sūtra concerning Aupamanyava; regarding this, Baudhāyana used to say that one should first strew around the Gārhapatya fire from the front, then from the south, then from the west, and then from the north; in this very same manner, one should strew around the Anvāhāryapacana fire, and likewise the Āhavanīya fire.
Regarding the placing of the vessels: thus it is said.

Regarding the Sūtra, Śālīki said that Baudhāyana [stated]: "Having strewn grass to the north of the Gārhapatya fire, one should place the vessels upon them"; Rāthītara, however, says that one should place the vessels to the north of the fire-hall and take them up as required.
Regarding the seating of the Brahman priest.
Baudhāyana says that one should step aside and sit down to the south of the Āhavanīya fire; Śālīki says that one should sit down to the south of the Āhavanīya fire without stepping aside at all.
Regarding the seating of the sacrificer.
"One should move away and sit down to the south," says Baudhāyana; "one should sit down to the south without moving away," says Śālīki.
"The spreading of the spine."
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana;
Śālīki says that one should spread the Pṛṣṭhyā line only during the Soma sacrifice.
Regarding the making of the two purifiers.
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana;
according to Aupamanyava, it refers to the grasses of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line; according to Śālīki, it refers to whatever other *kuśa* blades may be unused.
He remains silent while the *praṇītā* waters are being poured out and until the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*) has been made.
Baudhāyana says that one should converse with these [priests] while laughing inwardly during the ritual junctions; Śālīki says that one should do so with speech already released.
This refers to the exposition of the *hotṛ* priests.

"One [view] is that [the offerings] include the *graha* cups, the *ṛta* formula, and the *svāhākāra*; another is that they exclude the *graha* cups but include the *ṛta* formula and the *svāhākāra*; yet another is that all [of these] are included. Baudhāyana holds the first alternative; Śālīki holds both of the latter two."
This is the explanation of the *daśahotuḥ*.
"Having led forward the *praṇītā* waters, he should recite the *vandaśas* facing west toward the *hotṛ*," so say the two teachers; "only while about to take the handful [of grass]," says Aupamanyava.
Regarding the term "nirvapaṇa": it means the act of offering or pouring out.

Regarding the *sūtra* of Śālīki, Baudhāyana used to say: one should pour out [the grains] from the cart itself; having touched the two poles (*dhurau*), one should step over the axle-end with the formula, "May Viṣṇu step upon thee.
Having looked at the grains for the sacrificial cake, one should touch them with the formula, "Let the five restrain themselves.

For those who offer four portions (*caturavattin*), this is done three times with the *yajus* and once silently; for those who offer five portions (*pañcāvattin*), it is done three times with the *yajus* and twice silently; according to Kātya, however, all [portions] are taken with the *yajus*.
Regarding the departure of the five-fold offering.

Baudhāyana says that one should proceed with the fivefold cutting from the act of pouring out; Śālīki says from the act of cutting; Aupamanyava says from the act of offering; and Aupamanyavīputra says from the fourfold portion for consumption.
It is the sowing vessel for the remaining [grains].
"One should sow them either in a pit or in a fold," says Baudhāyana; "one should sow them right here," says Śālīki.
Regarding the pouring out of the clarified butter.
Regarding this, Śālīki said that Baudhāyana used to say: "Having reached the end of the vegetable offering, one should pour out the clarified butter;
in this way, its sprinkling is obtained together with the other oblations."
Regarding the term "paridāna": it means "complete surrender" or "entrustment."

"One should hand it over exactly as it was set out," says Baudhāyana; regarding this, Śālīki said that one should simply say, "O Agni, protect the oblation! and "O Viṣṇu, protect the oblation! for Viṣṇu is the guardian of milks, and Agni is the guardian of plants.
Regarding the purification of the *prokṣaṇī* waters.
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana; Śālīki says that one should recite this verse while actually purifying it three times.
Regarding the sprinkling of the materials for the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśīya*).
"One should sprinkle [the water] section by section," says Baudhāyana; "having recited the names of the deities together, one should do so three times," says Śālīki.
Regarding the sprinkling of the vessels: it is as follows.
Regarding the Sūtra, Śālīki said that Baudhāyana used to say: "Be purified for the divine rite, the vessels for the sacrifice to the gods."
"The lying down of those who remain."
"Baudhāyana says that one should pour these very waters over the two buttocks; Śālīki says that after pouring them, one should prepare other waters on top."
Regarding the shaking of the black antelope skin.

Having gone out from the fire-hall, one should shake out the black antelope skin in the northern or western intermediate direction—thus says Baudhāyana; Śālīki says that one should do so within the hall itself toward that same direction.
Regarding the spreading of the black antelope skin.

Baudhāyana used to say that one should perform these rites without releasing the sacrificial ground: from the shaking out of the black antelope skin until its spreading; likewise from the placing of the mortar until the pouring in of the grains for the sacrificial cakes; likewise from the setting down of the pestle until the two [acts of] adding fuel and piling on;

likewise from the *prastara* grass-bundle until the placing of the offering-ladles; likewise from the taking up of the spade until the digging; likewise from the *audumbarī* post until the offering over it; and likewise from the sacrificial post until the encircling with the cord—Śālīki says that one should perform these rites according to their actual occurrence.
"The receptacle for the portions of the sacrificial cake."
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana;
Śālīki says that one who offers five portions should pour out five handfuls.
"Striking the two millstones loudly with the roar of a bull."
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana; Śālīki says it should be done with the yoke-pin alone.
Regarding the winnowing-basket’s scattering.

Regarding this, Śālīki said that one should silently winnow with the *śūrpa* basket; however, Baudhāyana says that one should pour out the grains for the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśīya*) with the entire mantra: "Thou art increased by rain; may the rain-increased recognize thee."
Then, having turned toward the north, he purifies [the water].
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana;
Śālīki says that one should purify [the water] by turning toward whichever direction one wishes.
"The discarding of the husks."

Regarding this, Śālīke said; however, Baudhāyana used to say that one should take as much [of the grain] as is required from right there and scatter it from the neck of the black antelope skin with the formula, "Thou art the portion of the Rakṣases," and then touch water.
Regarding the re-spreading of the black antelope skin: [the rule is as follows].
Aupamanyava says that the thread for the two teachers should have its ends pointing eastward and be directed toward the northern stars.
Regarding the term "peṣaṇa" (grinding).

Regarding the *sūtra*, Śālīki said that Baudhāyana [prescribes]: "With the words 'For out-breathing (*prāṇa*),' one should push the furrow eastward; with 'For in-breathing (*apāna*),' westward; with 'For diffused-breathing (*vyāna*),' one should plow crosswise; then one should push it eastward with 'Along the long extension, may I bestow life.
He says that one should pour the flour onto the black antelope skin with the formula, "May the god Savitṛ, the golden-handed, receive you.

Regarding this, Śālīki said that there is no taking up of the fire-stirring stick (*dhṛṣṭi*) for a single oblation, nor for many. To this, Baudhāyana said: "One should take up the fire-stirring stick from the very beginning with the formula, 'Thou art the fire-stirring stick; grant me spiritual power (*brahman*). "

He should consecrate the *gārhapatya* fire with the mantra: "O Agni, drive away the Agni who is the consumer of raw flesh; expel the consumer of the corpse. He should then cast out a southern ember and arrange the others [of the fire] with the mantra: "Bring the one for the sacrifice to the gods.

Upon those [embers], he should place the pot for the *caru* offering with the formula: "Thou art firm; make the earth firm; make life firm; make offspring firm; encompass kinsmen for this sacrificer."
Then he should encircle it clockwise with embers, saying, "The Rakṣas is burnt up; the enemies are burnt up.
In this very same manner, he should place all the pots for the sacrificial porridge (caru) upon the fire.
Regarding the phrase "in the mouths of the Carus":

Baudhāyana used to say that one should take up the *dhṛṣṭi* from the very beginning and prepare the portions for consumption from the principal [oblation] itself; regarding this, Śālīki used to say that the taking up of the *dhṛṣṭi* occurs indeed at the joining of the potsherds (*kapāla*),
so one should take up the *dhṛṣṭi* while actually placing the potsherds.
One should prepare the portions for consumption from the sacrificial cake itself.
Regarding the placing of the skull-bowls:
