Regarding this, Maudgalya used to say that the Sāvitra formulas should apply to the other [fires] once the first fire-piling has been performed; however, Āñjīgavi said that one should not even do that.
Regarding the mounting of the two kindling woods (*araṇī*).

Regarding this, the Sūtra of the two teachers states that Gautama said: "The householder alone should first consign the fires into the kindling woods; the others [should do so] during the sacrificial session."
Regarding the word "śālāyāḥ" (of the hall).
According to the natural sequence, the Gārhapatya fire should be measured in the middle.
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana; regarding this, Śālīki used to say that it should be done on all sides with a step consisting of three paces.
The Trivṛt is in the eastern direction, the Pañcadaśa to the south, the Saptadaśa to the west, and the Ekaviṃśa to the north;
or rather, the Jyotiṣṭoma is on all sides, for all [the Stomas] are the sacrificial fees of the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Regarding the performance of the *pravargya* rite.
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana;
Śālīki says that one should not perform the Pravargya rite at the Ukthya sacrifice.
Regarding the term "yājamāna": it refers to that which pertains to the sacrificer.

"One should perform the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) with the *abhī* formulas," says Baudhāyana; "one should perform the duties of the sacrificer as occasion permits," says Śālīki; "those [rites] which are consecrations of the fires (*agnisaṃskāra*), one may perform them at will, while the rest [should be done] according to the common ritual procedure (*tantra*)," says Aupamanyava.
Regarding the "adding of fuel to the fires" (agnyanvādhāna).

The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana; however, Śālīki used to say in this matter: "The Gārhapatya fire should be enkindled once; the Anvāhāryapacana fire has its source in the village; having enkindled the Āhavanīya fire once, one may then go about his business as required."
Regarding "eating":
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana;
Śālīki says that one should place all the Ṛṣis together and consume [the portion] only once.
Regarding the term "mārjana" (cleansing).
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana; Śālīki says it should be done once in a single [instance].
Regarding the carrying away of the world-fires.
Regarding this, the Sūtra says that here the two teachers have stated: Dīrghavātsya said that the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) should indeed take place in the first [part].
Regarding the performance of the animal sacrifices for the *kratavaḥ*.

According to the Sūtra of Baudhāyana, the sacrificial animals belonging to the seasonal rites (kratupaśu) and those belonging to the set of eleven (aikādaśina) are optional alternatives; thus says Śālīki.
Regarding the term "samañjana": it means "smearing" or "anointing."
Regarding the sūtra of Aupamanyavīputra,
which states that one anoints with the *pracaraṇī* as many times as there are *stomas*, Baudhāyana holds this view.
"The Dadhigraha," it is said.
The Sūtra says: "With milk or with clarified butter for Maudgalya."
The former alternative is that of Baudhāyana; the latter is that of Śālīki.
Regarding the drawing of the Am̐śu and Śvadābhya vessels: [the rule applies].

The Sūtra follows Baudhāyana; however, Śālīki used to say that in the Vājapeya, the twelve-day sacrifice, the Sattra, the Tāṇḍinām Ayana, the Udbhid, and the Valabhid, it should be performed in this very manner with the Pṛśnigrahas and the Prāṇagrahas.
Regarding the taking up of the sixteen cups.
The Sūtra [states] that according to Baudhāyana they should draw [the cups] at each pressing; Śālīki [says] thus.
The oblation of the *atigrāhya* cups.
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana;
Śālīki says that they should offer the secondary oblation (anuvaṣaṭkāra) for the Māhendra cup.
"He introduces the Stotra of the Ṣoḍaśin."
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana;
"by whatever [means]" is the view of Śālīki.
"The expelling of heart-pains."
"One should remove them one by one," says Baudhāyana; "all of them together," says Śālīki.
"The final purificatory bath," he said.
According to the Sūtra of Baudhāyana, they should descend for the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) facing east; according to Śālīki, they should do so facing east.
Regarding the mounting [of the fires] onto the two kindling woods (*araṇī*).
Regarding this, the Sūtra of the two Teachers says that Gautama, the householder, said: "One should consign the fires into the two Araṇis; the other [should do so] afterwards.
One should observe the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) by means of five factors: by the *chandas*, by the Brāhmaṇa, by the *pratyaya*, by the *nyāya*, and by the *saṃsthāvaśa*.

Regarding "by the *chandas*"—as we have stated—that which is according to the traditional injunction, such as "this is the former" and "this is the latter"; furthermore, the mantra itself declares the action.
There is a restatement of ritual action (karmānuvāda), such as:

"The intellect has gone forth; go toward the sacrificial grass, toward the atmosphere! At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I offer what is pleasing to Agni.

Whatever one might not be able to arrange through a metrical formula (chandas), that one should seek to arrange by means of a Brāhmaṇa passage. Indeed, it is the Brāhmaṇa that ordains those mantras which are not clearly understood, specifying: "One does this with this [mantra], and one does that with that [mantra]."

Just as one cuts a branch with the words, "For sap thee! For strength thee!", or drives away the calves with the words, "Ye are winds, come hither!", so too he prescribes ritual acts that are devoid of mantras;

for example, the rule that "a Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fire at eight steps, a Rājanya at eleven, and a Vaiśya at twelve"—thus there is a fixed arrangement based on connection with specific castes. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "by means of conviction," this refers to the conviction of the Chāndogas, the Bahvṛcas, and the Adhvaryus.

As for the phrase "according to this principle," one who does not find the ordinary principle in the ordinary treatise should understand the village-principle, thinking: "This is the undertaking of the Arhats here."
As for this [saying], "By means of stability," when the Soma has been taken away, one should press *ādāra* and *phālguna* plants;
thus the mantras proceed by way of fourfold [application]: by praise, by designation, by benediction, and neither by praise nor benediction nor designation—this is the fourth.
Now, these are the five forms of oblation: plant-offering, milk, animal, Soma, and clarified butter.
Their respective rites and respective bases have been observed according to their bases;

one should not combine them with one another because there is no instruction to do so. Whichever oblation is completed by whichever [procedure], one should perform it with that very [procedure]; that is its specific basis.
The topics have been stated;
as for "sacrifice," what is its origin? Sacrifice has faith as its origin; it is auspiciousness.
"Where indeed is the sacrifice? It is in the person. And who indeed is the deity? It is the consecration (dīkṣā)."
"Speech"—
what indeed is the auspicious well-being?
"Speech alone," he said.
"What indeed is the one-syllabled Gāyatrī?
"Speech alone.
"What indeed is the beginning of the sacrifice? What is its foundation?"
It is known: "Svāhā! To the sacrifice with the mind, svāhā! To heaven and earth, svāhā! From the wide atmosphere, svāhā! I take hold of the sacrifice from the wind.
Indeed, the wind is the beginning of the sacrifice, and the wind is its foundation.

How, then, should one know that "this is the *tantra* (the main ritual framework) and this is the *āvāpa* (the insertion)"? The *tantra* begins from the adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*) up until the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*), except for the vegetable oblation (*auṣadha*).

In that ritual procedure (*tantra*), there are points for insertion (*āvāpasthāna*). These include, for example, the milking of the cows, the placing of the potsherds, the carrying away of the *stambayajus*, and the taking of the portions of clarified butter (*ājyagraha*). Whatever else one pours in after the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, that constitutes the insertion in the middle; in that very place where these oblations are poured, the items belonging to the insertion take their place within the ritual procedure. For instance, the *prāśitra*, the sacrificer’s portion, the Brahman’s portion, the *sviṣṭakṛt*, and the *iḍā* constitute an insertion from the point of view of the cutting of portions (*avadāna*), whereas the ritual procedure itself pertains to the point of offering (*pradāna*).
Where, indeed, does the *tantra* (the main ritual framework) attain the status of an *āvāpa* (insertion), or where does the *āvāpa* attain the status of a *tantra*?

In the *Maitrābārhaspatya* sacrifice and others, the *tantra* indeed begins from the pouring out [of the oblation], while the *āvāpa* begins from the offering. Then, in the *Vāruṇī* offerings and the *Sañjñānī* sacrifice, the *āvāpa* indeed begins from the pouring out, but the *tantra* begins from the offering. From the *anūyāja* offerings up to the offering of the *samiṣṭayajus*, it is the *tantra*.

"What deities indeed do the after-offerings (*anūyāja*) belong to? "One should say they belong to Agni," for it is known: "The gods found him through the after-offerings; in that he performs the after-offerings, he thereby kindles Agni. "What deities indeed do the fore-offerings (*prayāja*) belong to? "The seasons. Now, how many are the forms of the *pākayajña*, how many the forms of the *haviryajña*, and how many the forms of the *soma* sacrifice?

"The *huta*, the *prahuta*, the *āhuta*, the *śūlagava*, the *baliharaṇa*, the *pratyavarohaṇa*, and the *aṣṭakā-homa*—these are the seven forms of the *pākayajña*. Some, however, say they are innumerable.

Whatever else is offered elsewhere than in the *vihāra* (sacrificial fire-altar), all those are the forms of the *pākayajña*. Now, the forms of the *haviryajña* are: the *agnyādheya*, the *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *āgrayaṇa*, the *cāturmāsya*, the *dākṣāyaṇayajña*, and the *kauṇḍapāyinī*; some indeed mention the *sautrāmaṇi* as well. Now, the forms of the *soma-saṃsthā* are: the *agniṣṭoma*, the *atyagniṣṭoma*, the *ukthya*, the *ṣoḍaśī*, the *vājapeya*, the *atirātra*, and the *aptoryāma*—these are the seven *soma-saṃsthā*s. Whatever is the ritual performance (*kratukaraṇa*) of the *agniṣṭoma*, that is the same for the *atyagniṣṭoma*.
"That which belongs to the Ukthya belongs to the Ṣoḍaśin and the Vājapeya; that which belongs to the Atirātra belongs to the Aptoryāma.
Thus, among the seven stations of the Soma-sacrifices, two do not enter into the Sattras: the Vājapeya and the Aptoryāma.
How indeed, then, should one know: "This is the former series (tati), this is the latter"?

That which is the *prakṛti* (archetype) is the prior series (*pūrvā tati*); that which it ordains is the subsequent series (*uttarā tati*). The establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) is the prior series; the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*) is the subsequent series. The New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) are the prior series of the *iṣṭi* offerings; all optional (*kāmya*) *iṣṭis* are the subsequent series. The *Aindrāgna* animal sacrifice is the prior series of the independent animal sacrifices (*nirūḍhapaśubandha*); all optional animal sacrifices are the subsequent series. The *Jyotiṣṭoma* is the prior series of the Soma sacrifices; all Soma sacrifices are the subsequent series.

The first series of fires is the Śyenacit; all optional fires constitute the subsequent series. The first series of Ahīna sacrifices is the Dvirātra; all Ahīnas constitute the subsequent series. The first series of multi-day sacrificial sessions (ahargaṇas) is the Dvādaśāha; all ahargaṇas constitute the subsequent series. The first series of year-long sacrificial sessions (sattras) is the Gavāmayana; all year-long sattras constitute the subsequent series. Now, it is known how many Gavāmayanas there are: for example, when the Pṛṣṭha-stotras occur monthly, they might perform the Pṛṣṭhas only once in the final month; thus the third [Gavāmayana] consists of ten months.
There are seven cultivated plants and seven wild plants;
seven domestic animals and seven wild animals;
and the seven meters increasing by four syllables each.
There are seven cultivated plants: sesame, beans, rice, barley, millet, small grains, and wheat; some say that lentils are the seventh.
There are seven wild plants: *śyāmāka* millet, wild rice (*nīvāra*), wild sesame (*jartila*), *gavīdhuka*, *gārmuta*, *vāstūka*, and bamboo seeds; the last is the seventh.

Some say the *kuruvinda* beans; others say the seven domestic animals: the cow, the horse, goats and sheep, man, the donkey, the camel, and the mule as the seventh. Some say the seven wild animals: the cloven-hoofed, the beasts of prey, birds, reptiles, the elephant, the monkey, and the river-dwelling creatures as the seventh.

"The meters are seven, increasing by four syllables each: the Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī. Now, there are these three types of repetition: repetition of the ritual action (*karmābhyāvartin*), repetition of the deity (*devatābhyāvartin*), and repetition of the number (*saṃkhyābhyāvartin*). Now, this Sāvitra ritual involves the repetition of the ritual action; next, it involves the repetition of the deity, namely the *dhruvājya*, the *droṇakalaśa*, and the "all-pṛṣṭha" [offering]; then, it involves the repetition of the number, as one asks thrice, "O *śamitr*, is the oblation cooked? Furthermore, regarding the measurement of the King [Soma], where indeed should one apply an omitted mantra?
One should seek to connect [the formula] with a corresponding place, either by way of its form or by way of its excellence;
this is what we mean by "from place to place. One should arrange it together with that mantra which has been recited immediately preceding it, whether by means of the earlier time or the later time.

As for what was said regarding "by way of its form," it is as follows: "May he stand, bestowing excellent heroic strength, abundance of wealth, and good horses; made favorable by Bṛhaspati through wealth, for me, the sacrificer."
As for this [statement] "by means of the draft-ox," this [Aśvamedha] is indeed taught as being almost like fire (*agnikalpa*) and consisting mostly of bricks;
in that case, whatever mantra might be omitted would cause it to become predominantly bricks. However, this Aśvamedha is taught as consisting mostly of oblations (*āhuti*).

In that case, if a mantra should be omitted, one should remedy it by increasing the number of oblations; one should not initiate what has not been commenced, nor should one perform what has already been commenced. One should complete the rite silently through action.

Regarding what we said—that "one should not initiate what has not been commenced"—it is because this mantra for cutting the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is indeed recited as short, whereas the action is long.
The mantra would not be brought into effect merely for the sake of the performance. Furthermore, this mantra for the dismemberment of the animal is recited as short, while the action is long.
The mantra does not arise from the action; rather, on this naturally perforated stone (*svayamātṛṇṇā*), the mantra is traditionally handed down as long, while the action is short.
The mantra should not cease because of the action, just as it is said: "Three times with the *yajus* formula, once silently.
Having heard this regarding the fires of the worlds and their [corresponding mantras], there is the *stambayajus*.

As for the statement, "five times with the *yajus* formula and five times silently," this is done after having heard the measurement of those [grains] belonging to the King (Soma). As for the statement, "once with the *yajus* formula and once silently," this too is done after having heard the measurement of those belonging to the King.

As for the statement, "he pours out four handfuls of rice"—two for the deity, the third for the *sviṣṭakṛt*, and the fourth for the *iḍā*—all of these indeed have their corresponding *brāhmaṇa* explanations.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the acts performed according to specific injunctions. Although fire is not explicitly enjoined [for these], nevertheless, it happens as follows: one offers on the gambling-ground, one offers at the front of a chariot, one offers on the pole of a chariot, one offers at a crossroads, one offers on the two tracks, one offers on a stump that has been cut down, one offers on a footprint, one offers on a she-goat, one offers in the right ear of a goat, one offers on the right horn of a goat, one offers in the right hand of a Brāhmaṇa, one offers on a clump of *darbha* grass, one offers in water, one offers on a post of *udumbara* wood, and one offers on the mound of an anthill.

"He offers in the *aupāsana* fire; he offers in the *uttapanīya* fire; he offers in the *śāmitra* fire; he offers in the *āgnīdhrīya* fire; he offers in the *anvāhāryapacana* fire; he offers in the *gārhapatya* fire"—in such cases where no specific fire is designated, one must offer in the *āhavanīya* fire.

Furthermore, regarding the officiant who is not specifically designated—just as it occurs when one says "the *unnetṛ* offers" or "the *pratiprasthātṛ* offers"—in such cases where the *adhvaryu* is not designated, the offering must be made by the *adhvaryu* himself. The same applies when the vessel is not specifically designated.

Moreover, as it is said: "He offers with his joined palms; he offers with a winnowing basket; he offers with a fold of a black antelope skin; he offers with the middle leaflet; he offers with the terminal leaflet; he offers with an *arka* leaf; he offers with a ladle made of *parṇa* wood; he offers with a ladle made of *udumbara* wood; he offers with his two thumbs; he offers with two stalks of *visraṃsikā*; he offers with the throat of a *gomṛga*; he offers with a horse's hoof;
he offers with an iron water-pot"—in the absence of a specific injunction, one must offer with the *sruk* ladle alone.

If no specific fuel-wood is prescribed, one should understand that *samidh* (fuel-stick) itself is intended; for it is known from scripture: "One should not offer into a fire that is without fuel; if one were to offer into a fire without fuel, it would be as if one were to place food into a mouthless person—such is that act.
Therefore, one must offer only into a fire provided with fuel.
When no specific [fuel] is prescribed, one should offer after having added fuel."

Now, therefore, follows the ritual for the portions (*avadāna*). One draws out four [portions]; it consists of four cuttings. In the case of an unspecified offering, one should sacrifice after merely cutting off [the portion].

Regarding an unspecified oblation, one should understand it to be other than rice and barley only from a specific instruction; however, they indeed say that clarified butter (*ājya*) is the most quickly prepared among things not specified. Regarding an unspecified animal victim, one should understand it to be other than a goat only from a specific instruction. If the ritual procedure (*tantra*) involves a transference to Indra and Agni (*aindrāgna*), one should perform that transference; the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices involve a transference to Agni, while the *soma* sacrifice involves a transference to Indra.
The pouring out of the medicinal herbs is seen as belonging to [the offering] for Savitṛ;

what then belongs to the Sāṃnāyya? The milking belongs to the Sāṃnāyya, and the bringing forward belongs to the animal sacrifice; that which he measures out toward the Upāṃśusavana stone belongs to the King (Soma).
The carrying of fire around other oblations is well known; what indeed is the *rājña*?
It is when he subsequently carries around the *vasatīvarī* waters—that is the *rājña*.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśas*).

All [the cakes] on eight potsherds are dedicated to Agni, except for those belonging to the re-establishment of the sacred fires; all [the cakes] on eleven potsherds are dedicated to Indra-Agni, except for those belonging to the Āgrayaṇa and the Śunāsīrīya sacrifices;
all [the cakes] on eleven potsherds are dedicated to Indra, except for those belonging to the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice.

All the cakes for Agni and Soma consist of eleven potsherds, except for that of the *śyāmāka* grain; all the animal-cakes (*paśupuroḍāśa*) consist of eleven potsherds, except for those belonging to deities starting with Vāyu—for whichever deity the animal sacrifice is dedicated, the animal-cake belongs to that same deity, with the exception of the one for Vāyu;
all the cakes for Agni and Viṣṇu consist of eleven potsherds, except for that belonging to the *adhvarakalpā*.
In that very context, there are both an eight-potsherd and a twelve-potsherd [offering],
all of which are dedicated to Savitṛ except for those belonging to the Aśvamedha;
in that same context, there are also an eight-potsherd and an eleven-potsherd [offering], as well as an eight-potsherd offering to Savitṛ.

All Marut offerings consist of seven potsherds, except for the animal-cake offerings (*paśupuroḍāśa*) of the Aśvamedha, the animal-cake offerings of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, and the twenty-one-potsherd offering to the Maruts; and except for the animal-cake offerings of the Pañcaśāradīya offerings within the Rājasūya.

It is known: "What indeed are those 'anukhyā' potsherds that are to be marked? One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara in the deer-trap; these are the 'anukhyā' potsherds. Now follows the former arrangement.

Regarding the five *prayāja*s, the nine *prayāja*s, and the eleven *prayāja*s—the *prayāja*s are established as before; there is the carrying of fire around the victim (*paryagnikaraṇa*), the pressing of Soma for the victim, and the *agniṣṭoma* at the *gavāmayana*. Furthermore, it is known that its *stotrīya* verses amount to three hundred and sixty.
"There are as many nights in a year.

Now, the royal sacrifices are the Rājasūya, the Aśvamedha, the Puruṣamedha, the Sarvamedha, the Somasava, the Pṛthisava, the Mṛtyusava, the Kānāndhayajña, and the Śunaskarṇayajña. Furthermore, regarding the deity Aditi: at the establishment of the sacred fires (Agnnyādheya), she is the first *caru*; in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, she is the second; at the Prāyaṇīya and Udayanīya offerings, and at the Dīkṣaṇīyā, there are three [offerings]; at the Rājasūya, and in the Ratnimāna and Prāyujya rites, one offers a dewlap-bearing pregnant cow to Aditi—thus says one school; and in the Iṣṭikalpa, she is one [offering], and in the Vrātyastoma, she is one.

There are four [sacrifices] for Aditi: a pap-offering (caru) for Viṣṇupatnī Aditi, three for Ham̐sasāci Aditi, three reddish-brown ewes for Aditi, two for the Sautrāmaṇī, and a barren cow (vaśā) for Āditya as a draught-oblation; thus there are eighteen.
There are three systems of ritual procedure dependent upon the sacrifice: that with five fore-offerings (*prayāja*), that with nine fore-offerings, and that with eleven fore-offerings.
The *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices and the optional offerings (*kāmyeṣṭi*) proceed with five fore-offerings;
the seasonal sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*) with nine fore-offerings; and the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) and the Soma sacrifice with eleven fore-offerings.
These six rites in every ritual cycle fulfill all intentions:

namely, the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the fire-oblation (*agnihotra*), the new- and full-moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*), the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), and the Soma sacrifice.

This is also understood from the text: "Now, in that he takes out his fire, by that he obtains a thousand wish-granting cows; and in that he performs the fire-oblation, by that [he obtains] a thousand. This indeed is the measure of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, and this is the lowest among these.
From this or that, higher and better things arise;
the sacrificer of the animal sacrifice conquers all worlds. Indeed, other sacrificial rites are undertaken for a single desire, but the animal sacrifice and the Soma sacrifice are for all desires.
One who is about to establish the sacred fires (āgnīdhāsyamāna) should make himself prosperous; whatever in him is unwholesome, he should turn into something wholesome.

He should settle those debts whose time for payment has arrived, or else obtain permission [to delay them]. Furthermore, we shall first describe the selection of the officiating priests (ṛtvij) at the very establishment of the fires.
If his ancestors have been chosen [for the office], one should not bypass them, provided they have remained unbroken in their lineage, their Vedic study, their human conduct, and their character.
Regarding this, what indeed constitutes "bypassing" (ativaraṇa) or "choosing" (avaraṇa)? [The answer is:

"He practiced theft," "He committed violence," "He officiated for one for whom one should not officiate"—if such an act was performed and yet he has remained steadfast [in his duties], then in the case of these, there is either bypassing or choosing.
If he chooses them, let him choose only those whose limbs are unimpaired;
which one among them, indeed, should he choose first?
He who is most highly praised by him, that one he should choose first.

If he should seek others through that minister, he should indeed choose the Brahman first according to seniority, then the Hotṛ, then the Udgātṛ, and then the Adhvaryu; or the Adhvaryu immediately after the Brahman, whether before or after, according to the ritual action.
He should provide for the officiating priests with distributed wealth.

There are three legal cases concerning officiating priests (*ṛtvij*): "I shall sacrifice even without a priest," "I shall not give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) nor the portion for the *ājya* oblation," and "I shall not employ my wife [as a priest].
Now, what indeed is the duty regarding officiating priests?
It is that which pertains to the teacher (*ācārya*).
What constitutes the "worthy reception" (arhaṇa)?
One view is that it consists of [the offerings] at each arrival;

another is that it consists of [the offerings] at the beginning of each season; another is that it consists of [the offerings] at the completion of the year; and yet another is that it consists of the attainment of the sacrifice. Now, what indeed is the duty of the officiating priests?

One should not perform the office of a priest for one who has renounced it; nor for one who has not been invited; nor should one officiate for one who has not been purchased [as a priest]; nor for one who has not been chosen; nor for one who has been overchosen; nor should one officiate for one whose purpose is merely to be mentioned; nor for one for whom the sacrificial fee has already been taken away; nor should one officiate during the dark fortnight; nor for one who is distressed; nor for one who is dead; nor for one with three scars [on the forehead]; nor for one who has crossed a moat; nor for one who goes to the end [of his life]; nor for an outcaste; nor for one who has not studied the Vedas. However, among these, one may officiate for him who, while living by looking for a livelihood, breaks his potsherds.
That too is known from the *Daśataya*: "I cooked the entrails of a dog with a spit; I found no comforter among the gods. I saw my wife not being honored, and then the falcon brought me honey.
Regarding these [verses], it is said: "There is no one unfit for sacrifice who gives a thousand-fold dakṣiṇā," and [the text continues] regarding saline soil and sand.

Those [embers] which are like ashes at dawn, one should fetch them; or one should fetch them from the remains of a wild boar that has been slaughtered; or one should fetch them from a heap of refuse from a wild rat; or one should fetch them from a cook who is not fasting.

If such a cook is not available, one should fetch them from the hollow of a crab; if that is not available, one should fetch them from a tree struck by lightning; or if that is not available, one should fetch them from a tree struck by frost or wind, specifically from an *aśvattha* tree that has variegated markings.
From wherever a village or a city, or a river or a ford, is known, from there one should cause the horse to be brought; "one that has been driven before" means it is young— this is what is meant—
and "three pieces of gold."
One should have six [images] made:
those for the purpose of worship should be of gold, and those for the purpose of a grand gift should be of silver;
both should be adorned with human ornaments and dressed in new garments.
Every other human ornament is distinct [from this], except for the *nalada* grass; they prescribe this specifically for one who is afflicted.
Some, however, prohibit the wearing of garlands;
in that case, one should place them on [the body] a year prior [to the ceremony].

If, after three days, six days, twelve days, or even a year has passed, the fire goes out, what should he do in that case? He should once again prepare the *brahmaudana* rice-offering until the placing of the fuel-sticks; during that time, he should not have his hair or beard shaved.
Rather, one should observe this year beforehand for the sake of atonement; this has been stated,
and whenever it should go out, one should act in exactly this manner.

When it has been completed, he should not approach [the fire]; he should act in this very manner. When he approaches, the ritual procedure beginning with the Upavasatha-cow is extended. Some say there are two *brahmaudana* offerings: the one is for the leftovers, and the other is for the performance of conciliation (*sāntva*). Then, while pouring out the *uṣās* among the sacrificial materials, he should meditate in his mind upon whatever black spot he sees in the moon; "that also exists here," he should think. If he has not studied the *Sāmans*, he should recite their *yonis*; or else with the *vyāhṛtis*; or else with the *hiṅkāra*.
One should set the chariot wheel in motion with a refined light.
If, while he is placing it, the moon should appear in the east, what should he do?

He should complete whatever ritual procedure has been commenced, conclude it at the end of the sequence, and then finish it on the following day. Now, if the moon should appear once the fuel (idhma) has been placed upon the fire, what should he do?
Having performed the ritual up to the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), he should cease at the conclusion of the rite, thinking, "I shall complete it on the following day.
Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the seasons and the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). We shall first explain the seasons, and then the meters (*chandas*).
A Brāhmaṇa should establish his sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) in spring, a Rājanya in summer, a Vaiśya in autumn, and a Rathakāra in the rainy season.

The establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) belongs to all [classes], and it may be performed by all under the asterism Rohiṇī; however, according to their respective castes, there are also specific Vedic meters (*chandas*). Moreover, indeed, the installations of the fires (*agnyādheya*) are not restricted to specific desires, as it is said:

"One should establish the fire under the Kṛttikās; one should establish the fire under Rohiṇī; one should establish the fire under the two Punarvasus; under the two Pūrva-phalgunīs; under the two Uttara-phalgunīs; and under Citrā.
These [installations] are to be performed on the same day (*sadyaskālā*).

"A Kṣatriya in summer, a Vaiśya in autumn"—these two do not occur at the time of the *sadyaska* (immediate) rite. Now, therefore, we shall explain the *ārtija* forms of the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*). [One may establish them] during the waning half of the month or the waxing half of the month; "during the waning half" or "during the waxing half. One who establishes the fires during the waxing half of the month should fix upon whatever interval there may be [between the new moon and the full moon]. However, on the full moon day, it is an immediate rite. For one establishing the fires during the waning half of the month, no such interval exists for the sake of waiting.

One should perform all of this on the same day: the Caturhotṛ, the two Sārasvata oblations, and the Anvārambheṣṭi. Then, having performed the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha sacrifices, one should wait for the New-moon day. If, however, it is the New-moon day, one should complete the New-moon sacrifice on that very day.
Then, having offered the two Sārasvata oblations, one should join verse with verse; thus it is for the Pūrṇadarva offering, and thus for the Vāstoṣpatīya.

How indeed should one offer the full oblation? One should offer it with the formula: "To Agni, to the Earth, to Vāyu, to the Atmosphere, to Sūrya, to the Sky, to Varuṇa, to the Waters—Svāhā! Now, this silent *agnihotra* is seen as being for the purpose of consecrating the fire; therefore, one should offer it with clarified butter alone. Having wiped [the ladle] downwards, one wipes it upwards; thus, performing both these acts at the evening and morning *agnihotra*, one considers himself as having offered. On the night preceding the fast-day (*aupavasathikā*), when about to recite the *sāmidhenī* verses, one should explain the *daśahotṛ* formula, utter the *vyāhṛtis*, and then make the sound *hiṃ*; thereafter, one should recite the verses. This is the sequence here.

Now, regarding the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*) and the Soma sacrifice: having performed the sequence up to the *pūrṇāhuti* (full-offering), he should settle in the sacrificial hall. The *dīkṣaṇīyā* (initiation offering) follows an *āgneya* cake on eight potsherds; the *prāyaṇīyā* (opening offering) follows an *aindrāgna* and an *āditya* pap; the *ātithyā* (hospitality offering) follows an *āgneya* cake on eight potsherds for Agni Pavamāna; the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) for the Agniṣomīya follows offerings to Agni Pāvaka and Agni Śuci; and there is the *anvārambheṣṭi* (offering at the commencement) for the morning pressing. Alternatively, having completed all the oblations belonging to the establishment of the fires, he should settle in the hall, with the *udavasānīyā* (concluding offering) serving as the *anvārambheṣṭi*.

Now, as for this re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*): what indeed constitutes the re-establishment? It is when, after having established the fires, one thinks, "I have become worse off; my prosperity has failed; my son has died. This is what is observed within that same year. At what time, then, should one set it up?
That new moon which occurs before the full moon of the month of Āṣāḍha—on that day, once a year, the moon coincides with the *Punarvasu* asterism. On that day, one should establish the fires.

On the day of preparation for that [sacrifice], having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇī*), having moved away, having churned out the fires, and having spread them out, he should perform the *udvāsanyā* sacrifice; having sacrificed, he should consign the fires and go. He should have this very fire-hall renovated, or have another new one built; he should have these very sacrificial vessels scraped clean, or have other new ones made.
"A chariot repaired is the sacrificial fee"—by this it is meant that it has been renovated.
"A garment re-sewn"—by this it is meant that it has been restored.

The ox that is released again is said to be one whose strength has failed; now, these are the secondary rites (upāṃśu-dharmāṇi): namely, the establishment of the fires (agnyādheya), the re-establishment of the fires (punarādheya), the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), the initiation rite (dīkṣaṇīyā), the introductory offering (prāyaṇīyā), the guest-offering (ātithyā), the Upasad rites, the morning litany (prātaranuvāka), the offerings to the wives (patnīsaṃyāja), the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), the concluding offering (udayanīyā), the concluding settlement (udavasānīyā), the rite for carrying the fire-altar (citipraṇayanīya), the rite for the Tvaṣṭṛ-sacrifice, the rite for the sprouting of the sacrificial post (yūpavirohaṇīya), the eight-footed cow, and the pregnant cow—these are the corroborative cognitions (sahakāri-pratyayāḥ). Such is the ritual manual (kalpa) they declare to be that of Baudhāyana.

"One should establish the Gārhapatya fire with the verses of the Serpent Queen (sarparājñī)," it is said; having set aside those [verses], one should insert the *gharmaśiras* in their place and the verses of the Serpent Queen. Having performed the regular worship (*upasthāna*), one should perform the worship pertaining to the re-establishment of the fires (*paunarādheyika*). From this point onward, the procedure is established.
For one who has sacrificed and is now re-establishing the fires, there is a rule: "one should offer the *saṃnayya* (curdled milk), or one should not offer it."
"One should offer the *saṃnayya*," say some; "one should not offer the *saṃnayya*," say others.
For the sacrifice is in contact with the body. Only when one is to sacrifice again should one offer the *saṃnayya*.
They consist of a hundred syllables; these four are *akṣarapaṅkti*s, each consisting of twenty-five syllables.

Now, this third establishment of the fires (*tṛtīyādheya*)—upon what indeed does it depend? One should say: "Either on the original establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*) or on the re-establishment (*punarādheya*); it depends on the original establishment. Furthermore, for one whose fires have been carried off or whose fire-drills (*araṇī*) are lost, he proceeds by means of the *brahmaudana* (the sacrificial porridge for the Brahmins) alone; thus the original establishment of the fires is accomplished.

Now, regarding these Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the teachers declare that they begin with the full moon and conclude with the new moon. In this regard, they cite the following: after midnight on the day of the full moon, the moon begins to fill; it becomes full during the latter part of that night, throughout the entire following day, and until midnight of the subsequent night. Then, on the day of the fast (upavasatha) for the new moon, the sun overtakes the moon after midday.
He obtains this [time] during the afternoon, throughout the entire night, and from the middle of the following day until midday; one should sacrifice toward this junction (*sandhi*).

For on the full moon day, the night is to be joined; on the new moon day, the day is to be joined. There are two full moons and two new moons: the former full moon is *Anumati*, the latter is *Rākā*; the former new moon is *Sinīvālī*, the latter is *Kuhū*.
Gāyatrī is indeed Anumati and Triṣṭubh is Rākā—these are the names of the full moon; Jagatī is Sinīvālī and Anuṣṭubh is Kuhū—these are the names of the new moon.
Now, this moon consists of sixteen digits, and fifteen of them constitute its waxing fortnight.
This sixteenth digit, however, has entered manifoldly into the Brahmins, the waters, the herbs, the trees, and the animals.

When these [elements] are employed in the sacrifice, by that means this [digit] is gathered together. Furthermore, the portions of the Upavasatha day are the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the sixteenth;
however, the thirteenth and seventeenth do not exist.
On the day of the fast (upavasathīya), this Āhitāgni, prior to the morning Agnihotra, should set out the fire-sticks for kindling;
he should have the food for the vow (vratopāyanīya) cooked, and both of them shall eat thereof.
On this day, one should avoid all food mixed with ghee or curd, as well as alkaline substances, salt, meat, and inferior grains— with the exception of sesame seeds;
having first offered it to a Brāhmaṇa, one may eat it,
and on this day one should not give the remnants to a Śūdra.
On this day, he should give the remnants of his food only to his wife; he should not sleep on a couch, nor should he approach a woman.
However, he may sleep on a raised bed at will, but he should certainly not approach a woman; rather, he should remain as one observing a vow.
If he intends to have his hair and beard shaved, he should have his hair and beard shaved, have his body hair removed, and then have his nails clipped.

He should bathe, anoint himself, apply collyrium, assume the form for initiation, and add fuel to the fires: having made the Gārhapatya his lap, he should add fuel with upraised knees; the Anvāhāryapacana with bent knees; the Āhavanīya while standing; and he should recite the tenth [verse] while standing.

If the fires that have been consecrated should go out, or if the Āhavanīya fire of the *savanīya* sacrifice should go out from the Gārhapatya, one should remove the ashes, smear the ground with a lump of dung, draw out the flaming Āhavanīya fire, establish it, add fuel to it, re-consecrate it, and worship it with the *vyāhṛtis*. Now, if the Anvāhāryapacana fire should go out, one should carry it forth in exactly the same manner; for the Anvāhāryapacana is indeed an inviolable deity.

Having added fuel again, he should worship with the *vyāhṛtis*. Now, if the sun should set or rise while his fire has not been lifted up, he should either act according to the Sūtra or offer the *saṃtanī* oblations with the verses, "May the mind, the light, enjoy [the offering]" and "The thirty-three threads. Having offered these two spoon-oblations (*sruvāhuti*), he should worship with the *vyāhṛtis*. Then, if [the sun] has already set, having offered a spoon-oblation to Varuṇa, he should worship with the *vyāhṛtis*; and if [the sun] has already risen, having offered a spoon-oblation to Mitra, he should worship with the *vyāhṛtis*. He should likewise worship the *anvāhāryapacana* fire with the *vyāhṛtis*.

Now, when the fires have been mounted upon the two kindling woods (*araṇi*) or within oneself while traveling on a journey, the teachers do not prescribe an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Regarding this, they cite an example: "If the fires have been mounted within oneself, one may at will lower them onto the two kindling woods and churn [the fire]; or, having spread out the fires into the *āmātya* arrangement, one may lower them onto that and offer oblations. Or, if the fires have been mounted upon the two kindling woods, one may churn [the fire], spread out the fires, and offer oblations; or, having spread out the fires into the *āmātya* arrangement and placed the fires between the two kindling woods, one may offer oblations. As it is for the fires of kings and commoners, so it is for the fire churned for pleasure (*vṛthāgni*)."
Regarding that, some declare the established rule:

as far as a black antelope might sit, so far is the minimum distance for the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) when traveling; one should add fuel to the fires and enter upon the vow (*vrata*). Having entered the vow, one should cut a *parṇa* branch. This is the sequence here:
there are three kinds of *palāśa* trees—the smooth, the hairy, and the creeper-like.
This [stake] belonging to Lomaśaka is to be cut to the exact extent that a cow might graze;
one should not cut it beyond that, for what exceeds that is unfavorable to cattle.
If he should, however, be negligent regarding the remnants of the Agnihotra, he should offer the Agnihotra again. Now, these six inferior cows for the Sāṃnāyya are traditionally handed down.

If there should be three [cows], one should draw [the milk] from the first or the last four times; if there should be two, one should draw from each other three times each; if there should be only one, one should draw from that very one six times.
"Having released his speech, without taking breath, he should milk the subsequent ones"—this is said regarding those of unlimited number.
There are twelve pairs in the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
"These are to be prepared":
the wooden sword (sphya) and the potsherds (kapāla)—these are five;
"he lets the calf loose near [the cow] and he places the fire-pan (ukhā) on the fire"—these are seven.

These twelve [oblations] fall due only for one who performs the *saṃnayya* offering on the new moon day, not for one who does not; furthermore, this altar of the New and Full Moon sacrifices is either as large as the sacrificer or of unlimited size, so that it may encompass the oblations as they are placed; he raises the front part of the altar eastward to enclose the *Āhavanīya* fire.
He digs out the two buttocks toward the west for the sake of enclosing the Gārhapatya fire-altar;

it is narrower in front, wider behind, and more deeply concaved in the middle—for thus, indeed, is a woman—so he says of her. He digs it to this extent, commensurate with Prajāpati, the mouth of the sacrificer; "he digs for the sake of a firm foundation," they say.

Some say it should be dug two finger-breadths deep; some say three finger-breadths; some say four finger-breadths; some say the measure of a furrow; some say the measure of a chariot track; some say as far as the white [mark] of the heel.
According to others, this very same [depth] becomes more deeply excavated for the others.
One should not dig deeper than these measures; by digging on the south side, one makes it more abundant with rain.
They prepare a site provided with loose soil, sloping toward the east and the north, saying, "They finish it. He takes up a portion of this size;
regarding the *prastara* [grass-bundle], some say it should be taken up as large as a fingernail, while others say it should be taken up as broad as a finger-joint.
According to some, it should be taken as long as the handle of a *sruk* ladle; according to others, as long as the handle of a *sruva* ladle;
according to others, as long as a thigh bone; according to others, it should be measured by the joint of the thumb.
"An unlimited number should be taken," say some; "they should be this many," he says regarding the fuel-sticks (*samidh*);
"they should be made equal in measure to a span (*prādeśa*)," they say, for by this [measure] Prajāpati created creatures in the beginning.
"To which deity do the two strainers belong, and by whom are they purified?

One should reply: "They belong to Viṣṇu and are purified by Vāyu. They should not be cut with the fingernails. When leading forward the *praṇītā* waters, he should lead them forward while thinking in his mind, "I lead forward these waters," and he should meditate upon the earth.
He should perform these [acts] in common: the *praṇītā* waters, the Āhavanīya fire, the Brahman priest, and the fuel and sacrificial grass; for this is called "the head of the sacrifice."

"What indeed must the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇyaḥ*) be sprinkled with?"—thus it is known. The exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say: "You have sprinkled the oblations (*haviṣ*) with water; with what [did you sprinkle] the water?
"With the *brahman*."
They indeed become consecrated by Brahman.
He says, "O preparer of the oblation, come! for a Brāhmaṇa; "O preparer of the oblation, approach! for a Rājanya; "O preparer of the oblation, come hither! for a Vaiśya.
This [call] is said to be Parjanya himself. Furthermore, they also cite this: "He thus speaks as one who prepares the oblation."
It is known from the Brāhmaṇa: "One should strike the two millstones loudly with the roar of a bull. He says, "One should strike them loudly for the sake of victory;
as many of his rivals as hear the sounding of the sacrificial implements, they shall perish."
It is known from the tradition: "Twice on the lower grinding stone and once on the upper grinding stone, he prepares it nine times, [reciting]:
'O Agni, drive away the raw-eating fire!
Now, what indeed is this 'raw' (āma)? It is said to be the secondary fire (apara-agni)."
"Drive away the flesh-eaters"—this refers to the fire of the cremation ground; "bring hither the one who sacrifices to the gods"—this refers to the Āhavanīya fire.

"Who indeed is the carrier of the offerings to the ancestors?"—one should say, "It is the Anvāhāryapacana fire," for it is known from scripture: "O Agni, carrier of the offerings to the ancestors, sacrifice to the fathers who increase the cosmic order.
From where, then, should one pour the flour? One should say, "From the black antelope skin."
While pouring out the flour, he restrains his speech; he releases his speech with the words, "Cook this without burning it.
That which is burnt belongs to Nirṛti; that which is uncooked belongs to Rudra; that which is properly cooked belongs to the gods.
"May it be well-boiled," this is what is meant by saying "be united with the Brahman";
for it is known that the Brahman is speech; thus he unites him with speech.
"Where indeed is the mixed oblation cooked? [He replies:
"When he pours it out for the Āpyas with the formulas, 'Svāhā to Ekata! Svāhā to Dvita! Svāhā to Trita!'—who then is Ekata, who is Dvita, and who is Trita?"
Some say [the ancestors are] the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather;

some say they are the earth, the intermediate space, and the sky; some say they are fire, the sun, and lightning; some say there were three elder brothers of Agni; and some say they were sages who bore these names.
"Those gods purified themselves in the Āpyas," it is said; thus they are the gods named Āpyas.
But where, indeed, is that which is offered to the ancestors on the full moon day? It is when he pours [the water] out from the two buttocks.
"What indeed is the clarified butter (ājya) with which it is sprinkled?
"One should say: 'With truth. It is known: 'I sprinkle thee with truth; may I partake of thee.
"'I take thee for the restraint and support of the five winds'—the winds are according to the quarters, and the wind blowing in all directions is the fifth among them."
With the formula, "I take you for the restraint and support of the five seasons," winter and the cool season (*hemanta-śiśira*) here enter into a single unit;
with the formula, "I take you for the restraint and support of the five directions," this very upward direction becomes the fifth among them;
with the formula, "I take you for the restraint and support of the five peoples (*pañcajana*)," these are gods, humans, *asuras*, *rākṣasas*, and *gandharvas*, who constitute the fifth among them.
"With 'I take thee for the restraint and support of the five-holed cauldron,' this very space is the cauldron;

it has five holes, for the quarters are its five holes, and the wind is the stirring-ladle. Regarding this they also cite: "The year itself is the cauldron; it has five holes, for the seasons are its holes, and the wind is the stirring-ladle.
Now follows the entering of the Adhvaryu and the Hotṛ.

Between the Vedi and the *utkara*, the Adhvaryu enters from the east, and the Hotṛ from the west; the Adhvaryu should remain immediately adjacent to the fire. To one who does not know his lineage, [the Adhvaryu] says, "Recite the *pravara*. He should say, "Like Manu, like Bharata, like Manu," for it is known from the Brāhmaṇa that "all creatures are descended from Manu. Or, in the case of a king, the *pravara* may be that of his domestic priest (*purohita*). Now, if the kinship is unknown, he should declare him as the son of such-and-such a teacher (*āmuṣyāyaṇa*) and recite the *pravara* of that teacher. Then he should cause the Hotṛ to recite the *pravara*.

One should increase the portion for the deity with milk and that for the *sviṣṭakṛt* with curds. Having interlaced the fingers, one should cut the portions; the portions for the deities are the size of the joint of a thumb, while those for the *sviṣṭakṛt*, the *iḍā*, and the fourfold divisions are larger. Having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* with the formula "Brahman is the foundation," one should fill the ladle with water and pour it inside the enclosing sticks with the formula: "I offer this oblation in Vaiśvānara."
"What indeed has not yet arisen?"—one should say, "until the preliminary call for the *anūyāja* offerings.

Regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*), and the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*): some say the *agnihotra* has an *upadoha* as its fee;
others say the *agnihotra* has a *śarāva* (a shallow vessel) as its fee.
In that he offers the evening oblation, he thereby makes the night worthy of sacrificial gifts; in that he offers the morning oblation, he thereby makes the day worthy of sacrificial gifts;
and what he gives thereafter is the sacrificial gift itself.

When it says "he gives during the day and night," this is what is meant. Now, regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the fourfold division of both the *anvāhārya* rice and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is known; this is indeed his sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and furthermore, it serves to fill up any breach in the sacrifice.

Just as in that Soma sacrifice the sacrificial fees are led forth to the officiating priests according to the instruction, even so here, having divided the southern sacrificial cake into four parts, he places it upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

The optional *iṣṭis* have garments as their sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), while those for which no fee is specifically prescribed have a cow as their fee. The obligatory animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) has a cow as its fee, as does the regular *anvāhārya* rice-offering. Furthermore, regarding this ritual procedure taught by Śālīki—namely, that "all should walk around the Gārhapatya fire to the north during the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings"—the *phalīkaraṇa* oblation should be offered there without returning [to the starting point]. Now, some offer the oblations to Rākā, Sinīvālī, Kuhū, and Anumati, as well as the *patnīhoma*, the two *nāriṣṭha* oblations, and the oblation to Gṛhapati beforehand; [then] the wife [joins].

May they go with their husband through his meritorious deeds; may they become the two yoke-bearers harnessed to the sacrifice; being in harmony, may they cast off their enemies; may they attain the unaging light in heaven—svāhā!

O sacrifice, ten are your bodies worthy of worship; may the sacrificer gratify them with clarified butter. Praising the instruction of the two *nāriṣṭha* [sacrificial ladles], the sacrificer has become immortal within the divine assembly of the gods—*svāhā*!
"O you two of a hundred powers, that portion of strength which the gods have ordained for you—by this I gratify you; by this may you two be satisfied! *Am̐hahau svāhā*!
Now, the teachers declare that this Agnihotra begins in the evening and concludes in the morning;
regarding this they cite: "These two lights, of the sun and of the fire, come together."
One should not pass between them;

when taking out the Āhavanīya fire in the evening, one should deposit it while facing west from the east; when taking out the Āhavanīya fire in the morning, one should deposit it while facing east from the west.

When about to offer the evening *agnihotra*, he should offer after walking around by the front; when about to offer the morning *agnihotra*, he should offer after walking around by the back. In this way, these two lights of his remain unseparated. Now, this is the mantra for lifting [the fire]: "With speech as the *hotṛ*, with breath as the *udgātṛ*, with the eye as the *adhvaryu*, with the mind as the *brahman*, and with the ear as the *āgnīdh*—with these five divine officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) I lift you up. *Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ*, being lifted up, lift me up from whatever evil I have done unknowingly or knowingly."

He performs [the rite]: "Whatever sin or evil has been committed by day—released from all that, release me from it," thus in the evening; "Whatever sin or evil has been committed by night—released from all that, release me from it," thus in the morning.

He places the fire [with the mantra]: "I offer the immortal oblation into the immortal; I offer Agni into the earth for the conquest of immortality. Through this, may we conquer from here the infinite desire which Prajāpati first conquered. I offer immortality into Agni Vaiśvānara, Svāhā!"—thus in the evening; "I offer immortality into Sūrya Vaiśvānara, Svāhā!"—thus in the morning.

This indeed is the Agnihotra of the fire; the other is the milk-oblation. On the day of the new moon, one should sprinkle water around the fires as if they were already established; having offered the oblation, one should sprinkle water only around the Āhavanīya fire. On the day of the full moon, having offered the oblation, one should sprinkle water only around the Āhavanīya fire, or one should not sprinkle at all—this is another view. Now follows this indirect worship: "Remaining right here, O fires, I support you who are there with breath, speech, and mind. May life not desert me while I am away; I worship you with the Vaiśvānara light. Then, for one who is traveling, he should silently place this fuel-stick upon the fire.
One performs the sacrifice while traveling; now, regarding this complete oblation (*samastahoma*), the teachers say it exists according to the rule of the *yāyāvara* (wandering ascetics).
In this regard, they cite an example: there were indeed ancient seers named *yāyāvara*; they grew weary on the road and offered everything together as a single oblation.
Therefore, according to the dharma of the wandering mendicant, the entire [milk] must be offered while on the road; that is his unconditioned oblation.

He should conceal it by lying down, or by closing his eyes, or by extinguishing the fire. One should not offer the Agnihotra with the milk of a cow belonging to a Śūdra, nor of one whose calf is dead, nor of one that is over-milking, nor of one that is exhausted, nor of one that is estranged, nor of one whose calf belongs to another, nor of one received as a gift for a specific purpose (*anudeśya*), nor of one received as a funeral cow (*anustaraṇī*).

Many should not offer the oblation with the milk of a single cow, nor should a single person offer the milk of many cows. For one who obtains the milk of many cows, the consecration formula for spilled milk (*skannānumantraṇa*) applies from the time of the placing [of the milk] onwards.
While the fires are blazing and the oblations are being offered, one should count how many *agnihotra* offerings have been omitted and offer them in succession.
If he should offer after sunset, he must offer again at sunset; if he should offer at midnight, he must offer again at dawn.
Now, how indeed is the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) performed for one whose father is still living?
To those very same persons to whom the father gives, the son gives;
one whose father is living gives to two; one whose grandfather is living gives to one; some say that one should not give on behalf of a living person.
If one should inherit the estate of a paternal uncle who belongs to the same *gotra*, how is the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) performed in that case?
At the time when one offers the rice-ball to the father, at that very time one should offer a rice-ball for him.
Now, if one should inherit the estate of one who does not belong to the same *gotra*, how is the offering of the rice-ball performed in that case?

Having given [the portions] to his own [ancestors] and having spread the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the neighbor, he should offer the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) starting from the sacrificial grass; or else, having cooked the *sthālīpāka* in the house itself, he should offer the rice-balls starting from the sacrificial grass. How indeed does the offering of rice-balls take place for the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*)? It is as follows: "This is for you, O father of so-and-so, my grandfather, and those who follow you; this is for you, O grandfather of so-and-so, my great-grandfather, and those who follow you; this is for you, O great-grandfather of so-and-so, my great-great-grandfather, and those who follow you."

Or one may give according to the ritual for the distribution [of food]: "Svadhā to the fathers dwelling on earth; svadhā to the fathers dwelling in the intermediate space; svadhā to the fathers dwelling in heaven.

If one does not know the names of the father, grandfather, or great-grandfather, how should the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) be performed there? One should give according to the ritual for the distribution, saying: "This for you, O father, and for those who follow you; this for you, O grandfather, and for those who follow you; this for you, O great-grandfather, and for those who follow you. Furthermore, it is said: "In the latter part of life, one should have the hair cut."
"At what time, indeed, should this [hair] be cut? "After sixty-six years and eight months; at that very time it should be cut.

"How, then, does the Piṇḍapitṛyajña proceed for one who has not maintained the sacred fires? Having cooked a *sthālīpāka* of unoffered rice, having kindled the fire and strewn grass around it, and having offered the oblations, he should strew sacrificial grass with its points directed southward to the south of the fire, and beginning with the grass, he should offer the *piṇḍas*.

Alternatively, having cooked a *sthālīpāka* in the very house, he should offer the *piṇḍa* beginning with the *barhis* grass; wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), he should worship this fire with the verse addressed to Prajāpati.

As for that ritual procedure of Baudhāyana which they teach—namely, that one should release speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*) and then offer the *ājyānī* oblations—at what time, indeed, should he offer these? Having performed the ritual up to the point of the spilling [of the grain], he should offer them at this time.

How indeed does the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice take place for one who has not established the sacred fires? Having cooked a *sthālīpāka* (pot-offering) that has not been formally poured out, having kindled the fire and strewn grass around it, having offered the two *āghāra* libations and the two *ājyabhāga* portions, he should offer oblations to the deities of the *āgrayaṇa*, with the *Sviṣṭakṛt* as the fourth.
He may, if he wishes, offer the *ājyāni* (clarified butter offerings) before the *Sviṣṭakṛt*.

He should eat from this [remnant] with this very mantra: "O gods, you have led us from good to better. Or else, he may seek to obtain [the remnant] from the portion left over after the offering by a learned Brāhmaṇa.
The mantra for the consumption [of the remains] is the same.

How indeed should one know the *antarvirāja*, the *bahirvirāja*, and the *antarbahirvirāja*? Having performed the worship with the obligatory (*nitya*) rite, one should worship with the *virājakrama* verses; having gone abroad and returned again, one should worship with the *virājakrama* verses and then worship with the obligatory rite alone. By this very [method], the *bahirvirāja* and the *antarbahirvirāja* are explained. He goes abroad while sleeping on the ground, eating meat, and approaching women.

This [offering] has a contrary name; indeed, it is like this expiation which falls in the middle: one should perform the two-potsherd offering to the Aśvins at the very end. If it should be lost during the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, one should follow through with the *prāyaṇīyā*;

if it should be lost during the *prāyaṇīyā*, one should follow through with the *ātithyā*; if it should be lost during the *ātithyā*, one should follow through with the subsequent ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) for Agni-Soma. Now, if it should be lost during the fire-consecration (*agnidīkṣaṇīyā*), at what time, indeed, should one offer it?

Having offered the initiation oblations (*dīkṣā-āhuti*), one should offer this [oblation] at that time; or alternatively, before the drawing of the cups (*audgrahaṇa*). Furthermore, they teach this ritual procedure (*kalpa*) of Baudhāyana: for one who is traveling abroad, one should throw the sacrificer’s portion (*yajamāna-bhāga*) into the fire along with the *prastara* grass-bundle. Having spread a base of clarified butter (*ājya*) from the *dhruvā* vessel and having placed it in the *juhū* ladle, one should offer it, thinking: "The sacrificer’s portion attains the state of the *prastara*. Thus, for one traveling abroad, one should throw the sacrificer’s portion into the fire along with the *prastara*. Now follows this animal sacrifice together with the day of preparation (*upavasatha*).

What is the preparatory procedure for that rite? Having moved away with perpetual fires, having offered the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* oblation, having offered the *yūpāhuti*, having prepared the sacrificial post together with its formulas, having measured out the altar, and having eaten the food for entering the vow (*vratopāyanīya*), one should add fuel to the fires, enter upon the vow, bind the fuel-sticks and the sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*), and fast. Then, in the morning, one should sacrifice with a cake on eight potsherds for Agni—such is the ritual rule (*kalpa*) of Baudhāyana. One should not add fuel to the fires nor enter upon the vow;
rather, one should rub the hands together and strew the grass around the altar.

Having washed the vessels, he should set them down; he should seat the Brahman priest to the south. If the fire has been carried forward silently, he should sit down with the mantra at the northern altar. Having prepared the sprinkling waters, he should sprinkle the vessels; having poured out the clarified butter, placed it on the fire, and carried fire around it, he should go eastward with the wooden sword (sphya) in his hand and carry away the *stambayajus*. From this point onward, the procedure is established.

Then, having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods of the Śālīki rite, having gone down to the sacrificial ground, having churned out the fire, and having spread out the fires, he should likewise offer the six *hotṛ* oblations, offer the oblation for the sacrificial post (*yūpa-āhuti*), prepare the sacrificial post with its accompanying formulas, measure out the altar, add fuel to the fires, enter upon the vow, bind together the fuel and the sacrificial grass, rub his hands together, and strew the grass around the fires.

Having washed the vessels, he should set them down; he should seat the Brahman priest to the south. If the fire has been carried forward silently, he should sit down with the mantra at the northern altar-ground. Having prepared the sprinkling waters, he should sprinkle the vessels; having poured out the clarified butter and placed it on the fire, having carried fire around it, having melted the butter over the Gārhapatya fire and purified it, and having taken four portions into the ladle, he should offer a full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in the Āhavanīya fire while the firewood is burning. Then, going eastward with the wooden sword (sphya) in his hand, he should perform the Stambayajus rite. From this point onward, the procedure is established.
"The wooden sword (sphya) becomes the sacrificial post (yūpa).

How, then, do its splinter (svaru) and the two chips used for the churning (adhimanthana) come to be? One should have these carved from this very [wood], or one may make them from another tree of the same species;
this [post] remains without a top-ring (acaṣāla).

One should perform the recitation of the mantras beginning from the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) up until the third time of encircling (parivyayaṇa); at that third time, one should indeed encircle [the sacrificial post]. In this manner, for a post measured by the height of the sacrificer's upper body, there are posts for the animal sacrifice (pāśubandhika) starting from five cubits (aratni) up to nine cubits; for the Agniṣṭoma, the posts start from nine cubits up to twenty-one cubits. For the independent animal sacrifice (nirūḍhapaśubandha), the post is made of Palāśa wood and is either three or four cubits long.
Now, does the animal sacrifice succeed for one who is away on a journey, or does it not succeed?

"One group says it is accomplished; then another group says it is not accomplished. For they say that these fires of the worlds constitute a second establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), yet for one who is away from home, the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) is certainly not accomplished.
Now, how much of the ritual duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) are there in the animal sacrifice?"

Regarding the commencement of the vow (*vratopāyana*) and the dismissal of the vow (*vratavisarjana*), some say that at the re-undertaking of the sacrifice there is the *ājyāvakāśa* and the *upapraiṣa-āśrāvaṇa*. "To which deity does this [offering] belong? one should reply, "It belongs to Death (*mṛtyu*). Now, in the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), there are these six sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*): three with mantras and three silently; those containing barley are for Indra, and those for the sprinkling of the victim are silent.

If, in the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), one intends to offer the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) that have been consecrated by the mantras for the *paśupuroḍāśa*, the *prokṣaṇī* waters for the vessels, and the *prokṣaṇī* waters for the fuel and sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*), at what time indeed should he perform the offering?
Having proceeded with the *svāhākṛti-praiṣa*, he should offer them before the omentum (*vapā*).

"Some gods have their *svāhā*-utterances before [the offering], others have their *svāhā*-utterances after," they say; these are indeed the rays of the sun, moving both eastward and westward. Now, as for this animal cake-offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*), what is the commencement of its ritual action?
One should place the wooden sword (*sphya*) behind the *gārhapatya* fire.

Upon the wooden sword (sphya), he should place the vessel; into the vessel, he should pour the rice from the winnowing basket. The ritual procedure extends from the taking [of the rice] until the end, specifically up to the pouring out of the water for the *āpyas*. He should pour out the water for the *āpyas* behind the Gārhapatya fire.

With the remainder of the sprinkling-water (*prokṣaṇī*), he should mix the flour intended for the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*). In this same manner, he should do so for the *savanīya* offerings. Thus they teach the ritual rule of Baudhāyana.

One should cut off the *iḍā* for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering from this [cake] without having first made a base-layer. How, then, does the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*) come about here? By making a base-layer, dividing the cake into two parts, and pouring an over-layer [of clarified butter], thus his portion becomes fourfold. Now, some teachers set aside eleven ritual elements at the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*): the adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*), the undertaking of the vow (*vratopāyana*), the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, the *praṇītā* water, the sacrificer’s duties (*yājamāna*), the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, the *prāśitra*, the sacrificer’s portion, the Brahman’s portion, the division into four parts (*caturdhākaraṇa*), and the *viṣṇukrama* steps.
But how many *darvihoma* oblations are actually seen in the animal sacrifice?

Regarding the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ, the oblation for the sacrificial post, the *stokyās*, the offerings to the quarters, and the *upayaj* sacrifices—what deity indeed is the *manotā*? One should say: "It belongs to Agni.
What deity indeed is the *vanaspati*?

"One should simply say 'Vaiṣṇava,' for it is known that 'the trees indeed belong to Viṣṇu. Moreover, they cite: 'Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice. Now, this animal sacrifice is entirely in the Triṣṭubh meter: there are eleven *prayāja*s, eleven *anuyāja*s, the animal *puroḍāśa* is on eleven potsherds, there are eleven portions (*avadāna*s), and eleven *upayāja*s.

Regarding this, they teach the ritual procedure of Śālīki: "Having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇī*), one should depart for the *udavasānīyā* offering. If, while performing those rites there, the sun should set upon him, how is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) accomplished in that case—is it accomplished or not?"
"One [group] says it succeeds; then another says it does not succeed.
This space is encompassed by the sacrifice, and thus it does not succeed at all. Now, this animal is explained as being entirely connected with the *triṣṭubh*."
Now, therefore, we shall explain the animals for optional sacrifices. What indeed is their common characteristic?
They are those belonging to the Aśvamedha: those dedicated to Prajāpati, to Savitṛ, to Sarasvatī, to Pūṣan, to Yama, to the Pitṛs, to Heaven and Earth, to Vāyu, to Sūrya, and to Viśvakarman.
"They become pregnant"—how, in this case, is the expiation accomplished or not accomplished?

Some say it is accomplished; others say it is not accomplished. "These [sacrifices] are for the sake of prosperity," they say, "it is indeed not accomplished. Regarding the statement, "He offers a speckled, pregnant cow to Aditi," this is merely the name of a seer (ṛṣi).
"She has unbroken teeth" means that she has teeth that are not deficient; now, this [cow] is provided with ten bulls over the course of a year, and Kadrū herself becomes the tenth among them.
In this regard, how is the vow of studentship (*brahmacarya*) fulfilled or not fulfilled?
"It is accomplished," say some; "it is not accomplished," say others; it concludes thus:
"it is certainly not accomplished."
Regarding the statement "she becomes one that miscarries," some say it means "one who has aborted"; however, others say that she is indeed called "the barren cow" (vehat),
and they designate her as such.

"One should sacrifice a three-year-old animal dedicated to Soma and Pūṣan"—this is said to refer to exactly three [animals]; furthermore, they also cite: "One should sacrifice a stallion dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ, which sucks at three [teats]."
"He who mounts this [bull] while it is still a male—let him sacrifice a stallion on uneven ground," they say.

"Uneven ground" may refer to the sacrificial site (*devayajana*), or rather to that place where one sacrifices the animal; "at the junction of water and plants" means at the edge of the water, so some say. Now, others say: "In the rainy season or in autumn.
"He for whom the sun does not appear while the *Aśvina* hymns are being recited—let him sacrifice a multicolored bull to Sūrya," they say.

If [the victim] is not seen at the Prāyaṇīya Atirātra, one should perform the animal sacrifice for the Savanīya of the Ārambhaṇīya day; and if it is not seen at the Udayanīya Atirātra, they should perform the animal sacrifice for the Anūbandhya of the one-day rite, or having performed the Udavasānīya, they should sacrifice with this animal. Thus have these optional animals been explained. Now, how indeed does the subsequent performance of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices take place when they are undertaken for the duration of one's life?

On the full moon day of Phālguna or Caitra, one should sacrifice with the Śunāsīrīya offering; then one should fast for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, and having sacrificed with the Vaiśvadeva, one should sacrifice with the Full Moon and Vaimṛdha offerings. Now, if one should sacrifice with an *iṣṭi*, an animal sacrifice, or Soma, how should one proceed in that case? One should draw back [the ritual] and sacrifice with the Śunāsīrīya portion of this fortnight; then one may sacrifice with any one of these [other rites], and then one should fast for the Vaiśvadeva, and having sacrificed with the Vaiśvadeva, one should sacrifice with the Full Moon and Vaimṛdha offerings.

Regarding this, they teach Baudhāyana’s ritual manual: "The Cāturmāsya sacrifices should be performed throughout one's entire life, with pairings [of male and female deities] occurring within; however, in the very first year, one should observe the vow. How then are the *iṣṭis* and animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*) to be handled?
One may perform an *iṣṭi* at will, or an animal sacrifice at will.

Where indeed do the Cāturmāsya sacrifices come together? One should say: "In the Rājasūya and in the Soma-sacrifices of the Cāturmāsyas. Furthermore, they also cite this: "One may also sacrifice with the Cāturmāsyas during the Dvādaśāha;
having sacrificed with the Vaiśvadeva on the fourth day, with the Varuṇapraghāsas on the eighth, with the Sākamedhas on the ninth, and with the Śunāsīrīya offering on the twelfth."
It is known that the twelve nights are indeed a representation of the year;
the sacrificial grass is threefold,
the intermediate [days] are performed silently, and the outer [days] are accompanied by mantras.
"This very [procedure] is correct elsewhere, but in the case of a conjunction of *iṣṭis*, it becomes reversed.
"Where, then, do the *karambha* vessels first receive the mantra?
"One should say: at the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*)."
Together with the sacrificial offerings, he should carry fire around the *karambha* vessels.

"To which deity do the *karambha* vessels belong? one might ask; "They belong to Varuṇa," he should reply. For it is known: "He thereby offers a sacrifice to another Varuṇa. With the words, "Go home, O bounteous ones," he should look toward his house; this is what is meant by that.
If those two should exchange the *stambayajus* offerings while moving from here and there, the Pratiprasthātṛ should take hold of the Adhvaryu from behind.

Having poured out water from the portion already measured out, the Pratiprasthātṛ should cause the Adhvaryu to recite the formula over the clarified butter. Then, having taken up the two fuel-sticks before they are carried forward, the Adhvaryu steps aside and stands with his own fuel-stick.
Thereupon, this Pratiprasthātṛ, passing between the fuel-stick and the Āhavanīya fire, should take up his own fuel-stick.
Turning back by the side-ways, the two of them should carry the fuel;

then, having turned to the right from that point and having set down the two fuels, they return by the same way they came, and the Pratiprasthātṛ wraps himself around [the altar]. Between the two altars, he brings forward the *upayamanī* water-carriers to the east; then, taking these sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*) belonging to the Adhvaryu to the south of the Pratiprasthātṛ, he should set them down. In this way, he remains unencircled by these waters. Then this vessel for the Maruts goes to the southern altar; it is the seventh of the oblations to be placed on the fire. [The question is: "How do [the other offerings] become separated from this one?"

Having drawn this [offering] forward by its front with his right hand, he should remove it from the fire without pouring clarified butter over it; then, having placed it back on the fire and poured clarified butter over it, he should remove it and set it down within the altar. In this way, these [offerings] remain uninterrupted. Now, this Pratiprasthātṛ should cause the formula for the deity Marut to be recited only once and should cause the announcement (āśrāvaṇa) to be made only once; thus, in other respects, he acts as an imitator of the Adhvaryu.

In that case, when [the Adhvaryu] causes [the offering] to be heard here and sacrifices here, the Pratiprasthātṛ acts as a mere imitator; then, taking this stirring-stick belonging to the Maruts, he should throw it into the fire in front of the Uttaravedi.
