Furthermore, they teach the ritual procedure of Aupamanyava: "One should go down for the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) with the husks and the scrapings. Having offered the portion to the deity, he should hand over the Sviṣṭakṛt portion; having scattered the husks, he should cast them into the water at its edge. From this point onward, the rite is established. Now, this Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice concludes with the Ājyabhāgas and ends with the Iḍā.

In that [rite], there is no *prāśitra* portion; one should silently throw the smoothed *śakala* chips and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) into the fire. If a cow for milking is not available, one should cause a *saṃdhinī* cow to be milked.
Now, as for this Great Ancestor Sacrifice (*mahāpitṛyajña*), what is the commencement of its ritual procedure?

One should prepare the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the *yajus* formula: "Thou art strewn for the gods and the ancestors; thou art the sacrificial grass of the gods and the ancestors; let me not strike thee from behind nor across; may I succeed in thy joint. [With the formula] "Araru is driven away from the earth, the place of sacrifice for the gods and the ancestors," [and] "Araru is driven away from the earth, the non-place of sacrifice for the gods and the ancestors"—in these ways one should act upon these bases where the gods and the ancestors meet.
One should rub the hands together and strew around [the fire].

Having washed the vessels, he should set them down; having seated the Brahman priest to the south, and having placed a water-pot right there to the north, he should place the wooden sword (sphya) behind the Gārhapatya fire. Upon the wooden sword, he should place the vessel; into the vessel, he should pour the rice-grains. From the taking up of the winnowing basket until the end of the ritual, and up to the Āpyas, [the action takes place] behind the Gārhapatya. He should pour out the Āpya waters behind the Gārhapatya. These officiating priests move around in reverse order: the Adhvaryu should be closest to the fire, then the sacrificer, then the Brahman, then the Agnīdhra. Or rather, the Agnīdhra alone should be closest to the fire, then the sacrificer, then the Brahman, then the Adhvaryu.

They transpose the oblations: the cake is placed in front, the parched grains behind the cake, and the groats behind the grains. One should set aside each of these transposed oblations as they have been moved.

Now, where indeed are the Traiyambaka offerings set out? Having set aside the oblations with the formula, "I set out what is pleasing to Rudra Yāmbika," one should offer the portion for Kāya with the mantra, "To Kāya! if the mantras are intended for that deity.
He should recite "Recite for the body";
he should sacrifice with "Sacrifice to Ka. Now, where indeed does the *sauviṣṭakṛt* offering for the *traiyambaka* cakes take place?

Regarding the statement, "When he has already bound the victim," and "He gives a bull when [the sun] has not yet risen": this bull is to be given specifically at the Mahāhavis sacrifice when [the sun] has not yet risen; otherwise, the entire ritual duty (*yājamāna*) would perish in the Pitṛyajña, the Paśubandha, and the Soma sacrifice, because there are specific injunctions for its performance elsewhere.

In the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicaya*), every fire-rite is performed by the sacrificer; in the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), every metrical formula (*chandas*) is performed by the sacrificer.
One who intends to sacrifice with the *agniṣṭoma* should make himself prosperous;
whatever may be unfavorable for him, he should make that favorable.
Whatever debts may have become due, he should either settle them or obtain permission [to postpone them].
He prepares beforehand an abundance of barley-gruel for the debtor, as well as an animal, clarified butter, a cooking pot, a vessel, and a *kumbha*;

the *kumbha* is made of split bamboo and the *kurīra* is a net. A fee of one hundred and twelve is prescribed; this is known from the *Chandoga-Brāhmaṇa*: "He who presses the Soma is indeed a slayer of the heroes of the gods."

With a hundred [cows] he redeems the hero; with ten, the ten vital breaths; the eleventh is the self; and that which is the twelfth is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Now, some indeed sacrifice with a fee of twenty-one [cows], saying, "The *yajñāyajñiya* chant consists of twenty-one parts. Furthermore, some sacrifice with seven groups of three: the cow for purchasing Soma, the guest-offering cow, the *anūbandhyā* cow, and four in the middle. This is also known from the *Daśataya*: "The wise one, the seven-stepped one, whose thought is fixed on Truth... and so forth.

Now, therefore, follows the ritual for selecting the sacrificial ground (*devayajanakalpa*). He chooses this sacrificial ground as follows: it should have water to the east, be free from saline soil, not previously occupied, not containing excrement, not sloping away, not hollow, not fragile, and free from ant-hills; it should be rich in herbs where various kinds of plants grow intertwined; it should slope toward the northeast so that the waters flow toward the *catvāla* pit, yet not so steeply that they rush away; nor should one find another sacrificial ground closer than this to the east. Upon such a site, they cause a hall (*śālā*) with its ridge-pole facing east to be measured out.

"These Kṛttikās indeed do not abandon the eastern quarter; one should measure [the site] by their appearance—this is one view. One should measure it by the appearance of Śroṇā—this is another view. 'Between Citrā and Svāti'—this is yet another. 'It has openings toward the quarters'—it is by means of the doors that it has openings toward the quarters. Furthermore, they also cite: 'One should make the openings toward the quarters for the Vamśas themselves.'"
"Two *stomas* carry the morning pressing," thus the *trivṛt* and *pañcadaśa* carry the morning pressing;
the *pañcadaśa* and *saptadaśa* carry the midday pressing; the *saptadaśa* and *ekaviṃśa* carry the third pressing.
This indeed is the Catuṣṭoma;

for there are twelve stotras. Furthermore, regarding the ritual procedure of Aupamanyava that they teach, one should settle upon the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) before the threefold [stomas] have been reached; for it is known: "This earth is indeed the entire altar."
Now, some say that this offering to Agni and Viṣṇu occurs either before the consecration by water or after it.

Regarding the question, "At what point indeed should one perform the *barhis*-formula for the consecration-offering (*dīkṣaṇīyā*)?", [the answer is: having set down the ritual materials, before the touching of the hands, he leads the sacrificer to the vow, but he does not gird the wife. Thus he extends the vow for the consecration of the *adhvara*.

This entire offering becomes the "vow-inducing" (*vratopāyanīyā*). At the beginning, there is the girding of the wife; he does not prepare a portion for the sacrificer nor a portion for the Brahman priest. These two are said to be merely the joining of blessings.

"Beginning with what [act] should one pronounce the blessing for the sacrifice? Furthermore, it is said that there is an abundance of food for the preparatory rite of the vow (*vratopāyanīya*). For what purpose is this abundance? One should cut off a portion for the sake of the sacrificer's share; indeed, from the omission of the sacrificer's share, the Brahman's share is omitted, for these two—the sacrificer's share and the Brahman's share—are closely connected.

"He does not prepare the *barhiṣad* rice-cake, nor does he ask for the *anvāhārya* [mess of rice]"—these two are stated only in reference to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Indeed, other fees are well-known here;
"he does not perform the oblation of husks, nor does he offer the *samiṣṭayajus*"—these two are stated only in reference to those rites that conclude the ritual circuit.
"By what procedure does one bring the sacrifice to its conclusion?

[The response is: "He does not have the sacrificer recite the formula over the full vessel (pūrṇapātra), nor does he perform the Viṣṇu-steps. Indeed, the full vessel is prescribed for the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha);
however, in this case, there is another well-known purificatory bath, and the Viṣṇu-steps are for the purpose of completing the rite.
"By what means does one bring the sacrifice to its conclusion?
"They raised twelve *vātsabandha* [verses]."

"What indeed are these *vātsabandha* [offerings]? These are simply the ladle-offerings (*sruvāhuti*), excluding the utterance of "svāhā. Furthermore, they cite this: "The fire has a common number; there are three deities in the verse; those make twelve. Now, regarding this black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), it is explained etymologically: having bent the knee, one should crawl along its side toward the opening, as if toward a boat. If he should see something impure at night, he should worship the Āhavanīya fire with this very formula. Now, these are the observances (*vrata*) pertaining to initiation (*daikṣa*).

The rites of the Upasads begin in the evening and conclude in the morning, while those of the initiation (daikṣa) begin in the morning and conclude in the evening; furthermore, one should observe this initiatory vow only after having enclosed the sacrificial ground. Previously, the Agnihotra was offered at the Āhavanīya fire itself, thinking, "This belongs to the human realm. Now, however, this is the Prāyaṇīya [offering]; what, then, is the commencement of its ritual procedure?
If the sacrificial grass (barhis) has not been prepared with a Yajus formula beforehand,
one should touch the two hands together and then strew the grass.

Having washed the vessels, he should set them down; having seated the Brahman priest to the south and having placed a water-pot right there to the north, he should place the wooden sword (sphyá) behind the Gārhapatya fire. Upon the wooden sword he should place the vessel, and into the vessel he should pour the rice-grains. From the taking up of the winnowing basket until the end of the ritual, the procedure continues until the scattering [of the grains].

Having performed the rites up to the *praskandana* (the spilling of the grain), having offered a spoonful (*sruvāhuti*) into the *āhavanīya* fire, having gone out and issued the call (*saṃpraiṣa*), having entered [the hall] again, having poured water across the strainers and placed it over the fire, he should pour the rice grains across the strainers; then he should set out the clarified butter (*ājya*), then place the clarified butter over the fire, and having carried fire around both, he should go eastward with the wooden sword (*sphya*) in his hand and perform the *stambayajus* rite. From this point onward, the procedure is established as being concluded with the *śaṃyu*-formula.
What indeed remains of this ritual? Until the releasing of the ladles (*sruc-vimoka*), the pouring of the water for the cooked-rice oblations (*caru-havis*) is prescribed.
"One should offer the *caru* in pots"— this is indeed the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) of Baudhāyana.
As for the question, "To which deity does the *padāhuti* belong?", some say it belongs to Agni,
while others say it belongs to Viṣṇu.
Some say it belongs to Prajāpati; one should rather say it belongs to Vāk.
With a tuft of black wool, he pierces the two eyebrows of the Soma-seller from behind.

The sacrificer uncovers the King [Soma] with the verse, "The fair-winged birds have approached Indra. Now, if there should be no Soma-seller, one should drive in a Palāśa branch at the place where the pit for the sacrificial post is to be, tie it up, hang the King [Soma] upon the Palāśa branch, and wait. Furthermore, if someone should utter a word connected with impulsion—such as "quickly," "hurry," "do it"—then he should take up the King [Soma];
the conversations should not be interrupted.
He shall be the seller of Soma. Now, this first Subrahmaṇyā formula is said to end with the syllable *oṃ*. Then there is this guest-offering (*ātithya*); what is the commencement of that rite?
One should perform it with a *barhis*-formula, provided that no such formula has been used previously.
He should rub his hands together,
strew the sacrificial grass,

wash the vessels and set them down; having seated the Brahman priest to the south and unyoked the southern ox, he should place a water-vessel right there to the north, and set down the wooden sword (sphyam) behind the Gārhapatya fire.

Having placed the vessel upon the winnowing basket, he should pour the rice grains from the basket into the vessel. From the taking up [of the rice] from the basket until the end of the ritual action—that is, having performed the rites ending with the scattering [of the grains]—he should release the northern ox and cause the King [Soma] to enter.
One should understand that the Agniṣṭoma ritual procedure is established here up until the formal summons (*saṃpraiṣa*).
He performs the hospitality by merely shaking out the black antelope skin; from this point onward, the procedure is established.
Then he says, "Uproot a bunch of Darbha grass."
"What indeed is this bunch of darbha grass?
"It is that which one places upon the two godāna [hair-tufts].
"Having pierced through the seven mountains," he says.

"What indeed are these mountains? [he asks]. "They are said to be the fore-offerings (prayāja) and the after-offerings (anūyāja)," [it is replied]. "Of the Dīkṣaṇīyā, the Prāyaṇīyā, the Ātithyā, and the Agniṣomīya.
Furthermore, they also cite: "The Dīkṣaṇīyā, the Prāyaṇīyā, the Ātithyā, the Upasads, and the Agniṣomīya as the seventh."
"The sacrifice has hidden itself from the gods"—
what indeed is this sacrifice? It is that very *ātithya* (guest-offering) which concludes with the *iḍā*.
"The gods, grasping their hands together, sought it"—
this refers to when they touched that *tānūnaptra* [anointing butter] together;
"Indra stepped over it from above"— so it is said.
"When they perform with the Upasads," [it was asked], "he brought sacrifice itself as a sacrifice for them. But which sacrifice, indeed, brought this sacrifice?
"The Dīkṣaṇīyā, the Prāyaṇīyā, and the Ātithyā—this indeed is the sacrifice; 'He has carried off the sacrifice,' [they say].
This boar is 'vāma'; 'he steals vāma,' [they say]. Of the days of the Soma-pressing, it is the most excellent; thus he steals the desirable wealth from the sacrificer."

"What indeed are the after-offerings (anūyāja) of the guest-offering (ātithya)? "The Upasads," he should say. "Of what deity are the Upasads? "Agni's," he should say. "How, indeed, does the commencement of the Upasads take place?"
If the sacrificial grass (barhis) has been prepared without a formula (ayajuṣkṛta) at the beginning,
one should touch the hands together and then strew it around.

Having washed the vessels, he should set them down; having prepared the *madantī* water, he should sprinkle the vessels; having poured out the clarified butter (*ājya*) and placed it on the fire, and having carried fire around it, he should go eastward with the wooden sword (*sphya*) in his hand and perform the *stambayajus* rite. From this point onward, the procedure is established as in the archetype. In the first *upasad*, he should set down the offering-spoons (*srucaḥ*) so that they are raised up; in the second, they should be raised up even more; and in the third, they should be raised up still further. They should proceed with the *upasad* rites as if in a hurry; they should not concern themselves with what has not been completed.

"Taking the *sruva* ladle with all fingers joined, one should offer the *upasat* oblation as if about to eat. Where, then, should one perform the *barhis*-formula for the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice? Having removed the *pravargya*, before the leading forward of the *āhavanīya* fire and before the *savanīya* offerings, one should drive away the calves. When the *āhavanīya* has been separated [from the *gārhapatya*], one should scatter a third of a footprint [of earth] on the *gārhapatya*. Likewise, it should be done with the supporting-shovels (*upayamanī*). Now, this post of *udumbara* wood is to be made equal in height to the sacrificer; furthermore, this sacrificial stake (*yūpa*) is measured by the cubits (*aratni*) of the sacrificer.

Regarding this, some say that one should perform these [rites] together with the others; however, in this case, one should do them right here: having traced around the hole for the sacrificial post, one should rub the hands together, strew the grass around, wash the vessels, and set them down together.

Having prepared the sprinkling waters, he should sprinkle the vessels; having poured out the clarified butter and placed it on the fire, and having carried fire around it, he cleanses the offering spoons.

They carry those spoons and the sprinkling waters to the high altar. Then the Pratiprasthātṛ should gird the wife with the cord used for the cake-offering; then he should have her look at the Gārhapatya fire, and then, having had her look at the clarified butter, he should moisten her with the clarified butter.

The wife should look at it and take hold of it with the formula, "Thou art brilliance. Then, having taken hold of it with a chip of wood, he should carry it away with the formula, "Follow after the brilliance. Then he should place it over the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "May Agni not let thy brilliance perish. Then, having carried it and placed it to the north of the *prokṣaṇī* waters, he should look at it and purify it. He should pour out the *prokṣaṇī* waters while reciting the two verses containing the word *ājya*. The procedure for taking the clarified butter and the clotted butter (*pṛṣadājya*) near the Āhavanīya is well-established. From this point onward, as they teach the ritual rule of Śālīki: one should take the clarified butter for the Agniṣoma offering in the wife’s hall itself and place them upon the mound (*khara*).
Whether he has consecrated the fire or not, he should rub his hands together over the ancient *gārhapatya* fire,
strew the sacrificial grass around it,
wash the vessels, and set them down.
Having prepared the sprinkling waters, he should sprinkle the vessels; having poured out the clarified butter, placed it on the fire, and carried fire around it, he cleanses the offering spoons.
They set these down right here together with the sprinkling waters.
The Pratiprasthātṛ should not gird the wife with the cord used for the cake-offering.

He should not let her look at the *gārhapatya* fire; then, having had her look at the clarified butter (*ājya*), he should take up that which has been looked at by the wife with the formula, "Thou art luster. Then, having taken it up with a chip of wood, he should carry it forward with the formula, "Follow after the luster. Then he should place it over the *gārhapatya* fire with the formula, "May Agni not take away thy luster. Then, having carried it and placed it to the north of the *prokṣaṇī* waters, he should look at it and purify it. Having taken the *ājyavanti* and *pṛṣadājyavanti* portions of clarified butter in two ladles, and having handed them over to those who are to circumambulate, he should hand the King Soma over to the *brahmán*.

When they have been covered over, he should offer oblations with the *sruva* ladle; and they should proceed while remaining covered. From the *āhavanīya* fire, the King [Soma] should be on the southern side, then the fire, then the pressing-stones, and the *vāyavya* cups on the northern side, as well as the clarified butter (*ājya*). Alternatively, the fire may be on the southern side, then the King, then the pressing-stones, and the *vāyavya* cups and the clarified butter on the northern side.

Having gone out by the eastern door, having circumambulated the *sadas* to the north, and having placed the fire in the *āgnīdhra* shed and offered oblations into it, he proceeds with *prokṣaṇī* water in his hand toward the northern side of the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth. Following behind him, they offer the clarified butter (*ājya*) into the *āhavanīya* fire; then, having sprinkled the fuel-wood, sprinkled the altar, sprinkled the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and sprinkled the sacrificial grass that has been laid down, having poured water over it and taken the *prastara* bunch of *aśvavāla* grass from the front, he spreads the fivefold sacrificial grass and, holding the *prastara* in his hand, moves forward toward the east.

Having laid around the enclosing sticks made of *kārṣmarya* wood, having placed two upright fuel-sticks upon the fire, and having taken up the handful of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the two separating blades (*vidhṛti*), and the bunch of grass (*prastara*), he should turn to the right, enter the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door, and spread the handful of sacrificial grass on the northern half of the *khara* mound. Upon the grass he places the two separating blades; within the separating blades, the *prastara* made of *aśvavāla* grass; upon the *prastara*, the *juhū* ladle; and the other ladles upon the grass. Having touched them all together with the formula, "These have sat down," and having sipped water, he should take the King Soma from the Brahman priest and cause him to enter the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door, as if turning himself around [the Soma].

The ritual being established from this point upward, where indeed does the wood and sacrificial grass (idhmābarhis) reach its conclusion, as in the case of the *śilpavat* sacrifice? One should say: at the *agnīṣomīya*.
Where indeed does the *agnīṣomīya* follow upon the day of the Soma-pressing (*sutyamaha*)?
One should say, "The Sadyaskrī [sacrifice]. But as for where the Pravargya follows the day of the Soma-pressing, one should say, "It follows the Sadyaskrī. One should say, "The Sadyaskrī."
"Which deity indeed is invoked first as the Subrahmaṇyā?
"Speech itself; she invokes speech.
"Where indeed is the Pitāputrīyā Subrahmaṇyā invoked first? "When the omentum of the Agniṣomīya animal has been offered and the Vasatīvarī waters have been carried around, [that is] the second."

At the *prātaranuvāka*, the third [offering] is indeed the time for the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇās*); they say, "They call out. Now, as for that firm jar, he asks for it; by saying "firm," this very thing is meant.

"Prepare milk and groats"—these two are stated for the purpose of mixing. "Four ropes, four omentum-spits, and two sets of fuel and sacrificial grass"—these belong to both the *savanīya* and the *anūbandhya* offerings.

There are four vessels for Vāyu: the Soma-drawing vessel, the Āditya vessel, the Ukthya vessel, the Āgrayaṇa vessel, and the Dhruva vessel. Now, there are these twelve upright cups: the cup for the Dadhi-graha, the two cups for the Antaryāma, the cups for the dual-deity offerings, the Śukra and Manthin cups, the two Ṛtu cups, the supplementary cup for the Āditya vessel, and the supplementary cup for the Ukthya vessel.

Now, there are these eleven cups: for the sacrificer, the Brahman, the Hotṛ, the Udgātṛ, the Maitrāvaruṇa, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the Acchāvāka, the Sadasya, the Āgnīdhra, the Potṛ, and the Neṣṭṛ. One should have their handles made of the same form; they are known to be of *nyagrodha* wood. It is understood from the statement, "When they consume [the Soma] with cups having handles, they do so with *nyagrodha* cups," that they must indeed be of *nyagrodha* wood.
With the formula, "And my ray," this cup is declared to be the *adābhya*. With the formula, "And my overlord," this *dadhi-graha* (curd-offering) belongs to Prajāpati.

"May the draught for Sarasvatī be mine, and may the draught for Pūṣan be mine"—thus they say regarding the *vasatīvarī* waters; however, some say that this is the great draught (*mahāgraha*) belonging to the Rājasūya sacrifice:
it is called "for Pūṣan" because of nourishing (*poṣaṇāt*), and "for Sarasvatī" because of seizing (*grahaṇāt*).
Now follows this ritual procedure of the great night.
What is the commencement of that ritual?
Having washed their hands and feet, they proceed toward the sacrificial ground between the *cātvāla* pit and the *utkara* mound.

Their ritual acts are performed according to the respective directions. Then the Adhvaryu should touch the Āgnīdhra shed with a verse addressed to Agni, and the oblation-holder (*havirdhāna*) with one addressed to Viṣṇu. Now this Āgnīdhra, having first run to the wife’s hall (*patnīśālā*), kindles the fires, strews grass around them, washes the vessels, sets them down, melts the clarified butter (*ājya*), and waits. The other, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having prepared the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*), sprinkles the vessels, pours out the clarified butter, places it over the fire, carries fire around it, and cleans the offering-spoons (*sruk*).

They carry them to the high altar (uttaravedi) along with the sprinkling waters; then the Adhvaryu touches the spoons with a verse addressed to Agni, thinking, "The vessels, having been cleansed, shall be touched in two ways."

With the *vāyavyā* verse he [places] the *vāyavya* cups; with the *aindrī* verse, the *sadas*. Then this *unnetṛ*, having washed the pressing-stones and the *vāyavya* cup, and having placed the fringe of the *daśāpavitra* filter into the *droṇakalaśa*, sets it down in front of the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart. The *pratiprasthātṛ* prepares the curds for the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*). The *āgnīdhra* places the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*) nearby. Then the *pratiprasthātṛ* should gird the wife with the cord used for the cake-offering (*puroḍāśika*). Then he should make her look at the *gārhapatya* fire, and then, having made her look at the clarified butter, he should moisten her with the butter.

The wife should look at that very same [ghee] and take it up with the formula, "Thou art luster. Then, having taken hold of it with a splinter, he should carry it forward with the formula, "Follow after the luster. Then he should place it over the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "May Agni not take away thy luster. Then, having lifted it and set it down to the north of the *prokṣaṇī* waters, he should look at it; he should purify it, and [he should purify] the *prokṣaṇī* waters with the two [spoons] containing clarified butter. The procedure from this point onward is established: he takes the portions of speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) near the Āhavanīya fire. The rest is established.

Now, according to Śālīki, their ritual acts are performed exactly as directed by the calls (*saṃpraiṣa*). Then the Adhvaryu should touch the Āgnīdhra shed with a verse addressed to Agni, and the oblation-holder (*havirdhāna*) shed with one addressed to Viṣṇu; then he desists. Then this Āgnīdhra, having first run to the wife’s hall (*patnīśāla*), having added fuel to the fire, having strewn grass around it, having washed the vessels and set them down, having melted the clarified butter (*ājya*), waits. The other, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having prepared the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*), should sprinkle the vessels, pour out the clarified butter, place it on the fire, carry fire around it, and wipe the offering-spoons (*sruk*).

They carry those *prokṣaṇī* waters to the *āgnīdhra* shed; then the Adhvaryu touches the *sruca* ladles with a verse addressed to Agni. Having touched the vessels in two groups—those already cleansed and those yet to be cleansed—he touches the Vāyavya cups with a verse addressed to Vāyu and the Sadas with one addressed to Indra. Then this Unnetṛ, having washed the pressing-stones and the Vāyavya cup, and having placed the fringe of the *daśāpavitra* filter into the *droṇakalaśa*, sets them down in front of the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart. The Pratiprasthātṛ prepares the curds for the *pṛṣadājya*; the Āgnīdhra places the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*) nearby.
The Pratiprasthātṛ should not gird the wife with the cord used for the cake-offerings;
he should not let her look at the Gārhapatya fire. Then, having made her look at the clarified butter, he should moisten it with the butter.

He should take up what has been looked at by the wife with the formula, "Thou art brilliance. Then, having covered it with a chip of wood, he should carry it forward with the formula, "Follow after the brilliance."

Then he should place it on the Āgnīdhrīya fire with the formula, "May Agni not take away thy brilliance"; then, having carried it and placed it to the north of the *prokṣaṇī* waters, he should look at it and purify the *prokṣaṇī* waters with the two [spoons] containing clarified butter.

It is well known that, having taken the clarified butter mixed with clotted butter (pṛṣadājya) near the Āgnīdhrīya hearth and handed it over to the assistants, he proceeds northward past the Āgnīdhrīya mound with the sprinkling water (prokṣaṇī) in his hand, followed by the clarified butter. Then, having sprinkled the fuel (idhma), sprinkled the altar (vedi), sprinkled the sacrificial grass (barhis), and having sprinkled the sacrificial grass already laid down and poured water over it, he takes the Prastara-bunch from the front, spreads the single-layered sacrificial grass, and moving forward with the Prastara in his hand toward the east, he lays the enclosing sticks (paridhi) made of Udumbara wood and [places] the two upright [staves].

Having placed two fuel-sticks on the fire and having taken up a handful of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the two separators (*vidhṛti*), and the *prastara* bundle, he turns to the right, enters the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door, and spreads the handful of sacrificial grass on the northern half of the *khara* mound. Upon the grass he places the two separators; upon the separators, the *prastara*; and upon the *prastara*, the *juhū* ladle. Having touched them all together with the formula, "These have sat down: the two blades of grass, the two separators, the *prastara*, and the other ladles," he yokes them with the *yoga* formula.
From this point onward, the procedure is established.
It is known from scripture: "Is the consecrated one (*dīkṣita*) the Agnihotra? Is the one at the Upasads the Agnihotra? Is the one for whom the Soma has been pressed (*prasuta*) the Agnihotra?

Indeed, the vow itself is the Agnihotra of the consecrated; the remnants of the Gharma are the Agnihotra of the one at the Upasads; and the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups are the Agnihotra of the one for whom the Soma has been pressed.
That which he offers before sunrise is the portion of the evening Agnihotra; that which he offers after sunrise is the portion of the morning Agnihotra.
Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa, it is known from scripture: "They performed the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice with the Agnīṣomīya animal, and they performed the Darśa sacrifice with the Āgneya animal.

Furthermore, as for the ritual procedure (kalpa) taught by Aupamanyava: one should offer the *savanīya* oblations at the morning pressing itself for all three pressings; the potsherds (*kapāla*) should be placed on the fire only once, until the final covering of the cake; thus the combined ritual is performed.

One should remove each of those [cakes] at every pressing, whichever one he intends to use; or alternatively, he may let the remaining cakes of those that have been wiped away rest for the other two pressings. If a cake on a single potsherd (ekakapāla) is intended, he should proceed with those belonging to the morning pressing alone. He should resume the ritual procedure for the sacrificial cake (pauroḍāśika) from the point where it was interrupted. For the other two pressings, he should proceed at each pressing by merely placing embers upon the potsherds. From this point onward, the rite is established as already explained.

Regarding this, they teach the ritual procedure of Baudhāyana: one should draw the *vasatīvarī* waters which are bright on both sides and accompanied by the sun; those are the bright ones, with them one should cause [the Soma] to swell, and with them one should press. Having placed the *hotṛ*-cup so that its upper half is above, one should proceed even with this third [set of waters].

One should cause the three kinds of water—the *hotṛ*-cup water, the *vasatīvarī* water, and the *maitrāvaruṇa*-cup water—to enter the *havirdhāna* shed through the eastern door. Having taken them around the south of the *hotṛ*, one should bring in the *ekadhana* waters through the western door.
And at this time, he should pour out the contents of the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup entirely; he should pour down one-third of the *vasatīvarī* waters and one-third of the *ekadhana* waters.
In this way, his *śukra* cup becomes exclusively [Soma] beforehand.
"One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should draw the Soma-cup"—this cup of King Soma is to be drawn from that which has not yet been poured out.
"Which deities, indeed, consume the Soma first? "One should say: 'The Waters. For it is known [in the scripture]: 'Invited, drink of the Soma; invited, let the Soma drink of you.

Where, indeed, does the drinking of the Soma (somapītha) of the Soma take place? It is known: 'O Soma, that invincible, watchful name of yours which belongs to the Soma—for that Soma of yours, Svāhā! This, indeed, is also the drinking of the Soma of the Soma."
When they have assembled, there is this sequence:

having caused [the sacrificer] to recite over the *nigrābhya* waters, he should proceed with the *ādābhya* cup; then he should take up the *upāṃśusavana* stone, and then he should pour out the King Soma.
One should understand that the ritual procedure here follows the *agniṣṭoma* until the touching of the two fruit-stones.

Having touched the wooden plank, he should proceed with the *pṛśni* verses; then he should proceed with the *prāṇagraha* cups; then he should take up the *ām̐śu* cup; then he should proceed with the *ām̐śu*;
then at the proper time with the *upām̐śu* and the *antaryāma*—from this point onward it is established.

Regarding this, they teach Baudhāyana’s ritual procedure: at the drawing of the Āgrayaṇa cup, one should draw two streams at the morning pressing, three at the midday pressing, and four at the third pressing. There is a pouring together of the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups, and the Śukra cup is continuous; these two are for the morning pressing.

At the midday pressing, there is the continuous Śukra cup and the Āgrayaṇa with its scooping vessel (*udacana*); this is the third. At the third pressing, there is the remnant in the Āditya vessel, the pouring together of the King Soma and the Āditya cup, and the Āgrayaṇa with its scooping vessel; this is the fourth.
One should mix the purified King Soma with three things: milk, parched grain flour, and gold. Whatever cup one draws, he makes it have its bottom upwards on both sides and supported by gold.
The cups are to be offered while standing, except for the cup for Prajāpati and the residue of the Manthin cup.

Regarding this ritual procedure of Śālīki which they teach concerning the *drapsānumantraṇīyā* verses: one should offer these as oblations with the *sruva*-ladle. At what time, indeed, should one offer them?

One should offer them at this time, having offered the *saṃtanī* oblations. Then he says, "O Unnetṛ, cause the King [Soma] to flow forward toward the *pūtabhṛt*; having wiped the *ādhavanīya* with the fringes, turn it upside down. This is the formal command (*saṃpraiṣa*). Having remained standing until the *avakāśa* verses, and having wiped it with the fringes, he turns it upside down.
The ritual procedure is the same from the drawing of the Āśvina cup up to the pouring of the remnants over the hearths (dhiṣṇiya). This is the general outline.
But how, indeed, is the pouring over the hearths performed according to the order in which they were thrown?
Having poured with the formula, "To Vibhū, the carrier, svāhā," he pours over the Raudra hearth with the mantra: "With thy fierce host, O Agni, protect me; fill me; do not harm me."

"Seven he chooses"—thus the Hotṛ himself becomes the seventh among them. Regarding the subsequent days of the *ahargaṇa*, one might ask: "How should the morning pressing procession (*prasarpaṇa*) proceed? One should reply: "It should begin with the worship of the Āhavanīya fire. How many times should the worship of the *sphya* and *vighana* stones be performed? And how indeed should their movement through the space be arranged? [The answer is: Between the *dhiṣṇiya* of the Hotṛ and that of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin—those who have no *dhiṣṇiya* [should pass there]. Then those who possess *dhiṣṇiyas* should circumambulate each of their own respective *dhiṣṇiya* on the north side. Now, these two Adhvaryus do not carry the cups (*acamasau*).
"Where, indeed, does the consumption of these two take place?
"In the Hotṛ's cup," one should say.
"Which of the officiating priests, indeed, do not consume the Soma at the one-day sacrifice (ekāha)? "The Unnetṛ, the Grāvastut, and the Subrahmaṇya," one should say.
Where indeed, in the *sattra*, should those who have been consecrated (*dīkṣita*) consume [the Soma]?

The Unnetṛ should consume from the Neṣṭṛ’s cup; the Grāvastut from the Acchāvāka’s cup; the Subrahmaṇya from the Udgātṛ’s cup; or alternatively, all of them together should consume from the Āgnīdhra’s cup. It is known that in the subsequent performance (*uttarasyāṃ tatau*), he who is the Āgnīdhra is the Grāvastut, he is the Subrahmaṇya, and he is the Unnetṛ.

Furthermore, regarding this ritual procedure (*kalpa*) which they teach according to Baudhāyana: one should set out the Savanīya offerings on a single vessel; for this is seen to be the proper preparation (*alaṅkāra*) specifically for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

One should set out the sacrificial cake from the middle, having spread a base of clarified butter and poured butter over it; the fried grains to the east, the groats to the south, the parched grain to the west, and the curd-mixture to the north.
How, indeed, should there be a path for these?

The path for the oblation is well-known. Now, having carried it out through the eastern door and brought it into the *sadas* by the western door, one should carry it along the front of the performers, behind the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths, and past the north of the *acchāvāka’s* *dhiṣṇiya*. Having handed it over to another, one returns by the same way one came, goes around the north of the *sadas*, carries it out through the eastern door, and brings it around the north of the *āgnīdhrīya* shed; then, if the Adhvaryu has entered the *havirdhāna* shed, he should set it down within the altar, saying: "Come forth! (upaniṣkrāma mā).

One should simply say, "I shall carry you around. Furthermore, they teach this ritual procedure (kalpa) of Baudhāyana: regarding the two-cup offerings (dvidevatya), while the Pratiprasthātṛ stands to the north, the Adhvaryu hands over the secondary cup (pratinirgrāhya) to him. When the Adhvaryu carries the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) westward, he should take hold of the Pratiprasthātṛ as he enters the Havirdhāna shed. Having taken up the two cups, the Adhvaryu steps out; once he has stepped out, the Adhvaryu takes back the two cups. After [the Pratiprasthātṛ] has walked around by the rear, the Adhvaryu hands over the secondary cup to the Pratiprasthātṛ as he stands to the north.

Having offered the oblation and poured out the remnants, and having turned to the right, the Pratiprasthātṛ should take hold of the Adhvaryu; then the Adhvaryu, moving westward toward the Pratiprasthātṛ with the vessel, completes the rite from that point onward.
Now, these offerings to the dual deities are performed without a second *vaṣaṭ* call.

"Where indeed does their *anuvashatkāra* take place? Thus it is known: "The offerings to the dual deities (*dvidevatya*), the seasonal offerings (*ṛtuyāja*), and the cup for the wives' husband (*pātnīvata graha*)—the Āditya cup and the Sāvitra cups; do not perform the *anuvashatkāra* for these.

Furthermore, regarding this ritual procedure (*kalpa*) of Aupamanyava which they teach: one should consume the dual-deity cups with the long recitation (*dīrghabhakṣa*). Beginning with "O food, come hither, enter me," and continuing from "For power, for skill, for abundance of wealth, for heroic offspring," and so forth.

He touches himself [with the mantra]: "O King, do not terrify me; do not strike my heart with your brilliance! For the sake of virility, for strength, for life, and for splendor. Then, one should consume the draughts belonging to the openings of the pressings (*savanamukhīya*) by means of the consumption formula used at each pressing.
Now, where indeed does the *stotra* portion and the *śastra* portion of the *vasatīvara* water occur?
Its *stotra* portion occurs in the *viśvarūpā* verses, and its *śastra* portion occurs in the *prātaranuvāka*.
Where, indeed, does the participation of the two-cup deities (dvidevatya) in the stotra and śastra of the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma [libations] occur?
When there is the sound "upāṃśu" and "śaṃ", that constitutes the participation of the two-cup deities in the Prauga-uktha of the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma.

Now, this Pratiprasthātṛ becomes one who attends to the Adhvaryu from the north during the Ṛtu-graha offerings. As the Adhvaryu moves hither and thither, the Pratiprasthātṛ should hold him back; then the Adhvaryu, running westward toward the Pratiprasthātṛ, [takes] the vessel; the procedure from this point onward is established.
"To which deities, indeed, do the Ṛtu-yājas belong? "The seasons (*ṛtu*) are the deities"—this is one view. Now, another.
Indra, as the *hotṛ*, performs the sacrifice;
the Maruts, as the *potṛ*, perform the sacrifice;
the Goddesses, as the *neṣṭṛ*, perform the sacrifice; Agni, as the *āgnīdhra*, performs the sacrifice; Indra, as the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*, performs the sacrifice.
Mitra and Varuṇa [are the priests]; the Maitrāvaruṇa; the god Draviṇodas; the four Aśvins as Adhvaryus; the two Adhvaryus [serve] Agni Gṛhapati; Gṛhapati [serves] Agni.
Where indeed does the portion of the Stotra for Indra and Agni occur?
One should simply say, "The *bahis-pavamāna*"; for whatever cups (*graha*) are without a *stotra*, the *pavamāna* itself becomes their *stotra*.
As for where the *savanīya* offerings of the midday pressing are set out, one should simply say, "At the *stotra* of the minor *vaiśvadeva*."
"Where is the *stotra* of the *māhendra* cup belonging to the third pressing?"—one should say "here.
One should take this [cup] from the *hotṛ*'s goblet after the *nārāśamsa* has been offered.
There are two *nārāśamsas* in the morning pressing and the midday pressing, and one *nārāśamsa* in the third pressing; there are four *unnīyamāna-sūktas*.
At the openings of the pressings and at the cup of the Acchāvāka,
there are three long recitations for consumption; but where indeed does the Pravargya rite follow the day of the Soma-pressing?
One should simply say, "The curd-heat offering (dadhigharma)";
why [ask] about the surrounding of the Soma-vessel with the Upasads?
As for the statement, "He makes the pressing-stones resound upon the wooden boards across the hide," [it refers to this].
This is what they call the "dry pressing.

How, indeed, should one draw the Māhendra cup when the Rathantara is the Prstha? One should draw the Māhendra with this Gāyatrī verse: "Great is Indra, who [is] by might... But when the Bṛhat is the Prstha, one should draw the Māhendra with this Triṣṭubh verse: "Great is Indra, man-like, filling the people...
And when both are the Prsthas, one should draw it with whichever [verse] corresponds to the Prstha, and use the other as the Puroruṅ.

How indeed does the performance of the Savanīya animal sacrifice commence? Having spread the *iḍā-sūna*, having divided the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) and poured it into the *juhū* ladle, having gone out northward between the *cātvāla* pit and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), he should call for the *saṃvāda*, baste [the oblation], and set down the animal. With the *Pañcahotṛ* formula, he spreads [grass] in the four [ladles];
he should proceed from the *Manotā* verse until the end of the *iḍā*.
From this point onward, the procedure is established.

Now, regarding the Ukthya offerings: the very same drawing-formula used at the morning pressing is used for the midday pressing and the third pressing; it should manifest the deity for each individual cup, and one should cast three pieces of the sacrificial cake into each cup. "Nine [pieces] for the Hotṛ's cup"—this is said to apply to exactly three [cups]. Furthermore, this Āgrayaṇa vessel is drawn for thirty-three deities.
Where indeed are these [deities] known to be in the offering? It is known in the case of the Pātnīvata [offering]: "Of the husband of the wives (patnīvat), thirty-three gods."

How indeed should one consume the Pātnīvata [portion]? With the formula: "O divine Soma, belonging to the troop of Aditi, who art possessed of wisdom, of thee—the third pressing, having the Jagatī metre, drunk by Agni Vaiśvānara accompanied by the wives and by Tvaṣṭṛ, which is honeyed, invited, and to be consumed with invitation—I partake.
How indeed does it become an Antaryāma-ukthya?

Having drawn the Āgrayaṇa at the well-known third pressing, he should draw the Ukthya. Then, having set this [Ukthya] down near the Dhruva, he should distribute it into three upright vessels with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, agreeable to the gods, for the gods, eager for the Ukthas, for the Ukthas, for the life of the sacrifice, for Indra and Varuṇa.
Having touched the Ukthya-vessel again with the words, "Thou art a repeated oblation," and having wiped it, he sets it down with the formula: "This is thy womb; for Indra and Varuṇa, thee!"

At that very moment, he takes another [draught] with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, agreeable to the gods, longing for the gods, for the Ukthas, longing for the Ukthas, for the life of the sacrifice, for Indra and Bṛhaspati.

Having touched the Ukthya vessel again with the words, "Thou art a sacrificial oblation," and having wiped it around, he sets it down with the formula: "This is thy womb; for Indra and Bṛhaspati, thee!"

At that very moment, he takes another [draught] with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, agreeable to the gods, eager for the gods, for the Ukthya-vessels, eager for the Ukthya, for the life of the sacrifice, for Indra and Viṣṇu.
Here, he does not touch the Ukthya-sthālī again with the words "Thou art the oblation";
rather, having wiped it with the fringes of the cloth, he turns it upside down.
Having wiped it around, he sets it down with the formula, "This is thy womb; for Indra and Viṣṇu, thee! Then, having poured them into the *dhruva* vessel, he should pour them into the *hotṛ*'s cup;
he should pour the *stotra* verses into the *stotra* and the *śastra* formulas into the *śastra*.

Of that which has been offered, which has been drunk by Indra and Varuṇa, by Indra and Bṛhaspati, by Indra and Viṣṇu, by Agni Vaiśvānara, and by the Maruts—of this sweet, invited [portion], being invited, I partake. Or he may partake with this very formula; or rather, with the constant [formula] preceded by: "O divine Soma, belonging to the troop of Aditi, you who know the mind, of thee, the third pressing, having the Jagatī metre, drunk by Indra and Varuṇa, by Indra and Bṛhaspati, by Indra and Viṣṇu, by Agni Vaiśvānara, and by the Maruts—of this sweet, invited [portion], being invited, I partake."

Regarding this, they teach the ritual procedure of Aupamanyava: "One should offer the two *mindā*-oblations beforehand; having offered the two *mindā*-oblations, one should draw the *hāriyojana* cup. Now, some, having placed the *avabhṛtha* at the site of the *cātvāla*, pour oblations over the *soma-residue* (*nīrjīṣa*) with curds, milk mixed with honey, and the *naiṣṭyayana* formulas, saying: "O King Soma, that which they have cut from thee with the pressing-stone...
[and so on]. They say, "One offers the *avabhṛtha-yajus* formulas.
But what indeed are these *avabhṛtha-yajus* formulas?

When they perform [the rite] with wood-shavings (*śākala*) in the Āhavanīya fire, [they recite]: "Thou art the expiation for sin committed against the gods; thou art the expiation for sin committed against men; thou art the expiation for sin committed against the fathers"—this is at the *avabhṛtha* oblation. But what indeed is this *avabhṛtha* oblation? Having drawn up water, he offers it with: "O Lord of the Sacrifice, we worship thee with the oblations of the sacrifice, with the *sūktavāka*, and with the *namovāka*; Svāhā! Standing, they should proceed with the *avabhṛtha*.
Turning away, he should throw [the grass] toward the edge of the water with the forepart of his foot; from this point on, it is established.
Now, regarding this *udayanīya* sacrifice, what is the commencement of its ritual procedure?
One should prepare the sacrificial grass with the *barhir-yajus* formula, rub the hands together, and strew around the altar.

Having washed the vessels, he should set them down; having seated the Brahman priest to the south and having placed a water-pot right there to the north, he should place the wooden sword (sphya) behind the Gārhapatya fire. Upon the wooden sword, he should place the vessel; into the vessel, he should pour the rice from the winnowing basket. From the taking of the basket until the end of the sequence, that is, until the scattering [of the grains], the procedure continues as before.

Having performed the ritual actions up to the pouring out [of the grain], he should pour water across the strainer, place it over the fire, and then pour the rice grains across the strainer; then he should set out the clarified butter and place the clarified butter over the fire. Having carried fire around both, he should perform the *stambayajus* rite on the *aupasada* altar behind the *gārhapatya* fire. From this point onward, the procedure is established. The placing of the cooked oblation is as follows: having released the western joint of the enclosing sticks, or having moved the southern enclosing stick forward along its front, he should set down the *prāyaṇīya* offering facing east and the *udayanīya* facing west.
Here, the deities are worshipped with the fire at their head.
The Udayanīya sacrifice concludes with the Śayvant offering;
then, if an animal has been prepared, he should rub his hands and strew the sacrificial grass around the fire.
Having washed the vessels, he should set them down;

having prepared the *prokṣaṇī* waters, he should sprinkle the vessels; having poured out the clarified butter (*ājya*) and placed it on the fire, and having carried fire around it, he should take up the wooden sword (*sphya*).
From the formal summons (*saṃpraiṣa*) onwards, the ritual procedure pertaining to the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) is performed.

From this point forward, as they teach this ritual procedure of Śālīki—one should sacrifice with the curdled milk (āmikṣā) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa—the driving away of the calves for that offering takes place together with those for the Savanīya offerings; the evening milking is performed together [with them].
Having performed the Udayanīya sacrifice, he should rub his hands and strew the sacrificial grass around the altar.

Having washed the vessels, he should set them down; having prepared the *prokṣaṇī* waters, he should sprinkle the vessels. Then he should have the cows milked for the morning milking. Having cooked this [milk] over the *gārhapatya* fire, he should remove it from the heat without pouring *ājya* over it. Then he should pour out the *ājya*, place the *ājya* on the fire, and carry fire around both of them. Having laid the paridhis made of split bamboo around the *āhavanīya* fire, he should again place the milk on the fire, pour *ājya* over it, and set it down within the altar. Having performed the ritual up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, he has his hair and beard shaved and his nails clipped at the southern edge of the altar.

Then, having performed the *ājyabhāga* offerings, the sacrifice concludes with the *iḍā*. Now follows this *udavasānīyā* offering; for it possesses the characteristics of the *punarādheya* (re-establishment of the sacred fires).
Indeed, there is only a single carrying away of the *stambayajus* from the *mahāvedi*.
The wife, not being girt with the cord, sits by the tail of the sacrifice.
Now, they pile this fire-altar with three *upasads*, six *upasads*, or twelve *upasads*.

If he is about to pile one consisting of a thousand bricks with three *upasads*, having performed the *pravargya* and *upasads* in the forenoon, he piles the first layer together with the *purīṣa* and offers the *saṃcita* oblations;
having piled the second layer together with the *purīṣa*, he offers the *saṃcita* oblations.

On the following day, having performed the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites, and having laid down the third layer, the fourth layer, the fifth layer, and the sixth layer together with their *purīṣa*, he offers the two *saṃcita* oblations; the third [set of layers] is indeed that of the *aupavasathika* day. Now, if one is about to pile a thousand-brick altar consisting of six *upasad* days, he performs the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites in the forenoon, lays down the first layer together with its *purīṣa*, and offers the two *saṃcita* oblations.
On the following day, having performed the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites, he lays down the second layer together with its *purīṣa* and offers the two *saṃcita* oblations.
In this very manner, he remains for five days in the state of fasting;

then on the sixth day, if he intends to perform a sacrifice involving one thousand [bricks] with twelve *upasads*, it is according to the *sūtra*. But if he intends to perform a sacrifice involving two thousand [bricks] with three *upasads*, having performed the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites in the forenoon, and having laid down the first layer together with its *purīṣa* and offered the *saṃcita* oblations, he lays down the *āhāryā* brick with *ṛṣ-purīṣa*.
Having laid down the second layer together with its *purīṣa* and offered the *saṃcita* oblations, he lays down the *āhāryā* brick with *ṛṣ-purīṣa*.

On the following day, having performed the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites, and having laid down the third layer, the fourth layer, the fifth layer, and the sixth layer together with their *purīṣa*, and having offered the *saṃcita* oblations, he lays down the *āhāryā* layer with its *purīṣa*; this is indeed the third *aupavasathika* day. Now, if one intends to pile a two-thousand-brick altar with six *upasad* days, he performs the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites in the forenoon, lays down the first layer together with its *purīṣa*, offers the *saṃcita* oblations, and then lays down the *āhāryā* layer with its *purīṣa*.

On the following day, having performed the Pravargya and Upasad rites, and having laid down the second layer together with its loose earth (purīṣa) and offered the Saṃcita oblations, he lays down this [third] layer together with its loose earth.
In this very same manner he proceeds for five days;

the sixth day is the day of preparation (aupavasathika). Now, if he is about to pile a fire-altar of two thousand bricks with twelve Upasads, he performs the Pravargya and Upasad rites in the forenoon, lays down the first layer, and having spread the loose earth over it, he dwells for that night.

On the following day, having performed the Pravargya and Upasad rites, and having laid down the loose soil (purīṣa) and offered the Saṃcita oblations, he lays down the layer of loose soil brought from elsewhere.

Proceeding in this very manner according to the sūtra, having laid down layer after layer of loose soil and offered the Saṃcita oblations, he lays down the layer of loose soil brought from elsewhere; thus the twelfth day is indeed the day of fasting (aupavasathika).

Now, if he intends to pile a three-thousand-brick altar with three *upasads*, having performed the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites in the forenoon, having piled the first layer together with its *purīṣa* and offered the *saṃcita* oblations, he piles two additional bricks together with their *purīṣa*;
then, having piled the second layer together with its *purīṣa* and offered the *saṃcita* oblations, he piles two additional bricks together with their *purīṣa*.

On the following day, having performed the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites, and having laid down the third layer, the fourth layer, the fifth layer, and the sixth layer together with their *purīṣa*, and having offered the *saṃcita* oblations, he lays down two additional bricks (*āhārya*) each together with their *purīṣa*. This is the third [set] belonging to the day of preparation (*aupavasathika*). Now, if he is about to pile a three-thousand-brick altar with six *upasad*s, he performs the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites in the forenoon, lays down the first layer together with its *purīṣa*, offers the *saṃcita* oblations, and lays down two additional bricks together with their *purīṣa*.

On the following day, having performed the *pravargya* and *upasads*, and having laid down the second layer together with its *purīṣa* soil and offered the *saṃcita* oblations, he lays down two additional layers (*āhārye*) together with their *purīṣa*.

In this very same manner, it proceeds for five days; the sixth day is indeed the day of the fast (*aupavasathika*). Now, if he is about to pile a fire-altar of three thousand bricks with twelve *upasads*, he performs the *pravargya* and *upasads* in the forenoon, lays down the first layer, and having spread the *purīṣa* soil over it, he dwells for that night.

On the following day, having performed the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites, having laid down the loose soil (*purīṣa*), and having offered the *saṃcita* oblations, he lays down two *āhārya* bricks together with loose soil.

Proceeding in this very manner according to the sūtra, having at each stage laid down the loose soil and offered the *saṃcita* oblations, he lays down two *āhārya* bricks together with loose soil; thus the twelfth day coincides with the day of the fast (*aupavasathika*).

How indeed should one understand what is "with the Upasads inside," what is "with the Upasads outside," and what is "with the Upasads both inside and outside"? One should purchase the King (Soma) after twelve days remain of the year-long initiation-period (*daikṣa-saṃvatsara*); that is "with the Upasads inside. One should purchase the King when the year has fully elapsed; that is "with the Upasads outside. One should purchase the King after six days remain of the year-long initiation-period, and those [remaining] days should be the Upasads, followed by the subsequent six-night period; that is "with the Upasads both inside and outside. Thus it is said: "He makes this earth level with a hole."

"He places it on level ground"—this is what is meant by that. Then he stations these two, the horse and the donkey, either to the north or in front facing west. If they are in front facing west, the horse is to the south and the donkey to the north; if they are to the north, the horse is in front and the donkey behind. Regarding the statement, "He immolates the animals for the fires," there is a Brāhmaṇa passage concerning five animals.

If he performs the dedication of these animals, having carried out the ritual of the animal sacrifice (paśubandha) up to the placing [of the limbs] upon the sacrificial grass (barhis), they should cut the veins and cast the bodies into water; for it is known from scripture that "they cast the bodies into water. He observes celibacy (brahmacarya) for this month; he sleeps on the ground, eats sparingly, and avoids women. This is called the "prior initiation" (pūrvadīkṣā).
Thinking that he is being consecrated for this very thirteenth month, he causes the sacrificer to recite over the black antelope skin; he neither closes his fists nor restrains his speech.
This procedure, beginning from the black antelope skin until the end of the rite, continues until the announcement.
On the first *upasad* day, he measures out the altar and performs the *stambayajus* extraction.
"This indeed occurs through the power of karma. Now, while scattering the seeds of all herbs (*sarvauṣadhī*), he should meditate with his mind on that which is black in the moon; that too is here.

Plowing the successive furrows with successive oxen, scattering all the herbs, he should not step upon the space of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick. Now, some sing a Sāman over both the man [the altar] and the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, asking: 'What indeed is the secret significance of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*?'"

One should call a gold brick a "mandala-brick" and a "retahsic" (seed-shedding brick). Whichever group of bricks one lays down, one should not pass between them; the southern [group] to the south and the northern [group] to the north. If he were to lay down the bricks from the south or from the east, he should turn counter-clockwise (*apasavya*); but if from the north or from the west, having turned clockwise (*pradakṣiṇa*), he should lay down the bricks facing toward the *svayamātṛṇṇā* (self-perforated brick). Regarding the statement, "He lays down the Kṛttikās," what indeed are these Kṛttikās?

One should say "lightning" (vidyut) for the sake of non-flowing, according to Baudhāyana; there is a repeated piling (punaścit) in each fire-altar, and that is not a piling with loose earth (purīṣaciti), [but] with the sixth [layer], according to Vṛddhija; indeed, with the sixth, according to Śālīki.
Bringing forward the sixth covering, at what time indeed should he bring it?

One should say: "after having laid down the star-bricks. He proceeds by means of three rites: by the laying down of the loose soil (purīṣa), by the sprinkling accompanied by the thousandfold formula, and by the making of the cows.

He proceeds with eight rites toward the highest piled oblation: the Śatarudrīya, the prostrations, the sprinkling around, the drawing out, the serpent-oblations, the worship with Sāmans, and the Anuśamsana. Now, regarding the pouring out of various seeds, what is common (tantra)? The taking up of the ladle is common; the taking up of the winnowing basket is common; all the mantras for the cart, beginning with the yoke-pole, are common. Up to the Sāvitra formula, the seed is repeated for each individual seed; the Sāvitra rite is common; the Daśahotṛ, the advancing, and the entrusting are common.

The spreading of the black antelope skin is a common rite (*tantra*); the placing of the mortar is a common rite; the pouring of the grains for the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) is a common rite; the placing of the pestle is a common rite; the winnowing of the winnowing basket is a common rite. The mantra beginning with the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*) and continuing from the pouring onwards is repeated for each individual seed. This continues up to the scattering [of the grain], according to the ritual procedure taught by Śālīki: "One should step across together with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. This is appropriate only in the case of eleven fore-offerings (*prayāja*), not in the case of five fore-offerings.

Regarding this ritual procedure of Aupamanyava which they teach: one should sprinkle [the sacrificer] with as much [water] as is prescribed before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; here there is no black antelope skin, no two gold plates, and no parts belonging to the earth; having merely spread out *kuśa* grass, one should sprinkle him upon those [blades].

How, indeed, is the sprinkling of the performers of a sacrificial session (*sattra*) repeated? [The answer is: the announcement of the sprinkling on the first day, the sprinkling on the first day, the making the horse smell [the water] on the first day, and they should chant the *bahiṣpavamāna* at the beginning and at the end in the *āstāva*; every day, during the *yajñāyajñiya* chant, he should touch [the sacrificer] with two [verses].

How indeed does the performance of the eleven animals begin? Having spread the *iḍā*-grass, having divided the speckled butter and poured it into the *juhū* ladle, having gone out northward between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, he should call for the *saṃvāda*, sprinkle [the butter], and set down the animal. With the *pañcahotṛ* formula, he spreads [butter] in four [ladles];
having cut off the portion for the deity of the principal animal, and having placed the fat of the kidneys into the broth, he should cover the *juhū* with that.

One should sprinkle it with hot broth and then pour clarified butter over it. Then, having taken a single portion from each of the three limbs for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering into the *upabhṛt* ladle, one should place the fat of the kidneys into the hot broth and cover the *upabhṛt* with it; one should sprinkle it with hot broth but not pour clarified butter over it. Then, having placed the heart, tongue, breast, membrane, two kidneys, and the rectum into a vessel, one should sprinkle it with hot broth but not pour clarified butter over it. Then, having taken the *vasāhoma* (fat-oblation) in either a *kamaṇḍalu* or a *camasa* cup, one should sprinkle it with hot broth and then pour clarified butter over it.

He should touch the animal with his side; having offered the fat-oblation (*vasāhoma*), he should go around behind the *uttaravedi* from the rear of the *kumbha*; having circumambulated it, he should call for the *āśrāvaṇa*. At the half-verse of the *yājyā*, the *pratiprasthātṛ* should offer the fat-oblation and leave a remnant for the quarters. Then he should pour the remainder into the *vasāhomahavanī*. When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers the oblation. Without yet performing the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he steps northward and spreads an underlayer in both the *juhū* and the *vasāhomahavanī*.

Having taken the portion for the deity of the second animal, one should place the fat of the kidneys into the broth; having covered the *juhū* with it, one should pour the warm broth over it and then sprinkle it with clarified butter. Then, for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, one should take a single portion from each of the three organs into the *upabhṛt*, place the fat of the kidneys into the broth, and cover the *upabhṛt* with it.
Having poured the collected portions together with the broth, one should not sprinkle them with clarified butter.
Then, in that same vessel or a ladle, one should take the *vasāhoma* (fat-oblation); one should pour the broth over it and then sprinkle it with clarified butter.

He should touch the animal with his side; having offered the fat-oblation (*vasāhoma*), he should go behind the *kumbha* vessel and, having circumambulated the northern altar (*uttaravedi*), cause the announcement (*āśrāvaya*). At the half-verse of the *yājyā*, the Pratiprasthātṛ should offer the fat-oblation and leave a remnant.

When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers the oblation to the deities. He should do exactly the same for all the animals. Wherever he cuts off the portion for the *sviṣṭakṛt* of the animal dedicated to Varuṇa, there he should pour clarified butter over it twice.
One should pour hot water over it and sprinkle it with clarified butter;
likewise, one should take the fat-oblation (vasāhoma) either in a *kaṃsa* vessel or a *camasa* cup, pour hot water over it, and sprinkle it with clarified butter.

One should touch the animal along its side and proceed with the fat-oblation. Having gone around the northern altar from behind the *kumbha*, the Adhvaryu should call for the *śrauṣaṭ*. At the half-verse of the *yājyā*, the Pratiprasthātṛ should offer the fat-oblation.

Whatever remains from the [other] quarters, he should then pour that other portion into the *vasā-homa* ladle. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers the oblation. Then, prior to the offering to Vanaspati, he should offer to the common quarters. Then he should proceed with the offering to Vanaspati, and then with the *sviṣṭakṛt*.

From this point onward, it is established as follows: regarding the ritual procedure of Aupamanyava which they teach—one should sacrifice with the independent curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa—the ritual duties for the day of preparation (*aupavasathika*) should be understood as established here, just as they are for one who performs the *saṃnayya* at the new moon sacrifice, except for the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*.

"For a year he should not descend [from his status] toward anyone; he should not eat the flesh of headless animals nor the flesh of birds; having piled the fire-altar, he should not approach a woman with long hair; one who has piled the fire-altar should not run while it is raining; if he should run, he should turn back, for [the text says], 'He turns back toward food itself,' so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, in this Vājapeya sacrifice, there are seventeen chariots, each with three horses; these [horses] amount to fifty-one."
To the north, one should yoke a side-horse, thinking, "Twenty-four animals"; for both the Agniṣomīya and the Anūbandhya become twenty-four-fold.
Now it is indeed said: "One offers the Sāvitra oblation before each ritual act";
thus, when about to pour out the Dīkṣaṇīyā offering, one offers the Sāvitra oblation.
The Sāvitra [offering] comes from the Sāvitrī [verse] itself;
for one about to offer the initiation oblations, he offers the Sāvitra.
Having offered the Sāvitra, he should offer the initiation oblations.
"One offers the Sāvitra oblation when about to pour out the Prāyaṇīyā [oblation]";

thus, from the Sāvitra [rite] itself, it becomes the Sāvitra. "One offers the Sāvitra oblation while holding gold between [the fingers]"; having offered the Sāvitra, one should offer [the oblation] while holding gold between [the fingers].
Having proceeded with the footprint-rite, having purchased and carried back the King [Soma], and being about to pour out the Ātithyā [oblation], one offers the Sāvitra oblation.
The Sāvitra [offering] belongs to Savitṛ;
"when about to proceed with the first Pravargya and Upasad rites, he offers the Sāvitra";
having offered the Sāvitra, he should proceed with the first Pravargya and Upasad rites; "when about to perform the first tracing out of the Mahāvedi, he offers the Sāvitra."
"Having offered the Sāvitra oblation, one should take up the wooden sword (sphya) when about to lead forward the Āhavanīya fire;

'having offered the Sāvitra oblation,' [it is said] one should take up the fuel (idhma) when about to measure out the Sadas and Havirdhāna sheds on the chariot-stand (rathavāhana); 'having offered the Sāvitra oblation' [it is said]."
Having offered the Sāvitra oblation, one should erect the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds when about to lead forward Agni and Soma;

"having offered the Sāvitra oblation, he leads forward Agni and Soma"—having thus offered the Sāvitra oblation, he should lead forward Agni and Soma. When about to raise the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), [it is said] "he offers the Sāvitra oblation"; having offered the Sāvitra oblation, he should take up the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*).
Having set up the sacrificial post provided with a top-ring, and being about to dedicate the animal for Agni and Soma, he offers an oblation to Savitṛ;
having offered the oblation to Savitṛ, he should take two blades of *barhis* grass;
after performing the well-known ritual procedure with its omentum, and being about to take the *vasatīvarī* waters, he offers another oblation to Savitṛ.

Having offered the oblation to Savitṛ, he should take up the water-pot when about to offer the animal-cake; because it says "he offers the oblation to Savitṛ," the [second] oblation to Savitṛ arises from that very [first] oblation to Savitṛ.
Having established the horns according to the directions— saying, "It is hornless, four-cornered"— one should join together the *agniṣṭhā* (western) and *sūryasthā* (northern) horns;
and as for the statement, "One draws five *natigrāhya* cups for Indra," all of these must be drawn together with their respective *upayāma* vessels.

Having performed the Māruti offering, one should immolate these [animals]; this is the rule. The carrying of the firebrand is common to all; the *adhrigu*-precept would be repeated; there is an oblation for the immolated animals; one should split the two blades of sacrificial grass pointing upwards; at the *svāhākṛti*-precept, one should divide the clarified butter into two parts; the *stokīyā* verses belong to both portions; now, this chariot wheel is raised from the ground by the measure of a span (*prādeśa*).

"Turning around by the other side, he touches the two wings"—these refer to the two chariot wheels which he touches. Then he says, "The race-runners pass along the southern path"—these are said to be the Sūtas and Rājanyas.

"The Maruts, having gone around by the front of the Āhavanīya fire"—these are said to be the Kṣattṛs and Saṃgrahītṛs. Then he causes the sacrificer to put on a *tārpya* garment; this garment becomes satisfied with clarified butter. Moreover, they quote: "There are trees named *tṛpa*."

This thought occurs to them: "Now, some say that this Vājapeya consists entirely of seventeen-fold stomas; they say that one should chant the Bṛhat-sāman on twenty-one verses, using verses addressed to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa according to the instruction.
Now, this Rājasūya is completed in fifteen and a half months, or in fourteen and a half months;
in it there are five one-day Soma sacrifices, an Ahīna, and a two-night sacrifice.

There are six sheds and eight sacrificial posts; there are six *agniṣṭoma* offerings, two animals for the *paśubandha*, and the eighth in the *sautrāmaṇī*. There are exactly as many *avabhṛtha* (concluding purificatory) rites.
Where, indeed, is the oblation poured out from the oblation? One should simply say: "In the *ānumata*."
"A black garment with a black border as the sacrificial fee"—
by this it is meant that it has a black fringe;
"at will by means of an *iṣṭi* or an animal sacrifice."
Having performed the *saṃtani* sacrifice, one should sacrifice with either the *āgrayaṇa* or the *pārvaṇa*.
How indeed is the *sākamedha-parvan* [performed]?
The first *saṃtani* is at the deep of night; the second is on the following day at the onset of evening.
"What indeed has not yet arisen?"—one should say, "prior to the call for the after-offerings (anūyāja). He offers a pap (caru) dedicated to Bṛhaspati in the house of the Brahman priest;
[this refers to] whichever other Brahmin there may be who is not connected with the duties of the sacrificer (yājamāna).
"In the house of the favorite wife, a pap for Bhaga";
[this refers to] whichever queen is indeed fortunate.
"In the house of the discarded wife, a pap for Nirṛti."

"She is indeed called unfortunate" refers to the *pauṣṇa* oblation; "in the house of the *bhāgadugha*" refers specifically to the cook in the kitchen. Furthermore, they cite this: "He who milks for his share"—he is the one referred to here.
For twelve days there are the oblations of the Ratnins;

on the thirteenth day, the offering to Mitra and Bṛhaspati. When two days remain of this very same fortnight, one should sacrifice with the two Saṃtanī offerings. Now, if one should pile the fire-altar during the Ukthya Abhiṣecanīya rite, having offered the Agnicayana-related Sāvitra oblations during that very two-day period, and having gathered the fire-pans (ukhās) and the animal heads, one should sacrifice with the animal dedicated to Vāyu.

With "Thou art the lord of waters," these are the *apāmpatīyā* verses; they are said to belong to those [waters] that are oceanic. With "The vigor of the Maruts," these are the *niveṣṭyā* verses; they are said to belong to the whirlpools.
"Ye possess the splendor of the sun," with these words they are to be looked upon; these are said to be for those who are serene.
"The Śakvarī verses," with these words [the cow] is addressed; these are said to be for the birth-membrane of the cow.

"In this very case, one should sacrifice with an eight-potherd offering to Agni"; thus, when the Ukthya sacrifice concludes on the same day, this is the rule. But if it should be extended further, then one should sacrifice with an eight-potherd offering to Agni on that very day, and with an offering to Sarasvatī on the following day.
"Ten by ten they take charge of the cup here"—thus, seven each take charge of the Hotṛ’s cup and the Udgātṛ’s cup, while nine each take charge of the others;
these [rites] begin with the crawling forward and end with the Apsuṣoma. Then follows this Keśavapanīya Atirātra sacrifice, which has a reversed Stoma and includes the Ṣoḍaśin cup.

For him, the Agniṣṭoma chants are repeated: the Bahiṣpavamāna is twenty-one-fold, the Ājya-stotras and the Mādhyandina-pavamāna are seventeen-fold, the Pṛṣṭha-stotras and the Ārbhava-pavamāna are fifteen-fold, and the Yajñāyajñiya is threefold. Then he undergoes initiation for the Atirātra with reversed Stomas, the Keśavapanīya;
it has six initiation days and six Upasad days; the Soma-pressing takes place on the thirteenth day, and the concluding ceremony on the fourteenth.
Then, during the remainder of that very fortnight, he undergoes initiation for the Vyuṣṭi-dvirātra.
He remains consecrated for this one night of the waxing fortnight and two nights of the waning fortnight;

there are twelve *upasads* for these nights. Then he observes the fast-day (*upavasatha*). On the day of the fast, which is the new moon, the first day occurs; on the following day, the second. Thus concludes the *Vyuṣṭi*-sacrifice, a two-night rite. Then he should settle in the northern hall, and having churned the fire and distributed the fires, he undergoes consecration for the *udayanīya* *agniṣṭoma*.
He has three *dīkṣā*s and three *upasads*; on the seventh day, the pressing (*prasuta*) is completed.

This is the *udayanīya* *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice with a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*sahasradakṣiṇa*). Then, during the remainder of this very fortnight, he performs the *kṣatrasya dhṛti*, the *devikā* oblations, the *traidhātavīyā*, and the *sautrāmaṇī*.
Thus the *rājasūya* is completed in sixteen and a half months. According to Śālīki, it ends with the *keśavapanīya*.
These [days] are fifteen and a half;
then follow the Añjasas,
by which the first half-month is completed in the well-known manner.

The Cāturmāsya sacrifices take five days; the Saṃtanī takes two days; on the eighth day [is] the Indra [offering]; on the ninth day the former Devikā offerings; on the tenth day the latter [Devikā offerings]; on the eleventh and twelfth days [the Triṣaṃyukta offerings]; on the thirteenth day [the Vaiśvadeva]; on the fourteenth day the Vaiśvānara cake on twelve potsherds; on the fifteenth day the Vāruṇa oblation of barley; thus [constitutes] one month. The Ratninām havīṃṣi take twelve days; on the thirteenth day the offering to Mitra and Bṛhaspati; the Saṃtanī takes two days; the Abhiṣecanīya Ukthya sacrifice takes half a month.

Two months by means of a half-month: the Saptadaśa Daśapeya, for which one is consecrated for a half-month and observes the vows of consecration—this makes three months; the Pratīcīnastoma Keśavapanīya Atirātra with a half-month, and the Vyuṣṭi Dvirātra with a half-month—these make four months; the Kṣatrasya Dhṛti with a half-month—these are four and a half months. Now, according to Śālīki:
