The Agniṣṭoma, being pure, lasts for seven days; in this very manner, the remainder of the fortnight is accomplished up to the Vāruṇa offering by means of the twelve-day rite (dvādaśāha); on the thirteenth day, there is the offering to Mitra and Bṛhaspati; with a two-day period, the Saṃtanī rites; thus, the Abhiṣecanīya Ukthya sacrifice takes one month and a half-month; the Saptadaśa Daśapeya takes a half-month; with another half-month, the Pratīcīnastoma Keśavapanīya Atirātra; and with yet another half-month, the Vyūṣṭi Dvirātra—thus three months are completed; and finally, the Kṣatrasya Dhṛti.

These [days] amount to three and a half; then there is the Patantaka sacrifice with twelve *dīkṣā* days and twelve *upasads*, a seven-day *ahīna* sacrifice, and the *rājasūya*. He performs the other *rājasūya* oblations as occasion permits, then he performs the *devikā* oblations, then he sacrifices with the *traidhātavīyā*, and then he sacrifices with the *sautrāmaṇī*;
thus the *rājasūya* is completed.
Now we shall set forth this ritual procedure for the *iṣṭi*, involving both fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses and seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.

In that regard, the *yājamāna* (the duties of the sacrificer) is established according to Baudhāyana’s ritual manual as handed down by tradition; however, according to Śālīki, one should recite three triplets of verses.
Having recited the first verse three times, one should recite the next three verses once each, and recite the last verse three times;
thus one should recite fifteen [verses]. These eleven *sāmidhenī* verses we transmit;
of these, one recites the first three times and the last three times, making them fifteen.

"One should recite seventeen; one should recite twenty-one; one should recite twenty-four; one should recite thirty; one should recite thirty-two; one should recite thirty-six; one should recite forty-four; one should recite four hundred and four; one should recite four hundred and eight"—these are the *dhāyyā* verses in this context; they are to be inserted. All of them relate to Agni, all are in the *gāyatrī* metre, or one may recite them in all metres, or one may recite an unlimited number; these are indeed the *dhāyyā* verses to be inserted in this very context.
Not all of these are *gāyatrī* verses; the *puro'nuvākyā* is a *gāyatrī*, while the *yājyā* is a *triṣṭubh*.
The *puro'nuvākyā* has its characteristic mark at the beginning, and the *yājyā* has its characteristic mark at the end.
The *puro'nuvākyā* contains the word "head" (*mūrdhan*), and one sacrifices with a verse containing the word "team" (*niyutvat*). One performs the *upām̐śuyāja* between them. Thus it is said.
This applies only to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices and not elsewhere.
Now, these optional (kāmyā) offerings must be performed by one who is free from bodily waste;
he should observe a milk-vow for a year, or for twelve days, or as long as it takes to recover his strength.

Among those [offerings], if one were to offer even one of those that have common fetters (*saṃyojana*), all of them must indeed be offered. Regarding this point—that when the fire-attendant is not occupied with his duties, he takes out a small portion and then takes it out again—how is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) here accomplished? Is it accomplished or not?
Some say it is accomplished; others, however, say it is not accomplished.
If one of these two has its portion specified while the other has its portion unspecified, then both indeed become ones with unspecified portions, and thus [the ritual] is not accomplished.
Therefore, the taking of the *dhṛṣṭi* [should be done]: one should take the *dhṛṣṭi* from the vicinity of the *gārhapatya*;
with it, one should place the potsherds for Vaiśvānara upon the *āhavanīya*.

Having turned clockwise, he should pour the flour prepared for the Maruts into the *gārhapatya* fire, mix it, touch it, form two balls, carry one ball around the front of the [fire] for the Maruts, and then sprinkle the *vaiśvānara* cake on the *āhavanīya* fire. Having turned clockwise, he should cause the skin to be applied to the Maruts' offering on the *gārhapatya*, and likewise cause the skin to be applied to this [other] one. Having carried fire around that [Maruts' offering], he should carry fire around this one; having cooked that, he should cook this one. Or rather, he may perform both actions in both places.

The setting down of that boiled [milk] is performed by releasing the western joint of the enclosing sticks or the southern enclosing stick at its front; from this point onward, the procedure is established.
Or rather, it is on this [fire] that these two wipe themselves clean—those two who eat the food of those who hate each other; thus it is said: "one with the other."
"Those from whom the enemies might tremble, or whose kingdoms might be completely subdued"—
the neighboring kings are the "enemies," their own territories are the "kingdoms," and the subjects are the "people. He who is dejected in mind would be like one who has committed a sin himself.

Thinking, "If there is strength, he might become dejected in spirit like one who has committed sin himself," [one should act] so that what is given to one of noble form and lineage—who is himself sinful—might not be withheld as if it were a gift already bestowed; for such a thing becomes a gift that is not returned, being merely obstructed. Now, in this sacrifice which is like a *adhvara*, one should perform the first ritual procedure (*tantra*) ending with the *iḍā* offering, and carry forward the remainder together with the third [offering].
Regarding how the portions are to be consumed here:
one may consume them at various places as they arise, or having taken portions from all of them together and offered them, one should consume them at the end.
As for the statement "the ox is to be given by the Hotṛ," this ox is to be given specifically by the sacrificer from his own herd.
Having enclosed the altar, one should dig up half and not the other;
or rather, the southern half of the altar or the other half. Having taken a portion for Indra, he should take a portion for the Viśvedevas, and then [another] for Indra on top.
Thus, these two portions are indeed declared. "A garment preceded by a teacher is the sacrificial fee."

Whether they are woven or spun, the threads used are either copper-colored or blue; or rather, this is said to be merely the cord for the pillow. Now, at this *Sañjñāneṣṭi*, one should recite the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) only once and cause the announcement (*āśrāvayet*) only once, for she has two verses, both an invitatory and an offering verse (*yājyā*).

Furthermore, it is said: "If he does not obtain [the result], he should offer [the oblation] with the formula: 'I set aside this portion for the Ādityas, so that such-and-such a person from such-and-such a clan may obtain [the result]'"; having offered thus, he ceases.

Having performed the ritual actions up to the final dedication (*paridāna*), he should then pour these grains onto a black antelope skin and fix them on the northern part of the fire-hall. Once they have been understood [as ready], he should set them down and proceed with the ritual beginning from the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). From this point onward, it is established as being just like [the procedure] for one [the sacrificial cake] split by the fingernails; likewise for the one consisting of a hundred *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces. Alternatively, before the pouring of the rice grains, he should place a gold plate upon it. Or, even if it is boiled, he should take it while still boiling and, having enclosed it with gold and silver plates, set it down within the altar. He should then cause the [cakes] dedicated to Agni and Soma to touch those dedicated to Indra.
The portions that have been touched should be joined together before they are anointed with clarified butter;

by saying "he cuts off while making them all reach [the fire]," it is meant that this applies to the offering for the deities as well as the *sviṣṭakṛt* portion. Furthermore, it is said that the size [of the cake] should correspond to the number of years he expects to live;
if he is thirty years old, he should make it the size of one seventy-year-old.

If he should be forty years old, he should perform the sixty-year rite; this is his procedure for advancement. Now, regarding the offerings to Varuṇa and the Saṃjñāna sacrifice, he should recite the invitatory verses only once, give the call only once, and make the offerings only once, as they share a common deity. Having returned, he should offer a caru-oblation to Apām Napāt.
But who indeed is Apām Napāt?
One should say: "He is the lightning."

"Black and honey-colored"—this is what is meant by "produced by bees. "Not rough"—this is what is meant by "having three folds. Furthermore, they also cite this: "having three layers"—this is what is meant by that.
Just as it is for the threefold [offering], so too is the procedure for the cutting of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) when there is doubt;
"he created the serpents"—
these are said to be the months.
"He created the vayāmsi"—
these are said to be the meters;
"he himself indeed was it."
They point to the ancient Gārhapatya fire.

At the time for the animal sacrifice, having taken a firebrand from it, having carried it out by the southern door, having gone around the south of the Sadas, having carried it around the south of the Mārjālīya hearth, having brought it between the sacrificial post and the Āhavanīya fire, and having carried it out northward between the Cātvāla pit and the rubbish heap, they should cook the animal with it. Now, if there should be a firebrand from the Āhavanīya, they should carry it away together with the omentum.
"To which deity, indeed, do the Apāvya offerings belong? [he asks].

There are two [offerings] belonging to Prajāpati: that for Agni, and that for Vāyu; [then there is] that for the Viśvedevas—this is the "sacrifice of the sacrifice" (iṣṭarga), or rather, the Adhvaryu is the "sacrifice of the sacrifice" for the sacrificer. This is what is meant by the phrase "the hot tip. Furthermore, they also cite this: "The Adhvaryu himself is thus described [by the words] 'Protect me from the spell in the mouth, from every curse'. For the spell in the mouth is indeed a subsequent utterance (anuvyāhāra); therefore, "protect me from that"—this is what is meant.

Therefore, one must not enter upon the sacrificial site [during] day and night—this is one view; nor until the fires have grown cold—this is another; nor until it rains upon it—this is yet another. "The two oceans are spread out, undecaying"—these two are said to be day and night. "They revolve like feet in the belly"—by "belly" (udara) it is meant "feet" (pāda); this is what is expressed here. "Beholding them, they pass over one; not beholding them, they pass over the other by means of a bridge"—they pass over the day while beholding it, and they pass over the night by means of the bridge of sleep.
"Two garments, eternal, he wears; one"—by this it is meant that the Āditya wears day and night.

"Clothing himself in the black, he takes up the bright, having overtaken the aged"—clothing himself in the night, he takes up the bright [light] by hiding [the darkness]; by this it is meant that he wears the day.
Regarding the phrase "of that which is inhabited by an insect," what indeed is this insect that fashions these balls?
Regarding the constant taking [of the cups], it is said that one follows the Vaiṣṇava ṛc; thus, this [verse] is to be followed specifically with the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*).
Now, therefore, we shall explain the *atigrāhya* cups: these indeed are the *pṛṣṭhya-atigrāhyas*, five for Indra at the Vājapeya sacrifice.
The Paraḥsāmans and the Arvāksāmans; at the Viṣuvat [day], the Saurya and the Vaiśvakarmaṇāditya; in the Gavām Ayana, the Prājāpatya at the Mahāvrata.
The offering for Bṛhaspati is at the Bṛhaspatisava;

[the offerings] "Vaimṛdha," "Udbhid," and "Tviṣimat" are at the Vājapeya; and the two [offerings] beginning with "vṛṣā so aṃśuḥ pavate" are at the Aśvamedha. One should offer the omentum of the horse around the two Mahiman cups according to the specific instruction.

"How indeed does the consumption [of the Soma] belonging to another [cup] take place? "O Rudra, O God, of thee who art accompanied by the troop of Rudras, who knowest the mind, of the midday pressing, of the Triṣṭubh metre, drunk with waters, drunk with plants, drunk with offspring, drunk with Prajāpati, full of sweetness, being invited, I, invited, consume"—this is the consumption for those [cups] where the Sāmans are reversed; "eight-hoofed gold is the sacrificial fee"—by this it is meant that it is eight-pointed.
If there should be two embryos, there should be twelve enclosing-sticks; there should be one large receptacle and two intermediate receptacles.

Then, for a fetus that is bone, having gathered these bones together with clarified butter, he should pour them out inside the enclosing-sticks with the middle leaf-shoot, saying: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ."

"When there is no cloud over that which has been immolated"—if there should be no cloud when it has been immolated, one should simply stop; but if there should be no cloud when it has been dedicated (*upākṛtā*), one should dedicate another animal in its place and proceed with this sacrifice once the subsequent [animal] is provided by a cloud. Now, these *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings are seen for both the one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and the one who has not, except in the case of the sacrificial fire-enclosure (*vihāra*). However, the teachers have them offered as supplementary oblations before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, starting from "The eight Vasus.
But who indeed are these Vasus?

"Earth, the intermediate space, heaven, fire, wind, the sun, the moon, and the waters—these are the eight Vasus. Indeed, everything that exists here is established upon them. He who knows this becomes firmly established. 'The eleven Rudras'—these are said to be the vital breaths."
"The twelve Ādityas"—
these are said to be the months; five are taken up, nine by nine are taken up, and they are divided fivefold.
There are nine new births;
then that which is the tenth mantra is seen as intended for the grasping of these very [births].
Having milked her, one should give her to a Brāhmaṇa whose food one would not eat.
This [offering] is to be given only to one who has stood ready for alms.
Regarding the question, "To which deity do the *atirikta-soma* (excess soma) offerings belong?"—whatever cup they might exceed, it should belong to that very deity; this is one view.
Now, another point is indeed known as their *brāhmaṇa*: "Why is the sacrifice of Indra [performed] until the conclusion? Because they belong to Indra and Viṣṇu, they become cooled;

thus, they may desire the conclusion of the six-day period while it is still cooling. This is precisely the *brāhmaṇa* regarding the six-day period. Now, if a conjunction of days should occur such that even the nine middle days of the year-long session meet together, then at that very time, having made them cool, they should pile them up. And if it is on the *udayanīya* Atirātra, this very same [rule applies].
"Progeny indeed performed a sacrificial session (sattra), performing austerity and offering oblations. Regarding this, they ask: "Which is that sacrificial session?
[The answer is: "That which these who have not established the sacred fires perform as a futile exertion—that is the sacrificial session."
Regarding the Āśvina [fire-altar], which is said to be "eastward-facing" or "facing the Āśvins," how large indeed does the Āśvina become?

It is two yojanas, or as far as a horse might travel in a day; the altar (vedi) becomes twice that size. One should take the diagonal measurement of a square formed by the Agni-measure (āgnika-prakrama).
That shall be the step;
with that he should measure the altar. Alternatively, one should take a twenty-fourth part of twenty-one chariot-axles, twenty-one foot-steps, and eight finger-breadths;
that shall be the step.
With that [formula] he measures out the altar;
"Agni becomes threefold in praise," thus there are three [sets] of sevenfold [altars].
He is twenty-one-fold. Then he should choose these two ponds in the middle of the sacrificial ground.

"For what purpose, indeed, are these two ponds? [one might ask]. The southern one is for the horse-bath (*aśvaplāvana*), and the northern one is for the purificatory bath (*āvabhṛthika*). There are two slaves: the son of his paternal half-sister and the son of his maternal half-sister. He who is the son of his father’s half-sister leads in front; then he who is the son of his mother’s half-sister follows behind, having wrapped his left knee with an old cloth—this is said to be the cord for the supporting beam (*upadhānarajju*).
"Indeed, there are a hundred princes worthy of the couch"— by this, those who have been appointed as deputies are meant; "a hundred fierce kings"— by this, they are likewise described.
These very persons are not to be consecrated as kings; then, in the morning, he offers an eight-potherd cake to Savitṛ. This is the first [offering] to Savitṛ;

the second is in the section on the Vaiśvadeva; the third is in the afternoon. One should know that this is the ritual procedure for a one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*). And from the sacrificial ground, he should move away toward the north. Thus it is for the animals of the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*); thus for the animal dedicated to Vāyu; thus for the hornless goat. For seven days he should perform this sacrifice.
"How are there sacrificial portions here? [they ask].
"One may eat them at various places, or rather, having set up the sacrificial post for this seven-day sacrifice, one erects the *rājjudāla* post at the front, closest to the fire."
This is what is meant by "the *śleṣmātaka* tree.

Furthermore, they quote: "He fixes the *rājjudāla* tree at the center of the fire-altar for the removal of the sin of killing an embryo; on both sides there are two *pautudrava* trees for the attainment of a holy fragrance."

He gives the third of the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās). Of those pertaining to the fire-altar (āgnikās), he gives the third together with the Kāmapra; the third at the Atirātra, and the third at the Catuṣṭoma.
This Catuṣṭoma consists of four Uttarīyas; this Catuṣṭoma consists of [the offerings]: "Svāhā to one! Svāhā to two! and so forth.
"How indeed should one offer these recitations? [The answer is:

"They should be offered in their natural order, without interruption. Having taken twenty-four ropes, they approach the sacrificial posts; four each for the other assistants. "How should one bind the animals to these? [The answer is: "The horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal—these three share a common rope. There are three [ropes] for the forehead-straps."
For the animals tied to the side-posts, there are eight [mantras]: "To Agni Anīkavat, a red-marked ox," and so forth;

for those tied to the central post, there are seven: "To Soma Svarāj, two oxen that draw a cart," and so forth. Now, three of these [animals] have a common rope, and the fourth belongs to the chief animal alone. The ritual procedure is the same up to the carrying of fire around them (paryagnikaraṇa).

Of these animals that have been carried around the fire, twenty-nine are released; forty-one remain; there are forty-two shafts for them. Here, two [shafts] are joined together on the horse; as for the others, they are assigned one for each animal. "To Indra and Agni, the bestowers of vigor, the eight-year-old [bull]"—these two are said to be the yoke-animals (*prāsaṅgya*). Then, having mixed the flour of the *āśu* grain with *śalmali* resin...
These are the flour-pastes of *āśuka* rice mixed with the sap of the *śalmali* tree;
the Pratiprasthātṛs offer them separately.
For these, the Maitrāvaruṇas alone should recite the invitatory verses. There are exactly four offerings for these: "To the young bull, svāhā! To the draft ox, svāhā! and so forth.
These two are said to be the sun and the moon; moreover, they cite this: "The *saṃvatsara* is the draft-ox (*iluvarda*), and the *parivatsara* is the bull (*balivarda*).
He offers on its head with the formula, "To Jumbaka, svāhā!"—what deity, indeed, does this oblation belong to?
One should say "vāruṇī" [only];
as for "kikidīvi," it is "vidīgaya"; [it is] "vididihīvikīdīha," and thus one becomes "kikidīvi."
The spotted antelope, the moth, and the diver-bird—then he dedicates these animals: one for Agni, one for Indra-Agni, and one for the Aśvins.

These goats indeed have a common origin; their ritual performance has been explained in the same manner as that of the eleven sacrificial animals. Of what deities, then, are the seasonal animals? They have the seasons as their deities; this is one view.

Now, furthermore: the first [sets of offerings] are dedicated to Agni; the second to Indra; the third to the Viśvedevas; the fourth to Mitra and Varuṇa; the fifth to Bṛhaspati; the sixth to Savitṛ; and those for the year are dedicated to Prajāpati with the verse "nivakṣasaḥ.
Now, this twelve-day rite (dvādaśāha) is of two kinds: either an Ahīna or a Sattra.

If he performs it alone, it is an *ahīna*; if many perform it, it is a *sattra*. Whether it be an *ahīna* or a *sattra*, in both cases there are *atirātra* rites on both sides; for *ahīnas* have *atirātras* on one side only, while *sattras* have *atirātras* on both sides. An *ahīna* has *atirātras* on both sides only by specific injunction (*ādeśa*), whereas a *sattra* is without *atirātras* except by specific injunction—as in the case of the Agniṣṭomāyana, the Sārasvatāyana, and the Viśvasṛjāmayana. How, indeed, should their combination (*saṃnivāpa*) be performed? They should first combine them with the *sāvitra* offerings.

Having offered the *sāvitra* oblations and having descended from the fires, they should offer the *agnihotra*s; or else, for the sake of the animal sacrifice to Vāyu, they should pile the fires together. Having sacrificed with the animal to Vāyu and having descended from the fires, they should offer the *agnihotra*s. Now, if they were to pile them together for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering, those fires would remain piled together until the *vyudavasānīyā*. Having performed the *vyudavasānīyā*, they should perform the concluding rites (*yajñapuccha*) as neighbors. How indeed should those who have been consecrated together perform the *viṣṇukrama* strides?

If they are surrounded by great nooses, they may step forward, or having resolved upon the nooses, there may be a stepping forward; then he says, "Step forward! and again he says, "Step forward! Such a ritual procedure would be extremely heavy. Furthermore, this rule occurs in the text: "On the sixth day, having approached, they pile up the *uttaravedi*; or on the eleventh. This applies only when there is no piling of the fire-altar (*anagnicaya*), not when there is a piling of the fire-altar (*sāgnicaya*). How, indeed, does the continuity of the *ahīna* sacrifice remain uninterrupted?

The Adhvaryu maintains the continuity of the sacrifice by taking up the *vasatīvarī* waters and by preparing the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). The Brahman does so by the distribution of the milks and by restraining his speech. The Hotṛ does so by the *atipraiṣa* and by repetition. The Udgātṛ does so by the *subrahmaṇyā* litany. The sacrificer does so by re-appropriating the sacrifice. While they are performing these rites, they take up this *dhruvā* clarified butter.
Then they should collect these sacrificial grasses for the pressings; having risen at the deep of night, the Āgnīdhra should cause the fires to blaze while taking up the portions of clarified butter.

How indeed does the commencement of the day’s *prātaranuvāka* take place during the day? Having concluded the day’s ritual either with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings or with the *hṛdayaśūla*, having bound up King Soma, and at the proper time having taken up the *vasatīvarī* waters, having ensured the continuity of the *ahīna* sacrifice, and having washed the pressing stones and the *vāyavya* cup, and having placed the *daśāpavitra* strainer into the *droṇakalaśa* vessel, they run to the *āgnīdhra* shed; the fuel-bearers go forth, and having brought back the fuel-sticks, they set them down upon the *āhavanīya* fire.

When the *vasatīvarī* waters have been carried away, when the *subrahmaṇyā* has been invoked, he should place the *samidhs* for lying down upon the fire, bind together the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmā-barhis*), set aside the milk, run to the *āgnīdhra* shed, prepare the forms for lying down in the *āgnīdhra*, and proceed with the morning ritual according to the established procedure during the deep of night;
from this point onward, it is accomplished as prescribed.
The *atigrāhya* cups are indeed the support of the sacrifice. "The two wheels are the *pṛṣṭha* chants"—the threefold and the twenty-onefold are the wheels;

the cup for Agni is the support. The fifteenfold and the twenty-sevenfold are the wheels; the cup for Indra is the support. The seventeenfold and the thirty-threefold are the wheels; the cup for Sūrya is the support. As for this ritual procedure of Baudhāyana which they teach—that the fire-drilling is accompanied by mantras—the mantras here belong only to the office of the Adhvaryu; those for the churning of the fire do not recur.
On this day, one performs the seasonal sacrifice (ṛtuyāja) for oneself alone; on this day, one does not perform the seasonal sacrifice for another.

Having caused the announcement (*āśrāvya*), the Adhvaryu gives the cup to another, returns by the same way he came, sits down behind the two *havirdhāna* carts, utters the summons for the seasons (*ṛtusaṃpraiṣa*), stands up, makes the offering, pours out the remnants, turns to the right, and—sitting facing east where he previously offered—should consume the Hotṛ’s portion; sitting facing west, he consumes the Adhvaryu’s portion. The Hotṛ recites the *pārucchepīs*; the Maitrāvaruṇa arranges the *vālakhilyās*; the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin [recites] the *vṛṣākapi*; and the Acchāvāka [recites] the *evayāmarut*. The *śaṃsat* [formula] is uttered by each.

"What, then, is the duty of the Adhvaryu? "He should respond," one should say. Those *anuṣṭubh* verses which the Adhvaryu extracts and brings forward—these four are *gāyatrīs*. These three [of those] are *anuṣṭubhs*.
With only the foot of this *gāyatrī*, "O King Soma, come, descend," he should cause the King [Soma] to descend.
How, indeed, does the tenth day become entirely twenty-four-fold by its ritual application (*bhakti*) and yet remain a *triṣṭoma*, except for the silent *stoma*?
The Bahiṣpavamāna is twenty-fourfold; the Brahmasāman is fifteenfold; the Agniṣṭomasāman is thirty-threefold.

Of these, nine indeed come together, and they become twenty-four. Thus, by way of distribution, even this tenth day becomes entirely twenty-fourfold and also a Triṣṭoma, except for the Tūṣṇīṃ-stoma. [This is done] while letting loose the calf to its mother, with the verse: "Dharuṇa, sucking... (RV 9.82.1).
"To which deity does this oblation belong?
"One should say, 'To Prajāpati,'" he said.
"Now, let us arrange this twelve-day rite by means of the cups in their proper order."
Now, there are nine days that follow this rearrangement, which are other than the Prāyaṇīya and Udayanīya days and the tenth day; furthermore, there are the Chandomas, which are six in number.

For the first three-night period is established in its own place: at the morning pressing of the first three-night period, one should press the Soma for the first time eight times, for the second time eleven times, and for the third time twelve times. One should draw the cup for Mahendra with this Triṣṭubh verse, "Great is Indra, manly, filling the people"; the cup for Savitṛ with this Jagatī verse, "O Savitṛ, with thy undeceivable protections. One should prepare cakes on eight potsherds for the morning pressing, on eleven potsherds for the midday pressing, and on twelve potsherds for the third pressing.
One should consume the draughts of the morning pressing with the *vasumadgaṇa* and the *gāyatrī* metre; those of the midday pressing with the *rudravatgaṇa* and the *triṣṭubh* metre;

and those of the third pressing with the *ādityavatgaṇa* and the *jagatī* metre. Now, if the *jagatī* metre is used at the morning pressing during the second three-night rite, one should first press the *upāṃśu* stone twelve times, and the second [stone] eight times.

For the third time, eleven times over, he should draw the Māhendra cup with the Gāyatrī verse, "Indra, who [is] by might... He should draw the Sāvitra cup with the Triṣṭubh verse, "O Savitṛ, [grant us] what is lovely today... He should prepare the cakes for the morning pressing on twelve potsherds, those for the midday pressing on eight potsherds, and those for the third pressing on eleven potsherds.
He should consume the morning pressing cups with the *ādityavadgaṇa* formula and the Jagatī metre, and the midday pressing cups with the *vasumadgaṇa* formula and the Gāyatrī metre.

With the *ṛc* "O Rudra, with thy troop," using the *triṣṭubh* metre, [he offers] for the third pressing. Now, regarding the *triṣṭubh* at the morning pressing during the third *trirātra*: first, he should press the *upām̐śu* [cup] eleven times; second, twelve times; and third, eight times. He should repeat three times this *gāyatrī* verse, "Great is Indra, who by his might," without the *upayāma* formula; that becomes a *jagatī*, and with it he should take the *māhendra* cup. With the *gāyatrī* verse, "The golden-handed one for our aid," he takes the *sāvitra* cup.
One should prepare cakes on eleven potsherds for the morning pressing, on twelve potsherds for the midday pressing,
and on eight potsherds for the third pressing.
One should consume the portions of the morning pressing with the *rudravat* group and the *triṣṭubh* metre, and the portions of the midday pressing with the *ādityavat* group and the *jagatī* metre.
"With the *vasumadgaṇa* and the *gāyatrī* metre for the offerings of the third pressing"—thus [he says].

Now, some say that he should obtain the Vaiṣuvat day as the collection of months; there are seventeen *dīkṣā*s and twelve *upasad*s, and the Vaiṣuvat is the thirtieth. How indeed do the *stomas* come to be for the Go and Āyu sacrifices?

For the Go sacrifice, the *bahiṣpavamāna* is fifteenfold, the *ājya* chants are ninefold, the midday pressing is entirely seventeenfold, and the third pressing is entirely twenty-onefold, including the *ukthya*.

Now, for the Ayus, the *bahiṣpavamāna* is threefold (*trivṛt*), the *ājya* chants are fifteenfold (*pañcadaśa*), the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*) is entirely seventeenfold (*saptadaśa*), and the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) is entirely twenty-one-fold (*ekaviṃśa*), together with the *ukthya*.
Now, these two, the Viśvajit and the Abhijit, are *agniṣṭoma*s included in the sacrificial session (*sattra*).
What indeed are their *stoma*s? The Abhijit has a threefold rising and is fourfold in its repetition; the Viśvajit has a fourfold rising and is threefold in its repetition.

"How indeed does one become possessed of the Ekaviṃśati-garbha? Having approached the Abhijit, they should undertake the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha; then three Paraḥsāman days; then the Vaiṣuvata day; then three Pratyaksāman days; then the reversed Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha; and then the Viśvajit. "How indeed should one know the Go and Āyus as separated?
One should undertake the Go before the Abhijit; the Āyus remains in its own place.
"How many Agniṣṭomas are there indeed in the Gavāmayana?"

The Jyotis-Agniṣṭoma, the Trivṛt-Agniṣṭoma, the Viśvajit and Abhijit Agniṣṭomas, the Vaiṣuvat as the tenth day, and the Mahāvrata—these are the seven; indeed, they call this Gavām Ayana the one whose Stomas are well-known. Of that sacrifice, the northern wing is reversed; therefore, one should take the Tryanīka cups in reverse order, except for those belonging to the Go and Āyu [days] and the Daśarātra.
Now, there are these thirty-two sets of eleven [cattle] in the Gavām Ayana;

of these, sixteen are completed in the first fortnight, and seventeen remain for the set of eleven at the Viṣuvat day, including the Savanīya victim for Bṛhaspati. Thus, nine days remain without cattle.
"What indeed are these days?

[Thus asked. They are: the three *chandomas* following the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*, the tenth day, the *mahāvrata*, and the *udayanīya-atirātra*; and the *abhiplavas* and *akṣīyantis*—this is the *ayanam* of the Aṅgirases.
Here, in place of the *pṛṣṭhyas*, he places only the *abhiplavas*.

The *pṛṣṭhya* days diminish, and that is the course of the Ādityas; here, in place of the *abhiplava* days, he places only the *pṛṣṭhya* days. The *agniṣṭoma*s diminish, and that is the course of Prajāpati; here, in place of both the *pṛṣṭhya* and *abhiplava* days, he places only the *agniṣṭoma*s. Regarding "with *āghāṭī*s, *piñcholā*s, and *karkarīkā*s": the *āghāṭī*s are indeed gourds (*kola-uṣṭha*);
the *piñcholā*s are indeed lutes with broken necks (*vīṇā-kāṇabhraśa*); and the *karkarīkā*s are indeed lutes (*vīṇā*).
"At that very time he pierces with the knife"—by this it is meant that he should indeed pierce. Now, it is also said:
"The exponents of the Veda say: 'He indeed should sacrifice who, having sacrificed with the Agniṣṭoma, then sacrifices with the Sarvastoma.'"
There are four *ājya* chants consisting of fifteen verses each; these two constitute two groups of thirty. Of these, he offers three oblations in the latter group of thirty.
Those two [days] consist of the Triṇava and Trayastriṃśa stomas;

on the first day the Sāman for the Hotṛ’s Ājya-stotra is Gāyatra, and on the latter it is Traiṣṭubha—one should thus prepare these for the Hotṛ’s Ājya on the first day, and likewise for the Hotṛ’s Ājya on the following day.
Now, this thousandth cow—speckled in one place—is prepared and made ready.
By this, it is effectively stated:
"At what time, indeed, should one give a spotted four-year-old cow that slays enemies?
A Kṣatriya should give her after having won a battle.

How indeed should one sacrifice with the Garga-trirātra performed at the beginnings of the seasons? One should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma in either the month of Āṣāḍha or Śrāvaṇa. Having completed that day—ending either with the Patnīsaṃyājas or with the Hṛdayaśūla—and having bound the King (Soma), taken the Vasatīvarī waters at the proper time, and ensured the continuity of the Ahīna sacrifice, one washes the pressing stones and the Vāyavya vessel, places the *daśāpavitra* strainer in the Droṇakalaśa, and runs to the Āgnīdhra shed. The fuel-bearers go forth; having brought back the fuel-sticks, they place them near the Āhavanīya fire.

When the *vasatīvarī* waters have been carried around, the *saubrahmaṇyā* has been invoked, and the *saṃveśanīyā* fuel-sticks have been added to the fire, he should bind together the sacrificial grass (*idhma*) and the *barhis*, and having set aside portions of the milk, they fast. Then, on the following day, he should sacrifice with the *savanīya-iṣṭi*.
Thereafter, he performs the *stambayajus* rite.
In this very manner, carrying the *vasatīvarī* waters around day after day, he sacrifices with the *savanīya-iṣṭi* for four months.

He does not perform the *agnihotra* nor sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*. Then, when four months have elapsed, when the *vasatīvarī* waters have been carried around, and when the *subrahmaṇyā* has been invoked, he daily places the kindling-sticks for retiring upon the fire; having bound together the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and having set aside the milks, they observe the fast.
Then, on the following day, he sacrifices with the *ukthya*.

Having performed that very same day’s rites either ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings or ending with the heart-spit (*hṛdayaśūla*), having bound up the King Soma, taken the *vasatīvarī* waters at the proper time, ensured the continuity of the *Ahīna* sacrifice, washed the pressing-stones and the *vāyavya* cup, placed the fringe of the *daśāpavitra* filter into the *droṇakalaśa*, and run to the *Āgnīdhra* shed, they go as fuel-bearers; having brought back the fuel-sticks, they place them near the *Āhavanīya* fire.

When the *vastīvarī* waters have been carried around and the *subrahmaṇyā* litany has been invoked, he should place the *saṃveśanīyā* fuel-sticks on the fire, bind the sacrificial grass (*idhma*) and the *barhis*, and without leaving aside the milk, they fast. Then, on the following day, he performs the *savanīya* sacrifice;
there, in the same manner, he does not carry away the *stambayajus*.
In this very way, carrying the *vastīvarī* waters around day after day, he performs the *savanīya* sacrifice for another four months.

He neither performs the *agnihotra* nor sacrifices with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*. Then, when four months have elapsed, when the *vasatīvarī* waters have been carried around, and when the *subrahmaṇyā* has been invoked, he should daily lay on the fuel-sticks for retiring, bind together the sacrificial grass and faggot, set aside the milks, and remain in retreat. Then, on the following day, he sacrifices with the *atirātra*, including the tail of the sacrifice. Now, he should cause this thousandth cow to turn either toward the east or toward the north; he must not pass between her and the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*), nor between her and himself.
"What indeed are the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) for the Ahīna sacrifices? "Each session of days (ahargaṇa) should have a thousand as its fee—this is one view.

Each individual day should have a thousand as its fee—this is another. It should have twelve hundred as its fee—this is another. Or it should have fees according to one's faith—this is yet another. According to the traditional instruction (ādeśa), however, one gives a thousand [cows] following this Atirātra sacrifice."

The *ahīna* sacrifices begin with the two-night (*dvirātra*) and extend up to the eleven-night (*ekādaśarātra*). Now, these *sattras* (sacrificial sessions) are encompassed by the *ahīnas*; for instance, this eleven-night sacrifice contains the essence of the year. Indeed, the Bharata-twelve-day sacrifice is of both kinds: it consists of twelve *agniṣṭomas* with the *rathaṃtara* as their *sāman*, and that is the Bharata-twelve-day sacrifice. Furthermore, regarding those [sacrifices] where the *stomas* increase, one version is as follows: the first day should have the *trivṛt* [stoma], the second the *pañcadaśa*, the third the *saptadaśa*, and the fourth the *ekaviṃśa*. This is one way.
Now, for the other [form]: the morning pressing of the first day has the *trivṛt* stoma, the midday pressing has the *pañcadaśa*, and the third pressing has the *saptadaśa*;
then, for the second day, the morning pressing has the *pañcadaśa*, the midday pressing has the *saptadaśa*, and the third pressing has the *ekaviṃśa*;
then, for the third day, the morning pressing has the *saptadaśa*, the midday pressing has the *ekaviṃśa*, and the third pressing has the *triṇava*.

Now, for the fourth day: the morning pressing has twenty-one [verses], the midday pressing has twenty-seven, and the third pressing has thirty-three. Then follow these sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) belonging to the Upasad rites, beginning with the taking up of the winnowing basket and ending with the Āpya libations;
one should offer them all together once with an oblation from the dipping-spoon (sruva), according to the ritual procedure of Aupamanyava, as single-pot-sherd offerings to Agni.
"Follow along; they are going eastward"—saying this, he should throw a wooden pin (śamyā) from the vicinity of the Āhavanīya fire.

Wherever it falls, that shall be the site for the Gārhapatya fire; the Āhavanīya is to the east of that. Now, if they should come upon water that is not yet crossed, they should prepare a *caru* offering to Aponaptrīya as a subsequent oblation following the *tṛtīyasavanīya* offerings. Then, on the next day, when the sacrifice is to be concluded, he should indeed throw the wooden pin. There are three-day periods, there are five-day periods—these are the reductions of the *Abhiplava* sacrifices; on the eighth day is the Vājapeya.

In that regard, one should perform whatever ritual actions pertaining to the Vājapeya are encompassed by the Soma-pressing; furthermore, it is known from scripture that this [Vājapeya] is a *sattra* lasting for a year and is without *chandomas*.
Indeed, its *chandoma* portions are understood to be the twenty-fourth, the forty-fourth, and the forty-eightfold [stomas].

Now, this Atirātra is of two kinds: either an Ahīna or a one-day (Ekāha) sacrifice. However, its form is indeed that of an Ahīna, for it provides twelve Upasad days over many days. Yet, its form is also that of a one-day sacrifice, for he takes the Vasatīvarī waters only once, dedicates the animals only once, and there is only one performance of the ritual act (*kratukaraṇa*). When the sun has reached the midpoint of its setting, he introduces the *ṣoḍaśin* chant with gold; by saying "when half-set," this very point is expressed.

If the sun should set while his [fire] has not yet been properly established, he should offer three spoonfuls of oblations into the *gārhapatya* fire with the words: "Bhūḥ! Bhuvaḥ! Suvaḥ! Now, if [the sacrifice] should be exceeded at the *ukthya*, one should perform an *atirātra*; for indeed, his *dīkṣā* and *upasads* have been passed, the performance of the rite has been passed, and the drawing of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup has been passed.

Therefore, having prepared the *ṣoḍaśin* vessel at that very moment, he should draw [the soma] with three *ṛc*s, and then he should proceed with this before the three rounds (*paryāyas*) of the night.

In that case, the call is as follows: "O Pratiprasthātṛ, guard the third portion of the Āgrayaṇa, the third portions of the rectum, the tails, and the speckled butter; O Āgnīdh, let the two-potsherd cake for the Aśvins be cooked even during the latter part of the night. Now, at what time indeed is the two-potsherd cake for the Aśvins offered?
It is either together with the cakes of the third pressing, or before the final round of the night.

"The Trivṛt is indeed the lowest of the Stomas, and the Trivṛt is the highest"—this is the Brāhmaṇa passage concerning the Atirātra. Now, this Sautrāmaṇī liquor is either "foot-fermented" (*pādakiṇvā*) or "fivefold" (*pañcikā*).

The "shoots" (*śaṣpāṇi*) are of barley, and the "sprouts" (*tokmāṇi*) are of rice; the *māṣa* beans, however, are for the *nagnahu*. Furthermore, this *kārotara* [filter] is made of wood, or of split bamboo, or of clay; it should, however, be covered with a hide, for it is said, "This is the pressed-and-unpressed."
"He has indeed obtained what was to be obtained there, and he will obtain what is to be obtained here; therefore, one should perform the Upāṃśuyāja in this Dākṣāyaṇayajña.

Now, regarding this set of eleven sacrificial posts (*ekādaśinī*), the procedure for the oblation to the post (*yūpāhuti*) is that which is offered in the fire; furthermore, there is the portable [oblation] produced from the cutting-block.

The act of touching [the post] occurs thus: one should strike the first notch toward the fire-side once, the second twice, and the third thrice; in this very same manner for the others, in successive order, for the purpose of marking the cuts. Then, for the measurement of the altar, one should take a twenty-fourth part of ten chariot-axles, eleven steps, and eight finger-breadths;
that shall be the *prakrama*. By means of that, one should measure out the altar. Now, these two side-altars (*upasthāvānau*) should be separated by a distance of exactly four finger-breadths.

Then the others should be at the same distance as the interval between the axle and the rim. Now it is said: "One desirous of the world of the fathers should fix them level with the rim. They are of such a measure as the rim of the post standing nearest the fire. And it is said: "One desirous of power should fix them level with the *caṣāla*. They are of such a measure as the rope of the post standing nearest the fire.
"For one desiring a firm foundation, he makes them all equal"—thus he makes them all equal for one desiring a firm foundation.
"Those three which are in the middle, those he makes equal for one desiring cattle"—thus he makes those equal for one desiring cattle.
"He should interlink the others"—in this very manner, he interlinks the eight sacrificial posts (yūpas), placing the southern one next to the northern one. Now, it is indeed said:

If he should desire of someone, "May he be short-lived," he should erect for him a *gartamit* (pit-measured) altar, with the northernmost post being the tallest and the others progressively shorter. Here, he erects the northernmost post as the tallest and the southernmost as the shortest. Regarding this, the Brāhmaṇa says: "This is indeed a *gartamit*; for one who erects it in this manner, he quickly perishes. For one who desires heaven, he should erect the southernmost post as the tallest and the others progressively shorter.

One should erect each subsequent sacrificial post (yūpa) so that it is shorter than the preceding one by the measure of a thumb-joint; or rather, one may dig the sacrificial post-pits to this same measure. How indeed should the movement proceed for one who is tracing around the post-pits, erecting the posts, and dedicating the animals? Having passed between the post standing nearest the fire (agniṣṭha) and the post standing near the altar (upasthāvāna), and having walked around the rear of the high altar (uttaravedi), he should again pass between the agniṣṭha and the upasthāvāna, [and perform] for each one individually.

One should trace around, raise, or prepare [the sacrificial posts] one by one; whichever one he traces around, raises, or prepares, he should not pass between it and the next—keeping the southern post to the south and the northern post to the north.
Alternatively, having gone around all the posts from the front, he may trace around, raise, or prepare each one individually.
By this method, they become interconnected; thus, for these animals so interconnected, they should station the five animals on the southern side after first approaching them.

They should first carry forward the *vāruṇa* [animal], and then the others in due order. Having gone out toward the north between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, they should either strike down the *prastha* [stones] or, having made them circular, they should extract and carry away their omenta in such a way that they do not separate the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) from themselves by means of the omenta. Now, this *pātnīvata* [animal] should be smaller than the northern part of the sacrificial post by the measure of a thumb-joint; or rather, it should be as prescribed in the Brāhmaṇa: its height should be below the navel, without a *caṣāla* [top-ring], and without a base-covering.
Now, this *ayanam* of the Serpents is modified in terms of its *stomas*; but how might this *ayanam* of the Viśvasṛjs apply to people of the present day?
There are a hundred *dīkṣās*, a hundred *upasads*, and a thousand *prasutas*.
Now, regarding this *ayanam* of the Kuṇḍapāyins, some say it is preceded by the *Agnihotra*, while others enter upon it preceded by the *Soma* sacrifice.

Having concluded that day either with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings or with the heart-spit (*hṛdayaśūla*), and having bound the King Soma, he takes the *vasatīvarī* waters at the proper time; having ensured the continuity of the sacrifice (*ahīnasaṃtati*), he washes the pressing stones and the *vāyavya* cup, places the fringe of the *daśāpavitra* filter into the *droṇakalaśa*, and runs to the *āgnīdhra*.
The fuel-bearers go forth, and having brought back the fuel-sticks, they place them near the *āhavanīya* fire.

When the *vasatīvarī* waters have been carried around, the *subrahmaṇyā* litany has been invoked, and the *saṃveśanīyā* fuel-sticks have been placed on the fire, he binds together the sacrificial grass (*idhma*) and the *barhis*, and having set aside the milk for the *payasyā*, they fast. Then, on the following day, he sacrifices with the *āmāvāsya* oblation;
in that rite, he does not perform the *stambayajus* formula.
In this very manner, carrying the *vasatīvarī* waters around from day to day, they sacrifice with the *āmāvāsya* oblation for twenty-eight days.
They do not offer the Agnihotra oblations, nor do they perform the Full Moon sacrifice.
When he distributes the Dhiṣṇiya hearths at the third pressing, he makes the Mārjālīya hearth perpetual.
When the sacrificial offerings have been set down, having carried fire around the bowls of groats over the Gārhapatya fire, he proceeds with them at the Mārjālīya.

Having cooked the Piṇḍapitṛyajña offering on the Gārhapatya fire itself, he proceeds with it on the Mārjālīya fire. He chooses the ancestral lineages for them one by one; there are three balls of rice for each of them, which makes fifteen in total.

In the Mahāpitṛyajña, sacrificial grass is strewn; one does not mark out the altar, does not carry away the *stambayajus*, and does not take portions of clarified butter. When he distributes the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths at the third pressing, he makes the *mārjālīya* hearth perpetual. When the oblations have been placed near, having cooked the Mahāpitṛyajña oblations on the *gārhapatya* fire, he should proceed with them on the *mārjālīya*; he should proceed with the offering to the Maruts on the *āhavanīya*. The purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) should go to the very end. The altar is one-third [the size]; indeed, it is said that the ninth part of the earth becomes the third part of the steps.

Now, having performed the sacrifice of five oblations, one should perform the sacrifice again day by day with each single oblation. If only one or two oblations were to remain when the year is completed, what should one do in that case?
One should postpone the sacrifice of five oblations belonging to this [lunar] fortnight and perform it; then on the final day of the year, there shall be the sacrifice of five oblations.
Thus, one should pile the fire-altar during the first twelve-day period.

One who is building the fire-altar during the first twelve-day period should proceed for four days with the first *upasad* rite, for four days with the middle one, and for eight days with the last; then, for the remaining four-day periods throughout the year, he should resume each set of four months with one [additional] four-day period.

One should proceed for four days with the first *upasad*, for four days with the middle one, and for four days with the last; or alternatively, one should proceed for exactly four months with each individual *upasad*. Thus, on the final twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), one should pile the fire-altar (*agni*). While piling the fire-altar on the final twelve-day rite, one should proceed for a year minus eight days with the first *upasad*, for four days with the middle one, and for four days with the last; then, one should resume the remaining months minus four days each, taking up four months minus four days at a time.

One should proceed for four days with the first *upasat*, four days with the middle one, and four days with the last one; or alternatively, one should proceed for exactly four months with each individual *upasat*. Then, laying down the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks, one completes the month.

Having proceeded for a month while laying down the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks, on the thirtieth day one should cover the entire covering. Or else, having left space for the thirtieth [brick], one proceeds for the month while laying down the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks.

How should one proceed for this month? First, an *iṣṭi*; then, in the forenoon, the *pravargya* and *upasad*; then the bricks; then, in the afternoon, the *pravargya* and *upasad*. "For a month they proceed with the *vasordhārā* and the *purīṣa*"—how should one proceed for this month? First, an *iṣṭi*; then, in the forenoon, the *pravargya* and *upasad*; then the *purīṣa*; then, in the afternoon, the *pravargya* and *upasad*.
"He passes four months with the *upasad* rites":
what he performs there in one month, he performs here in ten nights;
"he presses [the Soma] for four months."
"What indeed are these months? [He replied:

"The first and last months of the Gavāmayana, and those two which are on both sides of the Viṣuvat, together with the month of the Viṣuvat itself; for one should place a lump of clay into the Vasatīvarī waters."
"For what purpose indeed does this lump of clay exist?
"It exists for the purpose of continuity.
When one jar is broken, he should place that same lump of clay inside another jar and bring water.

Having performed that day’s ritual either ending with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings or ending with the heart-spit (hṛdayaśūla), having bound the King Soma, having taken up the Vasatīvarī waters at the proper time, and having ensured the continuity of the Ahīna sacrifice, they wash the pressing-stones and the Vāyavya cup, place the fringe-filter (daśāpavitra) into the Droṇakalaśa, run to the Āgnīdhra fire-shed, and the fuel-bearers go forth; having brought back the fuel-sticks, they set them down near the Āhavanīya fire.

When the *vasatīvarī* waters have been carried around, the *subrahmaṇyā* has been invoked, and the *saṃveśanīyā* fuel-sticks have been added, they bind together the sacrificial grass (*idhma*) and the *barhis*, and having set aside the milk, they fast. Then, on the following day, they perform the *savana-iṣṭi*.
Therein, they do not perform the *stambayajus* rite.
In this very manner, carrying the *vasatīvarī* waters around day after day, they perform the *savana-iṣṭi* for a year.

They do not offer the Agnihotra oblations, nor do they sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices. Then, when the year has elapsed, when the Vasatīvarī waters have been carried around, and when the Subrahmaṇyā litany has been invoked, they should daily place the kindling-sticks used for retiring upon the fire, bind together the fuel and sacrificial grass, set aside the milks, and observe the fast. Then, on the following day, having performed the Abhijit sacrifice, they rise from the session. Now, it is indeed said: "One desiring cattle should pile the Chandaściti. He should perform the ritual formulas beginning with the taking up of the spades up until the Vāyavya cup.

He should sacrifice with a victim for Vāyu directly; he should perform the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering directly and accomplish the mantras beginning with the heating of the fire-pan (*ukhā*) up to the *vātsapra* and *viṣṇukrama* steps directly.
Having stepped with the *vātsapra* and *viṣṇukrama* steps directly, he should recite the other mantras in their proper order.
He should show the forms of Agni and go to a barren spot (*irīṇa*), where he should recite the mantras dedicated to Nirṛti.
He should worship the Gārhapatya fire directly, directly with the Prāyaṇīyā offering,
and directly with the Ātithyā offering.

One should accomplish the mantras beginning with the *kārṣṇājinī* through plowing and sowing; one should recite the first layer together with its soil-covering while performing the plowing and sowing directly.

In the same way for the second, and in the same way for the third. One should recite every layer together with its soil-covering, and every layer together with its clods and its soil-covering. Whatever *ahāntaḥśālīkā* oblations there may be, one should offer them; and whatever mantras belong to the high altar (*uttaravedi*), one should simply recite them.

"The Agnihotra is indeed the source (nidāna) of the Daśahotṛ; the New and Full Moon sacrifices are the source of the Caturhotṛ"—thus some declare this sequence. Now they also cite: "The establishment of the sacred fires (āgnyādheya) occurs in the first [season]; there is the eleven-prayāja [offering] produced from all together; 'the seasons' is the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ.

This is said to be the six-monthly animal sacrifice (paśubandha). Furthermore, they cite: "Every six months, one who has established the fires must sacrifice with an animal; he should sacrifice at both solstices (kāṣṭhe)."
When the sun moves northward with the *dhaniṣṭhā* stars in the month of Māgha, and returns southward with the *ārdrā* stars in the month of Śrāvaṇa, these two constitute the solstices (*kāṣṭhe*).
At the end of that [period], the year should not pass for one who has not sacrificed.

Then, in the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices and the *Soma* sacrifices, the Pañcahotṛ [formula] returns to the place of the Saptahotṛ. And that fire-drill (*nirmanthya*) which is used for the *Cāturmāsya* conjunctions, when it is extinguished, serves as the fire-drill for the animal sacrifices.

"One should bind the animals to the enclosing-sticks"—this is the Brāhmaṇa passage; thus they become our sacrificial posts (*yūpa*). Now, at the Mahāpitṛyajña, the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is already spread; he does not trace out the altar, he does not carry away the *stambayajus*, and he does not take portions of clarified butter (*ājya*). When he distributes the hearths (*dhiṣṇiya*) at the third pressing, he makes the *mārjālīya* hearth perpetual. Having performed the Mahāhavis offerings and when the oblations have been set down, having cooked the Mahāpitṛyajña oblations on the *gārhapatya* fire, he should proceed with them on the *mārjālīya*. He should proceed with the offering to the Maruts on the *āhavanīya*; the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) should go around the very end.
"His first layer is provided with loose soil and accompanied by mantras," it is said;

thus his very first layer becomes provided with loose soil and accompanied by mantras, while the others are silent. Whichever layer they declare to be provided with loose soil, that alone becomes his layer provided with loose soil and accompanied by mantras, while the others remain silent.
Now, these are the one-day sacrifices (*ekāhas*).

One should know that those days among them which are not specifically designated are *agniṣṭomas*. Furthermore, one should know that those days among the *ahīnas*, *rātris*, and *sattras* which are not specifically designated are *ukthyas*. "The cups of the midday pressing go toward him while wiping [the vessels]"—they go toward him as he sits in the *sadas*, the cups of the midday pressing going toward him while wiping [the vessels] for the purpose of consumption. This [stoma] is the twenty-fourfold;
"he sprinkles [him] with the residue of the *śukra* and *manthin* cups."
Having brought together the combined residue of the *śukra* and *manthin* cups, he sprinkles [the sacrificer] who is seated on the sacrificer’s seat;
this [rite] consists of the *catuṣṭoma*.

Seven oblations follow the morning-pressing: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Pūṣan, a cake on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ, a cake on eight potsherds for Tvaṣṭṛ, a cake on ten potsherds for Varuṇa, a pap for the Viśve Devas, and a cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts—these eight oblations follow the morning-pressing. [Furthermore: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, a cake on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ, a pap for Bṛhaspati, a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Soma, a pap for Sarasvatī, a cake on ten potsherds for Varuṇa, and a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth.

"Whatever belongs to the Rājasūya, with the exception of the Soma sacrifice, all that takes place here"— thus he prohibits the Maruta offering on twenty-one potsherds, as well as the rites of the Upasads; and by means of these thirteen and a half months,
it is completed— "whatever belongs to the Rājasūya, with the exception of the Uttaravedi, all that takes place here."

And here, with regard to the animal sacrifice, he prohibits the offering of two animals; and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices are completed within one and a half months. [Regarding the verse] "The tiger and also the viper..."—of which deity, indeed, is this oblation?
One should say, "Indra is the deity.

Having performed the animal sacrifice with seventeen animals and having collected the fire-pans (*ukhās*) and the heads of the sacrificial animals, he should sacrifice with an animal dedicated to Vāyu; or alternatively, having previously collected them silently, and having collected the clay for the mantra-rite, he coats [the pans] with that and binds [the head] with the formula: "Thou art taken with a base; for Agni, the possessor of the *bṛhat* [sāman], the possessor of vigor, the seeker of the *ukthya*, I take thee who art dear to Viṣṇu—[that which is] thy *bṛhat* vigor, O Agni, for that I take thee."
Having wiped it, he sets it down; he joins it with the formula: "This is thy womb; for Agni, thee, desiring the hymn.

He binds the head of the firm one, the messenger of heaven and earth, the bounteous one born for the sake of Truth—Agni, the sage, the sovereign, the guest of men—the gods generated as a vessel for their mouths.
"Thou art taken with a support; O Indra, I take thee, who art dear to Maghavan"—having wiped it thus, he sets it down. "This is thy womb; O Indra, [I set thee] who art dear to Maghavan.

He joins [the cup] with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; of thee, pressed by Bṛhaspati, Indra takes the draught of the Pātnīvata, as much as belongs to Indra, for Indra accompanied by the wives."

He joins [the cup]: "Thou art taken with a support for the Hāriyojana; thou art Rohit, whose yoke-horses are Rohit, whose charioteer is Rohit, the bearer of the thunderbolt, the lover of Pṛśni. For thee, O divine Soma, who hast the *iṣṭayajus*, whose *stoma* has been praised, and whose *uktha* has been recited, I take this cup accompanied by Rohit. Ye are Rohit; ye are the grains of Rohit together with Soma. To Agni, Svāhā!"

If there is contact with Indra in the Agniṣṭut, one should remove it; if there is contact with Agni in the Indra-stuti, one should remove it. The other deities are constant. "To which deity, then, do the additional stotras belong? One should say, "They belong to the Aśvins. Whatever exceeds the night, all that belongs to the Aśvins—this is one view.
Now, another.

The first [offering] is for Agni, the second for Indra, the third for the Viśvedevas, and the fourth for Viṣṇu. This takes place during the final days of summer when the barley has been harvested; by the term "harvested," it is meant that they have been trampled, as indicated by the context. It is said, "He causes the officiating priests (ṛtvij) to call out by means of their footstep"; this occurs either previously or subsequently. Then, having anointed him and purified him, he leads him away.

One should know that the ritual pertaining to the Agniṣṭoma is already established here; however, from the subsequent point of potential damage and at this specific time, one should prepare three bundles of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with a *yajus* formula—namely, for the *Dīkṣaṇīyā*, the *Prāyaṇīyā*, and the *Ātithyā*.

Then one should offer the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and the *Prāyaṇīyā*; one should proceed with clarified butter (*ājya*) from the *Ātithyā* until the chariots arrive. One should divide the butter offered together into three vessels: that which remains after the completion of the *Dīkṣaṇīyā*, one should use to complete the *Dīkṣaṇīyā*;
one should commence the *Prāyaṇīyā* with the *praṇītā* waters; and this indeed becomes the commencement of the *Ātithyā*.

"Having purchased the King [Soma] with a three-year-old castrated steer and brought him back, one performs the *Atithya* offering"—by this it is meant "with a three-year-old [heifer]"; how indeed should he adapt its formulas? [The formulas are: "Thou art consciousness (*cit*), thou art mind (*manas*), thou art intellect (*dhī*), thou art the right-hand one (*dakṣiṇa*), thou art worthy of sacrifice (*yajñiya*), thou art the Kṣatriya, thou art Aditi, the double-headed one; mayest thou arise for us well-disposed. The *Upasad* offerings consist of single groups.
These are indeed said to be the morning rites;
they make this very threshing-floor post their sacrificial stake,
and that is the threshing-floor post as the *yūpa*.
For her, the *kaṭa* becomes like a vessel for the *caṣāla*; thus this is what is meant by "it is bent. Then he dedicates these animals: the one for Agni-Soma, the one for Agni, and the *anūbandhya*.
These goats have a common origin;
their ritual procedure has already been explained.

Now, in this *sadyaskrī*, *anukrī*, *parikrī*, and *atikrī* [sacrifices], from the *avabhṛtha* onwards until sunset, the tail of the sacrifice (*yajñapuccha*) is performed. Among these, the first indeed has a single chariot; the first is the one for whom the Soma-purchase cow (*somakrayaṇī*) is present; the first is that for whom the vow consists of the remnants of the *agnihotra*. Now, in this [same set of sacrifices]—the *sadyaskrī*, *anukrī*, *parikrī*, and *atikrī*—they perform the forms of the vows consisting of three teats, two teats, and one teat.
Where, indeed, is the mixing (*saṃnivāpa*) seen in a one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*)?

In the Vrātyastoma, one should say "and for Indra and Agni, and for the Kulāya. Now, in this Vrātyastoma, many are consecrated for the sake of a single person; they cause them to sacrifice while they themselves remain unconsecrated.
[The equipment consists of] a staff, sandals, and a *śāmūla* skin; for the *śāmūlaka*s, there are blankets mixed with *dabhra* wool, and that skin is white, from a young goat.

This very sacrifice is the Agniṣṭoma for those who are senior; it is the Ukthya for those who are junior. The first day consists of the fourfold Stoma, and the latter day consists of the fivefold Stoma. One should make the Havirdhāna cart in the form of a couch; the northern Havirdhāna [should be so made], otherwise they would sink. There are two carts with the mantras of three and thirty [verses] respectively; these two middle Stomas exist. These two are the Pṛṣṭhya Stomas, proceeding in reverse order from here and from there. Then, on the new moon day, having combined them, one should offer the Piṇḍapitṛyajña according to the lunar month.

Sitting around him as he becomes the Brahman, they consume it; they consider that to be the Truth (*ṛta*). By this [truth], one should consume it from the Brāhmaṇa, for the Brāhmaṇa is the best of the social classes (*varṇa*) and Agni is the best of the gods. Or alternatively, one may consume it with the *vyāhṛtis*. This becomes the *Catuṣṭoma*; this is the fourfold increase (*caturuttarīya*), the *Catuṣṭoma* of the quarters.

Now, in this *kānāndha* sacrifice, from the *avabhṛtha* bath onwards at sunset, one performs the tail of the sacrifice; for that, having spoken of the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant ten times, a hundred times, a thousand times, ten thousand times, a hundred thousand times, a million times, ten million times, a hundred million times, a billion times, ten billion times, a hundred billion times, a trillion times, and so on—up to the middle, the end, the *parārdha*, the *padva*, and the *palva*—one considers oneself as having praised with the mind alone, thinking, "I have praised this much. Then, there is a single *pravargya* rite and a single *agnihotra*.
Now, in this *śunaskarṇa* sacrifice, having eaten food mixed with sesame and having consumed fish, one should drink only salt water and then lie down upon the path of the *sāman*.
Just as in a dream one goes from dream to dream,
so too it is said that he gives grain made into a heap, he gives grain made into a measure, and he gives grain made into a sack; this is what is meant by "made into a sack."

"They move forward and they move backward"—this means that the movement toward the west is performed from the south; by this very [principle], the fire-altar facing all directions is also explained, as is the thousand-halled altar. Now, regarding the statement "having purified him here, they purify him there," one should understand that the ritual procedure for the Agniṣṭoma is established here [as the model] for the northern hall alone.

He performs two three-night rites and one two-night rite; thus, by means of the consecrations (dīkṣā) and the Upasad days, he extends these days for him. One should not offer a sacrifice that is deficient in its arrangement; this is what has been declared regarding that which is not properly arranged according to the Sūtra.

Regarding the ritual application (*kratuyoga*), Baudhāyana says that one should observe each sacrifice within the sacrifice itself as a conventional rule (*sāmayika*). Thus, Baudhāyana says: "One should observe each sacrifice within the sacrifice.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the expiations (*prāyaścitta*) prescribed in the collections of mantras.

In all cases, if what has been performed with a mantra above should fall below, one should establish it with the mantra, "Brahman is the foundation of the mind," and then offer a spoonful (*sruvāhuti*) with that same mantra; or, having offered it, one should establish it. Having offered it, one should perform the subsequent rite. In this same way, one should not heed other rites that have been bypassed, provided they are no longer required by the purpose (*arthalupta*).

In all cases where the *āśrāvaṇa*, *pratyāśrāvaṇa*, or *vaṣaṭkāra* have been uttered too loudly, too softly, or omitted, one should offer a *sruva*-oblation with the verse: "The *āśrāvaṇa* has been [uttered] excessively.

In all instances of invoking the gods, if one fails to invoke the deity who is entitled to the portion and instead invokes another, one should offer a *sruva*-oblation with the verse: "Whatever, O gods, I may have overstepped. In all instances of the invocation of deities, if one fails to invoke the deity who is entitled to the portion and instead invokes another, one should offer a *sruva*-oblation with that same verse. Whenever one remembers this, one should rise up and invoke that deity mentally; then, one should sacrifice the surplus with clarified butter according to the order in which they were invoked.

If, at any point, drops should fall from things that have been refined, are being refined, or are refined, or if the cup should leak, one should fill it with water while reciting the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*, and then offer a spoonful oblation with the verse *tataṃ ma āpastadu tāyate punaḥ*.

If the sun does not appear during the performance of a sacrifice that has been spread everywhere—except in the case of a specific instruction—one should offer oblations with the *sruva* ladle while reciting these [verses]: "We have risen above the darkness," "Upward that [sun]," and "The bright one. If an eclipse of the sun or moon occurs, one should likewise do this. Furthermore, if there should be an emission of semen in a dream for the sacrificer or the officiating priests, one should offer two oblations with the *sruva* ladle while reciting these [two verses]: "Hear this my call, O Varuṇa" and "I go unto thee."

In all cases, when there is a failure or omission regarding the oblation, the deity, the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses, or the offerings—whether the offering has been made or not, or when there is an interruption or a transposition—one should offer two spoonfuls (*sruvāhuti*) with these two verses: "Thou, O Agni, art ours" (*tvaṃ no agne*) and "So thou, O Agni, art ours" (*sa tvaṃ no agne*).

In all cases, when there is cutting, burning, damage, loss, or destruction of the ladle, the *kūrca* grass-bundle, the *prastara*, the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the separating blades (*vidhṛti*), the strainers (*pavitra*), the *vedī* altar-mat, the fire-stirring stick (*upaveṣa*), the fuel-wood (*idhma*), or the ritual materials and collections, one should prepare another [item] according to its characteristic mark, set it down according to its characteristic mark, and offer two spoonfuls with these two verses: "Thou, O Agni, art the unerring" (*tvam agne ayāsi*) and "O Prajāpati" (*prajāpate*).
This applies everywhere in the course of the performed sacrifice.

If, prior to the offerings, the embers should roll back outside the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), one should perform the expiation prescribed by the Brāhmaṇa and offer a spoonful (*sruva-āhuti*) with the verse: "I set up this enclosure for the living.

In every case, if a failure in the sacrificial rite should occur while the sacrifice is being performed, one should offer eight spoonfuls with these [formulas]: "To those sacrificed for, svāhā! Vaṣaṭ to those not sacrificed for, svāhā! and so on.

If, during a sacrificial rite performed everywhere, a danger from enemies should arise, one should offer two spoonfuls with the two verses, "From which we fear, O Indra... and "The giver of well-being, the lord of the people..."; or, once the danger has passed, one should perform the sacrifice again.

In all cases, regarding the *upāṃśu* and subsequent stages up to the suspension of speech (*vācasthāna*), in the event of errors in accent, syllable, word, or meter, one should offer a spoonful with the verse, "By these songs, whatever of ours here is deficient...".
In all cases where no specific expiation is known, one should offer two spoonfuls with the two verses, "The unknown [expiation]... and "Equal to a man...".

In all cases where the *idhma* and *barhis* are used for the *prayāja* and *anūyāja* offerings during rites performed with cooked food (*pākayajña*), one should offer a spoonful (*sruva-āhuti*) with the verse: "O mind, that which is in the cooked food... (*yat pākatrā manasā*).

In all cases where [the fire] has been spilled, split, cut, broken, lost, diminished, or in the event of a reversal, a burning, or an excess or deficiency—whatever defilement of the self (*ātman*) has occurred—one should offer two spoonfuls (*sruva-āhuti*) with these two verses: "Punaragniś cakṣur adāt" and "Iti. In all instances of injury to the fires, one should place a fuel-stick (*samidh*) with the verse "Punaḥ tvā ādityā rudrā vasavaḥ samindhatām," and with that same verse one should offer a spoonful. In all sacrificial rites (*yajña-kratu*), having performed the *patnī-saṃyāja* offerings, having gone eastward, and having replenished the *dhruvā* ladle, [one proceeds] from the *dhruvā*.

He offers all the expiations with this Anuvāka, "Brahman is the foundation of the mind," verse by verse. Now, indeed, it is said: he offers the Samiṣṭayajus oblations for the completion of the sacrifice.

"Whatever in the sacrifice is cruel, whatever is disjointed, what it oversteps, what it does not overstep, what it does in excess, and what it omits—that very thing it propitiates through these," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

"These very [rites] are the restorations prescribed by the rule of the Brāhmaṇa, and they are accompanied by mantras," says Baudhāyana; "they are recited from the collection of mantras as occasional rites (*naimittika*)," says Śālīki.
Now, regarding the making of the potsherds, a space the size of a horse's hoof is prepared in the shape of a chariot wheel and a *citi*.

The resolve constitutes the qualification. Whether there be an increase or a decrease in the number of potsherds, if they do not spread out properly, one should offer oblations with a wooden spoon (sruva) into the Āhavanīya fire with the *vyāhṛtis*: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ. This applies equally to both insufficient spreading and excessive spreading. Now, regarding the sacrificial offerings: if it is undercooked, if it burns, if it overflows, or if it leaks, the expiation is as follows: for what is undercooked, one should offer a spoonful into the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra, "To Rudra, svāhā! For what is liquid, [one offers] to Vāyu; for what is burnt, to Nirṛti.

If that which was cooked therein should be burnt, he should proceed with what remains; but if everything should be burnt, he should drink water and offer two *mindā* oblations, then prepare another [offering], or he may proceed with clarified butter (*ājya*)—that indeed is the expiation (*prāyaścitti*) for that. To whichever direction it should spill, he should offer a spoonful (*sruvāhuti*) to that respective deity: if to the east, to Agni; if to the south, to Yama; if to the west, to Varuṇa; if to the north, to Soma; and if it should spill in all directions, he should offer spoonfuls to all these deities.

He causes it to swell with clarified butter using the two swelling verses, "Swell up" (*āpyāyasva*) and "Be united" (*saṃ te*). Then, at the time of taking out the sacrificial oblations, in the event of falling, splitting, breaking, overturning, spilling, or performing a reversal or improper union, he should offer oblations with the *sruva* ladle into the Āhavanīya fire with the *vyāhṛtis*: "Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Suvaḥ. Then, having gone out northward between the altar and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), and having stepped out further north until his shadow reaches the limit, he recites the *vyāhṛtis* and returns by means of the *vyāhṛtis* alone.
The *vyāhṛtis*, moreover, consist of four feet, nine syllables, and six letters;
they constitute the beginning, middle, and end of all four Vedas.
"Whatever may be deficient, excessive, or even improperly performed in a mantra, they dispel that evil; therefore, they are known as the Vyāhṛtis."
If a failure in the sacrifice should occur through the Ṛgveda, one should offer an oblation in the Gārhapatya fire with "Bhūḥ"; if through the Yajurveda, with "Bhuvaḥ" in the Anvāhāryapacana;
if through the Sāmaveda, with "Suvaḥ" in the Āhavanīya; and if it occurs through all three, one should offer in all of them.
But when the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) has been lifted up, or if it trembles, or likewise flows away, or if it is broken, or even if it slides together— what should be the expiation (prāyaścitta)?
It is known:
"If it is pulled out, he destroys his lineage; if it quivers, his offspring perish;
and if it breaks or even slips away, the sacrificer dies."

Then, having removed [the cake] that has become cracked, split, broken, or fallen out during the process of falling, splitting, breaking, being turned over, or shifting, and having placed it upon the sacrificial grass (barhis), he sprinkles it with abundant clarified butter and consecrates it with the mantra: "Why do you fly up? Why have you flown away? Being peaceful, come here for the sake of peace.
Becoming non-terrible and worthy of sacrifice, sit in your own place; sit in your own place. Having given a boon to the Brahman priest, he should place it within the altar (antarvedi).

When that [oblation] has been completed, one should offer the *surabhimatī*; when that has been completed, one should offer the *tantumatī*. The subsequent ritual acts belonging to the Vedic meters should be performed with the intent for long life.
This is the rule for the mishandling of the sacrificial oblation as ordained by those who perceive the truth.
In the event of a spillage during the taking up or the pouring out [of the oblation], or during the consecration of the substances—
at whatever time one becomes aware of it, one should perform that rite within the course of the ritual procedure.
The Praṇava and the Vyāhṛtis constitute this supreme and inferior sacrifice.
Therefore, whatever in the sacrifice may be spilled or performed erroneously,
