one should rectify all that with the Vyāhṛtis, except for that which has been consecrated by the Vaṣaṭ-call.
"What has been done by those who were ignorant, and what has been done by those who were in haste—
that which was done becomes truly accomplished through the employment of the Vyāhṛtis. One should state the measurements of the potsherds according to the ritual rules of the Adhvaryu.
They are equal and square, measuring two finger-breadths on all sides.
Baudhāyana says that one should increase the uneven portions according to the measure of the modifications of the oblation (*havirvikāra*).

Now, regarding the expiation for fires that have gone out—whether they reside in the two kindling woods (*araṇi*), within oneself, are perpetual (*ajasra*), have been rekindled (*anvāhita*), are situated at the Soma-pressing (*savana*), or have otherwise ceased—one should churn the fire from the kindling woods, arrange the sacrificial fires (*vihāra*), melt clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire, purify it, take four ladlings (*caturgṛhīta*) into the offering-spoon (*sruc*), and offer the *saṃtanī* oblation in the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra: "May the mind, as light, enjoy the clarified butter; may it join together this interrupted sacrifice."

"Those dawns and sunsets that have passed—I join them together with oblation and clarified butter, Svāhā! This is the expiation for [the fire] that has gone out, for that which was not offered, for that which has risen after [the sun], and for that which has set after [the sun]. This is for the one who has superseded his elder brother, for the one who has been superseded, for the one who is in the process of superseding; this is for the one who has vomited Soma, for the one whose Soma has flowed excessively, for the one whose consumption of Soma has been interrupted, for the one whose consumption of Soma has been omitted; this is for the one who has performed the *pari-iṣṭi* sacrifice, for the one who has caused the *pari-iṣṭi* sacrifice to be performed; and this very same [expiation] applies to him from whom a man, a chariot, a horse, a cow, a buffalo, a boar, a snake, a wild animal, a dog, or anything else [is lost].

If one should pass between a wild beast and the fires, or if someone should carry away even a portion of any fire, in all such misfortunes regarding the *agnihotra*, an expiation is performed with the *manasvatī* verse; having sacrificed thus, one becomes more prosperous—so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Now, regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices, there are four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); if one of them is absent, the other three should perform the rites, or even two. Furthermore, if there should be only one priest remaining, before the *prayāja* offerings, he offers the various *adhvaryava-prāyaścitta* oblations by dipping with the *sruva* ladle from the *ājyasthālī* vessel, [reciting]: "May I be pleasing to Speech; may I be pleasing to Vācaspati, O Goddess Speech!"
Or rather, place me in that which is the sweetest of speech; Svāhā to Sarasvatī!
Whatever in this sacrifice is deficient in speech or whatever is ill-performed, may the Aśvins mend that with their healing medicine; svāhā!

Indra the protector, Indra the savior, Indra who is easily invoked at every call, the hero—I now invoke Śakra, Indra who is invoked by many. May the bounteous Indra bestow well-being upon us; Svāhā! Whatever flaw there is in my mind, whatever in my speech, and whatever in my heart—
May the gods, Soma, and Bṛhaspati pacify that; svāhā!
Whatever the officiating priests do, whether knowing or unknowing, being deluded—may Agni and the goddess Śraddhā release me from that sin; svāhā!

Whatever offense we have committed against the atmosphere, the earth, or the sky, or against our mother or our father—may Agni Gārhapatya release me from that sin; may he free me from whatever misdeeds we have done, and make me free from blemish. Svāhā!

In the office of the Brahman, the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, the Āgnīdhra, and the Yajamāna—whatever in this single sacrifice is to be completed, may the gods protect that for me; may they not harm my vital breaths. Svāhā!

"I am Brahmā, I am the Hotṛ, I am the Adhvaryu, I am the Agnīdhra, I am the Sacrificer; I alone pervade the sacrifice. May the gods protect me; may they not harm my vital breaths. Svāhā! Having offered these single expiations for the Adhvaryu's errors, it is known that while seated within the sacrificial altar (antarvedi), he worships all the deities—this applies when the oblations have been omitted during the Parvan and Āgrayaṇa sacrifices. When the two kindling woods (araṇis) are being carried away, how is it that the ritual framework (tantra) is not lost?
The Śuci, the Pāvamānī, the Tantumatī, and the Pāthikṛt—these sacrifices should be performed; then the ritual procedure (tantra) is not lost.

"The pure one purifies evil; one should not let the thread drop from the thread. One should ascend the path with the *pathikṛt* [offering], and the *pāvamānī* verses shall purify. Such is the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) of Baudhāyana. When the new moon sacrifice (*darśa*) has been omitted, the *pāthikṛtī* [offering] must be performed; when the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsa*) has been omitted, the *vaiśvānarī* [offering] must be performed; when both have been omitted, both must be performed; and when many have been omitted, there should be an *anvārambhaṇīyā* [introductory offering], so says Śālīki.

Now, if the two fire-drills (*araṇī*) should become worn out—either by insects or by friction—one should procure two other new fire-drills. Having fasted on the new-moon day and performed the New-moon sacrifice on the following day, one should break the old drill into pieces, cast them into the *gārhapatya* fire, and kindle it. Then, taking the upper drill with the right hand and holding the lower drill over the fire with the left hand, he recites: "Awake, O Agni! Enter another womb, O Jātavedas, in order to carry out the sacrifice to the gods."

"O Forest-tree, enter into the fire-drill; drive away the worn-out body with the unworn. 'This is your seasonal womb,' [saying this] he consigns the fires into the two fire-drills. Having churned out the Gārhapatya fire according to the procedure for churning, and having arranged the sacrificial fires, he melts clarified butter over the Gārhapatya, purifies it, takes four ladlings into the offering-spoon, and offers the *saṃtanī* oblation in the Āhavanīya fire with the verse: 'May the mind, as light, enjoy the clarified butter; may it join together this interrupted sacrifice.'"

"Those dawns and those sunsets which have been desired, I unite them with the oblation of clarified butter, Svāhā! Then he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tantumant; he gives a shallow bowl as the sacrificial fee; that well-known sacrifice is thus completed.

Now we shall explain the destruction of the two fire-drills (*araṇī*). They perish due to eight causes: upon contact with impure matter, a dog, a *caṇḍāla*, a *śūdra*, a crow, a fallen person, a donkey, or a woman in her menses, the two fire-drills are destroyed.

Having discarded those two [fire-drills], he should fetch two other new ones that are equal [in quality] and bring back the fire-resident fire for the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punarādheya*). If the fire-drills are lost, he immerses them in water while reciting, "May you two be of one mind toward us. Then, having cut the upper [drill] into pieces, split it, and reduced it to splinters, he should perform the churning, the capacity for the ritual depositing (*āropaṇa*), the remainder of the churning, or the act of churning itself; thus the mishap regarding the fire-drills is concluded, provided all the fragments have been removed.

Now we shall explain the defects of sacrificial offerings (*havir-doṣa*). For instance, if it is contaminated by a blue fly, a *śātikā* insect, a bedbug, a louse on a garment or the head, a worm, or a small insect that forms a ball; or if it is defiled by excrement, urine, cats, mongooses, cocks, monkeys, crows, mice, or the dung of these; or by sweat, hair, dead nails, deformed nails, putrid matter, tears, blood, oil, tears from coughing, or mucus from sneezing; or if it is touched by any other such thing, or by a woman in her courses; or if it has been looked upon by one who is impure or by a killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahan*); or if it is placed in an unworthy vessel or in an impure place.
If the sacrificial oblation (havis) has spilled or become spoiled, they pour it into water or cause it to be placed in cold ashes.

Having offered two Mindā oblations, one should then prepare another [oblation] or proceed with clarified butter (ājya); indeed, they say that clarified butter is for the purpose of a swift restoration.
Having offered the two oblations of reproach (*mindāhuti*), he offers the *manasvatī* oblation;
that itself is the expiation for that.
Now, therefore, follow the expiations for fires that have gone out; oblations are seen as the means for their restoration.
Some say they are the Caturhotṛ formulas;
some say they are the Vyāhṛtis;
some say they are the Mindā oblations.
Some say [the verse] is *manasvatī*;

some say they are the *mahāvyāhṛtis*. Now, if all the fires should go out, one should consign the fires from their hearths into the two kindling woods (*araṇis*) and churn the *gārhapatya* fire according to the procedure for churning, with the mantra: "From here Agni was first born, Jātavedas, from his own womb;
may he, knowing, carry the oblation to the gods by means of the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, and the Jagatī."
"By means of the churning-sticks, he procreates him from his own womb," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Now, if [the fire] is not produced while being churned, one should fetch another wherever it is seen and offer with that; then, without hurrying, one should churn again. And if, once produced, it should go out, one should mutter the mantra for the re-ascension (*samāropaṇa*) and churn again. Then one worships it with: "Rejoice for the sake of food, for wealth, for power, for splendor, for vigor, and for offspring."

Then he kindles it with the formula: "May the two Sarasvatī springs kindle thee; thou art the sovereign (samrāj), thou art the radiant one (virāj). Then, having added fuel to it and having brought the Anvāhāryapacana fire, he takes out the blazing Āhavanīya fire, deposits it, and adds fuel to it. Having melted clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire and purified it, and having taken four portions into the ladle, he recites the Daśahotṛ formula mentally and offers it into the Āhavanīya while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, saying "Svāhā! Then, having turned to the right and returned toward the west, he offers the tenfold [oblation] into the Gārhapatya.

Regarding the section beginning with "The Brāhmaṇa is the Ekahotṛ," one offers ten spoonfuls (*sruvāhuti*). Now, if the *Anvāhāryapacana* fire should go out, one should take it out from the *Gārhapatya* and offer the Caturhotṛ formula in the *Anvāhāryapacana*, while offering the tenfold formula in the *Gārhapatya*.

If the *Āhavanīya* fire should go out, one should take it out from the *Gārhapatya* and offer the Pañcahotṛ formula in the *Āhavanīya*, while offering the tenfold formula in the *Gārhapatya*. If the *Āgnīdhrīya* among the fires belonging to the Soma-pressing should go out, one should take it out from the *Śālāmukhīya* and offer the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ formula in the *Āgnīdhrīya*, while offering the tenfold formula in the *Śālāmukhīya*.

Now, if the Āhavanīya fire on the high altar (uttaravedi) should go out, one should take it from the Āgnīdhrīya fire and offer the Saptahotṛ formula into that Āhavanīya on the high altar; into the Āgnīdhrīya, one offers the Daśahotṛ formula. By this same procedure, in the event of a single extinction or two, one should offer the Hotṛ formulas after dividing them accordingly. One should also offer the Vyāhṛtis both separately and collectively. Likewise, one should offer the two Mindā oblations. If the Manasvatī oblation is to be offered, one should offer it into the Āhavanīya. This is the expiation for fires that have gone out—whether they are the perpetual (ajasra) fires, those established for a specific rite (anvāhita), or those occurring during the pressings (savana). This very same procedure applies at the time of the oblation, with the exception of the anvādhāna.

Now, if the fire of one whose *agnihotra* has not yet been offered should go out after it has been taken out, he should either act according to the Sūtra, or he should kindle fuel from the *gārhapatya* fire and recite these mantras: "The churning," "the further churning," and "the kindling. Or he may perform the *jyotiṣmatī* sacrifice; or he may offer a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with two *jyotiṣmatī* verses; or he may offer a ladle-oblation (*sruvāhuti*) with a *jyotiṣmatī* verse, saying: "Svāhā to Agni Jyotiṣmat! Among the options of the sacrifice, the full oblation, and the ladle-oblation, the teachers declare that each preceding rule is more authoritative than the following.
Regarding this, they cite an example:
Whatever minor specialties are observed here and there, one should not perform work through attachment to them; that is wealth for times of distress.
One should diligently master the specific details from all the Vedas,
both for the sake of investigating ritual actions and to ensure their completion in times of adversity.

If, as a consequence, an offering has been made in the common fire by the ignorant or by children, or if the fires have been spread out by the wife, one should consign those fires into the two kindling woods, move away, churn out the fires, spread them out, and then perform the *pūrṇāhuti* and the *tantumatī* oblation. Now, if, not as a consequence, an offering has been made in the common fire by the ignorant or by children, or if the fires have been spread out by the wife, one should spread them out with the *vyāhṛtis*, and then perform the *pūrṇāhuti* and the *tantumatī* oblation.
Now, it is indeed said:

Nirṛti seizes the sacrifice of him for whom any oblation is burnt; even if they find the portions, they do not perform an expiation here. For this Adhvaryu burns the portions when he piles them together; he satisfies these very things.
Indeed, he burns them who offers the portions (avadāna) without first offering the clarified butter (ājya), and does not pour clarified butter over them from above;

the gods are not satisfied by those burnt portions, nor is the sacrificer. But he truly satisfies them who, having first offered the clarified butter, then offers the portions, and pours clarified butter over them from above.

When they are satisfied, the gods are satisfied; the sacrificer is satisfied. Now, if one were to sacrifice to Agni-Soma from the cake for Agni, or to Agni from the cake for Agni-Soma, it is said that this is not a true offering. One should therefore offer a spoonful (sruvāhuti) into the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra: "Whatever I may have overstepped, O Gods. The verses for recitation and invitation (yājyā-puro’nuvākyā) dedicated to Agni are a purification for the gods; those dedicated to Indra are a purification for the gods; those dedicated to Prajāpati are a purification for the gods; and the *vyāhṛtis* are a purification for the gods. Furthermore, if the Hotṛ priest should become confused regarding the verses for recitation and invitation, he should perform the sacrifice using all the verses dedicated to Agni.
It is known that "Agni is all the deities"; it is known by means of the verses addressed to Indra that "Indra indeed is all the deities";
it is known by means of the verses addressed to Prajāpati that "Prajāpati is all the deities";

and it is known by means of the *vyāhṛtis* that "all the *ṛc*s, all the *sāmans*, and all the *yajus* formulas are the *vyāhṛtis*. Now, if the sacrificer should become confused regarding the duties of the sacrificer, his entering between the altar and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*) shall be performed with the *vyāhṛtis*, his departing shall be performed with the *vyāhṛtis*, and his consecration shall likewise be performed with the *vyāhṛtis*.

It is known that all *ṛc*s, all *sāmans*, and all *yajus* formulas are indeed the *vyāhṛtis*. Regarding this, the gods are said to contemplate the sacrifice, thinking: "This oblation of ours has been omitted; it has not yet been offered. Some say [the interruption] is until the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; some say until the *iḍā*; some say until the *anuyāja*s; some say until the *śaṃyuvāka*; and some say until the *samiṣṭayajus*. If one should remember [the omission] after the *samiṣṭayajus*, one should conclude this sacrifice and perform another sacrifice that is free from defects. For it is known: "The sacrifice itself is the expiation for the sacrifice."

Now, if the calves should suckle from the cows that yield the *sāṃnāyya* milk, he should sacrifice in the evening with barley-gruel prepared for Vāyu. Even if only one cow has been milked, he should not cause her to be milked again once she has been sucked; he should conclude the rite with the milk already drawn, drive away the calves of the unmilked cows, and sacrifice with the *sāṃnāyya* on the following day. If the evening milking should meet with misfortune, he should pour out rice for Indra and fast. Or else, having divided the morning milking into two parts and having curdled one of them, he should perform it in place of the evening milking, while the other is used in place of the boiled milk (*śṛta*).

If the morning milking should suffer a calamity, one should offer a cake (puroḍāśa) for Indra or Mahendra and proceed with that curd. If both should suffer a calamity, one should offer five-platterfuls of rice for Indra. Having proceeded with the offering to Agni in the established manner, one should then proceed with the offering to Indra. If all the oblations should become spoiled, perish, or be stolen, one should perform this sacrifice after enumerating those deities with clarified butter; having performed this sacrifice, one should then perform another sacrifice that is not defective.

"It is known that sacrifice is indeed the expiation for sacrifice. Now, therefore, we shall explain the consecratory formulas (*anumantraṇa*) for oblations not recorded in the *Chandas* [Vedic meters]. He consecrates the *Vaimṛdha* sacrifice with: "Through the sacrifice to the god Vaimṛdha Indra, may I become free from rivals, heroic, and glorious"—or rather, "May I become free from rivals and heroic. [For the *Pārjanya* sacrifice: "Through the sacrifice to the god Pārjanya, may I become possessed of good pasture. [For the *Saumya* sacrifice: "Through the sacrifice to the god Soma, may I be propagated with offspring and cattle; may I be rich in seed; may I deposit seed. Or [alternatively]: "May I be rich in seed; may I deposit seed."

"Through the sacrifice to the god Savitṛ, may I become possessed of well-being and cattle; through the sacrifice to the goddess Sarasvatī, may I nourish speech and the food of sustenance; through the sacrifice to the god Sarasvant, may I become full of faith; through the sacrifice to the god Pūṣan, may I become possessed of prosperity and cattle; through the sacrifice to the Maruts, may I prosper in my vital breaths; through the sacrifice to the Viśve Devas, may I attain union with their vital breaths; through the sacrifice to Heaven and Earth, may I prosper in both worlds and attain abundance and a firm foundation"—thus [he thinks].

Through the sacrifice to the Vājins, may I become possessed of seed; through the sacrifice to Varuṇa, may I become a partaker of the sacred law (*dharma*); through the sacrifice to Ka, may I become most powerful; through the sacrifice to Viśvakarman, may I accomplish all works; through the sacrifice to the Ādityas, may I be released from laughter; through the sacrifice to Vāyu, may I become a partaker of jewels; through the sacrifice to Sūrya, may I become fair to behold;
through the sacrifice to Agni and Viṣṇu, may I become heroic; through the sacrifice to Viṣṇu, may I become *śipiviṣṭa*.

"By the sacrifice to the god Aryaman, may I go to the heavenly world"—with this, he consecrates the offering according to the deity. In this same manner, they declare that unassigned offerings on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) are modifications of the Agni-offering; those on eleven potsherds are modifications of the Agni-Soma offering; those on twelve potsherds are modifications of the Viśvedeva offering; and the single-potsherd and earth-potsherd offerings are modifications of the Heaven-and-Earth offering. Other than these, the *caru* offerings are modifications of the Agni-offering, and the *saumya* offerings are modifications of the Soma-offering.

Curd, milk, and clotted curd (*āmikṣā*) are modifications of the *sāṃnāyya*; the *vanaspati* offering is a modification of the *sviṣṭakṛt*; and they declare the *upāṃśuyāja* offerings to be modifications of the *upāṃśuyāja*. Now, moreover, they cite: "similarity of oblation, similarity of deity, and similarity of potsherds. When there is similarity of oblation, deity, and potsherds, similarity of oblation is the stronger; or rather, the formula for this sacrifice, "May I reach the conclusion of the *āgura*," is universal. Now, indeed, it so happens.

He who is seized by *pāpayakṣma*, or he who is excluded from the gods, the *ṛṣis*, the ancestors, the cows, or the Brahmins, or one who has been accused or is being accused, should sacrifice with the *rahasyā iṣṭi*. One intending to sacrifice with this *iṣṭi* procures gold. Its *upavasatha* is well known. Then, in the morning, after the *agnihotra* has been offered and before the carrying forward of the waters, having melted the clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire and purified it, and having taken four portions into the ladle, he offers it into the *āhavanīya* while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, [with the verse]:
"By which purifier the gods always purify themselves..."

With that [verse] "May the *pāvamānī* verses purify me in a thousand streams, svāhā!", he takes another four spoonfuls and offers them into the *āhavanīya* fire itself with [the verse]: "The purifier belonging to Prajāpati, consisting of a hundred threads and made of gold—with that we, the knowers of Brahman, purify the purified Brahman, svāhā. Having taken another four spoonfuls, he offers them into the *āhavanīya* fire itself with [the verse]: "May Indra purify me with good guidance, Soma with well-being, and Varuṇa with perfect harmony."

"May King Yama purify me with the *pramṛṇā* verses; may Jātavedas purify me with the *ūrjayantī*; Svāhā! Then, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and led forward the waters, he offers a sacrifice consisting of ten oblations, beginning with "To Agni, the deliverer from distress, [an offering] on eight potsherds. Having cooked them, he sets them down. For this sacrifice, there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.

Between the verse for the kindling fire (*samidhyamāna*) and that for the fully kindled fire (*samiddha*), he inserts two *dhāyyā* verses containing the word "purifier" (*pāvaka*): "This is the gathering-place of the waters," and "Homage to you"—these two.

The two butter-portions (ājyabhāga) contain the word "purifier" (pāvaka); [with the verses] "The immortal one with bright luster drives away the Rakṣases," and "The pure, purifying, worthy of praise," he recites the invitatory verse (puro'nuvākyā). Then, having recited [the offering verse]: "O Agni, that filter of yours which is spread within your flame—by that sacred prayer (brahman), we purify ourselves," he performs the sacrifice.

"Who, being pressed, flows all around with a purifying stream—the Indu, like a horse fit for action"—having recited this *puro'nuvākyā*, [the verse] "He runs toward the jars, is poured upon the filter, and is magnified by hymns at the sacrifices," he performs the *yajati* offering. Then, from this section beginning "I meditate on Agni, the first, the wise," the *yājyā-puro'nuvākyās* for the *saṃyājyās* occur. Then, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers oblations with the *sruva*-ladle using the section beginning "Pavamāna, the one who wins the light," verse by verse. Having performed the established *iḍā* ceremony, and having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives gold as a gift.

The ritual procedure up to the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings is the same; then, prior to the offering for the *gṛhapati*, he offers oblations with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) using this section of the text beginning with "Whatever offense, O gods, against the gods" (*yad devā devaheḍanam*), verse by verse. This sacrifice concludes with the pouring out of the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*) and the *viṣṇukrama* steps; he releases his vow (*vrata*).

One should perform this very sacrifice when there is a transgression of the seasons, a transgression regarding one's wife, or when semen has been discharged in a non-vaginal place; one should perform this very sacrifice when joined by a *pātaka* or *upapātaka*. One joined by a *mahāpātaka* should perform it for twelve days; one desiring merit should perform it for a month, a year, or a season. This very [sacrifice] they call the *Mahāpavitreṣṭi*, or the *Mṛgāreṣṭi*, or the *Rahasyeṣṭi*, according to Baudhāyana.

Regarding this statement, "He travels abroad for an unlimited time," it is actually meant that he does not travel abroad for more than a year. If, however, he should travel abroad for longer, he should perform the Pavitreṣṭi sacrifice. One who intends to perform this sacrifice prepares gold. Its fast-day procedure is well known. Then, in the morning, after the Agnihotra has been offered and before the carrying forward of the waters, he melts clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire, purifies it, takes four portions into the ladle, and offers it in the Āhavanīya fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, [with the verse]: "With that purifier with which the gods always purify themselves..."

With that [verse], "May the *pāvamānī* verses purify me in a thousand streams, Svāhā!"—having taken another fourfold portion [of ghee]—he offers it in the Āhavanīya fire itself with [the verse]: "The purifier belonging to Prajāpati, having a hundred openings, golden;

through it, we who know the Brahman purify the purified Brahman, Svāhā. Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers it in the Āhavanīya fire itself with [the verse]: "May Indra purify me with good guidance, Soma with well-being, and Varuṇa with perfect harmony."

"May King Yama purify me with the *prasṛṇā* [waters]; may Jātavedas purify me with the *mārjayantī* [waters]. Svāhā! Then, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having led forward the waters, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pavamāna; [he offers] curdled milk (*upāṃśu*) to Sarasvatī Priyā; [he offers] a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pāvaka; [he offers] curdled milk (*upāṃśu*) to Sarasvatī Priyā; [he offers] a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pāvaka; [he offers] curdled milk (*upāṃśu*) to Savitṛ Satyaprasava; [he offers] to Agni...

For Śuci he offers a cake on eight potsherds; for Vāyu with his team (niyutvat) [he offers] ghee. On the following day, for Agni Vratapati he offers a cake on eight potsherds; for Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa [he offers] ghee. On the following day, for Agni Vaiśvānara he offers a cake on eight potsherds; for Dadhikrāvan [he offers] ghee. Having cooked these, he places them down.
For this sacrifice, there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.

Between the verses for the fuel being kindled and those for it being fully kindled, he inserts two *dhāyyā* verses containing the word "purifier" (*pāvaka*), namely: "This is the gathering-place of the waters," and "Homage to you. The two *ājyabhāga* offerings likewise contain the word "purifier": "The immortal one with bright radiance," and "The pure, purifying, worthy of praise. Having recited the *puro'nuvākyā*: "O Agni, that purifier of yours which is spread within your flame," [he follows with the *yājyā*: "O Agni, you drive away the demons with your bright light."
"By that we purify the Brahman," with these words he sacrifices.

Having recited the invitatory verse (*puro'nuvākyā*): "The pressed drop, flowing all around with a purifying stream, like a horse fit for action," it runs toward the jars and is poured through the filter.

"May he grow through hymns at the sacrifices"—thus he sacrifices. Then [he recites] for the oblations: "O Agni, you purify our lives," "O Agni, purify yourself. For Agni Pavamāna: "And these dear [oblations] of ours among the dear [gods]," "Offering these with the ladle, from you. For Sarasvatī Priyā: "O Agni Pāvaka, be thou our purifier. For Pāvaka: "The Viśvadeva [is] by truth," for Savitṛ of true impulse. "Agni is most pure in his vows," "O Agni, thy purities," for Śuci. "Vāyu goes before," "O Vāyu, the bright [oblation] is offered to thee," for Vāyu Niyutvat. "Thou, O Agni..."

"Thou art the protector of vows; if we should violate thy vows"—this belongs to Vratapati. "May that which is thine today be fulfilled"—this belongs to Vratapati. "What, O Viṣṇu, was there to be concealed from thee?"—this belongs to Viṣṇu. "Of Śipiviṣṭa"—this belongs to Viṣṇu. "Vaiśvānara has been asked for our aid, he who is praised in heaven"—this belongs to Vaiśvānara. "I have performed [the praise] of Dadhikrāvan"—this belongs to Dadhikrāvan. "I have celebrated Dadhikrā"—this belongs to Dadhikrāvan. Now follows the consecration of the oblation (*hutānumantraṇa*): "By the sacrifice to the god Agni Pavamāna, may I become bright, purified, fit for sacrifice, free from evil, endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*), and an eater of food. [Likewise for] Agni Pāvaka, [and] Agni [Sviṣṭakṛt].

"By the sacrifice to the god Agni Vaiśvānara, who is pure, the lord of vows, may I become pure, cleansed, fit for sacrifice, free from evil, endowed with Vedic splendor, and an eater of food"—with this [formula] he offers the *upāṃśuyāja* (low-voiced offering), as in the case of the *upāṃśuyāja*. Then, before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he makes oblations with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) using this section beginning with "Pavamāna, the one who wins the light," verse by verse. The two *saṃyājyā* verses are those containing the word "guest" (*atithi*) and those containing the word "householder" (*damūnas*): "The beloved householder, the guest in the dwelling; come to this our sacrifice, O wise one!"
O Agni, having struck down all assailants, bring hither the enjoyments of those who act as enemies.
The domestic one, who is fond of being cleansed, is purified in his own home; he is the guest praised by the sages, auspicious for us.

"The bull with a thousand horns, whose strength is such—that Agni by his power surpasses all others. Having thus completed the *iḍā* ceremony and having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives gold as a gift.

The ritual procedure up to the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings is the same; then, prior to the Gṛhapati offering, he offers oblations with the dipping-spoon (sruva) using this Anuvāka beginning with "yad devā devaheḍanam," verse by verse. This sacrifice concludes with the pouring out of the full vessel and the Viṣṇu-strides, and he releases his vow. One who has been accused or is being accused should sacrifice with this very rite; one should also sacrifice with this very rite upon the lapse of a season, the lapse of a wife, or having spilled semen in a non-vaginal place; [this may be done] for a year, or for half a year, or for twenty-one nights.

He purifies ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first—himself and his lineage—including kinsmen who have entered the womb of animals and are obstructed by their evil deeds; he does not return to this world again.
Moreover, they cite this:
"The Vaiśvānarī, the Vrātapatī, and likewise the Pavitreṣṭi."
"Employing [this rite] at every season, he purifies ten generations.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the Nakṣatreṣṭis. Agni, indeed, desired, "May I be an eater of food among the gods. These have been explained by the Brāhmaṇa. That new moon which occurs prior to the full moon of Vaiśākha coincides with the Apabharaṇīs once a year; on that day one should begin.

On the day of preparation for that [sacrifice], having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods, having moved away, having churned out the fires, and having spread them out—or alternatively, having kept them burning continuously—one should perform the preparatory rite on either the full-moon or the new-moon day, whichever is marked by the appearance of its characteristic sign.

In this regard, it is known that this is the ultimate rule: the sacrificer observes the vow of eating only the remnants of the oblation. Alternatively, for one desiring long life, he should perform it under his birth-star; the performance may last for as long as he lives, or for a minimum of three years. He offers the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) with the verses containing the word "living" (*jīvan*): "O Agni, come to us with fair splendor," and "Thou, O Soma, [grant] great fortune. Then he pours out the offerings, saying, "I pour out what is pleasing to Agni and the Kṛttikās. He issues the command, "Sacrifice to Agni and the Kṛttikās. He attaches the formulas "to Agni an eight-potherd cake" and "to Anumati a pap" to every [offering]. Having cooked the oblations for the stars in the middle [of the sacrificial ground], he sets them down.

For this [offering], there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses. Between the verse for the fire being kindled and that for the fire already kindled, he inserts two glorious *dhāyyā* verses: "Whose splendors are self-arisen to behold" and "The invincible one who goes before. He offers the two *ājyabhāga* portions characterized by wealth and abundance: "Through Agni may he obtain wealth" and "Increasing prosperity, driving away disease. Then, for the oblations, he recites the invitatory and offering verses: "Agni is the head of the world," "May Anumati favor us today," and "O Anumati, do thou favor [us]. These are the invitatory and offering verses for the two concluding offerings.
"May Agni protect us with the oblation of the constellations, the Kṛttikās"—thus [he offers] according to the traditional recitation.

Then, before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he makes additional oblations with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), saying "To Agni, svāhā! To the Kṛttikās, svāhā! according to the traditional recitation. The two *saṃyājyā* verses contain the word *sviṣṭa*: "The bearer of oblations has offered well. This sacrifice concludes with the pouring out of the full vessel and the *Viṣṇu-strides*.
He releases his vow;
thus, following each successive ritual manual, he should sacrifice on each successive day;
we shall explain the specific details.
"Prajāpati Savitṛ" is the *upāṃśu* (whispered) formula; "for the serpents, for the Āśleṣās, a *karambha* [mixture] in clarified butter"—all these consist of barley.
At the time of placing [the oblations] on the fire, having poured the clarified butter across the strainer and placed it on the fire, he pours the *karambhas* across the strainer.

"For the Pitṛs, under the Maghā constellation, a cake on six potsherds"—by this [formula], the rites of pouring out, sprinkling, placing upon the fire, and mixing for the ancestral sacrifice are explained; by the Soma-oblation belonging to the third pressing, the procedure for the performance is explained; now follows this: "for Vāyu, under the Niṣṭyā constellation, milk from a cow that has calved once."

The consecration of the milk for the morning milking is performed with the calf; having sacrificed to the Viśākhās, he should then immediately perform the Full Moon sacrifice with clarified butter. Then, on the following day, having sacrificed to Mitra with the Anūrādhās using a pap, he should then immediately sacrifice to Abhijit. Then, on the following day, having sacrificed to Viṣṇu with Śroṇā using a cake on three potsherds, he should then sacrifice to the Uttara-proṣṭhapadas using a cake on "earth-potsherds"—that is, having merely traced out the number of potsherds on the ground, he places a glowing coal upon them.

The consecration of that [offering] consists of a single potsherd. Having sacrificed with the Āpabharaṇī verses, one should sacrifice with clarified butter on that very new moon day. Then, when the moon has become visible on the following day, one should pour out the flour for a cake on fifteen potsherds for the "visible" moon, perform the pouring out during the day, and proceed with the offering once the moon has risen.

They two prepared this *caru* offering from day and night, from two kinds of rice—white and black—milked from two cows that do not share the same calf, one white and one black. Having thus brought them together, he should offer it at daybreak and perform the ritual after sunset; or rather, he should offer it precisely at the junction [of day and night] and perform the ritual at the junction. He should offer it at dawn and perform the ritual thereafter. Then he prepares this *caru* for the lunar mansion, saying: "As you are among the gods, so may I be among men. At the time of the offering, the sacrificer, seated in his place, murmurs this prayer.

Having brought it forward, he should offer it during the day; when the stars have risen, he should proceed with the oblation to Sūrya and the Nakṣatras. Having brought it forward, he should offer it at night; when the sun has risen, he should proceed. Then he offers this oblation to Aditi, and then this oblation to Viṣṇu. "Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; thus he finds firm support in the sacrifice itself at the end," so says the Brāhmaṇa. A choice gift is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); thus it is known. Or rather, the animal sacrifice is well-established [in the standard manner].

Having performed the *Pāthikṛtīṣṭi*, one should sacrifice with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; having sacrificed with the *Nakṣatrasattra*, for the sake of infinite luster, and having sacrificed with the *Jyotir-āmayana*, one casts off evil and the state of being light (*jyotiṣṭva*) arises; thus he overcomes repeated death—so indeed said Baudhāyana.
One should sacrifice with new [grain] on either the new-moon day or the full-moon day, or one should offer the *Agnihotra* with new [grain].

Alternatively, having caused a cow that yields milk for the *agnihotra* to eat new grain, he should offer the oblation with her milk; or he should offer the morning and evening *agnihotra* with gruel made from new grain; or, having cooked four *śarāva*-measures of boiled rice on the *gārhapatya* fire, he should offer it to the deities of the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, with *Sviṣṭakṛt* as the fourth; or he should simply feed Brāhmaṇas with the new grain itself.

This very procedure for the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice involves the ritual treatment of green barley, śamī-grain, cultivated plants, herbs, trees, roots, fruits, and vegetables. Having performed the Āgrayaṇa, one may eat according to one’s desire until the next harvest, due to the variation in the ripening of crops. Having sacrificed with rice, one should sacrifice again with rice; having sacrificed with barley, one should sacrifice again with barley—not with rice after sacrificing with rice, nor with barley after sacrificing with barley. Or rather, one may sacrifice with either rice or barley. Thus the Āgrayaṇa offerings are concluded.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the expiations for animal sacrifices.

If the animal, once brought forward for sacrifice, should bleat, he offers this oblation: "That which is on the far side of the dust," and then he offers a second incidental oblation: "From whatever you fear we have bleated, from that grant us security;
be gracious to all our offspring; homage to Rudra, the bountiful one, svāhā!"

Because of fear from whom you trembled, fled, stood still, voided excrement, and passed urine—homage to him who performed these acts; to him, *svāhā*! With this formula, he offers the third oblation on these occasions. If he should sit down, having offered with the formula, "From fear of whom you sat down," he should raise him up with the staff of Mitrāvaruṇa, or with another made of Udumbara wood. For the Udumbara is strength (*ūrj*), and cattle are strength; verily, by means of strength, he wins for him strength and cattle—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
[He should offer] with "O bull, stand up! for a bull, and with "O horse, stand up! for a horse.
If a goat dies, [one should sacrifice] a goat;
if a ram, a ram;

if a cow, a cow. If it should die before the carrying of fire around it, one should perform whatever expiation is prescribed in the Aśvamedha, and then immolate another animal of the same deity, the same color, the same age, the same appearance, and of the same species.

For that [animal sacrifice], everything beginning with the *upākaraṇa* (dedication) is repeated, with the exception of the fire-drilling (*nirmanthya*), the *sāmidhenī* verses, the remainder of the *samidh* offerings, the *āghāra* libations, the *saṃpraiṣa* call, the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*), the *pravara* invocation, and the *prayāja* offerings.

Now, if one should not find an animal of that same species, [it is said] that goats, sheep, cattle, and horses serve as mutual substitutes for one another; therefore, in the absence of a goat or a ram suitable for dedication, one should sacrifice whichever of these is available.

The ritual procedure for the offering to Tvaṣṭṛ has been explained; then he causes his body to enter the waters with two verses: "Verily, you do not die here" and "Of all the quarters, thee, the quarter."

Now, if the animal is deficient in its limbs, whether in form or color, one should offer oblations to Agni, to Agni-Viṣṇu, to Indra, to Vāyu, and to Prajāpati, and then dedicate that very animal. Furthermore, if a hawk should snatch away or cause the loss of the omentum while it is being brought forward, one should place gold within the vessel, take four portions of clarified butter, and offer them in the Āhavanīya fire while the sacrificer maintains contact, with the verse: "The rising bird shines forth everywhere; golden-humped and seven-headed, he is in the east."

"O All-pervading One, having entered into all worlds, find a song for the sacrificer in this sacrifice; Svāhā! Then, whatever fatty substance remains in the place of that omentum, he should tear it out and proceed with it. Now, if he should find it again, he should not care for it. Furthermore, if the omentum, the sacrificial oblation, or the portioning should fall, he takes it up with the mantra: "I take you for glory and for heroism; O inviolable ones, may you bestow upon us vital power and milk," and having taken it, he offers it with the mantra: "That drop of yours, that surge of yours, the divine banner which has entered the entire world."

"May he protect us for our safety; Svāhā! Now, if a bird should perch on the *caṣāla* while the animal sacrifice has not yet been concluded, one should wash the *caṣāla*, sprinkle the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and offer an oblation of clarified butter in the same manner as before, saying: "Flow away or speak out for the drinking of Soma; find a path for the sacrificer in this sacrifice; Svāhā!
Now, therefore, we shall explain the intermediate vows of the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*);
while standing in that state, one does not speak untruth.
He does not eat with me,

nor does he approach his wife; they do not wash his garment by washing it [with soap], and he is one who drinks from vessels other than those made of clay and is not defiled by the leavings of a Śūdra.
He washes his own feet;
he does not eat salt or pulse-grain, except for sesame; he does not sleep on a couch.
One should not approach a woman out of lust;
one may approach one's wife during her season, provided he has not yet fathered a son. On both occasions, he undertakes the vow beginning with honey and eats honey;
this is called "ghee" in the Brāhmaṇa. This is what is meant.
It is known from scripture: "The divine honey. And [it is said]: "O Lord of the Forest, those seeking the gods anoint you with divine honey at the sacrifice.
One should not eat the remnants of another, nor should one perform the priestly office for another.
He should not anoint himself, he should not rub oil on his body, and he should not eat at a funeral feast (śrāddha).
He shall not have his hair shaved, nor shall he brush his teeth, nor shall he clip his nails.

"One may, at will, have one's hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved on the festival days (*parvan*), or one should let them grow back every four months"—this is the Brāhmaṇa. After a year has passed, they prescribe the very same vow as that of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). If the time for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice should not have elapsed, but if it should indeed elapse, he offers a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) to Agni Vratapati; this well-known sacrifice concludes up until the time of the New Moon. Thus they have been explained.
In cases of the lapse of time or in times of distress, one should sacrifice;

now, therefore, we shall explain the expiations for the consecration (*dīkṣā*) of the *adhvara* sacrifice. If the consecrated person should speak an untruth, he should mutter these four verses addressed to Varuṇa: "Hear this my cry, O Varuṇa," "To thee I go," "Do thou, O Agni, protect us," and "So do thou, O Agni, protect us."

"May the blessing of the sacrifice protect me from being severed from the black antelope skin or from the staff; may prosperity increase through curds and ghee; may the sacrifice release the lord of the sacrifice from sin"—thus he should mutter upon seeing anything impure or undesirable; it has been stated that he mutters this. It has also been stated that he mutters this when it rains or while it is raining. Having performed his vow and sipped water, he mutters: "O waters, become auspicious when drunk; be very kind to us in our womb, in our belly.
Rich in nourishment, free from disease, and sinless, be a blessing for our life."
Having vomited or spat out, he mutters: "Whatever of my essence I have here spat out or cast away, may Agni, Soma, and the Earth restore that again into my self.
He then addresses the spilled semen with the mantra: "Whatever semen of mine has been spilled through excessive passion, may you [O Agni] restore it."
"Like the *agnihotra* with Soma, I take that back again"—saying this, when about to urinate or void excrement, he takes a clod of earth from the ground, saying, "This is your sacrificial body.
Then he voids it, saying, "I release the waters, not my offspring; O deliverers from distress, being consecrated by *svāhā*, enter the earth."
He replaces it with a clod of earth, saying: "Be united with the earth!
You are named 'Repulsive' (bībhatsā), waters consecrated by *svāhā*; enter the earth! [He does so] for tears, saying:

"You are named 'Phlegmatic' (kaphasyā), waters consecrated by *svāhā*; enter the earth! [He does so] for the swelling of the nose, saying: "You are named 'Austere' (tapasyā), waters consecrated by *svāhā*; enter the earth! Having seen a bad dream, he mutters regarding the sweat: "The bad dream turns back toward itself; from the evil dream, away from misfortune."
"I shall not create a separation from Brahman, nor will I be bound by a dream," he mutters after eating food in a dream: "The food that is eaten at night does not satisfy hunger until morning;
may all that not harm me, for it is not seen as [real] by day."

If he sees blood that has flowed out or if he scratches himself, he murmurs: "Obeisance to the Rudras; svāhā to the waters! If it does not rain, he should run. If he runs, he should murmur this verse: "Obeisance to the Rudras, the lords of the dwelling. He should not associate with one who is initiated by another. If he should associate, he should murmur this verse: "In what manner may the wonderful one come to us? If the sun rises or sets while he is away from the sacrificial ground, he should murmur: "May the god Sūrya protect me from the gods. Baudhāyana says that these expiations apply to all initiations for the *adhvara* sacrifice.
Śālīki says [the expiation applies] from the release for the intermediate consecration (*āvāntaradīkṣā*).
Now, therefore, we shall explain the expiations (*prāyaścitta*) for all sacrifices.

In all cases where the oblation is spilled, cut, split, broken, lost, spoiled, inverted, or deficient; where it flows over, trickles away, falls, or cracks; or when non-twice-born persons, dogs, cats, crows, donkeys, wild animals, domestic animals, birds, reptiles, or other insects enter between the officiating priests and the fires—one should fill the *sruk* ladle with twelve portions of ghee and offer oblations with the *Durgā*, the *Manasvatī*, and the three *Mahāvyāhṛtis*. [The verse is: "We press the Soma for Agni Jātavedas; he burns up the wealth of the one who acts as an enemy."
"May he carry us across all difficulties; like a boat across a river, may Agni carry us beyond misfortunes—*svāhā*!

In the event of a reversal of ritual actions, one should offer only the *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa* portions. Regarding the grass-blades (*darbha*), fuel-wood (*idhma*), sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), the separating-strands (*vidhṛti*), the strainers (*pavitra*), the oblation (*havis*), the potsherds (*kapāla*), the large and small ladles (*sruk-sruva*), the fire-drills (*araṇi*), the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), and the removal of the consecrated water (*praṇītā-agnyudvāsana*)—whatever reversal of action may occur—one offers the expiatory oblations (*prāyaścitta*) by dipping with the *sruva* ladle from the clarified-butter vessel (*ājyasthālī*). He offers: "*Svāhā to Prajāpati! Svāhā to Hiraṇyagarbha!*" Then he offers to the Grandfathers (*pitāmaha*): "*Svāhā to the Lord of the Bhṛgus! Svāhā to the austerity of the Aṅgirases!*" And then...

He offers the Mahāvyāhṛtis: "Bhūr! To Agni and to the Earth and to the Great One, Svāhā! Bhuvaḥ! To Vāyu and to the Atmosphere and to the Great One, Svāhā! Suvaḥ! To Āditya and to the Sky and to the Great One, Svāhā! Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ! To the Moon and to the Stars and to the Quarters and to the Great One, Svāhā! Then he offers the Vyāhṛtis: "Bhūḥ Svāhā! Bhuvaḥ Svāhā! Suvaḥ Svāhā! Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ Svāhā!

[This applies] when the mantra is deficient or redundant, when it is poorly recited, when it is ill-acquired, when it is not yet arrived, when there is no *vaṣaṭ*-call, or even when the offering has passed.
If the oblation overflows, if the fire or the Hotṛ priest falters in their tone,
if there is excessive burning of the oblations, or if any vessel is broken;
In the case of the destruction or breaking of the skull-cup, when the fourfold [mantra] has been interrupted,
upon the loss of the purifying grass, or when the clarified butter is stirred;
When there is a transposition of the oblations, when the officiating priests are unpurified,
at the time of the expansion of the sacrifice, or when a state of duality has arisen;
The two oblations of self-reproach (mindāhutī) should be offered, as well as the vyāhṛtis beginning with oṃ,
the vāruṇī verses, the tantumatī verses, the anvagni verse, and the manasvatī verse.
The seven Mahāvyāhṛtis and likewise those belonging to Prajāpati—
these mantras are proclaimed for the purpose of restoring the sacrifice.
For a sacrifice devoid of expiation is consumed by the Asuras;
and a sacrifice consumed by the Asuras brings the gods into contact with guilt.

It would cause the officiating priests and the sacrificer to fall away from long life and spiritual luster; that [rite] is ill-performed, therefore one should eliminate its defects. Now, therefore, we shall explain the restorative rites (anugrahas).
One should perform the evening oblation before sunrise and the morning oblation before sunset, at their respective times without letting them pass.

It is known that for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices and the *agnihotra*, there is no lapse and no failure. The time for the evening oblation does not expire until the time for the morning oblation, nor does the time for the morning oblation expire until the time for the evening oblation. Now, if it is evening, one should offer the oblation with "To Doṣā Vastu, homage! Svāhā! and then perform the *agnihotra*. If it is morning, one should offer the oblation with "To Doṣā Vastu, homage! Svāhā! and then perform the *agnihotra*. Furthermore, if [the time has passed] while the first oblation is being offered...

If the Āhavanīya fire should go out while the oblation has been offered, one should place gold on a piece of wood, saying "The fire is in the wood, the wood is in the fire," and offer the subsequent oblation.

In cases of the lapse of time, there is the *āpaddhoma* (expiatory oblation). The time for the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsa*) must not pass beyond the time of the New Moon sacrifice (*āmāvāsya*); the time for the New Moon sacrifice must not pass beyond the time of the Full Moon sacrifice; the time for the first-fruits offering of rice (*vrīhyāgrayaṇa*) must not pass beyond the time for the first-fruits offering of millet (*śyāmākāgrayaṇa*); the time for the first-fruits offering of barley (*yavāgrayaṇa*) must not pass beyond the time for the first-fruits offering of rice; the time for the first-fruits offering of millet must not pass beyond the time for the first-fruits offering of barley; the time for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice must not pass beyond the time for the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices; the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices must not pass beyond the Śunāsīrīya; the Śunāsīrīya sacrifices must not pass beyond the Sākamedha sacrifices; and the Sākamedha sacrifices must not pass beyond the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.

The time for an animal sacrifice of the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) should not pass beyond the time for an animal sacrifice of the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana); nor should the time for an animal sacrifice of the southern course pass beyond the time for an animal sacrifice of the northern course. The time for the Jyotiṣṭoma of the later spring should not pass beyond the time for the Jyotiṣṭoma of the earlier spring. Because of the non-performance of sacrifices throughout the entire year, the seers were indeed in a state of distress; they offered the Agnihotra every half-month, taking fourteen portions in the evening on the first day of the lunar fortnight.
The oblation is offered once, there is one fuel-stick, one oblation, one act of approaching, and one wiping of the hands.

Thus, in the morning, for six months, having failed to offer the Agnihotra, having failed to perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Āgrayaṇa, the Cāturmāsya offerings, and the Animal Sacrifice, he should offer sacrificial cakes to Agni Pathikṛt, Agni Tantumat, Agni Vaiśvānara, and Agni Vratapati; then, having offered the Agnihotra and performed the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Āgrayaṇa, the Cāturmāsya offerings, and the Animal Sacrifice, [he remains thus] for one year, failing to offer the Agnihotra and failing to perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Āgrayaṇa, and the Cāturmāsya offerings.

Having offered sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) to Agni Pavamāna, Agni Pāvaka, Agni Śuci, Agni Pathikṛt, Agni Tantumat, Agni Vaiśvānara, and Agni Vratapati by means of the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), and having performed the *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the *āgrayaṇas*, the *cāturmāsyas*, and the *paśubandha*, one may then, for the purpose of the oblations, use rice and barley; in their absence, *priyaṅgu*, *kodrava*, and *dāravara* (excepted), as well as *mudga*, *māṣa*, *nīvāra*, bamboo-seeds, wild-rice, water-born plants, tubers, roots, fruits, water, and groats (*saktu*).

Clarified butter for the purpose of *ājya* must be that derived from a cow; this is the established rule. In its absence, one may employ clarified butter from a buffalo or a goat for the purpose of *ājya*.
Some consider [sesame oil] to be non-conflicting with foods;
in the absence of those two, oil is the substitute,
and in its absence, jartila oil.

Linseed, safflower, mustard, and vegetable oils—these are [used] according to the authority of the learned. In the absence of these, one should mix barley flour, rice flour, or millet flour with water and use them for the purpose of clarified butter (*ājya*).
*Kuśa* grass is for the purpose of spreading.

In the absence of these, [one may use] *śara* grass, *kutapa*, horse-tail hair, *muñja* grass, fragrant reeds, *arjuna* grass, *dāra* grass, *dūrvā* grass, *śyāmāka* millet, milky trees, or sugarcane from among these.

The sacrificial grass for the *prastara*, the *barhis*, the *vidhṛti*, the *pavitra*, the *yūpa*, the *raśanā*, the *paristaraṇa*, the *antardhāna*, the *āsana*, the *śayana*, and that for the *stotra-upākaraṇa* should be made from any grasses, excluding dry *śuṇṭhi*, *nalaba*, *lajjā*, *kṛṣṇatūla*, and *tṛṇa*. The fuel (*idhma*) should be of *palāśa* wood; in its absence, of *khadira*; or, if those are unavailable, of any one of the trees used for sacrifice. If even those are unavailable, some say that the fuel may be from any forest tree, with the exception of the *aralu*, *kapittha*, *kovidāra*, *śalmali*, *śleṣmātaka*, *nīpa*, *nimba*, *tilaka*, *vādhaka*, *vibhītaka*, *rājavṛkṣa*, *karañja*, and *palāṇḍu*.
At the time for sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), one should give a cow, gold, or clothing;

in their absence, one should give fruits, roots, or foodstuffs. However, one must never fail to perform the sacrifice; one should remain constantly engaged in the obligatory rites (nitya) as well as in those that provide immediate sustenance (ajasrika).
He for whom the daily rites have been omitted, as well as the occasional ones.

One who stands on the wrong path does not go to heaven, for he has fallen from grace. Therefore, one should always perform the obligatory rites with roots, fruits, honey, or meat, and never let the obligatory rites lapse.

And one should not omit the permanent [rites]. Now, if the *sadas* and *havirdhāna* sheds have been scorched, they should be constructed after covering the entire sacrificial ground, or they may be left uncovered; according to the opinion of Vādhūlaka, one should first take the *vasatīvarī* waters. Then, the others [the fires] should be established in their proper sequence. Now, if all [the oblations] should fall upon the broken potsherds, there one should take as much loose earth as is available, mix it with the *vasatīvarī* waters, pour it out, and proceed with the ritual; the expiation for that is that one should offer with one of the [Soma] cups. In the event of the destruction of the *āgnīdhrīya* fire, one should offer with a verse addressed to Agni: "Agni is the head of heaven... (*agnirmūrdhā divaḥ*).
With the verse addressed to Viṣṇu, "O Viṣṇu, you are our nearest," he offers upon the *havirdhāna*; with the verse addressed to Agni, "This Agni is thousandfold," upon the *sruk*s;
with the verse addressed to Vāyu, "O Vāyu, [bring] a hundred bay steeds," upon the *vāyavya* cups;
and with the verse addressed to Indra, "Indra have all strengthened," upon the *sadas*.

With the verse "O Viśvedevas, who are present before the Vaiśvadeva [offering], hear this invocation," he should offer two Mindā oblations at all [such occasions], as well as the Vyāhṛtis. He should perform an expiatory sacrifice (iṣṭi) in the event of a house fire; if there is total destruction, the Tantumatī sacrifice;

if the Soma plants have been burnt or lost, or if there is injury to or theft of the Soma, he should take whatever [Soma] is available, mix it with Vasatīvarī water, press it, and proceed with the ritual.
"If all [the soma] is destroyed, one should proceed after pressing with medicinal herbs;
having performed that, one should sacrifice again"— the Śruti says this very thing, and that is the expiation (prāyaścitti).

Now, if among the *hotṛ*-priests one should urge another, or if one should sacrifice for another using the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for that is as follows: the Adhvaryu, having failed to pronounce the principal deity, should offer an oblation with the first [verse] of the section beginning "The Brāhmaṇa is the single Hotṛ" for the Hotṛ; with the second for the Maitrāvaruṇa; with the third for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; with the fourth for the Potṛ; with the fifth for the Neṣṭṛ; with the sixth for the Acchāvāka; and with the seventh for the Āgnīdhra.

One should utter [the mantra] over the *yoni*; with the verse, "O gods, whatever I may have transgressed," one should offer a *sruva*-oblation. With the eighth and ninth [verses] consisting of ten [syllables], one should perform the previously mentioned expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

One should offer oblations in the *ukthya* rounds according to their sequence; with the tenth [verse], for the *ṣoḍaśin*, for the *rātri-paryāyas*, for the *rathaṃtara-saṃdhi*, and likewise for the *śipiviṣṭa-stotra* in the *vājapeya*.

Likewise, regarding the *ati-rātra* stotras: if one person is enjoined to sacrifice while another sacrifices, the first shall sacrifice or recite; if he himself is enjoined, he alone shall sacrifice. If it is the second [who acts], there shall be an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in the *soma* sacrifice; in other cases, one should act thus: the *hotṛ* should sacrifice with another [mantra], and the *maitrāvaruṇa* likewise. Or, he should perform the previously mentioned expiation. Similarly, if the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses are otherwise [than prescribed], there shall be another expiation. Furthermore, in the food-offerings (*anna-homa*) of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), regarding wild animals, if there is a deficiency, excess, repetition, or contradiction in the *sruva*-oblations, one should offer the *mindā-hutis*.

Likewise, if during the laying of bricks or the oblations of the *devasū* sacrifice, one should perform the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of one deity and that of another, one should abandon that [offering], produce it again, and sacrifice; or one may sacrifice together with what remains, or recite [the mantra], or perform the previously mentioned expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Now, we shall explain the expiations for when the sacrificial rite has already been commenced.

In that case, if the medicinal herbs, milk, animal victim, Soma, or clarified butter are deficient, lost, or stolen, one should produce them again and take them up. If one remembers [the deficiency] before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, the production [of the materials] takes place; if one remembers it after the *sviṣṭakṛt*, having concluded that [offering], one should sacrifice again with these very same materials, or sacrifice together with them. Furthermore, if one should remember [the error] after having poured out [the portion] for a deity, saying "for such-and-such," one should divide [the remainder] accordingly, touch it, and offer it all, saying "Svāhā to such-and-such!"

Wherever one should remember [the omission], there one should perform the rite in that very same manner, starting from the placing [of the materials]. Now, if one should remember it after having already placed them, one should pour the oblations back into their respective places and offer them; or else, one should perform the previously mentioned expiation (*prāyaścitta*). If other deities have been worshipped, or if the materials are lost or spoiled, or if the ritual procedure (*tantra*) has become defective, one should repeat the principal offering (*pradhāna*). Regarding the question of what the commencement of the entire sacrifice is for one who has performed it incompletely: having performed the rites for the entitled deity starting from the taking of the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), having cooked the oblation, and having placed it down, one should proceed with the rite in its own proper place.

In that case, as an expiation, one should offer the two *mindā* oblations and the *vyāhṛti* oblations; likewise, in the animal sacrifice, from the time of the *upākaraṇa* until the *sviṣṭakṛt*, one should perform the previously mentioned expiation. Now, if the sun should rise while the *prātaranuvāka* has not yet been commenced, what is the expiation for that? [The response is: "May Uṣas with her banner, together with the gods, graciously accept this sacrifice."

Having offered the two *mindā* oblations with the formula, "To the gods, the most honeyed, Svāhā! and having offered the *vyāhṛtis*, he should perform the *upākaraṇa*. Now, if the sun should rise while the *prātaranuvāka* is being recited, he should offer spoon-oblations (*sruvāhuti*) with these [verses]: "We have risen above the darkness," "Up from that," and "The bright one. Now, if the moon should not be visible, he should offer spoon-oblations with these two [verses]: "He becomes ever new as he is born" and "Whom the Ādityas swell with light. If an eclipse of the sun or the moon occurs, it is exactly this [same procedure].

Now, if one who is about to take up the cups (*graha*) should take them from another source without having first taken [the cup] for the deity entitled to a share, then at that very moment he should offer everything with the formula "Svāhā to such-and-such," and after taking the cup for the entitled deity again, he should offer the two *minda* oblations. Alternatively, he may offer with one of the cups, or with all the cups of the *hotrakas*—whether they be *grahas* or *camasas*—beginning with the formulas "O Vācaspati, Vidhe, Nāman," provided there is no defect in the sacrificial offering as previously described.

Likewise, having consumed that water and performed the expiation by offering an oblation, he should take it up again and offer it; or, having drawn it back into the cups, he should offer it; or, having offered it, he should place gold within it, pour water into it, and consume it—that indeed is the expiation for that. Now, if the time for the pressing should pass by, he should offer with the first Gāyatrī verse of this Anuvāka, "Agni is the head of heaven," at the morning pressing;
likewise, with the Triṣṭubh verse, at the midday pressing.

Likewise, at the third pressing of the Jāgata [stotra], if one should not reach the subsequent day of the Atirātra sacrifice, and if one were to reach it, a failure of the sacrifice (yajñabhreṣa) would occur;

the expiation for that is that one should offer oblations to all the Hotṛ-priests, for it is known: "The Caturhotṛ formulas are indeed the Brahman. Therefore, one should offer only the Caturhotṛ oblations. If one should not reach the count of days beyond this point, it applies to the Ekāhas. Now, as for the expiation regarding the Savanīya [offerings]: if there should be a foul odor, one should discard that, produce another, and proceed; or else, having washed it with warm water, placed it in clarified butter, and cooked it again, one should proceed.
In that case as well, if there should be a foul odor, one should discard it, produce it again, and proceed;
likewise for the *puroḍāśa* cakes of the *savanīya* offerings and for the *sāṃnāyya* oblations.

Now, if he should omit a *stotra*, a *śastra*, or a *pratigara*, he should offer the two *minda* oblations and then recite the opening formula (*upākaraṇa*). Furthermore, if he should omit a single *stotrīyā* verse, a hymn (*sūkta*), a verse of splendor (*varcas*), a half-verse (*ardharca*), or a *pratigara*, he should offer the two *minda* oblations and mutter [the following]:

"From the beginning of the *stotra*-recitation until the oblation, he should restrain his speech; if he should release his speech, he should mutter a verse addressed to Viṣṇu. Moreover, if he should release his speech after having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he should mutter a verse addressed to Viṣṇu: "O Viṣṇu, you are our nearest [kinsman]."

Having caused [the mantra] to be heard again, one should perform the sacrifice; in cases of deficiency, excess, repetition, contradiction, or other such faults, one should offer the *mindāhuti* oblations as an expiation elsewhere.
The Śruti states that the *mindāhuti* oblations are the body of the sacrifice;
therefore, this is the commendable practice of all the teachers.

Now, if the two Soma-libations, the offered and the unoffered, should become mixed together, one should draw out embers from the Āhavanīya fire toward the north and offer upon them: "For you two are the seasonal ones of the sacrifice, O Indra and Agni, the conscious ones;
satisfy yourselves with both the offered and the unoffered, with the unoffered and the offered."
"Of that which has been offered and that which has not been offered, of that which was not offered and that which was offered—O Indra and Agni, enjoy this Soma; drink it, take pleasure in it, Svāhā!
With these words, he follows the regular formula for consuming [the remnant]: "May darkness not seize the sacrificer, nor the officiating priests, nor these creatures."

"Let him not drink this Soma; both [the pure and the mixed] have been made together. Now, if the cups offered by one group were to be mixed with those offered by another group, or if one should take up Soma over Soma, then this very [formula applies]. Or, if priests chosen for one purpose were to be mixed with those chosen for another, except in the case of the Vrātyastoma or a Sattra, then this very [formula applies]. And if the pressed Soma should be rained upon, then having offered two spoonfuls with the verses, "This footstep for him who desires to drink," and "Indu has gone to Indu; Indra has drunk of Indu," he follows the regular consumption of that [Soma].

"Of that [Soma], O Indu, drunk by Indra, honeyed, invited, I, being invited, partake. Now, if the sacrificer should die or fear should come upon him while the Soma has been pressed, one should place all the oblations together in a vessel—the Soma in the *droṇakalaśa*, the clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle, and the animal victim in another—and offer a single oblation with the verse: "Those gods to whom this portion has become due, whose [are] the *prayāja*s and the *anūyāja*s..."

Having offered with the formula, "Svāhā to the gods, whose chief is Indra, whose king is Varuṇa, and who have Agni as their Hotṛ," one should thereafter proceed with the rites pertaining to the Pitṛmedha. Alternatively, one may sacrifice again when free from danger.

For one who is aged or incapable of performing the Agnihotra ritual, the internal depositing of the fires (ātma-samāropaṇa) is prescribed. When the fires have been deposited within oneself, one should not eat, nor drink, nor sleep on a raised bed, nor immerse oneself in water, nor engage in sexual intercourse. However, one may eat at will, drink at will, and indeed sleep on a raised bed at will; yet one must never immerse oneself in water nor engage in sexual intercourse.

Having washed his hands and feet and sipped water, he should sit facing the east; having consumed a small amount with the *agnihotra-yajus* formula, he should consume more silently while meditating on Prajāpati in his mind. In this very manner he should worship until the release of the sun. Now it is said: "Just as a son who is born dies, even so does he die whose *ukhya* fire goes out."
If he were to produce fire by friction, he would cut off his rival; he would cause that very rival to be born again.
Therefore, it should be wrapped around [the fire-drill];
thus he causes him to be born from his own womb.
"He does not produce a rival for him," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

If the fire-pan (ukhā) should break, one should cast the ashes into the water, smear the pan with a lump of dung, re-establish it, hand it over, and having made it capable of bearing oblations, he then offers libations over it with spoonfuls (sruva), saying: "The golden Gharma, svāhā! The golden Arka, svāhā! The golden Śukra, svāhā! The golden Jyotis, svāhā! The golden Sūrya, svāhā! With two verses containing the word *arka*, he places two *arka*-fuel sticks on the fire, [reciting]: "Arka is the purifier, the purifier is Arka; Arka is the measurer of the mid-region. With these two [verses].
One should proceed with the ritual beginning with the muñja-grass nest; then indeed it is said: "Darkness indeed seizes him whose fire in the ukhā pot goes out;
darkness is death."
"A black garment, a black cow as the sacrificial fee"—thus he gives a black garment, a black cow, and gold weighing a hundred mānas;
by means of darkness itself he strikes away darkness, that is, death; moreover, gold is indeed brilliance.
"He gathers splendor into himself," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Now, if the throne-seat, the sling, or the shed should be burned, one should place fuel-sticks upon the fire with the eight verses beginning, "Vaiśvānara, for our aid. Furthermore, if the Vasatīvarī water-jar, the foot-washing vessel, the Ekadhana jars, the brick-pots, or the boiling-pots should be spilled; or if the sacrificial post should break, the rope should snap, the top-ring should break, the Udumbara post should break, the pressing-stone should break, the Droṇakalaśa jar should crack, or any other object made of wood or clay in the sacrifice [should be damaged].

If the vessel should break, he should place it back in its own station with the same *yajus* formula used for setting it down, and having set it down, he consecrates it with: "O Earth, sustain my life; sustain my breath; sustain my offspring; sustain my cattle. May my life, breath, offspring, and cattle not be spilled away.

Then, if the vessel is made of wood, he should throw it into the *āhavanīya* fire; but if it is made of clay, he should cast it into the water with: "The earth has gone to the earth; the mother has gone to the mother.
May we abound in sons and cattle; may he who hates us be shattered!"

Now, therefore, we shall explain the worldly procedure for the Agnihotra. Before the Agnihotra, they consign the fires into the two kindling woods from the Gārhapatya fire with the verse, "This is thy womb, according to the season. Having placed the two kindling woods within the altar, one should offer the oblation in the worldly fire. It is known from tradition: "In the evening he draws out [the fire]; having offered the evening oblation, he draws it out again in the morning; having offered the morning oblation, he draws it out again in the morning. Furthermore, the Agnihotra is omitted on four occasions: by the burnt offering, by the ritual attendance, by the vow, and by the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
Having performed the Tantumatī sacrifice, one should perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices;
thus concludes the expiation for a broken [sacrificial sequence].
Now follows the combination of Agnihotra offerings in times of distress.
For example, when there is civil unrest, illness, travel on a journey, residence in the teacher's house, the unavailability of the proper place, time, or materials, or any other such obstacles,
what commencement of that ritual action can there be?

One may perform it at will in the forenoon, the afternoon, or at the time of the *agnihotra* sacrifice, either according to the sūtras or in a manner well-known to the sacrificer, provided there is no obstacle.

Having been born [into this state], on the first day of the lunar fortnight, he takes fourteen portions of four spoonfuls each in the evening; on the day of the fast or at the full-moon sacrifice, or otherwise on another day, fifteen. The rite from the kindling of the fire onwards is well-known, as are the mantras. Having set aside one calf, and having offered the evening *agnihotra* oblations, he should offer the morning *agnihotra* oblations.

One should not sacrifice at the time of the *pārvaṇa* [rite] if it begins in the evening and concludes in the morning; nor should one perform it after the fortnightly period has passed, nor in the context of another rite, nor for one who lacks faith. Furthermore, they cite this example: The beginning in the evening and the conclusion in the morning; At the time of the *pārvaṇa*, one should not sacrifice; Nor above the fortnightly limit; Nor in the context of another [rite]; Nor for one who is faithless.
