Then they also cite
Lack of faith is the supreme evil, for ignorance is said to be evil;
through ignorance dharma is destroyed, and one whose dharma is destroyed is considered base.
Through faith the intellect is purified; through faith the mind is purified.
Through faith Brahman is attained; faith is the destroyer of sin.

Therefore, one who is faithful and free from worldly attachment should perform the sacrifice to Tantumatī at the proper time; thus [is] the worldly practice, and likewise [it applies] when there is a failure of the injunction. Moreover, they cite this: "One should not extinguish the fires in vain, nor indeed except in times of distress;
for he who extinguishes the fire is a slayer of heroes among the gods.
Therefore, for one who is faithful and free from attachment, [this applies] even elsewhere.
Whichever minor particulars are observed in various places,
one should incorporate them into the ritual procedure so that it becomes endowed with propriety.
For one who, while his own scripture exists, conducts himself according to another's scripture and thereby disregards his own, that act is equal to the murder of an embryo.
The injunctions of one's own ancestral scripture (ārṣeya) are equal to those [of other scriptures] in their qualities;
they should be followed for the sake of investigating ritual acts and in times of distress.

As for the statement, "He travels abroad for an unlimited time, but he does not travel abroad beyond a year," because there is no specific distinction made, this is said to apply equally to both husband and wife when they have established the sacred fires (āhitāgni).

It is known that "the wife is indeed half of one's self. Now, if the sacrificer goes on a journey while his wife remains behind due to some reason for her own departure, the Adhvaryu, having offered the Vāstoṣpatīya oblation, should consign the fires by saying, "This is thy seasonal womb.
Wherever he may go, he should carry the fire with him;

having reached that place, having churned the fire and arranged the sacrificial ground, having melted the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya and purified it, and having taken four portions into the ladle, he offers the *saṃtanī* oblation in the Āhavanīya fire with the verse: "May the mind, as light, enjoy the clarified butter; may it join together this severed sacrifice."

"Those dawns and sunsets that have been desired, those I join together with oblation and clarified butter, Svāhā! Having said this, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tantumatī, and gives a shallow cup (śarāva) as the sacrificial fee.

That well-known sacrifice is completed. Now, if both the sacrificer and his wife go out [of the village], they may dwell at the edge of the village or at the boundary of the village; however, the Agnihotra itself would be lost. One should perform the Agnyādheya (the laying of the fires) without modification. When carrying the fires, they should not breathe over them; if they were to breathe over them, the fires would become worldly (profane). There is no concern regarding the fires as long as they have not been mounted upon the kindling woods (*samārūḍha*), because of the precedent seen in the *Sattra* sacrifices involving the throwing of the wooden pin (*śamyā*). Now it is indeed said: "He who, having added fuel to the fires, undertakes the vow, enters all desires into the fire. Therefore, if he were to depart without having sacrificed..."

When he is about to depart without having performed the sacrifice, he melts clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire, purifies it, takes four ladlings into the *sruva*-ladle, and offers it into the *āhavanīya* fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, [reciting]: "To thee, O best of the Aṅgirases...

This is explained previously regarding one who, having established the fires, enters upon the vow, and if his fires go out. If the fire of one who has established the fires goes out as far as the distance one can strike with a *śamyā*, if it goes out that far, he should collect it [rekindle it] with the verse: "This is one for thee, and yonder is another. Having collected it, he should throw it back into the fire at the times for the *agnihotra* or at other times.

If the other [the Adhvaryu] should go away further, he should follow after him and stay; he should indeed follow after him and stay. Wherever he stays, there they should take down [the milk]. For the plants and the cattle enter the milk of him whose calves, having been driven away for the sake of the oblation, suckle [their mothers]. If he were to milk them, he would sacrifice with an oblation that has lost its potency (*yātayāman*). If he were not to milk them, he would exclude the end of the sacrifice. He should offer a barley-gruel (*yavāgū*) to Vāyu. Then, having caused these [cows] to be milked and having poured water into that [milk], the rite from the pouring of the rice onwards is established; from that point upward, it proceeds as usual.

Now, if the evening milk-offering of one who has undertaken the vow should meet with disaster, he should pour out rice for Indra and fast; having performed the ritual up to the point of pouring out the grains, on the following day, having proceeded with the offering to Agni, he should proceed with the offering to Indra, and he should provide that which takes the place of the boiled milk. Furthermore, if both his offerings should meet with disaster, he should pour out five *śarāva* measures of cooked rice for Indra.

Regarding the injunction "one should offer either according to the archetype (prakṛti) or with a shallow bowl (śarāva)": some say that one should offer according to the archetype, while others say that the shallow bowl is for the purpose of measuring; thus, when it says "one should offer with four vessels," one should offer in the vessel itself and perform the ritual in place of the *sāṃnāyya*. Furthermore, if on the day of the vow (*vratya*) the wife becomes menstruating, one should exclude her and sacrifice.
One should sacrifice even without excluding her; thus one sacrifices with the entire sacrifice.

Having performed that sacrifice, he should invite her with the mantra: "I am this one. This is the mantra for approaching her during the fertile period. From the kindling of the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*) onwards, one should sacrifice without excluding her; likewise in the case of one-day rites (*ekāha*).

Now, if [the blood appears] during the initiation (*dīkṣā*) or the *upasad* days, or likewise on other days in multi-day sessions (*ahargaṇa*), or when three days have passed—as in the case of the three-day rite—one says, "Having cut the blood," and having washed it with cow's urine mixed with warm water, he purifies it with bunches of *darbha* grass.

It is known that *darbha* grasses are indeed water, for it is known that one becomes purified by bathing with them; for she remains there having assumed the color of the murder of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*).

Therefore, one should neither look at nor touch the sacrificial oblation (*havis*). Then, when ten days have passed since the birth, having performed the purification as prescribed, he should employ his wife in the ritual acts.
The son or a religious student (brahmacārī) should perform that rite;

the sacrificer should mutter its mantra. If the wife is unwell, he should have her perform it in this very manner. Now, if there is no milk when the *sāṃnāyya* or the *gharma* is about to be prepared, one should cause some milk to be milked by whatever means possible, mix it with water, and proceed; one must not perform it by bringing in any other milk. That itself is the expiation (*prāyaścitti*) for that. Furthermore, if from the commencement of the Soma-consecration until before the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering, she becomes menstruating and does not offer the *agnihotra*, [the following applies].
When three days have elapsed, the procedure beginning with the initiation in water is established; from that point onward [the ritual proceeds].

Now, if she becomes untouchable (*anālambhukā*) before the milking for the *vrata* milk, she should eat sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) for three days. If she has already drunk the *vrata* milk, she should consume sacrificial food as her *vrata* and then drink water.
When three days have elapsed, the procedure beginning with the cow’s urine is established; from that point onward [the ritual proceeds].

Now, if she should become one who must not touch [impure things] before the *pravargya* rite, one should not perform the *pravargya*; rather, having performed the purification starting from the sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) as prescribed, the procedure beginning with the cow-urine and so forth is established from that point onward. But if she becomes one who must not touch after the *pravargya* has been performed, one should set aside the sacrificial food for that day; when three days have passed, the procedure beginning with the cow-urine and so forth is established from that point onward.

Then, with the summons, "O initiated one, restrain your speech; O observer of the vow, restrain your speech; O wife, restrain your speech," she becomes unfit for sexual intercourse from the time of the single breast-offering onwards. Having performed the rites up to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) in the established manner, when three days have elapsed, they go down to the avabhṛtha.

On the day of the Soma-pressing, he should sit in the Mārjālīya shed after it has been strewn with sand and enclosed; on other days, he should sit only in the wife’s hall (patnīśālā). He should not enter the sacrificial ground before the morning libation.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the compendium of expiations (*prāyaścitta-samuccaya*).

In all cases where no specific rule has been prescribed, one should offer the *manasvatī*, the two *mindāhutī* oblations, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *hotṛ* formulas. For all violations of the vows, one should offer the two *mindāhutī*. In the event of the omission of the *pitṛyajña*, one should perform an additional offering with the *saptahotṛ* formula. Now, if they should depart while the entire *aupāsana* fire is still being established for the *agnyādheya*, one should offer a spoonful (*sruva-āhuti*) with the verse, "May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus kindle thee again," and then perform the domestic rites (*gṛhya-karmāṇi*) in a common (*laukika*) fire. If only half remains, or if the *brahmaudana* rice has been set aside, it should be treated like the *aupāsana* fire.

Likewise, if there is an extinguishing of the fires (*udvāta*), one should offer the *jaya* and other oblations after the cooking is finished. Now, if the sun should rise while the *gārhapatya* fire has not yet been established, one should establish it at another time starting from sunrise. If the destruction of the fire occurs in the middle [of the rite], this same [expiation] applies. Furthermore, if the wife should become pregnant, this same [expiation] applies until the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is given; beyond that, there is exclusion (*aparodha*) in the *agnihotra*, in the *soma* sacrifice, in the *avabhṛtha* and other rites, and everywhere in the *iṣṭi*, *paśu*, and *soma* sacrifices—either for that specific period regarding the wife, or for the whole [period].

Now, if both the *gārhapatya* and *āhavanīya* fires should go out, whether the sun sets upon them or rises upon them, the re-establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*) is the expiation (*prāyaścitti*) in that case.
Some say that there must be a re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*). Now, if the wife goes outside the boundary, there is a re-establishment.

Furthermore, if she should behave in an unrighteous manner while the fires have been consigned within her own body, or if the aforementioned defect regarding the destruction of the kindling-wood (*araṇi*) should occur, there is a re-establishment of the fires;

for it has been stated that the destruction of the fires follows from the destruction of the kindling-wood. Now, if they should carry the fires across the village boundary or a river, the two [the husband and wife] should maintain contact with these very fires as they are being carried.

When the sacrificer is away on a journey, his wife does not go with him; there is no expiation for this. If the *anvāhāryapacana* fire goes out while its source is intact, one should fetch it from its original place, or [fetch it] from separate fire-drills (*araṇi*). Now, if the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) rolls away, the Adhvaryu should set it back in its own place with the formula: "Follow the track of Prajāpati. The sacrificer follows with these two verses: "I establish myself in power, I establish myself in the kingdom; the other has increased everything. He should offer two spoonfuls (*sruva-āhuti*) with these two verses: "The sky has not fallen, nor has the earth; she has been born, she has procreated."

When one has set out on a journey, one should perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice; for it is known: "If he were to go toward the east, he would conquer the world of the gods; if toward the south, the world of the ancestors; if toward the west, they would destroy the sacrifice; if toward the north, he would conquer the world of men. Therefore, it must be offered while firmly established. Now, if an animal sacrifice or a Soma sacrifice should be interrupted, one should perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice and then sacrifice again.

If the entire day of the Soma pressing should be passed over, or if those who have taken hold of the ritual should be separated before sitting down, one should complete the rite and then sacrifice again.

"Once initiated for the Soma sacrifice, one should not give gifts, nor offer oblations, nor cook, nor recite prayers"—thus they say from the very beginning that he should divide [his duties]. One who is under a vow should not bathe, nor plunge into water, nor discard his garment, nor let dust settle [on him]. In all cases, they prescribe a vow for both the sacrificer and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) as long as the ritual action lasts. No other priestly office exists apart from that of the officiating priests; there is no collective performance (*samāsa*) among the great officiating priests, nor does the sacrificer perform the priestly office in every instance except during a sacrificial session (*sattra*).

In all *soma* sacrifices—whether there be transgressions regarding the *soma*, the passing of the proper time, intervening periods, reversals, intermixing, or combinations, and other such faults whether unknown or known—one should offer the *sarvaprāyaścitta* oblations by dipping with the *sruva* spoon from the *ājyasthālī* before the *samiṣṭayajus*. Some say [one should offer] the *jayas*; some the *abhyātānas*;
some the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*; some the *amātyahomas*;
and some the *chandāṃsi*.
Some say "belonging to Sūrya," some say "the bodies," and some say "the Hotṛ-priests."
Some say they consist of ten;
some say they are the Pauruṣīs;
others say they are the Vaiṣṇavīs.
Some say [he should recite] the Mahāvyāhṛtis;
some say the Vyāhṛtis;
others say the Prājāpatyā.
Some say it is the *praṇava*; the Teacher says it is all [the syllables]; the Teacher says it is all.
